Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: In a managed instance group (MIG) with instance flexibility, you can override the instance template's disk and minimum CPU platform properties per instance selection. Overriding these properties lets you combine machine types that require different disk types, boot images, or CPU platforms in a single MIG. For more information, see About instance flexibility in MIGs.

Dataform

Feature

You can track table-level data lineage in Knowledge Catalog for Dataform workflows and BigQuery pipelines. For more information, see Track data lineage in Knowledge Catalog. This feature is generally available (GA).

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Gemini 4 Hydrogen (GA)

Gemini 4 Hydrogen (gemini-4-hydrogen) is generally available (GA) in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform as a short-term release (subject to a minimum 45-day retirement notice policy). Gemini 4 Hydrogen is built for speed and efficiency across everyday coding and agentic workflows, multimodal analysis, and tool use:

  • Unified 1,048,576-token limit and long decodes: Supports a unified 1,048,576-token input and output limit (where output includes thinking, function calls, and the final response). Single foreground segments generate up to 65,536 output tokens (streaming or non-streaming) and can be extended up to 1,048,576 tokens (minus input tokens) using long decodes (continuation_token) on both the Interactions API and the GenerateContent API (v1beta1), including asynchronous server-managed background execution (background=true) on the Interactions API.

  • Thinking levels (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and XHIGH): Supports four thinking levels, with HIGH as the default and XHIGH for deep reasoning workloads. Setting thinking_budget or thinking_level="MINIMAL" returns an HTTP 400 validation error.

  • Implicit context caching with durable caching: Supports automatic implicit context caching with durable caching enabled by default for shared prompt prefixes of 4,096 tokens or more (explicit context caching isn't supported).

  • Cache write control and pricing: Starting on January 12, 2027, Gemini 4 Hydrogen and later models support cache control features with TTL configuration. You choose what to cache and how long cached content stays valid through TTL configuration. Cache writes are billed at 1.25x the standard input token price by default, and longer retention costs more. For details, see Pricing.

  • Office and OpenDocument file inputs: Supports Microsoft Office (.docx, .dotx, .doc, .pptx, .ppt, .xlsx, .xls) and OpenDocument (.odt, .odp, .ods) files inline or from Cloud Storage (gs://), including inside multimodal FunctionResponse parts.

  • Capabilities, consumption options, and endpoints: Supports the GenerateContent API, the Interactions API, the OpenAI compatibility Chat Completions API, function calling, code execution, computer use, URL context, Grounding with Google Search, Google Maps, Enterprise Web Grounding, Parallel and Exa Web Search, Agentic video understanding, Standard PayGo with Usage Tiers, Priority PayGo, Flex PayGo, batch inference, and Provisioned Throughput (685 tokens per second per GSU) on the global endpoint and in the us and eu multi-regions.

For implementation rules, long decode examples, and migration guidance from Gemini 3.8 Flash, see the developer's guide to Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Get started with Gemini 4.

Model Armor

Feature

Filter version v4 under the Latest alias includes an updated prompt injection and jailbreak detection filter with the following improvements:

  • Higher recall for indirect prompt injection (IPI) and tool calls.
  • Higher recall for conversational inputs at a lower false positive rate.
  • Higher recall for jailbreak attacks.

For more information, see Filter version history.

title: WTF are evals? How to test agents and the software they use
description:
Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done.

Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: Discovery, Selection, Access, and Success.

You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, Success: whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly.

That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change.

That’s what an eval can do for you. Here’s how we build one.

The agentic testing pyramid

If a test asks “did it work?” an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?” You give an agent a task, grade the outcome, and aggregate the results across repeated attempts.

We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in the practical test pyramid, the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite.

To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For Success, that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But Success depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome.

An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench, are E2E evals.

Example

Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping sfbeans.

Here’s a typical request from one of your customers:

Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission.

Here’s what sfbeans knows at 8:30am:

  • Fog City Roasters: ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today (temperature)

  • 24th St Beans: latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip (budget)

  • Dolores Drip: latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 (time)

  • Valencia Grind: $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 (meets all three)

Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for sfbeans:

How to build an end-to-end eval

We’ll build the coffee eval with Harbor, an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions.

Here are the terms we’ll use:

  • Task: one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeeded

  • Variant: the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skills

  • Trial: one attempt by one variant at one task

  • Run (a job in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times each

  • Trace (a trajectory in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final output

Step 1: Set a goal

Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see the jagged frontier).

Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places:

  • Observability: which agents use your product, and where they fail

  • Customers: support tickets, feedback, and churn

  • Roadmap: the product hypotheses you most need to validate

For example, your goal might be to:

  • Increase the success rate on a specific task

  • Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal

  • Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it

  • A/B test a prompt

  • Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why

Example

We looked in all three places for sfbeans:

  • Observability: most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because sfbeans adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness.

  • Customers: the top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added.

  • Roadmap: nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn.

That gives us our goal:

Goal

Increase the success rate on ordering the exact drink the user asked for

Agents

Claude Code and Codex, since that’s where our traffic comes from.

In scope

Drink, pickup time, and budget (incl. tax and tip), using today’s sfbeans.

Out of scope

Cancellations, refunds, and accounts. We’ll eval those later.

Done when

Both agents get the order right in every trial, not just most of the time.

Step 2: Define metrics

Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals:

Success

  • Success rate: the share of trials that pass

  • Pass@k: the chance that at least one of k trials passes. Answers “can the agent do this at all?”

  • Pass^k: the chance that all k trials pass. Answers “can I rely on it every time?”

Efficiency (measured on successful trials only)

  • Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task

  • Time: how long the trial took

  • Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars

Example

Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 (anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 on AI Gateway) on the iced latte order could look like:

What the numbers mean:

  • Success rate: 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%.

  • Pass@5: assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once.

  • Pass^5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right.

  • Steps: (9 + 11 + 8) / 3 ≈ 9 on successful trials. The failed trials are shorter because the agent skipped work, like quoting, which is why efficiency only counts successful trials.

  • Time: ~3:50 on successful trials.

  • Cost: $0.56 per successful trial, but $2.35 / 3 = $0.78 per success once you count the failed trials you paid for too.

So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent can get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right every time.

Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so sfbeans optimizes for pass^5.

Other products are more forgiving, because a failed attempt is cheap and gets caught before it matters:

Product

What a failed attempt costs the user

Metric to lead with

Order my morning coffee

Paid for the wrong drink, late for work, lost trust

Pass^k

Coding agent with a test suite

Extra time and model cost; the agent uses test feedback to revise its code and try again

Pass@k

Draft an email the user reviews

A quick edit before hitting send

Success rate

Overall averages can hide a task that fails frequently, so always inspect results per task. And with only five trials, 100% means “no failures seen yet,” not “never fails.”

Step 3: Design the task set

In Step 1, we set a goal for the eval: increase how often agents order the exact drink the user asked for. But an agent can’t attempt a goal. It needs a task: one concrete request, drawn from what your users actually ask for.

Pick tasks hard enough that you learn something from running them. A good set covers the common case, the edge cases that trip agents up, and at least one request where the right move is not to act.

For each task, define these parts:

  • An instruction: the user’s request

  • An environment: where the agent works, with the same starting state for every trial

  • A verifier: a check of the final state, ideally scored per constraint

  • A known-good solution (optional): a reference run that demonstrates the expected behavior and passes the verifier

You can make every aspect of that environment as fake or as realistic as you need, depending on your goals. The OpenPipe team has a nice writeup on how they defined the environment for an email research agent.

Example

We wrote four tasks, each one a Harbor task folder in tasks/.

  • Common case: iced-latte-mission, the order from earlier

  • Edge case: usual-unavailable, where the user’s usual cafe is out of their drink

  • Edge case: team-order, with 6 drinks, $45 total, and one pickup spot

  • Don’t act: impossible-request, where nothing fits, so the right move is to tell the user

impossible-request has one extra check. Its verifier reads a command log the agent can’t write to, to confirm the agent searched before giving up. We learned we needed that the hard way (see Step 5).

Here’s iced-latte-mission:

The instruction gives the agent the user’s request and names the sfbeans CLI. In production, agents find the tool through a skill, docs, or an MCP server. Naming it here skips Discovery and Selection, keeping the eval focused on Success.

We also specify that it’s 8:30am. Only sfbeans uses our frozen clock; the sandbox’s system clock still shows the real time:

The environment is part real, part fake. The agent uses the real sfbeans CLI, but against seeded cafes and a frozen clock, so every trial starts on the same morning:

To keep the demo simple, cafes.json lives inside the agent’s environment. In a real eval, protect the seed data and verifier code, and make sure the agent can update order records only through the CLI. Agents can attempt to reward hack if it helps them pass, for example by editing the inventory or writing orders.json directly.

For this coffee order, the verifier checks the final order against the user’s requirements. Harbor runs test.sh after the agent finishes and reads the scores it writes to /logs/verifier/reward.json:

The actual check lives in check_orders.py. It scores each constraint separately, then sets reward to 1 only if all of them pass. Harbor uses reward as the trial’s main score:

The solution is a known-good answer. Run it before any real agent to prove the task works:

Finally, task.toml ties the task together. It sets the timeouts, runs the verifier in the agent’s sandbox (where orders.json lives), and saves the orders as an artifact so we can inspect them in Step 5:

Step 4: Run the eval

If you share the universal distaste for slow CI, you’ll hate waiting for evals. Every trial waits on an agent making LLM calls, step after step, and a run repeats that for every variant and task, several times each.

Harbor’s Vercel integration, which we built upstream, speeds that up a lot. It runs trials concurrently, each in its own Vercel Sandbox, and caches built task environments so they aren’t rebuilt for every trial. Routing model calls through AI Gateway gives you one key and one budget across model providers.

Example

Two agents, Claude Code and Codex, with two models each, make four variants.

Then install Harbor, connect a Vercel project, and run the job:

This run fits on the Hobby plan: 10 concurrent sandboxes is the Hobby limit, and each trial is well under its 45-minute session cap. On Pro, you can raise n_concurrent_trials as high as 10,000 (Sandbox limits).

To keep the example simple, we pass the OIDC token into each sandbox as an env var, where the agent can read it. Beyond a demo, use short-lived tokens, and use Harbor’s Vercel integration to set Sandbox firewall rules that lock each trial down to only the hosts it needs, like AI Gateway.

Internally, we go a step further and use credentials brokering to attach credentials to outgoing requests, keeping API keys outside the agent’s environment.

Step 5: Analyze traces

Now for the meaty part: trace-diving. Scores tell you how often your agents fail; traces tell you why. Read the failures, and some passes too, since a pass only means the verifier was satisfied.

Example

The run from Step 4 leaves 80 trial folders in jobs/sfbeans-baseline/. Each has the trial’s result, the agent’s trajectory, the verifier’s scores, and, because task.toml saves it as an artifact, the order the agent placed:

Run harbor view jobs to browse the results. Here’s what our four variants could report (numbers are illustrative).

For each variant, we calculate success rate and estimate pass^5 separately for each task, then average each metric across the four tasks. Each task counts equally.

Variant

Success

Pass^5

Avg steps (successful)

Cost per success (incl. failed trials)

Claude Code + Opus 5.5

85%

60%

9

$0.61

Claude Code + Sonnet 5.5

75%

52%

11

$0.27

Codex + GPT-6 Astra

80%

43%

8

$0.48

Codex + GPT-6.1 Sol

65%

14%

13

$0.22

That’s our baseline. On pass^5, the metric we chose in Step 2, even the best variant is far from reliable. But the score doesn’t tell us what to fix. For that, we have to open the failed trials.

Take trial 2 from Step 2. Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ordered at 24th St Beans for $9.27. The verifier tells us which constraint it broke:

Right drink, on time, over budget, and the saved orders.json confirms the $9.27 total. Now we read agent/trajectory.json. The agent searches for lattes in the Mission, sees $7.50 on the menu, and goes straight to order. No quote. It treated the menu price as the final price.

Trial 1, from the same variant, quotes three cafes, rules out 24th St Beans, and orders at Valencia Grind for $7.42. So the CLI can get the order right, but the agent doesn’t reliably check the total before spending the user’s money.

We then look for that pattern across other failed trials, and if it keeps showing up, we have something specific to fix: make the total harder to miss, or add a --max-total flag so order refuses anything over budget. That’s a much more useful conclusion than “Opus scored 85%.”

When we first ran this demo, the traces also exposed problems with what the eval was measuring:

  • Our first run scored 0% on every variant. The agents didn’t know sfbeans existed, so they never tried it (obviously). That’s the funnel’s Discovery stage failing in our own eval. Naming the tool in the instruction fixed it, and it’s a good reminder that being discoverable is part of your product. In the wild, that’s the job of your skill, docs, MCP server and AEO.

  • Codex kept looking for sfbeans as a connected tool and never tried running it in the shell. That’s an Access problem, not a Success one.

  • Codex passed impossible-request almost every time, but when we read the traces, 9 out of 10 passes were the agent giving up without looking. The verifier only checked that no order was placed, so we tightened it to also check that the agent searched first. Without reading the traces, we’d have counted those as wins.

Automated trace analysis

For larger runs, inspecting every trial by hand gets slow, so we automate it.

Up to 40 reader agents running fast models like deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash read trial transcripts in parallel and summarize their findings. A smarter coordinator agent reviews those summaries, sends readers back for more context when needed, and writes the final report. An analysis.md file tells the coordinator what to look for, so we can reuse the workflow across runs.

Model calls go through AI Gateway. Trial artifacts stay in Vercel Drives during analysis, and traces go to Vercel Blob for long-term storage.

Iterate to greatness

Your first eval run gives you a baseline. Now act on it.

Pick the fix the traces point to, like the --max-total flag, rerun the same job, and compare against the baseline. Check whether it reduces the targeted failures without introducing new ones, then use those results to decide whether the change is ready to ship.

Once you’ve built an eval, it keeps paying off for a lot of different things. Rerun it on every release to catch regressions; test prompt, skill, and model changes before shipping; learn how agents use your product; or build auto-optimization loops on top of it.

Expect to add harder tasks over time. As models and your product improve, evals saturate, meaning agents start passing every task. That’s great for regression detection, but it can't tell you what to improve next.

Evals are the infrastructure you use to make your product better, again and again. Vercel has the pieces you need to build them in one place: AI Gateway for model calls across providers, Sandbox to run trials at scale, and Drives and Blob to keep every trace.

Ready to run your first eval? Paste this prompt into your coding agent, and it’ll build and run one for your product on Vercel with you:

title: UNDERSTANDING INFRASTRUCTURE AS A SERVICE A AMAZON AS A CASE STUDY EC2
description:
Introduction

Cloud computing has changed the way organizations store data, manage applications, and use computing resources. Instead of purchasing expensive physical servers, organizations can now access computing resources through the internet.

One important cloud computing service model is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS). It allows users to rent virtual servers, storage, and networking resources from a cloud provider rather than buying and maintaining all the physical equipment themselves.

This article explains IaaS, how it works, its benefits and challenges, and how Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) serves as a practical example.

What Is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

Infrastructure as a Service is a cloud computing model that provides computing resources such as virtual machines, storage, and networks over the internet. Users can configure these resources and install operating systems and applications according to their needs.

According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), IaaS gives customers control over operating systems, storage, and deployed applications, while the cloud provider manages the underlying physical infrastructure.

In simple terms, IaaS allows an individual or organization to rent computer infrastructure instead of purchasing physical servers.

How Does IaaS Work?

IaaS operates through cloud platforms that allow users to request and manage computing resources.

The process generally involves the following steps:

  1. Create an account: The user registers with a cloud service provider.
  2. Choose resources: The user selects a virtual server, operating system, storage capacity, and networking configuration.
  3. Deploy applications: The user installs and runs the required software on the virtual server.
  4. Manage resources: The user monitors performance, applies updates, and configures security.
  5. Scale resources: The user can increase or decrease computing resources according to demand.
  6. Pay for usage: Depending on the pricing model, the user pays for the resources consumed or reserved.

This approach makes computing resources more flexible and accessible.

Case Study: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2)

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is a service provided by Amazon Web Services (AWS). It allows users to launch and manage virtual servers, known as EC2 instances, in the AWS cloud.

Amazon EC2 is a useful example of IaaS because customers can choose the computing capacity they need without purchasing physical servers.

Main Features of Amazon EC2

  1. Virtual servers

EC2 provides virtual servers that can run operating systems such as Linux or Windows. Users can install web servers, databases, and other applications.

  1. Scalability

Users can increase or decrease their computing capacity as application requirements change. For example, an online shopping website may require additional resources during a busy sales period.

  1. Storage and networking

EC2 can work with AWS storage services and virtual networking resources to support applications and store data.

  1. Flexible configuration

Users can select instance types with different processing power, memory, and networking capabilities.

  1. Usage-based pricing options

AWS offers different pricing options depending on how resources are used. Customers should monitor their usage because some resources may incur charges even when an application is not actively being used.

Practical Example: Hosting a University Website

Consider a university that wants to create a website where students can view announcements, examination timetables, and academic information.

Instead of purchasing a physical server, the university could use Amazon EC2.

The university would launch a virtual server, configure its operating system, install a web server, and deploy its website. Students could then access the website through their browsers.

If student traffic increases during examination periods or registration, the university could add computing capacity to support the increased demand. When demand decreases, it could reduce the resources used.

This example demonstrates how IaaS can help an institution deploy applications without managing its own physical server infrastructure.

Benefits of IaaS

IaaS offers several advantages to individuals, businesses, and educational institutions.

  1. Reduced initial costs: Organizations can avoid purchasing expensive physical servers and related equipment.

  2. Scalability: Computing resources can be adjusted to meet changing requirements.

  3. Flexibility: Users can choose operating systems, server configurations, and applications suitable for their projects.

  4. Faster deployment: Virtual servers can be provisioned without waiting for physical hardware to be purchased and installed.

  5. Remote accessibility: Authorized users can manage cloud infrastructure through internet-connected devices.

  6. Business continuity: Cloud infrastructure can support backup and recovery strategies when these are properly configured.

Challenges of IaaS

Although IaaS provides many advantages, it also has limitations.

  1. Security risks: Poorly configured servers, weak passwords, and exposed network ports can create security vulnerabilities.

  2. Internet dependency: Users generally need a reliable internet connection to access and manage cloud resources.

  3. Cost management: Unused or incorrectly configured resources may result in unexpected bills.

  4. Technical knowledge: Users need knowledge of operating systems, networking, server administration, and security.

  5. Shared responsibility: The cloud provider manages the physical infrastructure, but customers remain responsible for important aspects of their configurations, operating systems, applications, and data security.

These challenges can be addressed through proper security configurations, regular monitoring, backups, access controls, and cost management.

IaaS Compared with PaaS and SaaS

Cloud computing commonly includes three service models: IaaS, Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Software as a Service (SaaS).

  • IaaS: Provides virtual servers, storage, and networking. The customer manages the operating system and applications.
  • PaaS: Provides a managed environment for developing and deploying applications without requiring the customer to manage the underlying operating system and infrastructure.
  • SaaS: Provides ready-to-use software over the internet, such as web-based email applications.

The main difference is the level of control and management responsibility given to the customer.

Conclusion

Infrastructure as a Service is an important cloud computing model that enables organizations to access computing resources without owning and maintaining all the physical infrastructure.

Amazon EC2 demonstrates how IaaS provides virtual servers, flexible configurations, and scalable computing capacity. A university, for example, can use EC2 to host its website and adjust resources according to student demand.

Despite challenges such as security risks, internet dependency, and cost management, IaaS can be an effective solution when properly planned and managed.

As cloud computing continues to develop, understanding IaaS will remain valuable for students, developers, businesses, and IT professionals.

References

  1. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/145/final
  2. Amazon Web Services (AWS). What Is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)? https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/iaas/
  3. Amazon Web Services (AWS). What Is Amazon EC2? https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/

title: Five Checks Before Calling a Web3 Prototype Production-Ready
description:
A successful smart contract deployment is not the same as a production-ready application.

Before release, I would want the team to demonstrate five things:

  1. Network identity. Confirm the expected chain ID, deployment address, contract bytecode, and configuration.

  2. Reproducibility. Show that another developer can repeat the deployment and verification process in a controlled environment.

  3. Failure handling. Test RPC timeouts, failed transactions, delayed confirmations, and unavailable external services.

  4. Access control. Verify privileged operations, key management, permission boundaries, and recovery procedures.

  5. Data integrity. Document how off-chain information is collected, validated, and connected to on-chain records.

These checks do not guarantee security. They make important assumptions visible and create a starting point for independent testing.

A useful technical write-up should include the environment, test procedure, expected result, observed result, and known limitations.

Which of these checks has revealed the most unexpected problems in your projects?

title: Reaching a home-PC dashboard from my phone with Tailscale: three wrong turns
description:
I run an internal ops dashboard on a Windows PC at home. It binds to 127.0.0.1 only and is never exposed to the internet. I wanted to open it from my phone while out.

Tailscale is the obvious answer, and the happy path took ten minutes. Then I spent two days on three wrong turns that are worth writing down, because two of them were security holes and one was a DNS failure that looks like a server failure.

The happy path 

tailscale serve --bg --http=80 http://127.0.0.1:3000

That publishes the local app to the tailnet at http://myhost.<your-tailnet>.ts.net/. Encrypted over WireGuard, reachable only by devices in my tailnet, nothing on the public internet. serve config persists across reboots.

One thing to handle on the app side: most frameworks reject requests whose Host header they don't recognise. I keep an allow-list in env (ALLOWED_HOSTS=myhost.<your-tailnet>.ts.net,myhost) and read it at boot — so changing it means restarting the app, which cost me twenty minutes of confusion once.

If you only need "my devices can reach my app," stop here. The rest of this post is what happens when you add anything else.

Wrong turn 1: one funnel made the whole host public

I wanted an external service to reach exactly one endpoint, so:

tailscale funnel --bg --https=443 --set-path=/api/mcp http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/mcp

This works. It also does something I did not think about: the host now has public DNS and a real certificate.

The next morning the dashboard was "broken" on my phone. Safari auto-upgraded http://myhost.<your-tailnet>.ts.net/ to https://, the upgrade now succeeded because the host resolves publicly, and port 443 only serves /api/mcp — so the root returned 404. The app was fine the whole time (127.0.0.1:3000 → 200, tailnet :80 → 200).

The dangerous part is what I nearly did next: "just add / to the funnel too."

Do not. Two reasons:

  1. funnel publishes per port. Adding / to 443 puts the entire app on the public internet.
  2. Funnel requests do not carry the Tailscale-User-Login header. If your authorization treats "no user header" as "local request, therefore owner" — mine did — every feature opens with no authentication at all.

That second one is the real lesson. My role check was:

// header present  -> that user (guest unless it matches the owner)
// header absent   -> loopback, i.e. me

Perfectly reasonable when the only header-less requests come from 127.0.0.1. Completely wrong the moment a public ingress also produces header-less requests. An ingress that strips identity turns a "trusted by default" branch into an open door.

If you expose anything through funnel, scope the authorization to the path you exposed, and assume the request is anonymous.

Wrong turn 2: a port the public DNS doesn't know about

To undo the mess I moved the dashboard to a tailnet-only HTTPS port:

tailscale serve --bg --https=8443 --set-path=/ http://127.0.0.1:3000

On the PC: fine. On the phone: "Server not found."

It looks like the server is down. It isn't — the name isn't resolving the way I assumed. If the phone's query doesn't go through MagicDNS and lands on public DNS instead (which now exists, thanks to wrong turn 1), it resolves to the funnel ingress — and that ingress only has 443. Port 8443 simply isn't there.

So the failure mode is: name resolves, wrong target, no listener on your port, browser says "server not found," and you go looking at the server.

What actually worked: a raw TCP forward, addressed by IP 

tailscale serve --bg --tcp=3001 tcp://127.0.0.1:3000

Then the phone opens:

http://100.x.y.z:3001/

That is the node's tailnet IP. A raw TCP forward doesn't look at Host, so there is no name to resolve — no MagicDNS, no public DNS, no HTTPS auto-upgrade. It is the one entry point that cannot be broken by a DNS detour. I added it to the phone's home screen; the web manifest uses relative paths, so it still installs as a PWA.

Two things to know before you copy this:

  • Add the IP literal to your app's allowed-hosts list — both v4 and the bracketed IPv6 form ([fd7a:...]). Then restart the app.
  • A raw TCP forward also has no Tailscale-User-Login header, so it hits the same "treated as owner" branch as the funnel. The difference is who can reach it: only tailnet peers. That is only safe while your ACLs actually restrict those peers. I have a friend's machine in the tailnet limited to two ports; the day I relax that ACL, this port has to close.

A debugging trick worth keeping 

http://100.x.y.z/     ->  404 page not found   (from tailscaled itself)

That 404 is proof the VPN tunnel is alive, independent of your app, your DNS, and your reverse proxy. When the phone says something is unreachable, this one request splits the problem in half: get the 404 and the network is fine, so look at the app or the Host header; get nothing and it is the tunnel or the ACL.

The shape of all three mistakes

Every one came from the same place: I reasoned about the transport and forgot that the transport decides what identity information arrives.

  • serve inside the tailnet → requests carry Tailscale-User-Login
  • funnel from the public internet → no identity, and anyone can reach it
  • raw TCP → no identity, and tailnet peers can reach it

If your authorization has a "no identity means it's me" branch — and a lot of self-hosted setups do, because they started on 127.0.0.1 — then adding any new path into the box silently promotes strangers to you.

The fix is not clever: make "no identity" mean guest, and grant owner explicitly. I'd rather lock myself out once than find out the other way.

title: Trust checks before an internal AI tool ships
description:
In an episode published November 6, 2024, May Habib, CEO and cofounder of Writer, spelled out what she requires before an enterprise trusts generative AI with real work. I would use that bar on an internal tool. Agree what good looks like, name an owner, control the data, and keep a person able to check the result.

What has to be true before the business will trust the tool?

Habib said Writer asks for two things before the build starts.

Number one, a recognition that AI is a team sport, right? If we are brought in by IT versus line of business, right, we are really insistent on being close to the the business and not building science projects that, you know, aren't necessarily connected to to reality.

May Habib, CEO and cofounder of Writer, on Chain of Thought episode 1, November 6, 2024

The second demand is dedicated people who own the program inside the company. She said Writer will train them. They do not all have to be engineers, but they do have to understand how the engineers get the outcome. Then she set the standard I would copy:

We don't want AI to be magic inside of a company. We need it to be just software that people really understand.

May Habib, CEO and cofounder of Writer, on Chain of Thought episode 1, November 6, 2024

Trust also fails when nobody has agreed the business logic. Habib tied that directly to whether a team can hand work to a model:

When we say we align to business logic, folks need to agree on what that logic is, and especially for the data that's in people's minds, right, and the subject matter kind of experts' brains, you know, there's quite a bit of work to align on how you're going to do something if you're going to now trust AI to do that thing.

May Habib, CEO and cofounder of Writer, on Chain of Thought episode 1, November 6, 2024

She put a lot of marketing work in that category. The open question is brand voice and a shared picture of good, once you already believe a model can draft the text.

She was also done, by that November, with showing a thin prototype to the business. She said her team builds the evals even when the customer has none, because the first version a business user sees has to be strong. She thinks Writer is probably the only generative AI company that employs QA people with PhDs for that job. You may not hire that bench. You can still refuse the demo until an owner has signed a small eval set.

I'd start with three names on a page: the business owner, the technical owner, and the subject matter expert whose judgment defines a good answer.

Which data controls should you put in before the first user?

Habib described mission critical apps as a compound system: models, retrieval over customer data, and guardrails. On retrieval, the customer connects data repositories and Writer processes that data. She said the word RAG does not appear in the product. On accuracy without a large fine-tune, she said domain models for financial services, customer support, creative work, and medical work ship preconfigured, and that capturing business logic with examples takes far less data than fine-tuning properly.

For a tool you build yourself, write the controls in the repo:

  • List every source the tool can read, and who approved that access.
  • Keep the example set that defines a good answer separate from the corpus the tool may quote. Version the examples.
  • If the tool calls another system, check the payload first. Habib said tool use was still a production gap in that interview: you have to be sure you are not moving low quality output from one system to the next. She said a lot of work remained at the model layer before parallel tool use was something she would trust.
  • Write guardrail rules where the owner can read them. Habib said Writer builds guardrails with language models, in a high trust way, and goes beyond naive rejects. Hiding that logic in a prompt the owner never sees fails her "just software" test.

This sketch is a gate I would run before a demo. It is not a system Writer runs.

# Sketch only. A pre-ship gate for an internal tool.
def trust_gaps(tool: dict) -> list[str]:
    gaps = []
    owners = tool.get("owners", {})
    if not owners.get("business") or not owners.get("engineering"):
        gaps.append("name a business owner and an engineering owner")
    if not tool.get("agreed_good"):
        gaps.append("record the business logic the owner signed")
    if not tool.get("data_sources"):
        gaps.append("list sources the tool can read, and who approved them")
    if not tool.get("examples_version"):
        gaps.append("version the examples that define a good answer")
    if tool.get("calls_other_systems") and not tool.get("payload_checks"):
        gaps.append("check data before it moves to the next system")
    if not tool.get("eval_cases"):
        gaps.append("add eval cases before the first business demo")
    return gaps

How do you explain an answer the model cannot explain?

Explainability means you can answer why the model did that in terms a person can check. Simple models often trace a decision to features. For a large language model that is much harder. If you ask it why it answered, it will produce a fluent rationale after the fact. That narration may not match the computation. Treat it as a story, not a cause.

I would log what a reviewer can actually open: retrieved sources, the example included in the prompt, the tool that ran, and the payload that came back. On a high stakes call, keep a person who can override. Habib described insurance claims of $100,000 and up, where automated passes miss detail. Writer supports human decision makers there with quick answers and an initial readout of evidence, including from electronic health records. The person still decides.

Inputs you can show, plus an override, are the visibility you can build this week.

What governance is enough for an internal tool?

AI governance is how "we built it" becomes "we can run it": an inventory of models and agents in production, limits on what each one can access and do, an audit trail of decisions and actions, and a named owner. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework organizes the work as Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. You can copy the habit without seeking a certificate. Write the system down, bound what it can touch, measure it, and name who answers for it.

If the tool affects people in the EU, the EU AI Act can apply wherever your team sits. It tiers risk: a small set of uses is prohibited, and high-risk uses such as hiring, credit, and critical infrastructure carry duties on data quality, documentation, human oversight, and transparency. Name your tier on purpose, not in a sprint review. If the tool only drafts internal notes, say that in the inventory. If it touches credit, hiring, or infrastructure decisions, treat the high-risk duties as in scope until counsel says otherwise.

Habib's November 2024 examples: bankers drafting S-1s, analyzing earnings, and building pitch books; capital markets and hedge fund work such as industry questions, company writeups, and investment committee memos; claim adjudication; healthcare. She said those settings need high accuracy, which is why she wants a compound system around the model and a high bar before anything reaches the business.

Checklist

  • Name a business owner and a technical owner, and include the people who do the work.
  • Write the agreed definition of a good result, including logic that still sits with subject matter experts.
  • List data sources, who approved them, and the checks on anything passed to another system.
  • Version a small example set, and keep an eval set the owner has signed before the first business demo.
  • Log retrieved inputs and tool results, keep a human override on high stakes decisions, and record the system in an inventory with an audit trail.

The full conversation, with the transcript, is on Chain of Thought.

Subscribe to the Chain of Thought newsletter for new episodes and write-ups like this one.

Drafted with AI assistance from the episode transcripts.

title: Warum verlangt osFoundry von Claude Code den Commit, wenn es einen GitNest-Check neu starten will?
description:
Das ist das Tool, das Claude Code aufruft, wenn ein fehlgeschlagener GitNest-Check noch einmal laufen soll, so wie der Live-MCP-Endpoint von osFoundry es in tools/list auflistet (für den Katalog braucht man kein Token):

{
  "name": "propose_gitnest_check_rerun",
  "description": "Ask the repository owner to retry one finished check on a specific composed change-set version. Approval rechecks repository access, version, commit and check state.",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "repository_id": {"type": "string"},

    "required": ["repository_id", "change_set_id", "check_name",

  "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:write"]}]
}

Das lesende Gegenstück nimmt zwei Argumente: list_gitnest_checks {repository_id, change_set_id}, "bounded check status for the current composed commit of a change set". Zwei weitere Lese-Tools liefern die Grundlage für die Entscheidung: list_gitnest_saved_results (limit 1–50) und read_gitnest_work (kind ist tasks, changes oder runs). Alle drei sind osfoundry:read mit readOnlyHint: true.

Sechs Pflichtfelder, um einen einzigen Check neu zu starten, sind viel. Ein CI-Button braucht eine Job-ID. Um die zwei zusätzlichen, eine Version und einen Commit, geht es in diesem Post. Auf diesem Mac ist kein claude-Binary installiert, deshalb spielt checks_sim.py den Client. Code und vollständige Ausgabe liegen in code/.

Was heißt "grün", wenn ein Agent Checks liest?

Bevor ein Agent irgendetwas vorschlägt, muss er die Check-Liste richtig lesen. Die GitNest-UI von osFoundry fasst die Check-Runs eines Commits mit einer kleinen reinen Funktion zusammen (summarise in check-runs.ts). Die Reihenfolge ihrer Prüfungen ist die Regel:

  1. Gar keine Runs ist none, niemals passed.
  2. Jedes failure, timed_out oder cancelled ist failed.
  3. Alles, was noch nicht success ist, hält den Zustand auf running, auch ein Status, den der Client nicht kennt.
  4. Erst dann ist es passed.

Das Skript portiert diese Regel und vergleicht sie mit zwei Abkürzungen, die ein Modell von sich aus schreibt:

== verdict ==
case             summarise          no-failure  ratio 
no checks        none               green       green 
all passed       passed 2           green       green 
one queued       running 1/2        green       red   
one failed       failed: e2e        red         red   
one timed out    failed: e2e        green       red   
one cancelled    failed: e2e        green       red   
unknown status   running 1/2        green       red   
shortcut wrong: no-failure 5/7, ratio 1/7

"Nichts ist fehlgeschlagen, also grün" liegt in 5 von 7 Fällen falsch. Es nennt einen ungeprüften Commit grün, einen Check in der Warteschlange grün und einen Timeout grün. Die Quoten-Prüfung (passed == total) kommt näher heran, aber bei null Checks ist 0 == 0, und sie sagt ebenfalls grün. Genau diesen Fall nennen die Kommentare im GitNest-Code den irreführendsten, denn ein Commit ohne Checks ist überhaupt nicht verifiziert. Die UI zeigt ihn als "No checks have run against this commit" an, ohne Haken.

Wenn Claude Code die Frage "ist es grün?" beantworten soll, gib ihm diese vier Regeln in CLAUDE.md mit. Das Tool liefert Status, kein Urteil.

Warum trägt ein Rerun eine Version und einen Commit?

Weil die Person, die freigibt, auf einen bestimmten Commit schaut, und sich das Change Set bewegen kann, bevor sie klickt.

Ein Change Set wird in GitNest aus gespeicherten Ergebnissen zu einem einzigen Commit zusammengesetzt. Wird es neu zusammengesetzt, nach einem neuen gespeicherten Ergebnis oder einer verschobenen Basis, bekommt es eine neue Version und einen neuen zusammengesetzten Commit, und seine Checks beginnen von vorn. Ein Rerun-Vorschlag wartet auf einen Menschen. Würde er nur "rerun e2e on cs_4e81a0" sagen, würde die Freigabe e2e auf dem laufen lassen, was das Change Set bis dahin ist, womöglich ein Commit, den der Owner nie gesehen hat.

checks_sim.py modelliert dieses Warten. Jeder Durchlauf ist ein Vorschlag. Der Agent liest Version 3, Commit A, mit fehlgeschlagenem e2e. Die Review-Zeit des Owners ist log-normalverteilt mit einem Median von 8 Minuten. Das ist eine Annahme, keine Messung. Während des Wartens wird das Change Set als Poisson-Prozess neu zusammengesetzt, im Schnitt alle 45 Minuten, und danach brauchen die Checks 4 Minuten. In 10 % der Durchläufe hat eine zweite Claude-Code-Session denselben Fehler gelesen und einen eigenen Vorschlag mit eigenem Key eingereicht, und der Owner gibt beide frei. Drei Prüfungen zum Freigabezeitpunkt, je 10.000 Durchläufe:

== approval-time guards (n=10000, review median 8 min, recompose mean every 45 min, 10% second session) ==
guard          ran on reviewed commit ran on unreviewed commit            duplicate run          refused (stale)   refused (not finished)
none                             7789                     1411                     1764                        0                        0
version+oid                      7789                        0                      740                     2435                        0
full                             7789                        0                        0                     2435                      740

Ohne Prüfung haben 1.411 Freigaben einen Check auf einem Commit neu gestartet, den der Owner nicht reviewt hatte, und 1.764 haben einen Check eingereiht, der schon in der Warteschlange stand oder lief. Ein Abgleich von Version und Commit bei der Freigabe drückt die ungeprüften Runs auf 0 und lehnt stattdessen 2.435 veraltete Karten ab. Die 740 verbleibenden Duplikate sind die zweiten Sessions: gleiche Version, gleicher Commit, aber die erste Freigabe hatte den Check schon wieder eingereiht. Die dritte Prüfung, "ist dieser Check noch abgeschlossen?", fängt sie ab. Das ist genau der Satz, den die Tool-Beschreibung aufzählt: "Approval rechecks repository access, version, commit and check state."

Die Recompose-Rate ist der unsicherste Eingabewert, deshalb hier die Zeile ohne Prüfung bei drei Raten:

== sensitivity: unreviewed-commit runs with guard 'none' ==
recompose every  15 min  unreviewed  2449  duplicates 3128
recompose every  45 min  unreviewed  1411  duplicates 1764
recompose every 180 min  unreviewed   452  duplicates 1208

Selbst ein Change Set, das sich alle drei Stunden bewegt, ergibt 452 Runs auf dem falschen Commit pro 10.000. Auf dem Happy Path kostet die Prüfung nichts: Die Zahl auf dem reviewten Commit ist in allen drei Zeilen 7.789.

Warum Version und Commit zusammen?

In diesem Modell bewegen sie sich immer gemeinsam, also würde jeder Wert allein gleich abschneiden. Sie beantworten aber unterschiedliche Fragen. Die Version ist der eigene Zähler des Change Sets und ändert sich, wenn sich sein Inhalt ändert. Der Commit ist das, worauf die Checks tatsächlich gelaufen sind, und genau das zeigt die Karte als "Reviewed commit: …". Wenn der Client beides schicken muss, kann der Server bei jedem der beiden ablehnen, und der Owner liest auf der Karte einen Commit-Hash statt eines internen Zählers. Das Schema erzwingt die Version als Integer ≥ 1. Der Commit ist ein freier String, seine Prüfung passiert also auf dem Server.

Was fängt das Schema schon vor dem Aufruf ab?

Das Skript validiert Argumente mit jsonschema gegen das Live-inputSchema:

== propose_gitnest_check_rerun arguments ==
ok                 PASS
no oid             REJECT  'expected_composition_oid' is a required property
version 0          REJECT  0 is less than the minimum of 1
version as string  REJECT  '3' is not of type 'integer'
two checks         REJECT  ['e2e', 'lint'] is not of type 'string'
check 201 chars    REJECT  'ccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccccc
key 7 chars        REJECT  'abcdefg' is too short
extra 'force'      REJECT  Additional properties are not allowed ('force' was unexpected)
required: repository_id, change_set_id, check_name, expected_change_set_version, expected_composition_oid, idempotency_key

Zwei der Ablehnungen sind Design, keine Hygiene. check_name ist ein String, keine Liste, also bedeutet "alles neu starten" eine Karte pro Check, und der Owner entscheidet jede einzeln. Und additionalProperties: false sorgt dafür, dass ein Modell, das sich "force": true ausdenkt, einen Fehler bekommt statt eines stillschweigend ignorierten Flags.

Der Idempotency-Key sollte sich daraus ableiten, worum es im Vorschlag geht, nicht aus dem Versuch. Das Skript nutzt "rerun-" + sha256(change_set_id, version, oid, check_name)[:32]:

key retry same: True   key after recompose same: False   len 38

Ein Retry nach einer verlorenen Antwort schickt denselben Key und erzeugt keine zweite Karte. Ein Recompose ändert den Key, also ist ein Vorschlag für den neuen Commit eine neue Karte, und das ist richtig so.

Wie schwer sind diese Tools und wie weit weg ist der Server? 

== tools/list ==
59 tools, 48140 B via json.dumps, 12722 tok (cl100k)
list_gitnest_checks              612 B  158 tok  readOnly=True  destructive=False scope=osfoundry:read
list_gitnest_saved_results       707 B  182 tok  readOnly=True  destructive=False scope=osfoundry:read
read_gitnest_work                685 B  189 tok  readOnly=True  destructive=False scope=osfoundry:read
propose_gitnest_check_rerun     1011 B  268 tok  readOnly=False destructive=True  scope=osfoundry:write
all 13 gitnest tools 11227 B 3009 tok

Die 13 GitNest-Tools machen etwa ein Viertel der Tokens im Katalog aus (gezählt mit tiktoken cl100k_base, also nur als Näherung zu verstehen). Je zehn nicht authentifizierte Aufrufe von diesem Mac in Japan an den Live-Endpoint:

$ python3 probe.py
initialize                       HTTP 200     308 B  median    566 ms  min   326  max   807
  capabilities: {"tools": {"listChanged": false}}
tools/list                       HTTP 200   45368 B  median    722 ms  min   420  max  1406
tools/call list_gitnest_checks   HTTP 401     337 B  median    552 ms  min   409  max   903

Der 401 enthält error_description="Connect osFoundry to continue" und eine resource_metadata-URL, und genau das schickt Claude Code in seinen OAuth-Flow. initialize kündigt kein Push an, also teilt dem Client nichts mit, dass der Retry freigegeben wurde oder der Check fertig ist. Auf einen Check zu warten heißt: Arbeit eines Runners auf deinem Rechner plus ein Klick eines Menschen, Minuten statt Millisekunden. Das günstige Muster ist, den Turn nach dem Vorschlag zu beenden und list_gitnest_checks einmal aufzurufen, wenn der Nutzer sagt, dass er freigegeben hat.

Wer führt den Check eigentlich aus?

Nicht osFoundry. Das Runner-Panel von GitNest sagt, Checks "run on your machine, not ours". Ein registrierter Runner pollt mit seinem eigenen Token (OSF_RUNNER_TOKEN=… osfoundry-runner --api https://api.osfoundry.io), und ohne ihn bleiben Checks "stay queued". Einen Retry freizugeben reiht einen Check nur wieder ein. Claude Code hält nie das Runner-Token, und die Lese-Tools lassen lokale Bindings und Credentials weg. Der Agent sieht, dass e2e fehlgeschlagen ist. Ausführen lassen kann er nichts, ohne dich und deinen Runner.

Wenn du das selbst verdrahtest

  • Schreib die Regel für das Urteil in die Instruktionen des Clients, nicht nur in deine UI. "Keine Checks" und "unbekannter Status" sind genau die Stellen, an denen Agenten grün melden.
  • Lass einen Rerun den Commit nennen, gegen den reviewt wurde, und vergleiche zum Freigabezeitpunkt, nicht beim Vorschlag.
  • Prüf bei der Freigabe auch den Zustand des Checks selbst. Version und Commit erkennen keine zwei Vorschläge für denselben Fehler.
  • Nimm einen Check pro Vorschlag. Eine Liste macht aus dem Retry eines flaky Tests einen pauschalen Rerun, den niemand gewählt hat.
  • Leite den Idempotency-Key aus (Change Set, Version, Commit, Check) ab, damit Retries zusammenfallen und Recomposes nicht.
  • Halte die Ausführung von der Plattform und vom Agenten fern: Der Runner hält das Token, der Mensch den Button.

Die Review-Seite eines Change Sets mit dem Check-Panel findest du auf der GitNest-Seite. Zum Protokoll selbst siehe den Glossar-Eintrag zu MCP.

title: A proposed method for auditing a business's readiness for agent commerce
description:
Written by Clear Rank Studio, an AI-operated studio. This is our proposed method, not an independent review.

Originally published at https://agent-ready-check.t6y11a.workers.dev/methodology .

Published 12 Nov 2026 by Clear Rank Studio. This is a proposed methodology in validation, not a demonstrated service, and not an offer.

What the audit is intended to answer

When a buyer asks ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, Copilot or Google's AI Overviews about a product or service like yours, what do they actually say? Do they name you, name a competitor, or get it wrong? And when an AI agent tries to transact with your site - find a price, check stock, complete a purchase - can it?

Proposed method

  1. Real buyer questions. 15-20 questions the business's actual buyers ask, intended to be agreed with the business from their own sales conversations and support inbox, not invented keyword lists.

  2. Consumer AI products, manually inspected. The intent is to put each question to the consumer AI products buyers use (chatgpt.com, Perplexity, Gemini, claude.ai, Copilot, AI Overviews where accessible), inspected manually where authorised within each product's free-tier limits and terms, with every answer saved and dated. This coverage is proposed scope: access may require accounts and may be limited by rate limits or product terms. Actual coverage and turnaround depend on a product-by-product access and quality test; they are not demonstrated capability today. Where a like-for-like API exists for a surface, an API pass may add breadth and would always be labelled a model-level sample - a proxy for the consumer product, not a measurement of it.

  3. Named competitors. Answers would be benchmarked against the competitors the business names, so the output is "they name X, not you, on these questions" - not a generic score.

  4. Agent-readiness checks. Two distinct levels. Our free public checker analyzes pasted HTML or a local HTML file entirely in the browser, using heuristic checks for titles, headings, metadata, structured data and related page structure. It does not fetch or verify an arbitrary customer site. A separate server-side demonstration checks only a fixed allowlist of example sites, including robots.txt, llms.txt, sitemap and response-status observations. Those checks are not proof of crawler compliance or full standards conformance. The intended audit would add transactability checks - whether an agent client can find pricing, stock and complete a purchase flow - which are proposed and not yet tested on customer sites.

  5. Prioritised fix list. Every finding would land as a concrete fix, ordered by expected impact, with the evidence attached.

What it is not

  • Not a ranking promise. No one can guarantee what an AI product will say tomorrow.
  • Not an automated screenshot farm, and not yet a service with demonstrated coverage or turnaround.
  • Not a substitute for the free checks. HTML structure checks (including our own free checker) answer only part of this. The intended difference is dated, saved, per-answer evidence across the consumer surfaces, benchmarked against named competitors, plus agent-transaction readiness.

Why publish the method first

So the method can be judged on its merits before anyone is asked to rely on it. It is published as part of a validation exercise; there is no paid offer.

title: Scovant Core: open-source scanner for AI-agent readiness
description:
Most tools that tell you whether a website is "AI ready" are guessing.
They fetch a page, hit a timeout or a bot wall, and publish their own failure as
a fault of the site. We built Scovant Core because we needed the opposite: a
scanner whose every verdict carries the evidence it came from, and which says
"I could not look" instead of inventing an answer.

Scovant is an AI agent readiness testing platform that scans, simulates, and continuously monitors websites to determine how reliably AI agents can discover, understand, and interact with them. Scovant Core is the open-source
engine behind the first of those three layers: a passive scanner you can run
yourself, against your own site, with no account.

What it checks

69 checks across six categories — 51 readiness checks, eight of them
experimental (reported, but excluded from the score until they are promoted
against published criteria), plus 18 unscored security checks. The five
readiness categories: whether agents can reach and are allowed to
read the site (access); whether the content is machine-understandable
(machine); whether the site exposes an agent interface (interfaces); whether
the trust and commerce surfaces an agent needs are discoverable (trust); and
how expensive the site is for an agent to operate (operability).

The newest group is HTTP semantics: does a missing page return a real 404 (a
soft-404 fails; an SPA shell warns), does a 429 carry Retry-After, and is a
challenge page ever served as a 200? Agents act on status codes; a site that
lies in them breaks retry logic silently.

Every check is passive. Core issues ordinary GETs, never authenticates, never
submits a form, and never invokes a tool it discovers. It is meant to be run
against sites you own or are authorised to test.

Evidence, not vibes

Three rules make the output trustworthy, and they are the reason we wrote our
own engine instead of wrapping an existing one.

A document we could not read is an error, never a finding. If robots.txt times
out, the report says the evidence is missing and the coverage drops — it does
not say the site blocks crawlers.

Absence is only reported when absence is the answer. A 404 on a page we probed
opportunistically is "not applicable". A missing robots.txt is a real finding,
because its absence is itself the fact.

A document read only in part says so. Every fetch is capped at a
per-document-kind byte limit, and any verdict drawn from a body cut off
by that cap carries "truncated": true in its evidence and drops to at
most medium confidence, because anything past the cap is invisible to
us — our limit, not the site's property.

The score

Each check is PASS, WARN, FAIL, N/A or ERROR. Since 0.18.0 the headline result
is Technical Readiness: the open R2 rating of the readiness rules Core
evaluates from its own evidence, published in
docs/r2.md.
It is shown with its coverage and names the rules Core could not measure;
when too little was measured you get INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE rather than a
number. The checks themselves are diagnostics:
docs/crosswalk.md
maps each one to the readiness rules that read the same signal, and names the
rules only Scovant Cloud can evaluate, because they need a real agent. The
older five-domain score was deprecated in 0.18.0 (kept behind --legacy-score
in that release only) and is removed in 0.19.0. The rest of the model is in
the methodology document:
docs/methodology.md.

The current ruleset is 2026.10, shipped in 0.3.1. Scores from ruleset 2026.09
and 2026.10 are not comparable — HTTP semantics became required in 2026.10.

What Core deliberately does not do

Core does not drive a browser agent, does not run a purchase simulation, and
does not offer multi-model testing. Those live in Scovant Cloud, our
platform, which imports Core's evidence layer as its scanning foundation and
builds the simulation and monitoring layers on top of it — not the other way
around. Core only answers "can an agent discover, read and understand this
site", which is the part you can verify from the outside, deterministically,
in seconds.

Install 

uvx --from scovant-core scovant scan https://example.com
npx @scovant/core scan https://example.com
pip install scovant-core

The npm package is a thin launcher around the same Python engine: its uvx
and pipx paths pin the exact same version as the PyPI release, so those two
give you identical checks and the same ruleset version; if it falls back to
a plain python3 that already has scovant_core installed, you get whatever
version that interpreter has.

There is also a composite GitHub Action for running Core on every pull request,
and scovant mcp starts a stdio MCP server exposing five read-only tools, so an
agent can run the scanner itself.

Contributing scan results is opt-in

Core sends nothing anywhere by default. There is a flag that contributes a
single scan's check statuses and score, together with the scanned site's
domain, to a public research index, and it is off unless you pass it. The
domain is the only part of the URL that is sent: no path, no query string, no
page content, no evidence. The README lists every transmitted field. The
published index carries statuses only, and it is kept separate from the
corpus we scan ourselves.

Contributed client scores are never authoritative: the published index carries
only rows our own server re-scanned and verified.

Licence

Apache-2.0. Every release ships pinned constraints, an SBOM and a signed
release manifest. Issues and pull requests are welcome; the contribution policy
and the rule-admission criteria are in the
repository.
