title: Remember your 404s until the next deploy
description:
Most caching advice is about remembering things that exist. This one is about remembering things that don't.

If you serve static files from object storage or a bucket behind a worker, every request for a missing file still costs you a lookup. Browsers ask for favicon.ico at the root even if you never had one. Bots probe for paths that were never there. Old links point at files that got renamed. Each of those is a round trip to storage that ends in the same answer: not here.

I added a small negative cache for this to a thing I run, and the rule that made it safe was simple: a 404 is only true until the next deploy.

Key it on the deploy

The set of files can only change when you deploy. So if you include the deploy ID in the cache key, you never have to invalidate anything. A new deploy means new keys, and the old entries just stop being read.

const key = `404:${deployId}:${url.pathname}`;

if (await cache.get(key)) {
  return new Response("Not found", { status: 404 });
}

const file = await bucket.get(objectPath);
if (!file) {
  await cache.put(key, "1");
  return new Response("Not found", { status: 404 });
}

That's most of it. Use whatever cache you already have. The important part is the key, not the store.

Why not just a TTL?

A TTL works, but it forces you to pick a number. Too long and a file you just deployed stays "missing" for a while. Too short and you get little benefit. Tying it to the deploy removes the guess: the answer is valid for exactly as long as the files are the same.

Things to watch

  • Only cache real misses. If storage errors or times out, that is not a 404. Don't remember it.
  • Normalize the path first. Otherwise /a/../b and /b become two entries, and someone can fill your cache with junk paths.
  • Bound it if you can. Bots generate a lot of unique paths. An expiry on top of the deploy key, or a cache that evicts on its own, keeps that in check.
  • Make sure the deploy ID is actually per deploy. If it's the same across releases, you've built a cache that never forgets.

Is it worth it?

It depends on how much junk traffic you get. It's a few lines, nothing to configure, and nothing to invalidate by hand. That's about the right size for a fix like this: small enough that it's hard to get wrong, and when it works nobody notices.

title: Before converting a bank CSV: check dates, signs and the target importer
description:
A bank CSV can look tidy and still describe the wrong transactions after an import. The useful question is whether the destination receives the same dates and amounts that you intended.

One starting check can save a conversion step: QuickBooks Online already supports CSV uploads. Intuit documents supported three-column and four-column layouts in its manual upload guide. Check the current instructions for your country and product first. You may not need another file format.

If your particular destination needs OFX, QBO or QFX, make a tiny example before moving a full statement.

Start with two transactions whose meaning you know

This is invented data for an asset-account example, not a real bank statement:

Date,Description,Amount
2026-11-01,Synthetic incoming payment,125.00
2026-11-02,Synthetic outgoing payment,-35.50

For this example, there are two transactions and a net movement of 89.50. Those are simple checks you can carry into the preview and destination. A converter producing a downloadable file does not prove the target application interpreted it correctly.

Check the date convention before exporting

03/04 cannot tell you by itself whether the date is March 4 or April 3. Use the convention documented by the source bank and inspect a transaction whose real date you know. Avoid letting a spreadsheet silently decide while you clean the file.

Check signs and column meaning

A balance column is not a transaction amount column. Separate money-in and money-out columns also need an explicit mapping. Inspect one known incoming and one known outgoing transaction in the target preview; do not apply this invented asset-account sign convention blindly to every statement type.

Check the exact import path

File extensions do not make formats interchangeable. The OFX 2.3 specification describes the move from SGML formatting to XML. Use the format and version supported by the destination; renaming a file is not a conversion.

Before a full import, review a small sample and check how the destination handles an overlapping date range. Two transactions with the same date and amount can be legitimate, so deleting apparent duplicates without checking the statement can create another error.

The tool we build, and the limit of our test

Our Luventra converter converts CSV to OFX/QBO/QFX in the browser. The current guest allowance is two files per day, up to 50 transactions per file.

In our 10 November synthetic browser check, a two-row OFX download preserved amounts of 125.00 and -35.50. That test did not include an accounting-application import, a payment, or a real customer statement. It supports a narrow claim about that export, rather than universal compatibility.

Keep the original export, inspect the preview and verify the target import before relying on a converted statement.

title: Zipkin has no built-in UI authentication, so exposure is an architecture decision
description:
Zipkin has no built-in UI authentication, so exposure is an architecture decision

Zipkin's architecture documentation states that there is no built-in authentication in the UI. The UI queries the Zipkin API to search traces and render service maps, spans, timing, and errors. That makes Zipkin an observability service with a clear access-control requirement: if the UI is reachable, the operator must provide the missing authentication and authorization at another layer.

On 13 November 2026 at 03:46 China Standard Time, a ZoomEye count-only query with sub_type=all, page 1, and page size 1 returned 39 matches for title="Zipkin" and 559 matches for app="Zipkin". The inversion is useful. A custom UI or proxy may change the title, and many instrumented applications can mention Zipkin without exposing the server UI. The application fingerprint caught a larger candidate set in this observation, but neither count proves that a particular endpoint is unauthenticated.

The API is the security boundary

The Zipkin UI is a client of the API. Protecting the HTML page while leaving the search or trace endpoints reachable is not a complete control. A caller who knows the API can query the same data without loading the UI. The inventory should list the UI path, the API paths, the query service, and any storage or collector endpoints that belong to the deployment.

Zipkin traces can include endpoint names, service names, span names, timestamps, durations, error tags, and sometimes request metadata. Even without credentials or payloads, the pattern can reveal internal architecture, deployment changes, dependency relationships, and failure paths. A trace search can also be used to enumerate service names and test whether a particular request appeared.

Authentication at a reverse proxy should be tested end to end. The proxy must validate the identity before forwarding to the backend and must not trust a client-supplied identity header. A proxy health route, a debug route, or an alternate backend port can bypass the policy. If the deployment uses network allowlists, verify that the collector and UI share the intended boundary or have separate policies.

Inventory the deployment as two planes

The collector plane receives spans from instrumented applications. The query plane serves searches and the UI. They may run in the same process or in separate services depending on the deployment. Record each listener, its protocol, its authentication control, and the identities that can reach it. A collector that accepts unauthenticated spans from a broad network can be abused to inject misleading traces or consume storage. A query plane that accepts unauthenticated searches can disclose real traces.

Limit what the collector accepts. Use a network boundary or an authenticated gateway where appropriate. Validate the size and rate of ingested spans and monitor for sudden changes in service names or trace volume. Those controls do not replace trace authorization, but they reduce the risk of a public collector becoming a low-cost data pollution path.

For the query plane, test an unauthenticated search against a harmless query. The expected result should be a denial at the proxy or application layer, not an empty UI page with an open API behind it. Then test a low-privilege identity and confirm that it cannot query services outside its intended scope if the deployment supports that separation. If the deployment has no per-service authorization, document the network-level trust boundary and the people who can query the whole trace store.

Make the observation useful without overstating it

The 559 application matches are a product-level discovery signal. The 39 title matches are a narrower page-title signal. Neither is a count of unauthenticated Zipkin servers. Validate an owned match with the response and the deployment record. Then inspect the proxy and backend configuration with secrets removed.

Monitor route changes and ingestion changes. A new ingress for the UI, a second query port, or a collector exposed during a migration can change the boundary without changing the Zipkin version. Keep a snapshot of the expected listeners and compare it with the running service.

Zipkin is designed to be operated behind controls that the product does not provide in the UI. The useful security claim is therefore architectural: identify the API, place it behind an authenticated boundary, restrict ingestion, and test both the UI and the API. The search count helps find candidates for that work; it does not decide whether the boundary exists.

Query evidence

  • Search: title="Zipkin"
  • Application: app="Zipkin"
  • Scope: sub_type=all, page 1, page size 1
  • Counts: 39 and 559
  • Observed: 2026-11-13 03:46 China Standard Time
  • Title query
  • Application query

References

  • Zipkin architecture
  • Zipkin server configuration
  • Zipkin Lens authentication and authorization

title: A check that cannot fail has never passed
description:
Originally published at erikhill.dev. The numbers below are checked against the repositories they come from.

A check that cannot fail has never passed

Yesterday I went to verify a number in my own portfolio: ten repositories, a recorded total of
290 tests. I ran every suite. The real number is 683 passing, and nine of the ten per-repo
figures I had written down were wrong.

That is not the interesting part. The interesting part is why nothing told me.

1. The build that reported a number it did not measure

One repo is a Java engine with 59 tests. I ran ./gradlew test, parsed the JUnit XML, and got
59 passed, zero failures. Correct answer.

Then I read the console output properly:

5 actionable tasks: 5 up-to-date

Gradle had decided nothing changed and skipped the task. The XML I parsed was from an earlier
run. The number was right by luck, and I had measured a file, not a test suite. Forcing it with
clean test gives a bare > Task :test with no UP-TO-DATE suffix, and an XML timestamp from
seconds ago rather than days.

If that suite had been broken since the last build, I would have reported it green, with
evidence, from a file.

2. The suite that reports zero tests instead of failing

Another repo keeps persistence behind an optional extra, which is a reasonable design: the base
install runs in memory and needs no ORM. Its test suite does not. On a base install:

ImportError while importing test module 'tests/test_store.py'
E   ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'sqlalchemy'
!!!! Interrupted: 1 error during collection !!!!

pytest never collects a single test. The output contains no count at all. If a pipeline keys on
"did any test fail", the answer is no, because no test ran. CI installs the dev extra and gets
29 passing, so CI is honest; the trap is anyone, including me, running the documented base
command and reading the quiet as calm.

3. The badge that had drifted by 163

The same audit against public surfaces: a tests badge reading 198 where execution gives 361. Six
of nine public claims understated. One README's prose said 39 while its own badge, in the same
file, said 42.

Understating is the benign direction, and I will take it over the alternative. But a README that
disagrees with itself gives a reader no reason to trust either number, and that costs more than
being three low.

4. The one that changes how I build checks

I keep a set of durable notes, each carrying a small shell command whose job is to detect that
the note has gone stale. The format stores the command and its expected output.

28 of 97 of those commands had recorded their own error as the expected output.

The cause is one missing separator. The field held the command and a human annotation with
nothing between them, so the annotation became arguments:

grep applicationId app/build.gradle -> must still read "com.example" (line 8 today); ...
zsh: no matches found: (line 8 today)

The shell aborts at glob expansion. grep never runs. Whatever wrote the baseline recorded the
failure, and the failure reproduces perfectly, every time. The check agreed with itself on
every evaluation it ever made. One of them had been pinning a repository's HEAD commit to a
date three months stale.

Then, repairing them, I wrote a check to count how many were still broken. It took three tries,
and all three failed the same way:

  1. Count occurrences of the error pattern across the notes. Returned one too many: it matched the pattern quoted in its own prose.
  2. Narrow to the right field. Returned one too many again: the pattern appeared inside its own command, because the command searches for it.
  3. Slice off everything before the separator and search only the recorded output. Correct.

Each fix was a real narrowing, and each one still counted itself. A measuring instrument stored
alongside the things it measures will include itself unless the unit explicitly excludes it.

The fourth failure was the best one. Repairing the last note drove the count to zero, and
grep -c exits non-zero on zero matches, so the check went red at exactly the moment it should
have gone green, and would have become the 28th instance of the defect it documents.

The thing they share

None of these are bugs in the usual sense. Nothing crashed. Every signal was green, and the
green was not false, it was empty. A skipped task, an uncollected suite, a baseline equal to its
own failure mode: each produces a passing result over a value that was never measured.

So the question I now ask of anything that reports a verdict is not "does it pass?" but "what
would make this go red, and has it ever gone red?" A check with no demonstrated failure mode is
a check with no demonstrated anything.

Which is easy to say and genuinely hard to apply to monitors, because a monitor cannot fail on
clean data by design, so you cannot mutation-test it the way you would a function. The only way
I have found that works is to pull the predicate out of the monitor and test the predicate.

I would like to be argued with on that last point, because it is the part I am least sure of.

title: Agentes LLM: permisos mínimos para email de prueba
description:
Un agente LLM puede crear un buzón, provocar un registro y leer un código de verificación en pocos pasos. Esa capacidad resulta útil para probar productos, pero también crea una frontera de seguridad poco visible: el modelo tiene acceso a una herramienta que puede generar datos, consultar mensajes y mantener recursos vivos.

La solución no es quitar la automatización. Es darle permisos mínimos, un tiempo de vida corto y respuestas que hagan evidente lo que acaba de ocurrir. Un correo de usar y tirar debe ser un recurso de prueba acotado, no una identidad que el agente pueda reutilizar sin límite.

El problema: una herramienta demasiado poderosa

Cuando se expone una sola función como email_tool, el modelo suele recibir demasiadas opciones: crear una dirección, listar mensajes, reenviar contenido, buscar por asunto y borrar recursos. Cada operación parece razonable por separado, pero juntas permiten que un fallo del prompt o una respuesta ambigua amplíe el alcance de la tarea.

El riesgo aparece en varios lugares:

  • Un reintento crea un segundo buzón y deja el primero sin dueño.
  • Una búsqueda amplia mezcla mensajes de ejecuciones anteriores.
  • El contenido completo del correo termina en el contexto del LLM, aunque solo se necesitaba un código.
  • Un flujo cancelado no libera la dirección ni sus mensajes.

En CI, este problema se parece a cualquier recurso temporal sin propietario. Un contrato de caducidad para emails de CI ayuda a pensar en el tiempo de vida antes de hablar de prompts. La pregunta no es solo si el agente puede llamar la herramienta, sino que puede hacer exactamente con cada llamada.

Define la frontera de permisos

Antes de diseñar el prompt, dibujo la frontera en palabras:

orquestador de la prueba
  ├─ crea un buzón con task_id
  ├─ dispara el evento de producto
  ├─ observa solo mensajes de esa ejecución
  ├─ extrae un dato mínimo
  └─ revoca el recurso al terminar

El agente no necesita conocer todas las operaciones internas. Puede tener tres capacidades pequeñas:

  1. create_fixture(task_id, expires_at): reserva una dirección asociada a una ejecución.
  2. wait_for_code(fixture_id, correlation_key, deadline): devuelve solo el estado y el código necesario.
  3. release_fixture(fixture_id): marca el recurso para eliminación, incluso despues de un fallo.

La diferencia importante es que el servidor aplica las restricciones. El prompt puede pedir un buzón con una duración razonable, pero nunca debe ser la única barrera. El backend comprueba que task_id pertenece a la ejecución actual, que expires_at no supera el máximo permitido y que el agente no está leyendo otra fixture.

Un límite de permisos así reduce la superficie de error sin convertir el sistema en una arquitectura enorme. Si el agente necesita consultar el asunto, se añade un campo específico. No hace falta darle una operación genérica para listar toda la bandeja.

Un contrato mínimo para el agente

Las respuestas de las herramientas también son una interfaz de seguridad. Un mensaje como “no encontrado” invita a improvisar; una respuesta estructurada limita mejor la siguiente acción:

{
  "status": "waiting",
  "fixture_id": "fx-1842",
  "remaining_ms": 18000,
  "observed_messages": 0,
  "next_action": "poll_after_3s"
}

Yo mantendría estos campos en todas las operaciones:

  • status: created, waiting, ready, expired o provider_error.
  • fixture_id: identificador opaco, sin exponer la dirección completa al modelo.
  • remaining_ms: tiempo disponible para el paso actual.
  • attempt: número de consulta dentro de la misma ejecución.
  • next_action: sugerencia limitada, no una instrucción libre.

El estado expired debe ser terminal. Si el agente recibe ese estado, no debería crear otra dirección automaticamente para repetir la prueba. El orquestador decide si se inicia una nueva ejecución y conserva la relación con el fallo original.

Este enfoque encaja bien con contratos de email para pruebas repetibles: cada prueba tiene una identidad, una condición de salida y una evidencia que se puede revisar sin abrir todo el buzón.

Evidencia, caducidad y rollback

Un agente confiable necesita una ruta de salida tan clara como la ruta feliz. Al terminar una ejecución, guardaría un recibo pequeño con:

  • task_id y fixture_id;
  • instante de creación y de liberación;
  • evento que originó el mensaje;
  • cantidad de consultas y tiempo consumido;
  • motivo de éxito, expiración o error.

El contenido del correo no debe entrar al recibo salvo que sea necesario para depurar. Para un código de verificación basta con almacenar un hash o los últimos caracteres, dependiendo del caso. Asi el equipo puede comprobar causalidad sin convertir los logs en otra bandeja de entrada.

La caducidad debería tener dos capas: una fecha aplicada por el proveedor y una limpieza de respaldo en el orquestador. Si una llamada queda a medias, el job de limpieza usa el fixture_id y elimina los recursos vencidos. No conviene depender de que el LLM recuerde llamar a release_fixture cuando ya recibió un error.

En documentación interna pueden aparecer búsquedas imperfectas como tempail mail. Las trato como señales de intención de prueba, no como nombres de herramientas que el agente deba resolver por su cuenta. También conviene registrar el motivo real del bloqueo, en vez de esconderlo detrás de un “falló el email”.

Q&A: decisiones prácticas

¿El LLM debe poder crear direcciones?

Sí, pero solo a través de una capacidad ligada a task_id, con duración máxima y cuota por ejecución. La decisión de permisos vive en el servidor, no en la personalidad del agente.

¿Por qué no exponer la bandeja completa?

Porque amplía el alcance de un error y hace difícil separar mensajes viejos de los nuevos. Una operación que espera un código concreto es mas fácil de auditar que una que devuelve todos los mensajes.

¿Qué hago cuando el proveedor de email falla?

Devuelve provider_error, conserva el recibo y ejecuta la limpieza. No repitas automáticamente con otra fixture si no sabes si el primer evento pudo llegar; primero marca la ejecución como inconclusa.

¿Dónde encaja tempmailso?

Puede servir como una temp mail so para aislar datos de una prueba, siempre que el equipo aplique su propia política de caducidad y no lo trate como una identidad real.

La arquitectura mínima es bastante concreta: una fixture con propietario, tres capacidades limitadas, respuestas estructuradas y una limpieza que no dependa del modelo. Con esos límites, los agentes LLM siguen siendo utiles para explorar flujos, pero sus herramientas de email dejan de comportarse como una caja negra.

title: Autonomous AI Agents in the Web: Integrating the Browser-Use Framework with SOCKS5 Proxies on Dedicated Hardware
description:
The current state of web automation feels like we are standing at a crossroads between the rigid past of Selenium scripts and a future where software "sees" and "thinks" its way through a DOM tree. If you have ever spent a weekend refactoring a scraper because a site changed a div class to a random hash, you know the pain of traditional automation. It is brittle, high-maintenance, and fundamentally dumb.

The emergence of autonomous AI agents—specifically those leveraging the Browser-Use framework—promises to end this cycle. However, moving these agents from a local "Hello World" demo to a production-grade environment requires more than just an API key. To achieve true autonomy, we must solve the two biggest hurdles in modern web interaction: environmental persistence (dedicated hardware) and identity obfuscation (SOCKS5 proxy integration).

This is not just about automation; it is about building a digital workforce that can navigate the web with the same nuance and resilience as a human operator.

Why is Browser-Use the "GPT-3 Moment" for Web Automation?

Most automation tools treat the web as a database to be queried. Browser-Use treats it as an environment to be perceived. Built on top of LangChain and Playwright, this framework allows Large Language Models (LLMs) to interact with a browser via natural language goals.

The shift is fundamental. Instead of telling the code to click(id="submit-button"), you tell the agent: "Find the most recent invoice in the dashboard and upload it to the accounting portal."

The framework handles the vision, the state management, and the execution loop. It interprets the visual layout, identifies interactive elements, and—most importantly—recovers when it hits an unexpected pop-up or a layout shift. It is the transition from a train on tracks to a self-driving car.

How Does Dedicated Hardware Change the Agentic Lifecycle?

Running an AI agent on your local machine is fine for debugging, but it’s a liability for production. When we talk about "dedicated hardware" in the context of Browser-Use, we aren't just talking about a VPS. We are talking about an environment where the agent has a persistent, high-performance lifecycle.

  1. Contextual Longevity: Web agents often need to perform long-running tasks—monitoring a market for hours or navigating complex multi-page workflows. Dedicated hardware ensures the agent isn't throttled by local CPU spikes or interrupted by a laptop going into sleep mode.
  2. Deterministic Latency: When an LLM "watches" a browser via screenshots, timing is everything. Dedicated hardware provides a stable network and compute baseline, reducing the "hallucinations" that occur when an agent tries to click an element that hasn't fully rendered due to local lag.
  3. The Sandbox Advantage: Running headless browsers is resource-intensive. On dedicated iron, you can optimize the memory overhead of Chromium, allowing for multiple agent instances to run in parallel without the "memory leak" death spiral common in shared environments.

The Stealth Layer: Why SOCKS5 is Non-Negotiable

If the browser is the agent's body and the LLM is its brain, the proxy is its passport. Modern websites have become incredibly sophisticated at detecting automated traffic. Simple HTTP proxies often leak headers that scream "I am a bot."

SOCKS5 (Socket Secure) acts at a lower level than HTTP proxies. It handles any traffic (TCP/UDP) and, crucially, does not rewrite your data headers. When you route a Browser-Use agent through a SOCKS5 proxy, you are achieving:

  • UDP Support: Essential for sites using modern protocols or those that perform WebRTC leaks to find your true IP.
  • Authentication Versatility: SOCKS5 allows for robust credential-based access, making it easier to rotate "clean" residential IPs.
  • Protocol Agnosticism: Since Browser-Use often interacts with complex web sockets and non-standard ports, SOCKS5 ensures the proxy doesn't break the connection mid-handshake.

Without this layer, your high-IQ agent will be neutralized by a simple 403 Forbidden error before it even finishes its first "thought."

The Architecture: Building the Autonomous Stack

To build a professional-grade setup, we need a clean integration of the Python-based Browser-Use framework, the Playwright driver, and a SOCKS5 tunnel.

1. The Environment Setup

On your dedicated server (ideally running a clean Ubuntu LTS), the first step is ensuring the browser dependencies don't conflict with the agent's logic.

# Core dependencies for Playwright in a headless environment
sudo npx playwright install-deps
pip install browser-use langchain-openai

2. Injecting the Proxy into the Browser Context

The beauty of Browser-Use is its deep integration with Playwright. You don't need to wrap your entire OS in a proxy; you can inject the SOCKS5 configuration directly into the browser instance the agent is controlling.

from browser_use import Agent
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from playwright.async_api import async_playwright

# Configuration for your SOCKS5 Proxy
PROXY_CONFIG = {
    "server": "socks5://your-proxy-provider.com:1080",
    "username": "your_username",
    "password": "your_password"
}

async def run_secure_agent():
    # We define the browser with the proxy settings
    # This ensures every request the agent makes is tunneled
    async with async_playwright() as p:
        browser = await p.chromium.launch(proxy=PROXY_CONFIG)

        agent = Agent(
            task="Research the latest trends in autonomous AI agents and summarize them in a Notion-ready format.",
            llm=ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o"),
            browser=browser
        )

        result = await agent.run()
        print(result)

3. Handling Persistence and Session States

One of the most powerful features of this setup is the ability to save the "State" of the browser. On dedicated hardware, you can store the storage_state (cookies, local storage), allowing the agent to "wake up" the next day already logged into the services it needs, without re-triggering 2FA alerts.

Framework for Resilience: The "3-Tier" Agent Strategy

When deploying agents on dedicated hardware, I recommend a tiered approach to ensure the system doesn't become a "black box" that fails invisibly.

Tier Component Purpose
Execution Browser-Use + Playwright Translates LLM intent into DOM actions (clicks, types, scrolls).
Network SOCKS5 + Residential IPs Masks the server's data center signature to mimic human traffic.
Observation Telemetry/Logging Captures the "thought process" and screenshots of failures for post-mortem analysis.

Overcoming the "Ghost in the Machine": Common Pitfalls

Even with dedicated hardware and SOCKS5, autonomous agents can fail in unique ways.

  • The Infinite Loop: Sometimes an agent gets stuck clicking a menu that won't open. Insight: Always set a max_steps parameter in Browser-Use. An autonomous agent should be a marathon runner, not a hamster on a wheel.
  • The CAPTCHA Wall: While SOCKS5 reduces the frequency of CAPTCHAs, it doesn't eliminate them. Integration with a third-party solver (like 2Captcha) as a custom tool within the Browser-Use agent is a mandatory "Plan B."
  • The Resource Leak: Headless browsers are notorious for "zombie processes." On your dedicated server, implement a cron job or a process supervisor (like PM2 or systemd) that cleans up orphaned Chromium instances every 24 hours.

Step-by-Step Checklist for Production Deployment

  1. Hardware Provisioning: Select a dedicated server with at least 8GB RAM (Chromium is hungry) and a high-bandwidth network.
  2. Secure Proxy Sourcing: Obtain a SOCKS5 provider that offers residential or mobile IPs. Data center IPs are often flagged by Cloudflare before the page even loads.
  3. Environment Isolation: Use Python virtual environments or Docker containers to isolate the Browser-Use dependencies.
  4. Logging Configuration: Redirect the agent's "thoughts" to a persistent log file. You need to see why it decided to click "Cancel" instead of "Submit."
  5. LLM Selection: Use a model with high reasoning capabilities (like GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet). Smaller models often lose the "thread" of a multi-step web task.
  6. Deployment: Run the agent as a background service. Monitor CPU and memory usage to ensure the browser isn't hanging.

The Ethical and Technical Horizon

As we move toward a web populated by as many agents as humans, the "Dedicated Hardware + SOCKS5" stack becomes the baseline for any serious enterprise. We are moving away from "scraping" and toward "participation."

The real insight here is that autonomy is a function of stability. You cannot have a truly autonomous agent if its connection is being blocked or its host machine is struggling to keep up with the rendering demands of a modern React app. By providing a stable "body" (dedicated hardware) and a stealthy "presence" (SOCKS5), you allow the "brain" (Browser-Use + LLM) to focus on the task at hand.

The question is no longer "Can an AI navigate the web?" We know it can. The question is: "Can you build an environment where it can do so reliably for 1,000 hours without human intervention?"

With this stack, the answer is finally yes.

Final Thought:
The web was built for humans. AI agents are currently "intruders" in that ecosystem. By using tools like Browser-Use with sophisticated network layers, we aren't just bypassing restrictions; we are teaching AI how to be a responsible and efficient citizen of the digital world. The future of work isn't just about writing code—it's about managing the machines that navigate the interfaces we've built.

title: UFORCE levanta 700 millones de dólares para llevar los drones probados en Ucrania a una industria global
description:
— 700 millones a 6.000 millones de valoración: UFORCE, la empresa ucraniana detrás de los drones navales MAGURA, cerró una Serie A coliderada por Valor Equity Partners y el National Wealth Fund del Reino Unido.

— De la guerra a la fábrica global: el dinero va a producción distribuida en Estados Unidos, Europa, Asia-Pacífico y Oriente Medio, con sistemas ya probados en combate.

— El matiz: las cifras de combate (más de una docena de buques destruidos, 300.000 vuelos) las reporta la propia empresa y no están verificadas de forma independiente.

UFORCE, empresa de tecnología de defensa fundada en Ucrania y con sede en Londres, anunció hoy una Serie A de 700 millones de dólares a una valoración de 6.000 millones, según el comunicado oficial. La ronda la colideran Valor Equity Partners y el National Wealth Fund del Reino Unido, con participación del Fondo de Inversión para la Reconstrucción de Estados Unidos y Ucrania.

La empresa construye plataformas autónomas no tripuladas por mar, tierra y aire, además del software de inteligencia artificial y la capa de mando y control que las opera. Su tesis es directa: hacer que la defensa cueste cien veces menos que la ofensiva. Su catálogo incluye la familia MAGURA de buques no tripulados, la familia NEMESIS de plataformas de ataque, la familia LIUT de robots terrestres, la familia PREDATOR de torretas contra drones y el software C2 que lo coordina todo.

Los MAGURA se han convertido en el producto insignia: según la empresa, han contribuido a la destrucción de más de una docena de buques de guerra rusos en el mar Negro y han derribado helicópteros y aviones de combate. Las fuerzas ucranianas los usan además como base marítima móvil para lanzar drones NEMESIS en ataques de largo alcance. Los NEMESIS, por su parte, suman más de 300.000 vuelos de combate y están adoptados por más de 100 unidades. Son cifras de la propia compañía, no verificadas de forma independiente, como advierte DroneLife.

El dinero no va solo a fabricar más unidades, sino a repartir la producción: Estados Unidos, Europa, Asia-Pacífico y Oriente Medio, cerca de los teatros donde se necesitan los sistemas y con capacidad de mantener el suministro aunque continúen los ataques a la infraestructura en Ucrania. En Estados Unidos, UFORCE anunció una alianza con ReconCraft para escalar la fabricación de los MAGURA, y en Reino Unido el National Wealth Fund respalda la expansión de la ingeniería y la manufactura. La empresa también es miembro fundador de la Alianza de Drones UE-Ucrania y trabaja dentro de las redes de la OTAN y la Fuerza Expedicionaria Conjunta.

El fichaje que acompaña a la ronda es el general retirado Christopher G. Cavoli, excomandante supremo aliado en Europa de la OTAN y socio de Valor Equity Partners, que se incorpora al consejo de UFORCE. «Ucrania ha mostrado al mundo lo rápido que puede moverse la innovación en el campo de batalla cuando los ingenieros trabajan codo a codo con quienes dependen de sus sistemas», dijo Cavoli. El director ejecutivo de UFORCE, Oleg Rogynskyy, lo resumió así: «Esta inversión nos ayudará a escalar la producción para Ucrania y a llevar a los aliados soluciones que pueden desplegar, integrar y sostener a la velocidad del combate moderno».

Para América Latina, el caso UFORCE importa por el costo, no por el frente de batalla. Los ejércitos de la región compran casi todos sus sistemas de defensa fuera, y la tesis de plataformas autónomas baratas y probadas en combate cambia la conversación sobre qué se puede permitir un país que no es potencia militar. México, en particular, ya tiene clústeres aeroespaciales y capacidad de manufactura avanzada, en Querétaro y Baja California entre otros, que en Estados Unidos y Europa se están reconvirtiendo para defensa. La pregunta es si la región quiere ser solo compradora de estos sistemas o también parte de su cadena de producción.

Qué NO se cubre: no hay precios por unidad de ninguna plataforma, ni especificaciones técnicas detalladas, ni contratos anunciados con gobiernos concretos, ni una verificación independiente de las cifras de combate que reporta la empresa.

Qué sigue: el arranque de la producción de MAGURA en Estados Unidos con ReconCraft, la expansión de ingeniería en Reino Unido, los próximos pasos de la Alianza de Drones UE-Ucrania y si la valoración de 6.000 millones se sostiene en la siguiente ronda.

title: The Importance of Software Engineering in Web Application Development: The Dangers of Vibe Coding
description:
INTRODUCTION,

Today, web applications are part of our everyday lives. We use them for online shopping, banking, education, communication and many other activities.

But creating a web application is not just about writing code and making it look attractive. It also involves planning, testing, security and maintenance. This is where Software Engineering comes in.

With the introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI), developers can now create applications by simply describing what they want. This is known as Vibe Coding. Although it makes development faster, it also comes with some dangers when people depend on AI without understanding the code.

  1. What is Software Engineering?

Software Engineering is the process of planning, designing, developing, testing and maintaining software to make sure it works properly.

For example, before creating a school management system, a developer should first understand what the school needs, who will use the system and how information will be stored.

This helps reduce mistakes and makes the application easier to manage.

  1. Importance of Software Engineering in Web Applications

Software Engineering is important because it helps developers create applications that users can trust.

Some of its importance includes:

  • Better quality: It helps applications work properly.
  • Security: It protects users' information from hackers.
  • Easy maintenance: It makes it easier to correct errors and add new features.
  • Saves time and money: Proper planning helps prevent costly mistakes.
  • Better user experience: It makes applications easier to use.
  • Future growth: It allows applications to support more users and features.
  1. What is Vibe Coding?

Vibe Coding is a method of developing software by giving instructions to AI tools instead of writing all the code manually.

For example, someone can ask ChatGPT to create a library management system with an admin dashboard, student registration and book management.

The AI can generate the code within a short time.

This is helpful, especially for beginners. However, the problem comes when developers simply copy and paste the generated code without understanding or testing it.

AI can make mistakes, and not every code it generates is safe or correct.

  1. Demerits and Dangers of Vibe Coding

Depending too much on Vibe Coding can cause several problems:

  1. Security problems: AI may generate weak code that allows hackers to access private information.
  2. Poor code quality: The generated code may be confusing and difficult to maintain.
  3. Hidden errors: An application may look good but still have features that do not work properly.
  4. Data loss: Poorly developed applications may expose or lose important information.
  5. Overdependence on AI: Developers may find it difficult to solve problems because they do not understand the code they are using.

  6. Maintenance problems: Adding new features or correcting errors may become difficult.

  7. Dangers of Developing Web Applications Without Software Engineering

Even when developers write code themselves, ignoring Software Engineering can create serious problems.

Some of these problems include:

  • System failure when users need the application.
  • Cyberattacks due to weak security.
  • Financial losses caused by errors or data theft.
  • Loss of users' trust.
  • Poor performance when many people use the application.

For example, a banking application without proper security may allow hackers to access users' accounts or interfere with transactions.

This shows that making an application work is not enough. It must also be properly tested and protected.

  1. How Can We Use AI Properly?

AI is a useful tool, but it should support developers rather than replace their knowledge.

Developers should:

  • Understand the code before using it.
  • Plan their applications properly.
  • Test all important features.
  • Check for security problems.
  • Protect users' private information.
  • Use Git and GitHub to manage their code.

AI should make development easier, but developers must still take responsibility for the applications they create.

Conclusion

Software Engineering plays an important role in web application development. It helps us build applications that are secure, reliable and easy to maintain.

Vibe Coding has made programming faster and easier, but depending on AI without proper understanding can lead to serious problems.

As upcoming software developers, we should learn to use AI while still following the principles of Software Engineering.

Creating an application that works is good, but creating one that is secure, reliable and can be trusted is even better.

References

  1. International Organization for Standardization (ISO). (2026). Systems and Software Engineering – Software Life Cycle Processes (ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207).
    https://www.iso.org/standard/90219.html

  2. Canadian Centre for Cyber Security. (2026). Managing Security Risks in Vibe Coding.
    https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/managing-security-risks-vibe-coding-itsm60043

  3. OWASP Foundation. (2025). OWASP Top 10: Web Application Security Risks.
    https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/

  4. IEEE Computer Society. Software Engineering Body of Knowledge (SWEBOK).
