title: How SteerDistill Shrinks 30‑Billion‑Parameter LLMs to 3 GB Without Losing Accuracy
description:
SteerDistill — How Closed‑Loop Teacher Steering Rescues Quantized LLM Agents

Lead

“Quantizing a 30‑billion‑parameter agent drops its success rate by 20 %—that’s the headline most engineers see.” Yet the arXiv pre‑print released on 10 Nov 2026 flips that narrative. The authors demonstrate a closed‑loop teacher‑steering pipeline that squeezes a 4‑bit LLM agent down to a 3‑GB footprint while keeping task success within four percentage points of the full‑precision baseline.

The paper, titled “SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed‑Loop Teacher Steering,” arrives just as the industry grapples with the cost explosion of deploying autonomous language agents at scale. If you run a SaaS chatbot, a code‑generation service, or a robot that talks to the world, you already feel the pinch of FP16 inference latency and memory consumption. SteerDistill promises to shrink those pain points without handing you a black‑box that behaves unpredictably.

Below I unpack the method, walk through a concrete debugging scenario, lay out the hard numbers, flag the remaining risks, and sketch where the technique heads next.

The Case Study: Debugging a Quantized Shopping Assistant

Imagine you built a WebShop agent on top of Llama‑2‑70B. In production you quantize the model to 4 bit using GPTQ to fit a single A100 GPU. After rollout you notice the bot starts adding the wrong item to the cart when the user mentions “blue” and “size M” together.

Step 1 – Isolate the Drift

You instrument the agent to log state‑transition tuples: (observation, hidden‑state, action) at each turn. Comparing logs from the quantized bot to the full‑precision teacher reveals a distribution shift: the hidden‑state vectors diverge after the third turn, especially when the observation contains color adjectives.

Step 2 – Deploy the Closed‑Loop Loop

SteerDistill injects a lightweight steering adapter (≈ 0.6 % of the base parameters) on top of the quantized model. The system runs a short rollout of the quantized bot in the same shopping environment, then asks the teacher to generate the ideal next‑step distribution for the exact same observation.

The pipeline computes a behavioral error signal in the space of state‑transition probabilities, not merely token‑level cross‑entropy. It feeds that error into the adapter, which learns a corrective linear map that nudges the quantized hidden state back toward the teacher’s trajectory.

Step 3 – Verify the Fix

After a few hundred online rollouts, the hidden‑state drift disappears. The agent now picks the correct “blue size M” variant 93 % of the time—only a 2‑point gap from the FP16 teacher. Crucially, you achieved this without retraining the entire 70‑B model or collecting a new dataset of shopping dialogs.

This micro‑debug illustrates SteerDistill’s core advantage: it treats quantization error as a runtime symptom and repairs it on the fly, rather than relying on a one‑shot offline distillation that often leaves hidden‑state bugs hidden.

The Meat: Hard Numbers from the Paper

Metric Full‑Precision (FP16/FP32) SteerDistill‑Quantized (4‑bit) Relative Change
Inference latency per step 12 ms 5 ms ‑58 %
GPU memory footprint (30 B model) 14 GB 3 GB ‑78 %
Task‑success rate (WebShop, MiniWoB) 92 % 88 % ‑4 %
Failure‑type reduction (environment‑condition mismatches) — 73 % fewer —
Adapter size — ≈ 0.6 % of base parameters —

“SteerDistill cuts inference latency by more than half while shrinking memory use by three‑quarters, and it slashes environment‑condition failures by 73 %.” – authors, arXiv 2611.13410

How the Numbers Add Up

  1. Closed‑Loop Error Measurement – The authors compute a Kullback‑Leibler divergence between the student’s and teacher’s state‑transition distributions after each rollout step. This metric captures both token‑level and hidden‑state drift, giving the adapter a richer learning signal than standard token‑loss.

  2. Adaptive Correction Adapter – The adapter consists of a low‑rank linear projection followed by a small MLP (two layers, 64 hidden units). Because it updates online, the system needs only a handful of gradient steps per failure case.

  3. Data Efficiency – Traditional imitation‑learning distillation consumes millions of expert trajectories. SteerDistill queries the teacher only on failure contexts, reducing required offline data by a factor of five.

  4. Quantizer Agnosticism – The authors plug the pipeline into three popular quantizers—bitsandbytes (8‑bit/4‑bit), GPTQ, and AWQ. All experiments show similar latency gains, proving the method does not hinge on a particular quantization algorithm.

The Pivot: Risks and Open Questions

Risk Why It Matters Mitigation
Residual performance gap (≈ 4 % task‑success loss) High‑stakes applications (medical advice, finance) cannot tolerate any drop. Combine SteerDistill with a fallback to the full‑precision teacher on critical queries; fine‑tune the adapter on a small task‑specific dataset.
Adapter overfitting to specific environments The steering head learns corrections that only work on the training rollout distribution. Periodically re‑sample diverse environments; employ domain randomization during the closed‑loop phase.
Teacher query cost Each corrective step requires the teacher to run a forward pass, which can double compute for the debugging window. Cache teacher hidden states for repeated observations; limit teacher calls to a budgeted number per hour.
Compatibility with non‑transformer agents Some LLM agents integrate external tools (e.g., tool‑use APIs) that produce non‑textual signals. Extend the state‑transition representation to include tool‑call embeddings; early experiments with Brain‑Grounded Axes show promising results.
Security of the steering loop An attacker could manipulate observations to force the adapter into a harmful correction. Harden the error‑signal pipeline with robust statistics (median‑based divergence) and monitor for outlier spikes.

The authors acknowledge these concerns in the discussion section and release a “risk‑assessment checklist” with the HF repo. Practitioners who treat SteerDistill as a plug‑and‑play solution without this due diligence risk deploying agents that behave unpredictably under distribution shift.

Outlook: From Research Demo to Production‑Ready Stack

Early Industry Adoption

  • Microsoft Azure AI rolled out “SteerDistill‑optimized LLM‑Agent images” on 15 Jan 2027, advertising ≤ $0.008 per 1 k token pricing for serverless agents.
  • Meta AI Research reported a 30 % cost reduction on internal recommendation‑policy simulations after quantizing 30 B agents to 3 bit with SteerDistill.
  • OpenAI added a steer-distill flag to its function‑calling agents, letting developers opt into the low‑cost pathway on custom hardware.

These moves indicate that the technique has cleared the proof‑of‑concept barrier and entered the productization phase.

What Comes Next

  1. Edge Deployment – With a 3‑GB memory footprint, 4‑bit agents equipped with a 0.6 % adapter can run on NVIDIA Jetson or even high‑end smartphones. Expect a wave of on‑device assistants that no longer rely on constant cloud calls.

  2. Multi‑Teacher Steering – Researchers are already experimenting with ensemble teachers to cover diverse domains (e.g., code, dialogue, robotics). The closed‑loop loop can aggregate error signals from several teachers, potentially shrinking the residual performance gap further.

  3. Standardization – The Hugging Face model hub now tags “SteerDistill‑compatible” models. A community‑driven ONNX‑compatible export will let hardware vendors bake the steering adapter directly into inference runtimes.

  4. Regulatory Audits – As LLM agents infiltrate regulated sectors, auditors will demand evidence that quantization does not introduce hidden bias. The closed‑loop telemetry that SteerDistill already records (state‑transition divergences, correction magnitudes) provides a natural audit trail.

Bottom Line

SteerDistill does not rewrite the rules of LLM scaling, but it rebalances the equation between cost and capability. By turning quantization error into a controllable, observable signal, the method lets engineers debug, adapt, and ship agents that were previously locked behind prohibitive hardware budgets.

If your organization already quantizes models for inference, you can plug in a steering adapter in two weeks using the Hugging Face reference implementation. Expect latency cuts of 50‑60 % and memory savings of 70‑80 %, while paying a modest price in task‑success accuracy that you can recover with targeted fine‑tuning or fallback logic.

The next generation of autonomous assistants will likely run on a tiny quantized core plus a smart steering layer that constantly checks its own behavior against a full‑precision oracle. SteerDistill provides the first, publicly available blueprint for that architecture.

Prepared by a senior tech columnist, based on the arXiv pre‑print 2611.13410 and accompanying industry announcements.

title: Beyond Writing Code: Why Software Engineering Still Matters in Web Application Development
description:
Introduction
The way we build software is changing rapidly. Today, with the introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, almost anyone can create a website or a web application without necessarily having strong programming knowledge.

Tools powered by AI can generate HTML, CSS, JavaScript and even complete application structures within minutes. What once required hours or days of coding can now be achieved by simply describing what you want to build.

This development is exciting, especially for beginners and people who are just getting into programming. However, it also raises an important question: Does being able to generate an application mean that we know how to build good software?

This is where software engineering becomes important.

Software engineering is not simply about writing code that works. It involves planning, designing, developing, testing, maintaining and improving software systems to ensure that they are reliable, secure, efficient and capable of meeting users' needs.

As web applications become part of everyday activities, from online banking and education to shopping and communication, the need to build them properly cannot be ignored.

Understanding the Role of Software Engineering in Web Applications

A web application is more than just a collection of web pages. It is a system that allows users to interact with information, perform activities and access services through a web browser.

Examples include online banking platforms, student portals, hospital management systems, e-commerce websites and employee management systems.

Behind these applications are several components that must work together, including the user interface, server-side logic, databases, authentication systems and security mechanisms.

Software engineering provides the principles and methods needed to bring these components together.

For instance, imagine developing an employee management system for an organization. The system may need to store employee information, manage attendance, calculate salaries and control access to confidential records.

Simply writing code to make these functions work is not enough. The developer must first understand the organization's requirements, plan the system's structure, design the database, consider security and test the different functionalities.

Without proper planning, the application may work initially but become difficult to maintain or develop further.

This is why software engineering is essential. It helps developers move beyond creating applications that merely work to building systems that can be trusted.

Why Software Engineering Practices Matter

There are several reasons why software engineering remains relevant in web application development.

1. Proper planning and requirement analysis

Before developing a web application, developers need to understand what users actually expect from the system.

Requirement analysis helps identify the features, limitations and expectations of the application.

Without this stage, developers may spend time building features that users do not need while ignoring important functionalities.

2. Better security

Security is one of the most important aspects of web application development.

Applications that handle personal information, passwords, financial records or organizational data must be properly protected.

Software engineering encourages developers to consider security during the development process rather than treating it as something to fix after deployment.

3. Easier maintenance

Web applications are rarely completed once and forgotten. They require updates, bug fixes, improvements and sometimes entirely new features.

Well-structured code, proper documentation and modular design make it easier for developers to understand and modify an application.

4. Reliability and quality assurance

An application should not only work under normal conditions. It should also handle unexpected situations appropriately.

Testing helps developers identify errors before users encounter them.

For example, a payment application should be tested to ensure that users are not charged twice when a transaction fails or that sensitive information is not exposed.

5. Scalability

As an organization grows, the number of people using its web application may increase.

A properly engineered system is easier to improve and expand to accommodate additional users and functionalities.

These practices make software engineering an important part of producing dependable web applications.

The Rise of Vibe Coding

One development that has attracted considerable attention in software development is something known as vibe coding.

Vibe coding refers to an approach to programming where a person uses natural-language instructions to tell an AI tool what to build, allowing the tool to generate much of the code.

Instead of manually writing every line, the developer describes the desired outcome, reviews the generated application and continues giving instructions until the result looks right.

For example, someone could tell an AI tool:

"Build an employee management system with a login page, an employee registration form, an attendance dashboard and a database."

The AI tool may generate much of the application without the user having to write every component manually.

Tools such as ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot and other AI-powered development assistants have made this approach increasingly accessible.

There is nothing inherently wrong with using AI to assist software development. In fact, it can improve productivity and help developers learn new concepts.

The problem begins when developers rely entirely on generated code without understanding, reviewing or testing what they are building.

The Disadvantages and Dangers of Vibe Coding

Although vibe coding makes software development easier to approach, it comes with several risks.

1. Security vulnerabilities

AI-generated code can contain security weaknesses. A developer who does not understand the generated code may unknowingly introduce vulnerabilities into an application.

For example, an application might store passwords incorrectly, expose sensitive database information or fail to protect restricted pages from unauthorized access.

If such an application is deployed, attackers may exploit these weaknesses.

2. Lack of understanding of the code

One major problem with vibe coding is that people can produce applications without understanding how the applications actually work.

A developer may generate hundreds of lines of code and successfully run the application without knowing what happens behind the scenes.

This becomes a serious problem when something breaks. If the developer cannot understand the code, identifying and correcting the problem becomes difficult.

3. Poor code quality

AI-generated code is not always well-organized.

It may contain unnecessary functions, duplicated code, poor naming conventions or complicated structures.

Although the application might work initially, these problems can make future modifications difficult.

4. Hidden bugs and unreliable functionality

An application looking good on the screen does not necessarily mean that all its functions work correctly.

For example, an AI-generated employee management system might display a registration form successfully but fail to save certain employee records correctly.

Without proper testing, such errors may remain unnoticed until real users begin using the application.

5. Overdependence on AI

Another concern is that excessive dependence on AI can weaken a developer's problem-solving and programming abilities.

Programming requires logical thinking, debugging and understanding how different components interact.

If beginners depend on AI to solve every problem, they may struggle when faced with situations where AI-generated solutions are incorrect or unsuitable.

6. Difficulty maintaining and expanding applications

When an application is generated without proper architectural planning, adding new features can become complicated.

A developer might discover that introducing one small change affects several unrelated parts of the application.

This can lead to more errors and increased maintenance costs.

What Happens When Web Applications Are Developed Without Software Engineering?

The dangers are not limited to vibe coding. Even when developers write every line of code themselves, ignoring software engineering practices can create serious problems.

Consider an organization that decides to develop its own employee management system.

The developers immediately begin coding without interviewing the intended users, documenting requirements or designing the database.

They create a login page, employee registration form and dashboard. Everything appears to work, so the application is deployed.

However, several problems eventually emerge.

Employees discover that their personal information can be accessed by unauthorized users. Some records are duplicated. The attendance system produces incorrect results, and adding new features becomes increasingly difficult.

These problems could have been reduced through proper software engineering practices.

Developing software without requirement analysis can produce the wrong system.

Ignoring security can expose confidential information.

Failing to test can allow serious errors to reach users.

Poor documentation can make it difficult for another developer to understand the application.

Neglecting maintenance can cause the application to become unreliable as technology and organizational needs change.

In some cases, these failures can result in financial losses, reputational damage and legal consequences.

This demonstrates that software development is not just about making something functional. It is also about taking responsibility for the system being created and the people who will depend on it.

Can Software Engineering and AI Work Together?

Absolutely.

The purpose of software engineering is not to prevent developers from using modern tools. Instead, it provides a structured way of using those tools responsibly.

AI can assist with writing code, explaining programming concepts, generating test cases, identifying possible errors and improving productivity.

However, developers must remain responsible for the decisions being made.

A better approach is to combine AI-assisted development with established software engineering practices.

For example:

  • Understand and document the requirements before generating code.
  • Design the application's structure before implementation.
  • Review AI-generated code instead of blindly accepting it.
  • Test individual components and the entire application.
  • Apply proper security practices.
  • Use version control to track changes.
  • Document important parts of the system.
  • Maintain and update the application when necessary.

This approach allows developers to enjoy the benefits of AI without sacrificing software quality.

AI should assist the developer, not replace the developer's responsibility to understand and verify the software being built.

Conclusion

The emergence of AI-powered development tools has changed how people approach programming. Building a web application is becoming easier, faster and more accessible than ever before.

However, accessibility should not be confused with expertise.

Being able to generate an application does not automatically mean that the application is secure, reliable or properly designed.

Software engineering remains relevant because it provides the foundation for building systems that can be trusted, maintained and improved over time.

Vibe coding can be a useful tool, particularly for experimentation, learning and rapid prototyping. However, using it without understanding the generated code or applying proper testing and security practices can expose users and organizations to serious risks.

Ultimately, the goal of a software developer should not simply be to create an application that works today. It should be to create an application that continues to work reliably, securely and efficiently tomorrow.

AI can help us write code faster, but software engineering helps us build software properly.

title: Google Expands Gemini Across Sheets, Search and Developer Tools With Staggered Rollouts
description:
Google is expanding Gemini across consumer, Workspace and developer surfaces, but this is not one uniform launch. The most concrete updates include Gemini in Google Sheets on Android for eligible Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, public Gemini API access through Google AI Studio, and Gemini coding assistance in Android Studio. Google Search's AI Mode and Gemini app capabilities are also continuing to evolve through separate releases and availability rules.

For businesses, the practical takeaway is straightforward: Gemini is becoming easier to encounter in everyday Google products and easier to build with, but teams need to check the specific product, subscription tier, device and usage limits that apply to their intended workflow. A feature available in one Gemini interface does not automatically mean the same capability, quota or audience is available elsewhere.

What Google has expanded, and where access differs

The clearest Workspace change is Gemini in Google Sheets on Android. Google says the mobile feature began rolling out on September 9, 2026, and is available to eligible Google AI Pro and Google AI Ultra subscribers. According to Google's official Sheets on Android announcement, the capability is designed to help users analyze data and surface insights from a phone or tablet. Google also notes that more complex spreadsheet edits remain better suited to Sheets on the web.

That distinction matters for teams hoping to replace desktop spreadsheet work with mobile AI assistance. Gemini in Sheets on Android can support faster review and analysis away from a desk, while the web version remains the appropriate place for detailed editing work. It is an extension of the spreadsheet workflow, not evidence that mobile and web editing are now equivalent.

Developer access follows a different path. The Gemini API is publicly available through Google AI Studio, where developers can create and manage API keys, associate keys with projects, and work within documented rate limits. This gives companies a route to test Gemini in their own applications, internal tools or automated processes instead of relying only on the Gemini app or Workspace interface.

Gemini is also available in Android Studio as AI-powered coding assistance. Google documents API-key-based access and notes that access, token usage and quotas can depend on the relevant tier. For Android development teams, that makes Gemini part of the development environment rather than solely a standalone chatbot.

Gemini surface Confirmed availability or access Practical use
Google Sheets on Android Eligible Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, rollout beginning September 9, 2026 Data analysis and insights on Android devices
Google AI Studio and Gemini API Public developer access with API keys, project association and documented rate limits Building Gemini-powered applications and integrations
Android Studio Gemini coding assistance with API-key access and tier-related token and quota considerations AI assistance during Android software development
Google Search AI Mode Available since late 2025, with continuing updates and tiered access in some markets Gemini-powered search experiences

Search and app updates should not be treated as a single entitlement

Gemini in Google Search has been available through AI Mode since late 2025, with Google continuing to update model routing, AI Overviews and the interface. Some Pro and Ultra access has been offered in the United States, while broader availability has been planned. That makes broad statements about availability difficult to apply universally without checking the user's region and product tier.

Google's later Gemini release notes also describe Gemini 4 Argon, released globally to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers on October 13, 2026. The update included new capabilities, Antigravity coding in the macOS Gemini app, and connectivity to more than 40 apps. These releases reinforce the wider direction: Gemini capabilities are spreading across Google's products, but they are introduced through product-specific schedules and plan requirements.

What to check before building with the Gemini API

The API can be useful for a focused business task, such as adding AI assistance to an existing application or prototyping a workflow. However, a successful test starts with the operational details rather than a broad assumption that every Gemini feature is available through the API.

Before committing engineering time, teams should verify:

  • The intended product surface, such as Google AI Studio, Android Studio, Sheets or Search.
  • The applicable plan and region, particularly where Pro or Ultra access is specified.
  • API-key and project setup requirements in Google AI Studio.
  • Rate limits and quota rules for the expected volume of requests.
  • Whether the task requires complex spreadsheet editing, which Google says is better handled in Sheets on the web.

This product-by-product approach also helps avoid a common implementation mistake: treating a consumer-facing Gemini capability as though it were automatically an API feature, or assuming an API integration carries the same limits as a subscription feature. Google documents these access paths separately, so the relevant documentation should guide the technical design and rollout plan.

For companies already using Google Workspace, the Android Sheets update provides a more immediate, low-friction way to evaluate where AI-generated analysis is useful. For software teams, AI Studio and Android Studio create a separate opportunity to test Gemini in products and coding workflows. The right starting point depends on whether the goal is improving an existing Google workflow or building a tailored capability.

Google's expanding Gemini footprint makes it more important to turn isolated AI experiments into dependable processes. Scalevise can help assess suitable use cases, map the required systems and plan practical AI implementation for business workflows without assuming that every new product feature fits your operation. This helps teams focus on work that can save time or reduce manual effort while accounting for access conditions, quotas and integration needs. Request an AI implementation consultation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who can use Gemini in Google Sheets on Android?

Gemini in Google Sheets on Android is available to eligible Google AI Pro and Google AI Ultra subscribers. Google says the rollout began on September 9, 2026.

Can developers access the Gemini API publicly?

Yes. Google provides public Gemini API access through Google AI Studio, including API-key management, project association and documentation for rate limits.

Does Gemini in Google Search have the same availability as Gemini in Sheets?

No. Google Search AI Mode and Gemini in Sheets follow separate rollout and access rules. Search availability has continued to expand, with some tiered access and regional differences.

What should a team review before using the Gemini API?

Teams should review the relevant API-key setup, project requirements, rate limits, quotas, product documentation and the access conditions for the Gemini capability they intend to use.

Conclusion

Google's Gemini expansion connects more of its consumer, Workspace and developer products, from mobile spreadsheet analysis to API-based development. The opportunity is real, but access is staggered rather than universal. Businesses will get better results by matching a defined use case to the appropriate Gemini surface, then confirming the plan, region, quota and workflow constraints before scaling it.

title: One Vue app, built by AI three times: no skill, vuejs-ai/skills, and vue-enterprise
description:
A few weeks ago I published vue-enterprise, an Agent Skill that teaches Claude Code and GitHub Copilot how I want Vue 3 + TypeScript code written in large, long-lived apps. People asked a fair question: does a skill change anything, now that models write decent Vue on their own?

So I measured it. One app, built by an AI agent with no skill, with the community vuejs-ai/skills, and with vue-enterprise. Two runs each, six apps in total.

I wrote one of the three skills, so I built the test to keep my hands off the result. The details are below, and everything (prompts, harness, the six apps, the reviews) is public, so you can check my work.

The app

A small support desk on top of a fake REST API I wrote for the test:

  • login, with every other page behind a route guard that sends you back where you wanted to go
  • a ticket list with text search, a status filter and pagination
  • a ticket detail page with comments and a comment form
  • create and edit forms, with client-side validation and the API's 422 errors shown next to the fields
  • a "Close ticket" button that updates the UI immediately and rolls back if the request fails

That fits in one agent session, yet it touches everything that separates a demo from a production app: server data, forms, routing, where state lives, tests and security.

Each build had two rounds. Round 1 was the prompt above. Round 2, in a fresh session, was a change request: add an assignee filter, and put search, filters and page in the URL so they survive a reload and work with Back and Forward. How the code takes a change matters as much as how it looks on day one.

Keeping it fair

  • Same everything. Every run started from the same create-vue scaffold (TypeScript, Router, Pinia, Vitest, Playwright, ESLint) with the same fake API, the same prompt, the same model and the same Claude Code version, headless. Nobody touched the code between rounds.
  • Clean environment. No user settings, plugins or other skills leaked in. The only difference between the arms was the contents of .claude/skills (plus, for vue-enterprise, the always-on rules file its README tells you to install).
  • Same nudge. Every prompt ended with "Use any Vue skills available in this project". The vuejs-ai README recommends saying that, so I gave it to all three arms.
  • Blind review. A stronger model reviewed the six apps without knowing which was which. It saw "app-K", "app-P" and so on, with a 12-point rubric. I ran the review twice with shuffled names to check that the scores held.
  • Black-box tests. I wrote Playwright scripts that use the apps the way a person would, without looking at their code.

The twist: all six apps work

I expected the no-skill apps to break somewhere. They didn't.

No skill vuejs-ai/skills vue-enterprise
type-check, lint, unit tests ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓
20 feature checks in a real browser 20/20, 20/20 20/20, 20/20 20/20, 20/20
8 harder checks (stale data, race conditions, expired session, open redirect, 404, double submit) 7/8, 8/8 8/8, 8/8 8/8, 8/8

Two runs per arm, so two results in each cell. Today's models write working Vue. If your bar is "does it run and pass the tests it wrote", you may not need a skill at all.

The differences show up in the code.

What the code review found

The blind reviewer scored each app out of 60. Here are the averages of the two reviews:

No skill vuejs-ai/skills vue-enterprise
Run 1 38 38.5 55
Run 2 29 44.5 57
Average 33.5 41.5 56

The two reviews never differed by more than four points on any app, and both put the same arm first.

In both reviews the two vue-enterprise apps came first and second, and the second no-skill app came last. vuejs-ai/skills landed in the middle, closer to "no skill" on structure and server data, but clearly better on details such as composables that take MaybeRefOrGetter and cleaning up after themselves.

Three differences explain most of the gap.

1. Server data: a cache, or an object you edit by hand

The no-skill and vuejs-ai apps fetch in each page and keep the result in a ref. To close a ticket optimistically, they flip one field on that object:

// no skill, run 2: src/lib/optimistic.ts
return optimistic(
  () => { ticket.status = 'closed' },
  () => { ticket.status = previous },
  () => update(ticket.id, { status: 'closed' }),
)

It works on the page you're looking at. Every other copy of that ticket (another list page, the list you came from) knows nothing about it until something refetches. In my browser test, a ticket closed while the "Open" filter was on stayed in the "Open" list (marked Closed) in all four apps without vue-enterprise. In the vue-enterprise apps it dropped out of the list.

Both vue-enterprise apps installed Pinia Colada, because the skill says server data is a cache, not state. The close becomes one mutation that updates every cached copy, rolls back only if nothing newer has replaced the optimistic value, and then invalidates so filtered lists correct themselves:

// vue-enterprise, run 2: src/features/tickets/useCloseTicket.ts
return useMutation({
  mutation: (ticket: Ticket) => api.updateTicket(ticket.id, { status: 'closed' }),
  onMutate(ticket) {
    queryCache.cancelQueries({ key: TICKET_KEYS.root })
    // ...set the detail entry and every cached list page to "closed"
  },
  onError(_error, ticket) {
    // ...restore, but only where the cache still holds the optimistic value
  },
  onSettled: () => queryCache.invalidateQueries({ key: TICKET_KEYS.root }),
})

Every request also gets an AbortSignal, so a slow, outdated search can't overwrite a newer one. (To be fair, the other apps guarded against that too, with a request counter. They just never cancel the request.)

2. One real bug, in both apps without a skill

Both no-skill apps serve "New ticket" and "Edit ticket" from the same component, which loads its data once, on mount:

// no skill, run 2: src/views/TicketFormView.vue
const isEdit = computed(() => !!props.id)
// ...
onMounted(load) // nothing watches props.id

Vue Router reuses the component when you go from /tickets/5/edit to /tickets/new. So if you click "New ticket" in the header while editing ticket 5, the "new" form opens filled in with ticket 5, and Save creates a duplicate. The reviewer spotted it in the code. My browser test confirmed it in both apps.

The vue-enterprise apps used separate create and edit pages around a presentational TicketForm (props in, typed events out), with the edit data coming from a query keyed on the route id. You can't hit that bug with that structure.

3. Accessibility and security nobody asked for

The prompt said nothing about accessibility. The vue-enterprise apps still tied every error to its input with aria-invalid and aria-describedby, gave each "Close ticket" button a label that names the ticket, and one moved focus to the first invalid field. One no-skill app has no aria-invalid anywhere, and its validation errors are plain <span>s a screen reader never announces.

On security, every app blocked the open-redirect trick I tried (/login?redirect=//evil.example), which surprised me. Only the vue-enterprise apps kept the token out of localStorage, which has a cost I come back to below.

Where my skill loses

This part matters more than the scores.

  • It costs more. The vue-enterprise runs took about 60% longer (about 4.9 minutes for round 1, against about 3 minutes) and cost about 45% more in tokens (about $1.18 per app at API prices, against $0.80 to $0.84). The agent reads reference files before writing, and writes more code: about 1,330 lines against 850 for no skill.
  • A reload logs you out. Both vue-enterprise apps kept the login token in memory, not in localStorage, because the skill says tokens don't belong in web storage. With this fake API (a bearer token, no cookie session, no refresh token) that means every reload sends you back to the login page. The redirect brings you back to the same URL with your filters, but a user would notice. The skill's real answer is a cookie session or a backend-for-frontend; my fake API didn't offer either, so the agent picked the safe option over the convenient one. In a real project you'd make that call yourself.
  • It doesn't make things pretty. The skill is about architecture, not design. Both vue-enterprise apps (and one vuejs-ai app) kept the scaffold's green link colour, which fails WCAG contrast; the no-skill apps happened to replace it.
  • Small sample. Two runs per arm, one app, one model, one tool. The gap between arms was much larger than the gap between runs of the same arm, but that's not a study. And an AI reviewer, even a blind one, is not a senior engineer's review. I checked its main findings with browser tests and they held, with one exception: it reported a double-submit bug that my test couldn't reproduce.

What I take from it

The model is no longer the bottleneck for "make it work". What a skill adds is the decisions an experienced team would make: where server data lives, how pages and components split, what a form must do for a screen reader, what you never put in localStorage. Without it, the agent makes reasonable local choices, and they add up to an app that works today and is harder to change tomorrow.

The change request showed that. All six apps got the URL filters working. The vue-enterprise apps did it with a tested parseListQuery and back/forward tests, touching only the list, the API layer and the tests. In one vuejs-ai app, the reviewer found a Back-button trap introduced along the way.

If you build long-lived Vue apps with AI, try it: github.com/AlinGhitu/vue-enterprise-skill. If you think the test was unfair, the prompts, the harness, all six apps, the agent transcripts and both reviews are here: evals/comparison-2026-11. Run it with your own skill and tell me what you get.

Originally published on ghitu.com.

title: Implementing Deadline-Delayed Renewal Reminders: Idempotency for Duplicate Queue Retries
description:
A renewal reminder for a subscription box can't go out whenever a worker happens to pick it up. Merchant policy puts it between 72 and 24 hours before the card is charged, consumer-protection rules in several jurisdictions put their own floor under that window, and the whole point of the notice is that the user still has time to cancel. So the job sits somewhere for days — and every day it sits is another chance for a queue retry, a redeploy, or an operator replaying a backlog to send the same message twice. Use a durable claim ledger keyed on the business fact, written before the send and committed after it, and treat the broker's delivery guarantee as at-least-once rather than as your deduplication layer.

That ledger becomes the only component allowed to answer "did this notice already go out?"

Examples here are Python. A Node.js worker needs the same three steps in the same order — pg instead of psycopg, node:crypto instead of hmac — because the ordering, not the language, is what keeps duplicate processing out of the customer's inbox.

What makes a delayed reminder queue send the same message twice after a retry?

Three different mechanisms produce the same symptom, and they need different answers.

The first is plain at-least-once redelivery. The worker renders the reminder, hands it to the mail provider, and dies before it acknowledges the message; the broker has no way to know how far the handler got, so it redelivers. Managed queues say this out loud — Pub/Sub documents at-least-once as its default delivery semantic — and any system built on visibility timeouts behaves the same way.

The second is subtler and it's the one that burns people: the visibility timeout expires while the send is still in flight. A slow TLS handshake with the SMTP relay, a provider throttling you to a few hundred messages a second, one retry on a 4xx — thirty seconds gone, ack deadline blown, and the broker hands the identical message to a second worker while the first is still talking to the provider. Both workers believe they are the first. Any dedupe check that lives in worker memory loses here, because the two workers don't share memory.

The third source isn't the queue at all. It's recovery. The scheduler gets paused for a database failover, the backlog builds, and someone re-enqueues everything due between 09:00 and 15:00 to catch up. Nothing in the broker remembers which of those notices already went out before the pause.

Broker-native deduplication doesn't reach any of this. A FIFO deduplication ID covers a five-minute window; a renewal reminder is enqueued up to 30 days before its deadline. The window closed weeks before the duplicate happened.

Deriving the idempotency key from the business fact

The identity of a reminder is a business tuple: this subscription, this billing period, this kind of notice. Not the message id the broker assigned, not the attempt number, not scheduled_for, and definitely not the worker hostname. Anything that changes when the job is replayed mints a fresh key and quietly re-enables the duplicate you were trying to stop.

I use a keyed digest rather than a bare hash — HMAC-SHA256 as described in RFC 2104 — mostly because the key ends up in places I don't fully control: log aggregators, the Message-ID header, provider metadata fields. A keyed digest keeps raw subscription identifiers out of those places. If your ledger never leaves your own database, a plain SHA-256 over the same tuple is fine and I wouldn't argue with it.

import hashlib
import hmac
import os

NOTICE_SECRET = os.environ["NOTICE_KEY_SECRET"].encode()


def notice_key(subscription_id: str, period_start: str, kind: str, revision: int = 0) -> str:
    """Stable identity for one user-facing notice.

    Business identity only. No broker message id, no attempt counter, no send
    timestamp: a replay days later must derive exactly the same key.
    """
    material = "|".join([subscription_id, period_start, kind, str(revision)])
    return hmac.new(NOTICE_SECRET, material.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()


notice_key("sub_8812", "2026-10-01", "renewal_notice_t72")

The revision field is there for the case that trips up most ledgers built without one. A customer downgrades the plan, the renewal amount changes, and the merchant decides a corrected notice has to go out before the same deadline. That is a different notice, not a retry, so it bumps to revision=1 and gets sent on purpose. Keep that decision in the producer, where someone can reason about it, and let the worker stay dumb.

Claim, send, commit — and the window where the worker dies

The order is not negotiable: claim the key and commit that claim, send, commit the result, then ack the broker. Each step exists because of a specific crash position.

CLAIM = """
insert into notice_ledger (notice_key, subscription_id, kind, state, claimed_at)
values (%s, %s, %s, 'claimed', now())
on conflict (notice_key) do nothing
returning notice_key
"""


def deliver(conn, job) -> str:
    key = notice_key(job["subscription_id"], job["period_start"], job["kind"])

    claimed = conn.execute(CLAIM, (key, job["subscription_id"], job["kind"])).fetchone()
    conn.commit()                       # durable before anything leaves the process
    if claimed is None:
        return "suppressed"             # another attempt owns it; ack and move on

    receipt = send_notice(
        to=job["email"],
        body=render(job),
        message_id=f"<{key[:32]}@notices.example.com>",
    )
    conn.execute(
        "update notice_ledger set state = 'sent', provider_id = %s, sent_at = now()"
        " where notice_key = %s",
        (receipt.provider_id, key),
    )
    conn.commit()
    return "sent"

Crash between the claim and the send and the row sits at claimed forever while the customer gets nothing. Crash between the send and the update and the row also sits at claimed — except this time the mail is already in flight. Those two states are indistinguishable from inside the worker, which is exactly why a stale claim must never be released automatically. An auto-release sweeper is a duplicate generator with a cron schedule.

Send them to a quarantine view instead and reconcile against the provider's event stream.

select notice_key, subscription_id, claimed_at
from notice_ledger
where state = 'claimed'
  and claimed_at < now() - interval '15 minutes'
order by claimed_at
limit 500;

Setting your own Message-ID is what makes that reconciliation cheap. Delivery, bounce and complaint webhooks echo it back, so a quarantined claim can be resolved against what the provider actually accepted instead of a guess. The quarantine stays small in practice, since it only fills from crashes inside a window of a few seconds, and clearing it is a lookup rather than a judgement call.

Never ack the queue message before the ledger commit. Ack-first loses notices; commit-first duplicates them, and duplicates are what the ledger absorbs.

Where the dedupe check lives Survives a multi-day delay Survives an operator replay Cost on the send path
Broker deduplication ID No — the window is minutes No Free, already in the queue
In-process cache No No Nanoseconds, lost on restart
Shared cache claim with TTL Only if the TTL outlives delay plus retries While the key is alive One round trip
Durable ledger row Yes Yes A write plus a commit

Replaying a backlog without re-sending yesterday's reminders

Treat a replay as an ordinary producer. It re-enqueues jobs, the ledger refuses the ones that already happened, and the operator never has to compute a safe time range by hand — which they will get wrong at 02:00 during an incident.

Before running it for real, count what it would mint: select the derived keys against the ledger and report how many are new. If a six-hour replay finds 4 unknown keys out of 900, the backlog was already delivered and the safest action is to stop.

Two things make replays go sideways even with a correct ledger. The first is throughput: 40,000 reminders released in one burst hits per-domain rate limits, and receiving mail systems read a sudden identical-content spike as exactly what it looks like. Push replay traffic through the same per-domain token bucket as normal sends and expect the pipeline, not the ledger, to be the bottleneck. The second is embedded credentials — if the reminder carries a one-time code or a signed cancellation link, a suppressed duplicate is correct behaviour, but a deliberate resend has to reuse the stored code. Mint a new one and the first message stops working, which produces a support ticket that is much harder to explain than a duplicate.

Put the replay batch id in logs and metrics. Never in the key.

Rolling this out on a live reminder pipeline

Run it in shadow first. Write claims, log the ones that would have been suppressed, enforce nothing, and let it ride through one full renewal cycle so that monthly and annual plans both pass through it. The suppression rate you observe is your real duplicate rate, and it's usually higher than the bug reports suggest, because customers silently ignore a second reminder more often than they complain about it. Backfill keys for notices already in flight before you flip enforcement on, otherwise the first enforced run treats every pending job as new.

Four metrics are enough: claims minted, duplicates suppressed, claims in quarantine, and the p99 gap between claim and commit. Alert on the quarantine count crossing zero and on that gap growing, since a widening gap means the crash window is getting wider too.

The catch is that every send now costs a durable write plus a commit before the network call, and that write is on the critical path. If the notice is harmless to repeat — an internal webhook, a metrics ping, a cache warm — stick with the broker's at-least-once guarantee and skip all of this. At millions of sends an hour, a shared cache claim with a TTL longer than the full delay window is the pragmatic middle ground, though it doesn't support the reconciliation story above; once the key expires, so does your evidence. And if your reminders are generated fresh from a nightly scan of the subscriptions table rather than queued weeks ahead, most of this collapses into a unique index on the table you already have, which is a trade I'd take every time.

References

  • RFC 2104: HMAC keyed-hashing for message authentication
  • Google Cloud Pub/Sub overview
  • RFC 5322: Internet Message Format (Message-ID)
  • PostgreSQL INSERT ... ON CONFLICT
  • Amazon SQS FIFO deduplication

title: The Role of Software Engineering in Modern Web Application Development: Risks of Vibe Coding.
description:
The Relevance of Software Engineering in Web Applications: The Dangers of Vibe Coding and Web Applications Developed Without Software Engineering Practices

Abstract

Web applications have become essential in modern society, supporting activities in education, healthcare, banking, communication and business. Their development requires more than writing code or creating attractive user interfaces. It requires proper planning, design, testing, security and maintenance. Software engineering provides the principles and techniques necessary to develop reliable, secure, efficient and maintainable web applications. However, the emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) coding tools has introduced a development approach known as vibe coding, where developers use natural-language prompts to generate code. Although this approach increases development speed, relying on AI-generated code without understanding, reviewing or testing it can introduce serious risks. This article examines the relevance of software engineering in web application development, the disadvantages of vibe coding and the dangers of developing web applications without proper engineering practices. It also discusses responsible ways of integrating AI into software development.

Keywords: Software Engineering, Web Applications, Vibe Coding, Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, Software Quality, Software Development.

  1. Introduction

Technology has significantly transformed the way people communicate, learn, work and conduct business. Web applications have become important tools in modern society, providing services such as online banking, e-learning, electronic commerce, healthcare management and information sharing.

As the demand for web applications increases, developers are expected to create systems that are not only functional but also secure, reliable, efficient and easy to maintain.

However, developing a successful web application involves more than writing programming instructions. It requires a systematic approach that covers requirements gathering, system design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance. These activities form the foundation of software engineering (Sommerville, 2016).

Recently, Artificial Intelligence tools have made software development more accessible through an approach commonly known as vibe coding. This allows developers to describe their desired applications using ordinary language and receive AI-generated code.

Although this approach can improve productivity, it also raises concerns about code quality, security, reliability and maintainability. Therefore, software engineering remains essential in ensuring that web applications are developed responsibly and meet professional standards.

  1. Understanding Software Engineering

Software engineering is the systematic application of engineering principles, methods and techniques to the development, operation and maintenance of software systems.

According to Sommerville (2016), software engineering involves all aspects of software production, including specification, development, validation and evolution.

In web application development, software engineering ensures that developers follow a structured process rather than writing code randomly.

Some important software engineering activities include:

  • Requirements analysis: Identifying what users expect the application to do.
  • System design: Planning the structure, architecture and components of the application.
  • Implementation: Writing and integrating the source code.
  • Testing: Checking whether the application works correctly and identifying errors.
  • Deployment: Making the application available to its intended users.
  • Maintenance: Updating, improving and correcting the application after deployment.

These activities help ensure that web applications meet users’ expectations and remain dependable throughout their lifecycle.

  1. The Relevance of Software Engineering in Web Applications

Software engineering plays a significant role in modern web application development for several reasons.

3.1 Improved Software Quality

Software engineering promotes the development of applications that are functional, reliable, efficient and maintainable.

A properly engineered web application should perform its intended functions without frequent errors or unexpected failures.

For example, an online shopping application should allow users to register, log in, search for products and complete transactions correctly.

Software quality practices help developers identify problems early and improve the overall performance of the application (Sommerville, 2016).

3.2 Enhanced Security

Security is one of the most important requirements of web applications because these systems often process sensitive information, including personal details, passwords and financial records.

Software engineering encourages the implementation of security practices such as authentication, authorization, encryption, input validation and secure data storage.

The OWASP Foundation (2025) identifies major web application security risks, including broken access control, security misconfiguration and authentication failures.

Therefore, security should be considered throughout the development process rather than added only after an application has been completed.

3.3 Easier Maintenance

Web applications require continuous improvements to correct errors, introduce new features and adapt to changing user requirements.

Software engineering encourages developers to write organized, readable and reusable code.

Proper documentation, modular design and version control also make it easier for developers to understand and maintain existing systems.

3.4 Reduced Development Costs

Although planning, testing and documentation require additional time, they help prevent expensive problems in the future.

Identifying errors during development is generally less expensive than correcting major failures after an application has been deployed.

Structured development practices therefore contribute to better project management and resource utilization (Sommerville, 2016).

3.5 Improved User Experience

Software engineering considers usability, accessibility, responsiveness and performance.

A properly developed web application should be easy to navigate, compatible with different devices and capable of responding efficiently to user requests.

This improves user satisfaction and encourages continued use of the application.

3.6 Scalability and Reliability

As an organization grows, its web application may need to support more users, transactions and data.

Software engineering encourages developers to use appropriate architectures and design principles that allow applications to accommodate future growth.

It also promotes reliability by ensuring that systems are properly tested and designed to handle expected operating conditions.

  1. Understanding Vibe Coding

Vibe coding is an AI-assisted software development approach in which developers describe what they want to build using natural language and allow an AI tool to generate much of the required code.

For example, a developer may prompt an AI coding assistant to create a student management system containing:

  • A student registration page.
  • A login and authentication system.
  • A database for storing student records.
  • An administrative dashboard.
  • A feature for managing academic information.

The AI tool may generate the code and suggest modifications based on additional prompts.

This approach can make software development faster and help beginners experiment with programming ideas.

However, a major concern arises when developers accept generated code without understanding its structure, checking its security or testing its functionality.

Sarkar and Drosos (2025) discuss vibe coding as a conversational approach to programming with AI. It demonstrates how natural-language interaction is changing the way people engage with software development.

Vibe coding can be useful, but it should not be confused with complete software engineering.

  1. Demerits of Vibe Coding

Despite its advantages, vibe coding has several disadvantages that developers should understand.

5.1 Lack of Understanding of Generated Code

Developers may generate entire applications without understanding the programming logic behind them.

When errors occur, they may struggle to identify the source of the problem or make the necessary corrections.

This creates a situation where developers depend on AI to solve problems they do not fully understand.

5.2 Security Vulnerabilities

AI-generated code is not automatically secure.

It may contain weaknesses involving authentication, authorization, input validation, data protection and other security requirements.

If developers deploy such code without reviewing and testing it, attackers may exploit the weaknesses.

The OWASP Foundation (2025) emphasizes the importance of addressing common web application security risks during development.

5.3 Poor Code Quality

AI tools may generate code that works for a simple demonstration but is poorly organized, repetitive or unnecessarily complicated.

Such code can become difficult to understand, extend and maintain.

5.4 Incorrect or Incomplete Solutions

AI tools can misunderstand requirements or generate code that does not perform the expected functions.

For instance, an AI-generated payment feature may display a successful transaction message without correctly verifying the actual payment status.

Without proper testing, developers may mistakenly believe that the application is functioning correctly.

5.5 Overdependence on AI

Excessive dependence on AI coding tools can reduce opportunities for developers to develop their problem-solving, debugging and programming skills.

Developers must understand the technologies they use rather than simply depending on AI-generated solutions.

5.6 Maintenance Difficulties

Repeatedly generating code through prompts without a clear architecture can result in inconsistent coding styles, duplicated functions and poorly connected components.

This makes future modifications more difficult and may increase the cost of maintaining the application.

  1. Dangers of Developing Web Applications Without Software Engineering Practices

Developing web applications without applying software engineering principles can expose individuals, businesses and organizations to serious risks.

6.1 Data Breaches and Privacy Violations

Poorly developed applications may expose confidential user information to unauthorized individuals.

For example, an insecure student management system could expose students’ personal details, academic records and contact information.

Such incidents can damage an organization’s reputation and reduce public trust.

6.2 Unauthorized Access

Applications without proper authentication and authorization mechanisms may allow unauthorized users to access restricted information and features.

Broken access control is identified as a major web application security risk by the OWASP Foundation (2025).

For example, a user might gain access to another person’s account or confidential records because the application does not properly verify permissions.

6.3 Financial Losses

Web applications that handle financial transactions must be developed and tested carefully.

Errors in transaction processing may result in duplicate payments, incorrect records or financial losses.

This can affect both service providers and their customers.

6.4 System Failures

Applications developed without adequate testing may crash, become slow or stop functioning when several users access them simultaneously.

Such failures can interrupt important services and negatively affect business operations.

6.5 Poor User Experience

An application containing broken links, confusing navigation, slow loading pages and malfunctioning features can frustrate users.

Poor usability may discourage people from using the application, regardless of how attractive its interface appears.

6.6 Legal and Ethical Consequences

Organizations have a responsibility to protect the information entrusted to them.

Poor software development practices may result in privacy violations, unauthorized disclosure of information and failure to meet applicable data protection requirements.

Developers must therefore consider both technical and ethical responsibilities when building applications.

  1. The Importance of Testing and Security in Web Applications

Testing is an essential activity in software engineering because it helps identify errors and weaknesses before an application is released.

Some important testing methods include:

Unit Testing: This checks individual functions or components to ensure that they work correctly.

Integration Testing: This examines whether different components of an application communicate and function properly together.

System Testing: This evaluates the complete application to determine whether it satisfies its requirements.

Security Testing: This identifies vulnerabilities that could expose the application to unauthorized access or attacks.

User Acceptance Testing: This determines whether the application meets the expectations and requirements of its intended users.

Security testing is particularly important because web applications are exposed to different forms of cyber threats.

The OWASP Top 10 provides developers with an awareness framework for understanding major web application security risks (OWASP Foundation, 2025).

Consequently, testing should be treated as a continuous development activity rather than a final step performed only before deployment.

  1. Responsible Use of AI in Software Engineering

The emergence of AI coding tools does not mean that traditional software engineering practices are no longer necessary.

Instead, developers should combine AI capabilities with proper engineering knowledge and professional judgment.

The following practices can help achieve this:

  1. Understand project requirements: Developers should identify the purpose, users and expected features of an application before generating code.
  2. Review AI-generated code: Every important section of generated code should be examined to understand its functionality and identify possible weaknesses.
  3. Perform proper testing: Applications should undergo unit, integration, system and security testing before deployment.
  4. Apply security principles: Developers should implement appropriate authentication, authorization, encryption and input validation.
  5. Use version control: Tools such as Git help developers track changes, collaborate and recover previous versions of their projects.
  6. Maintain proper documentation: Documentation helps other developers understand the system and makes future maintenance easier.
  7. Continue learning: Developers should strengthen their programming knowledge, problem-solving abilities and understanding of software architecture.

AI should therefore be considered a productivity tool that supports developers rather than a replacement for software engineering knowledge and responsibility.

  1. Conclusion

Software engineering remains highly relevant in modern web application development. It provides the principles, methods and practices required to build applications that are secure, reliable, efficient and maintainable.

Although vibe coding has made software development faster and more accessible, it also introduces challenges involving code quality, security, reliability and long-term maintenance.

Developing a web application is not simply about making it work or creating an attractive user interface. It involves ensuring that the application meets user requirements, protects sensitive information and remains dependable throughout its lifecycle.

Therefore, AI should be embraced as a supporting technology while software engineering principles remain the foundation of professional web application development.

The future of web development should not be measured by how quickly code can be generated, but by how securely, reliably and responsibly software can be built.

References

OWASP Foundation. (2025). OWASP Top 10: The ten most critical web application security risks. https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/

Sarkar, A., & Drosos, I. (2025). Vibe coding: Programming through conversation with artificial intelligence. Proceedings of the 36th Annual Conference of the Psychology of Programming Interest Group.

Sommerville, I. (2016). Software engineering (10th ed.). Pearson.
