title: Your error handling has never met a real 503. Here's how to introduce them.
description:
Staging is a terrible place to test failure. It only ever produces the happy path, so the code that handles timeouts, 500s and retries is the least-executed code in most apps, right up until production executes it for you.

This post is a practical way to fix that without changing the backend or the app: make the failures happen at the proxy, between the two.

Three kinds of failure worth testing

Slow. The request succeeds, eventually. What does the UI show at 200 ms, at 3 seconds, at 30? Is there a spinner, a timeout, a way out? Does the user tap the button twice?

Broken. 500, 502, 503, a dropped connection. Does the app retry, and how often? Does it honour Retry-After? On a checkout, does a retry charge the card twice?

Wrong. The one people skip. An HTTP 200 with bad data inside: a price that arrives as "49.00" instead of 49.00, a field that is suddenly null, an empty list on a screen that always had one item. These break more UIs than 5xx errors do, and no backend will produce them on demand.

Why the proxy is the right place

You could fake these in the app (a mock HTTP client, test fixtures) or in the backend (a broken build on staging). The proxy layer beats both for this job:

  • It needs no code change on either side, so you are testing the build you will ship.
  • It works for manual, exploratory testing on a real phone, where there is no test harness at all.
  • The same setup applies to the app, the automation suite and CI.
  • You can target one host and one path, and leave everything else alone.

The trade-off is the usual proxy setup: the device or runner sends its traffic through the proxy, and trusts the proxy's CA so HTTPS can be decrypted. That is the same for every tool in this post, and it is the part worth doing once, carefully.

What to look for when it fails

A checklist that has found real bugs for me:

  • Does a slow request ever give the user a way out, or is it a spinner forever?
  • After a 503, does Retry respect Retry-After, or hammer the server?
  • On payment or order endpoints, can a retry create a duplicate?
  • Does the error message make sense to a user, or does it print payment_unavailable?
  • When a number arrives as a string, does the screen crash, show NaN, or quietly do maths on text?
  • After the failure clears, does the app recover without a restart?

When the proxy has to be shared

Everything above runs on one laptop, which is fine until the failure you care about happens on a device in the lab, on a teammate's phone, or in a CI run. Then the proxy has to be somewhere everything can reach.

(15-second animated explainer, not a screen recording.)

Disclosure: that is the problem I build Proxycept for. It is a hosted debugging proxy: phones, emulators, teammates and CI runners point at one authenticated endpoint, and captures land in one shared web console. In it you can hold a request and change its response before releasing it, set delays and error rates per profile or per route, and add response rewrite rules that change one field of a real response (keeping its JSON type, or deliberately changing it) while the backend still answers for real.

What it does not do: it does not get past certificate pinning, it does not remove the CA step on each device (on Android that step is manual, like with any proxy), and it is for testing your own apps. If you work alone on one machine, a desktop proxy like Charles, Proxyman or mitmproxy is all you need.

If the shared version sounds useful, there is a free plan, and you can sign in with Google, GitHub or email: proxycept.com. If you are comparing it with Charles, this page covers when each one fits.

Have a failure case I missed, or a bug story like these? I'd like to hear it in the comments.

title: Look up a MAC address vendor (and spot randomized MACs) with one HTTP call
description:
Disclosure: I run the API described below (it is listed on RapidAPI, with a free plan), and this post was drafted with an AI assistant and reviewed before publishing.

Every network device has a MAC address, and the first three bytes (the OUI) say who registered it. Looking that up usually means downloading the IEEE registry files, parsing them, and keeping them fresh. Here is what the lookup involves, and a ready-made call if you would rather not maintain it.

What the registry contains

IEEE assigns address blocks in three sizes:

  • MA-L: 24-bit prefix (the classic 6-hex-digit OUI)
  • MA-M: 28-bit prefix
  • MA-S: 36-bit prefix (formerly IAB)

A correct lookup needs longest-prefix matching: a 36-bit block can sit inside an organization's range, so checking only the first 3 bytes can return the wrong vendor.

The randomized MAC trap

Modern phones use private (randomized) MAC addresses per Wi-Fi network. They are marked by the locally administered bit: the second-least-significant bit of the first octet. If it is set, the address was not assigned by a vendor, so a vendor lookup will not mean anything. Treat those as "unknown, privacy-randomized" rather than "no match".

One call

The endpoint is GET /lookup?mac=... and accepts any common format (colons, dashes, dots, or none):

import requests

resp = requests.get(
    "https://mac-address-lookup-oui-vendor-ieee-prefix.p.rapidapi.com/lookup",
    params={"mac": "3C:22:FB:12:34:56"},
    headers={
        "X-RapidAPI-Key": "YOUR_KEY",
        "X-RapidAPI-Host": "mac-address-lookup-oui-vendor-ieee-prefix.p.rapidapi.com",
    },
    timeout=10,
)
print(resp.json())

The JSON includes: found, vendor, prefix, block, prefix_bits (24, 28 or 36), registry, locally_administered, multicast, randomized and the data license note.

Listing and free plan: https://rapidapi.com/south-star-tools-2-south-star-tools-2-default/api/mac-address-lookup-oui-vendor-ieee-prefix

Doing it yourself instead

If you prefer to host it, download the IEEE MA-L, MA-M and MA-S CSV files, normalize the MAC to uppercase hex, and match the longest prefix first (36, then 28, then 24 bits). Check the locally administered bit before reporting a vendor.

If you hit a case that returns something wrong, tell me in the comments and I will fix it.

title: Distilling Frontier Agents into 0.5B CPU Models: How to Cut $500/Mo LLM Bills to Zero
description:
Distilling Frontier Agents into 0.5B CPU Models: How to Cut $500/Mo LLM Bills to Zero

Calling frontier models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro) for narrow, repetitive agent tasks is one of the most expensive architectural patterns in software engineering today.

Most production workflows—triaging alert tickets, converting logs to structured JSON, routing database queries, or interacting with a couple of CLI tools—don't require world-historical reasoning or creative flair. They require:

  1. Calling 2 to 5 specific tools with deterministic parameters.
  2. Adhering to strict validation schemas.
  3. Never hallucinating success when an underlying tool fails.

Yet, teams routinely rack up \$500 to \$2,000+ monthly API bills because smaller local models (0.5B–1.5B) traditionally collapse into hallucinated chaos when asked to execute multi-step tool calls.

Over the past few weeks, I built and open-sourced Task Model Distiller, a 3-pillar pipeline designed to distill frontier agent capabilities into sub-2B models (Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B) that run locally on ordinary CPUs at <1.5 GB RAM with zero external API fees.

Here is how the architecture works, why generic fine-tuning fails on small models, and how you can run this flywheel inside your own IDE or terminal.

⚠️ Why Traditional Fine-Tuning Fails on Sub-2B Models

If you take a base Qwen2.5-0.5B or Llama-3.2-1B model and fine-tune it on standard single-turn prompt-response datasets, you run into three critical failure modes:

  1. Context Loss: Agents operate in multi-turn feedback loops (system → user → tool_call → tool_output → response). Single-turn pairs fail to teach the model how to inspect prior execution state.
  2. Phantom Tool Claims: Small models love pleasing the user. If an error occurs, they will happily hallucinate: "I have paged the on-call engineer and restarted the service" even though the tool was never invoked.
  3. Silent Error Masking: When a tool returns {"status": "error", "code": 500}, naive models often ignore the error payload and proceed as if the action succeeded.

To fix this, we need more than just training data—we need adversarial calibration and deterministic evaluators.

🏛️ The 3-Pillar Distillation Pipeline 

                  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
                  │    Frontier Teacher (In-Workspace)     │
                  └───────────────────┬────────────────────┘
                                      │
               ┌──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┐
               ▼                                             ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────┐                   ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │        PILLAR 1         │                   │        PILLAR 2         │
  │   Full-Session Traces   │                   │   Adversarial Referee   │
  │   (Happy + Recovery)    │                   │   (Stage 1 + Stage 2)   │
  └────────────┬────────────┘                   └────────────┬────────────┘
               │                                             │
               │         ┌─────────────────────────┐         │
               └────────►│  CPU LoRA Fine-Tuning   │◄────────┘
                         │   (train_cpu_lora.py)   │
                         └────────────┬────────────┘
                                      │
                                      ▼
                         ┌─────────────────────────┐
                         │        PILLAR 3         │
                         │     The Scoreboard      │
                         │    (Private Locked)     │
                         └────────────┬────────────┘
                                      │ Failures
                                      ▼
                         ┌─────────────────────────┐
                         │   Targeted Flywheel     │
                         │  (Synthesize Fix Traces)│
                         └─────────────────────────┘

Pillar 1: Native Full-Session Synthetic Trace Generation

Instead of calling expensive third-party data generation APIs, your frontier AI coding assistant (inside Google Antigravity IDE, Claude Code, or Cursor) acts natively as the Teacher.

We generate complete multi-turn trajectories:

  • 40% Happy Paths: Normal user requests leading to clean tool execution.
  • 35% Edge Cases & Ambiguities: Tricky parameters, missing fields, or unrecognized entity names.
  • 25% Tool Failures & Recovery: Network timeouts, permission denied, or retry loops.

Every trace is verified before training using validate_traces.py to ensure schema integrity and strict ChatML formatting.

Pillar 2: The Two-Stage Adversarial Referee

Before training or benchmarking, we build and calibrate The Referee:

  • Stage 1 (Deterministic Invariant Engine): Validates raw execution logs using strict regexes and rule matrices. If a model claims "I paged Alice", Stage 1 verifies that page_engineer was physically executed and that its return code was not an error.
  • Stage 2 (Narrow Execution Judge): Strictly compares the assistant's final response against the tool logs (APPROVED vs REJECTED + offending sentence).
  • Adversarial Calibration (mutate_traces.py): Before benchmarking the model, we benchmark the judge. We synthesize deliberately sabotaged traces (phantom tool calls, silent failure masking) and calibrate the referee until it catches 100% of lies.

Pillar 3: The Scoreboard & Targeted Flywheel

We create a private, locked regression benchmark (benchmark_locked.jsonl) containing 30–50 tricky scenarios.

  • The un-tuned base model is benchmarked first to establish a baseline.
  • Any trivial cases the small model passes effortlessly are pruned.
  • The benchmark is locked and never mixed into training data.
  • After training, scoreboard.py runs and outputs a categorized failure report (e.g. {"tool_timeout": 3, "unauthorized_flag": 1}).
  • This report directly feeds back into Pillar 1: we synthesize 15 new targeted recovery traces covering the exact failure mode and retrain.

⚡ Real-World Case Study: incident-triager

Let's look at an imaginary production scenario:

  • Job: Inspect server alerts, check service health, and page on-call engineers if severity is critical.
  • Base Model: Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (0.5 Billion parameters).

Baseline Evaluation:

Running the untouched base qwen2.5:0.5b model through scoreboard.py:

  • Score: 6/25 (24%)
  • Failures: Hallucinated parameters, outputting chit-chat instead of JSON, and claiming the alert was resolved after the tool threw a timeout.

CPU LoRA Fine-Tuning:

We fine-tuned the model using train_cpu_lora.py with 4-bit LoRA target modules:

python scripts/train_cpu_lora.py   --base-model Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct   --dataset .distill/incident-triager/dataset/train_traces.jsonl   --output-dir .distill/incident-triager/training   --epochs 3   --merge
  • Training Device: Standard laptop CPU (16 GB RAM).
  • Training Time: ~12 minutes.
  • Output: Merged standard Hugging Face weights (safetensors).

Post-Training Scoreboard:

  • Score: 24/25 (96%)
  • Inference RAM: ~600 MB.
  • Inference Latency: Sub-40ms on CPU via Ollama or ONNX Runtime.

📦 Multi-Runtime Versatility (Beyond Ollama)

Because train_cpu_lora.py --merge exports a standard Hugging Face checkpoint, you are never locked into a single ecosystem:

Target Runtime Command / Export Tool Best For
Ollama (4-bit GGUF) ollama create my-bot -f Modelfile Instant local CLI & API (<1 GB RAM)
llama.cpp python llama.cpp/convert_hf_to_gguf.py merged_hf/ Native C++ embedded & edge devices
ONNX Runtime optimum-cli export onnx --model merged_hf/ onnx/ C#, C++, Rust, Windows DirectML
Apple Silicon (MLX) python -m mlx_lm.convert --hf-path merged_hf/ Unified memory Mac inference
vLLM / SGLang Load directly from merged_hf/ High-throughput server hosting

🤖 How to Use It with AI Coding Agents

The entire pipeline is packaged as a skill compatible with Google Antigravity IDE, Claude Code, Cursor, and Windsurf.

1. In Google Antigravity IDE

Install globally:

mkdir -p ~/.gemini/config/skills/task-model-distiller
cp -r * ~/.gemini/config/skills/task-model-distiller/

Then prompt your agent:

"Use the task-model-distiller skill to distill a local 0.5B model for my ticket-triage script."

2. In Anthropic Claude Code (CLI)

Add to your project's CLAUDE.md:

# Model Distillation Skill
When asked to build a local tool model, adhere to `SKILL.md` in `task-model-distiller`.

Then run:

claude "Initialize a model distillation pipeline for my GitHub labeler agent using task-model-distiller."

🔗 Try It Out (Open Source)

The entire codebase—including the synthetic trace validator, adversarial referee, scoreboard evaluator, and CPU LoRA training scripts—is open-source under the MIT license:

👉 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Virat-Ghatge/task-model-distiller

Give it a star ⭐ if you find it helpful, and start replacing expensive frontier agent calls with fast, ultra-reliable 0.5B local models!

title: DisplayLink Linux driver patents: the OIN codec exception
description:
The DisplayLink Linux driver patent dispute began with an ordinary hardware problem. Mike Lothian owned a Dell USB dock whose Linux driver kept crashing, according to Joe Brockmeier's November 10 report for LWN. He wanted better support, used Claude to help write a Rust driver, and asked the vendor for assistance. Synaptics responded with patent allegations and demands that eventually included a weekly monetary escalation.

TL;DR

  • Vino is Lothian's author-reported driver prototype. Its proposed upstream work has stalled, while the vendor's existing Linux software remains available.
  • Synaptics's October notice threatened US$25,000 for documentation, increasing by at least another US$25,000 each week without compliance. The published record establishes no court award or payment.
  • Open Invention Network coverage follows a defined list and exclusions. Its codec exception is central to this case.
  • GitHub Actions lockfiles and .NET 11 are the two shorter tooling updates in the episode. Their guarantees have explicit scopes too.

What the DisplayLink Linux stack actually contains

DisplayLink connects additional displays through USB docking hardware. Its Linux software includes the proprietary DisplayLink Manager and the open Extensible Virtual Display Interface module, usually called EVDI. These components have different jobs and different source availability.

The official EVDI README describes a kernel module and library that let applications manage virtual displays. It explicitly says the remaining driver is needed for full DisplayLink functionality. Seeing an open repository therefore tells you about that component. To understand whether the complete dock stack is available as source, you have to examine the rest of the software too.

LWN explains that the proprietary DL3 technology encodes a display stream for transmission and decodes it again for the connected devices. This is the machinery Lothian was trying to replace. The vendor continues to offer Ubuntu driver downloads, so the story should be described as the stalling of this attempted replacement.

That component distinction is useful when buying hardware. A project's name, an open kernel module and a supported operating-system logo each answer a narrow question. Check what software the device actually needs, which components have source, and which vendor support commitments apply to your platform. Those checks can prevent a surprise after the hardware arrives.

From an incomplete prototype to claim-mapping requests

Lothian's first Vino proposal was incomplete. Brockmeier reports that it reached the kernel development list in June and that Lothian was asking for help with communication to the dock. His later August version reportedly controlled three dock generations after the earlier attempts had never lit a panel. We have performed no hardware test or independent reproduction of that result.

Claude's involvement explains part of how he developed the prototype. It provides no evidence about the validity or application of a patent. That question remained attached to the work regardless of which editor, assistant or programming language he used.

In the July–October correspondence compiled by Lothian, Synaptics said an independently written or clean-room implementation could still implement patented inventions. The company alleged that Vino was progressing into technology covered by its patents. That is an allegation and a stated legal position requiring assessment in this particular case.

An August cease-and-desist notice included a long patent list and demanded withdrawal of allegedly infringing work. Lothian then asked which patent claims matched which code. A claim-mapping explanation would help him understand what the company believed he had implemented and what response was possible. A long list of patent identifiers leaves a developer with considerably more reading to do.

The distinction between source authorship and a claimed invention is the useful technical takeaway here. You can examine where code came from and still have a separate dispute about the method it implements. The correspondence documents Synaptics raising that second issue. It supplies no court determination that the prototype infringed valid claims.

What the October letter threatened

The October fifth letter contained a conditional monetary demand. It said Synaptics would seek US$25,000 to recover the costs of preparing documentation if Lothian failed to comply. It then said that amount would increase by at least US$25,000 per week until compliance.

The words “at least” and the condition are part of the actual notice. Removing them changes the account of what the company threatened. So does calling the demand an established debt, payment or court award. The published sources establish the threat and subsequent project status.

For an individual developer, a dispute can affect publication before any judge evaluates the implementation. The developer must weigh the usefulness of the work against the possible cost of defending it. A working prototype and an affordable defence are separate practical requirements. Lothian told LWN he could not afford to defend himself against Synaptics.

There was also an unusually awkward support interaction. On October seventh, Synaptics reviewed his older EVDI pull request. LWN quotes his response: “You can't threaten to sue me and then say 'can you update your pull request?'” That quotation captures the problem more clearly than another chart of patent identifiers would.

Why Open Invention Network coverage did not resolve this case

The Open Invention Network facilitates patent cross-licensing within a defined Linux System. Synaptics appears in its community directory. Lothian had joined too and asked how the network's commitments interacted with the company's allegations, according to LWN.

The scope is defined by software components and exclusions in the Linux System Definition. The pertinent codec clause excludes audio and image codecs unless expressly included in Table 0. The complete definition supplies the governing conditions and further member-specific limitations. Readers evaluating a different project should examine the actual agreement and its applicable scope.

This produces a concrete check beyond asking whether software runs on Linux. Identify the component involved, examine the definition and the express exceptions, then establish which commitments apply. An operating-system label alone cannot answer all of those questions.

Brockmeier reports that OIN investigated Lothian's situation. Chief executive Keith Bergelt said the protections did not extend to these attempted kernel contributions because of the codec exclusion. That reported conclusion is specific to this work. It establishes neither the validity of Synaptics's patents nor a universal exclusion for every codec or Linux driver.

Lothian told LWN he removed the public repository and Vino must remain local until the dispute is resolved. He may continue working on unaffected components. His proposed upstream replacement has stalled, and the vendor's existing Linux driver remains available. Keeping both parts of that status in view avoids exaggerating the practical consequence.

Also in the episode: locked actions and .NET support windows

Hugo van Kemenade's November 11 guide explains workflow lockfiles and links Python adoption examples. GitHub made the feature generally available in late October. A workflow can keep readable tags while its lockfile records the action commits to execute. Normal and transitive action dependencies are covered by the documented locking flow; this does not imply that arbitrary shell packages or every reusable workflow are frozen.

GitHub supports gradual onboarding and a Require lockfile policy. The practical benefit is control over the selected revision when a tag moves. Review that revision before locking it. Malicious code can be perfectly reproducible, which is an unfortunate definition of reliable.

Microsoft's .NET 11 release adds C# 15 union types with compiler-checked switch-expression coverage over declared cases. A product lookup can return a product or a missing-product case, with those alternatives visible in the type. That helps make a state model explicit while leaving application testing necessary.

.NET 11 receives two years of Standard Term Support. .NET 10 remains a supported Long Term Support option. Microsoft says quality and servicing policies are the same, with different support lengths. Choose the lifecycle that fits your maintenance plan; the release announcement provides no automatic migration of your application.

Verdict: REVERT

I stamped the escalating vendor pressure REVERT. A user trying to improve hardware he already owns ended up carrying the risk of an expensive defence, and the proposed driver stayed local. The verdict concerns that reported decision and its consequences. A legal assessment of patent validity or infringement requires different evidence and expertise.

The episode's recurring question is what each promise actually covers. Source access tells you about a component. OIN membership points you to an agreement and definition. A workflow lockfile selects a revision. A support policy specifies servicing and duration. Read the relevant boundary before relying on the larger assumption.

FAQ

Can an independently written driver face a patent allegation?

Synaptics raised that position in the correspondence: independently written source can still implement a claimed invention. The sources document its allegation, which requires legal assessment in this specific case.

Does OIN cover every project called a Linux driver?

Its scope follows listed components and exclusions. The codec clause has an express-list exception. LWN reports that OIN concluded these particular contributions were outside protection.

Was the weekly amount a court fine?

The primary notice threatened a conditional demand with escalation. The published record establishes no court award or payment.

Sources

  • Joe Brockmeier's LWN report
  • Synaptics October fifth notice
  • July–October correspondence
  • EVDI README
  • OIN definition and Table 0
  • Hugo's lockfile guide and GitHub's GA announcement
  • Microsoft's .NET 11 announcement

title: I built a Theme Studio where you plug a theme into a display and watch it stream in ⚡
description:
Hey everyone 👋

My portfolio has five themes: Classic, Terminal, Notebook, Midnight and Panorama. A dropdown would have been the easy way to switch between them.

I wanted switching themes to feel like plugging a cable into a screen. So I built a Theme Studio.

What you can do 🎮

  • Pick a theme from the row of cards, and it slides in under the display
  • Watch the display: it plays that theme's real page, live, and you can scroll it
  • Drag the display or a card around, and the wires follow on a spring
  • Hit Open: light races up the wires, a progress bar fills on the screen, and the theme opens
  • Press Esc mid-send to pull the plug

The wires 🔌

The connection isn't one line. It's a bundle of hairline strands, gold through orange, red and magenta to violet, pinched in the middle like a cable tie.

  1. Every strand is its own curve. Each one is a cubic bezier from a point on the card's edge to a point on the display's edge, so the bundle fans out at both ends.
  2. Light runs down it. Bands of brighter colour travel along the strands, and in dark mode they're blended additively so overlapping strands glow.
  3. It has weight. Drag a node and the bundle's middle trails behind on a spring, then settles.
  4. Sending is a volley. When you open a theme, a burst of bands and short sparks race up the strands into the display.

It's all one canvas over the stage, redrawn every frame.

The progress bar 🟩🟦🟪

While the light travels, the display's screen goes dark and a pixel progress bar fills on it.

  • One strict grid. Every cell sits on a 6px grid: lit cells are 4px squares (or dots), unlit ones are tiny specks.
  • Checkers, not noise. Which cells light up is an ordered dither of slowly drifting noise, so they gather into checker and diamond patterns that keep shifting.
  • A white-hot edge. The leading edge burns white with a soft bloom, and a few cells flare and go out as it fills.
  • Each theme gets its own bar. The wire's colours for Classic, GitHub greens for Terminal, blue dots for Panorama, and one colour per section for Midnight and Notebook.
  • It doesn't lie. The bar holds at 92% until the theme's page has actually loaded.

Under the bar, the site's sections (Intro, Work, Articles, Blocks) fill in turn as the bar passes through them, each with its own percentage. Point at one and its stretch of the bar lights up while the rest dims.

When it hits 100%, the screen grows out of the display and dives into the page.

Bonus: you're not alone 👀

If someone else is on the page, you'll see their cursor and their wire too. That runs through a small Cloudflare Durable Object.

Try it 🌐

👉 mahmad.me/theme-studio

Plug in Terminal and watch the greens fill up, then try Panorama.

title: Promptfoo vs DeepEval: The Same Support Bot, Tested Both Ways
description:
If you test LLM apps, you will run into Promptfoo and DeepEval within a week. Both are free and open source, both evaluate LLM output, and the comparison posts make them sound interchangeable. They are not. The quickest way to see the difference is to point both at the same app.

So I wrote a tiny stand-in "support bot" and tested it twice: once with Promptfoo, once with DeepEval. No AI model is involved, so you can run everything below in a couple of minutes for free. (Versions: Promptfoo 0.125.1, DeepEval 4.3.4.)

The app under test

A fake support bot with two known answers and a fallback:

# Stand-in for your real LLM app
ANSWERS = {
    "What is your refund window?": "30 days",
    "Do you ship to Canada?": "Yes, we ship to Canada in 5-7 business days.",
}

In a real project this would call your model or your RAG pipeline. The testing side stays the same.

Version 1: Promptfoo (YAML, any language)

Promptfoo treats your app as a "provider" and describes tests in YAML. A Python provider is just a function called call_api:

# bot.py
ANSWERS = {
    "What is your refund window?": "30 days",
    "Do you ship to Canada?": "Yes, we ship to Canada in 5-7 business days.",
}

def call_api(prompt, options, context):
    question = context["vars"]["question"]
    return {"output": ANSWERS.get(question, "Sorry, I don't know.")}

# promptfooconfig.yaml
description: Support bot checks
prompts:
  - "{{question}}"
providers:
  - file://bot.py
tests:
  - vars:
      question: What is your refund window?
    assert:
      - type: equals
        value: 30 days
  - vars:
      question: Do you ship to Canada?
    assert:
      - type: regex
        value: '\d+-\d+ business days'
  - vars:
      question: Can I pay with crypto?
    assert:
      - type: not-contains
        value: "I don't know"

Run it with npx promptfoo@latest eval. Result: 2 passed, 1 failed. The failure is deliberate: the bot has no answer about crypto, and the test says "never fall back to I don't know". That is exactly the kind of gap you want a test suite to surface before users do.

What stands out:

  • The tests are data, not code. A QA engineer, a PM or a prompt writer can add a case without touching Python.
  • It is language-agnostic. The provider could be an HTTP endpoint, a shell script or a hosted model, so it fits teams that aren't Python-first.
  • It scales sideways. Add a second provider and the same tests compare two models or two prompt versions in one run. Promptfoo also has a red-teaming mode for prompt injection and jailbreak checks (not used here, because it needs a real model).

Version 2: DeepEval (Pytest, Python-native)

DeepEval looks like ordinary Pytest. Each test builds an LLMTestCase and checks it against one or more metrics:

# test_bot.py
from deepeval import assert_test
from deepeval.test_case import LLMTestCase
from deepeval.metrics import ExactMatchMetric, PatternMatchMetric


def support_bot(question: str) -> str:
    answers = {
        "What is your refund window?": "30 days",
        "Do you ship to Canada?": "Yes, we ship to Canada in 5-7 business days.",
    }
    return answers.get(question, "Sorry, I don't know.")


def test_refund_window_exact():
    q = "What is your refund window?"
    case = LLMTestCase(input=q, actual_output=support_bot(q), expected_output="30 days")
    assert_test(case, [ExactMatchMetric()])


def test_shipping_mentions_days():
    q = "Do you ship to Canada?"
    case = LLMTestCase(input=q, actual_output=support_bot(q))
    assert_test(case, [PatternMatchMetric(pattern=r".*\d+-\d+ business days.*")])

Run it with deepeval test run test_bot.py. Result: 2 passed.

What stands out:

  • It lives next to your code. If your app is Python, tests sit in the same repo, run in the same CI job and fail the build the same way any Pytest test does.
  • The real strength is the metric library. The two metrics above are simple, deterministic ones. With a model configured, DeepEval adds LLM-judged metrics for things like answer relevancy, faithfulness and hallucination, which is where RAG and agent testing gets interesting.

So which one?

After running both on the same app, the split is clearer than most comparison tables make it:

  • Choose Promptfoo if you compare models or prompts, want non-developers to write tests, need red teaming, or your stack isn't Python.
  • Choose DeepEval if your app is Python, you want LLM tests as Pytest quality gates in CI, or you are evaluating RAG pipelines and agents.
  • Use both if you can afford the setup: Promptfoo for security and model selection, DeepEval for quality regression in CI. They don't conflict.

One honest caveat: this experiment uses a stand-in bot and deterministic checks only. The AI-judged metrics, Promptfoo's red-team generator and both dashboards need a real model and API spend, so I haven't covered them here.

The full comparison, with a feature table, CI/CD setup, costs and recommendations by role, is on my site: Promptfoo vs DeepEval: Which LLM Evaluation Framework Should You Choose?

What are you using to test your LLM features today? I'm curious whether teams lean to one tool or run both.

title: Certified kernels, guaranteed at install time
description:
Most GPU inference stacks find their kernel settings on your machine: the first time a new shape shows up, they stop, try block sizes, warp counts and pipeline stages, time them and keep the fastest. The result depends on your machine's mood at that moment.

NeuroBrix took the other road. Kernel settings are certified once per GPU class, checked against a float64 reference, and shipped inside the package. The fast path you get is the one we measured.

That raises a question few projects ask: how do you guarantee that what reaches a user's machine is complete? With the newest NeuroBrix, the answer is a release gate.

The build refuses an incomplete package

Every file the certified kernel tables need is tracked. When a release is built, the build checks the package against that list, and a package missing a single tracked file is refused. It never reaches PyPI. A pip install neurobrix therefore carries the certified tables, by construction, not by luck.

The engine refuses to guess

The second half of the guarantee lives at run time. If a table the engine expects is not there, NeuroBrix refuses to run on it and names what is missing, instead of silently falling back to guesswork. You either get the certified path or a clear message, never a quiet downgrade.

The same family as the V100 tensor cores

This is the same spirit as our work on the 2017 V100: its tensor cores sat unused on the Triton path, and NeuroBrix brought them back to life with its own kernels (the full story). On those V100s, our Triton engine beat the same model through PyTorch's kernels in 30 of 36 model-and-card pairs, up to 3.64x, every run reading its settings from the certified directory, none tuned during the measurement.

Fast kernels are half the work. Making sure every install gets them is the other half.

Try it 

pip install neurobrix
neurobrix doctor
neurobrix import TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0 --accept-license

title: Cross Post Video to TikTok, Reels and Shorts With Claude Code: Check the File, Write Three Texts, Send One Request
description:
Cross post video to TikTok, Reels and Shorts from your agent: Cross Post Video Skill is a free, MIT-licensed skill for Claude Code that takes one finished video and gets it ready for all three. It checks the file against every platform before anything is uploaded, helps you pick a cover, has the agent write a separate text for each platform, asks the settings only the account owner may choose, and shows every post on one plan page. After one clear yes, it sends all accounts in one request with a child per account. It also works in Codex, Cursor and OpenClaw.

Everything up to the upload runs on your own computer with Python and ffmpeg, and works without signing up for anything. This post walks through the NASA example in the repo, one command at a time.

npx skills add social-media-skills/cross-post-video-skill -g -a claude-code -y

Repo: github.com/social-media-skills/cross-post-video-skill

The plan page from the example: a 14-second NASA clip about why astronauts exercise in space, planned for TikTok, Reels and Shorts (NASA footage, no endorsement implied).

Why one video breaks on TikTok, Reels or Shorts

One vertical MP4 can be valid on all three platforms. What differs is everything around it, and each of these is easy to find only after the upload:

  • Length. TikTok's maximum belongs to the account, not the platform. A Short is square or vertical and up to 3 minutes; longer and YouTube makes it a normal video.
  • The file itself. Instagram is the strictest: 300 MB, up to 1920 px wide, 23 to 60 fps, AAC sound, the index at the start of the file, and no HDR.
  • The text. TikTok and Instagram take a caption. YouTube wants a title of up to 100 characters and counts the description in bytes. Instagram caps hashtags at 5.
  • The settings. TikTok makes the account owner choose who can see each post and whether comments, duets and stitches are on, with no defaults. YouTube asks whether a video is made for kids.

The skill moves all of that in front of the upload. Scripts do the checking and counting; the agent writes the texts and asks the questions.

The prompt

Post clips/microgravity.mp4 to my TikTok, Reels and Shorts on 12 January at 6 pm New York time. It's my own video with the original sound, no AI, not promotional. TikTok: everyone can see it, comments on, duets and stitches off. Not made for kids.

That prompt already answers what the agent would otherwise ask in its first message: is this the original export you have the right to post, what the sound is, whether it is AI-made or promotional, and the settings per account.

Step 1: check the file 

python3 <skill>/scripts/check_video.py clips/microgravity.mp4

clips/microgravity.mp4: 720x1280, 13.9 s, 29.97 fps, h264 yuv420p, aac 48000 Hz, 3.1 MB, 1.82 Mbps
  TikTok: ok
  Instagram Reels: ok
  YouTube Shorts: ok

This clip passes. When a file doesn't (4K, 120 fps, 5.1 sound, a MOV from a camera, HDR from a newer iPhone), --fix writes a re-encoded copy next to it as <name>.crosspost.mp4 and leaves the original alone. It keeps the picture size and only scales down a video over 1920 px wide. HDR is converted to standard colour when your ffmpeg has the zscale filter; when it doesn't, --fix writes nothing and tells you how to export a standard-colour file instead. It never trims, crops, pads or speeds up a video: length and shape stay your call.

Step 2: pick a cover

Without a cover, TikTok and Instagram show the first frame. cover.py makes a sheet of 12 frames with their times, with a dashed box on each for the middle 3:4, the part Instagram's profile grid shows.

python3 <skill>/scripts/cover.py clips/microgravity.mp4

In the example, the frame at 8.7 seconds looked good full screen and cut the astronaut's head off in the grid crop. The frame at 12.2 seconds didn't:

python3 <skill>/scripts/cover.py clips/microgravity.mp4 --at 12.2

The cover goes to TikTok and Instagram with the post. YouTube's cover is set in the YouTube app, so the plan and the by-hand page both say "Cover frame: 12.2 s" and you pick the same frame there.

Step 3: a text per platform, in one job file

The agent writes each text from what the video says, not from the other texts, and puts everything in crosspost.json: the accounts with their settings, the four answers, and the texts. Trimmed:

{
  "timezone": "America/New_York",
  "accounts": [
    {"name": "TikTok", "platform": "TIKTOK", "privacyLevel": "PUBLIC_TO_EVERYONE",
     "allowComment": true, "allowDuet": false, "allowStitch": false, "max_video_s": 600},
    {"name": "Reels", "platform": "INSTAGRAM"},
    {"name": "Shorts", "platform": "YOUTUBE", "privacy": "public", "madeForKids": false}
  ],
  "videos": [{
    "id": "microgravity", "file": "clips/microgravity.mp4", "when": "2027-01-12 18:00",
    "own_video": true, "audio": "original", "ai_generated": false, "promotional": "no",
    "text": {
      "TIKTOK": "Why astronauts work out for hours every day\n...",
      "INSTAGRAM": "Astronauts on the space station exercise for hours every day.\n...",
      "YOUTUBE": {"title": "Why astronauts exercise for hours every day in space",
                  "description": "...", "tags": ["space station", "ISS", "microgravity"]}
    }
  }]
}

The settings and the four answers are the owner's. If one is missing, plan.py lists it and the agent asks; it never fills one in. max_video_s comes from the connected TikTok account itself, because TikTok sets it per account.

Step 4: the plan page 

python3 <skill>/scripts/plan.py crosspost.json

3 posts planned -> plan.md, plan.html (0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes)
by hand (1): by-hand/
requests: requests/microgravity.json
next: show plan.html (or paste plan.md) and wait for a clear yes. ...

plan.py checks the file per account, every text and every setting, and counts each text the way its platform does. For the example: the TikTok caption is 198 of 2,200 characters with 3 hashtags, the Reels caption 329 of 2,200 with 4, the YouTube title 52 of 100 characters and the description 227 of 5,000 bytes. It also flags the things that aren't errors but are worth knowing: a link that won't be clickable, an @handle reused on another platform, a first line too long to stand alone, a hashtag that says nothing about the video.

The result is plan.html (the screenshot at the top) and plan.md: every account, its text, settings, cover and time, plus a list of what to do in the apps after it's live. The agent shows it and waits for one yes that covers these posts, these accounts and these times.

In the example only TikTok and Instagram are connected, so Shorts is planned by hand. by-hand/microgravity/shorts.md has the title, description, tags, settings, the cover frame and numbered steps for YouTube Studio or the app.

Step 5: one request, a child per account

After the yes, the agent uploads each file once, and plan.py --media media.json fills in the media IDs. The request is one post with a child per connected account, each with its own text in contentOverride. Trimmed from requests/microgravity.json:

{
  "schedule": {"type": "SCHEDULE_FOR_LATER", "scheduledFor": "2027-01-12T23:00:00Z"},
  "socialAccounts": [
    {"platform": "TIKTOK", "postMode": "DIRECT_POST", "privacyLevel": "PUBLIC_TO_EVERYONE",
     "allowComment": true, "allowDuet": false, "allowStitch": false,
     "isYourBrand": false, "isBrandedContent": false, "isAiGeneratedContent": false,
     "cover": {"type": "MEDIA_LIBRARY", "mediaId": "<cover>"},
     "contentOverride": [{"text": "Why astronauts work out for hours every day\n...",
                          "media": [{"type": "MEDIA_LIBRARY", "mediaId": "<video>"}]}]},
    {"platform": "INSTAGRAM", "postType": "REEL", "isAiGeneratedContent": false,
     "cover": {"type": "MEDIA_LIBRARY", "mediaId": "<cover>"},
     "contentOverride": [{"text": "Astronauts on the space station exercise for hours every day.\n...",
                          "media": [{"type": "MEDIA_LIBRARY", "mediaId": "<video>"}]}]}
  ]
}

The 6 pm New York time became 23:00Z: plan.py stops when a clock time has no time zone, and never assumes UTC. The order is fixed: the yes, the upload, posts_validate with the exact request, posts_create, then plan.py --posted with the post ID, then posts_get for the status per account. The request is validated as a whole: if one child is invalid, nothing is created. If validation forces a change, the agent plans again and asks for a new yes.

Nothing goes out twice

--posted writes the video and every account in that request to posted.json. From then on, plan.py leaves those accounts out of every new request for that video and shows them as "already posted". That matters for the most common next step: you connect the third account next week, plan again, and the new request holds only Shorts. The same goes for a failure. If one account fails, plan.py --failed releases just that account, and the accounts that went through are never sent again.

A scheduled post can't be checked before its time. After it, "check my cross-post" makes the agent read posted.json, call posts_get for each recorded post and report one line per account: live with its link, still processing, or failed and why.

The free plan math, said up front

Disclosure: the skill is made by the team behind WoopSocial, and posting goes through WoopSocial. It posts through each platform's own API with WoopSocial's approved apps, so you don't need a developer app or an app review of your own. The free plan covers 2 social accounts, no card. TikTok, Reels and Shorts are 3, so in its first message the agent asks which you want: it posts 2 and gives you the by-hand page for the third, posts all of them on a paid plan, or prepares everything and you post all of them by hand with nothing to sign up for. The connect step for your agent is on the WoopSocial setup page for AI agents.

WoopSocial posts the video and the texts. It doesn't write captions or change the video: the agent writes the texts, and the skill's own script does any re-encoding. Some things can't be set through it, and the plan lists them under "After it's live": the YouTube cover, YouTube's altered content and paid promotion answers, and Instagram's paid partnership label. A sound picked from an app's library can't be added either; for TikTok the agent can send the video as a draft to your inbox, where you add the sound and post it.

Several accounts per platform

The job file takes as many accounts as you have, including two on one platform (a Dutch and an English TikTok, say). Each account then gets its own text with "text": {"<account name>": ...} and its audience written down, and the plan warns once per job with what that platform's own rules say about the same video on several accounts. The skill never offers to speed up, crop or filter copies to make them look different, and it posts the original export only: no copy saved from another app, and nothing added to the picture.

It also makes no reach promises. No platform has said that posting order, a gap between platforms, a time of day or a hashtag count changes how a video is shown, so the plan doesn't suggest any, and it doesn't add #Shorts, which YouTube doesn't need.

Try it 

npx skills add social-media-skills/cross-post-video-skill -g -a claude-code -y

Then tell your agent "post this video to TikTok, Reels and Shorts" or "cross-post clip.mp4 everywhere tomorrow at 6". It needs Python 3.9+, ffmpeg and Pillow; scripts/check_setup.py prints the install command for anything missing. The full example, with every file the skill made, is in examples/microgravity/. Issues and pull requests are welcome, and there are more free skills for social media from the same team.

title: I built a zero-dependency, local-first Python & browser suite (SAST, contracts, invoices, tasks)
description:
Most everyday developer, security, and freelancer utilities either require heavy dependency trees or upload your sensitive files (contracts, invoices, source code, meeting notes) to third-party servers.

So I built IT Solutions Suite — a 100% offline, zero-dependency, MIT-licensed toolkit that runs either directly in your browser (pure client-side JS, zero server uploads) or via Python 3.9+ stdlib (pip install it-solutions-suite).

Try it right now (no signup, no uploads)

  • Live Browser Studio (Vercel): https://it-solutions-global.vercel.app/
  • Hugging Face Space: https://huggingface.co/spaces/itsolutions-global/it-solutions-suite
  • GitHub (MIT): https://github.com/itsolutions-global/it-solutions-suite
  • PyPI: pip install it-solutions-suite

What's inside the suite

  1. ClauseGuard — Contract & NDA Risk Scanner

    • Scans contracts, MSAs, and NDAs locally for risky clauses (uncapped liability, broad IP assignment, auto-renewal traps, non-competes, unilateral termination).
    • Note: Automated heuristic review — not legal advice.

  2. DocuPulse — Invoice & Receipt to CSV Extractor

    • Extracts vendor, invoice number, date, tax, total, and currency from pasted text or documents into clean CSV/JSON exports without sending financial data to an external API.

  3. NexusShield — Local SAST, Secret Scanner & SBOM

    • Scans repositories locally for hardcoded secrets, dangerous patterns, and dependency manifests using only the Python standard library.

  4. EchoStream — Meeting Follow-Up & Action-Item Extractor

    • Turns raw meeting transcripts into structured decisions, action items, owners, and follow-up drafts offline.

  5. CorePulse — Local-First Tasks & Life OS

    • Lightweight SQLite-backed task and workflow manager with zero external runtime dependencies.

Why zero-dependency?

  • Privacy by default: Sensitive PDFs, contracts, and source trees never leave your machine.
  • Instant startup: No Docker, no API keys, no node_modules bloat.
  • Auditable: Pure Python stdlib and vanilla HTML/JS/CSS under the MIT license.

If you try it out (either on the live browser studio or via pip install it-solutions-suite), I'd love feedback on what file formats or rules would make it more useful for your workflow!

title: I built a trading chart whose journal fills itself, on one FastAPI process and SQLite
description:
For a long time my trading "system" was three tabs: a charting site, an exchange demo account, and a spreadsheet journal I never kept up to date. So I built one page that does all three: Keelstone. It is in open beta and free.

This post is about the parts that were interesting to build.

The idea: a journal you cannot forget to fill in

You open a chart, press Trade and take a practice position with virtual funds. When you close it, the trade is already in your journal: entry, exit, leverage, result, the reason it closed, and a picture of the chart at both moments. Win rate, expectancy, profit factor, drawdown and the equity curve build themselves.

The detail that changed how the journal feels: a trade opened from the chart cannot be edited or deleted afterwards. Only the tag and the note can change. Once I could no longer tidy up my own history, the statistics finally told the truth.

Do not trust the browser with prices

The first version let the page send the fill price. That makes every result, and the monthly competition board, trivial to fake.

Now the server fills every practice order at the price it sees itself. A request whose price is more than a couple of percent away from the server's is refused. Stops, targets and liquidations are only accepted if the price range since the position opened really crossed the level. A position cannot lose more than its margin, the way an isolated position behaves on an exchange.

One process, one file

The whole backend is a single FastAPI process with SQLite in WAL mode, behind Caddy and a Cloudflare tunnel, in Docker Compose on one small machine. No queue, no cache server, no separate database.

That sounds reckless until you measure it. Live prices go straight from the exchanges to the browser over their public websockets, so the server never relays ticks. What is left is page loads, saved layouts, journal rows and a chat poll. In a load test with 600 simulated members, each sending a request every two seconds, the median response was 12 ms and the process used about two thirds of one core and 100 MB of memory.

Things that helped:

  • Keep hot state (rate limits, who is online, short caches) in memory and accept that it resets on restart.
  • Version static scripts by file time in the page, so a CDN can cache them for hours and a deploy is still picked up at once.
  • Write the boring housekeeping early: cap container logs, prune the build cache, keep the last 14 database backups. My disk grew by 9 GB in a day of deploys before I noticed.

Connecting a real exchange without holding anything

Members can connect their own Bybit Demo account and send orders from the chart. The server stores the API key encrypted and only passes instructions on; it refuses any key that is able to withdraw or transfer funds, and refuses read-only keys too, so a connected key can trade and nothing else. Positions opened from the chart are journaled with the exchange's own result once they close.

Security that fits a small project

  • Sessions are random tokens stored only as hashes; passwords use Argon2.
  • Two-step sign-in is plain TOTP from the standard library (hmac, struct, base64), with one-time backup codes stored as hashes.
  • The administrator console only opens in a session that gave an authenticator code in the last twelve hours, so a stolen password alone is not enough.
  • A tiny guard scores suspicious requests (probes for .env files, injection strings, bursts of 404s) and shuts an address out for an hour.

What I would do differently

I would write the "walk every endpoint as every kind of user" test on day one. Late in the project it found an admin page that had been quietly returning errors for days because a helper function had gained a parameter.

Try it

Charts for crypto and stocks, about 70 drawing tools, bar replay, a small script editor with backtests, a markets page with funding and open interest, and the journal: keelstone.online. Every account currently gets the top plan while the beta lasts.

It is software for studying markets and practising, not investment advice. I would love to hear what breaks.

title: Go Transactional SMS Alerts — Compare Europe Provider Delivery Before Report Replays
description:
Keeping notification transport replaceable is useful, but a logistics report loses its evidentiary value if a retry can quietly substitute a different attachment. TL;DR: compare transactional SMS alert providers for US and Europe utility-outage notifications against a reproducible dispatch record first. Bind the approved report revision to the email attachment, make the accompanying SMS refer to that dispatch, and choose the transport only after deciding how much provider-specific evidence the review requires. A low quoted rate cannot settle that decision.

Consider a hypothetical production review: a depot receives an outage report by email, an SMS tells its operator to check the report, and the report generator later produces a corrected PDF. A retry worker resolves the filename again. The filename is unchanged; the attachment bytes are different. The record now says that the original approval authorized a document it never examined. This is a design exercise, not an account of a measured incident.

Freeze the artifact.

The lesson is narrower than “log more”: an approval must identify a particular report revision, recipient, and dispatch purpose, and a replay must preserve that identity. A correction needs a new approval and a new dispatch identity. Submission acceptance, delivery observations, and a person's acknowledgment remain separate claims, even when the product interface puts them on the same screen.

Logistics teams should try Infrai for the accompanying transactional SMS alerts when they want to switch providers without changing code, and periodic event collection meets their evidence SLO. Infrai provides one REST API, one key, one bill: the capability contract stays stable when the vendor behind it changes. A single API key covers the email-and-SMS integration, reducing credential distribution work. Its consistent per-call vendor, latency, cost, and request metadata also reduces the custom normalization needed to attach operating context to each attempt. Those are useful integration properties. They don't establish that a particular email attachment reached, or was read by, its intended recipient.

How should teams compare transactional SMS alerts provider evidence in Europe?

Start the review by reconstructing one dispatch backward, from the recipient-facing report to the approval that authorized it. Can the reviewer recover the exact attachment bytes, the recipient reference, the report revision, the purpose, and the relationship between the email and its SMS reminder? These are application-owned records, not proposed provider request fields. If reconstruction depends on the current contents of a mutable file, adding another delivery receipt will not repair it.

For a concrete acceptance exercise, label the initial report revision 7 and its correction revision 8. Both can be legitimate documents. The error is allowing an approval for revision 7 to authorize revision 8 implicitly, because the retry reused a convenient path such as report.pdf. Keep the original artifact recoverable under the approved retention and access policy, and record a correction as a new action rather than rewriting the historical relationship.

A digest helps detect substitution. It does not prove authorization.

The approval record itself needs protection against unauthorized changes, and its recipient binding needs to refer to the approved destination rather than whatever address a customer profile contains today. Retain the raw transport observations alongside their interpretation so a later adapter change cannot silently redefine an older result. RFC 6376 describes DKIM domain-level signing; it does not make a signature evidence that an operator opened the report, nor does it replace the application's approval history. Keep that distinction visible in the review UI.

Capacity planning follows the artifact boundary. In a synthetic batch of 600 recipients, retaining a separate 2 MiB report copy for each recipient consumes 1,200 MiB before replication and indexes; retaining one immutable artifact with 600 controlled references changes that storage workload, although authorization still applies to every recipient. These are planning assumptions, not provider limits. Budget report retention, evidence ingestion, and reconstruction work separately from sending throughput. A submission SLO can look healthy while the evidence needed for tomorrow's review is unavailable.

Define an evidence SLO with the compliance owner: which dispatch population must be reconstructable, by what deadline, and how unresolved transport states are represented. Do not turn an unknown state into a successful one just to close the record.

Reject changed bytes before choosing a transport

The preventative path belongs before the send adapter. The following complete Go program checks a local attachment against an approval record, including the recipient reference and report revision, then retrieves Infrai's public email batch-send discovery contract for inspection. It performs no message send; attachment submission still needs qualification against that contract. Save it as main.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment, and run it with the approval-file path, PDF path, recipient reference, and revision, in that order. Discovery is public; the example uses environment-based Bearer authentication to demonstrate the integration convention. The read needs no write idempotency key.

The approval file is an application-owned JSON object with string fields named dispatch_id, recipient_ref, report_revision, and sha256. Its digest must come from the approved artifact through a trusted approval process. Generating a fresh approval from whichever file happens to exist immediately before a retry would defeat the check. No example values here are vendor fields or compliance certifications.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Approval struct {
    DispatchID string `json:"dispatch_id"`
    Recipient  string `json:"recipient_ref"`
    Revision   string `json:"report_revision"`
    Digest     string `json:"sha256"`
}

func inspectContract() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("GET", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/email.batch.send", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 2<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(retry, 10, 64); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 300 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("retry deferred beyond this program's wait budget")
                }
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(date); wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            if delay > 5*time.Minute {
                return fmt.Errorf("retry deferred beyond this program's wait budget")
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if !json.Valid(body) {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery response is not valid JSON")
        }
        fmt.Printf("contract for inspection: %s\n", body)
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func check(args []string) error {
    if len(args) != 4 {
        return fmt.Errorf("usage: go run main.go approval.json report.pdf recipient-ref revision")
    }
    data, err := os.ReadFile(args[0])
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var approval Approval
    if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &approval); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if strings.TrimSpace(approval.DispatchID) == "" ||
        strings.TrimSpace(approval.Recipient) == "" ||
        strings.TrimSpace(approval.Revision) == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("approval identity is incomplete")
    }
    if approval.Recipient != args[2] || approval.Revision != args[3] {
        return fmt.Errorf("recipient or revision differs from approval")
    }
    expected, err := hex.DecodeString(approval.Digest)
    if err != nil || len(expected) != sha256.Size {
        return fmt.Errorf("approval must contain a SHA-256 digest")
    }
    file, err := os.Open(args[1])
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer file.Close()
    hash := sha256.New()
    if _, err := io.Copy(hash, file); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    actual := hex.EncodeToString(hash.Sum(nil))
    if actual != strings.ToLower(approval.Digest) {
        return fmt.Errorf("attachment differs from approved bytes")
    }
    if err := inspectContract(); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    fmt.Printf("eligible dispatch=%s revision=%s sha256=%s\n",
        approval.DispatchID, approval.Revision, actual)
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := check(os.Args[1:]); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

There is a deliberate boundary here: checking a path and later reopening it for submission creates a substitution window. In the production adapter, submit the same verified immutable artifact, or use the verified bytes held by the send operation; do not reopen a mutable filename and assume the earlier check still applies. Protect the approval store as well. A digest comparison against an attacker-controlled approval proves nothing useful.

Nor is the printed eligibility result a send receipt. Persist the dispatch identity before submitting, retain it across retries of the same action, and apply the selected transport's documented idempotency behavior. A corrected report gets a different identity. A retry after an ambiguous outcome requires reconciliation rather than an automatic second business action.

Buy a stable contract or own the specialist record

Two architectures can preserve this invariant. In the shared-contract architecture, an application-owned approval and artifact store feeds a common transport interface, and a collector attaches observations to each dispatch. Its invariant is that swapping the vendor behind the capability leaves the approved artifact identity unchanged. Infrai is a deliberate option for the SMS part of that shape; its email and SMS event retrieval uses a pull model, so reserve collection capacity and choose a cadence that meets the evidence deadline.

In the direct-specialist architecture, the same approval boundary feeds separate provider adapters, and the application retains each provider's native observations alongside its normalized record. Its invariant is that normalization never discards evidence the review requires. Prefer this shape when direct ownership of specialist routing, reporting, or event handling justifies the adapter maintenance and on-call load. Neither architecture lets the transport approve a new report revision on the application's behalf.

The buy-versus-build decision is therefore about which contract the platform team will maintain. The comparison below identifies ownership differences and qualification work; it does not rank unmeasured regional delivery performance.

Candidate Contract the team chooses to buy Work the team retains Appropriate boundary
Infrai Shared capability interface with consistent per-call metadata Artifact approval, dispatch correlation, and periodic event collection Stable application code matters and pull-based evidence meets the SLO
Twilio Direct communications-provider contract Twilio-specific adapter and review of its native messaging evidence Own the specialist contract when its demonstrated workflow is a requirement
Amazon SNS AWS notification-service contract SNS integration and correlation with the separate report-email record Favor when AWS is already the selected operational ownership boundary
Telnyx Direct messaging-provider contract Telnyx-specific adapter and qualification of destination behavior Favor when qualification establishes a specialist messaging requirement
SendGrid A separate email-provider contract to qualify Attachment acceptance and report-to-SMS correlation Consider when the team wants an email-specific integration alongside its chosen SMS provider
Postmark Another direct email-provider contract to qualify Its own attachment acceptance case and evidence mapping Consider when that contract passes the report workflow's review requirements

Twilio, Amazon SNS, and Telnyx deserve the same replay acceptance case: an approved report, a corrected report, a retried notification, and a review that must distinguish all three actions. Sinch and MessageBird can undergo that same qualification. Brand recognition does not establish compliance, and no comparable US or European delivery measurements here support declaring a winner. Read the selected product's current documentation before treating an observation as evidence of anything beyond its documented meaning.

Keep the attachment decision separate. The email adapter must demonstrate submission of the actual report attachment and preservation of its relationship to the SMS dispatch; selecting an SMS provider alone establishes neither. For country-specific legal obligations, obtain the relevant contractual and compliance evidence directly. A common API is an integration boundary, not jurisdictional approval.

Where the replay rule stops helping

This design fits report dispatches whose approval and evidence requirements tolerate the chosen collection interval. Infrai is not a fit when the SMS escalation requires webhook-first handling; evaluate Twilio's specialist workflow against that deadline instead. The trade-off is ownership of a direct provider adapter and its evidence semantics. This design does not establish a life-safety alerting architecture, and the report evidence path must not delay an urgent notification.

That boundary matters.

Keep operating policy explicit: maintain destination allowlists and country-based spending circuit breakers in the application, record attribution by alert type in your own ledger, and retain an approved template inventory. Approve report emails before submission; where policy calls for retractable delayed reminders, SMS cancellation is a separate control. Keep this design scoped to report email and SMS rather than assuming it also qualifies voice, WhatsApp, RCS, SMTP relay, or email-based identity verification.

Then compare current commercial terms using the same destinations, traffic composition, and evidence obligations. The decision worth retaining is who can reconstruct the approved report dispatch after a retry, and who owns the work required to keep that promise.

Sources

References for message authentication and the direct-provider contracts to qualify:

  • RFC 6376, DomainKeys Identified Mail
  • Twilio Messaging documentation
  • Amazon SNS documentation
  • Telnyx Messaging documentation
  • SendGrid email documentation
  • Postmark developer documentation

If the shared-contract boundary fits your system, start with the first-party email-versus-SMS workflow discussion, then qualify the attachment and evidence requirements separately.

title: Healthcare Appointment Retrieval Deduplication Explained in Python: 5 Feeds (Trade-offs)
description:
Healthcare Appointment Retrieval Deduplication Explained in Python: 5 Feeds (Trade-offs)

Short answer: deduplicate appointment evidence before ranking by assigning each source a canonical identity, then keep a separate ledger of the records merged into that identity. For a healthcare appointment assistant, this reduces repeated slots and contradictory citations without hiding which scheduling system supplied each claim.

The useful unit is not a text chunk. It is a source-backed fact: clinic, service, location, provider, time window, and effective date. A cancellation feed and a public booking page may describe the same slot with different wording. If both survive retrieval, the language model sees confidence where there is only duplication.

The failure starts before the vector index

I initially treated duplicate detection as a similarity-search problem. That was a mistake. Embeddings can tell me that two documents talk about “Tuesday dermatology appointments,” but they cannot safely decide that the records refer to the same clinic, timezone, or booking authority. A false merge can erase a valid slot; a missed merge can make the assistant cite two answers.

Normalize fields at ingestion. Parse timestamps into UTC while retaining the clinic timezone, normalize phone numbers and URLs, and map provider identifiers through a controlled table. Keep the original payload and an ingest timestamp. Those details are boring until an auditor asks why a slot disappeared. In a real appointment stream, the same provider can arrive as “Dr. Lee,” “LEE, M,” or an internal UUID; collapsing those labels without a maintained crosswalk is a data-governance decision, not a clever string trick. The crosswalk needs an owner, a version, and a review path when a clinic changes its naming rules.

For five hypothetical feeds, I use a key made from stable identifiers rather than generated prose:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from hashlib import sha256
import json

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AppointmentRecord:
    clinic_id: str
    service_code: str
    provider_id: str
    starts_at_utc: str
    source_system: str
    source_record_id: str
    payload: dict

def source_key(record: AppointmentRecord) -> str:
    stable = {
        "clinic": record.clinic_id.strip().lower(),
        "service": record.service_code.strip().upper(),
        "provider": record.provider_id.strip().lower(),
        "starts_at": record.starts_at_utc,
    }
    encoded = json.dumps(stable, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")).encode()
    return sha256(encoded).hexdigest()

The hash is an implementation detail. The normalized fields are the contract. If a source cannot provide a stable provider or service identifier, mark the key as provisional and require a policy decision before merging it with a different authority.

Tiny detail, big consequence.

How should a healthcare appointment assistant resolve duplicate sources?

Use a two-stage pipeline. First, exact keys collapse records that represent the same appointment. Second, a source policy chooses the winning value for each field and records every losing record in a citation ledger. Retrieval then indexes one canonical record plus a compact list of provenance IDs.

A ledger entry should answer four questions: which records were merged, which source was authoritative for availability, when the decision was made, and what changed between versions. That makes the answer explainable without stuffing five copies of the same paragraph into the prompt.

Do not silently merge disagreements. If two systems report different times, retain both candidates, lower confidence, and route the turn to a clarification flow. Appointment booking is a consequential action; a fluent guess is not resolution.

Ranking quality versus response latency

Deduplication changes the retrieval distribution, so measure it as part of the search experiment. I track recall of the correct appointment, duplicate-rate in the top five results, time to first token, and citation agreement. The right threshold depends on the clinic data; your mileage may vary until you test representative cancellations, reschedules, and daylight-saving transitions.

A small evaluation set should include adversarial pairs: same provider and time but different locations, same slot with stale status, and two records that share a title but belong to different departments. Store expected identity groups as labels. Run the set on every parser or key change, and inspect failures by category rather than relying on one aggregate score.

Latency has a visible shape here. Exact-key grouping is cheap and bounded by the number of records. Fuzzy matching across the entire corpus is slower and harder to audit, so reserve it for a narrow candidate window after filtering by clinic and date. Cache normalized records, not model answers; cached answers can outlive a cancellation.

The catch: when source deduplication is the wrong choice

A single canonical record is not suitable when sources have independent legal or operational authority, or when the user explicitly asks for alternatives across locations. In those cases, preserve separate evidence and label the authority in the prompt. Stick with a broader multi-result retrieval strategy when freshness is more important than compact context.

There is also a boundary around identity resolution. If the input lacks a trustworthy identifier, the safe result is “possible duplicate,” not an automatic merge. Human review, a source-maintained crosswalk, or a later booking confirmation can resolve that uncertainty.

Keep the deduplication module independent from the embedding provider and the chat model. Its inputs and outputs should be plain JSON so a notebook fixture can become a batch job or an API worker without rewriting the policy. Log key versions, source IDs, and decision reasons; redact patient data from traces and enforce retention limits appropriate to your jurisdiction. Before launch, rehearse a stale-feed event, a provider rename, a timezone migration, and a partial replay. The assistant should state what it knows, cite the canonical source, and ask a focused question when identities remain ambiguous. That behavior is more valuable than squeezing another decimal point from a benchmark.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.hl7.org/fhir/
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-dm/
