title: Get the App Store and Google Play top apps list in Python (no libraries)
description:
Disclosure: I built the app store scraper used in this post and earn money when people run it. Free options are below.

Sometimes you just want the list: what's in the top 10 free apps right now, and is it the same on iPhone and Android? The store apps show you one chart at a time on one device, and you can't sort or save them. This post gets both charts into one CSV.

Free options first

  • Just looking? The Top Charts pages in the App Store and Google Play apps are free. If you only need a glance, stop here.
  • Apple only: Apple publishes free RSS feeds of its top charts at rss.marketingtools.apple.com. No key needed.
  • Android: the google-play-scraper packages for Python and Node are free. They're unofficial, so they can break when Google changes its pages.

I use the method below when I want both stores in one table, with the same columns, on a schedule.

Setup

You need Python 3 and a free Apify account (no credit card; it includes $5 of usage a month). There's nothing to install. Copy your token from Apify Console > Settings > API & Integrations:

export APIFY_TOKEN=your_token_here

The code 

import csv
import json
import os
import urllib.request

URL = ("https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/zahidthani~app-store-google-play-scraper"
       "/run-sync-get-dataset-items")

run_input = {
    "charts": ["top-free"],  # or top-paid, top-grossing
    "countries": ["us"],
    "maxResults": 10,        # per store and country
}

request = urllib.request.Request(
    URL,
    data=json.dumps(run_input).encode(),
    headers={
        "Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"],
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
)
with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=120) as response:
    apps = json.load(response)

columns = ["store", "rank", "name", "developer", "rating", "price", "genre", "url"]
with open("top_apps.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=columns, extrasaction="ignore")
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(apps)

print(f"Saved {len(apps)} apps to top_apps.csv")
for store in ("apple", "google"):
    rows = [a for a in apps if a["store"] == store]
    print(store, [a["name"] for a in rows[:3]])

The utf-8-sig encoding is there so Excel shows app names with accents and symbols correctly when you open the file.

Real output

This is the top free chart in the US from a real run on 1 November 2026:

Rank App Store Google Play
1 New York Road Runners Muse from Meta
2 TikTok Pro - Events ChatGPT
3 Muse from Meta TikTok Pro - Events
4 Vinted: Pre-loved marketplace TikTok - Videos, Shop & LIVE
5 ChatGPT WhatsApp
6 Capital One Mobile FreeReels - Dramas & Reels
7 Netflix Game Controller PineDrama - Short Dramas
8 Uber - Rides, Eats, Hotels Settings Home
9 PineDrama - Short Dramas DealSeek: Coupons & Discounts
10 Kalshi: Trade Sports & Events Vinted: Shop & sell pre-loved

Google Play rows also include a rating. App Store chart rows came back without one, so add "includeDetails": true if you need Apple ratings (it's charged at the higher details price).

What stood out: ChatGPT, Muse from Meta, TikTok Pro - Events and PineDrama are on both lists (Vinted too, under slightly different names), but about half of each top 10 isn't on the other. If you only watch one store, you miss a lot of what's moving. Charts also change daily, so your list will look different.

Adapting it

  • Another country or several: "countries": ["us", "gb", "de"]
  • Top grossing games: "charts": ["top-grossing"], "category": "games"
  • Only one store: "stores": ["google"]
  • Up to 200 per chart: "maxResults": 200 (Google Play goes up to 200, the App Store up to 100)
  • Track changes: run it daily with cron and add the date to the filename.

What it costs

$0.50 per 1,000 chart rows, plus $0.005 per run. This example (20 rows) costs about $0.015.

Limitations

  • Charts are a snapshot of what the stores show at that moment, and the two stores don't count things the same way, so a rank isn't an install count.
  • It reads public chart data only. There are no download numbers for the App Store.
  • The script waits for the result. Big multi-country jobs are better started with the Apify Python client and picked up afterwards.

Try it

  • App Store & Google Play Scraper on the Apify Store: https://apify.com/zahidthani/app-store-google-play-scraper
  • Runnable Python, Node.js and n8n examples: https://github.com/zahidthani/apify-data-tools-examples
  • Need reviews instead of charts? See my post on exporting app reviews to Excel: https://dev.to/zahidthani/export-app-store-and-google-play-reviews-to-excel-and-find-the-top-complaints-27m3
  • Rather have it set up for you? Details on my website.

title: Rate-Limited Job Processing Queue in Node.js Explained — Recovery-First Worker Design
description:
A B2B SaaS rate-limited job processing queue in Node.js should not depend on a web request staying alive. The request can enqueue a bounded batch, return, and let a worker own the slow and recoverable part.

Short answer: use a scheduler as a thin producer, a queue with a worker fixed at concurrency 1, and a durable idempotency key before each external call. Retry with backoff, nack transient failures, and send exhausted jobs to a dead-letter queue (DLQ).

That boundary is the useful design decision. Cron runs are capped at 900 seconds, while expired-record cleanup can take much longer and can be interrupted halfway through. A queue gives the work somewhere to wait after the trigger has finished.

Recovering nightly cleanup safely

Imagine a B2B SaaS product deleting expired exports every night. Each job contains a workspace ID, a cutoff timestamp, and the IDs of records eligible for deletion. The downstream storage API allows one active request from this tenant. Ten concurrent promises may look faster, but they turn a vendor limit into a burst of 429 responses.

Start with one worker. Measure later.

Standard queues are at-least-once. A process crash after the delete succeeds but before ack means the same message can be delivered again. FIFO deduplication does not solve this: its window is only five minutes. The worker must claim a business key such as workspace-42:exports:2026-08-21 in a durable store before calling the API, mark it complete after success, and acknowledge only then.

Keep queue messages small. The limit is 256 KB, retention tops out at 30 days, and an acknowledged message is removed. Put identifiers and a cutoff in the message; fetch the records from the source of truth. This is a work queue, not a Kafka-style replay log with several consumer groups.

For this cron-to-worker boundary, Infrai is a reasonable trial when self-describing HTTP matters. Its public discovery surface exposes request schemas and runnable examples, so wiring a capability is reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. One key and one bill also remove credential and invoice glue when the same account handles adjacent backend tasks. That is useful integration leverage, not a universal queue recommendation.

The worker contract is intentionally small

Treat the rate limit as an invariant in the worker loop. Consume one message, claim its key, call the downstream API, persist completion, and ack. A 429 is a scheduling signal, not permission to hot-loop: honor Retry-After when supplied, otherwise use exponential backoff, then nack for later delivery. After a bounded attempt count, send the message to a DLQ and redrive it deliberately.

I am not sure what reset window every vendor uses; your mileage will vary. Capture response headers and completion time from production-shaped batches before raising concurrency. The number 1 is a conservative starting point, not a universal benchmark.

Batching belongs on the producer side. It reduces publish round trips, but it must not change the worker's concurrency invariant. A stable batch idempotency key makes a retried publish safe during the platform's default deduplication period.

How should a Node.js queue handle concurrency 1, batch publish, retry, and idempotency?

The producer below calls the documented batch route. INFRAI_QUEUE_BATCH_JSON is the exact request body obtained from public discovery, so the example does not invent queue fields. The method, bearer header, status check, and 429 handling are explicit.

const required = (name: string): string => {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`${name} is required`);
  return value;
};

const wait = (milliseconds: number): Promise<void> =>
  new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

async function publishCleanupBatch(): Promise<unknown> {
  const body = JSON.parse(required("INFRAI_QUEUE_BATCH_JSON"));
  const apiKey = required("INFRAI_API_KEY");
  const batchKey = required("CLEANUP_BATCH_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish_batch", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": batchKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
      const seconds = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter
        : Math.min(2 ** attempt, 60);
      await wait(seconds * 1_000);
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Publish rejected (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return response.json();
  }
  throw new Error("Publish retry budget exhausted");
}

publishCleanupBatch().then((result) => console.log(result));

The worker adapter can be backed by any queue. This small TypeScript loop shows the important ordering and keeps concurrency at one without hiding retry state in a timer.

type Job = { id: string; idempotencyKey: string; attempt: number };
type Outcome = { ok: true } | { ok: false; retryAfterSeconds?: number };

interface Queue {
  consumeOne(): Promise<Job | undefined>;
  ack(job: Job): Promise<void>;
  nack(job: Job, delaySeconds: number): Promise<void>;
  sendToDlq(job: Job): Promise<void>;
}

interface IdempotencyStore {
  claim(key: string): Promise<"new" | "claimed" | "completed">;
  complete(key: string): Promise<void>;
  release(key: string): Promise<void>;
}

const pause = (seconds: number) =>
  new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, seconds * 1_000));

async function runWorker(
  queue: Queue,
  store: IdempotencyStore,
  callVendor: (job: Job) => Promise<Outcome>,
): Promise<void> {
  for (;;) {
    const job = await queue.consumeOne();
    if (!job) return;

    const state = await store.claim(job.idempotencyKey);
    if (state === "completed") {
      await queue.ack(job);
      continue;
    }
    if (state === "claimed") {
      await queue.nack(job, 1);
      continue;
    }

    const outcome = await callVendor(job);
    if (outcome.ok) {
      await store.complete(job.idempotencyKey);
      await queue.ack(job);
      continue;
    }

    await store.release(job.idempotencyKey);
    if (job.attempt >= 4) {
      await queue.sendToDlq(job);
      continue;
    }
    const delay = outcome.retryAfterSeconds ?? Math.min(2 ** job.attempt, 60);
    await pause(delay);
    await queue.nack(job, delay);
  }
}

The store needs an atomic claim operation. A process-local Map is fine for a test, but two worker processes must not both observe new. In production, make the idempotency record unique on the business key and treat a completed record as a successful duplicate.

Queue options under recovery pressure

The effective bill includes integration and incident work, not just a per-message number. Here is the comparison I use for this cleanup shape:

Option Good fit Recovery trade-off
AWS SQS Managed queue, DLQ and visibility controls in an AWS estate More AWS-specific IAM and client configuration; FIFO dedup is still time-bounded
BullMQ Node.js teams already running Redis and wanting familiar local tooling Redis durability, upgrades, and queue operations become your responsibility
Temporal Long, branching workflows, timers, and durable orchestration Heavier platform and a larger programming model for a single serial cleanup
Infrai queue A team wanting plain HTTP, public discovery, and one credential across backend capabilities It lacks DAG/workflow orchestration and fan-out joins; use Temporal or Airflow for those

Stick with SQS when your operational controls, IAM, and DLQ tooling already live in AWS. Choose BullMQ when Redis is already a reliable part of the product and keeping the worker in one Node.js codebase beats adding an HTTP boundary. Choose Temporal when cleanup is only one branch in a workflow with timers, compensation, or joins.

First, move the idempotency record to the same transactional boundary as the business state when possible. Otherwise a crash between “vendor succeeded” and “record complete” still needs a reconciliation job. Second, expose queue age, attempt count, DLQ depth, and 429 rate as operational metrics. Third, shard by tenant only after measuring the vendor's actual quota; sharding is a controlled increase in concurrency, not a free optimization.

The cron endpoint should remain boring: validate the schedule, publish a batch, and return. Cron tasks accept only public HTTP URLs, and a single run cannot exceed 900 seconds. Long cleanup belongs in the worker. There is no native debounce or throttle, so model those semantics in the producer or separate queues; missed triggers while cron is paused are not replayed automatically.

No giant framework required.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the queue capability details and request schemas at Infrai discovery. Then run the same recovery test against your real downstream limit before changing the worker invariant.

Sources

  • https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.publish
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/architecture
  • https://docs.temporal.io/workflows
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html

title: Font Loading Is a Layout Decision: Measured Shift for swap, optional, fallback and block
description:
Most advice about font-display stops at "use swap unless you can't stand the flash". That framing is wrong in two ways. First, swap is not a single behaviour — it is a three-phase timing contract, and what your page does depends on where the font lands inside those phases. Second, the layout shift it causes is not just "text gets slightly wider". On a page that sizes anything in ch, the swap changes the width of the container itself, which changes the line count, which moves everything below it.

I built a small harness to measure this rather than argue about it. Everything below is a number I actually got out of it, with the limits stated at the end.

The setup

One page, one viewport (1366×768), Chromium (system Chrome, driven by Playwright), served over http://127.0.0.1 so the font request can be genuinely intercepted and delayed. Three @font-face rules for Plus Jakarta Sans 400/600/700 — the font the Design Den site actually loads — and a fallback stack identical to the one in that site's index.html:

:root { --font: "Plus Jakarta Sans", system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, sans-serif; }

The page is a hero: a display heading on clamp(3rem, 7vw, 7rem) with line-height: .92, a lede paragraph at font-size: 19px; max-width: 52ch, and a pill button underneath. The font response is delayed by 1200 ms to simulate a cold fetch on a real network.

That 52ch is the whole story, and almost nobody notices it.

The mechanism people miss: ch re-resolves when the font swaps

ch is defined as the advance measure of the "0" glyph in the element's current font. So max-width: 52ch is not a fixed width. It is a width that is recomputed the moment the used font changes.

Sampled geometry from the harness, same page, same viewport, nothing else touching it:

Moment Used font 52ch resolves to Lede height Button top
t = 70 ms (fallback render) system-ui → Segoe UI 533 px 88 px (3 lines) 456 px
t = 1270 ms (after swap) Plus Jakarta Sans 723 px 59 px (2 lines) 427 px

The paragraph got 190 px wider — a 35.6 % jump in the column — not because the text grew, but because the "0" glyph in Plus Jakarta Sans is much wider than the "0" in Segoe UI. A wider column fit the same sentence in two lines instead of three. The document height went from 673 px to 644 px and the button moved up 29 px.

So the visible symptom is not "the text wobbles". It is "a paragraph changes its own width and everything under it slides". On a real page with a hero image, a sticky nav offset, or a min-height: 100vh section, that same reflow can push content across a fold.

For reference, the advance-width probe on a 68-character sample string at 700 112px:

  • fallback (system-ui → Segoe UI): 3716.51 px
  • Plus Jakarta Sans: 3885.39 px
  • the webfont is 4.54 % wider on that string

A 4.5 % width difference sounds trivial. Through ch, it became a 35.6 % container difference.

CLS per strategy, repeated three times

The only thing that moves on this page is the button, and it moves only because the lede reflows at the swap — so every layout-shift entry is attributable to the font swap. Each row below is 3 identical repeat runs.

font-display Font arrives at 1200 ms CLS Final 52ch
swap yes 0.00083 723 px
fallback yes 0.00083 723 px
block yes 0.00026 723 px
optional no — font never used for this load 0 533 px
swap + size-adjust/ascent/descent: 96%, line-gap: 0% yes 0.00779 694 px

All values were stable across the repeats — the same configuration gave the identical CLS three times. One earlier single-run sample of fallback reported 0.00581; the repeat run reported 0.00083, and I am quoting the repeat.

What optional is actually doing here

display: optional gives you a ~100 ms block period and a zero-length swap period. If the font is not available when the text is first laid out, the browser uses the fallback for the entire document lifetime and only considers the webfont on a later navigation.

That is why CLS is exactly zero and why the lede stayed at 533 px: the webfont never rendered at all on that load. optional does not fix the shift. It declines the font.

That is a legitimate engineering choice, and it is the one the Design Den homepage makes. Its markup is:

<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
<!-- Optional fonts avoid a late typography swap; generated local CSS is inlined for first paint. -->
<link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Plus+Jakarta+Sans:wght@400;600;700&display=optional"
      rel="stylesheet" media="print" onload="this.media='all'">

media="print" with an onload promotion to all keeps the Google Fonts stylesheet out of the critical path, and display=optional keeps the swap from happening mid-session. The cost is real and should be said out loud: on a first visit over a slow connection, a large part of your audience never sees your brand typeface. They see Segoe UI, or Roboto, or whatever the platform hands back. Your carefully chosen display face is a repeat-visit reward.

If brand typography is load-bearing for you — a studio, a fashion label, a luxury brand — optional may be the wrong trade. If legibility and stability are load-bearing — a form, a booking flow, a legal site — it is a strong one. Decide it deliberately instead of inheriting swap from a boilerplate.

Metric overrides made it worse, not better

The standard advice is to measure the fallback's metrics and apply size-adjust, ascent-override, descent-override and line-gap-override so the webfont occupies the same space. In this harness, applying a plausible-looking flat 96 % to all of them:

@font-face {
  font-family: 'PJS';
  font-weight: 700;
  font-display: swap;
  src: url('/fonts/pjs-700.woff2');
  size-adjust: 96%;
  ascent-override: 96%;
  descent-override: 96%;
  line-gap-override: 0%;
}

…moved the final column width closer to the fallback (694 px instead of 723 px, against 533 px), which is the intended direction — and increased CLS from 0.00083 to 0.00779, roughly nine times worse. The overrides changed the box metrics, not only the advance width, so they altered how many lines the paragraph needed and where things sat, producing additional shift entries.

I am not claiming overrides are bad. I am claiming that a copied percentage is a guess, and that a guess here made the metric you are trying to protect go up. Compute the values against your actual fallback font on your actual target platforms, then measure. If you cannot measure, do not ship them.

The naming trap: text-size-adjust is not size-adjust

While checking this, I found four matches for "size-adjust" in the Design Den CSS — and all four were text-size-adjust: 100% in responsive.css:

body {
  -webkit-text-size-adjust: 100%;
  text-size-adjust: 100%;
}

That is a completely different property. text-size-adjust stops mobile browsers from inflating font sizes when they think text is too small to read. size-adjust scales one font face's metrics. Having one in your CSS does not mean you have addressed font swap, and searching your codebase for one finds the other. Worth knowing before you tell yourself this is already handled.

How to measure it yourself

Two things that cost me time:

1. Do not trust document.fonts.check() for "was the font used". In this harness it returned true for display: optional runs where the font demonstrably never rendered. The reliable signal is geometry: measure the rendered width of a ch-sized element, or the document height, and compare against the known fallback value.

2. layout-shift entries are silently not delivered in some automation configurations. My first harness reported CLS 0 for every strategy, which looked like a clean result and was completely false. The cause was navigating with waitUntil: 'commit'. The same page, same observer, same mutation reported shifts correctly under waitUntil: 'load'. A zero you cannot explain is not a measurement — run a deliberate control shift (insert a 200 px block and confirm the observer fires) before you believe any CLS number coming out of a script.

The observer itself is short:

let cls = 0;
new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const e of list.getEntries()) if (!e.hadRecentInput) cls += e.value;
}).observe({ type: 'layout-shift', buffered: true });

buffered: true matters, or you miss the entries that happened before your script ran.

What I would decide before choosing a font

  1. Pick the font-display behaviour as a brand decision, not a default. optional buys stability and costs first-visit brand type. swap buys the typeface and costs a reflow. Both are defensible; an unexamined one is not.
  2. Stop sizing layout boxes in ch if you are swapping fonts. max-width: 65ch is a nice readable-measure heuristic, but it makes your layout depend on a glyph metric that changes during load. Use rem or a clamp() with a px ceiling for anything whose width affects line count below the fold.
  3. Reserve the space, then measure the reserve. The fix for font shift is the same fix for image shift: give the container a height that does not depend on which font won.
  4. Treat metric overrides as an optimisation with a verification step, not a checklist item.
  5. Preconnect to the font origin. It is one line and it moves the arrival time, which is the variable every strategy keys off.

Limits of this experiment

One machine, one viewport, one Windows fallback (Segoe UI), one font pair, one paragraph, no CPU throttling, no real network RTT — the delay was injected, not measured. These numbers rank strategies on this page; they do not describe your site or anyone's field data, and I would not quote them as a Core Web Vitals prediction. The ch mechanism, the optional behaviour and the override result are the parts I would generalise. The absolute CLS values are the parts you should re-measure.

Disclosure: this article was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy by Design Den; the accompanying cover is a conceptual AI-generated 3D illustration with the official Design Den Solutions logo composited unchanged, not a screenshot of any real page. All figures come from the harness described above.

Design Den Solutions builds and maintains responsive websites in Mohali / Chandigarh with performance basics, semantic structure and load-time checks handled as part of the build rather than bolted on afterwards — details on the web design and development service page.

title: Inside an enterprise AI agent: A governed, observable loop architecture
description: This post lays out a five-layer reference architecture for governed, observable enterprise AI agents on AWS: an API gateway, a five-phase agent runtime, a knowledge and state tier, platform services, and a cross-cutting trust and control framework. Each layer maps to managed AWS services, with the design patterns worth copying and the mistakes to avoid.

title: Database observability Dynatrace: slow queries with PostgreSQL
description:
It is 10:40, checkout takes eight seconds to respond, and the application dashboard points a finger at « the database ». Database observability Dynatrace offers a way past that vague suspicion: an application called Databases, fed by an extension that an ActiveGate uses to query PostgreSQL. Here is how I would run it, from the suspicious trace down to the execution-plan node that burns the time.

One framing note first: everything below is about Dynatrace SaaS. The pages I read talk about Grail, the Hub and the Platform Subscription, and nothing says Managed behaves the same, so I do not claim it. If you only want the extension itself, another post covers it: the database extension article. This one starts from the symptom.

Database observability Dynatrace: from symptom to query

A trace shows a SQL call lasting several seconds. That proves the database is making someone wait, nothing more. To act, you need three answers in order: which statement weighs most over the period, where its time goes (compute, disk, locks), and which node of its plan is responsible. The Databases app answers all three, provided the extension is in place. Without it, the tabs stay stubbornly empty.

No agent runs on the database servers: the extension reads metrics and query statistics remotely. The useful tabs are Overview (overall health), Explorer (CPU, memory, active sessions per instance), Databases, Tables and Indexes (including low-value indexes), Recommendations (extension version, databases found but unmonitored, missing plans) and Alert templates (ready-made alerts per vendor). Other engines are covered too: Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL, Snowflake, SAP HANA, DB2, MariaDB. I only read the PostgreSQL page closely.

Before opening the console: a field checklist

What has cost me the most time elsewhere is meeting a prerequisite halfway through a wizard. So I check these first:

  • the Databases app is installed from the Hub;
  • an Environment ActiveGate on 1.341.0 or later, with the Extension Execution Controller on, can reach the PostgreSQL server (see Environment ActiveGate or Cluster ActiveGate);
  • the PostgreSQL extension is at 3.2.4 or later (3.1.2 for MySQL);
  • you hold settings:objects:write on builtin:licensing.new-database-monitoring-experience, or the Settings Writer policy, and this monitoring is part of your Platform Subscription;
  • the connection goes straight to the monitored host: no load balancer, proxy or pooler such as pg-pool, otherwise a failover muddles the measurements;
  • log ingestion is on, since top queries are stored as logs.

Getting PostgreSQL ready without surprises

Two settings decide the quality of the data. First, pg_stat_statements must be in shared_preload_libraries; self-hosted, that means editing postgresql.conf and restarting, and also installing the hypopg binaries. On RDS, Cloud SQL or Azure, the provider’s parameter group is the source of truth. Second, track_activity_query_size must be raised to 4096: at the default 1024, long queries arrive cut off and become unreadable.

You then need a dedicated read-only account through the pg_monitor role, plus a dynatrace schema that will hold the function used to fetch plans. The capture below, taken from the documentation, shows the SQL to run.

The password behind the <PASSWORD> placeholder should come from your vault, not a shared file. On RDS or Aurora, IAM authentication removes that secret altogether (ActiveGate 1.325 or later).

Declaring the instance in the wizard

« Add DB instance » walks through six screens, which I summarise by what actually matters. Pick PostgreSQL as vendor, then the ActiveGate group: it will carry the polling load, so choose one with a network view of the database. Next comes configuration: frequency and feature sets, chiefly Queries and Index Recommendations. For the connection, the documentation advises one database per instance, often postgres. Finally, two scripts to download, install and validation, to run from a Unix machine with Bash and psql. Once validation passes, « Start monitoring » begins collection.

First check: in Recommendations, « Monitor extension status » should read « Up to date » with a clean extension log, and the instance should show in Explorer. Data lands in the Grail bucket default_database_monitoring.

Tracking down the guilty query

Three streams feed the analysis, all stored as logs and recognisable by their event.group:

  • top_queries: the 100 costliest statements by cumulative time, sampled from pg_stat_statements every 5 minutes;
  • longest_queries: the longest executions seen in pg_stat_activity, with the Queries feature set;
  • execution_plans: the plan of a top query, fetched through the helper function.

In the statement analysis view, I filter on a fragment of SQL text and flip between Time, CPU, Disk and Waits. My own rule of thumb (it is not from the documentation): lots of Time and little CPU means the query is waiting, on locks or I/O; lots of both means pure computation, and the plan probably has a problem.

Then open the plan. The diagram gives each node a cost and highlights the heaviest. In the example below, a single join absorbs 95.7% of the total cost across seven nodes, so there is no point fussing over the rest.

Source : docs.dynatrace.com

If the dominant node is a full table scan on a very frequent query, suspect a missing index: hypopg exists precisely to try hypothetical indexes without creating them. To cross-check against what applications write in their logs, the method in log pattern analysis pairs well with this work.

Where it can bite

  • ALTER statements are kept out of top queries, for security.
  • Getting a plan needs extensions:configuration.actions:write, and the request must come from the database that hosts the helper function.
  • On managed services, monitoring has limits and needs manual setup, per the documentation.
  • The extension is free but ingested metrics are billed, logs on top. The doc’s estimate: (68 × instances) + (40 × databases) + (1 × tablespaces) data points per minute.
  • After every extension update, re-run the install and validation scripts, or metrics, top queries or plans may stop.
  • Not verified here: MySQL details, Dynatrace Managed, and any DQL query on these logs (so I offer none).

My adoption plan

Start on a test database with a single feature set, watch the data-point bill, then widen. Reserve an ActiveGate group for databases, with validated network rules. Restrict read access to the default_database_monitoring bucket through a dedicated policy. Finally, tie a SQL latency threshold to an objective: the SLO and SLA learning path shows how.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need OneAgent on the database server?

Not for the extension, which runs without an agent on database hosts: an ActiveGate queries the database remotely. The host metrics shown in Overview, however, come from hosts running OneAgent.

Does this method work with MySQL?

The upgrade page lists MySQL 3.1.2 or later with the same wizard. MySQL grants and settings are not verified here; follow the MySQL extension page.

Where can I see slow queries without opening the application?

Top queries, longest queries and plans are logs tagged by event.group: look for them in the log tool, after checking the bucket and your read permissions.

In short

For Database observability Dynatrace, remember the sequence: prepared instance, extension set up by the wizard, then reading top queries, the Time/CPU/Disk/Waits axes and the execution plan. Source: Dynatrace documentation, Get started with database monitoring.

This blog is independent and not affiliated with Dynatrace LLC. The information comes from the official documentation, read in November 2026; check it before any production use.

Originally published on span.observer. French version: https://span.observer/fr/database-observability-dynatrace/.

title: Kubernetes Python client gets a modern overhaul for the AI/ML era
description:
by Yu Liao, Haowei Cai, and Federico Bongiovanni, Google Cloud Kubernetes Engineering & SIG API Machinery

When you train a large language model with Kubeflow, orchestrate distributed compute with Ray on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), serve inference traffic with KServe, or schedule thousands of ML pipeline pods with Apache Airflow, two technologies almost always meet under the hood: Python and Kubernetes.

Python is the undisputed lingua franca of artificial intelligence and machine learning. Kubernetes is the de facto operating system for AI infrastructure—scheduling GPUs and TPUs, orchestrating distributed training jobs, and scaling model serving endpoints. Connecting these two worlds is the official Kubernetes Python client (kubernetes-client/python).

Second only to Kubernetes's in-tree Go client (client-go) in popularity, the Kubernetes Python client is downloaded more than 73 million times per month on PyPI (~1.7 million times a day) and has earned over 7,500 GitHub stars.

Yet for the past several years, this critical bridge between Python and Kubernetes has operated in low-maintenance mode. As AI/ML workloads have exploded in scale and complexity, the gap between what modern AI infrastructure demands and what the legacy Python client was built to deliver has become impossible to ignore.

Today, we're sharing how Google Cloud engineers are partnering with open source contributors in Kubernetes SIG API Machinery to modernize the official Kubernetes Python client for the AI/ML era.

The historical problem: Legacy machinery meets hyperscale AI

As AI/ML clusters grew from dozens of nodes to 50,000-node hyperscale environments, the limitations of the Python client's aging architecture began surfacing as real-world production bottlenecks:

  1. Frozen on a decommissioned code generator: Up through Kubernetes 1.35, the Python client generated its ~400,000 lines of API and model code using OpenAPI Generator v4.3.0 (python-legacy)—a generator version that was deprecated in 2020 and completely removed from the upstream OpenAPI Generator project in May 2022. Staying pinned to v4.3.0 meant the client accumulated DeprecationWarning debt across newer Python releases, struggled with modern dependency resolution alongside PyTorch and TensorFlow, and couldn't easily receive upstream generator bug fixes.
  2. Synchronous-only execution in an asyncio world: Modern Python web frameworks, inference servers, and orchestrators have overwhelmingly shifted to asyncio to handle high-concurrency I/O without being bottlenecked by Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL). Because the official client lacked native asyncio support from the start, users were forced to turn to community clients like kubernetes-asyncio or third-party clients (kr8s, lightkube).
  3. Missing controller primitives (SharedInformer): In Go, controllers use SharedInformer to maintain a local, event-driven cache of cluster resources without repeatedly polling kube-apiserver. Without an equivalent primitive in Python, applications watching thousands of training pods or custom resources often hammered the API server or ran into watch disconnects.
  4. Slow model deserialization and HTTP/1.1 transport limits: In large clusters, listing pods or nodes in Python could take 30+ seconds due to excessive model reconfiguration during JSON deserialization (issue #1921). Combined with an underlying urllib3 transport layer restricted to HTTP/1.1, Python workloads missed out on the HTTP/2 multiplexing, flow control, and binary framing that make client-go fast at scale.

A principled approach: Built for AI/ML, not 1:1 parity

When we set out to modernize the Kubernetes Python client, we established two guiding principles to ensure our engineering investments deliver the highest possible return for the community:

  1. Target high-impact gaps, not 1:1 client-go parity: client-go is the in-tree Kubernetes client used by the control plane itself (kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler, and in-tree controllers). Attempting to replicate every long-tail client-go feature in Python would yield diminishing returns. Instead, we focus strictly on the primitives Python developers and operators actually need in production.
  2. Prioritize AI/ML workload requirements: Because AI/ML training, inference, and batch frameworks are the primary drivers of Python on Kubernetes today, every architectural improvement—from async concurrency and CRD ergonomics to large-cluster list performance—is prioritized through the lens of AI/ML scale.

How we're modernizing the Kubernetes Python client

Our roadmap focuses on three technical pillars: Machinery, Features, and Performance.

1. Machinery: Upgrading to OpenAPI Generator v7.20+

Every improvement to the Python client starts with its code generation pipeline (kubernetes-client/gen). Over the past few years, multiple community attempts to migrate off the decommissioned v4.3.0 python-legacy generator stalled due to the sheer scale of template and schema changes across hundreds of Kubernetes API models.

We are actively driving the migration to OpenAPI Generator v7.20.0+ and establishing continuous tracking with upstream generator releases. Completing this foundational upgrade:

  • Replaces dead python-legacy templates with actively maintained v7+ Python code generation.
  • Modernizes type annotations and packaging metadata, easing pip dependency resolution alongside heavy ML frameworks.
  • Unlocks the ability to contribute performance and serialization fixes directly to upstream OpenAPI Generator templates.

2. Features: Native asyncio, Shared Informers, and WebSocket v5

To prevent ecosystem fragmentation and give Python developers first-class Kubernetes primitives out of the box, we are bringing three major capabilities to the official client:

  • Official asyncio support: Rather than forcing developers to choose between the official synchronous client and third-party async libraries, we are introducing official asyncio support directly into kubernetes-client/python. Async-first ML orchestrators, FastAPI-based model control planes, and notebooks will be able to issue concurrent, non-blocking Kubernetes API calls natively.
  • Shared Informers (kubernetes-client/python#2515): We are bringing the SharedInformer pattern to the Python client. With built-in list-watch caching, automatic reconnection, and resource event handlers (on_add, on_update, on_delete), Python controllers and AI job managers can monitor cluster state and Custom Resources (TrainJob, RayCluster, InferenceService) with a fraction of the memory footprint and API server load.
  • WebSocket v5 streaming (KEP-4006, kubernetes-client/python#2486): As upstream Kubernetes transitions remote command streaming (exec, attach, port-forward) away from legacy SPDY to standard WebSockets via the v5.channel.k8s.io subprotocol, we are adding native WebSocket v5 channel support so interactive debugging and remote job execution work seamlessly against modern control planes.

3. Performance: Slashing deserialization overhead

For AI/ML platforms operating on multi-thousand-node clusters, client performance is an availability requirement. Our performance track targets the largest bottlenecks in Python client execution:

  • Eliminating model reconfiguration overhead: When deserializing large JSON responses (such as listing tens of thousands of Pods across a training cluster), the legacy generated model layer repeatedly instantiates and reconfigures schema validation objects (issue #1921). With the move to OpenAPI Generator v7+, we are revamping model initialization so large cluster queries deserialize in a fraction of the time.

What's next and how to get involved

The intersection of Python and Kubernetes is where modern AI infrastructure is built. By modernizing the code generation machinery, adding native asyncio and SharedInformer primitives, and closing the deserialization performance gap, we aim to give every ML engineer and platform builder a fast, reliable, and Pythonic official client—whether they are running a single notebook experiment or orchestrating a 50,000-node GKE training fleet.

This effort is happening in the open under Kubernetes SIG API Machinery, and we welcome feedback, use cases, and contributions from the community:

  • Explore the repository and roadmap: Check out kubernetes-client/python and kubernetes-client/gen on GitHub.
  • Join the conversation: Connect with us in the #sig-api-machinery channel on Kubernetes Slack or at the bi-weekly Kubernetes Python client triage meetings.

title: The Sitting of November 12–13, 2026 — Release Day, Two Bad Release Notes, and One PHPStan Bug
description:
A journal entry, written between pushes.

On November 9 I posted what I knew: the ecosystem was moving unevenly, and I was tired. Three days later, November 12 came around and the whole sitting lasted longer than I expected. The machine got hot. The logs were everywhere. Two packages released, two release notes broke, one bug made PHP cry TypeError on production-shaped data, and I went to bed with the CI green — finally.

I'm writing this the morning after, when the timestamps still mean something and the shame of the previous night is fresh enough to be useful.

Nov 12, late afternoon — the rewrite matures

The thing I've been carrying since v2.0.0 finally stopped being a workaround and became a finish line.

turso-api-client-php v2.0.0 is out, and the v1 API is gone. Just gone. No compatibility shim, no polite migration path from the old new Client('org', 'token'). The builder only entry point (Client::builder()->withToken(…)->withOrganization(…)) forced every consumer to decide what organization they were talking to — no implicit guessing from token. 53 of 53 operations from the pinned OpenAPI snapshot, SHA-256 328d56b8…, mapped into the coverage manifest. Typed exception hierarchy rooted at PlatformException. PSR-18/17/7 everywhere.

I spent most of this sitting writing about it in tests, docs, and a wiki that must not lie. That's the part nobody tells you: the rewrite was mostly verification. Making sure the pinned snapshot and the code agreed with each other — operation by operation — and then making sure the CI pipeline would enforce it forever after.

Nothing about this felt like progress. It felt like cleanup. But I have learned, the hard way, that cleanup at this layer is where the security and reliability actually live. Typed exceptions don't fix your app, but they do arguably stop you from catching a empty success body as if it were valid JSON.

Also, the upload-proof is real this time: a Docker harness that builds a clean PHP app (8.3 / 8.4 / 8.5) path-requiring the checkout, creates a scratch database with seed.type = 'database_upload', mints a JWT, uploads an SQLite dump with the correct PRAGMAs, reads the row back over Hrana /v2/pipeline, then — crucially — deletes the scratch database. All 8/8 checks green across three matrix legs, verified live against Turso Cloud on 2026-11-12.

I stopped believing "it compiles." I now believe "the scratch database was deleted."

Nov 12, evening — the envelope that lied

Here is the paragraph where I confess something.

DELETE /v1/organizations/{organizationSlug}/databases/{databaseName} replies with a scalar-string envelope:

{ "database": "my-app-production" }

The snapshot said that clearly. My implementation pretended it didn't. Databases::delete() declared : array and returned $decoded['database'] ?? $decoded.

For a short window of v2.0.0, every delete operation on a database — the most basic database administration — threw a TypeError and nothing else. In the Docker upload proof, everything passed except scratch_db_deleted. I stared at the log for about a second before remembering that “assuming the contract is right” is exactly the kind of assumption this rewrite is supposed to kill.

The fix took five minutes. The context took three months.

Databases::delete() now returns string|array, returning the scalar when present, verbatim otherwise. The test asserts {"database": "db1"} as a contract-correct shape instead of the objectified version I had been shipping. v2.1.0 followed later in the day with the fix, the hermetic temp-path tests, PHPStan level 6, and the green matrix across 8.3/8.4/8.5.

Nov 12, night — the Laravel adapter hour

Between v2.0.0 dropping lint and v2.1.0 marking green, the Laravel adapter — turso-platform-laravel — shipped too. It is not a big package: a service provider, a facade, a publishable config (turso-platform-config), and a thin manager around the SDK client. It binds lazily, aliasing the binding to Client::class, so controllers and jobs can type-hint the core SDK directly.

It shipped because it was ready, not because a blog post needed a new number. v1.0.0 went to Packagist 782 releases into the ecosystem. CI Matrix PHP 8.3/8.4/8.5 × Laravel 12 + package-discovery tests (7 tests / 14 assertions) all green, submitted manually because Packagist doesn't auto-bootstrap unprepared GitHub repos the same way.

And then PHPStan level 6 walked in and ruined something I had been very pleased with.

TursoPlatformManager::token() did:

$token = getenv('TURSO_PLATFORM_API_TOKEN') ?? '';
if ($token === '') {
    throw new ConfigurationException('…');
}

getenv() returns string|false. The ?? '' only catches null. So a fully unset env var produced false, false === '' was false, no exception was thrown, and false walked straight into withToken(). The documented “missing token → ConfigurationException” path never ran, anywhere, ever.

The fix is boring:

$token = getenv('TURSO_PLATFORM_API_TOKEN');
if (!is_string($token) || $token === '') { … }

PHPStan had found this before any of us had: it was the one error level 6 reported after we cleaned the ~50 iterableValue docblocks — and it was a real bug, not style. v1.1.0 followed hours later.

If you remember one thing from this, remember this sentence: static analysis that only catches style is a lint, static analysis that catches wrong code is a witness.

The Oh-No Moments Nobody Publishes

Three failures from this sitting that are not in most changelogs, but are in every honest one. They happened in this order:

First, .github/workflows/tests.yml got rejected on push. My token didn't carry the workflow scope. gh auth refresh -h github.com -s workflow — more specifically env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh auth refresh -h github.com -s workflow because GITHUB_TOKEN was set in the shell and masking gh's keyring — fixed it. The workflow file itself was fine. The credential discipline was not.

Second, the CI was red on all three legs. Not because of the code. Because tests/IntegrationsTest.php wrote its SQLite scratch files to /tmp/opencode/pu_test_xxx.db, which is a path that exists on one developer workstation in this entire universe. The runner cannot see it. SQLSTATE[HY000] [14] unable to open database file, and it failed 78 tests in three matrix legs at once. The fix was un-glamorous: sys_get_temp_dir() + bin2hex(random_bytes(4)). Two lines. A whole CI afternoon.

Third, the release notes were blank. Both v2.1.0 and v1.1.0 initially went out with the body text File not found:. The notes file had been created by a shell that glued together a multi-line heredoc incorrectly and secreted the literal string “File not found: ” into the markdown file. GitHub then rendered exactly that. You were the one who told me — “Release note hanya menampilkan File not found:.” Both bodies were rewritten within the hour, the family was scanned (all other releases were fine), and the lesson — verify the release body before announcing, not after — went into the global checklist.

I will keep this pattern on screen forever, as the fastest lesson to teach the next person who encounters my work: the hardest bugs are paths, the hardest errors are blanks, and the toughest days are the ones where nothing looks broken until you look at it sideways.

The Weekend Checklist

Between everything, the docs caught up. The PHP ecosystem now has:

  • An at-a-glance table in the ecosystem repo listing every package, version, and requirement — verified against Packagist and tags, not memory.
  • A map of 53/53 operations to their SDK resource classes (docs/api-map.md for the SDK, docs/facade-map.md for the Laravel adapter), with the live contract quirks documented — scalar-string delete envelope, empty-2xx bodies, v3 UUID-vs-slug, upload pre-flight PRAGMAs.
  • A troubleshooting doc for every failure we observed. No invented symptoms. No “might happen.”
  • Wikis mirroring all of it (repo docs remain the source of truth — wikis are projections, not originals).
  • A banner / art / README refresh for both package siblings — because ecosystems where your eyes land matter.

On November 13 the ecosystem README got its own correction: the Laravel and Symfony "Examples" sections were removed, per my own instinct that the example apps have earned their keep but not the cover page. They still exist; they are now merely not advertised.

Current Status

  • turso-api-client-php v2.1.0 — released, Packagist ^2.1, CI 3/3 green, 53/53 operations, upload-proof verified.
  • turso-platform-laravel v1.1.0 — released the same sitting, Packagist crawled via webhook (manual update-package rejected my .env token; the webhook wins every single time — always verify via the p2 metadata instead of assuming an HTTP request says either yes or no).
  • turso-client-http v3.0.1 shipped earlier in the week (verified green) — the HTTP layer of the family of "A thing you composer require and then forget exists."
  • turso-installer's README now carries correct requirements, PHP 8.1–8.5 extension coverage; its queue is honest about what's outstanding.
  • The ecosystem README posted today — Nov 13, 2026.

These are not ordinary numbers for someone doing this between client projects. None of this was planned to happen inside one sitting. That's the grace — and the pathology — of a solo-maintained ecosystem.

The Takeaway

I woke up November 13 with two virtual pages of what I had done and an eight-word summary of how it felt:

"It's not done until CI says so."

It wasn't a rule before the sitting. It is a rule now — one release, one badge, one verification at a time.

The AI didn't do the work. The AI helped with parts of the mechanism, but the judgment — what “done” means, when to stop designing versus start releasing, which env file contains a token that will be rotten tomorrow — none of that got delegated. I wrote every claim in the docs by verifying it, checking it off against a repo tag or a CI log. It took longer than "paint the API and ship it." It was also the only way I knew I could keep the library I was asked to maintain.

It is the second time I have said this somewhere public, and I still mean it: trust evidence, not résumés. Trust the scratch database being deleted and the next release shipping clean. Everything else follows.

The numbered list for the people who skimmed:

  1. turso-api-client-php v2.0.0 (2026-11-12) — typed rewrite against the pinned OpenAPI snapshot, 53/53 operations, builder-only, org-scope explicit.
  2. turso-api-client-php v2.1.0 (2026-11-12) — DatabaseUploader / RegionResolver integrations, scalar-string delete envelope fix, PHPStan level 6, hermetic CI 8.3/8.4/8.5, upload-proof matrix green live.
  3. turso-platform-laravel v1.0.0 (2026-11-12) — SP + Facade + publishable config, 7/14 Testbench suite green.
  4. turso-platform-laravel v1.1.0 (2026-11-12) — PHPStan level 6 + the getenv() bugfix, docs & wiki & art.
  5. turso-client-http v3.0.0 → v3.0.1 — v3 line live.
  6. Repo of record — turso-php-ecosystem README refreshed (2026-11-13).

Previous post in this series: Maintaining the Turso PHP Ecosystem in My Spare Time: What Happened on November 9, 2026.

title: Lambda Web Functions: reporte mide 5-7 min de memoria ociosa
description:
AWS Lambda Web Functions, el servicio que AWS anunció en octubre con servidores HTTP nativos y facturación por CPU activa, llegó con la promesa de reemplazar buena parte de la infraestructura casera que muchas empresas construyen sobre Lambda clásica. Easel.sh, una plataforma de despliegue, lo probó durante varias semanas y encontró un problema que la documentación de AWS no aclara: un entorno inactivo sigue facturando memoria entre 5 y 7 minutos después de atender la última petición, sin ningún parámetro para acortar ese margen. La empresa terminó construyendo su propio compute y, de paso, midió que respondía hasta 3,5 veces más rápido que AWS Lambda Web Functions.

A diferencia de Lambda clásica, que ejecuta una función por invocación y la apaga enseguida, Web Functions mantiene un servidor capaz de atender varias peticiones a la vez. Para una empresa como Easel, que opera infraestructura de despliegue para miles de aplicaciones de terceros, eso prometía reemplazar buena parte del trabajo que ya habían invertido en correr apps web eficientemente sobre Lambda clásica.

AWS Lambda Web Functions: nueve segundos para arrancar, cinco minutos facturando sin uso

Las primeras pruebas de Easel fueron buenas. Web Functions manejó 300 peticiones concurrentes sin errores y una función nueva ya atendía tráfico en menos de nueve segundos, según el reporte de la empresa. El problema apareció después: AWS documenta que Web Functions facturan memoria durante toda la vida del entorno de ejecución, incluso sin peticiones corriendo, pero no especifica cuánto tiempo sigue vivo un entorno ocioso antes de apagarse.

Easel midió seis entornos representativos y, según su propio reporte, encontró períodos ociosos de entre 313 y 411 segundos (poco más de 5 a casi 7 minutos), sin ningún timeout configurable para acortarlos. Para una petición de 200 milisegundos seguida de 345 segundos de inactividad, eso equivale a facturar memoria por un tiempo unas 1.700 veces mayor que la propia petición. En su comparación con AWS Cost Explorer, la memoria representó alrededor del 88% del costo calculado de cómputo y peticiones a precios de lista, aunque la aplicación de prueba solo usaba entre 160 y 210 MB.

El experimento completo costó apenas unos dos centavos de dólar a precios de lista, así que para una app con tráfico constante el problema puede no importar mucho: el mismo entorno atiende muchas peticiones y reparte el costo ocioso entre todas. Pero Easel aloja miles de aplicaciones con tráfico impredecible, muchas de las cuales reciben solo un puñado de peticiones al día. Multiplicado por miles de despliegues independientes, la cuenta cambia.

📌 Nota: Easel probó apagar sus propios entornos a los 10 segundos de inactividad. Eso redujo el tiempo de entorno facturado unas 20 veces, pero AWS registró cada cierre voluntario como un fallo de runtime, algo que la empresa no quiso arriesgar en producción.
Easel.sh midió entornos ociosos de 313 a 411 segundos antes de probar compute propio.

Compute propio: de 1,5 a 3,5 veces más rápido en el mismo Next.js

En vez de adoptar Web Functions, Easel movió la ejecución a servidores que opera ella misma, dejando la Lambda clásica solo para el desborde de tráfico. El primer host de compute propio entró en producción en el este de Estados Unidos el 2 de noviembre de 2026, sirviendo aplicaciones de clientes y el propio sitio de Easel.

Para comparar el rendimiento, la empresa desplegó la misma aplicación Next.js 16 en ambas plataformas y corrió benchmarks desde un cliente en Ashburn, Virginia, según su propio reporte. El resultado fue de 1,5 a 3 veces más rápido en tiempo de respuesta en caliente en los cuatro tipos de carga que probó: una API JSON tardó 9,3 ms en Easel frente a 27,0 ms en Web Functions (2,9 veces), el renderizado del lado del servidor pasó de 26,0 ms a 12,2 ms (2,1 veces), el primer fragmento de una respuesta en streaming bajó de 18,1 ms a 9,1 ms (2,0 veces) y una API con uso intensivo de CPU pasó de 61,4 ms a 39,7 ms (1,5 veces).

La diferencia no fue solo enrutamiento de red: 20.000 operaciones SHA-256 encadenadas tardaron 29,2 ms en el host de Easel frente a 43,8 ms en Web Functions, 1,5 veces más rápido en cómputo puro. En arranque en frío, tras dejar ambas aplicaciones inactivas 12 minutos, Easel respondió en 216 a 250 ms contra 810 a 854 ms de AWS en dos pruebas pareadas, unas 3,5 veces más rápido. Después de un período más corto de cinco minutos de inactividad, Web Functions ya había terminado su entorno y necesitó 908 ms para responder, mientras que Easel reanudó su entorno pausado en apenas 14 ms.

Lambda clásica y Vercel Fluid Compute: el mismo dilema, otro compromiso

Easel no es la primera en chocar con la facturación de memoria ociosa. En la discusión que generó el caso en Hacker News, un usuario identificado como Onavo apuntó que Fluid Compute de Vercel tiene un comportamiento "más correcto", posiblemente porque corre sobre la misma infraestructura de AWS (que además es inversor de Vercel). Es una opinión de la comunidad, no una medición de Easel, pero marca el punto de comparación obvio para quien evalúa estas tres rutas.
PlataformaQué resuelveRiesgo o límiteAWS Lambda clásicaFactura por invocación corta; no mantiene un servidor HTTP persistentePara manejar HTTP concurrente con eficiencia hay que construir infraestructura propia, justo lo que Easel ya tenía antes de probar Web FunctionsVercel Fluid ComputeSegún el comentario de Onavo en HN, mantiene el entorno vivo sin la misma penalización de memoria ociosaLa cifra es una opinión de un usuario de HN, no una medición de Easel; además es una plataforma administrada y cerrada, no compute propioCompute propio de Easel.shHost propio en EE.UU. desde el 2 de noviembre de 2026, con Lambda clásica solo de desbordeExige operar servidores y repartir capacidad entre clientes; no es una opción lista para un equipo que no quiere administrar infraestructuraEl host propio de Easel.sh entró en producción en EE.UU. el 2 de noviembre de 2026.

Qué significa esto para tu stack

Si administrás una API o un backend en Next.js sobre Lambda Web Functions con tráfico esporádico (un SaaS multi-tenant, microservicios internos, paneles que reciben pocas peticiones por hora), conviene abrir AWS Cost Explorer y separar cuánto del costo es memoria facturada contra cuánto es cómputo real. El 88% que midió Easel es la señal de qué buscar antes de comprometerte con esta opción.

Además de Cost Explorer, vale la pena revisar las métricas de CloudWatch por entorno de ejecución (duración por invocación versus tiempo total del entorno) para ver si tu propio tráfico se parece al patrón que describe Easel: peticiones cortas separadas por minutos de silencio. Si la proporción se acerca al 88% que midió la empresa, probablemente estás pagando mucho más por memoria ociosa que por trabajo real.

Un comentario en la discusión de Hacker News ofrece una pista concreta: el usuario torginus escribió que "si cerrás tu proceso de Lambda, el contenedor simplemente se apaga, y podés hacerlo después de devolver la respuesta". Antes de aplicarlo en producción conviene probarlo en un entorno de pruebas: Easel ya intentó algo parecido (apagar entornos a los 10 segundos de inactividad) y AWS registró cada salida voluntaria como un fallo de runtime en vez de un cierre limpio, así que el comportamiento puede no ser tan predecible como suena.

Para equipos con tráfico constante, nada de esto cambia mucho: el mismo entorno reparte el costo ocioso entre muchas peticiones. El problema aparece con tráfico intermitente o en plataformas multi-tenant que hospedan muchas apps chicas, justo el caso de Easel.

Los límites del experimento

Easel aclara que estos son resultados iniciales de una sola región de AWS y de un solo cliente de prueba en Ashburn, Virginia; no hay garantía de que se repliquen en otras regiones o con otro perfil de tráfico. La comparación de arranque en frío se basa en apenas dos pruebas pareadas, una muestra chica para sostener una diferencia de 3,5 veces. Y conviene tener presente que Easel vende compute propio: tiene un incentivo directo para que su infraestructura salga mejor en la comparación, algo que no invalida los números pero sí pide leerlos con ese contexto.

Referencias

  • Easel.sh: reporte original con las mediciones de memoria ociosa, benchmarks de latencia y arranque en frío.- Hacker News: hilo de discusión sobre la facturación de memoria ociosa en Lambda Web Functions.- Comentario de Onavo en Hacker News: comparación con el comportamiento de Vercel Fluid Compute.- Comentario de torginus en Hacker News: sugerencia de cerrar el proceso tras responder para apagar el contenedor.

title: Mocking Correlation IDs for Request Tracing
description:
Quick answer: A correlation ID is a single value that follows a request through several services, so their logs can be joined into one chain. Mock the header exchange by having the mock echo the ID, generate one when the client sends none, and return a mismatch or a missing value on demand. This lets you verify that the client generates, sends, reads, and logs the ID correctly without depending on a real distributed system.

What a correlation ID does

A request often crosses a gateway, one or more services, and a queue, and each component writes its own log. Without a shared identifier, those entries are hard to connect when something fails. The correlation ID, carried in a header such as X-Correlation-ID or X-Request-ID, gives every hop the same value. It has two common origins: the client generates one and sends it, or the entry gateway assigns one when the header is absent and returns it in the response. The response header usually carries the same value, so a support engineer can take the ID shown to the user and pull the matching logs.

Mock the header exchange

Use conditional responses to control what comes back, and inspect the recorded requests to see exactly what the client sent. Cover the cases below.

Scenario Request header Mock response header Client expectation
Client generated ID present Echoes the same ID Log that ID
Gateway generated No ID A newly generated ID Adopt the returned ID
Downstream differs ID present A different ID Follow the documented rule
Missing on response ID present No ID header Keep its own ID, no crash
Retry Same logical call Echoes the value Reuse or renew per convention

The mismatch row matters because a real downstream service can replace the value, and the client needs one clear rule for which ID wins rather than silently logging two unrelated values.

What the client must handle

Put ID generation and reading in one middleware layer so the behavior is consistent instead of being rebuilt per request. Generate a unique, well-formed value for each new logical request, send it on the header, and record it alongside the call. When the response carries an ID, read it and follow the agreed precedence, typically adopting the gateway value or keeping the one the client sent. Decide the retry convention up front: reusing the same ID keeps the attempts tied together, while a new ID distinguishes each attempt, and either is valid if the team applies it consistently. A desktop API workspace lets you set these conditional responses, inspect the recorded headers, and assert on each case in the same place. Powerduck works this way, so the header exchange is a fixed set of local responses.

Honest limits

A local mock runs in the desktop main process and verifies one hop of header handling, not the full behavior of a distributed trace. It does not model propagation across many real services, sampling, or a trace standard such as W3C Trace Context, and it does not prove the live services forward the ID or that the logging backend can actually query it. The echo and precedence rules are ones you define, while a real downstream service can truncate, replace, or drop the value. Confirm end-to-end propagation with a small set of genuine requests. Importing a schema does not deploy a backend, and a passing mock run is not evidence about production observability.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between a correlation ID and a trace ID? A correlation ID joins logs for one request across services. A trace ID is part of a tracing standard and often carries span and sampling context. They overlap, but the correlation ID is the simpler header-level value.

Who should generate the ID? Either the client or the entry gateway. If the client sends one, the gateway keeps it; if not, the gateway assigns one and returns it. The mock covers both paths.

What happens when the response has no ID? The client should keep the ID it sent and continue without crashing, rather than failing the request or logging an empty value.

Should a retry reuse the same ID? It depends on the convention. Reusing it links the attempts; renewing it separates them. Pick one and apply it consistently so the logs stay interpretable.

The bottom line

Use a correlation ID to connect the logs for a request, and mock the header exchange to prove the client handles the generated, gateway-assigned, mismatched, and missing cases. Keep generation and reading in one layer, define the precedence and retry rules explicitly, and verify real cross-service propagation separately. For more on this approach, see the API mocking guide hub.
