title: The Fundamentals of Database Creation
description:
By: Chia Jorine
Date: November 12, 2026 
Introduction
In modern software development, a database serves as the structured backbone of almost every application, responsible for securely storing, retrieving, and managing critical data. Creating a database goes far beyond writing a simple setup command; it requires careful planning to ensure data integrity, scalability, and efficiency.
•Requirement Analysis and Data Modeling
Before creating a database, a developer must determine what data the system needs to capture. This involves identifying key entities (such as Users, Products, or Orders), defining their attributes (such as usernames, prices, or dates), and mapping out how they relate to one another. Designing an Entity-Relationship Diagram (ERD) at this stage prevents structural flaws later in development.
•Choosing the Right Database Management System (DBMS)
Depending on the nature of the project, developers select between two primary models:
Relational Databases (SQL) Systems like PostgreSQL and MySQL organize data into strict tables with rows and columns, making them ideal for structured data and complex relationships.
Non-Relational Databases (NoSQL) Systems like MongoDB store flexible, unstructured data (such as JSON documents), suited for rapid prototyping and massive horizontal scaling.
•Schema Implementation and Constraints
Once the DBMS is selected, the physical database is initialized using Data Definition Language (DDL). Tables are constructed with specific data types and enforced constraints—such as ⁠PRIMARY KEY⁠, ⁠FOREIGN KEY⁠, ⁠UNIQUE⁠, and ⁠NOT NULL⁠.: Example

CREATE DATABASESschool_portal;
CREATE TABLE students (
• student_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
• full_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
• email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL
• );
These rules protect the database by ensuring that duplicate, incomplete, or invalid records cannot corrupt the system.
• Optimization and Security
To keep the database fast as records grow, developers apply indexes to frequently searched columns. Finally, securing the database through strong authentication, encrypted connections, and regular automated backups ensures that sensitive information remains protected against unauthorized access and data loss.
Conclusion
Proper database creation is a vital discipline in software engineering. By combining thoughtful data modeling, strict integrity constraints, and sound security practices, developers lay a reliable foundation capable of supporting scalable, high-performing applications.

title: Checkout custom_data arrived empty and the card was still charged
description:
When a signed-in user starts checkout, the backend opens a Lemon Squeezy checkout and sets custom_data.user_id to that account. The subscription_created webhook is what attaches the paid plan. The handler reads custom_data.user_id to know which account.

A subscription_created webhook arrived without user_id. The checkout had started from an authenticated session, so the field should have been there. It was not. One missing field on one event. That does not mean the provider always drops custom_data.

The refusal was intentional

I kept the handler from attaching a subscription when user_id is missing. A webhook that carries a payment and no owner is ambiguous. Attaching it anyway could put the paid plan on the wrong account.

The card was still charged. The subscription existed on the provider side, and the account stayed on the free plan.

What was added after

The refusal stays. If user_id is absent, the handler tries one recovery before it leaves the account path.

The rule, not the production source:

on subscription_created:
  if custom_data.user_id is present:
    attach to that account
  else:
    candidates = accounts whose email exactly matches the checkout email
    if exactly one candidate, and the conflict guards pass:
      attach to that candidate
    else:
      fall through to the guest path

The email has to match exactly, and it has to match one account. Two accounts on the same email, and the handler does not choose. Conflict guards run before anything is written.

If that step does not resolve, the subscription follows the guest path. It is not forced onto an account.

Retries

Webhooks get retried. Handling is idempotent, so a replayed subscription_created does not attach a second time, and it does not rewrite a state that is already settled.

A conflict is stored as subscription_created_conflict.

I build LiveSuggest, a meeting assistant that stays on the screen. No bot joins the call. This checkout is how a paid plan gets attached to an account.

title: Multilingual API Summaries Explained: Support Emails and Meeting Notes (3 Node.js Checks)
description:
Per-tenant visibility requires attribution, but recording every prompt would turn moderation telemetry into another sensitive content store. Keep the accounting record small and retain the review evidence separately. Short answer: a standard chat completions API is the simplest flexible starting point for summarizing multilingual support tickets, emails, and meeting notes in a US/EU SaaS application. For an edtech moderation workflow, use that interface to prepare a summary and proposed classification before human review, then account for each request against its tenant. Choose the service only after checking language coverage, attribution metadata, and the terms governing the data path.

Keep humans responsible. A concise report is useful; an unreviewed model judgment should not become a disciplinary action merely because it arrived as valid JSON.

The decision here concerns evidence retention: which records must survive long enough to explain a tenant's usage, and which content should disappear from operational telemetry immediately? That question changes the comparison more than a model's advertised unit price does.

What telemetry accompanies an API request to summarize multilingual support tickets?

Consider an illustrative moderation report submitted by a school tenant: a Spanish support email describing a classroom chat, an English staff note, and a request for human review. These are example inputs, not a measured deployment. A useful model response would summarize the allegation, propose a review category, preserve uncertainty, and identify what needs a reviewer. It should distinguish an allegation from an established event. One prompt pattern can accommodate the different text types without training a custom model, but the selected model's multilingual support and availability still require a catalog check.

The application should assign the tenant before making the request. Do not ask the model to infer billing ownership from a report's text. Associate the provider's request identifier with an internal operation identifier, the tenant, the chosen model, the processing tier, and the returned accounting metadata. Those are application design requirements; they are not a claim that every provider returns the same fields.

Count the dimensions.

Suppose a proposed metric has 200 tenant values, 4 workflow stages, 3 model choices, and 2 summary tiers. Its Cartesian upper bound is 4,800 combinations before adding status or region. Those are hypothetical design inputs, not observed traffic. Adding a unique report identifier to the labels would make the series population grow with the reports themselves. Put that identifier in a restricted accounting record instead. Per-tenant visibility does not require every accounting field to become a metric label.

This distinction matters when review traffic is uneven. A tenant importing historical complaints and a tenant processing live reports can produce similar totals while requiring different operational responses. Preserve a bounded workflow dimension so the distinction remains visible; avoid copying complaint text into the metric system to explain it.

Calculate storage amplification before setting retention

Retention is multiplication. In an illustrative workload of 100,000 reports per day, one 600-byte accounting record per report produces 60,000,000 bytes daily. Thirty days would retain 1.8 billion bytes before indexes, replication, or backups. Keeping a 6,000-byte content record for the same period would instead retain 18 billion bytes. This is storage arithmetic, not a provider benchmark or an assertion about actual record sizes.

The useful conclusion is that content and accounting need separate retention decisions. A reviewer may need the source report under the application's review policy, while an operator often needs only an operation identifier, outcome, and usage attribution. A longer accounting retention period should not silently extend the lifetime of student-related text. Set both periods explicitly, document their purposes, and include derived summaries in the content inventory.

Sampling introduces a different trade-off. Sample diagnostic traces if their purpose is debugging, but keep complete accounting records if they support tenant reconciliation. A sampled trace population cannot establish an exact tenant total when the unsampled requests have no other ledger. Retaining every request's accounting metadata is compatible with retaining very few prompt bodies.

Do not sample the bill.

For a US/EU application, language support and compliance suitability are separate questions. A multilingual model does not establish a processing location, retention agreement, or contractual right to send student information. Require evidence for those conditions before enabling a tenant's route. If the evidence is incomplete, the route has not passed that tenant's deployment review. No compliance conclusion follows from a familiar API shape.

Compare providers at the evidence boundary

A plain REST interface makes the transport requirement concrete: the caller needs to send an authenticated HTTP request, with no SDK installation or client-library version to maintain. A Node.js worker can use that contract just as a different backend language can. Transport simplicity is helpful, but it does not remove the work of joining request records to tenants.

The following comparison separates the roles of the alternatives. It makes no latency ranking or claim that their retention terms are equivalent.

Option Appropriate role in this workflow Boundary to inspect
OpenAI Direct chat-completions integration for preparing review summaries Verify the chosen model, processing terms, and accounting fields against the tenant's requirements.
OpenRouter A routing alternative when comparing model choices behind an API Examine the selected upstream path as well as the gateway; a model choice is also a data-path choice.
Anthropic A direct model-service alternative to evaluate for the same summary task Check its request contract before treating it as interchangeable; test language suitability and tenant accounting separately.
Weaviate A retrieval component when reviewed summaries need to become searchable Retrieval does not replace summary generation. Design the handoff and its separate accounting records.
Infrai A plain REST option with an OpenAI-compatible surface and per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata The same account covers AI runtime and retrieval; confirm the request schemas and tenant attribution in the application.

The metadata in the last row is useful because it gives the application material to join to its own tenant ledger. It is not proof of a built-in tenant ledger. Consolidation also means one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. Accept that concentration only if the operational ownership is appropriate for the school tenants involved.

An alternative stack using a Whisper API account plus Weaviate would require two service signups and two credential sets. The application would own the transcript-to-record mapping, the retrieval ingestion handoff, and reconciliation across the two services. For existing emails, tickets, or meeting notes, start with their text: introducing transcription adds a stage that this job does not require. Retrieval should receive an approved, minimized artifact when search is needed, rather than every raw complaint automatically.

The shared-account approach can reduce credential handling at that seam. It does not, by itself, prove that text remains in one processing location or never reaches an upstream processor. Those properties require separate evidence.

Test catalog discovery with curl

The first integration check is deliberately a read: inspect the available model catalog before selecting a production default. Run this curl request in the worker's deployment environment after setting INFRAI_BASE_URL to the service's API origin, without a version suffix, and INFRAI_API_KEY to its secret. This example applies to the catalog interface discussed above; it is not a universal discovery route for every comparison option.

curl --request GET \
  --url "${INFRAI_BASE_URL:?Set the API origin}/v1/ai/models" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${INFRAI_API_KEY:?Set the API key}" \
  --fail-with-body \
  --show-error \
  --retry 4 \
  --retry-max-time 60

The explicit method makes the request clear. Curl's retry behavior backs off on transient responses, including HTTP 429, and honors a supplied Retry-After header. The failure option preserves an error body while returning a failing exit status. This is a bounded catalog check, not a write-retry policy or a complete moderation application.

Use the catalog to establish available model identifiers, then evaluate language suitability before choosing a default. Do not substitute a price listing for availability evidence. For the eventual inference request, validate the response against the application's classification schema and leave unexpected outputs for human review. A chat model's structured response is still a proposal; schema validity does not establish that its allegation summary is accurate or that its suggested category is fair.

The next boundary is the approved-summary-to-retrieval handoff. Give the derived record an application-controlled identifier, maintain tenant access boundaries, and make reprocessing update the intended record rather than create accidental duplicates. Validate both request schemas before implementing that write. A shared key alone supplies none of those application invariants.

Migrate one tenant and verify deletion

Begin with a single tenant and text already intended for human review. First, establish attribution: every attempted summary must have an internal operation record, and returned accounting metadata must join to it. Second, check multilingual review quality using examples that include ambiguous allegations and mixed-language notes. Third, verify retention and access behavior for source reports, derived summaries, accounting records, and any retrieval copy.

Only then add historical imports. Batch processing suits imported records better than a live interaction path, and keeping that workload distinguishable prevents it from obscuring current review demand. Cost estimation can inform a basic summary tier and a more detailed tier, but let the extra review value justify the extra detail. Neither tier should change who owns the final decision.

Include a deletion exercise before expanding the rollout. Create an explicitly synthetic review record, let it pass through the summary and retrieval stages that the application enables, and then apply the configured content-retention policy. Check each derived copy separately. The accounting record should still explain which tenant owned the operation without retaining the allegation or a recoverable copy of the source text. This exercise tests the application's evidence boundary; a successful API response alone cannot establish it.

The rollout succeeds when a reviewer can inspect an appropriately retained report and an operator can explain its tenant attribution without reading that report. Keep less content in telemetry on purpose.

Sources

References for the comparison surfaces and the security review starting point follow. Model availability and deployment terms require checking the service selected for the tenant.

  • OpenAI API documentation
  • OpenRouter documentation
  • Anthropic documentation
  • Weaviate documentation
  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications

title: BigQuery MERGE Is Not a Uniqueness Constraint: A Replay-Safe Tutorial
description:
A MERGE can be atomic and still leave duplicate business keys. The missing ingredient is a clear key and version contract.

This tutorial builds a current-state orders table, not an event-history table. One row represents one order_id. It assumes a single writer and a source-provided, monotonically increasing integer version per order. Timestamps alone are not that contract.

Why the obvious MERGE fails

If two source rows match one existing target row and an update is required, BigQuery can reject the merge. If the key is absent from the target, multiple source rows can instead be inserted: rows inserted by the statement are not matched again within that same statement. Deduplicate the source before merging.

1. Create an isolated, runnable example

Run this GoogleSQL script in the BigQuery console. It uses temporary tables and does not modify your production tables.

CREATE TEMP TABLE orders (
  order_id INT64,
  status STRING,
  source_version INT64
);

INSERT INTO orders VALUES (101, 'created', 1);

CREATE TEMP TABLE incoming (
  order_id INT64,
  status STRING,
  source_version INT64
);

INSERT INTO incoming VALUES
  (101, 'paid', 2),
  (101, 'paid', 2),  -- identical delivery retry
  (102, 'created', 1),
  (102, 'paid', 2),
  (103, 'created', 1);

ASSERT (SELECT COUNT(*) = 0 FROM incoming
        WHERE order_id IS NULL OR source_version IS NULL)
AS 'Null key or version: quarantine this batch';

-- A version must identify one state. Do not pick a random
-- winner when two payloads claim the same key/version.
ASSERT (
  SELECT COUNT(*) = 0 FROM (
    SELECT order_id, source_version
    FROM incoming
    GROUP BY order_id, source_version
    HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TO_JSON_STRING(STRUCT(status))) > 1
  )
) AS 'Conflicting payloads for the same key/version';

CREATE TEMP TABLE batch_latest AS
SELECT order_id, status, source_version
FROM incoming
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
  PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY source_version DESC
) = 1;

-- Ties are harmless here only because the assertion above
-- guarantees identical payloads at a given key/version.
MERGE orders AS T
USING batch_latest AS S
ON T.order_id = S.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND S.source_version > T.source_version THEN
  UPDATE SET status = S.status,
             source_version = S.source_version
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (order_id, status, source_version)
  VALUES (S.order_id, S.status, S.source_version);

SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY order_id;

Expected result by inspection:

order_id status source_version
101 paid 2
102 paid 2
103 created 1

2. Check replay and late arrival

In the same script, repeat only the MERGE statement against the same temporary tables. The result should stay unchanged: equal versions do not update and existing keys do not insert.

Next, replace incoming with (101, 'created', 1), rebuild batch_latest, and merge again. Order 101 must remain paid at version 2. A delayed older event cannot overwrite newer state.

Finally, try two different statuses for the same key and version. The conflict assertion should stop the batch. In a real pipeline, persist those conflicting records to a quarantine table with enough metadata for investigation.

The SQL is an illustrative example; it has not been executed against a BigQuery project for this article. Run it in your own development environment before adapting it.

3. Close the production gaps

  • Existing target duplicates: this merge does not repair them. Before adopting it, check GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 and resolve duplicates using an authoritative version policy.
  • Cross-batch conflicts: also compare incoming equal-version payloads with the target. A different payload at an already stored version is a source-contract violation, not an ordinary retry. For wider rows, compare a canonical representation of all business fields.
  • Concurrency: keep one writer for the table or serialize overlapping key ranges. This example is not a global uniqueness guarantee for independent concurrent writers.
  • Keys: reject null keys. SQL null equality does not behave like ordinary equality. Composite keys need all their business-key columns in both the partition and join.
  • Deletes: define their semantics explicitly. Physically deleting the row also removes its version guard; an old replay can resurrect it. Retain a versioned deletion marker or a durable version ledger when that matters.
  • Partition filters: do not narrow the target to recent ingestion dates if older rows with the same key can still exist. A missed match becomes an insert.

BigQuery primary and foreign key constraints are not enforced, so declaring a primary key does not replace these checks.

A useful acceptance test

Test a new key with duplicates, an existing key with multiple versions, an exact replay, an older replay, null keys, conflicting equal versions and two overlapping writers. Verify both row count and final state. “The job succeeded” is not a data-quality assertion.

References: BigQuery MERGE semantics and BigQuery primary and foreign keys.

Saravana Kumar | TechX. Original tutorial generated by an AI assistant without human editing; example results are reasoned expectations, not a claim of production testing.

Check the notice you'd send them too. A silent change after a failed charge is how angry tickets start.

title: I measured what my Claude Code setup costs on every request. Most of my skills had gone blank.
description:
Claude Code sent 74,500 tokens with my first message of the day, before it had read a single word I typed. About 22,000 of those came from plugins, skills, MCP servers and hooks I had installed over a few months, most of which I had forgotten about.

That overhead is resent on every turn of every session. It drains your usage limit, fills the context window sooner (so sessions compact earlier), and, as it turns out, quietly makes Claude worse at picking the right skill.

Here's how I measured it, the one finding that surprised me, and the small open-source tool I built so you can check your own setup.

Where the numbers come from

Claude Code writes a transcript of every session to ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>.jsonl. Besides the conversation, it records what was loaded at startup as separate entries:

  • skill_listing: every skill name and description the model is shown
  • deferred_tools_delta: the names of all deferred tools, including every MCP tool, plus MCP servers that failed to connect
  • mcp_instructions_delta: instruction blocks MCP servers inject
  • agent_listing_delta: the subagent types on offer
  • hook_success: output of your SessionStart hooks, which often lands in context

And for each API call, the assistant entry carries the real usage:

"usage": {
  "input_tokens": 2,
  "cache_creation_input_tokens": 40260,
  "cache_read_input_tokens": 34273
}

Add those three and you get the exact size of the first request: no estimate, that's what the API billed. Every other number in this post is broken down from there.

The finding: past ~30,000 characters, your skills go blank

When I opened the skill_listing entry, most lines looked like this:

- some-plugin:some-skill
- another-skill
- yet-another:skill

No description. Just names.

The listing text was almost exactly 30,000 characters in every session I checked, no matter how many skills I had installed. Once your skills don't fit, Claude Code starts dropping descriptions and keeps only the names. In my setup, 220 of 283 skills were listed by name only. In an older session with 672 skills installed, 642 had no description.

Why that matters: the description is how the model decides when to use a skill. A bare name like review or start tells it almost nothing. So every skill you installed "just in case" isn't only costing tokens. It's pushing out the descriptions of the skills you actually rely on.

I haven't seen this documented anywhere, and the exact limit may change between versions, so treat ~30k as what I observed, not a spec.

What else was in there

Once everything was attributed to where it came from, a few other things showed up:

  • MCP servers that failed to connect at startup, every session, for weeks.
  • 36 MCP servers I had never signed in to, each still listing its authenticate and complete_authentication tools.
  • Duplicate skills: the same skill name shipped by two different plugins.
  • One skill whose description alone cost about 3,000 tokens per request. I had used it once.
  • And the obvious one: 272 of 283 skills hadn't been used in 30 days.

deadweight

I turned all of this into a CLI called deadweight. It reads the same transcripts and prints:

$ deadweight

  Before you type a word, every request carries 61.2k tokens
  measured from your latest session; median of recent sessions 63.8k
  ~19.4k from your setup · ~41.8k from Claude Code itself (system prompt + 18 tools)

  WHAT YOUR SETUP ADDS
  Deferred tool names (412)            ~7.1k  ████████████████████████
  Skill listings (214)                 ~6.2k  █████████████████████
  Hook injections (3)                  ~3.4k  ███████████▌
  MCP server instructions (4)          ~2.1k  ███████▏
  Agent listings (12)                   ~600  ██

  BIGGEST SOURCES
  name                           type           tokens    used  contents
  github                         mcp server      ~3.9k    212×  91 tools
  kitchen-sink                   plugin          ~3.6k   never  64 tools · 22 skills
  workflow-kit                   plugin          ~2.6k     14×  hooks 2.2k · 11 skills
  playwright                     mcp server      ~1.4k   never  33 tools

  PROBLEMS
  ✗ 151 of 214 skills are listed without a description: the skill listing is full
  ✗ 2 MCP servers failed to connect at startup
  ! 9 MCP servers never signed in, still listing 18 auth-only tools
  ! 198 of 214 listed skills were not used in 30 days (~5.1k per request)

  Run deadweight fix to disable 6 unused plugins and park 11 unused skills and save ~6.8k tokens per request.

(That's an illustrative example; your output will be your own setup.)

How it works:

  1. Measure: the total is the billed size of the first request in your latest session.
  2. Attribute: every skill line, tool name, instruction block, agent and hook injection is traced to the plugin, skill, MCP server or connector that added it. Hook commands are matched against each plugin's hooks.json.
  3. Check usage: every transcript from the last 30 days, subagents included, is scanned for Skill calls, MCP tool calls, agent launches and slash commands.

Then deadweight fix disables unused plugins and moves unused skills aside, and deadweight undo puts everything back.

Making "fix" safe

A tool that edits your config needs to be boring and predictable:

  • Read-only by default. Only fix and undo write, and both ask first.
  • Nothing is deleted. Plugins are set to enabledPlugins: false in settings.json, not uninstalled. Skills are moved into a backup folder.
  • Everything is backed up. Each run writes a manifest and a copy of settings.json to ~/.claude/deadweight/backups/<timestamp>/.
  • Plugins with hooks are skipped. A memory or safety plugin can do useful work without ever showing up as "used", so those need --include-hooked.
  • It refuses with too little history. With fewer than 5 sessions, "unused" doesn't mean much.
  • No secrets, no network. From .claude.json it only reads MCP server names, never commands, env vars or headers. A test asserts that secret values never reach the output.

Built in Rust, with Claude Code

deadweight is a single Rust binary. Transcripts get big (mine were 1.4 GB), so files are scanned in parallel with rayon, and lines are pre-filtered with a cheap substring check before any JSON parsing. A full scan of 41 sessions and 400+ subagent runs takes about a second.

I built it with Claude Code as my pair programmer: surveying existing tools so I didn't build yet another usage tracker, reverse-engineering the transcript format on my machine, writing the Rust and an end-to-end test suite that runs against a fake ~/.claude directory. The tests caught a real bug early: skill names like plugin:skill were being split on the wrong colon, which silently gave one skill's size to its neighbour.

Caveats

  • The total is measured. The per-item breakdown is estimated from text length, since there's no local tokenizer.
  • Claude Code deletes transcripts after cleanupPeriodDays (30 by default), so "unused" can only look that far back. Use --keep for things you use rarely.
  • The ~30k-character listing limit is what I observed, not documented behaviour.

Try it 

cargo install deadweight
deadweight

Prebuilt binaries for macOS, Linux and Windows, plus the source: github.com/msertdev/deadweight. It's free and MIT licensed.

I'm curious what numbers other people get, especially how many of your skills have lost their descriptions. If deadweight misattributes something in your setup, issues are very welcome.

title: I ran the same QLoRA 7B job 8 times on Vast.ai RTX 4090s. The bill went from $0.19 to $0.81. Here is what moved it.
description:
When people compare a rented RTX 4090 with a cloud A100, they multiply the hourly GPU price by the training time. I wanted to see
what actually shows up on the Vast.ai invoice for one fixed job on different hosts.

The job:

  • Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 4-bit QLoRA, yahma/alpaca-cleaned, 300 steps, checkpoint every 50 steps.
  • Image pytorch/pytorch:2.5.1-cuda12.4-cudnn9-runtime, dependencies installed at start.
  • One RTX 4090, host reliability >= 0.98, network >= 500 Mbit/s.

Three things from the invoices:

  1. Traffic: $0.81 against $0.19. On the first run the GPU hour looked cheap, but the bill was $0.81: $0.13 for the GPU and $0.66 for traffic, because the host charged for bandwidth and the job downloads a 15 GB model. After I started picking hosts by the full hourly price including expected traffic, the next run was billed $0.19 (0.44 h on the machine, about 19 minutes of it training).
  2. Same GPU, different bill: $0.21 to $0.38. On 4 November I ran the job six more times on six different 4090 hosts, with no failures. The most expensive run was on a host that trained at about 6 s per step instead of about 4, so training took 31 minutes instead of 17–19. I did not measure why that host was slower.
  3. Start-up is billed too. In those six runs the first training step came 4.5 to 8.5 minutes after renting. You pay for the image pull, the pip install and the model download.

For scale: the $0.19 run would be about $1.35–1.80 for the same job on one A100 at AWS on-demand rates. That is one job; I would not
generalise it.

How do you filter out slow 4090 hosts before renting? And do you bake everything into one large image to cut the start-up, or cache
the weights somewhere?

Disclosure: these runs were launched by a small supervisor service I build (NomadGPU), which is why I have the per-run billing.
Happy to share the logs.

title: A Free Tailwind CSS Curriculum — 81 Chapters, From Utility Classes to Engine Internals
description:
A Free Tailwind CSS Curriculum — 81 Chapters, From Utility Classes to Engine Internals

Most Tailwind tutorials teach the same thing: flex, p-4, text-lg, bg-blue-500, hover:, md:. Then they stop.

The real questions come after that. How does the scanner actually find class names? What changed in v4's Rust rewrite? How do you write a plugin? Why is my CSS bundle growing?

I found a curriculum that answers those. It's on KandZ Tuts, and it's 81 chapters, organized as a single progression from the utility-first paradigm to the internals of the engine.

Here's the breakdown.

Foundations (1–6)

The utility-first paradigm vs BEM, setup via @tailwindcss/vite and the CLI, the CSS-first configuration syntax (@import "tailwindcss" and @theme), the Lightning CSS Rust engine architecture, automatic content detection, and native CSS variables as design tokens.

Layout Primitives (7–19)

Spacing scale, sizing utilities, the OKLCH color system, arbitrary values (-[...]), typography, text alignment and truncation, Flexbox, flex grow/shrink/order/basis, Grid, dynamic grid sizes, box model, positioning, and z-index stacking contexts.

Visual Styling (20–29)

Backgrounds and color-mix(), gradients, borders and rings, shadows, opacity and backdrop filters, 2D transforms, 3D transforms, transitions, animations, and enter/exit animations with @starting-style.

Variants (30–41)

Pseudo-class variants, state variants, structural variants, the not-* variant, group-* and peer-*, named groups and peers, responsive breakpoints, custom breakpoints and container queries, dark mode strategies, media condition variants, arbitrary variants, and data attribute variants.

Architecture (42–55)

Cascade layers, @apply and custom utilities, @utility and @variant directives, @plugin, the typography plugin, form styling, the container query plugin, RTL with logical properties, accessibility utilities, headless component libraries, tailwind-merge and cva, the shadcn/ui pattern, CSS preprocessing and nesting, and upgrading from legacy configs.

Advanced Patterns (56–66)

Dynamic theme switching, fluid typography with clamp(), custom color functions, aspect ratio, Grid subgrid, custom scrollbars and scroll-driven animations, masking and clip-path, the View Transitions API, custom keyframes, Web Components and Shadow DOM, and micro-frontend CSS isolation.

Plugin Development (67–69)

Custom JavaScript plugins with the plugin API, dynamic functional utilities, and custom variant functions.

Engine Internals (70–74)

The Rust-based parsing engine, AST code scrapes and JIT generation, class name hashing and bundle minification, custom ESLint and Stylelint rules, and CI/CD unused-class auditing.

Beyond the Browser (75–79)

Email templates with Maizzle and react-email, Server-Driven UI, legacy CSS migration, performance profiling, and the standalone binary CLI for non-Node workflows.

Chapter 80: How the Scanner, Class Parser, and CSS Writer Work Together

Chapter 81: The Cheatsheet

Why the Engine Internals Matter

Chapters 70–80 are the reason to read this curriculum.

Most resources stop at "here's how @apply works." This one goes into how Tailwind actually generates CSS—the Rust-based Oxide engine, AST scanning, JIT on-demand class generation, class hashing, and the interaction between the scanner, parser, and writer.

That's what lets you diagnose a bloated bundle instead of guessing at content paths. It's the difference between using Tailwind and understanding it.

The v4 Rewrite

Chapters 3–6 cover what changed in Tailwind v4: the CSS-first configuration that replaced tailwind.config.js, the @theme directive, native CSS variables as design tokens, and the Rust engine that dropped full builds from seconds to milliseconds.

If you learned Tailwind on v3, these chapters are the migration path. If you're starting fresh, they're the reason v4 feels different from every tutorial written before 2025.

The Plugin Section

Chapters 67–69 are unusual for a Tailwind curriculum. Most stop at using utilities. This one teaches you to extend the framework—custom plugins with the plugin API, dynamic functional utilities, and custom variant functions.

If you've ever wanted to add a utility that Tailwind doesn't ship, this is where that gets explained.

Who This Is For

  • Beginners: Start at Chapter 1 and read in order.
  • Experienced Tailwind developers: Jump to Chapter 70 (the Rust engine), Chapter 67 (plugin development), or Chapter 74 (CI/CD auditing) if those are gaps.
  • Design system architects: Start at Chapter 6 (design tokens) and read through Chapter 56 (multi-brand theming).

The Link

Tailwind CSS — KandZ Tuts

Free, no signup, 81 chapters.

If you've been writing Tailwind for years but never understood how the scanner works, or you're starting from scratch and want a path that doesn't stop at flex, this is the most complete free curriculum I've found.

What Tailwind topics do you wish had better free resources? Let me know in the comments.

title: Make the database do the minimum: six rules I give my AI
description:
I build CRMs and back-office systems for small Italian companies, and I write most of the code with an AI assistant. That works well for a lot of things. It works badly for one thing in particular: the database.

My AI writes queries that are correct. They return the right rows, the tests pass, the page loads. With a hundred rows in the table. After a year of real use, the same page can take seconds, and the database plan you're paying for is suddenly too small.

The reason is simple. In my setups the database is the small, expensive resource, and the application server is the big, cheap one. Every query, every megabyte of database memory, has to justify itself. The AI doesn't know that. It writes the shortest code that works, and the shortest code usually asks the database to do more than it should.

One system I worked on had a sync loop that re-read calendars every minute "to see if anything changed". Nobody noticed it in development. In production, that one loop made most of all the requests the database received.

So I wrote the rules down. Here are six of them, the ones that make sense without any context.

1. No reads inside a loop

What the AI writes, if you let it:

const orders = await db.query('select id, customer_id from orders where day = $1', [day]);
for (const order of orders) {
  order.customer = await db.query('select name from customers where id = $1', [order.customer_id]);
}

One query for the list, then one more for each row. This is the classic N+1 problem, and Markus Winand explains it well on use-the-index-luke.com, in the section on nested loops: it's usually an ORM doing it silently, but an AI does it just as happily by hand. With 10 orders it's invisible. With 2,000 it's 2,001 round trips.

The rule: read each piece of data once per request, as a set. Independent reads start together, not one after the other.

const orders = await db.query('select id, customer_id from orders where day = $1', [day]);
const customerIds = [...new Set(orders.map((o) => o.customer_id))];
const customers = await db.query('select id, name from customers where id = any($1)', [customerIds]);

Two queries, whatever the number of orders.

2. Short, targeted reads

What the AI writes:

const all = await db.query('select * from contacts');
const open = all.filter((c) => c.status === 'open').slice(0, 50);

It reads every column of every row, ships them to Node, and throws most of them away. And on every page open it adds a select count(*) of the whole table, because the UI shows "1,234 contacts".

The rule: only the columns you need (never select * on a wide table), filtered by columns that have an index, with a limit. Never "read everything and filter later". No exact counts of a big table on every page load.

const open = await db.query(
  `select id, name, updated_at from contacts
   where status = $1 order by updated_at desc limit $2`,
  [ContactStatus.Open, config.contactsPageSize],
);

Plus an index on (status, updated_at). Winand's SQL Performance Explained is the book that taught me why the index has to match both the filter and the order, and why a limit only helps when the database can stop early.

3. Dashboards read a saved summary

Ask an AI for "a dashboard with the number of open deals per stage" and you'll get one of two things. Either a big group by over the live tables on every page view, or, if you said "make it fast", a trigger that updates a counter on every insert and delete.

The first one gets slower every month. The second one is worse: every write now pays for the dashboard, the counter drifts the first time a bulk import skips the trigger, and nobody can explain why the number is wrong.

The rule: a dashboard reads a small summary table with the numbers already computed. A background job rebuilds it on a slow schedule (the interval lives in configuration), and there's an "Update now" button next to "Last updated". The rebuild:

  • runs one at a time: it takes a database lock without waiting, and if the lock is taken it answers "already running";
  • replaces, never adds: it recomputes from the real rows, so a missed run can't leave a wrong total behind;
  • is checked every night against a real count, with an alert if they differ.

And no triggers for counters or summaries.

type RefreshOutcome = 'refreshed' | 'already-running';

async function refreshDealSummary(db: Db): Promise<RefreshOutcome> {
  return db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const [{ locked }] = await tx.query(
      'select pg_try_advisory_xact_lock($1) as locked', [LockKey.DealSummary]);
    if (!locked) return 'already-running';

    await tx.query('delete from deal_summary');
    await tx.query(`insert into deal_summary (stage, open_deals, computed_at)
                    select stage, count(*), now() from deals where closed_at is null group by stage`);
    return 'refreshed';
  });
}

pg_try_advisory_xact_lock returns immediately instead of waiting, and the lock goes away with the transaction. Two people pressing "Update now" at the same moment get one rebuild and one "already running".

4. External calls after the response

What the AI writes for "save the contact form and email me":

await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
  await tx.query('insert into messages (...) values (...)', [...]);
  await emailProvider.send(notificationFor(message)); // waits on the network
});

It looks tidy: everything in one transaction. But the transaction stays open, holding a connection and its locks, for as long as the email provider takes to answer. On a slow day that's seconds, and connections are exactly what a small database has the fewest of.

The rule: never keep a transaction open while you wait for an external service. Commit first, answer the user, then do the outside work (after the response, or through a queue).

const message = await saveMessage(db, form);   // short transaction, committed
scheduleAfterResponse(() => notifyOwner(message));
return { status: 'received' };

This is how my own site handles its contact form: the message is saved, the visitor gets the answer, and the notification goes out after the response. If the notification fails, that has its own path (I wrote about uncertain deliveries in the first article of this series), but it never holds the database hostage.

5. No state in the process

This one is not about queries, but it ends in the same place: a system that breaks when it grows.

My site runs headless Chrome to read web pages, fill in forms and print PDFs. Each Chrome is heavy, and the server is shared with other systems. So there's a brake: a small semaphore that lets at most 2 Chrome instances run at the same time, puts the next requests in a first-come-first-served queue, and fails cleanly if a request waits too long. The limit and the wait come from configuration.

It works. But here's the honest part: the semaphore lives in the memory of one process. With one copy of the server, the limit is 2. Start a second copy behind a load balancer and each copy has its own semaphore. The limit is now 4, and nobody changed a line.

This is the stateless processes rule from Adam Wiggins' The Twelve-Factor App, factor VI: the memory of a process is fine for a brief cache, not for anything the next request depends on. Counters, limits towards providers, queues, tokens: they belong in the database or another shared place.

I've seen the expensive version of this mistake. Another system I worked on kept its rate limit towards a phone service in memory. When it went to several copies, the limit multiplied with them, and the provider started saying "too many requests".

So my site's project file says, in plain words, that it runs as one copy only, and that the Chrome brake and a few other in-memory counters must be rewritten before a second copy exists. I'd rather have a known, written limitation than an invisible one. If you can't fix it today, write down where it breaks.

6. Measure first

Every rule above can be overdone. An AI that has read them will happily add indexes nobody uses and summary tables for pages nobody opens.

Donald Knuth's famous line, "premature optimization is the root of all evil", comes from his 1974 paper Structured Programming with go to Statements. People quote only that half. In the paper, the next sentence says we should not pass up our opportunities in the critical 3%, and then he says that programmers' intuitive guesses about which code is critical fail, and that measurement tools are what tell you. The point is not "don't optimize". It's "measure, then optimize what the measurement shows".

On Postgres, pg_stat_statements counts time and rows for every query shape, and a slow-query log catches the rest. My site's database has both turned on. The rule I give my AI: every performance fix comes with the number before and after, and the command that produced it. Martin Kleppmann, in the first chapter of Designing Data-Intensive Applications, makes the same point from the other side: you can't talk about scaling until you've described your load and measured your performance.

The check that blocks

As always with an AI, a rule in a document is a rule it will forget the next time it writes a new page. So the rule has to become a test that goes red.

The test I want on every important action counts the database queries it makes, and fails if the number grows with the data:

it('lists the day orders with a constant number of queries', async () => {
  const db = countingDb(testDb);              // wraps the client, counts every query

  await seedOrders(testDb, { count: 1 });
  await listDayOrders(db, today);
  const withOne = db.queriesMade();

  db.resetCount();
  await seedOrders(testDb, { count: 50 });
  await listDayOrders(db, today);

  expect(db.queriesMade()).toBe(withOne);     // 50 orders must not mean 50 more queries
});

There's no magic budget in it: the test only says that more rows must not mean more queries. When the AI brings back a read inside a loop, this goes red, and it has to explain itself.

I'll be honest: my rules file asks for this test on every action, but not every project of mine has it yet. It's the next check I'm adding, because it's the one that catches the mistake an AI makes most often.

The rules, in one line

The database stores and finds; the application server computes, waits and remembers nothing.

Further reading

The ideas here aren't mine. These explain them better:

  • Markus Winand, SQL Performance Explained (self-published, 2012), and its free web edition, use-the-index-luke.com: the chapters on indexes, partial results and the N+1 problem (section "Nested Loops").
  • Adam Wiggins, The Twelve-Factor App (12factor.net), factor VI, "Processes".
  • Donald E. Knuth, "Structured Programming with go to Statements", Computing Surveys, vol. 6, no. 4 (ACM, December 1974).
  • Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (O'Reilly, 2017): chapter 1, on describing load and performance.
  • The PostgreSQL documentation: "pg_stat_statements" and "Advisory Locks".

What I added is small: turning each of them into a sentence my AI reads before it writes code, and, when it matters, into a test that says no.

I'm Matteo Mazzocchi, an Italian developer. I build CRMs and back-office systems for small businesses, with an AI pair and a lot of tests that say no. More about my work: mazzocchimatteo.com.

title: Meta browser and server events need a shared deduplication identity.
description:
A browser purchase event and a server purchase event can each pass their own payload checks while describing the same order with different identifiers. The receiving platform then lacks the shared identity your integration intended to provide.

Meta's event model uses event ID and event name when deduplicating browser and server submissions. The application work begins earlier: establish one identity for the business event and preserve it through both delivery paths.

This walkthrough tests that propagation locally. It does not send Pixel or Conversions API requests, and its browser objects are application fixtures rather than Pixel API calls.

Create the identity when the business event becomes durable

Suppose checkout commits order order-1042. At the same durable boundary, store the identity for the purchase event that should represent that order in the intended destination.

The browser response and server delivery worker should read that stored identity. Generating a random value independently inside each adapter defeats the relationship before either request leaves your application.

A network transmission attempt needs its own operational identity. Keep that separate from the business-event ID. Retrying an event after a timeout is another attempt to deliver the same event, not necessarily another purchase.

If the browser never receives the checkout response, the server may still deliver its event. Your design should not require both paths to succeed before the order itself is considered committed.

Test both adapters against the same record

Save this complete example as a Node.js module and run it locally:

import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

function eventRecord(id, destination) {
  if (typeof id !== 'string' || id.trim().length === 0) {
    throw new TypeError('stable business-event ID required');
  }
  return { id, name: 'Purchase', destination };
}

function browserAdapter(event) {
  return { name: event.name, eventID: event.id,
    destination: event.destination };
}

function serverAdapter(event) {
  return { event_name: event.name, event_id: event.id,
    destination: event.destination };
}

function sameIdentity(browser, server) {
  return browser.name === server.event_name &&
    browser.eventID === server.event_id &&
    browser.destination === server.destination;
}

const stored = eventRecord('purchase-event-1042', 'synthetic-dataset-a');
const browser = browserAdapter(stored);
const server = serverAdapter(stored);
const retry = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(server));

assert.equal(sameIdentity(browser, server), true);
assert.equal(sameIdentity(browser, retry), true);
assert.equal(sameIdentity(browser, { ...server, event_id: 'retry-random-id' }), false);
assert.equal(sameIdentity(browser, { ...server, event_name: 'purchase' }), false);
assert.equal(sameIdentity(browser, { ...server, destination: 'dataset-b' }), false);
assert.notEqual(serverAdapter(eventRecord('purchase-event-1043',
  stored.destination)).event_id, server.event_id);
assert.throws(() => eventRecord('', stored.destination));

The destination field is local test metadata. It is not an additional CAPI event field. It ensures the fixture does not report a successful pairing when the two submissions are configured for unrelated destinations.

The example checks identity only. A complete server payload requires the rest of the destination contract, including appropriate event context and user data handled under the application's actual permissions and requirements.

Keep retries tied to the original event

Persist the event payload or enough immutable data to rebuild it consistently. A worker retry should not create a new event ID simply because it reconstructs the JSON.

Record an attempt number, send time, response metadata and error classification outside the business-event identity. Those fields let operators investigate delivery without changing what the event represents.

Consider the ambiguous-response case. The server may have accepted a request before your client timed out. Your local state should preserve that uncertainty and retry according to the documented destination contract. An HTTP timeout does not prove that the destination never received the first attempt.

Do not claim exactly-once reporting merely because you have a stable identifier. Stability is one input to the destination's deduplication behavior. Other conditions and delivery timing still apply.

Guard against the opposite identity bug

One constant event ID reused for every purchase is just as problematic as a new ID on every retry. Distinct business events need distinct identities within the intended scope.

Add a fixture for two different committed orders and assert that their event IDs differ. Add another fixture for a repeated delivery attempt and assert that its ID remains unchanged.

Also test browser refreshes or repeated confirmation-page renders. Decide whether they are re-presenting the same purchase event or representing a genuinely different operation. Generate identifiers from that business decision, not from page lifecycle events alone.

Avoid embedding personal information in IDs. Use an opaque identifier suitable for operational correlation. Keep any internal mapping to customer records in the application storage that already governs access to those records.

Check the actual outgoing requests

Unit tests on adapter objects can miss later tag-manager transformations or HTTP middleware. Capture the browser event arguments and serialized server body in a controlled integration test.

Compare exact event names and IDs, including case and whitespace. A value copied through a template can acquire a different representation even when the initial application record was correct.

Preserve the intended destination configuration with the captured pair. Two matching IDs in logs do not establish that the requests reached the same place.

If the browser and server are maintained by different teams, share a small identity contract and the same synthetic fixture. That gives both implementations a common expected result without requiring them to share all payload construction code.

Verify the outcome in destination diagnostics

Use a controlled event pair and inspect the destination's available event diagnostics. Retain the local record, request metadata and observed pairing outcome. Do not infer successful deduplication from a local equality assertion or a successful HTTP response.

If the result differs, investigate arrival, destination configuration, exact identity values and the currently documented matching conditions. Avoid changing several of those at once, since the next test would not identify which change mattered.

I maintain Pixellint. Its Meta Conversions API pack helps inspect the server payload. Keep the shared-identity tests beside the browser and server adapters because the relationship spans both paths and cannot be established from either payload alone.

Sources

  • Meta SDK event and deduplication documentation
  • Meta server-event implementation

Technical sources checked October 25, 2026. Drafted with AI; examples are synthetic unless explicitly stated otherwise.

title: My Cron Job Fired 50 Times While the Receiver Was Down. 10 Webhooks Vanished.
description:
Fifty POSTs, one per second, each carrying its own idempotency key. At fire 21, I killed the receiver.

That was the whole experiment. A dispatcher on my laptop, a receiver on the same laptop, and a kill signal in the middle. I wanted a number, not an opinion: when the thing on the other end dies mid-run, how much of a cron job's work actually arrives?

The dispatcher is a small Node script. It fires 50 POSTs to localhost, one a second, keys evt-001 through evt-050. Every POST carries an Idempotency-Key header with its key. If an attempt fails, it waits 500 milliseconds and tries once more, then moves on. It never asks why anything failed. It fires, it logs, it moves on.

The receiver is even smaller. It takes each POST, writes one JSON line to a log file, and answers 200. In phase 1 it ignores the idempotency key completely. It has no memory, no database, no queue. It is the dumbest possible webhook endpoint, which is the point. Most receivers I have actually built were not much smarter than this.

A controller script ran the outage. It watched the dispatcher log, killed the receiver after fire 21's ACK landed, and started it again after fire 31's retry failed. The outage is defined by delivery count, not by the clock, so exactly ten deliveries fell inside it: fires 22 through 31. No stopwatch, no guessing.

Phase 1, the dispatcher log for the first lost key:

{"ts":"2026-11-11T21:06:01.251Z","key":"evt-022","n":22,"attempt":1,"result":"error","error":"ECONNREFUSED"}

Ten keys, evt-022 to evt-031, each with two error lines: the first attempt, then the retry 500 ms later, also refused. Twenty error lines in total. Everything else got an ACK.

The receiver log, when the run finished: 40 lines, all "delivered", zero duplicates. First line evt-001, last line evt-050, with a hole in the middle where the outage was.

So the count is 40 delivered, 10 lost, 0 duplicated. The title of this post is the result, not a guess. Ten webhooks vanished, and nothing I had built noticed. The dispatcher logged the errors and carried on. The receiver had nothing to log because it was dead. If this had been a real cron job syncing orders or sending receipts, ten of them would simply not exist, and the only trace would be error lines in a log file nobody reads at 3 a.m.

The retry deserves a closer look, because it feels like it should have saved something. It saved nothing. The retry fires 500 ms after the failure, and the outage lasted about fifteen seconds of dispatcher time. A retry only helps when the outage is shorter than the retry delay. Mine was thirty times longer. A retry is a seatbelt for a stumble, not a parachute for a fall. I wrote it in because every tutorial says to add a retry, and it did exactly nothing for the failure I actually had.

Phase 2. Same fifty fires, same ten-delivery outage. Two changes: the receiver now honours the idempotency key, and after the run I replay the keys that never got an ACK.

First, the honest part. The header alone recovers nothing. I want to be plain about that, because the draft description I wrote before running this said "then added one header and ran it again", as if the header were the fix. It is not the fix. The header is a promise the receiver has to keep. Phase 2 before the replay looked exactly like phase 1: 40 delivered, the same ten keys lost, zero duplicates. The header changed nothing while the receiver was dead, because a dead receiver keeps no promises.

What changed the numbers was the replay. After the dispatcher finished, a second script read its log, picked out the ten keys with no ACK, and sent each one again. All ten came back {"status":"ok"}. Ten recovered, zero still lost.

Then I ran the replay a second time, with all fifty keys, to see what the header actually buys. Every single one came back {"status":"duplicate"}. Fifty out of fifty recognised, zero re-processed. The receiver log ended at 100 lines: 50 delivered, 50 duplicate entries, 50 unique keys. Every key delivered exactly once.

That is the whole story. The replay recovers the lost work, and the idempotency key makes the replay safe. Without the key, replaying all fifty would have delivered forty of them twice. With the key, the second pass is a no-op. The pieces only work together. A retry without a replay recovers nothing. A replay without an idempotency key doubles your deliveries. The header without either is decoration.

There are limits, and I should name them, because this ran on one laptop. Localhost has no real network latency, no half-delivered POSTs, no receiver that writes the log line and dies before answering. In production the failure modes are uglier: a POST can land and its response can still be lost, which is the one case where a retry does create a duplicate, and it is the case my setup could not produce. The numbers here are for this setup. They are not a promise about a queue in production.

What I would actually build, after watching this run, is boring. The dispatcher keeps an outbox: every event written down before it is sent, with its key. A sweeper re-sends anything with no ACK, on a timer, until it gets one. The receiver keeps every key it has seen in a real store, not a log file, and answers "duplicate" for repeats. That is three small pieces, and none of them is clever. The clever version is the one I started with: fire and forget, one quick retry, hope the other end stays up. It lost ten out of fifty.

Twenty-six posts in the last seven days on dev.to argued about cron webhook recovery patterns, and twenty-five more about rate-limited queues and dead-letter recovery. Most of them debate retry counts and backoff curves. After counting my own losses, I think the debate is pointed at the wrong piece. The retry count barely mattered. The replay sweep and the key were the whole game.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: Cheap Simple Webhook Task Processing with Rate-Limit Queue Backoff in Node.js SaaS
description:
Short answer: use a queue-centered design for delayed shipment webhooks when retries and basic rate-limited processing matter more than workflow orchestration. Three small worker lanes let a fintech SaaS smooth outbound traffic, while application code owns backoff and idempotency.

The data flow is deliberately plain: a shipment event enters a queue, workers consume at a bounded concurrency, and each subscriber gets a retry decision based on the downstream response. A queue is the pressure valve between your database and a partner API that says "429, try later." Infrai fits this early leg when you want a self-describing REST surface: its public discovery response includes schemas and runnable examples, so a Node.js service can inspect the contract before wiring a queue. One key and one bill cover the other backend capabilities you may add around shipment state, which avoids another credential handoff and keeps ownership clear for a small team. Infrai currently exposes 295 routes across 20 modules behind that convention, so adding an adjacent backend service does not require a new client library.

What should a Node.js SaaS measure for rate-limited webhook retries?

Run the same replayable fixture through each candidate: 10,000 shipment updates, 200 subscribers, a partner limit of 50 requests per second, and a 2% injected 429 rate. Record p95 delivery delay, duplicate deliveries, worker CPU, and operator steps after a forced worker restart. Pass only if every attempt is idempotent, the queue never exceeds the partner's limit for five consecutive minutes, and a poison message reaches a dead-letter path without blocking newer shipments.

That test is more useful than a vendor's headline number. Your decision rule is simple: choose the lowest-complexity option that passes the limit and recovery checks; accept higher latency only when it buys a failure mode you actually need. I would keep the fixture in CI and run it before changing queue settings.

A minimal worker keeps the control loop visible.

This TypeScript sketch keeps the sample small while showing the important edges. The standard queue is at-least-once, so the subscriber operation must tolerate duplicates. The eventId is the idempotency key in the downstream request.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function call(path: string, body: unknown, idempotencyKey?: string) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 6; attempt++) {
    const response = await fetch(`https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        ...(idempotencyKey ? { "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey } : {})
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body)
    });
    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
      const waitMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
    return response.json();
  }
  throw new Error("retry budget exhausted");
}

await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`, "Content-Type": "application/json", "Idempotency-Key": "ship_7f2-sub_42" },
  body: JSON.stringify({
  queue: "shipment-webhooks",
  message: { eventId: "ship_7f2", subscriberId: "sub_42", status: "in_transit" },
  delay_seconds: 30
})
});

// The consumer uses the same explicit POST pattern against /v1/queue/consume.
const batch = { messages: [] as Array<{ message: unknown }> };
for (const item of batch.messages ?? []) {
  // Persist eventId before acknowledging, then retry the delivery on failure.
  console.log(item.message);
}

The exact worker loop should cap concurrency at the partner's allowance, persist an attempt record, and acknowledge only after the subscriber accepts the event. This is the part worth stretching out in a real test: replay one shipment with a 429, kill the worker after the downstream call but before acknowledgement, then restart it. The second delivery is expected, and the idempotency record should turn it into one subscriber-side effect. If your audit table cannot explain that sequence, the queue setting is not the real problem. Backoff can be a delayed republish or a requeue decision in your application; there is no native debounce or throttle primitive. Keep delays at or below seven days, messages at or below 256 KB, and retention within 30 days.

Which queue, cron, or workflow runner should carry the shipment task?

Option Good fit Trade-off for shipment fan-out
Queue-centered workers Bounded concurrency, delayed retry, simple Node.js path You build backoff policy and duplicate protection
Cloudflare Workers Cron Triggers A periodic sweep that publishes due work A cron run is capped at 900 seconds and only calls a public HTTP URL; it is a trigger, not a worker pool
Inngest Durable function steps and managed retries More orchestration surface than a basic outbound queue needs
Temporal Long workflows, joins, and durable state Operational weight is hard to justify for one webhook delivery loop

Infrai is a reasonable leg of the experiment when you want the queue path over one REST API. Its discovery endpoint is self-describing and includes request schemas plus runnable examples, so wiring a capability is reading one endpoint instead of installing another SDK. One key and a consistent HTTP convention also reduce integration work when the same service later needs storage or observability.

My explicit recommendation: try Infrai for the shipment queue and worker lane if your team wants a plain HTTP integration and can own application-level retry policy. Keep the comparison honest by measuring it beside the alternatives above.

The boundary that changes the decision

The catch is fan-out. There is no built-in topic broadcast, so independent consumers need separate queues or an explicit publish loop. A standard queue also has at-least-once delivery, finite retention, and deletes on acknowledgement; it is not a Kafka-style replay log. Store an audit record separately when reconciliation matters.

Choose Inngest or Temporal when the shipment process grows into a multi-step workflow with joins, compensation, or long-running state. Stick with Cron Triggers when the work is a short, public-URL sweep and sub-minute delivery jitter is acceptable. Your mileage may vary on latency because this method intentionally trades some immediacy for a controlled rate.

Before shipping, check four things in prose: the partner limit is represented as worker concurrency, each event has a durable idempotency record, retries stop at a defined attempt budget, and a dashboard can show queue age plus dead-letter counts. I started by assuming a cron schedule would be cheaper to operate; the recovery test changed my mind because rate-limit handling belonged next to the consumer.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the queue documentation.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs/learn/why-inngest
  • https://docs.temporal.io/workflows
  • https://nodejs.org/api/globals.html#fetch
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs

title: Designing Autism-Friendly Websites: Accessibility Principles Every Developer Should Know
description:
Most of us have shipped a feature that looked great in a demo and felt exhausting in real use. An auto-playing hero video, a sticky banner that follows you down the page, and a toast notification that appears out of nowhere. For some users, these are minor annoyances. For others, they can make a site hard to use at all.

This is where autism-friendly website design earns its place in a developer’s toolkit. It isn’t a niche concern or a special mode. It’s a set of choices that make interfaces calmer, clearer, and more predictable, and those choices tend to help everyone: people on a noisy commute, people with migraines, people using a screen reader, and people who are simply tired.

This article walks through practical principles you can apply today, with code you can copy into your own projects.

Why Inclusive Web Design Matters

Web accessibility is often discussed in terms of screen readers and keyboard navigation, and those matter a great deal. But accessibility also covers cognitive and sensory experience, and that’s where neurodivergent users, including many autistic people, are frequently overlooked.

The goal of inclusive web design isn’t to build a separate “autism version” of your site. It’s to reduce friction by default and give people control over the parts of the experience that affect them most.

Sensory Differences Are Individual

Many autistic people report differences in how they process sensory input, such as light, sound, motion, or visual clutter. But these experiences vary widely. One person may find flashing elements distressing, another may be unbothered by motion but need very clear structure, and another may prefer dense, information-rich layouts.

That variation is the key design lesson: don’t design for a stereotype, design for choice. For a deeper understanding of autism and sensory needs, educational resources like AutismCue offer helpful information that can help developers and design teams build awareness before creating digital experiences.

With that in mind, here are the principles that matter most for sensory-friendly website design.

1. Reduce Unnecessary Motion

Animation can add polish, but unrequested motion can be distracting or uncomfortable. Auto-playing carousels, parallax scrolling, and looping background videos are common culprits.

CSS gives you a built-in way to respect user preferences:

/* Default: subtle, purposeful animation */
.card {
  transition: transform 0.3s ease;
}
.card:hover {
  transform: translateY(-4px);
}

/* Respect the user's OS-level setting */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *,
  *::before,
  *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}

Note that prefers-reduced-motion depends on users having set that preference in their system. Many haven’t, which is why an in-page control (covered below) is still valuable.

2. Avoid Overwhelming Visual Elements

Visual noise competes for attention. Pop-ups, stacked banners, autoplay media, and dense layouts all raise the cognitive load.

Practical guidelines:

  • 1. Limit each screen to one primary call to action.
  • 2. Avoid auto-playing audio or video. If media must play, start it muted with visible controls.
  • 3. Don’t use flashing content. WCAG sets limits on content that flashes more than three times per second.
  • 4. Delay or avoid modal pop-ups, especially on first load.
  • 5. Use white space deliberately to group related content.

3. Readable Typography and Spacing

Clear typography reduces effort for nearly everyone. A solid baseline:

body {
  font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif;
  font-size: 1.125rem;   /* ~18px, respects user zoom */
  line-height: 1.6;
  max-width: 70ch;       /* comfortable line length */
}

p {
  margin-block: 0 1.25em;
}

h1, h2, h3 {
  line-height: 1.25;
  margin-block: 1.75em 0.5em;
}

Use relative units (rem, em) so text scales with user settings. Avoid long blocks of centred or justified text, which can create uneven spacing and make it harder to read.

4. Simple, Predictable Navigation

Predictability is a major part of accessible UX design. Users should always know where they are and what will happen next.

  • Keep navigation in the same place on every page.
  • Use clear, literal labels (“Contact us”, not “Let’s talk”).
  • Avoid mega-menus that change layout unexpectedly.
  • Indicate the current page with aria-current="page".
  • Don’t open links in new tabs without warning. 
<nav aria-label="Main">
  <ul>
    <li><a href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="/guides">Guides</a></li>
    <li><a href="/contact">Contact</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>

Add a “Skip to main content” link as the first focusable element so keyboard users can bypass repeated navigation.

5. Clear Instructions and Understandable Content

Ambiguous language can create real barriers. Idioms, sarcasm, and vague microcopy (“Oops, something went sideways!”) may be confusing for literal-minded readers and for non-native speakers too.

  • Use plain, direct language.
  • Say exactly what a button will do: “Download PDF” beats “Get it”.
  • Break long processes into numbered steps.
  • Tell users what to expect before they act (“This takes about two minutes”).
  • Write error messages that explain what went wrong and how to fix it.

6. Accessible Forms and Buttons

Forms are where friction becomes failure. A few habits go a long way:

<form>
  <div class="field">
    <label for="email">Email address</label>
    <p id="email-hint" class="hint">We'll only use this to send your receipt.</p>
    <input
      type="email"
      id="email"
      name="email"
      autocomplete="email"
      aria-describedby="email-hint"
      required
    />
  </div>

  <button type="submit">Submit order</button>
</form>

input, button {
  min-height: 44px;      /* comfortable touch target */
  padding: 0.5rem 0.75rem;
  font-size: 1rem;
}

:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #1a5fb4;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

Key practices: always use visible <label> elements (not placeholders as labels), show hints before errors happen, avoid time limits where possible, and never remove focus outlines without replacing them.

7. Maintain Sufficient Colour Contrast

WCAG 2.x requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and UI components. But also consider excessive contrast: pure black on pure white can feel harsh for some users, so a slightly softened palette is often more comfortable.

:root {
  --text: #1f2933;   /* dark gray, not pure black */
  --bg: #fafafa;     /* soft off-white */
}

Never rely on colour alone to convey meaning. Pair error colours with icons and text.

8. Give Users Control

Because preferences differ, the strongest approach is letting people adjust their own experience. A simple motion toggle is a good start:

<button id="motion-toggle" aria-pressed="false">Reduce motion</button>

.reduce-motion *,
.reduce-motion *::before,
.reduce-motion *::after {
  animation: none !important;
  transition: none !important;
}

const btn = document.getElementById("motion-toggle");
const root = document.documentElement;

btn.addEventListener("click", () => {
  const on = root.classList.toggle("reduce-motion");
  btn.setAttribute("aria-pressed", String(on));
  localStorage.setItem("reduceMotion", on);
});

if (localStorage.getItem("reduceMotion") === "true") {
  root.classList.add("reduce-motion");
  btn.setAttribute("aria-pressed", "true");
}

The same pattern can extend to theme, text size, or hiding non-essential elements like promotional banners.

How to Test Your Work

Automated tools catch only part of the picture, so combine methods.

Automated checks

  • Lighthouse (built into Chrome DevTools) for a quick accessibility audit.
  • axe DevTools or the axe-core library for catching common WCAG issues.
  • WAVE for a visual overview of structural problems.

Manual checks

  • Navigate your entire site using only the keyboard.
  • Turn on prefers-reduced-motion in your OS and confirm animations calm down.
  • Zoom to 200% and check that nothing breaks.
  • Test with a screen reader such as NVDA, VoiceOver, or JAWS.
  • Read your microcopy aloud. If it’s ambiguous, rewrite it.
  • Ask: is there anything on this page that moves, flashes, or interrupts without my permission?

Most importantly, include autistic and neurodivergent people in user testing where possible. No checklist replaces lived experience.

Conclusion

Good autism and technology practices come down to a few habits: reduce unnecessary stimulation, be predictable, write clearly, and give people control. None of these require a redesign from scratch. You can start with one change, like honouring prefers-reduced-motion or rewriting a vague button label.

Inclusive design isn’t about guessing what users need. It’s about building flexible interfaces that let people shape their own experience. When we do that well, the web becomes calmer and more usable for everyone.

What’s one small accessibility improvement you could ship this week? Share it in the comments.
