title: Proof Driven Development: can the agent prove it works?
description:
One of the problems with using agents is that you can ask them to implement something, add tests, run everything and explain why it works, and still end up with a bug. You can ask another agent to review the result, which helps, but then you have to check whether the review makes sense too. We've made producing code incredibly easy, and now we're trying to figure out how to keep up with checking all of it. Asking the same LLM “are you sure?” a few more times doesn't give us much of a guarantee.

So I found this announcement from GitHub Next pretty interesting. Microsoft Research is working on Proof Driven Development Kit, or PDD Kit, which brings formal verification into the agent's development workflow. The idea is that we can ask for a mathematical proof that the implementation satisfies a specification, and have a separate verifier check that claim. What makes this interesting to me is that the correctness argument has to survive something more demanding than the agent's own explanation of why its code is correct.

If formal verification is new to you, I wrote an introduction to how it works and why it matters for AI-generated code.

// Detect dark theme var iframe = document.getElementById('tweet-2112936525457740139-333'); if (document.body.className.includes('dark-theme')) { iframe.src = "https://platform.twitter.com/embed/Tweet.html?id=2112936525457740139&theme=dark" }

Ok, what are they doing?

According to the announcement, PDD Kit discusses the code with you, figures out what you're trying to achieve and proposes a formal specification. You review that specification, approve it, and the implementation gets checked against it using Verus, a verification tool for Rust. The demo follows a login flow from the initial intent to a verified pull request. It also integrates with Chopin, GitHub Next's collaborative planning environment, so the team can work through the plan together. Where formal proof isn't possible, the workflow uses tests and computer-use agents to check the behavior. The announced language support is Rust, and Verus adds syntax for specifications and proofs around the Rust code.

Chopin

A real-time multiplayer, agentic planning environment

githubnext.com

What I like here is that there's something outside the LLM checking the formal claim. The agent can propose an implementation, but it doesn't get to declare its own homework correct just because the explanation sounds convincing. The Verus documentation describes this as static verification: checking that code satisfies the specified properties for all executions covered by the model, without adding runtime checks. Think about the amount of time we spend wondering whether there's some input we forgot to test. For properties we can express and verify this way, that's a much stronger guarantee. But there's a very important word in all of this: specification.

This is where the questions matter

Imagine you're implementing session validation. You want users with valid sessions to access the application, and everyone else to be rejected. You ask the agent to implement the check, and it gives you something like this. I'm using JavaScript here to keep the example familiar; the announced formal verification support in PDD Kit is for Rust.

function canUseSession(session, now) {
  return session.signatureValid && now < session.expiresAt;
}

Looks reasonable. A valid signature and a session that hasn't expired. You test a valid session, an expired session and an invalid signature. Everything passes. Then a user logs out, you mark the session as revoked, and... the function still accepts it. We never checked session.revoked. We could add a test for that. We should. But now imagine we had formally specified the function as: Accept the session if and only if its signature is valid and it hasn't expired. The implementation satisfies that rule. We could prove it and still have the exact same bug, because we forgot revocation in the requirement too.

This is exactly the kind of gap Chopin and PDD Kit are meant to help us catch. PDD Kit discusses the intended behavior before proposing a formal specification, and Chopin gives the team a shared place to question the plan and resolve those decisions. For this example, that conversation should include: “Does logging out revoke the session immediately?”, “What happens at the exact expiration time?” and “Should every otherwise valid session be accepted?” The tools can help turn “make session validation work” into a set of explicit decisions, with the answers carried into the specification. That's a useful part of the workflow: you don't have to arrive with a perfect specification already written.

After working through those questions, the rule could become: Accept the session if and only if its signature is valid, it hasn't been revoked, and the current time is strictly before its expiration time. Now the expiration boundary is settled: at the exact expiration time, access is denied, so an implementation using <= would violate the specification. The “if and only if” also requires valid sessions to be accepted. Without that, an implementation returning false for everyone could satisfy a narrower rule that only requires invalid sessions to be rejected. Congrats, nobody can log in anymore. This is why the discussion and the proof belong together: the tools help us work out what we mean, then verification checks that the implementation follows what we agreed. The tools can still miss a requirement, but helping us uncover those requirements is part of their value.

Perfectly built according to the plan. Still doesn't get you across.

An admin, but whose admin?

For an application beyond Microsoft's login demo, I'd want to try this workflow on tenant permissions. Imagine you're building a SaaS application and an admin can delete documents. The agent checks whether the user is an active admin, and everything looks fine in your tests because every user and document in the fixtures belongs to the same company. Then someone passes a document ID from another company and discovers that being an admin was apparently a global achievement. Oops. The rule needs to connect the user's membership to the document's tenant. A simplified postcondition in Verus syntax could look like this, assuming those values are already available to the function:

ensures
    allowed == (
        active_member
        && is_admin
        && member_tenant == document_tenant
    ),

Here I'd want the agent to consider an active admin in the right tenant, an active admin in a different tenant, an inactive admin, and a regular member. That second case is the interesting one: the role is valid, but the relationship is wrong. A proof against this contract would have to cover different tenant IDs too, rather than only the company IDs someone happened to put in a test. We still need to establish that the application supplies the actual document tenant and the right membership record. If it passes the user's tenant ID for both arguments, the decision can follow this rule perfectly while the application still leaks access.

Someone still has to know what to ask

I've said this before: you cannot prompt what you don't know exists. If you don't know sessions can be revoked, you probably won't notice that revocation is missing from the specification. This is also a research problem. Microsoft Research calls the translation from informal requirements to checkable specifications intent formalization. Shuvendu Lahiri's article identifies validating those specifications as a central bottleneck. Someone still needs to establish whether the formal statement matches what the user meant.

Intent Formalization: A Grand Challenge for Reliable Coding in the Age of AI Agents - Microsoft Research

microsoft.com

There's another detail in our session example: signatureValid is an input. The function doesn't verify a signature. Same with now: we give it a timestamp, and it trusts that value. A proof of this decision doesn't establish that the cryptography is correct, that the clock is right, or that every protected endpoint actually calls the function. Those need their own guarantees or checks. So when a PR says “verified”, I'd want to know what was verified. The session decision? The HTTP handler? The whole login flow? Which parts were proved, tested, or assumed? That's where PDD Kit's combination of formal and empirical verification makes sense to me. You can prove a decision follows a rule and still use integration tests to check that the application supplies the right inputs and calls it in the right places.

The proof covers what's inside the boundary. The inputs still have to come from somewhere.

How I'd apply this to JavaScript

I don't work in Rust, so Verus isn't something I can apply to my JavaScript projects. But I can borrow PDD Kit's approach: agree on the contract before generating the implementation. I'd use Chopin for the shared plan, questions and decisions, with its MCP server connecting the coding agent. Then turn those agreed rules into unit and integration tests, use fast-check to exercise generated input combinations, and add browser checks for the user flow. For our session example, that means explicitly checking revocation, expiration boundaries and valid sessions being accepted. This doesn't give JavaScript the same formal guarantees, but it gives the agent concrete requirements to implement and us something specific to check before merging.

At Rocket.Chat, we're already increasing code coverage significantly, and every new feature has to come with a decent amount of testing. PDD's approach could help us get more out of that effort by making the expected behavior explicit before we write the tests. For a room-permissions change, for example, the agent could help us work through who should have access, who shouldn't, and what happens when membership changes. Those agreed rules would give us something concrete to connect to the implementation and its tests during review, and make missing cases easier to spot.

Why Property-Based Testing? | fast-check

Learn about the benefits and advantages of property-based testing. If you have never encountered property-based testing before, it is best to start with the definitions in What is Property-Based Testing?.

fast-check.dev

title: Scovant Core 0.26.0: MCP endpoint detection that reads real evidence
description:
A scanner that asks "does this site expose an MCP server?" usually starts at
one URL: /.well-known/mcp.json. Many sites answer that URL with something: a
catch-all page, a JSON error, a redirect to the homepage. Until this release,
Scovant Core counted an HTTP 200 there as a sign of an endpoint. That was wrong,
so before changing it we measured how wrong.

What we measured

In a corpus of 8,523 sites:

  • 0 published a valid /.well-known/mcp.json
  • 239 answered that path with another document
  • 33 published a valid AI Catalog (/.well-known/ai-catalog.json)
  • 19 had an MCP server card we could resolve

So the one place everyone looks was, in practice, never the place a real server
was described, while the sites that did describe an MCP server mostly did it
through a catalog the old check never read.

What changes in 0.26.0

A discovery file has to be one. A 200 at /.well-known/mcp.json that is an
HTML page, or JSON without an mcpServers server, no longer counts as an
endpoint. The finding now says what was served instead, so the fix is obvious.

Server cards are recognised, not assumed. A card at the well-known card
paths counts only when it looks like a server card: a JSON object with a
non-empty name and a remotes list, a version or a $schema. A JSON error
page at those paths is no card.

The AI Catalog is followed. Core reads /.well-known/ai-catalog.json and
fetches up to three server cards it lists — https and public addresses only,
following up to five redirects on each. A card found that way counts as an MCP
surface, so a site that publishes its server through a catalog stops getting a
false "no MCP endpoint" finding.

No answer is not a "no". If the catalog or a listed card times out, answers
429 or 5xx, or is cut off at our read limit before it parses, the rule reports
not measured instead of a finding. Our failure to read a document is never
evidence about the site — the same rule Core has applied to every other
document since its first release.

What it costs

At most four more requests per scan (the catalog and up to three cards), plus
any redirect hops. Core stays passive: ordinary GETs, no authentication, and it
never calls an MCP endpoint or invokes a tool it discovers.

Model change

The Technical Readiness model id moves to R2.1@7b46d2ed7f8b, and the rule
behind this check, MCP_ENDPOINT_ABSENT, moves to rule version 2.0. Results
produced before and after the release carry different model ids, so a change
in a site's result can always be told apart from a change in how we measure.
Every model change is listed in the
methodology changelog.

Upgrade 

pip install -U scovant-core
uvx --from scovant-core scovant scan https://example.com
npx @scovant/core scan https://example.com

The GitHub Action Scovant/scovant-core@v0 picks up 0.26.0 automatically; pin
@v0.26.0 for an exact version. The full list of changes is in the
changelog.

title: PIX, Retries and Approval Rates: Phoenix365 on LatAm Payment Cascades
description:
A player in Mexico tries to deposit through SPEI shortly before a major football match. The payment provider times out, the cashier keeps spinning, and the player leaves before placing a bet. For an ordinary retailer, a failed payment might mean a purchase postponed until tomorrow. In iGaming, it can mean losing the session and the customer. At Phoenix365, a B2B casino and sportsbook technology provider working with Latin American operators, payment reliability shapes the operator experience as much as it shapes the finance team’s numbers. Effective orchestration depends on provider routing, PIX-specific behaviour, safe retries, and honest measurement of approval rates.

Why One Payment Provider Isn't Enough in LatAm

Latin America is not one payment market. Consumers have different local rails, bank arrangements, card acceptance patterns, and wallet preferences. An operator using one international checkout configuration may offer a technically functioning cashier that still fails to serve important customer segments.

Common methods illustrate the variation:

  • PIX, Brazil: Instant account-to-account transfers initiated through banking apps.
  • SPEI, Mexico: An interbank transfer system operated by Banco de México.
  • PSE, Colombia: A bank-account payment option used for online purchases.
  • Local cards and e-wallets: Familiar alternatives whose coverage varies by country and provider.

A single payment processor may create several points of weakness:

  • Peak-time interruptions: Timeouts during popular matches can interrupt deposits precisely when demand rises.
  • Issuer differences: Card approval may vary significantly by issuing bank or acquisition route.
  • Coverage gaps: One connection may not support the required local method, currency, or customer segment.
  • Provider limits: Transaction caps, volume limits, and maintenance windows can unexpectedly restrict availability.

Our Payments Hub lets each operator build its own set of providers and methods for its market, while the operator chooses the providers and holds the contracts. Which methods an operator can offer for gambling depends on the rules in each market.

A payment cascade is an ordered sequence of eligible processors: a payment starts on the preferred route and can move to a fallback only when the earlier outcome makes switching safe and permitted.

How PIX Changes the Cascade

This section uses PIX as an example of how instant account-to-account payments change cascade design; the same pattern applies to similar rails in other markets.

PIX is the instant payment system created by Brazil's central bank. It works around the clock and lets customers pay through a QR code or a copy-and-paste payment code. For a European reader, the distinction from a card authorisation is important: the customer actively initiates a bank transfer, while with a card the issuer approves or declines the charge.

In a card cascade, routing can be revised around a declined authorisation, subject to network rules. With PIX, routing largely occurs before the payment request and QR code are generated. Once the customer sees the code, the request is tied to a particular payment flow. Silently creating a second request through another provider risks duplicate payment instructions and customer confusion.

Three failure points need distinct handling:

  • Request creation fails: The provider never returns a usable payment instruction, so a fallback may be considered after checking the original request's status.
  • Customer does not pay: The QR code expires or remains unpaid; the cashier should say the payment has not arrived and offer a clear, new payment option.
  • Payment settles but confirmation arrives late: The system must match the late confirmation to the original payment and credit it once.

PIX can also be used for payouts to registered recipient keys or eligible account details, and refunds should follow the applicable refund mechanism and the original payment record. A payout flow still needs account-ownership checks: a PIX key on its own does not verify who the recipient is.

Designing the Cascade: Routing Rules and Order

Good routing depends on the transaction in front of it. A route that performs well for one bank or transaction value may be inefficient for another. The decision engine should consider:

  • Payment method, country, and currency.
  • Transaction amount and applicable provider limits.
  • Issuing bank or card BIN, where relevant.
  • Provider health, recent errors, and response time.
  • Transaction fees and total processing cost.

The first provider should usually be the eligible route with the strongest reliable results for that segment, even when a cheaper one is available. Backup providers follow a defined order. Commercial decisions balance acceptance, latency, settlement reliability, fraud exposure, and fees.

A few examples of how routing signals can affect the cascade:

  • High recent timeout rate: Temporarily reduce or suspend traffic to the affected route.
  • Strong approval for a bank segment: Prefer that processor for matching card transactions.
  • PIX request not created: Check the status before issuing a new code through another provider.
  • Increased processing cost: Reassess the ranking without sacrificing legitimate approvals.

A circuit breaker helps automate provider health management: when error rates cross a threshold, the system pauses new traffic on that route and later tests recovery before returning it to service. Thresholds, cool-down periods, and partial recovery need deliberate configuration.

Retries Without Double Charges

A retry is not automatically safe merely because the customer has not seen a success message. Timeouts can conceal a transaction that was accepted downstream. Before switching providers, the cashier must establish whether the earlier attempt is definitively failed, still pending, or successfully settled.

Distinguish recoverable and definitive outcomes:

  • Potentially retryable: Confirmed temporary gateway unavailability, issuer downtime, or a soft decline when the relevant provider and network explicitly allow another attempt.
  • Do not retry: Fraud blocks, stolen or blocked cards, explicit “do not retry” responses, and unresolved transactions that may already have succeeded.

Every logical deposit should have a stable identifier and idempotency protection so repeated API calls do not create an additional charge or a second wallet credit. Individual processor attempts also need their own tracking references. Idempotency must work alongside reconciliation across providers; reusing one key on separate processors is not sufficient protection by itself.

Asynchronous confirmations complicate the flow. A deposit can remain pending while the provider processes the transfer or delivers a webhook. Wallet balance should increase only after verified success, and duplicate or delayed webhooks must be handled safely. When status is uncertain, query the provider and reconcile first; retry only once the earlier attempt is confirmed as failed.

Set a maximum number of attempts, minimum delays between retries, and stop conditions for hard declines. The player should see a helpful status message such as “Payment pending confirmation” with a way to refresh or contact support.

Measuring Approval Rates the Right Way

A single payment approval rate can hide more than it reveals. A cascade creates additional processor attempts, so dividing successful payments by all attempts produces a different number from dividing successful deposits by unique customer payment intents. PIX also needs a distinction between request creation and actual payment completion.

Track separate measures:

  • First-attempt approval and final completion after fallback.
  • Success rates by method, provider, bank, and relevant segment.
  • Time from initial request to verified confirmation.
  • Abandonment or failure at each stage of the deposit journey.
  • Total processing cost per successfully credited deposit.

Consider 100 unique deposit intents. Seventy succeed on the initial route; ten more succeed after allowed fallback attempts. Final completion is 80%, and first-attempt success is 70%. If the system made 140 processor attempts altogether, attempt-level approval is about 57%. All three figures are mathematically valid but answer different questions.

Risk controls must be analysed alongside payments performance. Tougher fraud screening may reduce approvals while preventing harmful transactions; relaxing checks solely to increase the headline payment approval rate can worsen outcomes. At Phoenix365, we use three-layer fraud analysis, while payment and risk teams should agree on shared definitions and escalation criteria. Compare new customers with returning players separately, because their verification status and checkout behaviour can differ substantially.

What to Get Right Before Building One

  1. Route by segment. Build routing rules from payment type, market, bank, amount and real provider performance.
  2. Handle PIX before showing the code. If creation fails, resolve the first attempt, then show the customer a clearly labelled replacement request.
  3. Retry only safe failures. Respect decline instructions, cap attempts, use idempotency keys, and reconcile pending transactions before modifying wallet balances.
  4. Measure both stages. Report initial approval independently from final unique-intent completion, with latency, fraud, and processing cost beside them.

A well-designed cascade can recover legitimate payments, but it cannot compensate for weak provider coverage, unclear status handling, or careless risk policies. What signals do you use to remove a provider from the cascade automatically?

title: The API Worked. My Team IDs Didn't.
description:
How a basketball side project taught me that perfectly valid data can become completely misleading on its way to a database.

It started with basketball

I'm an Olympiacos supporter.

I'm also a data engineer, which means that occasionally, instead of simply enjoying something, I decide it needs a database.

That's more or less how RED Observatory started.

I wanted to build a sports analytics platform where I could explore basketball games beyond the usual final score.

Shot charts, shooting patterns, player performances, historical comparisons. The sort of things I enjoy looking at, combined with the sort of engineering I enjoy doing.

The initial architecture was fairly straightforward:

  • Python for data collection and processing.
  • SQLite for storage.
  • FastAPI for serving the data.
  • React for the frontend.
  • EuroLeague data as the starting point.

Nothing particularly exotic.

I expected the interesting challenges to involve statistics and visualisation.

Instead, one of the most useful engineering lessons came from something considerably less glamorous.

Three characters in a team identifier.

The first dataset looked promising

The first substantial historical collection covered Olympiacos's 2023–24 EuroLeague season.

Forty-one games.

The early integration used a mixture of a community-maintained Python client and direct requests to EuroLeague endpoints.

The client helped with schedule and shot information. Direct requests handled additional game statistics.

It was a reasonable starting point for a personal project.

And data was making its way into the database.

At that stage, it's tempting to focus on the next visible feature.

Can I render a shot chart?

Can I display a box score?

Can I compare games?

But there's a question that should come before all of those.

Does the database actually represent the games correctly?

When we later examined the original database, the answer was rather uncomfortable.

Forty-one games. Half the picture.

The original database contained all 41 games.

That sounds promising.

But a closer inspection revealed something unexpected.

It contained 489 player-match records, all assigned to the away side.

Not a single player-match record was assigned to the home side.

The database also lacked stored fixture dates and final scores.

In other words, we had a collection of basketball games without a complete representation of what happened in those games.

That's an impressive achievement, if your goal is to build an analytics platform for exactly half a basketball court.

Unfortunately, it wasn't mine.

There was another problem.

Two fixtures involving Bayern Munich had been associated with Barcelona.

And this one had a particularly simple explanation.

The three-character problem

In the original importer, team identifiers were generated from the first three characters of a club's name.

The relevant logic looked like this:

home_code = home_name[:3].upper()
away_code = away_name[:3].upper()

At first glance, this might seem like a convenient shortcut.

Many team names have distinctive beginnings.

But consider two EuroLeague clubs:

FC BARCELONA
FC BAYERN MUNICH

Apply our transformation:

"FC BARCELONA"[:3].upper()
# 'FC '

"FC BAYERN MUNICH"[:3].upper()
# 'FC '

There it is.

Two different teams.

One identifier.

Including the trailing space.

Beautiful.

The importer reused existing team records based on this generated identifier. Once two distinct clubs shared the same key, their identities could become mixed.

In the preserved database, two games that the source schedule identified as Bayern Munich fixtures instead referenced Barcelona.

No malformed JSON was required.

No mysterious server failure.

No dramatic API outage.

We introduced the ambiguity ourselves.

And because the resulting values were still perfectly valid strings, a database could happily accept them.

A valid record isn't necessarily a correct record

This is what makes data-quality problems particularly interesting.

Imagine a pipeline that:

  1. Successfully retrieves data from an upstream service.
  2. Parses the response without errors.
  3. Transforms the records.
  4. Inserts them into a database.
  5. Serves the result through an API.
  6. Displays it in a polished interface.

Every operation might succeed.

The frontend might render exactly what the backend returned.

And yet, somewhere in step three, Bayern Munich quietly became Barcelona.

From the application's perspective, everything might appear operational.

From the perspective of someone trying to analyse basketball games, the result is wrong.

A successful request tells us that communication worked.

A successful database transaction tells us that the database accepted the operation.

Neither tells us that the information still means what it meant at the source.

That's a different kind of validation.

And it's the kind that matters most in analytical systems.

Fixing the identity problem

The repair wasn't simply a matter of changing three characters to four.

The real solution was to stop inventing team identities from display names.

Where the source provides authoritative club codes, use them.

A club's display name is useful for a human interface.

It is not necessarily a stable identifier.

Names can change, contain prefixes, use different alphabets or appear in multiple formats.

Even without an obvious collision, a name-derived key introduces assumptions that the source data may not support.

For RED Observatory, the repaired import process used source club codes and the fixture's home/away designation to restore the correct associations.

The historical data was rebuilt into a separate database rather than blindly changing the accepted one.

But correcting team identities was only part of the work.

The missing player statistics required a more complete approach to box-score ingestion and validation.

Both teams have to exist

The original importer had another weakness.

Its parsing logic conditionally processed the home and away sections when the expected structures were present.

If a section wasn't available in the form it expected, that side could be skipped without treating the incomplete result as a fatal problem.

We don't have enough preserved evidence to establish exactly why every home-side player record went missing in the original capture.

And that's worth being explicit about.

We know what the original database contained.

We can identify the team-code collision in the importer.

But the complete historical debugging sequence wasn't preserved.

What mattered for the repair was ensuring that incomplete game data could no longer pass through the pipeline unnoticed.

The newer importer requires both teams' statistical blocks.

It also handles details that are easy to overlook until they become problematic:

  • Player identifier formats.
  • Playing-time values.
  • Team-level and player-level statistics.
  • Reconciliation against final scores.
  • Shot-event identifiers and team associations.
  • Missing spatial coordinates, without pretending they're zero.

These aren't especially glamorous features.

Nobody opens a basketball analytics website hoping to admire its identity-reconciliation logic.

But without them, the more interesting visualisations become considerably less trustworthy.

Rebuilding the season

The repaired database provided a useful before-and-after comparison.

Metric Original database Repaired database
Captured games 41 41
Team records 17 18
Player-match records 489 979
Games with both roster sides 0 41
Fixture dates and scores Missing Restored
Known Bayern/Barcelona mismatches 2 0

The repaired import also introduced automated checks for the relationships between fixtures, teams, player statistics and recorded results.

That doesn't prove that every source value is perfect.

Nor does matching shot-event counts establish that every coordinate is spatially accurate.

But it gives the system explicit conditions that must hold before the collected information can be trusted for the analyses we want to perform.

The objective wasn't to make the database bigger.

It was to make the database more faithful to the source.

The architecture grew up a little

The ingestion process also evolved beyond the original collection scripts.

RED Observatory now separates collecting source responses, normalising records, validating relationships and preparing data for publication.

A simplified view looks like this:

EuroLeague source endpoints
           |
           v
     Raw data capture
           |
           v
   Normalise and identify
           |
           v
   Candidate SQLite DB
           |
           v
 Validate and reconcile
           |
           v
    Static JSON export
           |
           v
 Verify before publication
           |
           v
    RED Observatory

An important detail is that updates are prepared as candidates.

They don't automatically become the accepted public dataset just because a collection process completed.

The new data must pass validation and publication checks first.

If it doesn't, the previously accepted baseline is retained.

For a small hobby project, that may sound rather elaborate.

But it solves a real problem.

I don't want a temporary upstream issue or an importer regression to quietly replace trustworthy data with something incomplete.

And I certainly don't want to discover another basketball club masquerading as Barcelona.

One was enough.

What about the Python library?

There's an important clarification here.

The original integration used the community-maintained euroleague_api package alongside direct HTTP requests.

But the investigation didn't establish that the library was responsible for the problems in our historical database.

In fact, inspection of the preserved package showed functionality for retrieving full player statistics for both teams.

So this isn't a story about a broken open-source dependency.

The verified identifier collision was in our own code.

And the original integration's incomplete validation was our responsibility too.

That distinction matters.

It's easy to blame an abstraction when a data integration behaves unexpectedly.

Sometimes the abstraction really is responsible.

Sometimes the upstream source changes.

And sometimes you write name[:3] and accidentally merge two basketball clubs.

Engineering has a way of keeping us humble.

Why side projects are excellent teachers

I work professionally in data engineering.

I spend a lot of time thinking about how data moves between systems, how transformations behave and what happens when assumptions turn out to be wrong.

But RED Observatory is different.

Nobody commissioned it.

There isn't a customer waiting for a delivery.

I started it because I enjoy basketball, enjoy engineering and wanted to see what I could build.

That freedom is part of what makes it valuable.

I can explore problems that interest me, change direction when something unexpected appears and spend time understanding the parts that aren't immediately visible to users.

I originally wanted to make basketball shot charts.

Instead, I ended up revisiting data identity, ingestion design, reconciliation and safe publication.

All useful engineering problems.

Just with considerably more Olympiacos involved.

The lesson I'll keep

If there's one thing this experience reinforced, it's that data correctness is not something you can infer from a successful pipeline execution.

You need to define what correctness means for the domain.

For basketball, that might involve checking that both teams exist, game identifiers match, statistics reconcile and missing values remain distinguishable from real zeros.

For geospatial data, it might involve coordinate systems, geometry validity, source resolution and geographic coverage.

Different domains.

The same underlying responsibility.

A pipeline should do more than move data successfully.

It should preserve the meaning of that data.

Because otherwise, you can build a perfectly functioning application around a beautifully organised misunderstanding.

And if you'll excuse me, I have some basketball statistics to investigate.

This time, preferably involving the correct teams.

RED Observatory is an independent, fan-built sports analytics project. It began with basketball and continues to evolve as an engineering experiment.

More projects and writing: ptzivras.pages.dev.

title: How to Handle 3 Failed Job Retries: AWS SQS vs RabbitMQ Recovery Paths
description:
A failed job retry in AWS SQS or RabbitMQ is not just a queue choice. It is a recovery-boundary choice. For a developer-tools service that fans out one shipment update to many subscribers, I would separate the publisher, each delivery attempt, and the exhausted work item. That gives operators a place to retry one subscriber without replaying every subscriber.

Short answer: use a durable work record with an idempotency key, explicit attempt state, bounded backoff, and a dead-letter path. SQS and RabbitMQ can both carry the work. Neither one decides whether a repeated shipment update is safe. Your handler and storage model do that.

The useful comparison is operational: what can you recover, what can you inspect, and what happens when a consumer disappears halfway through a batch?

Start with the recovery unit, not the broker

The recovery unit should be one subscriber delivery. Suppose shipment shp_4821 changes to in_transit and 37 subscribers need the event. Put 37 delivery records behind one event identity, not one opaque job that retries the whole fanout. A timeout from subscriber 12 should not make subscribers 1 through 11 run again.

I use an attempt number and a stable key composed from the event and subscriber IDs. The attempt number is for policy. The stable key handles idempotency. They solve different problems.

The smallest useful record looks like this:

type DeliveryState = "pending" | "leased" | "delivered" | "retryable" | "dead";

type Delivery = {
  id: string;
  eventId: string;
  subscriberId: string;
  idempotencyKey: string;
  attempt: number;
  state: DeliveryState;
  nextRunAt: string;
  lastError?: string;
};

The queue message carries id, not the complete shipment payload. The worker loads the delivery record, checks that it still owns the attempt, and sends the payload with idempotencyKey. If the process dies after the remote service accepts the request but before the worker acknowledges the message, the redelivery is expected. The receiver must treat the key as a duplicate-safe operation.

That is the first hard limit. A queue can redeliver. It cannot infer whether an external side effect already happened.

Should AWS SQS or RabbitMQ handle failed job retries?

Classify the result before choosing a retry delay. A connection reset, a 429 response, and a malformed destination are three different operations. Retrying all three with the same delay is configuration bloat disguised as reliability.

type Outcome =
  | { kind: "delivered" }
  | { kind: "retry"; reason: string; delayMs: number }
  | { kind: "dead"; reason: string };

function classify(status: number | "timeout" | "network"): Outcome {
  if (status === "timeout" || status === "network") {
    return { kind: "retry", reason: String(status), delayMs: 30_000 };
  }

  if (status === 429 || status >= 500) {
    return { kind: "retry", reason: `remote_${status}`, delayMs: 60_000 };
  }

  if (status >= 400) {
    return { kind: "dead", reason: `permanent_${status}` };
  }

  return { kind: "delivered" };
}

function nextDelay(attempt: number, baseMs: number): number {
  const capped = Math.min(baseMs * 2 ** attempt, 15 * 60_000);
  const jitter = Math.floor(capped * 0.2 * Math.random());
  return capped - jitter;
}

The numbers here are policy examples, not universal defaults. Set them from the subscriber contract and measured latency. A delivery endpoint that permits 30 seconds of work needs a different lease and timeout from one that answers in 200 milliseconds. Keep the worker timeout shorter than the queue lease only when the worker can renew the lease safely; otherwise a slow request creates concurrent attempts.

This is where the two common choices differ. SQS provides visibility timeout semantics: a received message becomes visible again when the timeout expires unless it is deleted, and a dead-letter queue can receive messages after a configured receive count. RabbitMQ uses acknowledgements, and unacknowledged messages can be requeued when the channel or connection closes; dead-lettering is configured through queue arguments or policies. Those are useful mechanics, but they are not a retry strategy.

A third option, Redis Streams, makes consumer groups and pending entries visible in a different way. That can be convenient when the team already operates Redis, but pending-entry recovery and retention still need explicit operational rules. The comparison is about recovery behavior, not which logo belongs in the architecture diagram.

Keep the implementation boring enough to inspect

The worker should make one decision per delivery and record it before it disappears from an operator's view. Here is the control flow I want to see in a code review:

async function processDelivery(delivery: Delivery): Promise<void> {
  const lease = await store.claim(delivery.id, delivery.attempt);
  if (!lease) return;

  try {
    const status = await sendToSubscriber(delivery.subscriberId, {
      eventId: delivery.eventId,
      idempotencyKey: delivery.idempotencyKey,
    });
    const outcome = classify(status);

    if (outcome.kind === "delivered") {
      await store.markDelivered(delivery.id, delivery.attempt);
    } else if (outcome.kind === "dead") {
      await store.markDead(delivery.id, delivery.attempt, outcome.reason);
    } else {
      await store.scheduleRetry(
        delivery.id,
        delivery.attempt + 1,
        new Date(Date.now() + nextDelay(delivery.attempt, outcome.delayMs)),
        outcome.reason,
      );
    }
  } catch (error) {
    await store.scheduleRetry(
      delivery.id,
      delivery.attempt + 1,
      new Date(Date.now() + nextDelay(delivery.attempt, 30_000)),
      error instanceof Error ? error.message : "unknown_error",
    );
  }
}

The queue acknowledgement belongs after the state transition is durable. If the transition fails, leave the message eligible for redelivery. If the state says delivered, a later redelivery should be a cheap no-op. That ordering is less clever than trying to coordinate a distributed transaction, and it gives the operator a concrete record to inspect.

Measure more than queue depth. I want retry age, attempts by subscriber, time from nextRunAt to claim, dead-letter rate, duplicate-key responses, and the oldest pending delivery. A flat “jobs processed” counter hides the failure that matters: one subscriber failing 10,000 times while the rest succeed.

Three recovery paths I would keep at scale

At small volume, one queue and one worker can be enough. At scale, I would split the paths by operator action:

  1. The normal path handles pending and retryable deliveries whose nextRunAt is due.
  2. The delayed path holds work until its retry time, with a bounded attempt count and jitter.
  3. The dead path preserves the payload reference, error class, last attempt, and subscriber identity for replay or repair.

Replay must create a new attempt deliberately. Do not edit a dead record in place while an old consumer can still see it. A repair command should verify the subscriber contract, create an audit entry, and enqueue only the selected delivery IDs. This is where operational recovery beats a slightly simpler producer API.

The broker trade-off is then straightforward. Choose SQS when managed visibility and queue-level redrive behavior fit the team’s operating model. Choose RabbitMQ when acknowledgement and routing control are central to the design. Consider Redis Streams when its pending-entry model fits an existing operational boundary. In every case, keep the delivery ledger outside the message body and test crashes between send, state update, and acknowledgement.

I would start with a 37-subscriber fixture, kill the worker at each of those three boundaries, and assert four things: no subscriber is silently lost, a successful subscriber is not needlessly replayed, a permanent error reaches the dead path, and a redelivery remains idempotent. That test tells me more than a benchmark that only measures messages per second.

Further reading

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/dlx
  • https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/streams/
  • https://nodejs.org/api/abort_controller.html
  • https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/crontab.5.html

title: How to Test Your MCP Server with Coding Agents
description:
When an AI agent works with your product, it needs a way to find information and take action. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives AI applications a shared way to access those capabilities. Through an MCP server, you can provide tools for checking deployments or updating tickets, along with context such as documentation. The same server can work across compatible applications, reducing the need for separate integrations.

The ecosystem around that connection has grown quickly. In December 2025, Anthropic reported more than 10,000 active public MCP servers. By July 2026, MCP’s maintainers reported nearly 500 million monthly downloads across its Tier 1 software development kits. For developer products, that growing ecosystem creates more opportunities to reach users through the AI applications they already use. Agent evaluations build on that by showing how coding agents use MCP to choose tools, interpret responses, and complete developer tasks.

Building and connecting your MCP server

Developers have traditionally worked with products through interfaces, CLIs, and APIs, using documentation to find their way. As coding agents take on more of that work, MCP gives them a shared way to discover and use your product’s capabilities.

Building an MCP server starts with choosing which operations agents can use and exposing them as tools. Each tool has a name, a description, and a definition of the inputs it accepts, and connects to your existing APIs or application code. The official MCP SDKs handle communication between your server and the AI application.

Building and connecting your MCP server

Once connected, an agent can call a tool with the required inputs. Your server runs the corresponding code and returns the result, such as deployment logs or a ticket’s current status. Setup may also include signing in or supplying credentials so the tools operate with the connected user’s account permissions.

Test your MCP server with MCP Inspector

Once the server is connected, you can check its behavior directly with MCP Inspector. It shows which tools are available and lets you follow a call from its inputs to the returned result. With known starting data, you can see whether the operation reaches the correct resource and returns what you expect.

You can then explore how the server responds when a request is incomplete or the connected account lacks access. Your team writes the product-specific error messages that explain what happened and what would help the task continue. Running these workflows as agent evaluations lets you see whether agents can access your tools, understand the feedback, and take a useful next step inside the applications your users work with. For tools that change data, the evaluations can also check that the correct resource was created, updated, or deleted and that unrelated data stayed unchanged.

Evaluate MCP tool use with coding agents

In our previous post, we covered how to build evaluation tasks that test how well agents handle the work developers do with your product. The same approach applies to MCP evaluations, with a closer look at which tools agents use and how they use them.

Before interpreting a missing tool call, check whether the tool was available to the agent. If it wasn’t, review setup and discovery. If it was, consider whether its name, description, and accepted inputs made it a clear choice for the task.

The table below shows which trace evidence can help explain how agents use your MCP tools. Some applications don’t show discovery steps or identify which server handled each call. Client and server logs can help fill those gaps, while separate outcome checks verify whether the task produced the intended result.

What to look for in an MCP agent trace

MCP behavior Evidence in the trace
MCP tool use Whether the agent called relevant tools on your MCP server.
Correct inputs Whether calls used valid arguments and targeted the intended resources.
Use of results Whether the agent used your server’s responses to guide its actions and support its answer.
Error recovery Whether the agent adjusted after errors and checked uncertain writes before retrying.

Some tasks can explicitly ask the agent to use your MCP server, with successful use included in the evaluation criteria while allowing different valid tool sequences. Other tasks can leave the approach open so you can see whether agents choose your MCP tools. Recording the route separately from the outcome helps distinguish task success from successful use of your server. Repeating each task from the same starting conditions helps you assess consistency across runs.

Keep these tasks as a repeatable evaluation set and rerun them after changing your tools’ names, descriptions, inputs, or responses. When comparing server versions, restore the starting data and keep the client, model, permissions, and other available tools consistent. Compare the trace evidence above alongside verified outcomes across repeated trials to see where behavior improved or regressed.

Conclusion

Testing your MCP server with coding agents shows how the integration supports real developer workflows. Following the agent’s choices reveals how it selects tools, supplies inputs, and responds to errors. That evidence helps you identify where clearer tool descriptions, more useful results, or better error messages could make the experience more dependable.

title: ChronoLock: The Anti-SaaS Secret Link
description:
Most “secure share” tools still touch your secret.

They encrypt on their servers, require accounts, log metadata, or retain the ability to decrypt later. ChronoLock does none of that.

It encrypts in the browser. The server only ever sees ciphertext. There is no account and no telemetry. When the lifetime ends or the secret is revealed once (if you choose), it is gone.

The full source is public: github.com/Nuem8/ChronoLock (GPL-3.0).

The core rule

Everything sensitive happens in the browser using the Web Crypto API.

A random 32-byte key and 12-byte IV are generated locally. The secret is encrypted with AES-GCM before anything is uploaded. The server receives only the ciphertext plus a few flags (TTL, burn-after-read, whether it is locked to a public key).

You can verify this in two ways:

  1. Open DevTools → Network while creating a secret. Only ciphertext leaves the browser.
  2. Read the source. The encryption path is in the web client; the server never sees key material.

Two ways to lock a secret

1. Key in the link (default)

The raw AES key is placed in the URL fragment (after #). Browsers never send the fragment to the server. Anyone with the complete link can decrypt; a truncated link cannot.

2. Locked to a recipient public key

You paste the recipient’s public key. The secret is encrypted so that only the matching private key can open it. The link itself contains no decryption material. The private key never leaves the recipient’s browser and is never sent to ChronoLock.

If the private key is lost, the secret is unrecoverable. That is intentional.

What the server actually stores

  • Ciphertext
  • Chosen lifetime (5 min / 1 h / 1 day / 7 days)
  • Whether to delete after one successful reveal
  • Whether the secret is locked to a public key

Nothing else. No plaintext, no key, no user identifier, no visit log that identifies the secret.

On reveal the browser downloads the ciphertext and decrypts it locally. If “Delete after one reveal” is enabled, the ciphertext is removed only after a successful decryption with the correct key. A wrong key does nothing. The row is also deleted when its lifetime ends.

The server can run with an in-memory store (dies with the process) or SQLite (keeps unexpired ciphertext across restarts, still without the key).

Limits and deliberate constraints

  • Maximum payload: 8 KB
  • Encryption only works over HTTPS or localhost
  • No accounts, no key recovery, no admin override
  • Longest lifetime is 7 days by default

These are not missing features. They are the design.

Run it yourself 

cargo run --release -- --listen 127.0.0.1:8787 --store sqlite --data chronolock.db

Or memory-only:

cargo run --release -- --listen 127.0.0.1:8787 --store memory

Put it behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS. WebCrypto will refuse to encrypt on a public http:// page.

Why this exists

I needed a way to hand someone a temporary credential or recovery code without putting it in email, Slack, or a service that could still read it later. Existing tools either required accounts, kept the ability to decrypt, or added more surface than I wanted.
ChronoLock is the smallest thing that satisfies the requirement:

  • Encrypt in the browser
  • Store only ciphertext
  • Expire or burn after one use
  • Leave no account trail
  • Source available under GPL-3.0 Live instance: chronolock.nuem8.com Source: github.com/Nuem8/ChronoLock

I invite users to test and give me feedback on how to improve it. Thanks.
