title: Do You Actually Need a Headless CMS for Your Blog?
description:
Skip a headless CMS if you write the posts yourself: use Markdown. If someone else writes them, they need an editor, and a headless CMS still leaves you building the blog. That's what DropInBlog is for.

Ask how to add a blog to an Astro or Next.js site, and you get a list. Sanity, Payload, Strapi, Contentful, Directus. Pick one, wire up the API, build some templates, and ship it.

Quick disclosure: I founded DropInBlog and have been building blog software since 2015. I also use it on my own Astro site, so I'm biased, and you should weigh everything below accordingly.

Some of you should skip us too.

Who's going to write the posts?

I started building websites at 19, back when "layout" meant Dreamweaver and a lot of nested tables. That turned into a web agency, and our clients had custom-built sites. Sooner or later, every one of them asked for a blog.

The standard fix was WordPress on a subdomain with a custom theme built to match. It worked. It was also cumbersome. Every one of those installs turned into technical debt: a second site to keep updated and patched, with a theme that had to keep looking like the real one.

That's where I learned that the developer who builds a site is rarely the person who writes its blog. Usually it's someone in marketing, and sometimes it's the founder at 11pm.

If it's just you, use Markdown

If you're the only person writing, and you live in a code editor anyway, you don't need a CMS. You need a folder.

Astro content collections handle this well. One config file:

// src/content.config.ts
import { defineCollection } from 'astro:content';
import { glob } from 'astro/loaders';
import { z } from 'astro/zod';

const blog = defineCollection({
  loader: glob({ pattern: '**/*.md', base: './src/data/blog' }),
  schema: z.object({
    title: z.string(),
    pubDate: z.coerce.date(),
  }),
});

export const collections = { blog };

Drop Markdown files in src/data/blog, pull them with getCollection('blog'), and you have a blog. Not on Astro? Eleventy, Hugo, and Jekyll have been doing this for years. Hat tip to all of them.

Every post is a commit and a deploy. If you're already deploying the site yourself, that's just how you publish, and your posts get versioned with the rest of your code.

If this is you, you can close this tab. You're set.

If other people write, they need an editor

The moment someone outside the dev team writes, Markdown in a repo gets awkward. They need Git access. They break the front matter with one stray colon. They want to see the post before it goes live.

So you need an editor. There are a lot of ways to get one, and they mostly differ on where the content lives:

Option Examples Where content lives What you still build Good when
Git-based CMS Decap, Sveltia, Keystatic, TinaCMS Markdown or JSON files in your repo Templates and SEO pages, and publishing is still a commit You want posts versioned in your repo
Self-hosted headless CMS Payload, Strapi, Directus Your own database Templates and SEO pages, plus running the CMS You want to own the data and host it yourself
Hosted headless CMS Sanity, Contentful The vendor's cloud Templates and SEO pages You don't want to run anything (both have free plans)
Classic CMS used headless WordPress (REST API), Ghost (Content API) Its own database Templates and SEO pages, plus running the CMS Your team already uses WordPress or Ghost
Blog layer DropInBlog The vendor's cloud Very little (more on that below) You're adding a blog to a site that's already built

All of these are real options. Plenty of good blogs run on each. Payload comes up more than anything else in dev threads right now, and I get why.

But look at the "What you still build" column. With every headless option, the CMS gives you content and an editor. Your app still needs the rest: the post template, the list with pagination, category and author pages, the sitemap, the RSS feed, and the meta tags and schema on every page.

If you already have Sanity, Payload, or something else for the rest of the site, that's fine. A lot of teams keep that CMS and use DropInBlog for the blog, because the blog stays compartmentalized from the rest of the site, and it's already done. Since blogs are all we do, we can go deep on them, instead of the blog being an afterthought in a much larger system.

The difference is our Rendered API. Instead of JSON you have to turn into templates, it returns the finished HTML: the post, the list, categories, authors, the sitemap, the feed, the meta tags. You don't design those pieces yourself. When we ship a new blog feature, it shows up for your marketing team without a frontend pass.

What teams get wrong when they add a blog

The teams that find us usually show up after one of three things: a site migration, a blog nobody wants to touch anymore, or an SEO problem.

Most teams build the post page and call it done. Then the requests start: author pages, categories, a redirect because someone changed a slug. Every one lands in the dev backlog, and the blog becomes a second product nobody planned to maintain.

For us, the hardest part has always been everything around the posts. Matching each site's design. Keeping every page crawlable and indexable.

On Astro, our integration handles that part. Install it and add your keys:

npm install @dropinblog/astro

# .env
DROPINBLOG_BLOG_ID=your_dropinblog_blog_id
DROPINBLOG_API_KEY=your_dropinblog_api_key

Then one entry in your config:

// astro.config.mjs
import { defineConfig } from 'astro/config';
import dropInBlog from '@dropinblog/astro';

export default defineConfig({
  site: 'https://yoursite.com',
  integrations: [dropInBlog()],
});

That registers the blog, category, and author routes, plus a sitemap, RSS feeds, and JSON-LD on every page. It works in static, server-rendered, or Server Islands mode. On a static build, point our build hook at your host's deploy hook. Every publish triggers a rebuild that skips the posts that didn't change.

Your marketing team writes in our editor. Nobody opens a pull request to fix a typo.

An AI assistant can do the same work through our MCP server. Posts come out the way the editor writes them, so they stay easy to open and edit by hand. SEO analysis is the same 0-100 score the panel already shows. Team permissions apply there too: the assistant can only do what that person's role allows in the editor.

When you shouldn't use us

Here's when DropInBlog is the wrong pick:

  • You're the only writer and happy in Markdown.
  • You're a creator or a newsletter-first publication. There are tools built for that, and we aren't one of them.
  • You want something free. We're paid, with a free trial.

If you want the full setup, we have an Astro package and packages for other frameworks.

What's your blog stack, and who actually writes on it?

title: Edtech Reminder Backpressure Explained: Node.js Queues Before a 900-Second HTTPS Timeout
description:
Short answer: let the public HTTPS cron webhook admit due reminder IDs to a durable queue, return before the 900-second timeout, and let rate-limited workers drain that queue under explicit retry and acknowledgement rules.

For an edtech reminder system, the deciding constraint is not cron accuracy. It is whether a burst of class reminders can cross a narrow delivery limit without turning webhook lifetime into job lifetime. The queue absorbs that mismatch. More worker concurrency lowers latency until the downstream rate limit becomes binding; after that point, extra concurrency adds retry traffic and cost without draining the backlog faster.

That is the decision record: cron owns when to scan, the HTTPS handler owns admission, and workers own delivery. Keep those boundaries separate.

How should Node.js user reminders recover when a cron webhook hits a 900-second timeout?

Treat the timeout as a boundary error in the design, not as permission to make the cron request run longer. A public scheduler has to reach the HTTPS endpoint, but reachability only starts the operation. If that request also scans every learner, waits on every notification, and retries each slow delivery inline, its completion time grows with the day's reminder volume. A 900-second ceiling then becomes part of application correctness, which is a poor bargain: one unusually dense course timetable can move a routine scheduling run from “slow” to “ambiguous.” The caller may no longer know whether work finished, while the application may already have sent some reminders.

The safer contract is smaller. On each cron tick, the handler selects a bounded page of due records, derives a stable delivery key, publishes those records, persists the scan cursor, and returns. If more rows are due, another bounded admission pass continues from that cursor. The worker pool acknowledges a message only after its durable state says the delivery has reached the intended terminal outcome. RabbitMQ's documentation draws the relevant distinction: a consumer acknowledgement concerns delivery from broker to consumer, while publisher confirms concern transfer from publisher to broker. They solve different uncertainty windows, so don't treat one as proof of the other.

This is the invariant that matters: a reminder may be attempted more than once, but its delivery key may produce at most one accepted delivery outcome. The data model, not a long-lived request, enforces that rule.

Fast failure helps. If DNS, TLS, routing, or access policy prevents the scheduler from reaching the public endpoint, alert on the missing admission heartbeat; don't quietly interpret an empty queue as “no reminders were due.” A queue depth of zero and a scheduler that never arrived look identical unless the admission path emits its own timestamp.

Decision boundaries and failure ownership

Three identifiers keep the system auditable: a run_id for one scheduled admission pass, a reminder_id for the user-facing intent, and a stable delivery_key for the channel attempt. The first explains scheduler behavior. The second supports product and compliance review. The third is the idempotency boundary. Reusing one identifier for all three makes investigation harder because “the cron ran twice” and “the message was delivered twice” are different claims.

The failure boundaries should be equally plain. The scheduler can fail to invoke the public HTTPS endpoint. The admission handler can stop after publishing only part of a due page. A worker can lose ownership before recording an acknowledgement. The downstream delivery channel can accept work more slowly than the producer creates it. None of those cases requires the webhook to wait for the final send; each requires an observable checkpoint and a replay rule.

For email, SMS, and OTP-like flows, retry policy also has a compliance edge. An old classroom reminder is not automatically useful merely because it is still queued. Give each job an expiry derived from the event time and product policy, then suppress it after expiry rather than “catching up” with stale messages. The exact expiry is a product decision, and I'm not sure there is one defensible global value: a lesson starting soon, an account notice, and an authentication code have different harm profiles. Resolve that uncertainty with the product owner and compliance reviewer, then encode the result as data workers can enforce.

Keep the following invariants close to the code review:

  • A cron retry can repeat admission without creating a new delivery identity.
  • Publishing and advancing the scan cursor must leave a recoverable record of which page was admitted.
  • A worker never exceeds the configured downstream rate budget, even while draining a large backlog.
  • Expired work is recorded as suppressed, not silently discarded and not sent late.
  • Admission, queue age, attempts, accepted outcomes, and suppressions have separate counters.

One warning deserves its own line.

Queue depth alone lies.

A stable depth can mean balanced flow, a stalled consumer, or a rate ceiling matched exactly by arrivals. Queue age exposes the user impact; attempt counts expose churn; the admission heartbeat separates “nothing due” from “cron couldn't reach us.” Those signals let an operator distinguish latency pressure from wasted work before raising concurrency.

Comparing the latency and cost choices

The useful comparison is between ownership models, not queue brands. Each model can be implemented with several tools; the operational shape is what determines whether it fits a reminder burst.

Model Latency behavior Cost behavior Failure boundary Best fit
Synchronous cron webhook Low overhead for a tiny batch, then latency grows with work No standing worker pool, but retries can repeat expensive work Caller timeout overlaps delivery progress Small, strictly bounded batches that always finish well inside the request budget
Queue admission plus fixed workers Backlog adds predictable waiting Stable worker allocation; idle capacity is possible Admission and delivery are independently replayable Regular course schedules with known rate limits
Queue admission plus elastic workers Can reduce queue age during bursts until the downstream limit binds Capacity follows demand, with scaling and retry overhead Autoscaling, rate limiting, and delivery each need telemetry Spiky enrollment or timetable events where latency has explicit value

Choose a target queue age first, then size workers from measured service time and the permitted downstream rate. Don't start from a fashionable concurrency number. If the channel accepts at most a fixed number of requests per interval, total worker issue rate must remain below that boundary; otherwise the “faster” pool spends its budget producing retries. For a cost-sensitive nightly digest, a fixed pool that drains gradually may be correct. For a reminder tied to the beginning of a live class, paying for temporary capacity may be reasonable, but only until the delivery limit is saturated.

The catch is that queue admission adds state, operational alarms, and replay semantics. It is not suitable when every run contains a demonstrably tiny, bounded set and the whole operation comfortably fits the request deadline. Stick with a synchronous handler in that case, provided it still uses stable delivery keys and records completion. At the other extreme, use a continuously running dispatcher rather than cron when deadlines are finer than the scheduler's trigger granularity or when due work arrives continuously. The valid rejected option depends on the workload; “always use a queue” is not an architecture decision.

GitHub Actions illustrates another boundary worth documenting. Its scheduled workflows run from the default branch, the shortest interval is five minutes, and scheduled runs can be delayed during periods of high load. Those characteristics can be acceptable for a coarse maintenance scan, but they do not define a precise user-notification clock. A reminder architecture should state whether trigger delay is allowed and how a later scan discovers work that became due since the prior cursor.

The critical path in Python

The production application may expose its admission handler in Node.js, but the control loop below is intentionally language-neutral Python. It shows the contract without coupling the decision record to a framework or a commercial service. The store and queue interfaces are abstractions; their implementations must provide the durability guarantees selected by the team.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Protocol


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ReminderJob:
    reminder_id: str
    delivery_key: str
    expires_at: datetime


class ReminderStore(Protocol):
    def claim_due_page(self, now: datetime, limit: int) -> list[ReminderJob]: ...
    def already_accepted(self, delivery_key: str) -> bool: ...
    def mark_accepted(self, delivery_key: str) -> None: ...
    def mark_suppressed(self, delivery_key: str, reason: str) -> None: ...


class DurableQueue(Protocol):
    def publish(self, job: ReminderJob) -> None: ...
    def acknowledge(self, job: ReminderJob) -> None: ...
    def retry_later(self, job: ReminderJob) -> None: ...


class Channel(Protocol):
    def send(self, job: ReminderJob) -> bool: ...


def admit_due_reminders(
    now: datetime,
    store: ReminderStore,
    queue: DurableQueue,
    page_size: int = 200,
) -> int:
    jobs = store.claim_due_page(now=now, limit=page_size)
    for job in jobs:
        queue.publish(job)
    return len(jobs)


def process_one(
    job: ReminderJob,
    now: datetime,
    store: ReminderStore,
    queue: DurableQueue,
    channel: Channel,
) -> None:
    if store.already_accepted(job.delivery_key):
        queue.acknowledge(job)
        return

    if now >= job.expires_at:
        store.mark_suppressed(job.delivery_key, reason="expired")
        queue.acknowledge(job)
        return

    if channel.send(job):
        store.mark_accepted(job.delivery_key)
        queue.acknowledge(job)
    else:
        queue.retry_later(job)

There is a deliberate gap between send and mark_accepted: a worker can lose ownership after the channel accepts a request but before local state is updated. The final integration therefore needs a channel-supported idempotency token or a reconciliation mechanism keyed by delivery_key; a local pre-send check cannot close that window alone. This is also why consumer acknowledgements belong after durable outcome recording. A premature acknowledgement trades visible retry risk for invisible loss.

The page_size of 200 is example configuration, not a benchmark or universal recommendation. Load tests should vary page size, worker count, channel latency, and injected ownership loss. Assert outcomes, not merely throughput: no unexpired reminder disappears; no delivery key reaches two accepted outcomes; expired jobs remain suppressed; a repeated cron run resumes from a durable boundary. Then deploy with worker concurrency below the known downstream budget and raise it while watching queue age rather than request count alone.

Rejected option and deployment rule

The rejected design is a webhook that holds the cron request open until all reminders are sent. It remains valid for a bounded administrative task where the maximum input size is enforced, partial completion is transactionally visible, and the worst-case duration stays far below the caller's deadline. It is a poor default for class reminder fan-out because enrollment and timetable clustering make the amount of work part of runtime.

Ship the queued design in two stages. First, run admission with workers consuming but delivery disabled, and compare admitted IDs with the existing due-set calculation. Next, enable a constrained worker pool and verify queue age, acknowledgement rate, accepted outcomes, retries, suppressions, and the admission heartbeat. Rollback should stop new admission while allowing a deliberate choice between draining or preserving already admitted work; deleting the queue erases the evidence needed to make that choice.

The final rule is compact: use the public HTTPS cron call as a recoverable trigger, not as a container for delivery work. Select worker capacity from the latency target and the actual rate boundary, accept the operational cost of a queue only when the workload is unbounded or bursty, and preserve a synchronous path for genuinely small jobs. That keeps a 900-second timeout from deciding which learners receive a reminder.

References

  • RabbitMQ, “Consumer Acknowledgements and Publisher Confirms”: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • GitHub Docs, “Events that trigger workflows”: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows

title: Getting to Know the Options File Settings
description:
Options

CodeBehind provides a dedicated options file located at code_behind/options.ini. This file contains various configuration options that allow developers to customize the framework's behavior without modifying the framework's source code.

The options file includes settings for View compilation, file paths, routing, Controllers, WebForms Core integration, WebSocket connections, Server-Sent Events (SSE), and other framework features.

The default options file in CodeBehind looks like this:

[CodeBehind-options]
view_path=wwwroot
move_view_from_wwwroot=true
dll_path=wwwroot/bin
move_dll_from_wwwroot_bin=true
rewrite_aspx_file_to_directory=false
access_aspx_file_after_rewrite=false
ignore_default_after_rewrite=true
start_trim_in_aspx_file=true
inner_trim_in_aspx_file=true
end_trim_in_aspx_file=true
set_break_for_layout_page=true
convert_cshtml_to_aspx=false
show_minor_errors=false
error_page_path=/error.aspx/{value}
prevent_access_default_aspx=false
default_role=guest
web_forms_script_path=/script
auto_create_web_forms_script=true
recreate_web_forms_script_after_recompile=false
use_default_controller=true
default_controller=DefaultController
use_segment_in_default_controller=true
set_break_for_default_controller=true
access_controller_by_lower_case=true
just_access_controller_by_lower_case=true
ignore_prefix_controller=.
ignore_suffix_controller=.
put_two_underlines_equal_to_dash_for_controller=false
set_default_pages=true
max_web_socket_connections_per_client=3
web_socket_buffer_size=4096
send_view_only_in_get_method=false
ignore_layout_for_post_back=false
set_text_html_content_type_for_post_back=true
sse_interval=1000
max_sse_connections_per_client=3

In the following sections, we will examine these settings and explain how they can be used to customize CodeBehind applications.

View File Configuration

Change View Path

(view_path=wwwroot)

This setting specifies the directory in which CodeBehind stores and compiles View files (.aspx). Developers can move their View files out of the wwwroot directory and place them in a directory of their choice.

This is particularly useful when View files contain server-side code. Keeping these files outside the publicly accessible wwwroot directory helps prevent direct access to their source files and improves application security.

Operation location: View file compilation

Move Views from wwwroot

(move_view_from_wwwroot=true)

When enabled, this setting automatically moves all .aspx and .astx files from the wwwroot directory to the directory specified by view_path during recompilation.

This eliminates the need to manually relocate View files when changing the View directory.

Operation location: View file compilation

Rewrite ASPX File Paths as Directory Paths

(rewrite_aspx_file_to_directory=false)

One of the interesting features of CodeBehind is the ability to access ASPX files through directory-style URLs without their file extensions.

When this option is enabled, a URL that corresponds to an ASPX file can also be accessed using a path without the .aspx extension.

For example, the following file:

/page/about.aspx

Can also be accessed through:

/page/about

This feature provides cleaner URLs without requiring additional routing configuration.

Note: You can safely enable this option because the rewriting process does not introduce additional processing overhead.

Operation location: View file compilation

Allow Access to ASPX Files After Rewriting

(access_aspx_file_after_rewrite=false)

When rewrite_aspx_file_to_directory is enabled, this option determines whether the original ASPX file path remains accessible.

If enabled, both the extensionless URL and the original .aspx URL can be used to access the same View.

If disabled, access is limited to the rewritten directory-style URL.

Operation location: View file compilation

Ignore Default.aspx After Rewriting

(ignore_default_after_rewrite=true)

In CodeBehind, a file named Default.aspx is automatically recognized as the default View of its containing directory. Therefore, developers do not need to include its filename in the URL.

When ASPX-to-directory rewriting is enabled, this option determines how Default.aspx files are handled in the rewritten directory structure.

When enabled, Default.aspx is treated as the default View of the corresponding directory rather than allowing the Default path to be treated as a separate directory.

Operation location: View file compilation

Change DLL Path

(dll_path=wwwroot/bin)

This setting specifies the directory where CodeBehind stores and loads compiled DLL files.

Developers can move DLL files from the default wwwroot/bin directory to a directory of their choice. Keeping DLL files outside the publicly accessible wwwroot directory helps prevent direct access to compiled assemblies and improves application security.

Operation location: DLL compilation

Move DLLs from wwwroot/bin

(move_dll_from_wwwroot_bin=true)

When enabled, this setting automatically moves all DLL files from the wwwroot/bin directory to the directory specified by dll_path during recompilation.

This eliminates the need to manually move compiled DLL files when changing the DLL directory.

Operation location: DLL compilation

Whitespace Management During View Compilation

CodeBehind provides three options for automatically removing unnecessary whitespace from ASPX files during compilation.

These options make it possible to write cleaner and more readable View code without worrying about extra line breaks, tabs, or spaces affecting the resulting HTML.

Trim at the Beginning of ASPX Files

(start_trim_in_aspx_file=true)

When enabled, this option removes unnecessary line breaks, tabs, and spaces from the beginning of ASPX files during compilation.

This means you no longer need to place the DOCTYPE declaration or the opening HTML tag immediately after the Page directive. You can start writing them on the next line.

For example, instead of writing:

Standard syntax:

<%@ Page %><!DOCTYPE html>

You can write:

<%@ Page %>
<!DOCTYPE html>

The same applies to Razor syntax:

@page
<!DOCTYPE html>

This makes View files easier to read and maintain.

Operation location: View file compilation

Trim Inside ASPX Files

(inner_trim_in_aspx_file=true)

When enabled, this option removes unnecessary line breaks following server-side code blocks during compilation.

This prevents unwanted blank lines from appearing between HTML elements in the resulting output.

For example, both Razor and standard syntax support server-side code blocks:

Razor syntax:

@{ code }

Standard syntax:

<% code %>

With this option enabled, unnecessary line breaks following these code blocks are removed.

Operation location: View file compilation

Trim at the End of ASPX Files

(end_trim_in_aspx_file=true)

When enabled, this option removes unnecessary line breaks, tabs, and spaces from the end of ASPX files during compilation.

This helps prevent unnecessary whitespace from being included in the compiled output.

Operation location: View file compilation

Prevent Direct Access to Layout Files

(set_break_for_layout_page=true)

When enabled, Layout files are automatically excluded from direct access. This means users cannot access these files directly through their URLs.

Layout files are intended to be used as part of the View composition process rather than executed as independent pages.

Operation location: View file compilation

Support the CSHTML Extension

(convert_cshtml_to_aspx=false)

CodeBehind provides an option to support .cshtml files. This allows developers to use the familiar CSHTML extension and take advantage of code highlighters that recognize Razor syntax.

When enabled, CSHTML files can contain both Razor syntax and standard CodeBehind syntax. During compilation, these files are converted into ASPX files.

For default pages, the filename must be Default.cshtml. Files named Index.cshtml, for example, will not automatically become the default page.

Important: CSHTML files should not be added to Visual Studio projects as compilation items. The reason is that, in addition to CodeBehind, the default .NET compilation process may also attempt to compile these files. This can cause compilation conflicts, unstable behavior, and potential security issues.

Also note that Visual Studio's default code highlighter may display unnecessary errors in CSHTML files that use CodeBehind-specific syntax.

Operation location: View file compilation

Show Minor Compilation Errors

(show_minor_errors=false)

When enabled, this option displays minor compilation issues that do not prevent successful compilation but indicate that the code could be improved or optimized.

These messages are written to the views_compile_error.log file in the code_behind directory.

This option is useful for identifying potential problems and improving the quality of View files without interrupting the compilation process.

Operation location: View file compilation

Error Handling and Default Pages

Configure the Error Page Path

(error_page_path=/error.aspx/{value})

The default CodeBehind template includes an error page. This option specifies the path used to display that page when an error occurs.

The default path contains a variable named {value}. CodeBehind replaces this variable with the corresponding error code.

For example:

/error.aspx/500

In this example, {value} is replaced with 500.

This allows developers to handle different types of errors through a single error page and customize the displayed content according to the error code.

For more information about configuring error pages, see the following tutorial:

Error Handling

Operation location: Every request

Prevent Direct Access to Default.aspx

(prevent_access_default_aspx=false)

In CodeBehind, a file named Default.aspx is automatically recognized as the default View of its containing directory.

For example, if a Default.aspx file exists in the root directory, accessing:

example.com

will execute:

example.com/Default.aspx

Similarly, if a Default.aspx file exists in the dir directory, accessing:

example.com/dir

will execute:

example.com/dir/Default.aspx

However, the original Default.aspx URL remains accessible by default.

When this option is enabled, direct access to the Default.aspx file path is disabled, while access to the directory itself remains available.

For example:

  • example.com/dir/Default.aspx will not be accessible.
  • example.com/dir/ will remain accessible.

This helps prevent multiple URLs from accessing the same page, which can contribute to cleaner URL structures and better SEO.

Operation location: Every request

Set the Default User Role

(default_role=guest)

This option specifies the default role assigned to users in the application. Its default value is guest.

Developers can change this value to customize the default role used by CodeBehind.

WebForms Core Integration

WebFormsJS Script Path

(web_forms_script_path=/script)

This option specifies the directory path used for the WebFormsJS client-side script.

For example, with the default value:

web_forms_script_path=/script

The WebFormsJS file will be available at:

/script/web-forms.js

Developers can change this path to place the script in a different directory.

Automatically Create the WebFormsJS Script

(auto_create_web_forms_script=true)

When enabled, CodeBehind automatically creates the WebFormsJS file.

This eliminates the need to manually create or copy the client-side script into the project.

Recreate WebFormsJS After Recompilation

(recreate_web_forms_script_after_recompile=false)

When enabled, CodeBehind recreates the WebFormsJS file after each recompilation.

This is useful when the WebFormsJS script needs to be regenerated to reflect changes in the framework or its configuration.

Controller Configuration

Use the Default Controller

(use_default_controller=true)

When enabled, accessing the application's root URL causes the default Controller to execute.

This provides a convenient way to define the Controller responsible for handling requests to the root path.

Specify the Default Controller Name

(default_controller=DefaultController)

This option specifies the name of the Controller class used as the default Controller.

The default value is DefaultController.

Developers can change this value to use a different Controller class for the root path.

Enable Segments in the Default Controller

(use_segment_in_default_controller=true)

When enabled, the default Controller can access URL segments.

This allows developers to handle additional path information through the default Controller.

Note: If another Controller matching the requested route is found, that Controller will be executed instead of the default Controller.

Restrict the Default Controller to the Root Path

(set_break_for_default_controller=true)

When enabled, the default Controller is excluded from the list of Controllers used during route configuration.

As a result, the default Controller is executed only for requests to the root path, rather than being considered for other routes.

Allow Lowercase Controller Names in URLs

(access_controller_by_lower_case=true)

When enabled, Controller class names can be accessed through URLs using lowercase letters.

This provides greater flexibility when defining routes and accessing Controllers.

Allow Only Lowercase Controller Names in URLs

(just_access_controller_by_lower_case=true)

When enabled, Controller class names can only be accessed through lowercase URLs.

This option can be used to enforce a consistent lowercase URL structure.

Ignore a Prefix in Controller Names

(ignore_prefix_controller=.)

This option allows developers to exclude a specified prefix from the Controller name when generating its accessible URL.

For example, if the prefix Route is specified, a Controller named:

RouteContent

can be accessed through:

example.com/Content

This makes it possible to use naming conventions in Controller classes without including those prefixes in the URLs.

Ignore a Suffix in Controller Names

(ignore_suffix_controller=.)

Similar to the previous option, this setting allows developers to exclude a specified suffix from Controller names when generating their accessible URLs.

For example, if the suffix Controller is specified, a Controller named:

ContentController

can be accessed through:

example.com/Content

This is particularly useful when following naming conventions that require a common suffix for Controller classes.

Convert Double Underscores to Dashes in Controller Routes

(put_two_underlines_equal_to_dash_for_controller=false)

When enabled, this option treats two consecutive underscores in a Controller class name as a dash in its corresponding URL.

For example, a Controller named:

active__page

can be accessed through:

example.com/active-page

This provides an alternative way to create readable URLs from Controller class names.

Automatically Create Default Pages

(set_default_pages=true)

When enabled, CodeBehind automatically creates the default project template and its associated pages.

This makes it easier to initialize a new application without manually creating the initial files.

WebSocket and SSE Configuration

Maximum WebSocket Connections per Client

(max_web_socket_connections_per_client=3)

This setting determines the maximum number of simultaneous WebSocket connections allowed per client.

When the number of connection requests exceeds this limit, the oldest active WebSocket connection is terminated, and a new connection is established in its place.

This helps control the number of active connections maintained for each client.

WebSocket Buffer Size

(web_socket_buffer_size=4096)

This setting determines the size of the buffer used for WebSocket communication.

Choosing an appropriate buffer size is important. A buffer that is too large may consume unnecessary memory, while a buffer that is too small may limit the amount of data that can be handled efficiently.

The default value is 4096 bytes.

Send View Only for GET Requests

(send_view_only_in_get_method=false)

When enabled, this setting restricts View content delivery to GET requests.

For all other HTTP methods, including POST, PUT, and DELETE, the server does not include the View content in the response.

This helps prevent unnecessary View transmission during requests intended for data submission or modification.

Ignore Layout for Post-Back Requests

(ignore_layout_for_post_back=false)

When enabled, the server automatically excludes the Layout from the response whenever it detects a Post-Back request sent by WebFormsJS, identified by the Content-Type header.

This eliminates the need for developers to manually check whether a request originates from WebFormsJS and conditionally disable Layout rendering.

Set HTML Content Type for Post-Back Responses

(set_text_html_content_type_for_post_back=true)

When enabled, this setting instructs CodeBehind to set the response Content-Type header to text/html; charset=utf-8 whenever it receives a Post-Back request identified by the corresponding header from WebFormsJS.

This ensures that the browser interprets the response as HTML rather than attempting to process it as another content format.

SSE Transmission Interval

(sse_interval=1000)

This setting specifies the time interval, in milliseconds, between consecutive SSE data transmissions from the server to the client.

For example, a value of 1000 means that SSE data is transmitted every second.

Developers can adjust this value to control how frequently SSE data is sent.

Maximum SSE Connections per Client

(max_sse_connections_per_client=3)

This setting defines the maximum number of simultaneous SSE connections allowed per client.

When the number of connection requests exceeds this limit, the oldest active SSE connection is terminated, and a new connection is established in its place.

This helps prevent an excessive number of SSE connections from being maintained by a single client.

Conclusion

The CodeBehind options file provides a centralized way to customize many aspects of the framework, from View compilation and file management to Controller routing and real-time communication.

Instead of modifying framework code or implementing additional configuration logic, developers can adjust these settings directly through code_behind/options.ini.

More customization options may be added to the options file in future versions of CodeBehind.

Related links

CodeBehind on GitHub:
https://github.com/elanatframework/CodeBehind

CodeBehind in NuGet:
https://www.nuget.org/packages/CodeBehind/

CodeBehind page:
https://elanat.net/codebehind

title: Node.js Marketplace Webhooks: Rate-Limit Queues, Retries, and Delivery Guarantees
description:
Short answer: use a queue-centered design for delayed marketplace webhooks when you need retries and basic rate-limited processing without complex orchestration. Let a scheduler enqueue work, then let workers control concurrency. Pick a workflow engine when the delivery contract needs durable fan-out, joins, or replay.

A marketplace webhook usually starts as an event such as order.paid or shipment.updated. The producer should record the event and enqueue a delivery task. A worker owns the call to the partner API. That boundary keeps the scheduler from becoming a hidden worker pool.

Infrai fits this narrow handoff because its queue surface is plain REST: no SDK install, no client-library version to babysit, and any language that can send HTTP can publish work. Infrai's operating model is one key, one bill across the wider backend capability set, so the same service does not need a new credential each time the workflow adds storage or observability. I would still keep the event ledger in Postgres; the queue is transport, not the system of record.

Cron is useful as a trigger. It is a poor place to drain a rate-limited backlog. A cron-fired job can wake up every minute, but it does not naturally express worker concurrency, per-attempt backoff, or an idempotency key for each delivery. The queue does.

The queue model is intentionally boring: publish a task, consume one, call the destination, then acknowledge only after the destination accepts the request. Standard delivery is at-least-once, so the consumer must be idempotent. A retry can happen after a timeout even when the partner already processed the request.

Ship it.

Keep an audit row in Postgres before publishing. Acknowledgement deletes the message, retention is finite, and this is not an event-stream replay system. If support needs to reconstruct a month of deliveries, the queue alone cannot do that job.

How can a cheap Node.js webhook task queue handle rate limits?

The right comparison axis is the delivery guarantee, not the number of knobs in a dashboard. Here is the short matrix I use when reviewing a marketplace integration:

Option Delivery shape Rate limiting and retry fit Choose it when Main catch
Queue plus worker At-least-once task delivery Worker concurrency and application backoff You need a small, explicit pipeline No native debounce, throttle, or topic fan-out
BullMQ on Redis At-least-once jobs with Redis state Rich delayed jobs, backoff, and concurrency controls Your team already operates Redis and wants a Node.js-first library Redis operations and retention become your responsibility
Inngest Durable function/workflow execution Built-in retries and step history You need multi-step workflows with clear execution history More orchestration than a single delivery task needs
Cloudflare Workers Cron Triggers Scheduled HTTP invocation Trigger timing, not a durable task queue The work is short and a public HTTP endpoint is enough A cron run has a 900-second limit and missed runs are not replayed

For the common case, I would put the queue between the marketplace event log and the outbound HTTP client. Backoff can be modeled in application logic by requeueing or delayed republishing. There is no native debounce or throttle primitive, so encode the partner's policy in the worker and persist the next-attempt timestamp.

That is a trade-off, not a defect. A simple queue is easier to inspect than a workflow graph, but it cannot give you a built-in join when three independent seller checks must all finish before settlement.

The following example uses the documented queue surface. It creates a queue, publishes one delayed task, and consumes it. The retry wrapper honors Retry-After, uses exponential backoff for 429, and sends an idempotency key on writes. The queue's delay must stay at or below seven days; retention must stay within 30 days.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function publish(init: RequestInit, idempotencyKey: string) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const headers = new Headers(init.headers);
    headers.set("Authorization", `Bearer ${apiKey}`);
    headers.set("Content-Type", "application/json");
    if (idempotencyKey) headers.set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey);
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish", { ...init, headers });
    if (response.status !== 429) {
      if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
      return response.json();
    }
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
    const waitMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
  }
  throw new Error("rate limit retries exhausted");
}

const queue = "marketplace-webhook-delivery";
await publish({
  method: "POST",
  body: JSON.stringify({
    queue,
    body: JSON.stringify({ eventId: "evt_7421", kind: "order.paid" }),
    delay_seconds: 30
  })
}, "evt_7421");

Create the queue once, then run this publisher from the event handler. The worker consumes and acknowledges after a successful partner response; on a retryable response, leave the message unacknowledged or publish a new attempt with a deterministic event id. Do not assume one consumer receives a message only once.

For a long-running drain, have a cron trigger enqueue a bounded batch and let workers consume it. Cron tasks accept a public http_url, have a 900-second execution ceiling, and do not catch up missed triggers after a pause. Push subscriptions also require a public HTTPS target. Those constraints define where the provider boundary ends.

Reliability: what survives a worker crash?

The queue model forces an explicit contract. A standard queue is at-least-once; the consumer owns deduplication and must make the partner call idempotent. FIFO deduplication lasts five minutes, which is useful for a burst but not a substitute for a durable event id. Delayed messages last at most seven days, message bodies are capped at 256 KB, and retention tops out at 30 days. Ack deletes the message.

That makes an audit table non-optional for a marketplace that needs chargeback evidence. Write event_id, destination, attempt count, and the next eligible time before you publish. On a worker crash, reconcile the table with the partner's idempotency key. I am not sure every team needs a full replay log, but if the answer is yes, choose a stream or a workflow product before you ship a queue-only design.

Infrai is a reasonable fit for delayed webhook buffering and worker-side rate control when a single HTTP integration matters more than workflow primitives. Its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas and supplies runnable examples in ten languages, which removes a second integration tax when a CLI or a small Go helper joins the Node.js service. The recommendation is narrow: use it for the queue handoff, while your application retains ownership of partner-specific retry rules.

That consistency matters during a migration. A marketplace team can inspect the public discovery document before writing a client, compare the declared method and path with its test fixture, and keep the same Authorization header convention in a tiny worker and an internal command-line tool. It does not remove operational work: you still need a dead-letter policy, metrics, and a database transaction around the event record. It does remove a class of glue where every provider has a different SDK shape, retry exception, and credential loader. The payoff is a smaller handoff surface, not a promise that the queue will design the delivery policy for you.

The catch is real. There is no built-in topic fan-out, so independent consumers need separate queues. Delayed messages top out at seven days, message bodies at 256 KB, and FIFO deduplication at a five-minute window. For Kafka-style replay, durable multi-consumer history, or DAG orchestration, use a specialist instead.

BullMQ is the pragmatic choice when Redis is already a production dependency and you want queue-native backoff and concurrency controls in one Node.js package. Inngest is better when a webhook starts several durable steps and the final action depends on a join. Cloudflare Cron Triggers fit a short, public HTTP call that can tolerate schedule jitter and does not need message retention.

Your mileage may vary here; the deciding test is failure recovery. Send a duplicate event, kill a worker after the partner responds, and pause the scheduler. If the resulting state is explainable from your audit table and idempotency key, the queue boundary is doing its job.

Three words: measure the handoff.

If this boundary matches your system, start with the queue capability guide.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.push_subscribe
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs
  • https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: Understanding IaaS: A Practical Look at AWS EC2
description:
Introduction

A few years ago, if you wanted to put a website online, you had to buy a physical server, find a place to keep it, and look after it yourself. Today, you can get a server running in minutes, and you only pay for the time you use it. That is the idea behind Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).

As a networking and security student, I wanted to understand how this works in practice. In this article, I explain what IaaS is, what it is made of, and how it looks in real life, using Amazon EC2 as a case study.

What is IaaS?

IaaS is a cloud computing model where a provider rents out basic computing resources over the internet: virtual machines, storage, and networking. You don't buy or maintain any hardware. You use what you need, when you need it, and pay for what you use.

It is one of the three main cloud service models:

  • IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): You get the raw infrastructure and manage the operating system, runtime, and applications yourself. Examples: AWS EC2, Azure Virtual Machines, Google Compute Engine.
  • PaaS (Platform as a Service): The provider also manages the operating system and runtime, so you only deploy your code. Examples: Heroku, Google App Engine.
  • SaaS (Software as a Service): You simply use a finished application. Examples: Gmail, Google Docs.

In short, IaaS gives you the most control, but it also gives you the most responsibility.

Key Components of IaaS

  • Compute: Virtual machines (VMs) that run your applications.
  • Storage: Block storage (like virtual hard disks), object storage, and file storage.
  • Networking: Virtual networks, IP addresses, load balancers, firewalls, and DNS.
  • Virtualization: A hypervisor splits one physical server into many isolated virtual machines. This is what makes IaaS possible.

Case Study: Amazon EC2

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) is the IaaS compute service of Amazon Web Services (AWS). It lets you launch virtual servers, called instances, in just a few minutes.

Main building blocks of EC2

  • Instances: The virtual servers themselves. You choose the CPU, memory, and network capacity through instance types, such as general purpose, compute optimized, or memory optimized.
  • AMI (Amazon Machine Image): A template that contains the operating system and software. When you launch an instance, you pick an AMI such as Ubuntu, Amazon Linux, or Windows Server.
  • EBS (Elastic Block Store): Persistent virtual disks that you attach to your instances.
  • VPC (Virtual Private Cloud): Your own isolated virtual network inside AWS.
  • Security Groups: Virtual firewalls that control which traffic can reach your instance.
  • Key Pairs: SSH keys used to log in securely to Linux instances.
  • Elastic Load Balancing and Auto Scaling: Tools that spread traffic across instances and automatically add or remove instances based on demand.

Launching an instance

Here is the basic process:

  1. Sign in to the AWS Management Console and open the EC2 service.
  2. Click Launch instance.
  3. Choose an AMI, for example Ubuntu.
  4. Choose an instance type. A small general-purpose type is enough for testing.
  5. Create or select a key pair.
  6. Configure the network and a security group, for example allow SSH on port 22 and HTTP on port 80.
  7. Add storage and launch the instance.
  8. Connect using SSH and install what you need, such as a web server.

"bash
ssh -i my-key.pem ubuntu@
sudo apt update && sudo apt install nginx -y"

Within minutes, you have a working web server on the internet, without buying any hardware.

EC2 pricing models

  • On-Demand: You pay for the time you use, with no long-term commitment. Good for testing and unpredictable workloads.
  • Reserved Instances / Savings Plans: You commit to 1 or 3 years in exchange for a lower price. Good for steady, long-running workloads.
  • Spot Instances: You use spare AWS capacity at a big discount, but AWS can take it back with short notice. Good for flexible jobs that can be interrupted.

Real-world use cases

  • Hosting websites and web applications
  • Running backend APIs and databases
  • Development and testing environments
  • Batch processing and data analysis
  • Handling sudden traffic spikes

Advantages of IaaS

  • No upfront hardware cost: You don't need to buy or maintain servers.
  • Scalability: You can add or remove resources in minutes as demand changes.
  • Pay-as-you-go: You only pay for what you use.
  • Flexibility and control: You choose the operating system, software, and configuration.
  • Global reach: You can deploy servers in many regions, close to your users.
  • Disaster recovery: Backups and replication across regions are easy to set up.

Disadvantages of IaaS

  • More responsibility: You are the one who patches, secures, and maintains the operating system and applications.
  • Costs can grow unexpectedly: Forgotten running instances and poorly sized servers can lead to high bills.
  • Shared security: Under the shared responsibility model, AWS secures the hardware and data centers, but you secure your data, access, and configuration. A misconfigured security group is a common cause of breaches.
  • Learning curve: There are many services and options to learn.
  • Internet dependency: You need a reliable internet connection to manage and use your resources.

Conclusion

IaaS has changed how people and companies build and run software. By renting virtual infrastructure instead of owning it, teams can move faster, scale easily, and avoid big upfront costs. Amazon EC2 is a good example: with a few clicks, you get a fully configurable server, backed by flexible pricing and strong networking and storage tools.

The trade-off is responsibility. With IaaS, security, updates, and cost control are in your hands. Used well, it is a powerful foundation for almost any modern application.

Thanks for reading! Feel free to leave questions or feedback in the comments.

title: Amazon MWAA now supports fine-grained access control with IAM Identity Center and multi-team environments
description:
Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) now supports fine-grained access control, giving administrators precise control over who can access which workflows and resources in an Apache Airflow environment. Fine-grained access control is delivered through two new capabilities: IAM Identity Center integration and multi-team environments.

With IAM Identity Center integration, users sign in to the Apache Airflow UI with their corporate identity provider. Authorization is evaluated per request using IAM policies attached to IAM Identity Center Permission Sets, with condition keys that scope access by resource type (DAGs, connections, variables, pools, and more), action, and specific resource ID.

With multi-team environments, several teams can share a single MWAA environment. Each team gets its own DAG folder in Amazon S3, and users see only shared DAGs plus their own teams' DAGs based on IAM Identity Center group membership. Teams reduce cost through shared infrastructure and simplify management by configuring environment settings once. Multi-team environments are based on the Apache Airflow multi-team feature, which is currently in preview.

These features are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon MWAA is available.

To learn more, visit the IAM Identity Center integration documentation and the multi-team environments documentation.

title: Why I Built a 100% Ad-Free, 3-Second Daily Expense Tracker PWA (React + Firebase + GitHub Actions) published: true
description:
Most "free" expense trackers are bloated with loan ads and slow forms. Here is how I built a lightweight, ad-free PWA with automated 11:00 PM IST email audits.
tags: webdev, react, firebase, showdev

cover_image:

Most "free" expense tracking apps on the Play Store and App Store share the same problem: bloat and ad spam.

You open the app just to log a ₹20 cup of chai or a ₹150 auto ride, and you are hit with full-screen personal loan banners, credit card pop-ups, and multi-step forms. After three days, you stop logging altogether.

To solve this for my own daily spending, I built Daily House Expense Tracker Pro—a lightweight, 100% ad-free Progressive Web App (PWA) designed to log micro-spends in under 3 seconds and send an automated summary email every night.

🔗 Try it live (no app store download needed): Daily House Expense Tracker Pro

What Makes It Different?

  1. Zero Ads, Zero Loan Spam, 100% Free: Built purely as a utility tool at Zunaro Labs. No trackers, no banner ads, and no forced bank-account linking.
  2. 3-Second Micro-Spend Logging: Open the PWA from your home screen, enter the amount and category (Chai & Snacks, Groceries, Transit, Utilities), and save immediately.
  3. Automated 11:00 PM IST Nightly Email Ledger: Every night at 11:00 PM IST, an automated job reconciles your daytime inflows and outflows and emails a clean daily statement straight to your inbox.
  4. Installable PWA (0MB Bloat): Works directly in Chrome or Safari and installs to your mobile home screen like a native wallet app.
  5. Instant Financial Statements: Filter between variable daily habits and fixed monthly overheads, and export clean reports whenever you need them.

The Tech Stack & Architecture

I kept the stack lean so the app loads in under a second on mobile networks:

  • Frontend: React + Vite + Tailwind CSS
  • Authentication & Database: Firebase Auth (1-click Google Sign-In) & Cloud Firestore for real-time sync
  • Hosting: Firebase Hosting
  • Automated Nightly Audits: GitHub Actions cron workflows (11:00 PM IST daily cutoff reconciliation & email dispatch)

What's Next?

I am currently rolling out improvements based on early user feedback—including faster category shortcuts and monthly surplus visual breakdowns.

If you are tired of clunky finance apps, give it a spin and let me know what feature you would add next in the comments!

👉 Launch App: https://daily-house-expense-trackerpro.firebaseapp.com/

title: Lucide vs Font Awesome: Pick the Right Icons in 2026
description:
Icons look like a tiny decision until you ship. Then you notice the navbar loads a font file you barely use, the stroke weights do not match, or a license question lands in your inbox from a client.

That is exactly the moment the Lucide vs Font Awesome decision stops being cosmetic. One is a lean, open source, stroke based SVG library that took over the React and Tailwind world. The other is the old guard, with years of history, a huge catalog, brand logos and a paid tier behind it.

Neither is the winner for every project. This guide compares them the way a working developer would: licensing, bundle impact, styles, framework support, accessibility, cost and the small gotchas that only show up in production. By the end you will know which one fits your stack, and you will have copy ready code for both.

Quick Answer: Lucide or Font Awesome?

Choose Lucide if you want a clean, consistent outline icon set, you build with React, Vue, Svelte or Next.js, and you care about small bundles and a permissive license.

Choose Font Awesome if you need a very large catalog, brand logos, multiple visual styles, or you work on a team or CMS that already runs on Font Awesome classes.

Many projects end up using Lucide for interface icons and a separate brand icon source for social logos. More on that below.

What Is Lucide?

Lucide is an open source icon library made of SVG icons drawn on a 24 by 24 grid with a consistent 2 pixel stroke. It started in 2020 as a community fork of Feather Icons, which had only 286 icons and slowed down in development. Lucide kept the same clean look, stayed backward compatible with Feather, and grew to more than 1,500 icons. You can browse the full set on the Lucide official site.

Key facts:

  • License: ISC, which is functionally close to MIT.
  • Style: Outline only. One visual language, one stroke width by default.
  • Customization: Size, color and stroke width are all adjustable, because the icons are real SVG.
  • Packages: Official packages exist for vanilla JavaScript (lucide), React (lucide-react), Vue (lucide-vue-next), Angular (lucide-angular), Preact (lucide-preact) and a static asset package (lucide-static). Community packages cover other frameworks.
  • Adoption: lucide-react sits around 5 million weekly npm downloads according to a January 2026 snapshot. It is also the icon library behind many shadcn/ui setups.

What Is Font Awesome?

Font Awesome is one of the oldest and best known icon toolkits on the web. It was created for Bootstrap era projects, later grew into a company backed product, and is now on version 7, which launched in July 2025. Version 7.2 followed in February 2026 with new Free icons such as moon phases and zodiac signs, plus new Pro icons and a new hand drawn Pro+ pack called Graphite. The Font Awesome official site has the current catalog and release notes.

Key facts:

  • Free tier licenses: Icons under CC BY 4.0, fonts under SIL OFL 1.1, code under MIT.
  • Styles in Free: Solid, Regular (a limited set) and Brands.
  • Pro: A paid subscription that adds many more icons and styles, plus extra icon packs and Kits with extra features. Check the Font Awesome site for current pricing, since plans have changed over the years.
  • Delivery options: Web fonts via CSS classes, SVG with JavaScript, individual SVG files, npm packages, and hosted Kits.
  • Version support: Version 6 is on long term support with critical fixes only. Versions 3, 4 and 5 are end of life.

Lucide vs Font Awesome: Side by Side

Feature Lucide Font Awesome (Free)
Icon style Outline only, consistent stroke Solid, Regular (limited), Brands
Catalog size 1,500+ icons Larger catalog, plus a bigger Pro catalog
License ISC CC BY 4.0 (icons), SIL OFL 1.1 (fonts), MIT (code)
Attribution Keep the license file in your package Required by the licenses, usually satisfied by the comments inside the files
Brand logos Not a focus Yes, large Brands set
Delivery SVG, per icon imports Web font, SVG, npm, CDN, Kit
Tree shaking Excellent with named imports Good with the SVG packages, not applicable to the web font
Stroke width control Yes, via strokeWidth No, since most styles are filled glyphs
React support Official lucide-react Official @fortawesome/react-fontawesome
Paid tier None Pro, Pro+ and higher plans
Best for Modern app UIs, dashboards, design systems Marketing sites, CMS themes, brand icons, broad coverage

Licensing: The Part Most Developers Skip

This is where the two libraries differ most in day to day risk.

Lucide's ISC license

ISC is short and permissive. You can use Lucide in commercial products, modify it and redistribute it. You need to keep the copyright notice and license text. If you install through npm, the license file ships inside the package, so simply do not strip it from your build output. The Lucide GitHub repository contains the exact license text for the version you install.

Font Awesome Free's three licenses

Font Awesome Free splits licensing by file type. The Font Awesome Free repository documents each one:

Component License Typical files
Icon artwork CC BY 4.0 SVG files
Fonts SIL OFL 1.1 .woff2, .ttf
Code MIT CSS and JavaScript

Attribution is required across these licenses. In practice, the comment headers embedded in the official files cover it. The catch is your build tool. Bundlers such as Webpack, Vite and esbuild often move /*! and @license comments into separate .LICENSE.txt files or strip them. If that happens, add a visible credit in your footer or your legal page.

Practical licensing tips

  • Check your production build output for the license notices, not just your source folder.
  • Individually copied SVGs from a website may not include any header. Add a license comment inside the file.
  • Brand logos carry their own trademark rules. A permissive icon license does not give you rights to a company's logo.
  • Pro needs a token. Font Awesome Pro packages come from a private registry, so your CI needs an auth token stored as a secret, never committed in .npmrc.

This is general information, not legal advice. Read the actual license files for the exact version you ship.

Performance and Bundle Size

Icon choices show up in your Lighthouse score more often than people expect. When we moved a client dashboard from a full icon font to per icon SVG imports, the page stopped downloading glyphs it never rendered and the first contentful paint improved without touching any other asset. That experience is why this section gets as much space as the visual comparison.

Lucide: import only what you use

Each Lucide icon is a small SVG component. With named imports, a bundler includes only the icons you reference. Independent estimates put a single tree shaken icon at roughly half a kilobyte, though exact numbers depend on your bundler and version.

import { Search, Menu, X } from "lucide-react";

export function Header() {
  return (
    <header>
      <Menu size={20} />
      <Search size={20} strokeWidth={1.5} />
      <X size={20} color="currentColor" />
    </header>
  );
}

One trap to avoid: importing the whole icons object to look icons up by name at runtime. That pulls the whole catalog into the bundle. If you need dynamic icons, map a short list of allowed names to imported components.

Font Awesome: pick the delivery method on purpose

Font Awesome gives you more ways to load icons, and each one has a different cost.

Method How it loads Performance note
Web font (CSS classes) One font file per style Simple, but you ship glyphs you never use
SVG with JavaScript Script swaps in inline SVG Flexible, adds runtime work
npm SVG packages Import specific icons Smallest output, closest to Lucide's model
Kit Hosted script, tuned for your icons Convenient, depends on an external request

If bundle size matters to you, use the npm SVG packages with named imports rather than loading a whole font.

import { FontAwesomeIcon } from "@fortawesome/react-fontawesome";
import { faHouse, faMagnifyingGlass } from "@fortawesome/free-solid-svg-icons";

export function Nav() {
  return (
    <nav>
      <FontAwesomeIcon icon={faHouse} />
      <FontAwesomeIcon icon={faMagnifyingGlass} />
    </nav>
  );
}

Performance tips that apply to both

  1. Import named icons only. Never import a full set.
  2. Self host or bundle instead of depending on a third party CDN when you can.
  3. Preload critical font files if you use the web font route, and use font-display: swap.
  4. Measure with your real build. Run your bundle analyzer before and after switching, because the best answer depends on how many icons you really use.

Design and Visual Style

Lucide's look

Lucide is calm, consistent and slightly rounded. Every icon shares the same grid, stroke and corner treatment, so a page full of them looks like one set. This is why it pairs so well with minimal interfaces, dashboards and developer tools. Because the stroke is adjustable, you can make icons feel lighter or heavier with a single prop. A strokeWidth of 1.5 reads as more refined, while 2 feels sturdier.

The limitation is range. Lucide is outline only. If your brand needs bold filled icons, duotone effects or a playful look, you will not get it from Lucide alone.

Font Awesome's look

Font Awesome Free leans on solid glyphs, with a smaller Regular outline set. It looks familiar because it has been everywhere for years. That familiarity is a plus for marketing pages and admin panels, and a minus if you want your product to look distinct. Pro and the newer icon packs add more personality, but they are paid.

If your design is starting to look generic, our guide on how to avoid AI slop in website design covers small choices like icon style that make a site feel intentional.

Framework and Tooling Support

Stack Lucide Font Awesome
React / Next.js lucide-react @fortawesome/react-fontawesome
Vue lucide-vue-next @fortawesome/vue-fontawesome
Angular lucide-angular @fortawesome/angular-fontawesome
Preact lucide-preact Community options
Vanilla JS / HTML lucide or lucide-static CSS classes, SVG with JS, or Kit
Static site generators (Hugo, Astro) Inline SVG or static files CSS classes or Kit
Tailwind CSS Works naturally with currentColor Works, but web font sizing needs more care

Using Lucide without a framework 

<i data-lucide="menu"></i>

<script type="module">
  import { createIcons, Menu, Search } from "lucide";

  createIcons({
    icons: { Menu, Search },
  });
</script>

Passing a small object of icons keeps the output lean. Passing every icon works, but it defeats the point.

Using Font Awesome with plain HTML 

<i class="fa-solid fa-house"></i>
<i class="fa-brands fa-github"></i>

This is the fastest setup of any icon library, which is exactly why so many WordPress themes and Bootstrap projects still use it.

If you run a Hugo site, the same decision applies, and our Hugo SEO guide covers other performance choices worth making at the same time.

Accessibility

Icons often carry meaning, so treat them as content, not decoration.

  • Decorative icons next to visible text should be hidden from screen readers with aria-hidden="true". Both libraries commonly do this for you by default, but verify in the rendered HTML.
  • Icon only buttons need an accessible name. Add aria-label="Search" on the button, or visually hidden text inside it.
  • Do not rely on color alone to show state.
  • Check contrast for icons that act as controls, since low contrast outline icons are harder to see. 
<button aria-label="Open menu">
  <Menu aria-hidden="true" />
</button>

Cost: Free vs Paid

Lucide is entirely free and open source. There is no paid tier to think about.

Font Awesome Free covers a lot, and plenty of professional projects ship with it only. The paid Pro plans add more icons, more styles and extra packs, and they require a private registry token. Pricing and plan names have shifted over the years, so check the Font Awesome site on the day you decide rather than trusting an old blog post, including this one.

A simple budget rule: if you are about to pay mainly to get more outline icons, look at open source options first. Our list of Font Awesome alternatives compares several free ones.

Brand Icons: The Gap Lucide Does Not Fill

Social and company logos are a common reason people stay on Font Awesome. Lucide mostly stays away from brand logos because of trademark concerns. If you need GitHub, X, LinkedIn or YouTube marks next to Lucide's interface icons, add a dedicated brand source such as Simple Icons rather than forcing one library to do everything.

Which Should You Choose? A Practical Decision Guide

Pick Lucide when

  • You are starting a new React, Next.js, Vue or Svelte project.
  • You use shadcn/ui or a Tailwind based design system.
  • You want one consistent outline style.
  • You care about small bundles and per icon imports.
  • You prefer a plain, permissive license with no paid plan.

Pick Font Awesome when

  • You need brand logos and a very wide catalog in one place.
  • Your project is a CMS theme, a Bootstrap site or a legacy codebase already using fa- classes.
  • You want filled glyphs, or you plan to buy Pro for extra styles.
  • Non developers on your team add icons through class names or a Kit.

Use both when

  • Interface icons come from Lucide and brand logos come from Font Awesome Brands. Keep it to one visual style per area so the page does not look mixed.

How to Migrate From Font Awesome to Lucide

A full switch is usually a few hours of work on a mid sized app. Here is a safe order.

  1. Inventory your icons. Search your codebase for fa- classes and FontAwesomeIcon usage and list every distinct icon.
  2. Map each one to its closest Lucide name. Most common interface icons (search, user, settings, trash, check, arrow) have direct matches.
  3. Create a wrapper component. Export a small Icon component so future swaps touch one file.
  4. Replace in batches, one page or feature at a time.
  5. Handle brand icons separately with a brand icon source.
  6. Remove the old package and font files, then run your bundle analyzer to confirm the size drop.
  7. Re-test accessibility, especially icon only buttons. 
import { Search, User, Settings } from "lucide-react";

const icons = { search: Search, user: User, settings: Settings };

export function Icon({ name, size = 20, ...props }) {
  const Component = icons[name];
  return Component ? <Component size={size} {...props} /> : null;
}

This wrapper keeps dynamic lookups safe, because only the icons you list get bundled.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Mixing icon styles inside one screen. Stroke icons next to filled glyphs look unplanned.
  • Importing a whole icon set to use five icons.
  • Forgetting license output after bundling Font Awesome.
  • Using icons without labels on buttons that have no visible text.
  • Choosing by popularity alone. Pick the library that matches your design and your stack.
  • Hardcoding icon sizes everywhere. Use one size token or one wrapper component.

For more help choosing visual direction before you pick assets, see our roundup of UI and UX design inspiration resources, and our explainer on design system files for AI agents if you want your icon rules to be followed consistently by coding assistants.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the main difference between Lucide and Font Awesome?

Lucide is a free, open source library of consistent outline SVG icons built for modern JavaScript apps. Font Awesome is a larger toolkit with solid, regular and brand icons, several delivery methods and an optional paid Pro tier.

Is Lucide better than Font Awesome?

Neither is better in every case. Lucide is usually better for clean app interfaces, small bundles and permissive licensing. Font Awesome is usually better when you need brand logos, a bigger catalog or filled icon styles.

Is Lucide free for commercial use?

Yes. Lucide uses the ISC license, which allows commercial use. You only need to keep the copyright notice and license text included with the package.

Is Font Awesome free for commercial projects?

Font Awesome Free can be used in commercial projects under its CC BY 4.0, SIL OFL 1.1 and MIT licenses, as long as you meet the attribution requirements. Pro features need a paid subscription.

Does Lucide have brand icons like GitHub or Twitter?

Lucide mostly avoids brand logos for trademark reasons. If you need them, use Font Awesome Brands or a dedicated brand icon library such as Simple Icons alongside Lucide.

Which icon library has better performance, Lucide or Font Awesome?

Lucide's per icon SVG imports are small and tree shake well. Font Awesome can match that when you use its npm SVG packages with named imports, but loading the full web font ships more data than most pages need.

Can I use Lucide and Font Awesome together?

Yes. A common pattern is Lucide for interface icons and Font Awesome Brands for social logos. Keep sizes and visual weight consistent so the mix looks deliberate.

Does Lucide work with React, Vue and Svelte?

Yes. Official packages exist for React, Vue, Angular and Preact, plus a vanilla JavaScript package and static assets. Svelte users can use community packages or inline the SVGs.

Which is better for Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui?

Lucide is the more common choice, because its SVG icons inherit currentColor and scale with utility classes, and it is the default icon set in many shadcn/ui projects.

Key Takeaways

  • Lucide is a free, ISC licensed, outline only SVG library with more than 1,500 icons, forked from Feather in 2020.
  • Font Awesome is now on version 7, with a Free tier under CC BY 4.0, SIL OFL 1.1 and MIT, and paid Pro plans for more icons and styles.
  • Lucide wins on consistency, per icon imports and licensing simplicity.
  • Font Awesome wins on catalog breadth, brand logos and multiple styles.
  • Tree shaking only helps if you import named icons. Avoid loading a full set.
  • Check your build output for Font Awesome license notices, because bundlers can strip them.
  • Add accessible names to every icon only button.
  • Using Lucide for UI and a separate source for brand logos is a common, clean setup.
  • Wrap icons in one small component so you can swap libraries later with little pain.

Conclusion

The Lucide vs Font Awesome question has a boring, useful answer: match the library to the job. If you are building a modern app interface, Lucide gives you a consistent outline set, tiny per icon bundles and an ISC license you do not have to think about. If you need broad coverage, brand logos and filled styles in one place, Font Awesome still earns its place, provided you use its SVG packages instead of shipping the whole font.

Start by listing the icons your product actually uses, then pick the delivery method that keeps the page light. The rest is consistency and labels, which cost nothing and prevent most of the bugs people blame on the icons themselves.

title: Catch N+1 Queries Before They Catch You
description:
A common N+1 example: load 100 records, then run one more query per record to fetch a relation. One line of application code can result in 101 database queries.

It's the most common performance bug in ORM-based backends, and it's easy to miss because each query is fast on your laptop.

ZinTrust provides an N+1 detector in RequestProfiler. It analyzes SQL entries in QueryLogger; it does not automatically intercept every ORM/database query. Instrument the queries you want to inspect, then use eager loading with with() to avoid one relation query per record.

Three rules that keep N+1 out of your app:

  1. Load relations you'll use with with() in the same query chain.
  2. Capture and inspect query logs for new list endpoints before you merge.
  3. Add indexes on foreign keys and columns you filter on.

The detector is only as useful as the query log you give it. Make query capture part of profiling when you want it to flag repeated SQL.

Try it: npm install -g @zintrust/core && zin new my-app
https://zintrust.com/profiling
