title: Node.js Nightly Reconciliation: Idempotency Across Delayed Webhook Queue Redelivery
description:
Short answer: use a queue for delayed webhook retries, and make the consumer idempotent because at-least-once delivery means the same payment event can arrive more than once.

For a customer-support system reconciling payment-provider events each night, the operational constraint is event-specific timing. A failed webhook may need its next attempt in 30 seconds while another is ready in 20 minutes. A cron sweep can discover work, but it is a poor clock for thousands of independent retry schedules. Put each retry on a delayed queue, retain the business payload in the application database or object store, and send only its reference and stable event key through the queue.

My recommendation is specific: teams that want a plain HTTP queue alongside other backend capabilities should try Infrai for the delayed publish-and-consume boundary, because its broad production modules share one REST contract and one credential rather than adding another SDK and key. Its public discovery surface also exposes request schemas and runnable Go examples before integration, which shortens the path to a first useful request. The consumer-side idempotency record remains your responsibility.

What integration boundary lets at-least-once queues duplicate delayed webhook retry jobs?

Standard queue delivery is at least once. A worker can complete the payment-provider call and still fail to acknowledge the message, so the queue may deliver that message again. Two workers can also observe attempts close together. Neither case proves that the queue is broken; redelivery is part of the delivery contract, and the application has to decide what “already done” means.

The dangerous assumption is that a queue message ID is the business operation ID. It isn't necessarily. For nightly reconciliation, define a key from the payment event and the intended effect, such as provider_event_id + operation. Store that key in a durable processed-event record governed by a uniqueness constraint. On receipt, claim the key before making the effect visible, then acknowledge only after the application's success state is durable. If a duplicate claim loses the uniqueness race, acknowledge it without repeating the effect.

Be precise here.

An HTTP timeout is ambiguous — the provider may have accepted the call even though the worker did not receive the response. If the payment provider accepts an idempotency key, send the same stable key on every attempt. The local processed-event record prevents duplicate application work; the provider key protects the remote side of the boundary. If the provider has no such contract, reconciliation must query authoritative provider state before issuing a second mutation. I'm not sure what latency target is right for every support operation; an on-call escalation update and a nightly ledger repair have different urgency. Measure that policy in your own service, but don't trade away idempotency to shave a retry interval.

Compare credential inventory before selecting retry machinery

Developer experience matters at 02:00. Count credentials, client libraries, moving parts, and the number of contracts an operator must inspect during a retry storm. Also count what the product cannot do, because a short setup is worthless when the execution model is wrong.

Option First integration surface Good fit here Boundary that changes the choice
BullMQ A Node.js queue library and its documented setup A Node.js team that wants the queue close to its application stack Stick with BullMQ when direct control of the Node.js queue stack matters more than a shared HTTP capability surface
Infrai One REST API, one credential, and public capability discovery Delayed webhook work where a small HTTP contract reduces SDK and credential sprawl Not suitable when the design needs DAG orchestration, fan-out/fan-in joins, Kafka-style replay, or multiple consumer groups
Temporal A specialist workflow system Multi-step durable workflows whose orchestration is the product requirement The extra workflow model is unnecessary for one delayed callback with a durable idempotency record
Airflow A specialist scheduler and DAG model Scheduled data workflows where dependencies between steps matter It is a heavier conceptual fit for per-event webhook retry timing

Infrai's primary advantage in this decision is breadth behind a consistent surface: the same key reaches 295 routes across 20 modules, so adding another supported backend capability is another HTTP contract rather than another vendor SDK. The supporting benefit is inspectability. Discovery is public, self-describing, and includes full request and response schemas plus runnable examples in ten languages. That doesn't make a general queue a workflow engine, and it doesn't remove application state from the design.

There are hard limits to put in the runbook. An Infrai delayed message cannot exceed 7 days, its payload cannot exceed 256KB, retention is at most 30 days, and acknowledgement deletes it. FIFO deduplication covers only a 5-minute window. There is no native debounce, throttle, topic fan-out, or Kafka-style replay. For a retry beyond seven days, store next_attempt_at in the application database and let a scheduler enqueue it when it enters the supported window. For a payload near the size ceiling, publish a reference, not a compressed mystery bundle.

Latency versus cost is therefore a policy choice, not a vendor slogan. A support-visible payment mismatch can enter the delayed queue immediately, while low-priority nightly reconciliation can batch discovery work and enqueue only unresolved references. Fewer wake-ups may reduce operational work, but a longer interval increases time-to-repair. Keep the interval explicit and observable.

Implementation example: publish the smallest useful reference

The safe worker is a state machine: claim, execute, commit, acknowledge. Before writing that consumer, publish the smallest useful message. This runnable Go program sends a stable payment-event reference to Infrai's verified queue publish route with a 30-second delay. It retries rate limits, honors Retry-After when present, and reuses an idempotency key so retrying the publish does not create a second logical write.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type publishRequest struct {
    Queue        string         `json:"queue"`
    Payload      map[string]any `json:"payload"`
    DelaySeconds int            `json:"delay_seconds"`
    Priority     int            `json:"priority"`
}

func retryDelay(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(response.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if at, err := http.ParseTime(response.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
        if wait := time.Until(at); wait > 0 {
            return wait
        }
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    body, err := json.Marshal(publishRequest{
        Queue: "payment-reconciliation",
        Payload: map[string]any{
            "event_id":  "pay_evt_1042",
            "operation": "reconcile-payment",
        },
        DelaySeconds: 30,
        Priority:     0,
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequest(
            http.MethodPost,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish",
            bytes.NewReader(body),
        )
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        request.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        request.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "pay_evt_1042:reconcile-payment")

        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(response, attempt))
            continue
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("publish failed: HTTP %d: %s", response.StatusCode, responseBody))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(responseBody))
        return
    }
    panic("publish exhausted its retry budget")
}

The API idempotency header protects the publish operation. It does not make the webhook consumer idempotent. That consumer still needs a durable unique key and explicit states such as processing and completed, an ownership lease, and a transaction. Only completed is a terminal duplicate. An expired processing claim can be recovered according to a documented policy, while a successful remote mutation is confirmed with the provider's idempotency contract or authoritative state. In Node.js, the language changes; this invariant does not.

Don't acknowledge early.

Backoff belongs in the message schedule. A retry that outlives a normal HTTP request should become a delayed message, and the worker should return control rather than sleep while holding a delivery. Cap attempts, preserve the stable event key, and route exhausted work into an operator-visible state. The queue's delivery count is diagnostic metadata; it is not a substitute for business identity.

How do you test redelivery before the nightly run?

Start with a synthetic payment event that cannot alter a real ledger. Publish one reference, consume it, and deliberately exercise the same consumer twice with the same business key. The expected result is one completed reconciliation record and one duplicate acknowledgement. Then interrupt the worker after the provider action but before acknowledgement. On redelivery, the worker must resolve the same key without applying the action again.

Record enough evidence for an operator to answer three questions: which business key ran, which attempt observed it, and whether the outcome was completed, retryable, or duplicate. Avoid storing the full webhook body in queue diagnostics when it can contain sensitive payment context. The authoritative payload stays behind the reference in application-controlled storage.

Test the ceilings too: reject or externalize a payload before 256KB becomes a publish-time surprise, and verify that scheduling policy never asks the queue for more than 604800 seconds of delay. Confirm the 30-day retention boundary against the support team's investigation window. These are configuration assertions, not tribal knowledge.

For rollback, stop new publishes first, keep the durable reconciliation rows, and let already claimed operations reach a known state. Switching a consumer off without preserving its claims creates ambiguity. If the queue is paused, remember that delayed work and nightly discovery are separate concerns: the database still holds the source of truth, so a controlled replay can select unresolved business keys rather than blindly republishing every historical message.

Latency and cost set the final operating rule

Use delayed queue messages when every failed webhook needs its own backoff clock and can complete inside the seven-day delay boundary. Keep the consumer idempotent for every delivery. Use a cron trigger only to discover unresolved nightly reconciliation rows or enqueue long-running work; Infrai cron calls public HTTP targets, does not host the code, has a 900-second execution ceiling, and does not backfill triggers missed while paused.

Choose BullMQ when the team wants a Node.js-native queue stack under its direct control. Choose Temporal when retries belong to a durable, multi-step workflow, and Airflow when a scheduled DAG is the real abstraction. Choose Infrai when one small REST integration and a shared credential across backend capabilities remove meaningful setup and operating friction, provided its queue limits match the workload.

The catch is simple: no queue product can infer the business identity of a payment reconciliation. That key, its durable state transition, and the provider-side duplicate defense are application design. Keep them in the runbook.

References

  • BullMQ documentation: https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • Temporal documentation: https://docs.temporal.io/
  • Apache Airflow documentation: https://airflow.apache.org/docs/
  • OWASP SSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • Infrai queue publish discovery schema: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.publish

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai queue documentation.

title: My VPS bill is one number. Here is what each app on it actually costs
description:
My VPS bill is one number. Here is what each app on it actually costs

My server bill arrives as one line. Six dollars a month, four apps, and a Postgres database I forgot about. When I wondered which app was costing me the most, I had no answer, because the bill does not know about apps.

Levelrail has two features that attack this from different sides. One splits your real server bill across the apps by measured usage. The other estimates what an app would cost on typical metered cloud pricing. I ran both on a throwaway local instance. This post covers exactly what each computes, what I saw, and where the numbers stop being trustworthy.

TL;DR

Question Feature Input Output
What does each app cost me on my server? Usage and cost Your monthly bill, vCPUs, memory, measured usage Per app, project, environment and team cost, plus idle capacity
What would this app cost elsewhere? Cost estimate The app's CPU and memory Three reference prices per month
Am I on track this month? Cost explorer The same daily snapshots Trend, forecast and budgets

Both are showback, not billing. Levelrail pulls nothing from a cloud provider and sends no invoice.

Splitting the bill by usage

You enter what each server costs per month, with its vCPUs and memory. Levelrail divides the bill by the days in the month, and each app gets a share of the day by how much of the server it used:

share = cpu_weight * (cores used / server vCPUs) + (1 - cpu_weight) * (memory used / server memory)
app cost for the day = daily bill * share

cpu_weight defaults to 50 percent. Whatever no app used is idle capacity. By default it shows as Unallocated, so you can see how much of the bill nobody used. If the apps together use more than the server, Levelrail scales their shares down so the total never exceeds the bill.

Here is the setup I ran, with a made up bill that matches a small VPS:

levelrail-cli usage settings set --mode node --node local=6:2:4 --reprice-month

The --node value is NAME=MONTHLY[:VCPUS[:GIB]], so this says a node called local costs 6 a month and has 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB. The --reprice-month flag applies the new prices to the month so far. Without it, past days keep the prices they had when recorded, so a price change never quietly rewrites last month.

Then I asked for the report:

levelrail-cli usage report --period mtd --by resource

Period: 2026-11-01 to 2026-11-11 (node)
Total: 2.04 USD (- vs previous period)
Unallocated (idle capacity): 2.04 USD
Forecast month end: 6.00 USD

RESOURCE              COST  PREVIOUS  CHANGE
database:w2f-main-db  0.00  0.00      -
app:w2f-web           0.00  0.00      -

I should be plain about what that shows. My instance had two idle containers, a whoami web app and an empty Postgres, and they had run for five minutes. Their measured usage rounds to zero cents, so the whole 2.04 is idle capacity. The forecast of 6.00 is the full monthly bill, which is the right answer for a server doing nothing. The report fits a quiet server. It tells you nothing about load. I did not generate load.

A worked example you can check

Since my test box was idle, here is the arithmetic from the docs formula, not a measured result. Take the same 6 per month server with 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB. November has 30 days, so the daily bill is 6 / 30 = 0.20. Say an app averages 0.5 cores and 1 GiB for the day:

share = 0.5 * (0.5 / 2) + 0.5 * (1 / 4) = 0.125 + 0.125 = 0.25
app cost for the day = 0.20 * 0.25 = 0.05

That app costs 0.05 a day, about 1.50 a month at that usage. The other 75 percent of the day's bill is Unallocated. That is why the method helps on a small server: it shows the idle share, which a per app invoice would hide.

Two settings change the picture. The idle spread, a percent from 0 to 100, distributes idle capacity over apps by usage, so the report adds up to the whole bill. I set it to 100 and repriced:

levelrail-cli usage settings set --idle-spread-pct 100 --reprice-month
levelrail-cli usage report --period mtd --csv

The CSV then showed small idle shares on the database and the app (0.0313 and 0.0063 for the current day), while the earlier days stayed Unallocated, because nothing had logged usage on them. The docs say history starts when recording starts.

What counts as usage

The collector already keeps the metrics behind this, sampled every 15 seconds. For each day Levelrail records the average and the median (p50) CPU and memory, plus how many seconds the container was reporting. A stopped container accrues nothing, so downtime costs nothing. You choose in the prices dialog whether allocation uses the average or the p50.

You can also price storage per GiB per month and egress per GiB. Storage counts the app's local named volumes at the moment the day was recorded, and only volumes on the control plane's own Docker daemon count.

If you have no single bill to split, the other mode takes a price per vCPU hour and per GiB of memory hour, and an app costs cores * hours * cpu price + GiB * hours * memory price.

The other number: what would this cost elsewhere

The cost estimate is a different tool, and people over-read it, so the docs say plainly: an estimate, not a real bill. It never calls a live pricing API. For one app:

levelrail-cli apps cost w2f-web

I had declared resources: { memory: 128Mi, cpu: 0.25 } for the app, and this is what came back:

size: 0.25 vCPU (declared), 0.12 GiB memory (declared)

  Generic cloud VM                 $4.00/mo (provider minimum)
    cpu $1.00 + memory $0.50
  Generic managed VM               $10.00/mo (provider minimum)
    cpu $2.00 + memory $0.75
  Generic metered container PaaS   $7.50/mo
    cpu $6.25 + memory $1.25

The size comes from the declared limit first. With no limit, it uses the p95 of CPU and memory over the last 7 days. With neither, you get a response priced at each profile's floor, and the basis fields say there is nothing real behind the number.

The formula per profile is max(cpu_cost + memory_cost, floor), using three built in rate profiles:

Profile Represents $/vCPU/month $/GiB/month Floor/month
vm A bare unmanaged cloud VM 4 4 4
managed_vm A managed VM with backups and support bundled 8 6 10
paas Metered container PaaS pricing 25 10 7

The docs say these are round numbers and not any provider's rate card, and I checked the arithmetic against my output: 0.25 * 25 = 6.25 and 0.125 * 10 = 1.25, which gives 7.50. The 0.25 vCPU and 0.125 GiB on the vm profile come to 1.50, under the 4 floor, so the floor applied. The formula has no discounts, sustained use pricing, egress or storage costs. Correct the rates with APP_COST_ESTIMATE_<KEY>_CPU_USD, ..._MEMORY_USD and ..._MINIMUM_USD, then restart the control plane.

I use this number to compare rough sizes, nothing finer. It says nothing about what your actual provider charges.

Budgets and forecasts

The Cost explorer builds on the same snapshots. The docs list grouping by app, project, tag, node or kind, a month end forecast from the mean of the last full days (up to seven), and budgets that alert at thresholds or throttle or pause apps at 100 percent. The CLI forms are levelrail-cli costs explore --by tag --period 30d and levelrail-cli costs budgets create .... I ran costs explore once and it printed 0.00 for my idle app, so I cannot tell you more than the docs do about how the forecast behaves with real traffic.

FAQ

Is this an invoice or a billing integration?

No. The docs call it showback, a report of who used what. Levelrail bills no one and queries no cloud provider.

How accurate is it?

Only as accurate as the bill you enter and the usage it measured. If a server bill is wrong, every cost on it is wrong by the same factor. Days are UTC, and storage is a single reading per day.

Does the platform itself show up as a cost?

Not as its own line. A server has one bill, and the platform and the operating system fall into the idle share.

Can I get the data out?

Yes. levelrail-cli usage report --period 30d --csv > usage.csv writes the resource breakdown, and every command takes --json.

The bottom line

On a small VPS the useful number is rarely the cost of one app. The idle share matters more, the part of the six dollars nobody used. My idle test box says 100 percent of the bill is idle, which is honest and dull. I plan to run this on a server with real traffic for a month and see how close the forecast gets.

If this saved you time, a star on the repo helps others find it.

title: How to read a peptide certificate of analysis, section by section
description:
Most certificates of analysis for research peptides get a two second look. Here is what each part actually tells you, in the order I check it.

1. Who ran the test

A real certificate names the laboratory, its address, and a report or accession number. "Third-party tested" with no lab name is a claim, not a document. If the lab has a public lookup, search the number there yourself instead of following a link the seller gave you. The lab's copy and the seller's copy should match on compound, lot, date and results.

2. Identity comes first

Mass spectrometry answers a simple question: is the molecule in the vial the molecule on the label? The report should list an expected mass and an observed mass that agree within the instrument's tolerance. A purity number with no identity result tells you the sample is one thing, but not which thing.

3. HPLC purity

HPLC separates the sample and reports each peak as a share of total peak area. A figure like 99.4% means the main peak makes up 99.4% of the detected area at the wavelength used, usually 214 nm for peptides. Things worth noticing:

  • Purity is an area percentage, not a weight percentage.
  • The chromatogram matters as much as the headline number. Look for a clean main peak and small, separated minor peaks.
  • If every lot from one seller reads exactly 99.9%, ask whether each lot was really tested.

4. Net peptide content

This is the line most people skip. A vial labelled 10 mg can hold 10 mg of powder, but part of that powder is counter-ion salt and moisture. Net peptide content reports how many milligrams of actual peptide are in the vial. A result near or above the label means the label is honest. A result far below it means you are comparing prices per vial, not per milligram of peptide.

5. Match the lot to the vial

The lot printed on the vial must be the lot on the certificate. One good certificate reused across many lots or many months is a red flag. Dates should also make sense: a test date before the manufacture date means something is wrong.

6. Quick red flags

  • The lab name does not lead to a real lab with a working website.
  • The report number returns nothing at the lab, or returns a different compound or lot.
  • The file is an image only, with fonts or alignment that look edited.
  • The "verify" link points to the seller's own domain.

A small checklist

  1. Find the lab and the report number.
  2. Look the number up on the lab's own site.
  3. Confirm identity, then purity, then net content.
  4. Match the lot to the physical vial.
  5. Keep a copy with the date you checked it.

I work on lab documentation at Luvaminos, a US supplier of research-use-only materials, and we publish one certificate per lot, so these are the checks we expect people to run on ours as well. If you handle lab reports in your own work and see something I missed, leave a comment and I will add it.

title: Mocking API Version Negotiation: Headers, Paths, Fallbacks
description:
Quick answer: A client declares the API version it wants, through a versioned path, a header, or a query value, and the server picks the matching contract or applies a documented fallback. Mock this by matching the version declaration with a conditional response for each branch, including the default, deprecated, and unsupported cases. This lets you test how the client handles a changed schema, a deprecation warning, and an upgrade error without keeping a real old version running.

How a client declares a version

There are four common mechanisms, and many APIs use one consistently. A versioned path such as /v1/resources and /v2/resources makes the version obvious in the route. A dedicated header such as X-API-Version: 2 keeps the URL stable. A vendor media type such as Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json carries the version inside content negotiation, and a query parameter such as ?version=2 is simple but easier to leak into links and caches. Whichever one the API uses, the server has to answer three questions: what to do when a version is explicit, what to return when none is given, and how to reject a version that is no longer supported.

Mock each negotiation branch

Use conditional overrides that match the version declaration and return a response that genuinely differs between versions, since identical bodies cannot prove the client handles a schema change. Cover the branches below.

Client sends Server choice Response Client expectation
Version 2 explicit v2 contract 200, v2 schema Parse the new fields
Version 1 explicit v1, deprecated 200 plus deprecation headers Warn, keep working
No version Documented default Default schema Stable, predictable behavior
Unsupported version None match 400 or 404 Show an upgrade message
Old versioned path Routed v1 v1 response Route-specific handling

The deprecated row should include the deprecation and sunset headers a real API emits, so the client can surface a warning without treating the response as a failure. The unsupported row is the one that catches a client blindly parsing an error body as data.

What the client must handle

Set the version declaration in one place rather than scattering it across requests, so a change does not leave some calls on the old contract. On a deprecated version, read the warning headers and log or surface them while continuing to parse the response. On an unsupported version, treat the status as an error and show the upgrade path instead of retrying the same call. Where v1 and v2 differ in fields or types, keep the parsing logic tied to the version returned so the client does not assume every response has the new shape. Inspect the recorded requests to confirm the version marker the client actually sent. A desktop API workspace lets you match these version branches with conditional overrides, inspect the recorded requests, and assert on each response in the same place. Powerduck works this way, so negotiation is a fixed set of local responses.

Honest limits

A local mock runs in the desktop main process and does not replace the real backend, so the version map, default, and fallback rules are ones you define. The mock does not model real gateway routing, traffic splitting, or canary rollout, and it does not prove the live service keeps old versions available or retires them on the same schedule. Confirm the real default version, deprecation headers, and unsupported-version status with a small set of genuine requests. Importing a schema does not deploy a backend, and a passing mock run is not evidence about the production version lifecycle.

Frequently asked questions

Is version negotiation the same as content negotiation? No. Content negotiation selects a representation such as JSON or XML through Accept. Version negotiation selects a contract such as v1 or v2, even when a vendor media type carries the version.

What should happen when no version is sent? The server should return a documented default version rather than guessing. Mock that branch so the client relies on a predictable response.

How do I test an unsupported version without an old server? Mock the rejection as a 400 or 404 and assert the client shows an upgrade message instead of parsing the error body.

Should a deprecated version still work? Usually yes, while returning deprecation and sunset headers. The client should warn and keep working, then migrate before the sunset date.

The bottom line

Treat version negotiation as a defined set of branches, not an implicit default, and mock each one with responses that actually differ between versions. Cover the explicit, default, deprecated, and unsupported cases, keep the version declaration centralized, and verify the real gateway and lifecycle separately. For more on this approach, see the API mocking guide hub.

title: Why AWS Built an Emulator to Give Coding Agents a Local Feedback Loop
description:
If you have ever tried pointing an autonomous coding agent at an AWS backend, you have probably watched it thrash. Deploying a test stack to a cloud sandbox to check if an SQS visibility timeout works or if a DynamoDB conditional write fails takes 45 to 120 seconds per cycle. The agent burns through context polling status endpoints, runs up token bills, and loses its reasoning chain while waiting on remote state.

On November 11, AWS released AWS Emulator under a CC0 public domain dedication. The project is an offline, in-memory implementation of more than 200 AWS services generated from 438 Smithy API models. You can test S3, SQS, DynamoDB, Lambda, and hundreds of other services locally on your laptop without an AWS account, network calls, or cloud credentials.

The part of the release that caught everyone's attention on Hacker News is that the entire emulator codebase was written, tested, and maintained by autonomous AI agents without human code review.

Three teams and a coloring book

In his launch write-up, Matt Goldberg, a Senior Principal Engineer on the AWS Developer Tools team, compared agents to children working in a coloring book. Without explicit structural boundaries, agents drift into strange implementation choices, such as attempting to write a custom Python interpreter from scratch to handle Lambda invocations.

To keep hundreds of concurrent agents from wandering off course, AWS split the work across three separate teams:

  1. Test writers create customer scenarios based on public Smithy API models. Each scenario is run against the live AWS cloud until it passes, ensuring the test captures true cloud behavior. Once verified, these scenarios become static fidelity tests stored in CodeCommit. They can be replayed repeatedly on local hardware without touching AWS again.
  2. Issue finders replay that fidelity test suite against the local emulator code. When an endpoint returns unexpected XML, mishandles a header, or violates a timeout contract, the finding agent groups related failures and logs a ticket in an issues directory.
  3. Issue fixers check out the repository, address one ticket at a time, and send the patch through an automated merge gate.

That merge gate decides what actually lands on mainline. In addition to compiler checks and zero-regression runs against the fidelity suite, the gate runs multiple specialized security agents performing adversarial reviews alongside general code quality linters. If any check fails, the patch gets rejected back to the fixer agent for rework.

Four nights without tests versus two hours with a harness

On All Things Distributed, Werner Vogels and Swami Sivasubramanian connected this release to the early architecture of AWS. Twenty years ago, Swami and Al Vermeulen built Alf, the Paxos-based distributed lock service that still underpins core primitives in S3 and DynamoDB. Testing Alf required a custom JVM simulation to inject dropped packets and test concurrency edge cases under strict correctness guarantees.

Recently, Swami tried using Amazon's Kiro agent to rebuild Alf's Paxos replication engine. He supervised the agent for four nights while it struggled to produce workable code. The bottleneck was simple: the agent had no local environment to run its code and verify whether state transitions actually held. Once Swami provided an exact specification and a local test harness, the agent completed the rebuild in two hours.

When an agent cannot execute and test its output immediately, it generates plausible guesses. When it has a local execution target with immediate assertion feedback, it iterates toward correctness.

Why local emulation changes coding agent workflows

For developers using AI coding agents on infrastructure or backend services, cloud dependencies create massive friction. Having an agent write code against live AWS services usually means one of two bad options.

The first option is running tests against live cloud sandboxes. Every test cycle requires provisioning resources, waiting on CloudFormation or Terraform state transitions, and dealing with remote network latency. A single verification loop that takes two minutes destroys the agent's context efficiency, burns through tokens on repetitive status polls, and risks orphaned cloud resources if the agent exits unexpectedly.

The second option is relying on hand-rolled mocks. Hand-rolled mocks almost always diverge from real AWS semantics. An agent might assume SQS visibility timeouts behave one way, write application logic that passes local mock assertions, and fail immediately upon hitting production infrastructure.

AWS Emulator changes that dynamic by placing 200+ AWS services directly into the agent's local execution loop. An agent running in your terminal can spin up a local emulator, create an SQS queue, push sample payloads, verify dead-letter queue routing, test DynamoDB conditional writes, and confirm the code works before touching Git.

In an agent-driven development loop, the engineer focuses on the surrounding harness: defining interface specs, verifying ground-truth fidelity tests, and enforcing merge gates that keep the generated code correct.

title: A created_at-only cursor lost 587 rows, even with clock_timestamp() and microseconds
description:
A reader on one of my Postgres posts asked a fair question: why put id in the pagination index at all? With clock_timestamp() instead of now(), it's hard to create two rows at exactly the same time.

So I measured it.

The setup

PostgreSQL 16, a 4-vCPU machine. The table is the one every app has:

CREATE TABLE concurrent (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(),
  n int
);

Then I filled it two ways:

  1. Concurrent inserts: pgbench with 16 clients, one INSERT per autocommit transaction, for 20 seconds (about 29,000 inserts a second).
  2. One bulk insert: INSERT ... SELECT of 1,000,000 rows, like an import or a backfill.

How many timestamps collided

Table Rows Distinct created_at Rows sharing a timestamp
Concurrent inserts 583,817 572,945 10,872
Bulk insert 1,000,000 869,925 130,075

timestamptz stores microseconds. Two rows written in the same microsecond get the same value, and on a busy table that happens thousands of times. clock_timestamp() makes it rarer than now(), which is fixed for the whole transaction, but it does not make it unique.

What it does to keyset pagination

Then I walked each table newest-first, 20 rows a page, the way an infinite-scroll API does, with two cursors:

-- cursor on the timestamp only
WHERE created_at < $last_created_at
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- cursor on (timestamp, id)
WHERE (created_at, id) < ($last_created_at, $last_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
Table Cursor Rows returned by walking every page Rows lost
Concurrent inserts created_at only 583,230 of 583,817 587
Concurrent inserts (created_at, id) 583,817 of 583,817 0
Bulk insert created_at only 993,090 of 1,000,000 6,910
Bulk insert (created_at, id) 1,000,000 of 1,000,000 0

Why rows disappear

When a page ends on a row whose timestamp is shared, the other rows with that timestamp are on the far side of the cursor. The next request asks for created_at < last_created_at, strictly less, so they are skipped. No error, no duplicate, just a user who never sees a few posts in their feed.

Using <= instead doesn't fix it: then the rows that were already shown come back on the next page as duplicates, and if more than a page shares one timestamp, the walk never advances.

The id makes the sort key unique. (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) is a row comparison: "strictly before this exact row", so every row is returned once.

The fix 

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_posts_created_id
  ON posts (created_at DESC, id DESC);

SELECT id, title, created_at
FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
  • Put both columns in the cursor you hand to the client, and both in the ORDER BY.
  • Keep the row comparison as one tuple; Postgres can use the composite index for it directly.
  • Any unique, stable column works as the tiebreaker. The primary key is the obvious one.

How to check your own table 

SELECT count(*) - count(DISTINCT created_at) AS rows_sharing_a_timestamp
FROM posts;

If that's above zero and your cursor holds only the timestamp, some users are missing rows today.

Checklist

  • Cursors for keyset pagination encode the timestamp and a unique tiebreaker.
  • WHERE uses the row comparison (created_at, id) < (...), never created_at < alone.
  • ORDER BY and the index list the same columns in the same direction.
  • A test walks every page of a table with duplicate timestamps and checks no row is missing or repeated.

Making Claude Code write it this way

Ask for "cursor pagination" and you often get a timestamp-only cursor, because it looks complete and passes a small test. The cursor-pagination skill in my Claude Code skills pack for TypeScript + GraphQL + Postgres backends always uses a unique tiebreaker, and the pack's starter backend tests a full page walk in CI.

  • Two skills are free (GraphQL N+1 fixes and safe Postgres migrations): github.com/adnan909/free-sample
  • The full pack, with the cursor-pagination skill, 6 more skills and the starter backend: Backend Skills Pack on Gumroad

title: Your Node.js AI App Needs a Budget, Not Just an API Key
description:
Connecting an application to an LLM is relatively straightforward.

You send a prompt, receive a response, and integrate the result into your application. A basic AI feature can be built in a few hours.

But what happens when that feature starts getting real traffic?

One user asks a simple question. Another uploads a 100-page document. Someone else maintains a conversation containing 50 previous messages. Meanwhile, background jobs are generating summaries, processing files, and calling AI models.

Your application might be working perfectly from a functional perspective, but your API consumption keeps increasing.

And the problem isn't always the model.

It is often the way your application manages AI requests.

As AI features become part of production applications, managing token consumption, request frequency, and model costs becomes an architectural responsibility.

For applications using multiple models and providers, a centralized approach can make these controls easier to maintain. This is one reason AI gateway architecture becomes increasingly useful as an application grows.

In this article, let's look at how to introduce practical AI cost controls in a Node.js application without building unnecessarily complicated infrastructure.

1. Understand What Actually Drives AI Costs

Before implementing cost controls, understand where the consumption comes from.

Most LLM providers calculate usage based on input and output tokens, although pricing can also vary by model, caching, and supported modalities.

Input tokens include:

  • System instructions
  • User prompts
  • Previous conversation messages
  • Retrieved documents and knowledge
  • Tool definitions and structured inputs

Output tokens include generated content and, depending on the model, other generated tokens that may not appear in the visible response.

Consider a customer support chatbot.

A user sends:

"How can I reset my password?"

The actual request might contain much more than that sentence:

System instructions
+ Customer support guidelines
+ Previous conversation history
+ Retrieved knowledge base documents
+ Current user question

The application pays for the complete request, not just the latest user message.

This is particularly important in applications that maintain long conversations or process large documents.

The first architectural decision should be to measure the complete AI request rather than looking only at the user's input.

2. Put a Maximum Output Limit on Every Request

Never allow your application to generate unlimited output when a feature has a clearly defined purpose.

A document summary does not need 5,000 generated tokens. A classification operation might need only a few.

Set limits based on what the feature actually requires.

Here's an example using the OpenAI Node.js SDK:

import OpenAI from "openai";

const openai = new OpenAI({
  apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY
});

export async function generateAnswer(prompt) {
  const response = await openai.chat.completions.create({
    model: process.env.OPENAI_MODEL,
    messages: [
      {
        role: "system",
        content: "Provide clear and concise answers."
      },
      {
        role: "user",
        content: prompt
      }
    ],
    max_completion_tokens: 500
  });

  return {
    content: response.choices[0]?.message?.content ?? "",
    usage: response.usage
  };
}

Here, max_completion_tokens establishes an upper limit on generated tokens.

One important detail: this limit can include reasoning tokens that are not visible in the final response. It is not necessarily a limit on the number of words the user receives.

Also, this example uses the Chat Completions API. Other providers and API endpoints may expose different parameter names.

The objective isn't to make every response short. It is to prevent features from generating significantly more content than their purpose requires.

3. Control Input Size Before Calling the Model

Output limits solve only half the problem.

Your application must also control input consumption.

Consider a document summarization feature that accepts uploaded files.

A user uploads a small PDF. Another uploads a document containing several hundred pages.

Without input controls, your application could attempt to send a huge amount of content to the model.

Start with basic request validation:

function validatePrompt(prompt) {
  if (typeof prompt !== "string") {
    throw new Error("Prompt must be a string");
  }

  if (!prompt.trim()) {
    throw new Error("Prompt cannot be empty");
  }

  const MAX_CHARACTERS = 12000;

  if (prompt.length > MAX_CHARACTERS) {
    throw new Error("Input exceeds the allowed size");
  }

  return prompt.trim();
}

This is an initial payload-size check, not an actual token limit.

Why does that distinction matter?

The number of tokens represented by a string depends on the content and tokenizer. Images, files, and tool definitions introduce additional complexity.

For more predictable control:

  1. Use a tokenizer compatible with the selected model for text-only estimates.
  2. Use a provider's token-counting endpoint when available.
  3. Account for system instructions, conversation history, and retrieved context.
  4. Set separate limits for different AI features.
  5. Reconcile estimated usage with the actual usage returned by the provider.

A chatbot, translation feature, and document summarizer should not necessarily share the same input limits.

A single global limit rarely works well across different AI workloads.

4. Introduce Distributed Rate Limiting

One user should not be able to generate unlimited AI requests.

A common implementation is request-based rate limiting.

For example:

  • Free users: 10 requests per minute.
  • Standard users: 30 requests per minute.
  • Enterprise users: Custom limits.

These are illustrative values. Actual limits should depend on your application's traffic and infrastructure.

In a distributed Node.js application, Redis is a practical choice because multiple application instances can share the same counters.

However, there is an implementation detail worth considering.

The following approach looks simple:

const count = await redis.incr(key);

if (count === 1) {
  await redis.expire(key, 60);
}

But INCR and EXPIRE are separate operations. If the application fails between them, the counter might remain without an expiry.

A better approach is to execute both operations atomically using a Redis Lua script.

The following example uses the Redis Node.js client v4 interface:

const RATE_LIMIT_SCRIPT = `
  local current = tonumber(
    redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0'
  )

  local limit = tonumber(ARGV[1])
  local window = tonumber(ARGV[2])

  if current >= limit then
    return {
      0,
      current,
      redis.call('TTL', KEYS[1])
    }
  end

  current = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])

  if current == 1 then
    redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], window)
  end

  return {
    1,
    current,
    redis.call('TTL', KEYS[1])
  }
`;

async function checkRateLimit(redis, userId) {
  const key = `ai:requests:${userId}`;

  const result = await redis.eval(RATE_LIMIT_SCRIPT, {
    keys: [key],
    arguments: ["10", "60"]
  });

  const [allowed, count, ttl] = result;

  return {
    allowed: Number(allowed) === 1,
    count: Number(count),
    retryAfter: Math.max(0, Number(ttl))
  };
}

The Lua script executes the counter update and expiry logic as one atomic operation.

This is a fixed-window rate limiter. It is simple and useful for many applications, although it can allow bursts around window boundaries. For smoother traffic control, consider a sliding-window or token-bucket algorithm.

Also, use the authenticated user or tenant identity when constructing the Redis key. Do not trust an arbitrary user ID supplied by the request.

One more important distinction: request rate limiting controls how frequently users call your application. It does not guarantee control over how much those requests cost.

For that, you need usage-based budgets.

5. Track Actual Token Consumption

Do not rely entirely on your provider's billing dashboard.

Your application should know how much each feature and user consumes.

LLM APIs generally return usage information after a successful request.

For Chat Completions, the response includes fields such as:

  • prompt_tokens
  • completion_tokens
  • total_tokens

For the Responses API, the corresponding fields include:

  • input_tokens
  • output_tokens
  • total_tokens

You should normalize these fields inside your application so that the rest of your system doesn't depend on a particular provider's response format.

For example:

function normalizeUsage(response) {
  const usage = response.usage ?? {};

  return {
    inputTokens:
      usage.prompt_tokens ??
      usage.input_tokens ??
      0,

    outputTokens:
      usage.completion_tokens ??
      usage.output_tokens ??
      0,

    totalTokens: usage.total_tokens ?? 0
  };
}

Now you can maintain a common usage format irrespective of the provider adapter.

A simple usage record could look like this:

{
  "userId": "user_123",
  "feature": "document_summary",
  "provider": "openai",
  "model": "configured-model",
  "inputTokens": 2400,
  "outputTokens": 450,
  "totalTokens": 2850,
  "status": "success"
}

Avoid storing sensitive prompts or personal information unnecessarily. Usage metadata is often sufficient for cost monitoring.

Over time, this information helps answer important questions:

  • Which AI feature consumes the most tokens?
  • Which customers generate the highest usage?
  • Which models are being used most frequently?
  • Are costs increasing because of longer prompts or larger responses?
  • Is a particular workflow generating unnecessary requests?

You cannot optimize what you cannot measure.

6. Introduce Per-User or Per-Tenant Spending Budgets

Rate limiting controls request frequency.

Usage tracking tells you what happened.

A spending budget controls how much a user or tenant is allowed to consume.

Imagine a SaaS application where every customer receives a monthly AI allowance.

Instead of relying only on request counts, calculate the estimated cost of each operation.

A simplified cost calculation looks like this:

function estimateCost({
  inputTokens,
  outputTokens,
  inputPricePerMillion,
  outputPricePerMillion
}) {
  return (
    inputTokens * inputPricePerMillion +
    outputTokens * outputPricePerMillion
  ) / 1_000_000;
}

The pricing values must come from configuration based on the selected provider and model.

For more accurate estimates, account separately for cached input, image or audio usage, and other billable categories where applicable.

For financial accounting, use integer units such as currency micros or an appropriate decimal type rather than accumulating floating-point currency values.

Now comes an important architectural problem.

Suppose a customer has a monthly budget of $5.

Two requests arrive at almost exactly the same time.

Both requests check the current balance and see that enough budget remains. Both proceed to the model.

The combined cost exceeds the allowance.

This is a concurrency problem.

The solution is to reserve the estimated cost before sending the request.

For example, in MySQL:

UPDATE ai_user_budgets
SET reserved_micros = reserved_micros + ?
WHERE user_id = ?
  AND spent_micros + reserved_micros + ?
      <= monthly_limit_micros;

The estimated cost is supplied for both placeholders. Check the number of affected rows.

If no row was updated, the reservation could not be made, so reject the request.

This makes the budget check and reservation a single atomic database operation.

After the LLM responds:

  1. Calculate the actual cost using the returned usage.
  2. Convert the reservation into actual spending.
  3. Release any unused reserved amount.
  4. Record the final usage against the request.

If the request fails, release the reservation according to your failure-handling policy.

For a production implementation, give each reservation a unique request ID and expiration time. This makes it possible to recover reservations left behind by crashed application instances.

Also account for cases where actual consumption exceeds the estimate. A reservation should be based on a conservative estimate, ideally including the maximum permitted output, and the final reconciliation must have an explicit overrun policy.

The distinction between checking a budget and reserving a budget becomes especially important when multiple application instances process requests simultaneously.

7. Stop Sending Entire Conversation Histories

Conversation history is another source of unnecessary token consumption.

Consider a chatbot that has been running for 50 messages.

Does every new request really need all 50 previous messages?

In many cases, it doesn't.

A more practical architecture combines:

  • A rolling summary of older conversation messages.
  • A limited window of recent messages.
  • The current user message.

For example:

function buildMessages(
  summary,
  recentMessages,
  userMessage
) {
  return [
    {
      role: "system",
      content: "You are a helpful support assistant."
    },

    ...(summary
      ? [{
          role: "system",
          content: `Conversation summary: ${summary}`
        }]
      : []),

    ...recentMessages,

    {
      role: "user",
      content: userMessage
    }
  ];
}

This reduces the amount of repeated context sent to the model.

However, summarization itself has a cost.

It should not run after every message. Choose an appropriate threshold and preserve important information such as customer preferences, decisions, unresolved issues, and previous actions.

The objective is to maintain useful context without repeatedly transmitting unnecessary information.

8. Use the Right Model for the Right Task

Not every AI feature needs the same model.

Consider an application with these features:

Feature Architectural consideration
Text classification A smaller, lower-cost model may be sufficient
Translation Prioritize language quality and predictable output
File summarization Consider input size and context requirements
Complex reasoning Use a capable reasoning model where justified
Data extraction Prefer structured output and validation

Using an expensive model for every operation can increase costs without providing meaningful improvements.

A model-selection layer can help:

function selectModel(task) {
  const models = {
    classification: process.env.CLASSIFICATION_MODEL,
    translation: process.env.TRANSLATION_MODEL,
    summarization: process.env.SUMMARY_MODEL,
    reasoning: process.env.REASONING_MODEL
  };

  const model = models[task];

  if (!model) {
    throw new Error(`Unsupported AI task: ${task}`);
  }

  return model;
}

The application can choose a model based on the task rather than hardcoding one model throughout the codebase.

Of course, model selection should be validated against output quality, latency, reliability, and actual cost. Cheaper does not automatically mean better.

9. Add Caching Where It Makes Sense

Another opportunity is avoiding repeated calls for identical or safely reusable requests.

For example, your application might receive the same request multiple times:

"Explain what a database index is."

Generating the same answer repeatedly may be unnecessary.

An application-level cache can help with suitable workloads.

async function getCachedResponse(
  redis,
  cacheKey,
  generate
) {
  const cached = await redis.get(cacheKey);

  if (cached) {
    return JSON.parse(cached);
  }

  const result = await generate();

  await redis.set(
    cacheKey,
    JSON.stringify(result),
    { EX: 3600 }
  );

  return result;
}

This is a simplified example.

A production cache needs a carefully designed key containing the relevant model, prompt version, configuration, and tenant or access scope. It also needs an invalidation strategy.

Do not share cached answers across users or tenants when the underlying context contains private information.

Caching is particularly useful for repeated reference questions, stable knowledge, and deterministic operations.

It is less suitable for requests that depend on changing data, real-time information, or user-specific context.

Track cache hits separately. A cache hit avoids a provider call, so your application-level request count and provider-level token consumption should not be treated as the same metric.

10. Pay Special Attention to AI Agents

Traditional chatbots usually respond to individual requests.

AI agents are different.

An agent might make several model calls, invoke external tools, retrieve information, evaluate its results, and repeat the process before completing a single task.

A user might submit one request, but the application could generate ten or twenty LLM calls behind the scenes.

This makes cost estimation much more complicated.

For agent-based applications, consider enforcing:

  • Maximum model calls per task.
  • Maximum total tokens per execution.
  • Maximum execution time.
  • Maximum spending per task.
  • Maximum tool invocations.
  • Explicit retry limits.

A runaway agent loop should never be able to consume unlimited resources.

These limits should apply to the entire task, not just individual model requests.

This is particularly important when designing AI agent architectures, execution workflows, and guardrails.

11. What Should You Monitor in Production?

A production AI application needs more than an API usage counter.

I would start with these metrics:

Metric Why it matters
Input tokens Measures prompt consumption
Output tokens Measures generation consumption
Cost per request Identifies expensive operations
Cost per tenant Tracks customer-level spending
Requests per minute Detects excessive usage
Average response time Measures performance
Failure rate Identifies provider problems
Model distribution Tracks model selection
Cache hit ratio Measures cache effectiveness
Budget reservation failures Detects budget exhaustion
Cost per completed task Measures overall execution efficiency

A basic dashboard can provide enough information to identify problems early.

As the application grows, introduce alerts for unexpected consumption spikes, unusual request patterns, and approaching customer budgets.

One important operational consideration is deciding what happens when Redis, the usage database, or the provider becomes unavailable.

For example, a system that cannot verify a customer's spending allowance should not silently allow unlimited AI requests. Define fail-open and fail-closed behavior according to the risk of each feature.

Cost controls are not simply monitoring features. They are part of your application's operational reliability.

12. Bring Everything Together

These controls become much easier to manage when they are not scattered throughout your application.

A practical architecture could look like this:

              User Request
                   |
                   v
             Authentication
                   |
                   v
              Rate Limiter
                   |
                   v
             Input Validation
                   |
                   v
             Context Manager
                   |
                   v
             Usage Estimator
                   |
                   v
           Budget Reservation
                   |
                   v
                AI Gateway
                   |
                   v
              LLM Provider
                   |
                   v
            Response Processing
                   |
                   v
           Actual Usage Capture
                   |
                   v
          Budget Reconciliation
                   |
                   v
                Response

Each component has a specific responsibility.

Application layer: Handles user permissions, subscription plans, and business rules.

Rate limiter: Controls request frequency.

Context manager: Controls conversation history and retrieved information.

Usage estimator: Estimates the potential cost before execution.

Budget manager: Reserves, tracks, and reconciles spending.

AI gateway: Handles provider communication, timeouts, retries, and model selection.

Monitoring layer: Provides visibility into application-wide AI consumption.

If you haven't already considered the gateway layer, our article on what an AI gateway is and how it works explores the architecture, provider abstraction, routing, rate limiting, and cost tracking in more detail.

This separation also makes it easier to introduce additional providers without rewriting your business logic.

Final Thoughts

Building an AI feature is no longer the most difficult part of integrating AI into an application.

The real engineering challenge begins when that feature becomes part of a product used by hundreds or thousands of people.

An application that works perfectly with ten test requests might behave very differently under real production traffic.

You need to think beyond API integration.

Token limits, distributed rate limiting, usage tracking, budget reservations, context management, caching, and model selection should be treated as architectural responsibilities rather than features added after an unexpectedly large API bill.

My recommendation is simple: build these controls into your AI integration layer from the beginning.

It is much easier to design an application with predictable AI consumption than to retrofit spending controls after customers are already using it.

How are you controlling AI costs in your applications? Are you tracking usage at the API level, per user, or per tenant?

I'd be interested to hear how other developers are approaching this in production.

Further Reading

If you're exploring production AI architecture, these articles may also be useful:

  • What Is an AI Gateway? How It Works and Why It Matters
  • AI Agents Explained: How They Work, With Real Examples
  • AI Governance Consulting: What It Is and When You Need It

You can also read my previous DEV.to article: Stop Calling Your LLM Directly: Build a Small AI Gateway in Node.js.

Explore more AI and software architecture insights at VoidSyntax.

title: Cloud for Cheap: What It Actually Costs to Run Your Own
description:
I did the arithmetic on a Google One bill last month, then did the same arithmetic on the server sitting under my desk. The cloud won. Not narrowly — by enough that I closed the tab and went to make coffee.

That's the answer most self-hosting guides won't give you, because "run your own cloud" is a hobby that sells a feeling, and the feeling is free while the electricity isn't.

Here's the real arithmetic, with every price checked on 10 November 2026: what Google One actually charges, what a cheap VPS actually costs, what a home server burns in electricity, and the one rule that tells you which of the three to pick.

Every option, priced

One table, because the whole argument is in it. The Google One and Hetzner prices were checked against the vendors' own pages on 10 November 2026; the electricity figures are calculated at the German household rate of 36.18 euro cents per kWh, which is what Eurostat recorded for the first half of 2026.

Option What you get Monthly Yearly Over five years
Google One Free 15 GB, shared $0.00 $0.00 $0.00
Google One Basic 100 GB, shared $1.99 $19.99 $99.95
Google One AI Plus 2 TB, shared $9.99 $99.99 $499.95
Google One AI Pro 5 TB, shared $19.99 $199.99 $999.95
Hetzner CX23 2 vCPU, 4 GB, 40 GB NVMe €5.99 €71.88 €359.40
Hetzner CX33 4 vCPU, 8 GB, 80 GB NVMe €8.99 €107.88 €539.40
Pi 5 and an 8 TB disk, home 3.0 W idle, electricity only — €9.51 €47.55
N100 mini PC, home 10 W idle, electricity only — €31.70 €158.50
Old desktop tower, home 50 W idle, electricity only — €158.46 €792.30

Read the last three rows next to the first four and the argument is already over for most people. A desktop tower left running all day costs more over five years than Google One 2TB does. That is not a self-hosting setup, that is an expensive way to store photographs.

Where the electricity comes from

The bottom three rows are the ones nobody puts in a spreadsheet, so here is the calculation. German households paid 36.18 euro cents per kWh in the first half of 2026 — the second most expensive rate in the EU, which makes the maths harsher than most guides admit.

A Raspberry Pi 5 idles at about 3.0 W headless, or 3.6 W with Ethernet and a USB SSD attached. A cheap N100 mini PC idles around three times that. A refurbished office box from 2020 can sit at 18 W doing nothing at all.

Here is the whole calculation in one line: at 36.18 cents per kWh, every watt of continuous draw costs €3.17 a year. A machine that idles at 50 W is spending more on electricity than a cheap VPS costs for the whole month.

Measure your own machine instead of trusting someone else's table. On a Pi, the power supply reports real numbers:

# Instantaneous watts on a Raspberry Pi 5
cat /sys/class/power_supply/*/power/now | awk '{printf "%.2f W\n", $1/1000000}'

# On a desktop with a supported kernel: total and per-process draw
sudo powertop --interval=2

And if you want the annual figure for your own hardware instead of mine:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Annual electricity cost of a machine that draws $1 W continuously.
# Usage: ./power-cost.sh 3.0          # watts, 36.18 cents/kWh
#        ./power-cost.sh 18.0 0.30    # watts, your own price per kWh
awk -v w="${1:-3.0}" -v p="${2:-0.3618}" 'BEGIN {
  kwh = w * 8760 / 1000
  printf "%.1f W -> %.1f kWh/year -> EUR %.2f/year\n", w, kwh, kwh * p
}'

What a cheap VPS actually costs

Hetzner raised its cloud prices twice in 2026. On 1 April most lines went up about a third, and on 15 June every line went up again for new orders and rescales. The cost-optimised CX23 went from €2.99 to €3.99 to €5.49 a month.

Compare that with DigitalOcean's comparable Droplet at $24 a month and the gap is embarrassing in Hetzner's favour.

But note the catch: the cheap lines are capacity-limited. Since September 2026 the cost-optimised plans are frequently marked unavailable and sell out within minutes of a restock. Budget for the possibility that your €5.99 server isn't there when you want it.

The three ways to run your own cloud

  • Home server — a machine you own, in your house. Cheapest in electricity, most expensive in your time.
  • Cheap VPS — a rented box in a datacentre. One flat monthly price, nobody else's hardware in your hallway.
  • Nothing at all — sync between your own devices, no server involved. Costs nothing at all.

The third option is the one nobody sells you, and for a lot of people it's the correct one. Syncthing is free, open source, and it syncs folders directly between your laptop, your phone and your parent's laptop without a server in the middle. If what you need is "my photos are on my phone and I want them on my laptop", you don't need a cloud. You need a peer-to-peer sync tool and a free afternoon.

Where self-hosting genuinely wins

It wins when you're billed per seat and your files are measured in gigabytes, not terabytes.

A ten-person team with a shared document library doesn't need a storage plan, it needs a box. And the box costs the same whether ten people use it or fifty. Google Workspace Business Standard is roughly $14 per user per month on an annual plan — about $140 a month for that team, and it climbs with every hire. One CX33 covers the same library and the price doesn't move.

It also wins when privacy is the point and price isn't. A password manager, a photo library, a calendar — those aren't storage problems, they're trust problems, and no amount of money buys the trust you get from a box in your hallway.

Where it never wins

  • Cheap bulk storage. Google One 2TB is $9.99. You aren't beating that with a VPS.
  • Zero administration. You're buying an unpaid job. Every disk that fills, every certificate that expires, every backup you never tested is now yours.
  • Anything that needs a phone number. A mail server on a residential connection will get you blocked, and the block will outlast your patience.
  • When the apps already work. The most underrated saving in the whole self-hosting world is the subscription you didn't cancel.

The costs nobody puts in the spreadsheet

Electricity is the smallest of the three real costs. The other two are bigger and they're both paid in the same currency: your time.

The 3am restore. Every self-hosted system has a bad day, and the difference between a bad day and a lost weekend is whether you tested the backup. A backup you've never restored is a hypothesis, not a backup.

The update treadmill. Six services means six things to patch, and the one you don't patch is the one with the advisory on it. This is the cost that makes a modest cloud bill look cheap.

The migration. Moving a photo library onto a new server takes an evening, and the evening after that you find the folder structure doesn't match what you expected and you start again.

What to do next

If the goal is saving money, start with the free option: Syncthing between your own devices costs nothing and needs no server. Then look at what you actually pay for, and whether that subscription is per-seat or per-terabyte.

If the goal is owning your data, the Build Your Own Cloud guide has the stack and the order to install it in. Budget for a backup disk, and for the evening.

If the goal is learning, the home lab beginner's guide is the gentler version of the same question.

Don't buy the hardware until you've done the arithmetic above for your own machine. The number that decides it is how many watts it draws while idle, and that's a number you can read in five minutes with a €12 plug meter.

Self-hosting isn't a cheaper cloud. It's a different kind of bill — sometimes smaller, sometimes much larger, and always paid in your own time.
