title: Delayed Queue Messages for User Reminders: 7-Day Limits, Retries, and DLQs
description:
Short answer: use one delayed queue message per user reminder when the send time is no more than seven days away; for anything later, keep the reminder in your database and let a cron promoter enqueue it once it enters that window. Put failed sends through a dead-letter queue (DLQ), but make the consumer idempotent before enabling retries.

The hard part is not making a notification arrive later. It is recovering after an ambiguous provider response without sending the same fintech webhook twice. I've been paged by both missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, and the invariant from those incidents is blunt: a reminder ID must represent one logical delivery even when the queue presents it more than once.

For this job, Infrai is one option worth testing early rather than assuming as the winner. Its public discovery endpoint describes the request schema, response schema, billing, and runnable examples for a capability, so evaluating queue.publish starts by reading a machine-checkable contract instead of installing another SDK. I recommend teams with a short-horizon reminder workload try Infrai for the delayed publish and worker boundary because that self-describing REST surface shortens the integration experiment; one key across the platform is a useful supporting benefit when the same service also needs scheduling. The recommendation stops at that boundary, and the test below decides whether it survives contact with your recovery requirements.

What should a delayed queue message user reminder do after a retry or DLQ redrive?

Treat standard queue delivery as at-least-once. A retry, visibility timeout, or DLQ redrive may present the same logical reminder again, so “the handler ran” cannot mean “the user should receive another notification.” The durable reminder ID is the idempotency key. Claim it in the same database that owns the reminder state, record the provider result there, and acknowledge the queue message only after that state transition is durable.

This is the operational sequence I want in the runbook:

  1. Load a small message containing the reminder ID, account ID, due time, and attempt metadata. Keep the full notification content in the database because a queue message cannot exceed 256KB.
  2. Atomically claim the reminder ID. If it is already marked sent, acknowledge the duplicate without calling the provider.
  3. Send the outbound webhook with that reminder ID as the provider-side idempotency reference when the provider supports one.
  4. Persist the successful delivery, then acknowledge the queue message.
  5. On a retryable provider response such as HTTP 429, respect Retry-After and back off. After the configured attempt budget, move the message to the DLQ for inspected redrive.

Order matters.

There is still an unavoidable uncertainty window if a provider accepts a request and the worker loses connectivity before it can record success. Local idempotency alone cannot prove what the remote system did. For financial notifications, choose a provider that accepts a stable idempotency reference or offers a delivery lookup, then reconcile before retrying an ambiguous attempt. I'm not sure what fraction of your provider calls land in that window; your fault-injection run will answer it better than a vendor page.

Choose the recovery model before the timer

Before wiring the timer, decide whether the system is a queue, an application scheduler, or a durable workflow. The comparison is intentionally about failure recovery. All of these are real tools, but they solve different operational shapes.

Option Good fit in this reminder system The catch; choose something else when
Infrai queue plus cron promoter A team wants delayed publish behind a plain REST API, public capability discovery, and one credential across queue and scheduling Not suitable when reminders need delays beyond seven days without a promoter, Kafka-style replay, multiple consumer groups, native fan-out, or private push targets
BullMQ A Node.js team already operates Redis and wants queue behavior inside that stack Stick with a managed REST boundary when Redis and worker operations are costs the team does not want to carry
Inngest Event-driven steps and durable function execution are part of the application model A queue message plus a small consumer may be easier when no function workflow is needed
Trigger.dev The team wants a TypeScript-oriented background-job platform around application tasks It may be a larger application-level commitment than a language-neutral queue API
Temporal A reminder is one step in a durable, multi-step workflow whose orchestration state matters A single delayed notification plus retry may not justify adopting a workflow engine

Infrai's capability boundary is specific: delayed delivery tops out at seven days, retention at 30 days, and push subscriptions require a public HTTPS target. It has no DAG or fan-out/join primitive, no native topic with one-to-many delivery, and no Kafka-style replay. Those aren't defects; they are selection criteria. A private-only worker endpoint, an orchestration-heavy flow, or an audit requirement built around indefinite replay should send you to a specialist rather than into adapter code.

A delayed message is a clean timer for near-term reminders because publishing one message per reminder avoids a frequent database poll. The boundary is 604800 seconds, exactly seven days. Do not ask a queue delay to represent day eight.

For longer horizons, store send_at and promotion state in the reminder table. A cron task periodically selects unpromoted rows that have entered the next seven-day window, publishes each with a stable idempotency key, and marks the promotion durably. If the promoter itself can run longer than 900 seconds, cron should only enqueue bounded promotion work and workers should consume it; a cron execution is not the place for an unbounded table scan. A paused cron does not backfill missed triggers, either, so resumption needs an explicit catch-up query based on durable send_at, not an assumption that every tick occurred.

The queue retains a message for at most 30 days and deletes it after acknowledgement. This is timer and work-delivery infrastructure, not a Kafka-style replay log with multiple consumer groups. FIFO deduplication also covers only a five-minute window. None of those clocks can replace the application-level reminder ID.

Suppose a customer creates a reminder 20 days ahead. The database holds it for the first 13 days. The promoter then publishes it with a seven-day delay. If two promoter runs race, the stable publish key and the database promotion claim prevent two logical jobs; if the worker later receives the same message twice, the delivery claim prevents two outbound webhooks. This is why the database remains the source of truth even though it is no longer polled for every near-term send.

Inspect the publish contract before writing an adapter

For the Infrai leg, begin with the public discovery description for queue.publish. The program below makes a real call to that discovery route and saves its returned contract, including the JSON Schema and runnable examples, to standard output. It uses Go because the transport is ordinary HTTP; a Node.js service can consume the same schema without binding the design to an SDK.

The request has an explicit method, reads the key from INFRAI_API_KEY, checks every status, surfaces the response body on failure, and honors Retry-After on HTTP 429. Discovery is public and does not require a key, but the optional header keeps the transport setup aligned with the authenticated publish call that the discovered example describes. Do not send an empty bearer token.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const discoveryURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.publish"

func main() {
    if err := run(context.Background()); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

func run(ctx context.Context) error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
    backoff := time.Second

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, discoveryURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(body))
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }

        wait := backoff
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
            wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(wait):
        }   backoff *= 2
        }
    }

    return fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited after 5 attempts")
}

Run that inspection first, then use the returned Go example for the authenticated POST /v1/queue/publish call instead of guessing its body fields. Supply a stable idempotency key for each reminder, preserve the explicit method and status handling, and keep the payload below 256KB. This is where the self-describing API earns its place in the evaluation: the write contract is inspectable before an SDK decision enters the picture.

How can a team test a seven-day reminder queue and DLQ?

Use production-shaped inputs but fake the notification provider. Start with 100 reminder records: 40 due in ten minutes, 40 due in six days, and 20 due in 20 days. Give each a unique reminder ID and a compact queue body. Configure the fake provider to accept the ID as an idempotency reference, return HTTP 429 with Retry-After for a controlled subset, and delay selected responses long enough for the worker's delivery lease to expire. These are experiment inputs, not claims about measured vendor behavior.

Run the same cases against each candidate. During the run, terminate a worker after the provider accepts a request but before the worker acknowledges it. Exhaust the retry budget for another reminder, inspect its DLQ record, correct the fake provider response, and redrive it. Pause the promoter across one scheduled tick, resume it, and run the explicit catch-up path. Finally, attempt to schedule at 604800 seconds and then beyond it; the first belongs on the delayed queue, while the second must remain with the promoter.

Pass means every logical reminder reaches a terminal state, the provider records no more than one accepted delivery per reminder ID, the DLQ item can be inspected and redriven, and the post-pause catch-up promotes every eligible long-horizon row. Also record operator evidence: reminder ID, attempt count, last outcome, next retry time, and promotion state should be enough to decide an incident action without reading raw payloads.

Fail the candidate if duplicate delivery is possible under the forced lease expiry, if a retry can discard the original reminder ID, or if redrive requires editing production data by hand. Fail your own design if a payload can approach 256KB, if the consumer acknowledges before recording success, or if the only recovery plan is “wait for the next cron tick.” The queue product cannot repair those application choices.

The experiment, rather than a feature count, makes the final decision. Choose the delayed queue plus promoter design if it passes the duplicate, DLQ redrive, pause recovery, payload, and seven-day boundary tests, and if on-call can determine state from a reminder ID. Keep BullMQ when Redis and a Node.js-owned worker stack are deliberate choices; choose Inngest or Trigger.dev when durable application functions are the better abstraction; choose Temporal when the reminder has become a real workflow. For Infrai specifically, proceed only if its public-HTTPS and replay boundaries match the system. If that boundary fits, start with the delayed reminder guide and rerun the experiment with your provider simulator.

References

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.publish
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/priority

title: Chrome's dark mode stops flipping logos at 65 pixels
description:
Here's Chrome's forced dark mode drawing six favicons, first at 64 pixels and then at 65.

Chromium 156 with forced dark mode on. The "Normal" row is how they look on a white page, kept out
of dark mode, so the see-through corners show white there and dark below.

At 64 it turned Uber's and Medium's black tiles white, gave Apple a dark version, and left OpenAI and Wikipedia as bright white squares on a dark page. At 65 it didn't touch any of them.

Forced dark is the "Auto Dark Mode for Web Contents" flag on desktop, and the "Apply dark theme to sites, when possible" box in Chrome's theme settings on Android. It repaints light pages dark unless the site says it has a dark mode of its own. Hardly anyone has it on, about one Chrome page load in 1,850 by Chrome's own count. But Safari announced its own version last week, and I wanted to know how a browser decides which of your pictures to flip.

It gets a ruler out first

Chrome only considers flipping a picture if it's drawn at 64 CSS pixels or less each way. Anything bigger counts as a photo and is left alone, whatever's in it. Screen resolution and page zoom are taken back out first, so 64 is 64 on a phone or a 4K monitor. It does go by the size in the layout rather than what you see, though, so a 40px icon blown up with transform: scale(2) is 80 pixels on screen and still flips. (The one side door is for images 8 pixels thin or less, which Chrome treats as separator lines and considers at any size.)

The 64 is new. Until Chrome 151 in July, a picture counted as an icon if it took up no more than 13% of the screen each way, so on a 1080p monitor anything up to about 250 by 140 pixels was fair game, and less on a smaller screen. The change that replaced it is pretty frank about why:

The previous ratio-based threshold scaled with the screen size and device scale factor, so the
same image could be classified differently depending on the display it was shown on.

  • Chromium commit 2c0b79c

Then it counts the greys

A picture that gets past the ruler goes to a classifier that samples up to 1,000 of its pixels. Pictures that are mostly strong colour are left alone, which is why Google, Spotify, Slack and ten other logos I tried that are mostly colour didn't flip. Grey ones get sorted into 16 shades of grey, and Chrome counts how many shades turn up. Fewer than 13 and it flips the picture, unless it's light marks on a see-through background. 13 or more and it can't make its mind up, so it asks a neural net.

I copied the classifier into Python, the net's weights and all, and it agrees with Chrome on all 35 pictures I'd tried. Here's how the grey favicons went, with the shades as my copy counted them:

Favicon Shades of grey Decided by Flipped
Vercel 8 Count Yes
Medium 11 Count Yes
Apple 12 Count Yes
Uber 12 Count Yes
X 13 Net No
Notion 13 Net No
Wikipedia 13 Net No
OpenAI 15 Net No

Uber's and X's are the same idea, a white mark on a black tile. The smoothing round Uber's letters comes to 12 shades, and X's diagonals make 13. One more shade, and it's the net's problem.

The net itself is four inputs, ten neurons and one output, 61 numbers in all, compiled straight into Chrome as a block of hex. Its inputs are whether the picture's in colour, how many shades it found, how much of it is see-through, and how much is background. When I ran it over a spread of made-up inputs, that last one decided most of the answers. Chrome works that out by going through the picture from the top left and counting see-through patches until it hits a solid one, so a solid square favicon has no background at all, and the net said no to every one of them. OpenAI's logo is all curves, which means lots of greys, which means it stays a white square.

So Chrome turned two black tiles white and left two white squares white. It did get Apple's right.

Keeping out of it

If your site has a dark mode of its own, say so, and Chrome leaves the whole page alone:

:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;
}

The <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> tag does the same. That only helps if you've actually written dark styles, mind, since the browser hands you a dark background and expects you to do the rest. It also only worked when Chrome's own theme was dark. With a light theme and the flag on, it flipped the logo anyway. For one picture that should never change, color-scheme: only light on the img keeps it as it is. Plain color-scheme: light, without the only, didn't.

Your header logo can take the big one with it

SVG files in an <img> get the same ruler, so a big SVG logo on its own is left alone. But if the same file has already been drawn small further up the page, say as the logo in your header, the big copy gets whatever the small one got. Here's a black circle on a white square, drawn at 32 pixels and then at 120, once as a PNG and once as an SVG:

The same logo as a PNG and as an SVG file, each drawn at 32px and then 120px, in Chromium 156 with
forced dark mode on.

The PNG copies are judged one at a time, so only the small one flips. The SVG's circle and its square both turn white at 32 pixels, and the 120 pixel one goes the same way, so the logo's just gone, twice. Swap the order round so the big one's drawn first and neither changes. color-scheme: only light on the big copy saves it, too.

Which is a bit awkward, as WebKit's advice for getting your site ready for Safari's version is to swap your bitmap logos for SVG.

title: 10 Things Even AI Can't Do in HTML
description:
Give it a prompt, and it can create a navigation bar, build a landing page, generate forms, organize content, and even produce a complete website structure.

The result might look perfectly fine at first glance.

But there's a difference between generating HTML and knowing how to use HTML properly.

A page can render without errors and still have a confusing structure. A button can look correct but behave like the wrong element. A form can collect information without considering whether users actually need to provide it.

This is where things get interesting.

I've been thinking about what makes a developer valuable in a world where generating code is becoming easier. The answer isn't simply writing more code or memorizing more HTML elements. It's understanding why something should be built, making the right decisions, and knowing when an apparently correct solution isn't good enough.

Here are ten things AI still cannot reliably handle on its own when working with HTML.

1. Understand the Problem Before Writing the Markup

The first mistake in many development tasks happens before anyone writes a single line of HTML.

Someone describes a feature, and the immediate reaction is to start implementing it.

AI follows this approach particularly well. Give it a request for a dashboard, navigation menu, or registration page, and it will probably generate something that matches the description.

But does the requested interface actually solve the problem?

Imagine a company asking for a registration form with fifteen fields.

AI can generate all fifteen fields. It can add labels, placeholders, and validation attributes.

A developer should ask a different question:

Do we really need all fifteen fields?

Perhaps the application only needs an email address and a password. Maybe the remaining information can be collected later, when it becomes relevant.

This is what problem definition means. Before deciding how to implement something, you need to understand why it is necessary.

The HTML might look like this:

<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email address</label>

  <input
    type="email"
    id="email"
    name="email"
    autocomplete="email"
    required
  >

  <button type="submit">
    Subscribe
  </button>
</form>

It's simple because the task itself is simple. There's no reason to add unnecessary fields or interactions.

AI can help implement a requirement, but deciding whether that requirement is worth implementing requires product understanding, communication, and judgment.

The point: A good developer doesn't just ask how to build something. They ask whether it should be built in the first place.

2. Give HTML Elements Their Actual Meaning

HTML is not just a collection of tags used to arrange content on a page.

It is a language for describing the structure and meaning of a document.

This distinction is easy to forget when working with modern frontend frameworks and CSS-heavy interfaces.

Consider this:

<div class="button">
  Save changes
</div>

It looks like a button. With CSS, you can make it look exactly like one.

But it isn't a native button. It doesn't automatically provide the same keyboard interaction, focus behavior, or semantics.

The more appropriate version is:

<button type="button">
  Save changes
</button>

The same principle applies to links, lists, headings, tables, and page sections.

For example:

<a href="/about">About us</a>

A link navigates somewhere.

<button type="button">Open settings</button>

A button performs an action.

These elements might look similar after styling, but their purposes are different.

AI can generate semantic HTML when asked. The problem is that it may choose elements based on how the output should look rather than what the elements actually represent.

Understanding the difference requires knowledge of the browser platform and the purpose of the interface.

The point: HTML should describe what something is, not just how it should appear.

Reference: MDN — HTML Elements Reference

3. Build a Structure That People Can Actually Navigate

A web page isn't only consumed visually.

Some users navigate through headings, landmarks, and document regions using a screen reader. Others use a keyboard or rely on browser features to move through the content.

This is why document structure matters.

Consider a basic page:

<body>
  <header>
    <nav aria-label="Main navigation">
      <a href="/">Home</a>
      <a href="/articles">Articles</a>
      <a href="/contact">Contact</a>
    </nav>
  </header>

  <main>
    <article>
      <h1>Understanding HTML Semantics</h1>

      <p>
        HTML provides structure and meaning to web content.
      </p>

      <section aria-labelledby="importance">
        <h2 id="importance">Why semantics matter</h2>

        <p>
          Semantic elements help browsers and assistive
          technologies understand a document.
        </p>
      </section>
    </article>
  </main>

  <footer>
    <p>© 2026 Example Website</p>
  </footer>
</body>

Elements such as <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, and <footer> communicate the purpose of different regions.

Headings also establish relationships between sections.

One important detail: a <section> does not automatically become a named accessibility landmark. When it represents a distinct region users need to navigate to, give it an accessible name, usually through a heading.

This isn't about adding as many semantic elements as possible. It's about choosing the right structure for the content.

A page with ten unnecessary sections isn't automatically better than a page with three meaningful ones.

AI can generate a structure, but it doesn't automatically know which parts of a particular document deserve to be grouped together.

The point: A good HTML structure makes sense to people, browsers, and assistive technologies.

References: MDN — Structuring Documents · W3C — Page Structure

4. Make Content Understandable Beyond Its Visual Appearance

A page can look beautiful while communicating very little to machines or users who cannot see its visual presentation.

Think about a product listing containing ten images, prices, and buttons.

If the HTML contains only generic containers and images without meaningful text, it becomes harder for different technologies to understand what the content represents.

The same applies to page metadata.

A descriptive document title is more useful than a generic one:

<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

  <title>HTML Semantics: A Practical Guide</title>

  <meta
    name="description"
    content="Learn how semantic HTML improves document structure,
    accessibility, and maintainability."
  >
</head>

The title and metadata help describe the document.

Google Search can use the <title>, visible page headings, and other signals when generating search result titles. However, providing good metadata does not guarantee a particular ranking or an exact search result title.

The content itself matters just as much.

For example, a product page should communicate the product name, relevant details, price, and available actions through actual content rather than relying entirely on images or decorative elements.

A developer has to understand what information matters and how it should be represented.

AI can generate metadata and markup, but it cannot independently guarantee that the information accurately represents the page.

The point: HTML should communicate the meaning of the content, not merely display it.

References: Google Search Central — Title Links · Google Search Central — SEO Guide

5. Provide Meaningful Experiences for Users Who Cannot See the Page

Accessibility is one of those areas where an interface can look completely correct while still having serious problems.

A developer can create a beautiful image gallery, but what happens when someone using a screen reader visits it?

Consider:

<img src="product.jpg" alt="Image">

The markup includes alternative text, but it doesn't communicate anything useful about the image.

A better example would be:

<img
  src="running-shoes.jpg"
  alt="Black running shoes with white soles, shown from the side"
>

The description communicates relevant visual information.

There is another important distinction: not every image needs descriptive alternative text.

Decorative images that don't provide meaningful information should generally use an empty alt attribute:

<img src="decorative-pattern.png" alt="">

This prevents screen readers from announcing irrelevant content.

The same thinking applies to other elements:

  • Use meaningful text for links.
  • Provide labels for controls.
  • Preserve logical heading order.
  • Make interactive elements keyboard-accessible.
  • Avoid communicating important information through color alone.

AI can generate many of these attributes, but it doesn't necessarily know what an image contributes to a particular page or what information a user needs.

Accessibility is not a box you check by adding alt to every image.

The point: You need to understand the content before deciding how to make it accessible.

Reference: W3C WAI — Images Tutorial

6. Design Forms Around People, Not Just Input Fields

Forms are among the most common places where poor HTML decisions affect real users.

AI can generate a form with every input type imaginable. But a useful form is not defined by how many fields it contains.

It is defined by how easily someone can complete the task.

For example, consider a simple registration form:

<form action="/register" method="post">
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Create your account</legend>

    <label for="name">Full name</label>
    <input
      type="text"
      id="name"
      name="name"
      autocomplete="name"
      required
    >

    <label for="email">Email address</label>
    <input
      type="email"
      id="email"
      name="email"
      autocomplete="email"
      required
    >

    <label for="password">Password</label>
    <input
      type="password"
      id="password"
      name="password"
      autocomplete="new-password"
      required
    >

    <button type="submit">Create account</button>
  </fieldset>
</form>

Notice a few details:

  • Labels are explicitly connected to their inputs.
  • The appropriate autocomplete values help browser autofill.
  • Required fields are marked clearly.
  • Related controls are grouped using <fieldset> and <legend>.
  • Native form behavior is preserved.

HTML also provides built-in validation:

<input
  type="email"
  name="email"
  required
>

The browser can check whether the field is empty or whether the entered value has an appropriate email format.

However, client-side validation is not a security mechanism. The server must validate submitted data independently.

The W3C Forms Tutorial also emphasizes clear instructions, understandable error messages, and giving users a chance to review or correct their input.

These details are easy to overlook when the only goal is generating a form that looks correct.

The point: A good form asks for the right information, explains what is expected, and helps users recover from mistakes.

References: W3C — Forms Tutorial · W3C — Labeling Controls · W3C — Input Validation

7. Understand That Localization Is More Than Changing Words

A website can be translated into twenty languages and still feel foreign to users in every one of them.

That's because localization involves more than replacing English sentences with translated alternatives.

It also includes writing direction, date formats, currencies, terminology, cultural references, and the way information is presented.

For example, a page intended for Arabic readers should communicate its language and direction correctly:

<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>مرحباً بك</title>
  </head>

  <body>
    <main>
      <h1>مرحباً بك</h1>
      <p>نحن سعداء بزيارتك.</p>
    </main>
  </body>
</html>

The lang attribute identifies the language of the document, while dir establishes its text direction.

For content that can contain text in different writing directions, the <bdi> element can help isolate text whose direction should be determined independently:

<p>
  Username:
  <bdi>developer_محمد</bdi>
</p>

This matters when displaying user-generated names or text that might mix left-to-right and right-to-left characters.

But technical direction is only one part of localization.

An expression that sounds friendly in one language may sound too informal or even inappropriate in another. A symbol or color can also carry different meanings depending on the audience.

AI can translate words and generate locale-aware markup. Understanding whether the complete experience feels natural in a particular culture requires local knowledge and human review.

The point: A localized website should feel like it was designed for its audience, not simply translated for it.

8. Preserve the Browser's Native Capabilities

Modern frontend development often involves JavaScript frameworks, custom components, and complex application architectures.

Sometimes, developers forget that the browser already provides a lot of useful functionality.

A simple link can navigate between pages:

<a href="/articles">
  Read articles
</a>

A native form can submit information:

<form action="/search" method="get">
  <label for="search">Search articles</label>

  <input
    type="search"
    id="search"
    name="q"
  >

  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

Neither example requires JavaScript to provide its basic browser behavior.

You can add JavaScript later to improve the experience, but the essential functionality already exists.

This is closely related to progressive enhancement.

The idea is simple: start with meaningful HTML that provides the core experience, then add CSS and JavaScript to improve it.

For example, a navigation link should still be a useful link before any client-side routing enhancement is added.

Not every interface needs to be a fully custom JavaScript component.

Sometimes the native element is the better solution.

The PDF's discussion of smart reuse is relevant here. Originality doesn't require rebuilding everything from scratch. It often comes from combining existing tools and capabilities in a more appropriate way.

The point: Knowing when not to write additional code is also a development skill.

Reference: web.dev — Learn Forms

9. Create Something Original Without Ignoring Existing Standards

This is probably the most interesting part of the discussion.

What does originality actually mean in software development?

Does writing an entirely new HTML structure make a developer original? Does avoiding existing patterns automatically make a project better?

Not necessarily.

The PDF introduces an important distinction: originality is not simply creating something that has never existed before. It can come from the creator's distinctive contribution and the way existing knowledge is combined.

I think this idea applies directly to HTML development.

Consider the following three dimensions:

Product-focused originality

The structure and content should serve the specific product. A documentation website, an online store, and a portfolio do not need the same document structure.

Person-focused originality

The content, writing style, presentation, and decisions should reflect a meaningful identity rather than simply copying a generic template.

Social and strategic originality

The implementation should make sense for the intended audience, the team, and the goals of the project.

For example, using <details> and <summary> to create an FAQ section is not a completely new invention.

<section aria-labelledby="faq-heading">
  <h2 id="faq-heading">Frequently Asked Questions</h2>

  <details>
    <summary>What is semantic HTML?</summary>
    <p>
      Semantic HTML uses elements that describe
      the meaning and purpose of content.
    </p>
  </details>

  <details>
    <summary>Why should I use it?</summary>
    <p>
      It helps browsers, developers, and assistive
      technologies understand the document.
    </p>
  </details>
</section>

The originality is not in inventing a new element. It's in recognizing that a native HTML feature is the right solution for a particular problem.

A developer who understands HTML can combine existing elements, patterns, and ideas in ways that produce a more useful experience.

AI can suggest combinations, but choosing the right combination depends on understanding the product and its users.

The point: Originality doesn't mean avoiding existing solutions. It means knowing how to use them in a way that creates something valuable.

10. Take Responsibility for the Final Result

This is where technical knowledge, experience, and professional judgment come together.

AI can produce a complete HTML document, but that doesn't mean the document is ready for production.

Someone still needs to check whether:

  • The markup follows the HTML standard.
  • Interactive elements behave correctly.
  • The document has a logical structure.
  • Forms are usable and provide appropriate feedback.
  • Accessibility requirements have been considered.
  • The content and metadata are accurate.
  • The implementation fits the existing codebase.

And importantly, someone needs to take responsibility when something goes wrong.

A useful starting point is validating the generated markup with the Nu HTML Checker.

But passing validation doesn't guarantee a good user experience. You should also test the page using a keyboard, screen reader, different browsers, and realistic content.

There is another part of responsibility that often gets overlooked: working with other developers.

The PDF makes a valuable point about shared coding conventions. A developer's originality should not mean introducing a completely different style into every project.

Imagine joining an established codebase where every page follows consistent naming, indentation, component boundaries, and document conventions.

Adding your own personal style everywhere might feel creative, but it can make the code harder for the next developer to understand.

A professional developer knows when to follow an existing pattern and when there is a strong reason to improve it.

That decision often requires discussion, explanation, and collaboration.

The point: Generating code is an activity. Owning the quality and consequences of that code is a responsibility.

So, What Makes a Developer Valuable in the AI Era?

I don't think the answer is writing HTML faster than an AI model.

AI can generate basic markup, create forms, suggest semantic elements, and explain unfamiliar parts of the standard. It can save a considerable amount of time on repetitive work.

But speed alone doesn't define a good developer.

The more important skills are becoming increasingly clear:

  • Defining the right problem before implementation.
  • Understanding the technology beyond copying examples.
  • Combining existing solutions in useful ways.
  • Making thoughtful architectural and design decisions.
  • Communicating with teammates and understanding users.
  • Maintaining code that other people can work with.
  • Continuously learning and developing deeper expertise.

One idea from the PDF is especially relevant here: technical execution is becoming easier to automate, while the value of judgment, problem-solving, and meaningful contribution becomes more important.

That doesn't mean technical knowledge is becoming irrelevant. Quite the opposite.

The deeper your understanding of HTML, browser behavior, accessibility, and web standards, the better you can evaluate generated code and recognize when something is wrong.

AI can help you move faster, but understanding what deserves to be built is still a major part of the job.

title: Linux cloud server unreachable? A five-layer troubleshooting checklist
description:
A server that responds on localhost can still be unreachable from the internet. Before changing instance size, test each layer separately.

1. Confirm the application is listening

Run these commands on your own Linux server:

ss -lntp
curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8080

Replace 8080 with your application's port. A process bound only to 127.0.0.1 accepts local connections. When using Nginx as a reverse proxy, this is often intentional. Keep the backend private and expose the proxy's HTTP/HTTPS ports.

2. Check the host firewall and cloud security group

These are separate controls. Inspect the operating-system firewall and the inbound rules attached to the instance. Open only the intended public service ports. Restrict SSH to trusted source addresses where practical. Avoid opening every port to diagnose a single endpoint.

3. Test the reverse proxy

Check configuration syntax before reloading Nginx:

sudo nginx -t
curl -I http://127.0.0.1

If the backend responds but Nginx returns 502, inspect the upstream address, port, application status and proxy error log. If the wrong site appears, check the server_name and matching virtual host.

4. Verify DNS and HTTPS separately

An old A record or unexpected AAAA record may send visitors elsewhere. Compare the resolved addresses with the intended endpoint. A valid certificate must cover the requested hostname. Test from an external network as well as from the instance.

5. Record a reproducible result

Keep a small checklist with the hostname, expected port, HTTP status, test time and network used. Redact cookies, authorization headers and private IP details before sharing logs. This makes intermittent failures much easier to investigate.

About the author

Yunzhihui Cloud publishes cloud-server deployment and operations guides. Our cloud-server consulting page describes how to prepare configuration requirements. For service enquiries, contact Telegram @ak6793.

title: Key Considerations: Storing AI-Generated Images in Cloud Storage
description:
Short answer: for a property-management system that turns incoming receipts into AI-generated images, keep the original object in a private, retention-controlled cloud archive and keep processing state in a database. Put a signed access boundary between users and storage. If the original must be legally immutable, use an archive with native versioning or WORM controls; a convenient object API without those guarantees is not enough.

The decision is architectural, not a choice of SDK. A receipt image is both a working input and an audit record, and those roles have different failure boundaries. I would choose the split archive when deletion, retention, and reconciliation matter more than having one uniform storage surface. I would choose a single object service only when the organization can provide the missing immutability and concurrency controls outside that service.

Infrai is a deliberate candidate for the private processing side of this workflow: its public discovery surface describes schemas without a key, and one REST API can keep the adapter independent of a particular storage vendor. That convenience is useful only when the archive's stronger retention guarantees are supplied elsewhere.

No SDK is required.

For this workflow, Infrai's one key, one bill model can remove a small but recurring operating burden when the same account coordinates storage, database, and processing calls. The one REST API is plain HTTP, so the Go worker and separate review service do not need parallel provider-specific SDKs merely to cross the same integration boundary. The documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That is an integration benefit, not evidence that the storage service supplies legal retention.

What are the key considerations when storing AI-generated images in cloud storage?

The useful invariants are small enough to write down before comparing products. These are the key considerations, not a checklist to hand to a vendor and forget:

  1. The original bytes are retained separately from derived images and thumbnails.
  2. Every derived object points back to an immutable application record containing the receipt identifier, source digest, creation time, and retention decision.
  3. A user receives a time-limited signed URL, never a permanent public URL.
  4. A retry cannot create a second logical receipt or silently replace the original.
  5. Deletion is a recorded business event, not merely a successful object-delete response.

Those rules expose the central boundary. Object storage can hold bytes and enforce access; it does not automatically know whether a property manager is allowed to destroy the source receipt. The database, queue, and retention policy must carry that meaning.

A useful test is unpleasantly direct: after a worker crashes between writing a thumbnail and recording its metadata, can reconciliation find the orphan? If the answer depends on a human remembering which request ran, the system has already lost its audit trail.

The original is the boundary.

Keep that sentence close to the design record.

For example, imagine receipt 2026-000184 has an original, a normalized PNG, and a thumbnail. The worker writes the thumbnail, loses its database connection, and retries. A stable object key plus an idempotency key prevents a second logical write, but only the database can say whether the original is still under review, eligible for deletion, or attached to an export. That is why storing files and storing their meaning are separate operations, even when both happen in one cloud region.

Which architecture fits a retention-sensitive receipt workflow?

There are two defensible shapes. They solve different problems.

Architecture Invariants Failure boundary Best fit
Split archive and processing store Original is retained under a separate policy; database is the source of business state; derived objects are replaceable A storage write can succeed while the database transaction fails, so reconciliation is required Property-management workflows with review, deletion requests, and audit export
Single object service with application controls One private bucket holds originals and derivatives; database records object identity and retention state Missing native versioning, object lock, or conditional write must be supplied by an external archive or coordination layer Smaller workflows where operational simplicity matters and legal immutability is handled elsewhere

The first architecture is my default for receipts. It accepts one extra coordination problem in exchange for making the original's retention policy explicit. The second can be sound, but only if “single service” does not become a euphemism for “the bucket is the database.”

The distinction matters during deletion. A lifecycle rule can remove objects after a minimum age, but it cannot decide whether an unresolved dispute, tax review, or export request has priority. The shortest lifecycle period supported by this storage surface is one day, and multipart fragments do not receive an automatic cleanup rule, so incomplete-upload cleanup belongs in an operational job rather than a hopeful assumption.

How should the critical path preserve the original?

The write path should make identity and retries boring. Generate an application receipt ID first, derive stable object keys from it, and record the source digest before any worker is allowed to publish a derivative. The exact database transaction depends on the application, but the storage call should still be explicit about private access and should surface non-success responses.

Here is a minimal Go client shape for the object-write boundary. It is intentionally narrow: the receipt system owns retention metadata, while the object service owns the private bytes. The concrete route and payload schema should be generated from the current discovery response before production rollout.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func putReceipt(ctx context.Context, endpoint, bucket, key string, image []byte) error {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    url := endpoint + "/" + bucket + "/" + key
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPut, url, bytes.NewReader(image))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/png")
    req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "receipt-2026-000184-original")
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        return fmt.Errorf("object write failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, string(body))
    }
    return nil
}

The idempotency key is not a substitute for a database uniqueness constraint. It protects a retried logical write; the receipt ID and source digest establish what the write means. In a production worker I would also use bounded exponential backoff for transient failures and treat a 429 response as a scheduling signal, not an invitation to loop. A permanent URL is deliberately absent from this flow.

For reads, request a presigned URL only after the application has checked the viewer's role and the receipt's retention state. Do not forward the service Authorization header to that returned URL. A signed URL is an access handoff with an expiry, not a public ACL, and its lifetime should match the human action that needs it.

What do the real storage options preserve for you?

The comparison should start with failure semantics rather than a feature-count race. Amazon S3 provides presigned URLs and has mature controls for versioning and Object Lock; that makes it a strong candidate when regulatory retention is a first-class requirement. Its breadth also means that the team must understand which account, bucket, and object policy is actually enforcing each boundary.

Cloudflare R2 is attractive for teams that want an S3-compatible object surface and a simple placement in an edge-oriented stack. It is a reasonable processing store for private derivatives, but its fit for an audit archive still depends on the exact retention and replication controls selected for the account. Compatibility with an API shape is not proof of identical guarantees.

Azure Blob Storage is a natural choice for organizations already governed through Microsoft identity and policy tooling. Its blob versioning and immutable storage capabilities can support an archive design, while the application still has to model receipt ownership, legal holds, and reconciliation. Identity integration reduces one class of operational work; it does not remove the need for an audit record.

The fourth option is a unified REST abstraction such as Infrai. Its useful angle here is that the application contract can stay stable while the capability's underlying vendor changes, which keeps the receipt workflow from spreading provider-specific clients through every worker. The public discovery surface describes request and response schemas, and the platform exposes one key and one REST interface across backend capabilities. That supporting consistency matters when the same service also needs database, queue, or processing integrations.

I would recommend Infrai to a property-management team using it as the private processing and access layer, provided the actual legal archive remains a service with the required immutability guarantees. That recommendation is conditional: Infrai's storage surface does not provide public-read ACLs, object versioning, or Object Lock, and it does not expose an If-Match conditional write. It is therefore a poor fit for permanent public image hosting or for a financial-grade WORM archive by itself. Strict concurrent overwrite rules need coordination in a queue or database, and browser-direct uploads cannot rely on a self-configured CORS route.

This is why vendor substitution should happen behind the contract. The receipt service should expose storeOriginal, getSignedReceipt, and markRetentionDecision; only the adapter should know how a particular object API presigns or writes. The abstraction is valuable when it preserves that boundary. It becomes dangerous when it hides the missing guarantees.

The rejected shortcut: one bucket, one delete, one truth

The tempting design stores original receipts, thumbnails, OCR intermediates, and review exports under one prefix, then deletes by prefix when a retention timer fires. It is operationally neat. It is also the wrong default for an auditable workflow because an object listing is not a retention decision, and a failed delete can leave the database claiming something that the storage system does not reflect.

I would keep that shape for a low-risk image cache, a disposable preview pipeline, or a system where an authoritative archive already exists outside the bucket. I would not make it the source of truth for original receipts. The difference is not philosophical; it is the recovery path after a partial failure.

Reconciliation should be a normal process. Compare the database's expected object keys with prefix-filtered listings, inspect object metadata where available, and route unknown or missing records to review. This storage surface cannot perform server-side metadata search, so the database must remain the index for receipt number, property, retention class, and deletion authorization.

One more boundary deserves emphasis: a trial credit cannot pay for persistent storage writes. A receipt archive must use an account and billing path that permits those writes before the first production document is accepted. That is a deployment prerequisite, not an optimization.

Decision

Use the split architecture when original receipts need defensible retention, independent deletion approval, and an audit trail that survives worker retries. Keep private originals in a service with native archival guarantees, keep derived images replaceable, and put application state in a database that can reconcile every boundary crossing.

Use a single private object service when the archive guarantee is supplied elsewhere and the workflow primarily needs secure access, scaling, and straightforward backend integration. Infrai is a deliberate option in that second role: its stable REST contract and discovery surface can keep provider choice behind an adapter, while its storage limitations remain visible in the design record.

That is the useful decision rule. Optimize the bytes after you have decided who is allowed to delete them. If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage capability schema at Infrai's discovery endpoint and verify the current request and response contract before wiring the adapter.

References

  • AWS S3 presigned URLs
  • Amazon S3 Object Lock
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility
  • Azure Blob immutable storage
  • Infrai storage discovery

title: Backend Security Best Practices for Mobile Apps (With Code You Can Actually Use)
description:
Mobile developers spend a lot of time on the app and a lot less on the server behind it. That's understandable: the app is what users see, and the backend is "just an API."

But here's the uncomfortable truth: your mobile app is not a security boundary. Anyone can download it, decompile it, intercept its traffic, and call your API directly with curl. Whatever your app "prevents" in the UI, an attacker can simply skip.

So the real security of a mobile product lives in the backend. This article walks through the practices that matter most, with code examples in Node.js/TypeScript (Express). The principles apply to any language or framework.

The mindset: assume the client is hostile

Before any code, adopt this rule:

Never trust anything that comes from the client: not the request body, not the headers, not the "user ID" field, not the app version, not "this button is hidden for free users."

Everything below follows from it. If a check only exists in the app, it doesn't exist.

Most real-world API breaches don't come from exotic cryptography attacks. They come from boring mistakes: missing authorization checks, leaked secrets, no rate limiting, and over-trusting input. The OWASP API Security Top 10 is a good checklist, and the top items are consistently authorization failures and broken authentication.

  1. Always use TLS, and know what it does and doesn't give you

HTTPS is non-negotiable. It protects data in transit from passive eavesdropping and tampering on public Wi-Fi and hostile networks.

Practical rules:

Enforce HTTPS everywhere and redirect or reject plain HTTP.
Use a modern TLS configuration from your host or load balancer rather than hand-rolling one.
Send an HSTS header so clients don't downgrade.
ts
import express from 'express';
import helmet from 'helmet';

const app = express();

// Helmet sets several protective headers, including HSTS
app.use(helmet());
app.disable('x-powered-by');

About certificate pinning: it can protect against some man-in-the-middle scenarios, but it's a trade-off. If you pin incorrectly or rotate certificates carelessly, you can lock out your own users with a broken app until they update. If you pin, pin to something you can rotate safely, include backup pins, and have a kill-switch plan. Also know that a determined attacker with a rooted device can often bypass pinning, so treat it as defense-in-depth, not a guarantee.

  1. Authentication: don't invent your own

If you can, use a proven identity provider (Auth0, Firebase Auth, AWS Cognito, Keycloak, or your platform's equivalent) instead of building password handling yourself. It's not that you can't build it. It's that the edge cases (account recovery, brute force, MFA, session revocation) are where homemade systems fail.

If you do handle passwords yourself, use a slow, memory-hard password hashing algorithm such as Argon2id (or bcrypt/scrypt). Never store plain text, and never use fast hashes like plain SHA-256 or MD5 for passwords.

ts
import argon2 from 'argon2';

export async function hashPassword(password: string): Promise {
return argon2.hash(password, { type: argon2.argon2id });
}

export async function verifyPassword(hash: string, password: string): Promise {
return argon2.verify(hash, password);
}

Extra habits that pay off:

Return the same generic error for "wrong email" and "wrong password" so you don't reveal which accounts exist.
Support MFA for sensitive apps (finance, health, admin tools).
Check new passwords against known-breached password lists if you can.
Make login, signup, and password reset the most rate-limited endpoints in your API.

  1. Tokens: short-lived access, rotating refresh

Mobile apps typically use a short-lived access token plus a longer-lived refresh token. Done right, this limits the damage if a token leaks.

Access tokens

Keep them short-lived (minutes, not days). If you use JWTs, always specify the allowed algorithm when verifying, and never accept alg: none or let the token choose its own algorithm.

ts
import jwt from 'jsonwebtoken';

const ACCESS_SECRET = process.env.JWT_ACCESS_SECRET!; // from a secrets manager, not source code

export function signAccessToken(userId: string) {
return jwt.sign({ sub: userId }, ACCESS_SECRET, {
algorithm: 'HS256',
expiresIn: '15m',
issuer: 'api.example.com',
audience: 'mobile-app',
});
}

export function verifyAccessToken(token: string) {
return jwt.verify(token, ACCESS_SECRET, {
algorithms: ['HS256'], // pin the algorithm
issuer: 'api.example.com',
audience: 'mobile-app',
});
}
Refresh token rotation

Refresh tokens are powerful, so treat them like passwords:

Generate them with a cryptographically secure random generator.
Store only a hash of the token on the server.
Rotate on every use: issue a new refresh token and invalidate the old one.
If an old token is ever reused, assume theft and revoke the whole session family.
ts
import crypto from 'crypto';

function newRefreshToken() {
return crypto.randomBytes(48).toString('base64url');
}

function hashToken(token: string) {
return crypto.createHash('sha256').update(token).digest('hex');
}

export async function rotateRefreshToken(oldToken: string) {
const oldHash = hashToken(oldToken);
const record = await db.refreshTokens.findByHash(oldHash);

if (!record) throw new Error('invalid_token');

if (record.usedAt) {
// Token reuse detected: someone may have stolen it.
await db.refreshTokens.revokeFamily(record.familyId);
throw new Error('token_reuse_detected');
}

await db.refreshTokens.markUsed(record.id);

const fresh = newRefreshToken();
await db.refreshTokens.create({
userId: record.userId,
familyId: record.familyId,
tokenHash: hashToken(fresh),
expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000),
});

return { accessToken: signAccessToken(record.userId), refreshToken: fresh };
}

(The db object here is pseudocode for your data layer.)

On the device

Where the app stores tokens matters too. Use the platform's secure storage rather than plain preferences or local files:

iOS: Keychain
Android: EncryptedSharedPreferences or the Android Keystore
Flutter and React Native have wrappers around these (for example flutter_secure_storage or Keychain/Keystore-backed libraries for React Native).

And give users a way to log out everywhere, which means server-side revocation, not just deleting the token locally.

  1. Authorization: the bug that causes the most breaches

Authentication answers "who are you?" Authorization answers "are you allowed to do this, to this object?" The second question is the one teams forget.

The classic bug is BOLA / IDOR (Broken Object Level Authorization): the API trusts an ID from the request and returns whatever it points to.

Vulnerable:

ts
// Any logged-in user can read ANY order by guessing IDs
app.get('/orders/:id', requireAuth, async (req, res) => {
const order = await pool.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]);
res.json(order.rows[0]);
});

Fixed: always scope the query to the authenticated user (or check ownership explicitly):

ts
app.get('/orders/:id', requireAuth, async (req, res) => {
const result = await pool.query(
'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2',
[req.params.id, req.user.id]
);

if (result.rowCount === 0) {
// Same response whether it doesn't exist or isn't yours
return res.status(404).json({ error: 'not_found' });
}

res.json(result.rows[0]);
});

Rules to live by:

Derive identity from the token, never from the request body. If your signup or update endpoint accepts userId or role in JSON, an attacker will set it.
Check authorization on every endpoint and every object, not just at login.
Watch for mass assignment: don't blindly spread request bodies into database updates.
Use random, non-guessable IDs (UUIDs) as defense-in-depth, but never as a replacement for real checks.
Keep admin and privileged functions on separately protected routes and test them explicitly.
ts
// Don't do this: attacker can send { "role": "admin" }
await db.users.update(req.user.id, req.body);

// Do this: allow-list the fields users may change
const { displayName, avatarUrl } = req.body;
await db.users.update(req.user.id, { displayName, avatarUrl });

  1. Validate input, and validate it on the server

Client-side validation is for user experience. Server-side validation is for security. Use a schema library so validation is consistent and hard to forget.

ts
import { z } from 'zod';

const SignupSchema = z.object({
email: z.string().email().max(254),
password: z.string().min(12).max(128),
displayName: z.string().min(1).max(60),
});

app.post('/signup', async (req, res) => {
const parsed = SignupSchema.safeParse(req.body);

if (!parsed.success) {
return res.status(400).json({ error: 'invalid_input' });
}

// parsed.data is now typed and constrained
// ...create the user
});

And for databases, always use parameterized queries. Never build SQL by concatenating strings.

ts
// Vulnerable to SQL injection
const sql = SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}';

// Safe: parameterized
await pool.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', [email]);

The same principle applies to NoSQL queries, shell commands, file paths, and any template or interpreter. If untrusted input reaches an interpreter as code, you have an injection bug.

Other input-related habits:

Set maximum body sizes and timeouts so one request can't exhaust your server.
Validate file uploads: type, size, and content, and store them outside the web root or in object storage with restricted access. Never trust the filename or the client-reported MIME type.
Whitelist URLs if your server fetches user-supplied links, to avoid SSRF (server-side request forgery) against your internal network or cloud metadata endpoints.

  1. Rate limiting and abuse protection

Without limits, your API is a free brute-force and scraping service.

ts
import rateLimit from 'express-rate-limit';

// General API limit
const apiLimiter = rateLimit({
windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,
limit: 300,
standardHeaders: 'draft-7',
legacyHeaders: false,
});

// Much stricter for sensitive endpoints
const authLimiter = rateLimit({
windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000,
limit: 10,
standardHeaders: 'draft-7',
legacyHeaders: false,
});

app.use('/api', apiLimiter);
app.use('/api/login', authLimiter);
app.use('/api/password-reset', authLimiter);

Notes from the field:

Limit by user and IP, and use a shared store (like Redis) if you run multiple server instances. In-memory counters don't work across instances.
Add progressive delays or temporary lockouts after repeated failed logins, but be careful that lockouts can't be weaponized to lock out real users.
Put a WAF or CDN in front of the API for volumetric abuse.
For high-value actions (signup, checkout, SMS/OTP sending), consider bot protection or CAPTCHA, and watch your SMS costs: OTP endpoints without limits are a known way to run up bills.

  1. Secrets: nothing sensitive in the app, nothing sensitive in git

This one is simple and violated constantly.

Anything you ship inside the mobile app can be extracted. That includes API keys, "obfuscated" strings, and hardcoded credentials. Obfuscation slows attackers down; it doesn't stop them.

So:

Don't put private keys, database credentials, or third-party secret keys in the app. Have the app call your backend, and let the backend call the third party.
Some keys are designed to be public (for example, many map or analytics keys). For those, restrict them by app identifier, bundle ID, and API scope in the provider console.
Keep server secrets in environment variables loaded from a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Vault, or your host's equivalent), not committed to the repository.
Add secret scanning to your repo and CI so accidental commits get caught. If a secret ever lands in git history, rotate it: deleting the commit isn't enough.
ts
// Fail fast at startup if a required secret is missing
function requireEnv(name: string): string {
const value = process.env[name];
if (!value) throw new Error(Missing required env var: ${name});
return value;
}

const JWT_ACCESS_SECRET = requireEnv('JWT_ACCESS_SECRET');

  1. Verify webhooks and third-party callbacks

Payment providers, subscription systems, and messaging services call your server with webhooks. If you don't verify them, anyone can POST a fake "payment succeeded" event.

Verify the provider's signature using the raw request body and a constant-time comparison:

ts
import crypto from 'crypto';

function verifySignature(rawBody: Buffer, signatureHeader: string, secret: string) {
const expected = crypto
.createHmac('sha256', secret)
.update(rawBody)
.digest('hex');

const a = Buffer.from(expected);
const b = Buffer.from(signatureHeader);

// timingSafeEqual requires equal lengths
return a.length === b.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b);
}

(Use your provider's official SDK helper if it has one. Signature formats differ between providers, and the SDK handles details like timestamps and replay protection.)

The same logic applies to in-app purchases and subscriptions: validate receipts and entitlements on the server with the store's APIs. If the app alone decides "this user is premium," a modified client can decide that too.

  1. Don't leak information in errors or logs

Two opposite mistakes:

Too verbose errors that return stack traces, SQL errors, or internal paths to the client.
Too little logging, so when something goes wrong, you can't tell what happened.

Return generic errors to clients and keep the details in server logs:

ts
app.use((err: Error, req: express.Request, res: express.Response, _next: express.NextFunction) => {
// Detailed log for you (with a request ID for correlation)
logger.error({ err, requestId: req.id, path: req.path });

// Generic message for the client
res.status(500).json({ error: 'internal_error', requestId: req.id });
});

Logging guidelines:

Never log passwords, full tokens, card numbers, or sensitive personal data.
Log security-relevant events: failed logins, permission denials, token reuse, password changes, admin actions.
Set up alerts on suspicious patterns (spikes in 401/403, many failed logins from one source).
Know your data retention and privacy obligations (for example GDPR/CCPA) before deciding what to store and for how long.

  1. Protect the supply chain and the infrastructure

Your code might be perfect while a dependency or a misconfigured cloud bucket is not.

Dependencies: run automated audits (npm audit, Dependabot/Renovate, or similar) and update regularly. Pin versions with a lockfile and review what you add.
Least privilege: the database user your API uses shouldn't be a superuser. Cloud roles should have only the permissions they need.
Network: keep databases in private networks, not exposed to the public internet.
Storage: check that cloud buckets are private by default. Public buckets with user data are a repeat headline.
Backups: encrypt them, test restores, and restrict who can access them.
Environments: keep dev, staging, and production separate, with separate credentials.
CI/CD: protect your pipeline credentials. A compromised pipeline can ship malicious code under your name.

  1. Device and app attestation (helpful, not magic)

You can't fully verify that a request comes from your genuine, unmodified app. But platform attestation services let your backend ask for a signal that raises the bar:

Android: Play Integrity API
iOS: App Attest / DeviceCheck

These can help reduce automated abuse, fake clients, and emulator farms, particularly for signups, promotions, and payments. Use them as one signal among several, combined with rate limiting, anomaly detection, and server-side rules. Don't rely on them as the only gate.

A quick API security checklist

Copy this into your project:

Transport & headers

HTTPS enforced, HSTS enabled
Security headers set (e.g., via Helmet or your gateway)

Authentication

Passwords hashed with Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt (or delegated to an identity provider)
Short-lived access tokens, rotating refresh tokens stored hashed
JWT algorithm pinned; issuer/audience checked
Server-side logout and session revocation

Authorization

Every endpoint checks the user's permission for the specific object
Identity taken from the token, never the request body
Field allow-lists for updates (no mass assignment)

Input & data

Schema validation on all inputs
Parameterized queries only
File upload validation and safe storage
SSRF protections on any server-side URL fetching

Abuse & monitoring

Rate limits, with stricter ones on auth and OTP endpoints
Security event logging and alerting
No sensitive data in logs or error responses

Secrets & infrastructure

No private secrets in the app or in git; secret scanning on
Webhooks verified; purchases validated server-side
Dependencies audited; least-privilege roles; private databases and buckets
Final thoughts

You don't need to do everything on day one. If you're short on time, focus on the highest-impact items first:

Authorization on every object (stops the most common real-world data leaks)
No secrets in the app or repo
Server-side validation and parameterized queries
Rate limiting on login and sensitive endpoints
Short-lived tokens with proper refresh handling

Security is not a feature you finish. It's a habit: review it when you add endpoints, test it before release, and revisit it as your app grows. And remember, the app is just a client. The backend is where your users' trust is actually kept.

If you found this useful, I'd love to hear which of these you've seen go wrong in the wild. Share your story in the comments.

This article was originally published on the Koderspedia blog. Koderspedia builds mobile apps, games, and web products for startups and enterprises. Learn more at koderspedia.com.
