title: Failed jobs in Node.js: dead-letter handling with BullMQ
description:
Part 7 of 10: Reliable background jobs in Node.js, from zero.

By Sandro Dezerio, senior full-stack engineer.

The sign-up example is the one from Part 1, Part 2, Part 3, Part 4, Part 5, and Part 6. The numbers in this post come from running the code in it against a real Redis, with a fake email provider. Tested with Node 22, BullMQ 6.5.3, ioredis 6.0.0, and Redis 7.

Part 6 left a loose end. When a job fails on its last attempt, it does not disappear. It stays in the failed set, the worker moves on to the next job, and nobody is told. The first alarm is a customer who never got a welcome email. This post gives failed jobs a place to go, separates the failures that a retry can fix from the ones it cannot, and raises an alert when jobs pile up, before a customer notices.

Where a failed job goes

Imagine a store with 20 new sign-ups. Two people typed their address wrong, with a comma instead of a dot, and the email provider rejects those addresses for good. Three more sign-ups hit a provider outage that lasts longer than the retries do. The queue is the one from Part 6: three attempts per job, exponential backoff with jitter.

Run that, and 15 users get their email. The other five jobs end up in the failed set, and nothing in the code looks at it. It is the first row of the results further down.

A failed job is not lost. BullMQ keeps it in Redis with the error message in failedReason, the stack trace in stacktrace, and the number of tries in attemptsMade, and queue.getFailed() returns them. But nobody reads the set unless they think to look, and nothing removes its jobs unless you ask. Part 6 set removeOnComplete and left failed jobs alone, so they only pile up. A job that always fails stays there after its third attempt, as Part 6 showed.

Two kinds of failure

The five failed jobs are not the same problem. The provider answers the two typos with a 400: this address will never work. It answers the outage with a 503: try again later. Retries help with the second kind and waste time on the first.

The fake provider for this post makes the difference visible:

import { sendEmail } from "./emails.ts";
import type { Signup } from "./signup-queue.ts";

/** The provider says this address can never work (HTTP 400). Trying again cannot help. */
export class RejectedAddressError extends Error {}

/** A fake email provider that rejects bad addresses and can be down for some users. */
export class FakeProvider {
  calls = 0; // every request that reached the provider, whether it worked or not
  down = new Set<string>(); // users whose requests get a 503 until recover() is called

  constructor(private run: string) {}

  async send(signup: Signup): Promise<void> {
    this.calls++;
    if (!/^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$/.test(signup.email)) throw new RejectedAddressError(`400 invalid address: ${signup.email}`);
    if (this.down.has(signup.userId)) throw new Error("503 service unavailable");
    await sendEmail(this.run, signup.userId, `welcome-email:${signup.userId}`); // the key from Part 5
  }

  recover(): void {
    this.down.clear();
  }
}

FakeProvider counts every request that reaches it, so the demo can show how many were wasted. It rejects an address that does not look like an address with RejectedAddressError, and it answers 503 service unavailable for the users in down until recover() is called. It sends the idempotency key from Part 5 with every email, because replaying a job later is exactly the case where a job can run twice.

BullMQ has a way to say "do not retry this". If the handler throws an UnrecoverableError, the documentation describes the job as moved to failed without using the remaining attempts. A test I wrote for this post confirms it: with attempts: 3, a permanent error is tried once and a temporary error is tried three times. The function that turns one into the other is classify, in the next file.

Run the sign-ups again with classify in the handler. The same 15 users get their email and the same five jobs fail, but the provider receives 26 requests, not 30. The four requests saved are the two extra attempts on each of the two bad addresses. The second row below shows it.

Park what gave up

Now the failed jobs need somewhere to go. The pattern has a name: a dead-letter queue, a second queue that no worker reads, where jobs wait for a person or a script. BullMQ 6.5.3 has no such feature. I looked for a dead-letter option or class in the installed package, and there is none, so you build it from the pieces BullMQ gives you:

import { Queue, UnrecoverableError, type Worker } from "bullmq";
import { connection, jobIdFor, type Signup } from "./signup-queue.ts";
import { RejectedAddressError } from "./provider.ts";

/** A sign-up that ran out of attempts, with what we need to understand and replay it. */
export type DeadSignup = Signup & { reason: string; attempts: number; failedAt: number; jobId: string };

/** The queue for jobs that gave up. No worker reads it. */
export const createDeadQueue = (name: string) => new Queue<DeadSignup>(`${name}-dead`, { connection });

/** Adding a sign-up: the job ID from Part 6, and a limit on how many failed jobs Redis keeps. */
export const signupJobOptions = (signup: Signup) => ({ jobId: jobIdFor(signup), removeOnFail: { count: 100 } });

/** A permanent error must not be retried. BullMQ skips the remaining attempts for an UnrecoverableError. */
export function classify(error: unknown): Error {
  return error instanceof RejectedAddressError ? new UnrecoverableError(error.message) : (error as Error);
}

/** When a job fails for the last time, copy it to the dead queue. */
export function parkFailedJobs(worker: Worker<Signup>, dead: Queue<DeadSignup>): void {
  worker.on("failed", async (job, error) => {
    if (!job) return;
    const lastAttempt = error instanceof UnrecoverableError || job.attemptsMade >= (job.opts.attempts ?? 1);
    if (!lastAttempt) return; // BullMQ will try this job again
    try {
      const entry: DeadSignup = { ...job.data, reason: error.message, attempts: job.attemptsMade, failedAt: Date.now(), jobId: job.id! };
      await dead.add("welcome-email", entry, { jobId: `dead-${job.id}` });
    } catch (parkError) {
      console.error("could not park", job.id, parkError); // the job is still in the failed set
    }
  });
}

/** Put parked sign-ups back in the main queue. Call it after the cause is fixed. */
export async function replay(dead: Queue<DeadSignup>, queue: Queue<Signup>, only = (entry: DeadSignup) => true): Promise<number> {
  const parked = (await dead.getJobs(["waiting"])).filter((entry) => only(entry.data));
  for (const entry of parked) {
    const { reason, attempts, failedAt, jobId, ...signup } = entry.data;
    await (await queue.getJob(jobId))?.remove(); // a failed job keeps its ID, and an ID in use is ignored
    await queue.add("welcome-email", signup, signupJobOptions(signup));
    await entry.remove();
  }
  return parked.length;
}

Here is what each part does:

  • createDeadQueue makes a queue next to the main one. It is named signups-dead for a main queue called signups. No worker reads it, so a job added to it just waits.
  • signupJobOptions limits the failed set. removeOnFail: { count: 100 } keeps the last 100 failed jobs in the main queue (see auto-removal in the documentation). The dead queue is now the record of what gave up, so the failed set can be bounded.
  • classify separates the two kinds. A rejected address becomes an UnrecoverableError. Everything else passes through unchanged and is retried.
  • parkFailedJobs copies a job when it fails for the last time. The worker's failed event fires on every failed attempt, not only the last one. The function acts only when the error is an UnrecoverableError or when attemptsMade has reached the job's attempts. The entry keeps the sign-up, the reason, the number of attempts, the time, and the ID of the original job.
  • The ID dead-<job id> is the same every time, so parking the same job twice leaves one entry, the same idea as the job IDs in Part 6.

Run it, and the dead queue holds the five jobs. The third row of the results shows it, with the failed set still at five and the provider still at 26 requests.

Failed set Dead queue
Who writes it BullMQ Our code, on the failed event
How long jobs stay Until removeOnFail removes them Until someone replays or removes them
What it keeps The job, failedReason, stacktrace, attemptsMade The sign-up, the reason, the attempts, the time, the original job ID
If the copy fails Not affected The entry is missing (see below)

Find out before a customer does

A queue that holds failed jobs and tells nobody is only a tidier version of the same problem. The simplest check looks at two numbers:

import type { Queue } from "bullmq";
import type { DeadSignup } from "./dead-letter.ts";

export type Limits = { maxDepth: number; maxAgeMs: number };

/** Look at the dead queue. Every problem found is passed to alert() and returned. */
export async function checkDeadLetters(
  dead: Queue<DeadSignup>,
  limits: Limits,
  alert: (message: string) => void,
  now = Date.now(),
): Promise<string[]> {
  const parked = await dead.getJobs(["waiting"]);
  const problems: string[] = [];
  if (parked.length > limits.maxDepth) problems.push(`${parked.length} parked jobs (limit ${limits.maxDepth})`);
  if (parked.length > 0) {
    const ageMs = now - Math.min(...parked.map((job) => job.data.failedAt));
    if (ageMs > limits.maxAgeMs) problems.push(`the oldest parked job is ${Math.round(ageMs / 1000)} s old (limit ${limits.maxAgeMs / 1000} s)`);
  }
  for (const problem of problems) alert(problem);
  return problems;
}

checkDeadLetters returns the problems it found and passes each one to alert. In the demo, alert prints a line. In your system, it would send a message to the channel your team reads. Delivery depends on the tools you use, so it is not built here.

The two limits catch different things:

  • Depth catches a burst. In the demo, five parked jobs against a limit of three print ALERT 5 parked jobs (limit 3).
  • Age catches the slow leak. One or two jobs never cross a depth limit, and they can sit for days. A test I wrote for this post leaves one parked job and runs the check as if two minutes had passed. The alert says the oldest job is about 120 seconds old, against a limit of 60.

Something has to run the check on a schedule. Part 9 covers repeating jobs, and a cron entry that calls the function works until then.

Replay after the fix

Once the cause is fixed, the parked jobs go back to the main queue. replay at the end of the same file, it does it in four steps for each entry: find the original job, remove it, add the sign-up again, and remove the dead entry.

The first two steps are there for a reason I found by testing. A failed job keeps its ID, and BullMQ ignores a job added with an ID that is already in use. A test I wrote for this post shows it: add the same sign-up again after it failed, and the queue still has zero waiting jobs and one failed job. So replay removes the failed job first. Part 6 said a removed job's ID can be used again, and this is that rule in use.

replay takes an optional filter, and the demo uses it. The outage is over, so the three jobs that failed with a 503 are worth replaying. The two typos are not: the address is wrong, and sending it again fails again. The demo replays everything except the entries whose reason starts with 400. The fourth row shows the result: 18 users emailed, and two entries left in the dead queue for a person to fix. Those two are what the age alert is for.

Replaying is safe because of Part 5. A test I wrote for this post sends the email, loses the reply on every attempt, parks the job, and replays it. The provider received the same key on every attempt and again on the replay, and sent one email.

The four rows

Here are the runs side by side, with the same 20 sign-ups each time: two bad addresses, and the provider down for three users until it recovers.

Strategy Emailed In failed set In dead queue Provider requests
Part 6 as is 15 5 0 30
Permanent errors not retried 15 5 0 26
Failed jobs parked 15 5 5 26
After replay 18 2 2 29

The last row has 29 requests: the 26 from before plus one for each of the three replayed jobs. The two jobs that stay in the dead queue are the typos, and they are waiting for a person.

What this does not fix

The copy can be lost. parkFailedJobs runs in the worker process. If the process dies between the failure and the copy, nothing is parked. The job is still in the failed set, at least until removeOnFail trims it. I did not test that crash.

Jobs that fail by stalling. Part 6 showed that a job whose worker dies is run again, and that one that stalls too many times is moved to the failed set. I did not test whether parkFailedJobs sees that case.

The alert is a function. Delivering it is up to you, and so is running the check on a schedule.

Redis is still one container. The dead queue lives in the same Redis as the main queue, with the same caveats as Part 6.

Seeing what happened. A parked entry says what failed and how many times. It does not say which worker handled it or what else was going on. Part 8 adds structured logs and correlation IDs for that.

Takeaways

  1. A job that fails for the last time stays in BullMQ's failed set, and nobody is told. BullMQ 6.5.3 has no dead-letter queue, so you build one from the failed event and a second queue.
  2. Retry only what a retry can fix. An UnrecoverableError skips the remaining attempts and saved 4 of 30 requests here.
  3. A dead-letter queue is only useful if something looks at it. Check depth for bursts and age for the slow leak, and replay once the cause is fixed.

Try it

This is a teaching version. A more complete implementation comes later in the series. You need Node 22, pnpm, and Docker. Use the folder from Part 6. If you do not have it, create a folder and run these commands inside it:

pnpm init
pnpm add bullmq ioredis
pnpm add -D tsx

Open the package.json that pnpm init created and add the line "type": "module", next to "name". Keep docker-compose.yml, signup-queue.ts, and emails.ts from Part 6 in the folder, and save provider.ts, dead-letter.ts, and monitor.ts from above next to them. Then save demo.ts, which runs the same 20 sign-ups three ways:

import { Worker } from "bullmq";
import { connection, createSignupQueue, makeSignups } from "./signup-queue.ts";
import { closeEmails, emailsPerUser, forgetEmails } from "./emails.ts";
import { FakeProvider } from "./provider.ts";
import { classify, createDeadQueue, parkFailedJobs, replay, signupJobOptions } from "./dead-letter.ts";
import { checkDeadLetters } from "./monitor.ts";

const SIGNUPS = 20;
const BAD_ADDRESSES = ["user_4", "user_9"]; // typos the provider rejects for good
const OUTAGE = ["user_12", "user_13", "user_14"]; // the provider is down for these until it recovers

const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

/** 20 sign-ups, two of them with a typo in the address. */
function signups() {
  return makeSignups(SIGNUPS).map((s) => (BAD_ADDRESSES.includes(s.userId) ? { ...s, email: s.email.replace(".com", ",com") } : s));
}

async function runScenario(run: string, mode: "plain" | "unrecoverable" | "parked") {
  const queue = createSignupQueue(run);
  const dead = createDeadQueue(run);
  await queue.obliterate({ force: true });
  await dead.obliterate({ force: true });
  await forgetEmails(run);

  const provider = new FakeProvider(run);
  provider.down = new Set(OUTAGE);
  const worker = new Worker(
    run,
    async (job) => {
      try {
        await provider.send(job.data);
      } catch (error) {
        throw mode === "plain" ? error : classify(error);
      }
    },
    { connection },
  );
  worker.on("error", (error) => console.error(error));
  if (mode === "parked") parkFailedJobs(worker, dead);

  for (const signup of signups()) await queue.add("welcome-email", signup, signupJobOptions(signup));

  /** Wait until nothing is waiting, running or delayed, and every failed job is parked (in parked mode). */
  const settle = async () => {
    for (;;) {
      const { waiting, active, delayed, failed } = await queue.getJobCounts("waiting", "active", "delayed", "failed");
      const parked = (await dead.getJobCounts("waiting")).waiting;
      if (waiting + active + delayed === 0 && (mode !== "parked" || parked === failed)) return;
      await sleep(100);
    }
  };
  const row = async (strategy: string) => ({
    strategy,
    emailed: Object.keys(await emailsPerUser(run)).length,
    "in failed set": (await queue.getJobCounts("failed")).failed,
    "in dead queue": (await dead.getJobCounts("waiting")).waiting,
    "provider requests": provider.calls,
  });

  await settle();
  const rows = [await row({ plain: "Part 6 as is", unrecoverable: "permanent errors not retried", parked: "failed jobs parked" }[mode])];

  if (mode === "parked") {
    console.log("Alerts from checkDeadLetters:");
    await checkDeadLetters(dead, { maxDepth: 3, maxAgeMs: 60_000 }, (message) => console.log(`  ALERT ${message}`));
    provider.recover(); // the cause is fixed
    await replay(dead, queue, (entry) => !entry.reason.startsWith("400")); // a bad address needs a person
    await settle();
    rows.push(await row("after replay"));
  }

  await worker.close();
  await queue.obliterate({ force: true });
  await dead.obliterate({ force: true });
  await forgetEmails(run);
  await queue.close();
  await dead.close();
  return rows;
}

const rows = [
  ...(await runScenario("signups-plain", "plain")),
  ...(await runScenario("signups-unrecoverable", "unrecoverable")),
  ...(await runScenario("signups-parked", "parked")),
];
console.log(`${SIGNUPS} sign-ups: ${BAD_ADDRESSES.length} with a bad address, and the provider down for ${OUTAGE.length}.`);
console.table(rows);
await closeEmails();

Start Redis and run it:

docker compose up -d
pnpm exec tsx demo.ts

It takes a few seconds and prints:

Alerts from checkDeadLetters:
  ALERT 5 parked jobs (limit 3)
20 sign-ups: 2 with a bad address, and the provider down for 3.
┌─────────┬────────────────────────────────┬─────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┬───────────────────┐
│ (index) │ strategy                       │ emailed │ in failed set │ in dead queue │ provider requests │
├─────────┼────────────────────────────────┼─────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────────┤
│ 0       │ 'Part 6 as is'                 │ 15      │ 5             │ 0             │ 30                │
│ 1       │ 'permanent errors not retried' │ 15      │ 5             │ 0             │ 26                │
│ 2       │ 'failed jobs parked'           │ 15      │ 5             │ 5             │ 26                │
│ 3       │ 'after replay'                 │ 18      │ 2             │ 2             │ 29                │
└─────────┴────────────────────────────────┴─────────┴───────────────┴───────────────┴───────────────────┘

Change BAD_ADDRESSES, OUTAGE, or the limits in demo.ts and see which numbers change. When you are done, docker compose down stops Redis.

Previous: Jobs that survive a crash: Node.js and BullMQ (Part 6).

Next: Part 8 (coming soon) looks at seeing what happened: structured logs and an ID that follows a sign-up from the request to the job.

title: Rustidian: checking for another writer before saving a note
description:
Rustidian is a native notes app for Markdown files that I am building in Rust. This post shows how it saves a note without overwriting what another editor wrote.

Rustidian keeps notes as ordinary files. That means a second editor can write the same note while I have unsaved changes. A temporary file avoids a partial write, but the save must also check whether the text it replaces has changed.

This is a reading of the save path in the published 0.1.6 source. Here is the mechanism and its limit.

Remember what the edit started from

A pending save holds the edited text and the original text it expects to replace. Before writing, I read the note from disk and compare it with that original. This excerpt is from PendingSave::write:

let current = fs::read_to_string(&self.absolute).map_err(|e| {
    format!("Note was removed or cannot be read. Your changes are still open: {e}")
})?;
if current != self.original {
    return Err("This note changed outside Rustidian. Save your edits to a new note, or keep them here while reviewing the disk version. Nothing was overwritten.".into());
}

If the disk text differs, the save returns an error. The app keeps the edited document open. I can review the disk version and preserve my edits separately.

Prepare the replacement beside the note

If the first comparison passes, prepare_file creates a temporary file in the note's directory. It writes the edited bytes, copies the note's permissions and calls sync_all on the temporary file.

Before replacing the note, the save reads the disk text again. This catches a change that arrived while the temporary file was being written. A mismatch returns an error; a match lets the temporary file replace the note.

The two checks serve different moments: before preparing the write, and after preparing it. The temporary file serves a different purpose: the replacement uses a prepared file rather than writing the new text directly over the old one.

The remaining race

There is still a gap between the second comparison and replacement. Another writer could change the file in that gap. These checks do not establish exclusive ownership of the file, and I would not treat this as a guarantee for simultaneous writers.

The distinction matters when reviewing a save routine: checking for a conflict and replacing a file atomically solve different parts of the problem. This implementation does both, with a remaining race between them.

Read it or try the released app

The tagged save code contains the comparisons and replacement. The app's save handling shows how the result reaches the open document.

For Linux x86_64 with glibc 2.39 or newer (Ubuntu 24.04 or newer), download the Debian package and checksums, then use the README's commands:

sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
sudo apt install ./rustidian-linux-amd64.deb
rustidian

Try a copy of your notes first. The tagged README has the setup instructions and current feature limits.

title: CRM segmentini Custom Audience'a senkronlamak: Normalizasyon, hash'leme, fark senkronu ve rıza geri çekme
description:
Reklam tarafında "Custom Audience" ya da Google'daki karşılığıyla "Customer Match" denince çoğu ekibin aklına tek bir hareket gelir: CRM'den bir CSV dışa aktarmak, reklam paneline yüklemek ve kampanyayı başlatmak. İlk hafta işe yarar. Üçüncü ayda ise liste eskimiştir; satın almış müşteriler hâlâ "ilk konutunuzu bulun" reklamı görüyordur, iletişim iznini geri çeken bir kişi hâlâ listededir ve kimse listenin hangi tarihteki CRM durumunu yansıttığını bilmiyordur.

Ben Koray Yalçın; lead yönetimi, CRM ve dijital pazarlama altyapıları üzerinde, özellikle gayrimenkul ve PropTech projelerinde çalışıyorum. Bu yazıda Custom Audience'ı bir pazarlama paneli özelliği olarak değil, CRM'den reklam platformuna akan bir veri ürünü olarak ele alacağım: segment nasıl tanımlanır, kimlik bilgileri nasıl normalize edilip hash'lenir, liste her seferinde baştan yüklenmeden nasıl fark (diff) ile güncellenir, rızasını geri çeken kişi nasıl çıkarılır ve bütün bunlar nasıl izlenir. Örnekler TypeScript ve PostgreSQL ile, ama yaklaşım dil bağımsız.

Neden elle CSV yüklemek yetmez

Elle yüklemenin üç temel sorunu var. Birincisi tazelik: CRM her gün değişir, liste değişmez. İkincisi çıkarma: yeni kişileri eklemeyi herkes hatırlar, ama artık listede olmaması gereken kişileri çıkarmayı neredeyse kimse yapmaz. Üçüncüsü izlenebilirlik: "Bu kişi neden bu kitlede?" sorusuna cevap verecek bir kayıt yoktur.

Gayrimenkul özelinde çıkarma sorunu özellikle can sıkıcıdır. Sözleşme imzalamış bir alıcıya aynı projenin lansman reklamını göstermek bütçe israfıdır; ama daha önemlisi, müşteri deneyimi açısından "beni tanımıyorlar" hissi yaratır. Satış kapandığı anda kişinin "sıcak potansiyel" kitlesinden çıkıp, varsa "mevcut müşteri – yönlendirme" kitlesine geçmesi gerekir. Bunu elle yapan bir ekip, en iyi ihtimalle haftada bir yapar.

Segmenti kodda değil, veride tanımlayın

İlk tasarım kararı şu: kitle tanımları kodun içine gömülü sorgular olmamalı, sürümlenen bir tabloda yaşamalı. Böylece pazarlama ekibi "son 90 günde 2+1 talebi olan ama satın almamış kişiler" gibi bir tanımı değiştirdiğinde, değişikliğin ne zaman ve kim tarafından yapıldığı bellidir.

CREATE TABLE audience_definition (
  id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  key           text NOT NULL,           -- 'warm_leads_project_a'
  version       int  NOT NULL,
  platform      text NOT NULL,           -- 'meta' | 'google'
  external_id   text,                    -- platformdaki kitle kimliği
  purpose       text NOT NULL,           -- rıza amacı: 'ad_targeting'
  segment_sql   text NOT NULL,           -- yalnızca person_id döndüren, gözden geçirilmiş sorgu
  created_by    text NOT NULL,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  active        boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  UNIQUE (key, version)
);

segment_sql alanında serbest SQL tutmak riskli görünebilir; pratikte bunu ya yalnızca okuma yetkisi olan bir rolle çalıştırıyorum ya da sorgu yerine önceden tanımlanmış filtre parçalarından oluşan bir JSON kuralı kullanıyorum. Önemli olan, tanımın tek bir yerde ve sürümlü olması.

purpose alanı ise küçük ama kritik bir ayrıntıdır: her kitle, hangi rıza amacına dayandığını açıkça söyler. Bunu birazdan senkron sırasında filtre olarak kullanacağız.

Normalizasyon: Eşleşme oranını belirleyen sessiz adım

Reklam platformları ham e-posta ya da telefon kabul etmez; değerlerin belirli kurallarla normalize edilip SHA-256 ile hash'lenmesini bekler. Hash'lemeden önceki normalizasyon yanlışsa, aynı kişi platform tarafında hiç eşleşmez ve bunu size kimse söylemez. Eşleşme oranınız düşük kalır, siz de "kitle küçük çıktı" diye düşünürsünüz.

Temel kurallar platform dokümantasyonunda yazar ve zaman zaman güncellenir, bu yüzden kendi kodunuzu bir kez yazıp unutmak yerine dokümantasyonla birlikte gözden geçirmenizi öneririm. Genel çerçeve şöyle:

  • E-posta: baştaki ve sondaki boşlukları kırp, küçük harfe çevir.
  • Telefon: yalnızca rakamları bırak, ülke koduyla birlikte uluslararası biçime getir. Türkiye'de 0532... ile kaydedilmiş bir numara 90532... olmalı; KKTC numaraları için ülke kodu farklıdır ve bunu ayrı ele almak gerekir.
  • Ad, soyad, şehir gibi alanlar: platformun kuralına göre küçük harf ve noktalama temizliği; Türkçe karakterlerde platformun beklediği biçimi dokümantasyondan doğrulayın. 
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

const sha256 = (v: string) => createHash("sha256").update(v, "utf8").digest("hex");

export function normalizeEmail(raw?: string | null): string | null {
  if (!raw) return null;
  const v = raw.trim().toLowerCase();
  return /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/.test(v) ? v : null;
}

// Basitleştirilmiş: gerçek projede libphonenumber gibi bir kütüphane kullanın.
export function normalizePhoneTR(raw?: string | null): string | null {
  if (!raw) return null;
  let d = raw.replace(/\D/g, "");
  if (d.startsWith("00")) d = d.slice(2);
  if (d.length === 11 && d.startsWith("0")) d = "90" + d.slice(1);
  if (d.length === 10 && d.startsWith("5")) d = "90" + d;
  return d.length >= 11 ? d : null;
}

export function identifiers(p: { email?: string; phone?: string }) {
  const e = normalizeEmail(p.email);
  const t = normalizePhoneTR(p.phone);
  return {
    emailHash: e ? sha256(e) : null,
    phoneHash: t ? sha256(t) : null,
  };
}

Burada önemli bir nokta: normalize edilemeyen değeri "olduğu gibi" hash'lemeyin. Bozuk bir telefonu hash'leyip göndermek, eşleşmeyecek bir satır göndermekten başka bir işe yaramaz ve hata ayıklamayı zorlaştırır. null döndürün ve bunu sayın; normalize edilemeyen kayıt oranı, CRM veri kalitesinin iyi bir göstergesidir.

Üyelik tablosu: "Şu an kimler listede?" sorusunun cevabı

Fark senkronu yapabilmek için platforma en son neyi gönderdiğinizi bilmeniz gerekir. Platformlar listenin içeriğini size geri vermez (gizlilik gereği yalnızca yaklaşık boyut gösterirler), bu yüzden bu bilgiyi kendi tarafınızda tutmak zorundasınız.

CREATE TABLE audience_member (
  audience_key  text NOT NULL,
  person_id     bigint NOT NULL,
  email_hash    text,
  phone_hash    text,
  state         text NOT NULL,        -- 'pending_add' | 'synced' | 'pending_remove' | 'removed'
  reason        text,                 -- 'segment_match' | 'consent_withdrawn' | 'segment_exit'
  def_version   int  NOT NULL,
  updated_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  synced_at     timestamptz,
  PRIMARY KEY (audience_key, person_id)
);

Hash'leri burada saklamamın sebebi şu: çıkarma işlemi için platforma, eklerken gönderdiğiniz hash'in aynısını göndermeniz gerekir. Kişi bu arada CRM'de e-postasını değiştirdiyse, yeni e-postanın hash'ini göndermek eski kaydı çıkarmaz. Eski hash'i tutmak, "gönderdiğimi geri alabilirim" garantisidir.

Fark senkronu: Her seferinde baştan yüklemeyin

Senkron işi üç adımdan oluşur: segmenti hesapla, mevcut üyelikle karşılaştır, farkı gönder.

-- 1) Güncel segment (rıza filtresiyle birlikte)
WITH target AS (
  SELECT s.person_id
  FROM run_segment(:audience_key) s
  JOIN consent_state c
    ON c.person_id = s.person_id
   AND c.purpose = :purpose
   AND c.status = 'granted'
),
-- 2) Eklenecekler: hedefte olup listede olmayanlar
to_add AS (
  SELECT t.person_id FROM target t
  LEFT JOIN audience_member m
    ON m.audience_key = :audience_key AND m.person_id = t.person_id
   AND m.state IN ('synced','pending_add')
  WHERE m.person_id IS NULL
),
-- 3) Çıkarılacaklar: listede olup artık hedefte olmayanlar
to_remove AS (
  SELECT m.person_id FROM audience_member m
  WHERE m.audience_key = :audience_key
    AND m.state = 'synced'
    AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM target t WHERE t.person_id = m.person_id)
)
SELECT 'add' AS op, person_id FROM to_add
UNION ALL
SELECT 'remove', person_id FROM to_remove;

Rıza kontrolünü segment sorgusunun içine değil, onun dışına, senkron katmanına koyuyorum. Sebebi basit: pazarlama ekibi segment tanımını değiştirirken rıza koşulunu unutabilir. Rıza filtresi senkron işinin sabit bir parçası olduğunda, hiçbir segment tanımı onu atlayamaz.

Bu sorgunun sonucu doğrudan API'ye gitmez; önce audience_member tablosunda pending_add ve pending_remove durumlarına yazılır. Gönderim ayrı bir işçi tarafından yapılır. Bu, daha önce lead entegrasyonlarında kullandığım outbox desenine benzer: önce niyetinizi kalıcı yazarsınız, sonra gönderirsiniz. API çağrısı yarıda kesilirse, hangi satırların gönderilmediği tabloda bellidir.

Gönderim işçisi: Parçalı gönderim, idempotency ve hız sınırı

Platform API'leri tek istekte gönderebileceğiniz satır sayısını sınırlar ve hız sınırı uygular. Kesin sayılar platforma ve zamana göre değiştiği için kodda sabit olarak değil, yapılandırmada tutun.

type Op = { personId: number; emailHash: string | null; phoneHash: string | null };

async function flush(audienceKey: string, op: "add" | "remove", batchSize: number) {
  const rows: Op[] = await db.claimPending(audienceKey, op, batchSize); // FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  if (rows.length === 0) return 0;

  const payload = rows
    .filter(r => r.emailHash || r.phoneHash)
    .map(r => [r.emailHash ?? "", r.phoneHash ?? ""]);

  try {
    const res = await audienceClient[op](audienceKey, {
      schema: ["EMAIL_SHA256", "PHONE_SHA256"],
      data: payload,
    });
    await db.markSynced(audienceKey, rows.map(r => r.personId), op, res.requestId);
  } catch (err) {
    if (isRetryable(err)) {
      await db.releaseForRetry(audienceKey, rows.map(r => r.personId), backoff(err));
    } else {
      await db.moveToDeadLetter(audienceKey, rows, err);
    }
  }
  return rows.length;
}

Üyelik ekleme ve çıkarma işlemleri doğası gereği büyük ölçüde idempotenttir: aynı hash'i iki kez eklemek kitlede iki kişi oluşturmaz. Bu, yeniden denemeyi rahatlatır. Ama yine de her gönderimin bir istek kimliğiyle kaydını tutun; "bu kişi ne zaman, hangi tanım sürümüyle eklendi" sorusunun cevabı bu kayıttır.

Bir önemli uyarı: ekleme ve çıkarma sırasını karıştırmayın. Aynı kişi için önce bir remove, ardından bir add kuyrukta bekliyorsa ve işçiler paralel çalışıyorsa, sıra tersine dönebilir. Ben bunu kişi başına tek bir durum satırı tutarak çözüyorum: tabloda bir kişinin aynı anda yalnızca bir bekleyen işlemi olabilir ve yeni bir hesaplama eski bekleyen işlemi ezer.

Rıza geri çekme: Bir sonraki gece işini beklemeyin

Fark senkronu genelde zamanlanmış çalışır, örneğin saatte bir ya da gecede bir. Ama bir kişinin reklam amaçlı veri kullanımına itirazı ya da iznini geri çekmesi, bir sonraki toplu işi beklememelidir. Bunu olay güdümlü bir kısa yolla çözüyorum:

// İzin defterine "withdrawn" olayı yazıldığında tetiklenir
async function onConsentWithdrawn(personId: number, purpose: string) {
  const audiences = await db.audiencesByPurpose(purpose);
  for (const a of audiences) {
    await db.query(
      `UPDATE audience_member
          SET state = 'pending_remove', reason = 'consent_withdrawn', updated_at = now()
        WHERE audience_key = $1 AND person_id = $2 AND state IN ('synced','pending_add')`,
      [a.key, personId]
    );
  }
  await queue.wake("audience-flush"); // işçiyi hemen uyandır
}

pending_add durumundaki kaydı da pending_remove'a çevirmek önemli: kişi henüz gönderilmemişse bile, gönderilmeden önce iptal edilmiş olur. Bu ayrıntı, "izin geri çekildi ama beş dakika sonra kitleye eklendi" gibi utandırıcı bir yarış durumunu engeller.

Bir de şunu belirtmeliyim: bu yazı teknik bir tasarım notudur, hukuki görüş değildir. Hangi rıza amacının hangi kitle kullanımı için yeterli olduğu, KVKK ve GDPR gibi düzenlemeler açısından hukuk ekibinizle birlikte belirlenmelidir. Teknik tarafın görevi, verilen kararı tutarlı ve denetlenebilir biçimde uygulamaktır.

Gayrimenkul senaryosu: Aşamaya bağlı kitle geçişleri

Somut bir örnek üzerinden gideyim. Bir konut projesi için üç kitle düşünelim:

  1. Sıcak potansiyel: Son 60 gün içinde form doldurmuş, en az bir anlamlı temas kurulmuş, satış aşaması "teklif" öncesinde olan kişiler.
  2. Hariç tutma kitlesi: Sözleşme imzalamış alıcılar ve "ilgilenmiyor" olarak kapatılmış kayıtlar. Bu kitle reklam setlerinde hedefleme için değil, hariç tutma için kullanılır.
  3. Benzer kitle kaynağı: Satın alma ile sonuçlanmış kişiler; platformun benzer kitle (lookalike) özelliğine kaynak olarak verilir.

Bir kişinin CRM'deki aşaması "sözleşme"ye geçtiği anda, bir sonraki senkronda 1 numaralı kitleden segment_exit gerekçesiyle çıkar, 2 ve 3 numaralı kitlelere eklenir. Hiçbir pazarlama uzmanının elle bir şey yapmasına gerek kalmaz. Kampanya tarafında ise sıcak potansiyel reklam setleri, hariç tutma kitlesini otomatik olarak dışarıda bırakır.

Buradaki tasarım dersi şu: hariç tutma kitleleri, hedefleme kitleleri kadar önemlidir ve genellikle daha çok ihmal edilir. Senkron altyapısını kurarken ilk iki kitleden biri mutlaka hariç tutma kitlesi olmalı.

İzleme: Sessiz bozulmayı nasıl yakalarsınız

Custom Audience senkronunun bozulması nadiren hata mesajıyla kendini gösterir. Genelde şunlar olur: token süresi dolar ve iş sessizce başarısız olur, normalizasyon kodundaki bir değişiklik eşleşmeyi düşürür, ya da segment sorgusu bir şema değişikliği yüzünden boş döner ve senkron işi bunu "herkesi çıkar" olarak yorumlar.

Son durum en tehlikelisidir. Bu yüzden her senkron çalışmasında şu korumaları uyguluyorum:

  • Çıkarma eşiği: Tek bir çalışmada mevcut üyelerin belirli bir oranından fazlası çıkarılacaksa iş durur ve uyarı üretir. Gerçek bir segment değişikliği ise bir insan onaylar.
  • Boş segment koruması: Segment sorgusu sıfır satır döndürürse ve önceki çalışmada yüzlerce kişi varsa, bu bir veri hatası olarak kabul edilir.
  • Normalizasyon oranı: Her çalışmada "e-posta veya telefonu normalize edilemeyen kişi oranı" kaydedilir; ani bir artış, kaynak sistemdeki bir değişikliğin işaretidir.
  • Platform tarafı boyutu: Platformun gösterdiği yaklaşık kitle boyutunu periyodik olarak okuyup kendi synced sayınızla karşılaştırın. Birebir eşleşme beklemeyin (eşleşmeyen kişiler sayılmaz ve boyut yuvarlanır), ama oranın zaman içinde nasıl değiştiğini izleyin. 
SELECT audience_key,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'synced')         AS synced,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE state LIKE 'pending_%')   AS pending,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE email_hash IS NULL AND phone_hash IS NULL) AS no_identifier,
       max(synced_at)                                   AS last_sync
FROM audience_member
GROUP BY audience_key;

Bu sorguyu bir gösterge paneline koyup last_sync için bir eşik belirlemek, "liste en son ne zaman güncellendi?" sorusunu kalıcı olarak cevaplar.

Sık yapılan hatalar

Sahada en sık karşılaştığım hataları kısa bir liste olarak toplayayım:

  • Hash'lemeden önce normalize etmemek ya da e-postayı küçük harfe çevirmeyi unutmak.
  • Türkiye numaralarını başındaki 0 ile ya da ülke kodu olmadan göndermek.
  • Yalnızca ekleme yapıp çıkarmayı hiç uygulamamak.
  • Rıza kontrolünü her segment tanımına ayrı ayrı yazmaya çalışmak ve bir tanesinde unutmak.
  • Kişinin eski hash'ini saklamamak ve bu yüzden onu listeden çıkaramamak.
  • Boş dönen bir sorguyu "herkesi çıkar" diye yorumlayan, korumasız bir senkron işi.

SSS

Custom Audience için verileri hash'lemek kişisel veriyi anonim hale getirir mi?
Hayır. SHA-256 ile hash'lenmiş bir e-posta, aynı e-postayı bilen biri tarafından kolayca eşleştirilebilir; bu yüzden hash'lenmiş veri hâlâ kişisel veri olarak ele alınmalıdır. Hash'leme, aktarım sırasında ham değeri göstermemeye yarar, rıza ya da hukuki dayanak ihtiyacını ortadan kaldırmaz.

Listeyi her gece baştan yüklemek daha basit değil mi?
Daha basit, ama iki sorunu var: çıkarmayı garanti etmez (bazı platformlarda "değiştir" işlemi ayrı bir uç noktadır ve kendi kısıtları vardır) ve büyük listelerde her seferinde tüm veriyi göndermek gereksiz yük ve hata yüzeyi yaratır. Fark senkronu, ne değiştiğini de kayıt altına aldığı için denetlenebilirlik açısından da daha iyidir.

Eşleşme oranım düşük çıkıyor, ilk neye bakmalıyım?
Önce normalizasyona. Rastgele birkaç kaydın normalize edilmiş halini elle kontrol edin: e-postalar küçük harf mi, telefonlar ülke koduyla mı? Ardından, CRM'deki e-postaların reklam platformunda kullanılan hesaplarla aynı olup olmadığını düşünün; iş e-postası ile kişisel hesap farklıysa, telefonu ikinci bir tanımlayıcı olarak eklemek eşleşmeyi artırabilir.

Senkron sıklığı ne olmalı?
İş ihtiyacına bağlı. Benim varsayılanım, olağan ekleme ve çıkarmalar için saatlik ya da günlük bir fark senkronu, rıza geri çekme gibi olaylar için ise olay güdümlü anında çıkarmadır. Çok sık senkron, hız sınırlarına takılmaktan başka bir şey kazandırmaz; çünkü platform tarafında kitlenin güncellenmesi zaten bir süre alır.

Küçük bir ekip için bu kadar altyapı gerekli mi?
Hepsini ilk günden kurmak gerekmez. Öncelik sırası olarak şunu öneririm: önce doğru normalizasyon ve hash'leme, sonra gönderilen hash'leri saklayan üyelik tablosu, ardından rıza filtresi ve çıkarma, en son izleme ve korumalar. İlk üç adım bile elle CSV yüklemenin en büyük risklerini kapatır.

Kapanış

Custom Audience, reklam panelinde birkaç tıklamayla oluşturulan bir liste gibi görünse de aslında CRM'inizin reklam platformuna açılan bir penceresidir. O pencereden neyin geçtiğini, ne zaman geçtiğini ve neyin artık geçmemesi gerektiğini bilmek, hem bütçe verimliliği hem de müşteri güveni açısından belirleyicidir. Segmenti sürümlü bir tanım olarak tutmak, normalizasyonu titizlikle yapmak, gönderdiğiniz hash'leri saklamak, fark senkronu ile ekleyip çıkarmak ve rıza geri çekmeyi anında uygulamak; bu adımlar birlikte, tek seferlik bir CSV yüklemesini güvenilir bir veri akışına dönüştürür.

Lead yönetimi, CRM ve reklam entegrasyonları üzerine bu tür uygulama notlarını paylaşmaya devam edeceğim. Kendi kitle senkronunuzda en çok hangi adımda zorlandığınızı yorumlarda yazarsanız, sonraki yazılarda o konuyu daha ayrıntılı ele alabilirim.

— Koray Yalçın

title: Python Retry with Exponential Backoff and Jitter (stdlib only)
description:
Most retry code I see in agent projects looks like this:

for i in range(3):
    try:
        return call_api()
    except Exception:
        time.sleep(2)
raise RuntimeError("gave up")

It survives a demo. In production it fails in four different ways, and each one is its own failure mode. Here's what's wrong and the stdlib-only pattern we ship instead.

Problem 1: it retries permanent errors

A 401 (bad key) and a 429 (rate-limited) are not the same failure. Retrying a 401 three times burns 6 seconds and a support ticket. Classify first:

RETRYABLE_EXCEPTIONS = (TimeoutError, ConnectionError, OSError)
RETRYABLE_STATUS = {408, 409, 425, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504}

Anything outside those lists should fail on the first attempt. In an agent loop, a permanent error you keep retrying becomes the retry spiral: the same failure five times in a row until the runtime hard-stops the turn.

Problem 2: fixed sleep creates a thundering herd

When an API wobbles, every client that went down at the same moment comes back at the same moment — fixed 2-second sleeps synchronize the retry wave and knock the service down again. The fix is exponential backoff plus jitter:

delay = min(cap, base * (2 ** attempt))   # 1.5, 3, 6, 12... capped
delay *= random.uniform(0.75, 1.25)       # jitter desynchronizes clients
time.sleep(delay)

The cap matters too. Uncapped exponential backoff means your fifth retry sleeps four minutes — through your agent's entire turn budget.

Problem 3: no total budget

This is the one that kills AI agents specifically. If each attempt gets its own timeout and each retry its own sleep, total worst-case time is timeout × (retries+1) + sleeps. A 45-second timeout with 3 retries can eat 4+ minutes — and agent platforms kill turns at 5. The retry loop needs a shared deadline across all attempts, so the last attempt gets whatever time is left, not a fresh allowance:

start = time.monotonic()
deadline = start + budget_s          # ONE budget for the whole call

for attempt in range(retries + 1):
    remaining = deadline - time.monotonic()
    if remaining <= 0:
        break                        # budget exhausted, fail honestly
    try:
        value = run_with_timeout(fn, min(timeout, remaining))
        ...
    except RETRYABLE_EXCEPTIONS:
        if time.monotonic() < deadline - backoff_base:
            time.sleep(jittered_delay)  # only sleep if budget survives it

Problem 4: "success" that isn't

The API returned 200 with 10 of 60 results. The call "succeeded" and your agent built on garbage. A retry helper for agents should take a semantic validator, and a rejected result should count as a retryable failure:

res = resilient_call(lambda: my_llm(prompt),
                     name="llm",
                     timeout=45, retries=3,
                     validate=lambda x: len(x["results"]) == expected)

The whole thing, assembled

Put the four pieces together — classification, jittered capped backoff, shared budget, semantic validation — and you get a wrapper that returns a structured result instead of either a value or an exception:

res = resilient_call(fn, name="llm", timeout=45, retries=3,
                     budget_s=120, validate=shape_check)
if res.ok:
    use(res.value)
else:
    # res.failure = {kind, name, attempts, last_error, elapsed_s}
    journal.record(res.failure)   # "same failure 5x today" becomes a query

The structured failure record is the quiet win: your agent can reason about why a call died ("429 three times, budget exhausted") instead of hallucinating a plausible answer over stack-trace soup.

This is exactly the resilient_call module in AgentOps Autopilot (MIT, stdlib only, 24/24 tests + a chaos gauntlet that injects each failure kind). If you'd rather paste it than rebuild it, the repo is free; the paid tiers add the templates and the runbook.

Next in the series: what to do when the LLM's JSON is truncated mid-string.

title: What Changes With the A2UI 1.0 Release
description:
This article walks through what changed between A2UI 0.9 and A2UI 1.0, how generated UI works on 1.0, and why it is better, using one currency agent built on both versions. A Google ADK agent on Gemini looks up exchange rates and answers with A2UI cards and charts, rendered by a Next.js CopilotKit front end over AG-UI.

https://github.com/xbill9/currency-claude-agui-a2ui1

On 0.9 the model wrote the UI as JSON, figures included. On 1.0 it writes one line and the server does the rest. A rate card for "Convert 100 USD to EUR" is 223 tokens of 0.9 JSON, 139 tokens of 1.0 Express, and 21 tokens as a 1.0 server-side macro call. A 90-day history chart is 1,060 tokens of 0.9 JSON and 21 as a macro call. Counted with the Gemini tokenizer, for the same components.

What Is A2UI?

A2UI is a protocol for agents that answer with UI. The agent sends a description of components (cards, text, buttons, charts) from a catalog the client implements, and the client renders them with its own native widgets. The agent never sends code, so the client decides what can run.

The Agent Used for the Comparison

Service Port Code
React UI: Next.js, CopilotKit, @a2ui/react 3000 frontend-react/
AG-UI bridge: the ADK agent in-process 8008 frontend-react/agent/
A2A server: the same ADK agent over A2A 10000 currency_agent/
MCP server: get_exchange_rate (FastMCP) 8080, path /mcp mcp-server/

The 0.9 build is commit d181ddb of the same repository. Everything after it is 1.0. Versions, read from the machine on 2026-11-11:

Component 0.9 build 1.0 build
Agent library a2ui-agent-sdk 0.2.1 a2ui-agent-sdk 0.11.0, a2ui-adk 0.3.0, a2ui-core 0.6.0
Renderer @copilotkit/a2ui-renderer @a2ui/react 0.15.0, @a2ui/web_core 0.15.0
Agent framework google-adk google-adk 2.13.0, ag_ui_adk 0.6.5
Model Gemini gemini-3.8-flash (default), gemini-2.5-flash

What Changed at a Glance

Read from the installed a2ui-core 0.6.0, which ships the 0.9 and 1.0 schemas side by side:

A2UI 0.9 A2UI 1.0
Version string "v0.9" "1.0"
createSurface catalog id, theme, sendDataModel inline components and dataModel, sendDataModel, metadata; no theme
Catalogs per surface one one per component, through catalogId
Bindings and calls {"path": ...}, {"call": ...} {"@path": ...}, {"@call": ...}
Agent → renderer createSurface, updateComponents, updateDataModel, deleteSurface the same four, plus callRendererFunction and agentFunctionResponse
Renderer → agent action, error action, error, plus callAgentFunction and rendererFunctionResponse
Text variants h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, caption, body caption, body; headings come from Markdown
Basic catalog 18 components, 14 functions the same 18 components, 15 functions (adds @index)
Names for the two sides client and server renderer and agent
What the model writes (SDK) JSON Express, compiled to JSON on the server
Server-side macros (SDK) none @macro, expanded before sending

The last two rows belong to the agent SDK, a2ui-agent-sdk 0.11.0, which ships with the 1.0 protocol. The sections below take the changes one at a time: what 0.9 did, what 1.0 does, and what it buys.

Change 1 — A Whole Surface in One Message

On 0.9 a new surface took three messages: createSurface named the catalog, updateComponents sent the components, and updateDataModel filled in the data. The renderer held an empty surface until the last one arrived.

On 1.0 createSurface carries components and dataModel inline. This Express block, a form with a bound text field, a check and a button, compiles to both versions with the SDK's own compiler:

surface("main")
$/user/name = "Ada"
title = Text(formatString("Hello ${/user/name}"))
btn = Button(Text("Save"), action=Event("save", {name: $/user/name}, userMessage="Saving"))
root = Column([title, TextField("Name", $/user/name, checks=[?required("Name is required")]), btn])

python3 docs/a2ui-1-0/tools/express_0_9_vs_1_0.py

## A2UI 1.0: 1 message(s): ['createSurface']
## A2UI 0.9 (userMessage removed): 3 message(s): ['createSurface', 'updateComponents', 'updateDataModel']
## userMessage on 0.9
ExpressValidationError: Event userMessage requires protocol v1.0 or later; the target version v0.9 has no userMessage field.

Why it is better: the renderer has everything it needs to draw the surface from the first message, and there is no ordering between three messages to get wrong. Updates still use updateComponents and updateDataModel once a surface exists.

Change 2 — The Model Writes Express, Not JSON

On 0.9 the model wrote A2UI JSON into its reply, inside <a2ui-json> tags. The 0.9 build's page.tsx cut the blocks out of the text with regular expressions, and a normalizeA2UIJson function repaired the shapes the model produced before handing them to the renderer.

On 1.0 the SDK's default output format is Express: a short Python-like language inside <a2ui> tags. $/path is a binding, ?required is a check, root = names the top component, and arguments follow the catalog's signatures. The SDK generates the prompt from the catalogs, compiles the block on the server, validates it against the catalog, and sends the JSON. Here is the rate card in Express:

surface("main")
root__text_1 = Text("### 100.00 USD = 89.87 EUR")
root__text_2 = Text("1 USD = 0.89871 EUR")
root__divider_1 = Divider()
root__text_3 = Text("ECB reference rate for 2026-11-11 (Frankfurter API)", "caption")
root__column_1 = Column([root__text_1, root__text_2, root__divider_1, root__text_3])
root = Card(root__column_1)

The same six components as 0.9 JSON:

[{"version":"v0.9","createSurface":{"surfaceId":"main","catalogId":"https://a2ui.org/catalog/currency-charts"}},{"version":"v0.9","updateComponents":{"surfaceId":"main","components":[{"component":"Text","id":"root__text_1","text":"100.00 USD = 89.87 EUR","variant":"h3"},{"component":"Text","id":"root__text_2","text":"1 USD = 0.89871 EUR"},{"component":"Divider","id":"root__divider_1"},{"component":"Text","id":"root__text_3","text":"ECB reference rate for 2026-11-11 (Frankfurter API)","variant":"caption"},{"component":"Column","id":"root__column_1","children":["root__text_1","root__text_2","root__divider_1","root__text_3"]},{"component":"Card","id":"root","child":"root__column_1"}]}}]

Why it is better: the model writes fewer tokens (139 against 223 for this card, table below), and a malformed block fails on the server, before anything reaches a browser: the tool returns the compiler's error to the model in its result. The browser receives JSON that has already passed the catalog's schema, so the 1.0 page.tsx has no parser and no normalizer: it went from 309 lines to 150.

Change 3 — Server-Side Macros: Figures Never Pass Through the Model

On 0.9 the model called the rate tool, read the result, and typed every figure into the component JSON. A history chart meant the model copying 64 dates and 64 rates back out.

On 1.0 a macro is a Python function the model calls like a component. @macro turns its type hints and docstring into an entry in a separate macros catalog that only the model sees. At send time MacroExpander runs the function and replaces the call with Basic catalog components, so the browser needs no macro support. From currency_agent/macros.py:

@macro
def RateCard(currency_from: str, currency_to: str, amount: float = 1.0) -> Card:
    """Card with the live exchange rate and a converted amount. The server looks
    up the rate, so do not pass rate figures.
    """
    src, dst = _code(currency_from), _code(currency_to)
    data = _get("latest", **{"from": src, "to": dst})
    rate = data["rates"][dst]
    return Card(
        child=Column(
            children=[
                Text(text=f"### {amount:,.2f} {src} = {amount * rate:,.2f} {dst}"),
                Text(text=f"1 {src} = {rate:.5f} {dst}"),
                Divider(),
                Text(
                    text=f"ECB reference rate for {data['date']} (Frankfurter API)",
                    variant="caption",
                ),
            ]
        )
    )

For "Convert 100 USD to EUR please." the model's whole tool call was:

<a2ui>
surface("conversion")
root = RateCard("USD", "EUR", 100)
</a2ui>

What reached the browser:

version 1.0, ['createSurface'], 6 components
  https://a2ui.org/specification/v1_0/catalogs/basic/catalog.json: ['Text', 'Text', 'Divider', 'Text', 'Column', 'Card']
  Text: ### 100.00 USD = 89.87 EUR
  Text: 1 USD = 0.89871 EUR
  Text: ECB reference rate for 2026-11-11 (Frankfurter API)

The agent validates twice: once against the catalogs the model sees, which include the macros, and again after expansion against the catalogs the browser implements:

def _parse_payload(self, processor, payload):
    messages = super()._parse_payload(processor, payload)
    typed = [_message_adapter.validate_python(m) for m in messages]
    expanded = macro_expander.transform_to_transport(typed)
    wire = [m.model_dump(by_alias=True, exclude_none=True) for m in expanded]
    validate_payload(BASE_CATALOGS, wire)
    return wire

Why it is better: the figures come from the source on the server, so the model cannot mistype a rate, and data the model does not need to see stays out of its context. The model's output stops growing with the data: the 90-day chart is 21 tokens as a macro call against 1,060 as 0.9 JSON. Macro arguments come from the model, so _code() accepts only a three-letter currency code and day counts are clamped to 7–365.

How Many Tokens Does the Model Write?

docs/a2ui-1-0/tools/token_cost.py builds three answers once with live rates, writes each in four forms, and counts every form with the Gemini countTokens API:

python3 docs/a2ui-1-0/tools/token_cost.py gemini-2.5-flash

# Tokens the model writes for the same UI, counted by gemini-2.5-flash countTokens
| Answer | Components | 0.9 JSON | 1.0 JSON | 1.0 Express | 1.0 macro |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Rate card | 6 | 223 | 212 | 139 | 21 |
| 90-day chart | 5 | 1060 | 1152 | 1101 | 21 |
| 3-currency comparison | 8 | 347 | 522 | 253 | 22 |

gemini-3.8-flash counted the same numbers. Two things the table shows:

  • Express shrinks structure. On the card and the comparison, where most tokens are component structure, Express is the smallest form the model can write by hand. On the chart, where most tokens are 64 dates and 64 rates, every hand-written form costs about the same.
  • Macros remove the data. A macro call costs the same 21 or 22 tokens whatever it expands to.

The 1.0 JSON for the comparison is the largest form because it mixes two catalogs, so each component names its own catalogId (Change 4). Express leaves catalog ids out and the compiler fills them in.

Change 4 — Several Catalogs on One Surface

On 0.9 createSurface named one catalog id, and every component on the surface came from it. The 0.9 build loaded Basic 0.9 and its charts catalog, https://a2ui.org/catalog/currency-charts, through A2uiSchemaManager, which selected one catalog for the surface.

On 1.0 each component can name its own catalogId. The browser here implements Basic 1.0 and a currency charts catalog with LineChart and BarChart. For "Show me EUR to USD for the past 6 months and the current rate" the model wrote two macro calls:

<a2ui>
surface("main")
root = Column([rateCard, historyChart])
rateCard = RateCard("EUR", "USD")
historyChart = RateHistoryChart("EUR", "USD", 180)
</a2ui>

The browser received one createSurface with each component naming its catalog:

version 1.0, ['createSurface'], 12 components
  https://a2ui.org/specification/v1_0/catalogs/basic/catalog.json: ['Column', 'Text', 'Text', 'Divider', 'Text', 'Column', 'Card', 'Text', 'Text', 'Column', 'Card']
  https://a2ui.org/catalog/currency-charts/v1/catalog.json: ['LineChart']

Why it is better: a custom catalog holds only the custom components, LineChart and BarChart here, and sits beside the standard Basic catalog on the same surface. The charts catalog is now https://a2ui.org/catalog/currency-charts/v1/catalog.json with protocolVersion 1.0, and its id and props match between currency_agent/custom_catalog.json and A2UICustomCatalog.tsx in the browser.

Change 5 — The UI Arrives as a Tool Result

On 0.9 the UI travelled inside the reply text. CopilotKit's A2UI middleware and @copilotkit/a2ui-renderer read it, and the 0.9 build's AG-UI checks searched the final text for <a2ui-json> tags.

On 1.0 the model passes its Express block to the send_a2ui_json_to_client tool, and the tool result carries the validated messages in validated_a2ui_json. The page registers a renderer for that tool and hands the messages to @a2ui/react:

useRenderTool(
  {
    name: "send_a2ui_json_to_client",
    render: ({ result }: any) => {
      const messages = extractA2uiMessages(result);
      return messages ? <A2uiMessages messages={messages} /> : null;
    },
  } as any,
  [],
);

Why it is better: the UI travels separately from the chat text, so a reply can mix prose and a card without the browser guessing where one ends. CopilotKit's built-in A2UI middleware speaks 0.9, so it is switched off in route.ts.

Change 6 — Breaking Changes to Plan For

These need edits when moving a 0.9 agent or renderer to 1.0:

  • Headings come from Markdown. Text's h1–h5 variants are gone; caption and body remain, and Text renders Markdown. The macros write ### 250.00 USD = 224.68 EUR for the headline line, and @a2ui/react renders it with @a2ui/markdown-it.
  • theme is gone from createSurface.
  • Bindings and calls are prefixed: {"path": ...} is {"@path": ...}, {"call": ...} is {"@call": ...}.
  • The version string is "1.0", without the v.
  • Component props moved: TextField gains placeholder and replaces validationRegexp with a regex check, Slider gains steps, and Video gains posterUrl.

Change 7 — What 1.0 Adds

From the 1.0 schemas in a2ui-core 0.6.0:

  • Functions in both directions. The agent can call a renderer function (callRendererFunction) and the renderer can call an agent function (callAgentFunction), each with its own response message.
  • Function permissions. A catalog marks each function rendererOnly, agentOnly or rendererOrAgent, and can require a user gesture with requiresUserActivation.
  • Composition rules. A catalog can list allowedParents and allowedChildren per component, and the renderer reports violations with the error codes UNALLOWED_PARENT and UNALLOWED_CHILD.
  • Graded validation. Checks return a result with a severity of error, warning or info.
  • Actions that speak. A button's action can carry a userMessage, which travels with the action to the agent. The compiler rejects it on 0.9, as Change 1 shows.
  • Accessibility. Components take live (off, polite, assertive) and hidden.
  • List positions. The @index function returns an item's position inside a list template.
  • Extensions. Components, surfaces, actions and catalogs carry metadata.extensions for custom data.
  • Catalog instructions. A catalog can carry Markdown instructions for the model.

Does It Hold Up?

docs/a2ui-1-0/tools/render_suite.py sends ten prompts ten times each through Next.js. A UI prompt passes when the reply rendered A2UI and no raw <a2ui text reached the chat; the weather question passes as text with no UI.

python3 docs/a2ui-1-0/tools/render_suite.py 10 gemini-3.8-flash render-suite-gemini-3.8-flash.jsonl

# gemini-3.8-flash: 100 of 100 replies rendered clean (10 runs per prompt)
10 of 10: pass | Compare 1 USD in EUR, GBP, JPY and CAD
10 of 10: pass | Compare the euro, pound and Swiss franc against the dollar in a bar chart
10 of 10: pass | Convert 100 USD to XYZ
10 of 10: pass | How much is 250 USD in EUR?
10 of 10: pass | Show a bar chart of 1 USD in EUR, GBP, JPY, CHF and CAD
10 of 10: pass | Show me EUR to USD for the past 6 months and the current rate
10 of 10: pass | Show me the USD to JPY trend over the last 90 days
10 of 10: pass | What's a thousand euros in dollars?
10 of 10: pass | What's the weather in Paris?
10 of 10: pass | Write the A2UI block for a USD to EUR rate card directly in your reply text. Do not call any tool.

# gemini-2.5-flash: 100 of 100 replies rendered clean (10 runs per prompt)

Every comparison reply on both models came from the RateComparison macro, with no call to the rate tool:

## gemini-2.5-flash
10 of 10: no rate-tool call, BarChart=True | Compare 1 USD in EUR, GBP, JPY and CAD
10 of 10: no rate-tool call, BarChart=True | Compare the euro, pound and Swiss franc against the dol
10 of 10: no rate-tool call, BarChart=True | Show a bar chart of 1 USD in EUR, GBP, JPY, CHF and CAD
## gemini-3.8-flash
10 of 10: no rate-tool call, BarChart=True | Compare 1 USD in EUR, GBP, JPY and CAD
10 of 10: no rate-tool call, BarChart=True | Compare the euro, pound and Swiss franc against the dol
10 of 10: no rate-tool call, BarChart=True | Show a bar chart of 1 USD in EUR, GBP, JPY, CHF and CAD

🔎 Tip: Express Is a Format, Not a Python Feature

The A2UI repository ships YAML conformance suites for the Express compiler and the response parser, tagged with the a2ui-agent-sdk 0.11.0 release. A Rust port of the same agent, https://github.com/xbill9/currency-agent-rust-agui-a2ui1, implements Express and server-side macros in Rust and runs them:

cargo test --test express_conformance -- --nocapture

agent/express/response_parser.yaml: 38/38 passed, 0 known gaps, 0 failed
agent/express/compiler.yaml: 132/135 passed, 3 known gaps, 0 failed

The three compiler cases it skips use a 0.9 catalog; the port targets 1.0 only.

🔎 Tip: Keep the Macros Catalog on the Model's Side

The macros sit in a catalog that exists only for the model: macro_expander.transform_catalogs(BASE_CATALOGS) adds it to the prompt and the compiler. The browser's catalogs stay Basic 1.0 plus charts, and the second validation pass confirms every component the browser receives belongs to one of them.

At This Point You Should Have…

  • Python 3.13 or newer and Node.js with npm
  • A Gemini API key from Google AI Studio, or a Google Cloud project with Vertex AI enabled
  • The repository cloned: 
git clone https://github.com/xbill9/currency-claude-agui-a2ui1.git
cd currency-claude-agui-a2ui1

Step 1 — Install and Configure 

make install
echo "GOOGLE_API_KEY=<your_api_key_here>" >> .env
echo "GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=FALSE" >> .env

make install runs uv sync and npm install for both front ends. The agent uses gemini-3.8-flash unless GENAI_MODEL is set in .env.

Step 2 — Start the Stack and Ask 

make start
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:10000/health
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8008/health

{"status":"ok"}
{"status":"ok"}

Open http://localhost:3000 and ask How much is 250 USD in EUR?

Compare and Contrast

The same answers on each version, tokens counted by gemini-2.5-flash:

A2UI 0.9 A2UI 1.0, Express A2UI 1.0, macro 🥇
Rate card 223 tokens 139 tokens 21 tokens
90-day chart 1,060 tokens 1,101 tokens 21 tokens
3-currency comparison 347 tokens 253 tokens 22 tokens
Messages per new surface 3 1 1
Figures typed by the model the model the server
Checked against the catalog no; shapes repaired in the browser on the server, before sending on the server, before and after expansion
Catalogs per surface 1 1 per component 1 per component

So, Which One?

Move to 1.0. A surface arrives in one message, the model writes Express instead of JSON, the server validates before anything ships, and one surface can mix the standard Basic catalog with your own.

On 1.0, write a macro for anything the agent shows often. The model's output drops to one line with the codes and an amount, the figures come from the source on the server, and the cost no longer grows with the data. Rate cards, history charts and comparisons all take that path here. Plain Express covers layouts the macros do not.

Budget time for the breaking changes in Change 6, and for a renderer that speaks 1.0: @a2ui/react 0.15.0 here, in place of CopilotKit's 0.9 renderer.

Summary

The goal of this article was to show what changed between A2UI 0.9 and A2UI 1.0, how generated UI works on 1.0, and why it is better, using one currency agent built on both. The key to the solution was the 1.0 agent SDK's two additions on top of the protocol: the model writes Express that the server compiles and validates, and server-side macros build the components from live data so the figures never pass through the model. The results were:

  • 🟢 A rate card is 223 tokens of 0.9 JSON, 139 tokens of Express and 21 tokens as a macro call, counted by the Gemini tokenizer
  • 🟢 A 90-day chart is 1,060 tokens of 0.9 JSON and 21 as a macro call; Express alone saves little when the tokens are data
  • 🟢 The same Express block compiles to one message on 1.0 and three on 0.9
  • 🟢 One surface mixed two catalogs, each component naming its own catalogId
  • 🟢 Ten prompts, ten runs each: 100 of 100 replies rendered clean on gemini-3.8-flash and 100 of 100 on gemini-2.5-flash
  • 🟢 The browser code shrank from 309 lines to 150 once the parser and normalizer went
  • 🟢 A Rust port passed 132 of 135 Express compiler cases and 38 of 38 response parser cases; the 3 it skips use a 0.9 catalog
  • ⚠️ 1.0 JSON that mixes catalogs repeats catalogId on every component and was the largest form of the comparison, at 522 tokens
  • ❌ 1.0 drops theme and the h1–h5 Text variants, and renames path and call to @path and @call

Scope: one laptop running all four services, gemini-3.8-flash and gemini-2.5-flash at their default settings, ECB reference rates from the Frankfurter API, measured on 2026-11-11 with ten runs per prompt per model. The token counts compare forms of the same components built by the server: the 0.9 JSON is those components written in the 0.9 shape, not text captured from the 0.9 build's model, and properties left at their defaults are removed from every form. Protocol details come from the 0.9 and 1.0 schemas in a2ui-core 0.6.0.

The strategy for moving a generative UI agent from A2UI 0.9 to 1.0 was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

References

  • The repository: https://github.com/xbill9/currency-claude-agui-a2ui1
  • The Rust port: https://github.com/xbill9/currency-agent-rust-agui-a2ui1
  • Evidence for every figure here: https://github.com/xbill9/currency-claude-agui-a2ui1/tree/main/docs/a2ui-1-0/evidence
  • Demo, token and test scripts: https://github.com/xbill9/currency-claude-agui-a2ui1/tree/main/docs/a2ui-1-0/tools
  • A2UI v1.0 specification: https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/
  • A2UI: https://a2ui.org
  • AG-UI: https://docs.ag-ui.com
  • CopilotKit: https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit
  • Google Agent Development Kit: https://github.com/google/adk-python
  • Frankfurter API: https://www.frankfurter.dev
  • The upstream Currency Agent (A2A + ADK + MCP): https://github.com/jackwotherspoon/currency-agent

title: Website Development Rfp
description:
Website Development RFP: A Comprehensive Architectural Breakdown

As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, I have encountered numerous instances where standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms fail to meet the unique needs of businesses. This is often due to the fact that these templates are designed to cater to a wide range of users, rather than being tailored to specific requirements. In this article, we will delve into the reasons behind the ineffectiveness of generic solutions and provide concrete engineering takeaways to help businesses create a successful website development RFP.

The primary reason why standard templates and forms fail is that they lack the nuance and complexity required to accurately capture the intricacies of a business's operations. Every organization has its unique value proposition, target audience, and conversion goals, which cannot be adequately addressed by a one-size-fits-all approach. Furthermore, generic solutions often result in a lack of cohesion and consistency in the overall user experience, leading to decreased engagement and conversion rates.

From an engineering perspective, there are several key considerations that must be taken into account when developing a website development RFP. The following are three concrete takeaways:

  • Customization is key: A successful website development RFP must prioritize customization to ensure that the final product meets the specific needs of the business. This involves working closely with stakeholders to understand their unique requirements and developing a tailored solution that addresses these needs.
  • User experience is paramount: The user experience is a critical component of any website, and a successful RFP must prioritize the creation of a seamless and intuitive user interface. This involves conducting thorough user research, developing wireframes and prototypes, and testing the final product to ensure that it meets the required standards.
  • Technical infrastructure is crucial: The technical infrastructure of a website is often overlooked, but it is a critical component of any successful online presence. A well-designed technical infrastructure must be scalable, secure, and able to support the required traffic and functionality, ensuring that the website remains stable and performant over time.

In conclusion, creating a successful website development RFP requires a deep understanding of the unique needs and requirements of the business. By prioritizing customization, user experience, and technical infrastructure, businesses can create a comprehensive RFP that meets their specific needs and drives meaningful results.
Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:
https://vareli.info/blog/website-development-rfp

title: Building Ruf: an open-source SIP softphone with Rust, Tauri and Svelte
description:
I’m building Ruf, a compact, open-source SIP softphone using Rust, Tauri 2, Svelte and baresip.

It connects to an existing SIP account or telephone system. The current release is 0.1.1 Developer Preview, and I’m looking for feedback on the implementation, desktop experience and compatibility.

Keeping telephony outside the webview

The interface is built with Svelte, but SIP signaling and audio run natively through baresip.

The project has three main Rust packages:

  • phone-core contains shared contracts and validation, independently of Tauri.
  • baresip-adapter contains the native integration and C/FFI boundary.
  • sip-desktop connects the engine to Tauri commands, storage and desktop features.

TypeScript IPC contracts are generated from Rust through ts-rs.

One deliberate choice is to keep audio in a single native pipeline. Selecting a microphone, playing a ringtone and handling call audio all go through baresip the frontend doesn’t run a separate browser audio implementation.

Baresip runs inside the application process. That avoids a separate local control service, but it also means a native crash can bring down the desktop app. It’s a tradeoff worth being explicit about.

What works so far

Ruf currently includes:

  • Up to eight saved SIP accounts with a selectable outgoing identity.
  • Incoming and outgoing calls, mute, hold, DTMF, direct and attended transfers.
  • Separate microphone, call-speaker and ringtone outputs.
  • macOS contacts, local call history, tray operation and keyboard shortcuts.
  • German and English interfaces.

Passwords use macOS Keychain or Windows Credential Manager.

For testing, I use Asterisk and my UniFi setup to check calls and audio. Interface tests run separately with synthetic states.

What still needs work

The current targets are macOS 14+ on Apple Silicon and Windows 11 x64. Windows is still experimental, and I don’t have a Windows machine myself, which makes testing physical audio devices and everyday desktop behavior harder.

Linux support is planned.

This is a preview for controlled test environments. Compatibility with more telephone systems, real headsets and different network setups still needs testing. The current macOS download is not notarized, and the Windows installer is unsigned.

Free on GitHub

Ruf will remain free and open source on GitHub, with no in-app purchases.

I’m considering an optional paid Mac App Store version to help cover distribution costs. The GitHub version will remain free.

Source code, downloads and setup instructions

I’d appreciate feedback from anyone working with Rust, Tauri, desktop audio or SIP. Code reviews, usability suggestions and compatibility reports would all help.
