title: Token de API de IONOS Cloud: el DCD no es el Control Center, cuánto dura y cómo hacerlo de solo lectura
description:
La guía de IONOS Cloud de este sitio explica en cuatro pasos cómo generar el token en el DCD y pegarlo. Search Console me mostró que la gente llega con preguntas que la guía no contesta: "ionos controlcenter", "dcd ionos", "ionos api token". Las junté acá: dónde se crea cada credencial de IONOS, cuánto dura el token, cómo se arma un usuario que de verdad sólo puede leer y cómo se revoca. Todo sale de la documentación de IONOS: docs.ionos.com, la referencia de la Auth API y la de ionosctl.

DCD, Control Center y Developer Portal: tres lugares, dos credenciales

  • El DCD (Data Center Designer, dcd.ionos.com) es la consola de IONOS Cloud: data centers virtuales, servidores, LANs, IP blocks. El token de la Cloud API se genera ahí, en Menu → Management → Token Manager.
  • El panel de cliente de my.ionos.com, el que muchos buscan como "IONOS Control Center", es donde se contratan los productos. El token de la Cloud API no se crea en ese panel: el Token Manager vive en el DCD.
  • El Developer Portal de hosting (developer.hosting.ionos.com) emite otra cosa: API keys con un public prefix y un secret, que se mandan en el header X-API-Key, después de activar el acceso a la API de hosting desde my.ionos.com. Según su propia documentación, esas APIs configuran productos de hosting (dominios, DNS, SSL). Si buscabas un token para los servidores del DCD, esa key no es.

La Cloud API (https://api.ionos.com/cloudapi/v6) acepta el token como Authorization: Bearer o usuario y contraseña por Basic. El token es la opción que vence sola y se revoca sin cambiar la contraseña de nadie.

Tres formas de generar el token, y cuánto dura

Desde el DCD: Menu → Management → Token Manager → Generate Token. El TTL se elige de una lista (1 hora, 4 horas, 1, 7, 30, 60, 90, 180 o 365 días), y el valor del token se muestra una sola vez; en ese momento se puede descargar como archivo de texto. En la lista quedan el ID, la fecha de creación y la de vencimiento, nunca el valor.

Por API o con ionosctl, el TTL va en segundos (o como 30D en la CLI), con un mínimo de 60 segundos y un máximo de un año, que también es el valor por defecto si no lo pedís:

# Auth API: un token de 30 días (2.592.000 s) con usuario y contraseña
curl -s -u "$IONOS_USERNAME:$IONOS_PASSWORD" \
  "https://api.ionos.com/auth/v1/tokens/generate?ttl=2592000"

# lo mismo con ionosctl
ionosctl token generate --ttl 30D

# qué tokens tiene el usuario y cuándo vence cada uno
ionosctl token list

Dos límites que figuran en la referencia de la Auth API. La autenticación Basic de ese endpoint sólo funciona si el usuario no tiene 2FA; con 2FA, el token se genera en el Token Manager del DCD. Y hay un tope de 100 tokens activos por usuario, que un script que genera uno nuevo en cada corrida alcanza rápido. ionosctl token delete --expired limpia los vencidos.

Para una integración que sólo lee, yo elijo 90 días y anoto la fecha de vencimiento: ese día la integración deja de leer, y prefiero que pase con aviso. Un año es el valor por defecto de la API, no una recomendación.

Solo lectura: el token no tiene scopes, el usuario sí tiene límites

El token no lleva permisos propios: actúa con la identidad del usuario que lo generó. El dueño del contrato y los administradores ven y pueden modificar todo (la página Users & Groups aclara que los administradores tienen acceso a todos los recursos del contrato sin estar en ningún grupo), así que un token generado desde tu usuario administrador es un token de administrador, lo uses para lo que lo uses. Un token de lectura sale de un usuario que no es administrador: mínimo privilegio armado con el RBAC de IONOS, que la misma página describe como usuarios, grupos, privilegios y recursos compartidos. En el DCD, Menu → Management → Users & Groups:

  • Users → Create: un usuario nuevo, con su email y contraseña, sin promoverlo a administrador.
  • Groups → Create: un grupo, y en la pestaña Privileges no marcás nada. Los privilegios son acciones sobre el contrato (crear data centers, reservar IP blocks, crear snapshots o clusters de Kubernetes); un grupo de lectura no necesita ninguno.
  • Members: sumás el usuario al grupo.
  • Resources of Group → Grant Access: cada data center y cada IP block que tiene que ver. Según la documentación, asignar el recurso habilita la lectura; Edit y Share son casillas aparte, que quedan sin marcar.
  • Entrás al DCD con ese usuario y generás el token en su Token Manager. Ese es el token que va en cualquier herramienta de inventario.

Con ionosctl se arma igual. La referencia de share create dice que el share, por defecto, da acceso de lectura y uso; editar es el flag --edit-privilege:

# grupo sin privilegios, con el usuario adentro
ionosctl compute group create --name "solo-lectura"
ionosctl compute group user add --group-id "$GROUP_ID" --user-id "$USER_ID"

# IDs de los recursos que se pueden compartir
ionosctl compute resource list

# un share por data center, sin --edit-privilege ni --share-privilege
ionosctl compute share create --group-id "$GROUP_ID" --resource-id "$DATACENTER_ID"

Antes de pegarlo en ningún lado, comprobá qué es. ionosctl token parse muestra el ID del token, el usuario, el contrato y el rol, y con --privileges los privilegios de ese usuario. La Cloud API dice qué data centers ve:

ionosctl token parse --token "$IONOS_TOKEN"
ionosctl token parse --token "$IONOS_TOKEN" --privileges

# data centers visibles para este token
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $IONOS_TOKEN" \
  "https://api.ionos.com/cloudapi/v6/datacenters?depth=1" | jq -r '.items[].properties.name'

Si la lista sale vacía, el token está bien: la documentación avisa que los recursos que creó el dueño del contrato no son visibles para otros usuarios hasta que se comparten con su grupo. Falta el Grant Access de ese data center.

Las métricas son un caso aparte. La referencia de ionosctl describe el privilegio "access and manage monitoring" como acceso a métricas y gestión de alarmas. Si querés ver CPU y red de los servidores con ese usuario, es el único privilegio que le sumaría, sabiendo que con él deja de ser lectura pura.

Revocar: Token Manager, API y el detalle de 2FA

En el Token Manager, Delete invalida el token en el momento, aunque no haya vencido. Por API y CLI se borra por ID (DELETE /auth/v1/tokens/{tokenId}) o por criterio: CURRENT (el que estás usando), EXPIRED o ALL.

ionosctl token list # ID, creación y vencimiento
ionosctl token delete --token-id "$TOKEN_ID"
ionosctl token delete --expired
ionosctl token delete --current # el de IONOS_TOKEN

Con 2FA activado, la referencia de la Auth API dice que el borrado sólo se puede hacer desde el Token Manager. Y hay otra forma de cortar el acceso sin tocar el token: sacar el data center del grupo (Revoke Access en Resources of Group). El token sigue vivo, pero deja de ver ese recurso.

Lo que hace Control Cloud con ese token

El formulario de Control Cloud ofrece token o usuario y contraseña, pero el inventario y las métricas de cada organización se leen con el token, así que es lo que conviene pegar. Lo guarda cifrado y lo usa contra la Cloud API v6 para listar data centers, servidores, LANs e IP blocks y dibujarlos en el mapa, y contra la Telemetry API para las métricas de un servidor cuando abrís su panel. Con el usuario de solo lectura de arriba el mapa funciona; prender o apagar servidores desde Control Cloud necesita Edit sobre ese data center. Un detalle que salió del uso: el código detecta un token pegado dos veces seguidas y se queda con uno. El paso a paso para conectarlo está en la guía de IONOS Cloud; si querés probarlo con tu contrato, pedí acceso.

title: Token de API da IONOS Cloud: o DCD não é o Control Center, quanto tempo dura e como deixá-lo somente leitura
description:
O guia da IONOS Cloud deste site explica em quatro passos como gerar o token no DCD e colá-lo. O Search Console me mostrou que as pessoas chegam com perguntas que o guia não responde: "ionos controlcenter", "dcd ionos", "ionos api token". Juntei aqui: onde cada credencial da IONOS é criada, quanto o token dura, como montar um usuário que de fato só pode ler e como revogá-lo. Tudo sai da documentação da IONOS: docs.ionos.com, a referência da Auth API e a do ionosctl.

DCD, Control Center e Developer Portal: três lugares, duas credenciais

  • O DCD (Data Center Designer, dcd.ionos.com) é o console da IONOS Cloud: data centers virtuais, servidores, LANs, IP blocks. O token da Cloud API é gerado ali, em Menu → Management → Token Manager.
  • O painel de cliente do my.ionos.com, o que muita gente procura como "IONOS Control Center", é onde os produtos são contratados. O token da Cloud API não é criado nesse painel: o Token Manager fica no DCD.
  • O Developer Portal de hospedagem (developer.hosting.ionos.com) emite outra coisa: API keys com um public prefix e um secret, enviadas no header X-API-Key, depois de ativar o acesso à API de hospedagem pelo my.ionos.com. Segundo a própria documentação, essas APIs configuram produtos de hospedagem (domínios, DNS, SSL). Se você procurava um token para os servidores do DCD, essa key não é.

A Cloud API (https://api.ionos.com/cloudapi/v6) aceita o token como Authorization: Bearer, ou usuário e senha por Basic. O token é a opção que vence sozinha e pode ser revogada sem trocar a senha de ninguém.

Três formas de gerar o token, e quanto ele dura

Pelo DCD: Menu → Management → Token Manager → Generate Token. O TTL é escolhido de uma lista (1 hora, 4 horas, 1, 7, 30, 60, 90, 180 ou 365 dias), e o valor do token aparece uma única vez; nesse momento dá para baixá-lo como arquivo de texto. Na lista ficam o ID, a data de criação e a de vencimento, nunca o valor.

Pela API ou com o ionosctl, o TTL vai em segundos (ou como 30D na CLI), com mínimo de 60 segundos e máximo de um ano, que também é o padrão se você não pedir outro:

# Auth API: um token de 30 dias (2.592.000 s) com usuário e senha
curl -s -u "$IONOS_USERNAME:$IONOS_PASSWORD" \
  "https://api.ionos.com/auth/v1/tokens/generate?ttl=2592000"

# o mesmo com o ionosctl
ionosctl token generate --ttl 30D

# quais tokens o usuário tem e quando cada um vence
ionosctl token list

Dois limites que constam na referência da Auth API. A autenticação Basic desse endpoint só funciona se o usuário não tiver 2FA; com 2FA, o token é gerado no Token Manager do DCD. E há um teto de 100 tokens ativos por usuário, que um script que gera um novo a cada execução alcança rápido. ionosctl token delete --expired limpa os vencidos.

Para uma integração que só lê, eu escolho 90 dias e anoto a data de vencimento: nesse dia a integração para de ler, e prefiro que isso aconteça com aviso. Um ano é o padrão da API, não uma recomendação.

Somente leitura: o token não tem escopos, o usuário tem limites

O token não carrega permissões próprias: ele age com a identidade do usuário que o gerou. O dono do contrato e os administradores veem e podem modificar tudo (a página Users & Groups esclarece que administradores têm acesso a todos os recursos do contrato sem estar em nenhum grupo), então um token gerado pelo seu usuário administrador é um token de administrador, seja qual for o uso. Um token de leitura sai de um usuário que não é administrador: mínimo privilégio montado com o RBAC da IONOS, que a mesma página descreve como usuários, grupos, privilégios e recursos compartilhados. No DCD, Menu → Management → Users & Groups:

  • Users → Create: um usuário novo, com e-mail e senha, sem promovê-lo a administrador.
  • Groups → Create: um grupo, e na aba Privileges você não marca nada. Privilégios são ações sobre o contrato (criar data centers, reservar IP blocks, criar snapshots ou clusters de Kubernetes); um grupo de leitura não precisa de nenhum.
  • Members: adicione o usuário ao grupo.
  • Resources of Group → Grant Access: cada data center e cada IP block que ele deve ver. Segundo a documentação, atribuir o recurso habilita a leitura; Edit e Share são caixas à parte, que ficam desmarcadas.
  • Entre no DCD com esse usuário e gere o token no Token Manager dele. Esse é o token que vai em qualquer ferramenta de inventário.

Com o ionosctl é igual. A referência do share create diz que o share, por padrão, dá acesso de leitura e uso; editar é a flag --edit-privilege:

# grupo sem privilégios, com o usuário dentro
ionosctl compute group create --name "somente-leitura"
ionosctl compute group user add --group-id "$GROUP_ID" --user-id "$USER_ID"

# IDs dos recursos que podem ser compartilhados
ionosctl compute resource list

# um share por data center, sem --edit-privilege nem --share-privilege
ionosctl compute share create --group-id "$GROUP_ID" --resource-id "$DATACENTER_ID"

Antes de colá-lo em qualquer lugar, confira o que ele é. ionosctl token parse mostra o ID do token, o usuário, o contrato e o papel, e com --privileges os privilégios desse usuário. A Cloud API diz quais data centers ele vê:

ionosctl token parse --token "$IONOS_TOKEN"
ionosctl token parse --token "$IONOS_TOKEN" --privileges

# data centers visíveis para este token
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $IONOS_TOKEN" \
  "https://api.ionos.com/cloudapi/v6/datacenters?depth=1" | jq -r '.items[].properties.name'

Se a lista vier vazia, o token está certo: a documentação avisa que os recursos criados pelo dono do contrato não ficam visíveis para outros usuários até serem compartilhados com o grupo deles. Falta o Grant Access desse data center.

As métricas são um caso à parte. A referência do ionosctl descreve o privilégio "access and manage monitoring" como acesso a métricas e gestão de alarmes. Se você quer ver CPU e rede dos servidores com esse usuário, é o único privilégio que eu acrescentaria, sabendo que com ele o usuário deixa de ser somente leitura.

Revogar: Token Manager, API e o detalhe do 2FA

No Token Manager, Delete invalida o token na hora, mesmo que não tenha vencido. Pela API e pela CLI se apaga por ID (DELETE /auth/v1/tokens/{tokenId}) ou por critério: CURRENT (o que você está usando), EXPIRED ou ALL.

ionosctl token list # ID, criação e vencimento
ionosctl token delete --token-id "$TOKEN_ID"
ionosctl token delete --expired
ionosctl token delete --current # o de IONOS_TOKEN

Com 2FA ativado, a referência da Auth API diz que a exclusão só pode ser feita pelo Token Manager. E há outra forma de cortar o acesso sem mexer no token: tirar o data center do grupo (Revoke Access em Resources of Group). O token continua vivo, mas deixa de ver esse recurso.

O que o Control Cloud faz com esse token

O formulário do Control Cloud oferece token ou usuário e senha, mas o inventário e as métricas de cada organização são lidos com o token, então é ele que convém colar. Ele fica guardado cifrado e é usado contra a Cloud API v6 para listar data centers, servidores, LANs e IP blocks e desenhá-los no mapa, e contra a Telemetry API para as métricas de um servidor quando você abre o painel dele. Com o usuário somente leitura acima o mapa funciona; ligar ou desligar servidores pelo Control Cloud precisa de Edit nesse data center. Um detalhe que saiu do uso: o código detecta um token colado duas vezes seguidas e fica com um. O passo a passo para conectar está no guia da IONOS Cloud; se quiser testar com o seu contrato, peça acesso.

title: IONOS Cloud API token: the DCD is not the Control Center, how long it lasts and how to make it read-only
description:
This site's IONOS Cloud guide explains in four steps how to generate the token in the DCD and paste it. Search Console showed me people arrive with questions the guide does not answer: "ionos controlcenter", "dcd ionos", "ionos api token". I gathered them here: where each IONOS credential is created, how long the token lasts, how to build a user that really can only read, and how to revoke it. Everything comes from IONOS documentation: docs.ionos.com, the Auth API reference and the ionosctl reference.

DCD, Control Center and Developer Portal: three places, two credentials

  • The DCD (Data Center Designer, dcd.ionos.com) is the IONOS Cloud console: virtual data centers, servers, LANs, IP blocks. The Cloud API token is generated there, under Menu → Management → Token Manager.
  • The customer panel at my.ionos.com, the one many people search for as "IONOS Control Center", is where products are ordered. The Cloud API token is not created in that panel: the Token Manager lives in the DCD.
  • The hosting Developer Portal (developer.hosting.ionos.com) issues something else: API keys with a public prefix and a secret, sent in the X-API-Key header, after you enable API access to hosting services from my.ionos.com. According to its own documentation, those APIs configure hosting products (domains, DNS, SSL). If you wanted a token for your DCD servers, that key is not it.

The Cloud API (https://api.ionos.com/cloudapi/v6) accepts the token as Authorization: Bearer, or a username and password over Basic. The token is the option that expires on its own and can be revoked without changing anyone's password.

Three ways to generate the token, and how long it lasts

From the DCD: Menu → Management → Token Manager → Generate Token. The TTL comes from a list (1 hour, 4 hours, 1, 7, 30, 60, 90, 180 or 365 days), and the token value is shown only once; you can download it as a text file at that moment. The list keeps the ID, the creation date and the expiration date, never the value.

Through the API or ionosctl, the TTL is given in seconds (or as 30D in the CLI), with a minimum of 60 seconds and a maximum of one year, which is also the default if you do not ask for one:

# Auth API: a 30-day token (2,592,000 s) with username and password
curl -s -u "$IONOS_USERNAME:$IONOS_PASSWORD" \
  "https://api.ionos.com/auth/v1/tokens/generate?ttl=2592000"

# the same with ionosctl
ionosctl token generate --ttl 30D

# which tokens the user has and when each one expires
ionosctl token list

Two limits stated in the Auth API reference. Basic authentication on that endpoint only works if the user has no 2FA; with 2FA, the token is generated in the DCD Token Manager. And there is a cap of 100 active tokens per user, which a script that generates a new one on every run reaches quickly. ionosctl token delete --expired clears the expired ones.

For an integration that only reads, I pick 90 days and write down the expiration date: that day the integration stops reading, and I would rather it happen with a heads-up. One year is the API default, not a recommendation.

Read-only: the token has no scopes, the user has limits

The token carries no permissions of its own: it acts with the identity of the user who generated it. The contract owner and administrators can see and modify everything (the Users & Groups page notes that administrators have access to every resource in the contract without being in any group), so a token generated from your administrator user is an administrator token, whatever you use it for. A read token comes from a user who is not an administrator: least privilege built with IONOS RBAC, which the same page describes as users, groups, privileges and shared resources. In the DCD, Menu → Management → Users & Groups:

  • Users → Create: a new user, with an email and password, not promoted to administrator.
  • Groups → Create: a group, and on the Privileges tab you tick nothing. Privileges are contract-wide actions (create data centers, reserve IP blocks, create snapshots or Kubernetes clusters); a read group needs none of them.
  • Members: add the user to the group.
  • Resources of Group → Grant Access: every data center and IP block it should see. According to the documentation, assigning the resource enables read access; Edit and Share are separate checkboxes that stay unticked.
  • Log in to the DCD as that user and generate the token in its Token Manager. That is the token that goes into any inventory tool.

With ionosctl it is the same. The share create reference says a share grants read/use access by default; editing is the --edit-privilege flag:

# a group with no privileges, with the user in it
ionosctl compute group create --name "read-only"
ionosctl compute group user add --group-id "$GROUP_ID" --user-id "$USER_ID"

# IDs of the resources that can be shared
ionosctl compute resource list

# one share per data center, without --edit-privilege or --share-privilege
ionosctl compute share create --group-id "$GROUP_ID" --resource-id "$DATACENTER_ID"

Before pasting it anywhere, check what it is. ionosctl token parse shows the token ID, the user, the contract and the role, and with --privileges that user's privileges. The Cloud API tells you which data centers it sees:

ionosctl token parse --token "$IONOS_TOKEN"
ionosctl token parse --token "$IONOS_TOKEN" --privileges

# data centers visible to this token
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $IONOS_TOKEN" \
  "https://api.ionos.com/cloudapi/v6/datacenters?depth=1" | jq -r '.items[].properties.name'

If the list comes back empty, the token is fine: the documentation warns that resources created by the contract owner are not visible to other users until they are shared with their group. The Grant Access for that data center is missing.

Metrics are a separate case. The ionosctl reference describes the "access and manage monitoring" privilege as access to metrics and alarm management. If you want to see the servers' CPU and network with that user, it is the only privilege I would add, knowing that with it the user is no longer purely read-only.

Revoking: Token Manager, API and the 2FA detail

In the Token Manager, Delete invalidates the token immediately, even if it has not expired. Through the API and the CLI you delete by ID (DELETE /auth/v1/tokens/{tokenId}) or by criteria: CURRENT (the one you are using), EXPIRED or ALL.

ionosctl token list # ID, creation and expiration
ionosctl token delete --token-id "$TOKEN_ID"
ionosctl token delete --expired
ionosctl token delete --current # the one in IONOS_TOKEN

With 2FA enabled, the Auth API reference says deletion can only be done from the Token Manager. And there is another way to cut access without touching the token: remove the data center from the group (Revoke Access in Resources of Group). The token stays alive, but it stops seeing that resource.

What Control Cloud does with that token

The Control Cloud form offers a token or a username and password, but each organization's inventory and metrics are read with the token, so that is what to paste. It is stored encrypted and used against Cloud API v6 to list data centers, servers, LANs and IP blocks and draw them on the map, and against the Telemetry API for a server's metrics when you open its panel. With the read-only user above the map works; starting or stopping servers from Control Cloud needs Edit on that data center. One detail that came from real use: the code detects a token pasted twice in a row and keeps one. The step-by-step to connect it is in the IONOS Cloud guide; if you want to try it with your contract, request access.

title: Kafka Streams API
description:
Taming the Real-Time Data Beast: A Deep Dive into Kafka Streams API

So, you've got data. Lots of it. And it's not just sitting there, is it? It's moving. Streaming. Flowing in like a digital river, carrying valuable insights, user actions, and system events. In today's world, waiting for batch processing is like trying to catch a train after it's left the station – you'll miss the crucial moments. This is where the magic of real-time data processing comes in, and at the heart of this revolution for many lies the Kafka Streams API.

If you're already swimming in the Kafka ecosystem, you know it's a powerful beast for ingesting and storing massive amounts of data. But what if you want to do something with that data as it arrives? That's where Kafka Streams steps onto the stage, not as a clumsy sidekick, but as a sophisticated conductor, orchestrating your data streams into meaningful actions and insights, all without leaving your beloved Kafka.

This article is your friendly guide to understanding Kafka Streams API. We'll demystify its concepts, peek under the hood, and see why it's become a go-to solution for many real-time processing needs.

What's the Big Idea? Why Kafka Streams?

Imagine you're running an e-commerce platform. Orders are coming in, products are being viewed, customers are adding items to their carts. You don't want to wait until the end of the day to know which products are trending, or if a customer is about to abandon their cart. You want to react now.

This is the domain of stream processing. And Kafka Streams is essentially a client library that lets you build distributed applications and microservices that process data stored in Kafka topics. Think of it as a set of powerful tools that empower you to read from Kafka, transform that data, and write the results back to Kafka, or to external systems. The beauty is that it does all this in a fault-tolerant and scalable manner, leveraging the robust foundation of Apache Kafka.

Getting Your Hands Dirty: Prerequisites

Before we dive headfirst into the code and concepts, let's make sure you're prepped. You don't need a PhD in distributed systems, but a basic understanding will go a long way.

  • Java Knowledge: Kafka Streams is primarily a Java library, so being comfortable with Java (and ideally some object-oriented programming principles) is essential. You'll be writing Java code, so get ready to embrace the JVM.
  • Apache Kafka Fundamentals: You should have a grasp of core Kafka concepts:
    • Producers and Consumers: How data gets into and out of Kafka.
    • Topics: The streams of data.
    • Partitions: The units of parallelism within topics.
    • Brokers: The Kafka servers themselves.
    • Zookeeper (or KRaft): For cluster coordination (though KRaft is becoming the preferred way). Understanding these will make the "why" behind Kafka Streams' design much clearer.
  • Maven or Gradle: You'll need a build tool to manage your dependencies. Maven and Gradle are the standard choices in the Java world.
  • A Running Kafka Cluster: You'll need a local or remote Kafka cluster to experiment with. Docker Compose is a fantastic way to spin up a local Kafka instance for development.

The Core Concepts: Building Blocks of Your Stream Processing Empire

Kafka Streams isn't just about writing some Java code. It introduces a few key concepts that are crucial to grasp:

1. Streams and Tables: The Dual Nature of Data

This is arguably the most important concept in Kafka Streams. Data in Kafka can be viewed in two ways:

  • Stream (KStream): This represents an unbounded, continuously updating sequence of records. Think of it as a log of events. Each record is an independent piece of data, like an order event, a click, or a sensor reading. When you read from a Kafka topic, you're primarily dealing with a KStream.
    • Example: A stream of incoming user clicks on your website.
  • Table (KTable): This represents a changelog stream, where each update to a record effectively overwrites the previous version. It's like a database table where you can query the current state. In Kafka Streams, a KTable is often derived from a KStream by performing a stateful operation, like aggregating events.
    • Example: A table representing the current count of product views for each product ID. Each new view updates the existing count.

These two abstractions are not mutually exclusive; in fact, they often work hand-in-hand. You can transform a KStream into a KTable and vice-versa. This duality is key to modeling real-world data scenarios.

2. Kafka Streams DSL: Your Toolkit for Transformation

Kafka Streams provides a high-level Domain Specific Language (DSL) that makes it easy to express stream processing operations. This DSL is built upon the lower-level Processor API, but for most use cases, the DSL is your best friend. It offers a fluent, chainable API for common operations.

Here are some of the core DSL operations you'll encounter:

  • map and mapValues: Transform each record's key and/or value.

    KStream<String, String> sourceStream = builder.stream("input-topic");

// Transform the value of each record
KStream<String, String> mappedStream = sourceStream.mapValues(value -> value.toUpperCase());

  • filter and filterNot: Select records based on a condition.

    KStream<String, String> filteredStream = mappedStream.filter((key, value) -> value.length() > 10);

  • flatMap and flatMapValues: Transform a record into zero, one, or more records. Useful for splitting strings or extracting multiple values.

    KStream<String, String> wordsStream = sourceStream.flatMapValues(value -> Arrays.asList(value.split(" ")));

  • groupByKey and groupBy: Group records by their keys. Essential for stateful operations. groupBy allows you to define a new key for grouping.

    KTable<String, Long> wordCounts = wordsStream
    .groupBy((key, value) -> value) // Group by the word itself
    .count(Materialized.as("word-counts-store")); // Aggregate to count occurrences

  • reduce and aggregate: Perform stateful aggregations. reduce is simpler, while aggregate offers more control.

    // Example using reduce for summing values (simplified)
KTable<String, Integer> sumTable = sourceStream
    .groupByKey()
    .reduce((value1, value2) -> value1 + value2);

  • join: Combine records from two different streams or tables based on a common key. This is where the real magic happens for correlating data.

    KStream<String, UserInfo> userStream = builder.stream("user-topic");
KStream<String, OrderInfo> orderStream = builder.stream("order-topic");

KStream<String, JoinedInfo> joinedStream = userStream.join(
    orderStream,
    (userInfo, orderInfo) -> new JoinedInfo(userInfo, orderInfo),
    JoinWindows.of(Duration.ofMinutes(5)), // Window for time-based joins
    Serdes.String(), // Key Serde
    new JoinedUserInfoOrderInfoSerde() // Value Serde
);

  • windowed operations: These are crucial for performing aggregations or joins over time windows (e.g., "count clicks in the last 5 minutes"). You'll see concepts like TumblingWindows, HoppingWindows, and SessionWindows.

3. State Stores: Remembering for Stateful Operations

Many stream processing operations (like aggregations, joins, and filtering based on history) require the application to remember past events. This is where state stores come into play. Kafka Streams manages these state stores locally within your application instances.

  • Local State: State stores are typically backed by embedded key-value stores like RocksDB. This provides fast, in-memory access for your operations.
  • Fault Tolerance: Importantly, Kafka Streams also captures all changes to the state stores in Kafka changelog topics. This ensures that if an application instance crashes, its state can be rebuilt from the changelog topic when it restarts or when a new instance takes over. This is a fundamental aspect of Kafka Streams' fault tolerance.

You'll often interact with state stores implicitly through operations like count(), reduce(), or aggregate(). You can also explicitly manage them using the Processor API.

4. Kafka Streams Builder: The Architect of Your Application

The StreamsBuilder is your entry point to defining your Kafka Streams application. You use it to create KStream and KTable instances from Kafka topics and then chain together the DSL operations to build your processing topology.

import org.apache.kafka.streams.StreamsBuilder;
import org.apache.kafka.streams.Topology;
import org.apache.kafka.streams.kstream.KStream;

public class WordCountApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StreamsBuilder builder = new StreamsBuilder();

        // Define the processing topology
        KStream<String, String> textLines = builder.stream("input-topic");

        KTable<String, Long> wordCounts = textLines
            .flatMapValues(text -> Arrays.asList(text.toLowerCase().split("\\W+")))
            .groupBy((key, word) -> word)
            .count(Materialized.as("counts-store")); // Materialized view for the count

        wordCounts.toStream().to("output-topic", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()));

        Topology topology = builder.build();

        // ... (Code to run the Kafka Streams application)
    }
}

Advantages: Why Fall in Love with Kafka Streams?

So, what makes Kafka Streams so appealing?

  • Lightweight and Simple: Compared to heavier stream processing frameworks, Kafka Streams is a Java library. This means no separate cluster to manage, no complex deployments. Your stream processing logic lives alongside your other application code.
  • Tight Kafka Integration: It's built by the Kafka team, for Kafka. This means seamless integration, leveraging Kafka's strengths for data ingestion, storage, and fault tolerance. You're not bolted on; you're part of the family.
  • Scalability and Elasticity: Kafka Streams applications are inherently scalable. You can run multiple instances of your application, and Kafka Streams will automatically distribute the processing load across them based on Kafka partitions. Need more processing power? Just add more instances!
  • Fault Tolerance: As mentioned with state stores, Kafka Streams is designed for fault tolerance. If an application instance fails, its tasks are automatically reassigned to other healthy instances, with minimal data loss thanks to changelog topics.
  • Exactly-Once Processing Semantics (EOS): Kafka Streams supports exactly-once processing semantics, meaning each record will be processed exactly once, even in the face of failures. This is a critical guarantee for many mission-critical applications.
  • Low Latency: Designed for real-time processing, Kafka Streams offers very low end-to-end latency, making it suitable for interactive applications and immediate decision-making.
  • Rich API: The DSL provides a powerful and expressive way to define complex processing logic without diving into the low-level details.

Disadvantages: The Not-So-Glamorous Side

No technology is perfect, and Kafka Streams has its limitations:

  • Java-Centric: If your team isn't proficient in Java, or your organization prefers other languages, this can be a barrier. While there are community efforts for other languages, Java is the primary and most well-supported option.
  • Limited to Kafka as a Source/Sink: Kafka Streams is designed to work with Kafka. While you can write to external systems, the core processing happens between Kafka topics. For complex integrations with a multitude of external systems as primary sources/sinks, other frameworks might offer more built-in connectors.
  • State Management Complexity: While powerful, managing state can become complex for very intricate scenarios. Understanding state store rebalancing, restores, and potential performance bottlenecks is crucial for large-scale deployments.
  • No Built-in UI for Monitoring: Unlike some dedicated stream processing platforms, Kafka Streams doesn't come with a comprehensive built-in UI for monitoring and debugging. You'll rely on Kafka's own monitoring tools and potentially custom dashboards.
  • Learning Curve for Advanced Features: While the DSL is intuitive, mastering advanced concepts like custom processors, interactive queries, and detailed state management can require a significant learning investment.

Features that Make You Go "Wow!"

Let's highlight some of the standout features:

  • Interactive Queries: This is a game-changer. It allows your applications to directly query the local state stores of running Kafka Streams instances. Imagine asking your application, "What's the current count of product X?" – and getting an instant answer! This enables building rich, real-time UIs or dashboards that can directly access processed data.

    // Example of querying a local state store
KafkaStreams streams = new KafkaStreams(topology, streamsConfig);
streams.start();

// Get a handle to the queryable state store
ReadOnlyKeyValueStore<String, Long> countStore = streams.store("counts-store", QueryableStoreTypes.keyValueStore());

// Query the store
Long countForWord = countStore.get("your-word");

  • Kafka Streams DSL Extensions: Beyond the basic DSL, you can leverage extensions for more specialized tasks, like windowing, aggregations with different merging strategies, and more.

  • Processor API for Customization: For situations where the DSL isn't flexible enough, the lower-level Processor API gives you fine-grained control over how data flows through your application and how state is managed.

  • Stream-Table Duality and Conversions: The ability to seamlessly convert between KStream and KTable and perform operations like toStream() and toTable() makes modeling complex data transformations intuitive.

  • Serde Management: Kafka Streams relies on Serializers/Deserializers (Serdes) to convert your Java objects into bytes for Kafka and back. It provides built-in Serdes for common types and allows you to define custom ones.

When to Choose Kafka Streams?

Kafka Streams shines brightest in these scenarios:

  • Real-time Microservices: Building microservices that need to react to events as they happen, like fraud detection, real-time recommendations, or personalized user experiences.
  • Data Enrichment and Transformation: Augmenting incoming data with external information or transforming it into a more usable format before storing or further processing.
  • Stream Analytics and Aggregations: Performing calculations, aggregations, and windowed analysis on high-volume, real-time data streams.
  • Event-Driven Architectures: Acting as the backbone of an event-driven system, where components communicate and react to events flowing through Kafka.
  • When You're Already Invested in Kafka: If you're already using Kafka extensively, Kafka Streams is a natural extension that allows you to leverage your existing infrastructure and expertise.

Beyond the Basics: A Glimpse into Advanced Usage

As you delve deeper, you'll encounter:

  • Custom Processors and Sources/Sinks: For ultimate flexibility, you can write your own Processor, Source, and Sink implementations to integrate with any system or perform highly custom logic.
  • Interactive Queries for Real-time Dashboards: Imagine a dashboard that shows live metrics directly from your stream processing application, powered by interactive queries.
  • Complex Event Processing (CEP): While not a full-blown CEP engine, Kafka Streams can be used to detect patterns of events over time, enabling sophisticated event correlation.
  • Testing Strategies: Unit and integration testing your Kafka Streams applications is crucial. You'll learn about the TopologyTestDriver for simulating Kafka input and verifying output.

Conclusion: Your Real-Time Data Companion

Kafka Streams API is a powerful and elegant solution for building real-time data processing applications within the Apache Kafka ecosystem. Its lightweight nature, deep integration with Kafka, and robust feature set make it an attractive choice for developers looking to harness the power of streaming data.

While it has its limitations, particularly its Java-centric nature, the advantages it offers in terms of scalability, fault tolerance, and ease of development for many common stream processing tasks are undeniable. By understanding the core concepts of streams, tables, state stores, and the DSL, you'll be well on your way to taming the real-time data beast and unlocking valuable insights and actions from your flowing data. So, go forth, experiment, and build something amazing with Kafka Streams!

title: Treat agent-suggested any / as casts on UI props as a merge blocker
description:
The component compiles. That’s because the agent wrote props as any, or value as string, or sprinkled // @ts-expect-error on a <Select> that now takes a number. The runtime still blows up when the form submits "".

I’ve started treating new any / as on UI props as a merge blocker, not a typing nit. The cast is often hiding the actual bug the PR was supposed to fix.

Where the casts show up

Typical patterns in agent diffs:

  • ...(props as any) to spread into a design-system component
  • onChange={(e: any) => ...} because the event type didn’t match
  • items as Foo[] after a filter that TypeScript correctly widened
  • <Button {...(rest as ButtonProps)}> when rest still contains a href
  • as unknown as Props — two casts, still one lie

Agents do this when the types are right and the call site is wrong, or when a union wasn’t narrowed. A cast makes the screenshot possible. It does not make the state valid.

A simple policy

  • No new any, as any, or as unknown as on component props, event handlers, or JSX spreads in feature UI
  • as is allowed only for a documented boundary (a JSON parse you already validate, a DOM API, a test fixture) and must sit next to that validation
  • @ts-expect-error needs a one-line reason and a follow-up; it is not a way to land a Select
  • If the system component’s types are wrong, fix or wrap that type in a named helper — don’t punch through at every call site

Existing casts in untouched lines can stay until you edit that component. New ones in the diff should justify themselves.

What to put in the prompt 

Do not use `any`, `as any`, `as unknown as`, or empty
@ts-expect-error to make this UI compile. If props don’t
match, change the component’s prop type or the caller.
If you must assert, name the type and explain the runtime
check that makes it safe. Prefer narrowing (typeof, in,
discriminated unions) over casts.

Paste the existing prop type and one correct call site. The agent is much less likely to invent as any when it can see a working example.

How to catch it in review 

git diff -U0 -- '*.ts' '*.tsx' | rg -n "\bas any\b|as unknown as|: any\b|@ts-expect-error|@ts-ignore"

For each hit in the new hunks:

  1. Is there a runtime check next to it?
  2. Could a narrowed type or a better prop definition remove it?
  3. If it’s on a JSX spread, what extra keys might leak through?

CI can fail on new : any / as any in src/ (a simple diff grep, or @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any on changed files). Use that if the team already agrees. Review still catches as SomeType that is merely hopeful.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • as any / as unknown as on props to “just get it compiling”
  • Event handlers typed as any to skip ChangeEvent
  • Spreading an object into a component through a cast because it has extra fields
  • A new // @ts-expect-error with no reason

Accept

  • A tightened prop type, or a caller that now passes the right union member
  • A named, validated boundary (parseResult.data after Zod / Valibot)
  • An existing cast you didn’t touch, called out if you’re aware of it

Tiny habit

When the agent’s UI PR “compiles now,” search the diff for any and as. If a cast appeared to paper over a prop mismatch, send it back and ask for a real type fix. The compiler was trying to help. Don’t disable it in the JSX.

title: Long Live Rails
description:
When DHH took the stage at Rails World 2026 and talked openly about going "pencils down" on hand-typing code—and about just how much Rust he and 37signals are shipping now—a predictable subset of the internet treated it like a concession speech.

Even the creator of Ruby on Rails, who joked in the same breath that reading Rust is like "pouring acid in my eyes," was raving about 30x to 100x speedups, minuscule binaries, and sub-millisecond startups once AI agents handle the borrow checker. If he is reaching for Rust, what does that say about Ruby and Rails?

I think that reaction gets the story completely backwards.

Over the past month on Forem (the Rails monolith that powers DEV), we have been gradually replacing dozens of our own internal Ruby modules with Rust. As I wrote in Our Looping Factory Cut DEV Page Load Time by 75% and Counting, one of the autonomous workflows running continuously against our codebase is a dedicated rust-loop that ports CPU-bound and allocation-heavy Ruby hot paths into an in-process Rust extension (gems/forem_native) via magnus and rb-sys.

Far from making me question Rails, watching this happen in production has made me appreciate Rails more than ever. The fact that dropping Rust into a Rails codebase is this accessible is a feature, not a bug.

Rust inside the monolith is a superpower

There used to be an unspoken cliff in dynamic web frameworks: Ruby got you to product-market fit with unmatched developer happiness, and then the day your string parsing, feed scoring, or serialization paths started choking the garbage collector, someone pitched splitting off a Go or Rust microservice. Suddenly one cohesive application became two deployments, a network hop, duplicate auth assumptions, and an operational tax you paid forever.

Today, that cliff is mostly gone—both ergonomically and architecturally.

Inside Forem, we split gems/forem_native into a pure-Rust forem_core crate (with zero Ruby dependencies) and a ~15-line-per-function magnus wrapper that borrows Ruby string buffers in place with zero serialization or memory copies. Our rust-loop—monitored alongside eight other maintenance loops in the control panel I described in Ask More of Your UI—has steadily moved hot leaf and pipeline modules over to Rust:

  • Markdown pre-processing, frontmatter normalization, and reading-time tokenization (~54x faster with zero Ruby heap allocations).
  • Home feed ranking and dynamic pgvector SQL expression assembly (~20x faster with 97% fewer Ruby objects allocated).
  • HTML sanitization, inline SVG icon rendering, @username mention parsing, URL normalization, Public Suffix subdomain routing, constant-time CSRF/JWT verification, and 51-pattern secret scrubbing on agent transcripts.
  • Entire pure-Ruby dependencies (gemoji, emoji_regex, wcag_color_contrast) deleted outright from our Gemfile.

And yet nobody cloning Forem needs cargo installed to run bin/dev. Tiny (~300 KB) precompiled platform binaries load in under a millisecond on macOS and Linux, our Containerfile compiles a stripped shared library in a multi-stage builder with zero Rust toolchain left in the production image, and every ported function is locked down by RSpec differential specs testing 1,000+ randomized inputs against the legacy Ruby reference.

In Design for Churn, I argued that AI-era codebases behave less like static buildings and more like gardens: when rewriting implementation code gets cheap, your real investment goes into the perennial beds—the schemas, routing, boundaries, and contracts that hold steady while the annuals inside them turn over. (It is the same principle we used when bringing System One models like Jev into our AI stack: keep the policy and domain structure clean in Ruby, and swap in specialized engines underneath.)

Rails is the perennial bed. As @techie_raj captured well in Your Rails App Is Already AI-Ready. You Just Don't Know It., twenty years of shared conventions—config/routes.rb, app/services/, declarative Active Record scopes, self-describing background jobs—gave Rails a legibility that both new hires and coding agents navigate effortlessly. And as @ttebify noted in Rust is amazing, as long as I’m not the one writing it, strict compilers give agents a tight, unforgiving feedback loop for low-level compute. Pairing Rails' high-level coherence with Rust's bare-metal leaves isn't abandoning Rails—it's Rails doing what it has always done best: orchestrating the whole system cleanly while getting out of the way when native speed matters.

Making the intuitive thing first-class

If you want a concrete example of why Rails keeps winning over the long arc, look at this gem of an addition landing in Rails 8.2 (already backported to Rails 7.2, 8.0, and 8.1 via rails-query-command):

// Detect dark theme var iframe = document.getElementById('tweet-2120569126150127666-369'); if (document.body.className.includes('dark-theme')) { iframe.src = "https://platform.twitter.com/embed/Tweet.html?id=2120569126150127666&theme=dark" }

Every team putting AI coding agents to real work eventually runs into the exact same wall: agents reading static source files in isolation guess wrong about production bottlenecks, and you obviously cannot hand an autonomous agent an unrestricted rails console or rails runner against live data. (I wrote recently in AI Engineering Has Entered Its Audit Era about how scoping agent authority and proving output has become the real engineering work, a theme @oleksandr_sainchuk also explored on the write side in How we keep AI agent actions under server side control in rails.)

At Forem, unlocking our 70ms-to-16ms latency drop required building our own bespoke workaround for this: a read-only Postgres gateway (forem-db-query) wrapped in a privacy guard so our performance loops could inspect live query plans, sequential scans, and row distributions safely before touching a line of code. Plenty of other teams have quietly cobbled together their own read-only wrappers, MCP tools, or custom rake tasks to solve the exact same problem.

Even when we and others already have workarounds for something like this, the whole point of Rails is that it makes intuitive, necessary things first-class in a way that pays off in the long run.

When bin/rails query becomes a standard verb across the entire ecosystem—read-only by contract, emitting structured JSON, with schema, models, and explain built right in—twenty bespoke team scripts collapse into one shared convention. Every developer, every operational runbook, and every coding agent immediately knows how to ask a Rails app a safe question about its data.

Meeting the moment

Frameworks fade when they treat their boundaries like a purity test—insisting that every problem must be solved in one language, or ignoring how software is actually being built today.

Rails has lasted, and continues to lead, because its core competency has never just been Ruby syntax. Its core competency is taste and integration: looking at the messy, pragmatic things developers actually need to ship—from migrations, background jobs, and zero-downtime Kamal deploys to painless native Rust extensions and agent-safe database introspection—and pulling them together into defaults that feel obvious in hindsight.

We are going to keep replacing hot compute loops with Rust where it makes DEV faster. And we are going to keep doing it happily inside a Rails monolith that keeps rising to meet the moment.

Long live Rails and Happy Coding ❤️

title: What Is Cloud Telephony? How It Works and the Rules That Apply
description:
"Cloud telephony" covers products that have very little in common, from a hosted PBX to a raw voice API. This post follows one call through the stack, separates what's sold under the name, works out what media location does to delay, and maps the rules that apply.

Cloud telephony is a business phone service whose switching, call logic, and media processing run on a provider's servers instead of hardware at your site. Calls still reach ordinary phones through telecom operators. You manage everything through a console or API, and you pay by usage or per seat rather than buying a PBX.

This guide follows one call through the stack, separates the products sold under this name, works out what media location does to delay, and maps the rules that apply, each linked to its source.

Note: Key takeaways

  • Cloud telephony moves the switch, not the phone network. Your calls still cross operator networks, so numbers, caller ID, and telecom rules all still apply.
  • The name covers several products. Hosted PBX, contact centre software, voice APIs, and SIP trunks leave very different work with your team.
  • Media location sets delay. In our illustrative example, sending Frankfurt-to-Frankfurt audio through Virginia lifts one-way delay from about 91 ms to about 175 ms.
  • Your own application becomes part of the call path. On a programmable service, a slow webhook (callback) means silence for the caller.
  • Telecom rules still apply. Authorisation, number series, automated-call rules, and data laws vary by country, and several changed in 2026.

What is cloud telephony?

Cloud telephony means renting the brain of a phone system as a service. The provider runs the software that decides where each call goes, and you reach that software through a browser or an API.

Something else stays exactly as it was. A customer calling your number from a mobile phone still uses their operator's network, and the provider connects to that network at its edge. Only the part that used to sit in your server room has moved.

The term is loose, and sources use it differently. TechTarget files it under unified communications as a service and separates shared multi-tenant platforms from dedicated hosted setups. Vendors in markets such as India often frame it around virtual numbers, call flows, APIs, and a dashboard. Both are describing real products, so ask which one a vendor means before you compare prices.

How does a cloud telephony call work?

Every call runs on two separate tracks. SIP and your application decide what should happen, and RTP carries the sound. The diagram follows one inbound call, and the steps below match its numbers.

  1. The caller dials your number. Your DID routes to the provider, so the operator network hands the call to the provider's interconnect.
  2. The edge admits it. A session border controller sits between the outside network and the provider's core. RFC 5853 catalogues the jobs these devices do, including topology hiding and NAT traversal.
  3. Call control decides. It looks up what your number should do. A hosted product runs a flow you built in its dashboard. A programmable service sends a webhook (callback) to your server and waits for instructions.
  4. The media server handles audio. It plays prompts, collects keypresses, records, and can copy audio to another system.
  5. A second leg connects the other party. That can be a mobile number, a softphone, a browser, or an AI agent. Each adds a call leg with its own state.
  6. The call ends and leaves a record. The provider writes a call record with duration, hangup cause, and quality data, and then notifies your application.

An outbound call runs the same stack in reverse: your API request or dialler starts at call control, and the operator network delivers the call last.

What this design adds to your failure list

A PBX in your building fails in familiar ways. A cloud stack adds an HTTP dependency and a longer audio path, so each stage has its own signature:

Stage Depends on What the caller notices when it fails
Operator to provider Interconnect and number routing The call never connects, or the caller hears a network message
Provider to your application Your server's reachability and response time Silence after answer, or the call drops
Media path Packet loss, jitter, and distance Clipped words, one-way audio, or people talking over each other
Agent leg The agent's network or mobile coverage The caller waits, or the transfer fails
Capacity Concurrent-call and calls-per-second limits A busy tone, or a campaign that runs slowly

Which products count as cloud telephony?

Four product families use the label, and each one divides the work differently. The first column in this matrix is the on-site PBX they replace or connect to.

  • Hosted PBX (UCaaS) replaces office extensions, usually with desk phones or softphone apps, and often bundles chat and video.
  • Contact centre software (CCaaS) adds queues, agent desktops, supervisor views, and reporting, so your team can start without building anything.
  • A voice API (CPaaS) gives you numbers, call control, and media as building blocks. You write the logic and the interface.
  • SIP trunking supplies only the carrier connection. Your PBX or AI stack stays in charge of the call.

The billing model tends to follow the split. Retell's guide describes per-user monthly subscriptions, while other services bill pay-as-you-go. As a rule of thumb, seat pricing grows with headcount and usage pricing grows with minutes, so model both against your own traffic.

How does cloud telephony differ from VoIP, PBX, SIP, and IVR?

These terms get compared as rivals, yet they answer different questions. Cloud telephony describes where the system runs, and the others describe a technology, a function, or a feature.

Term What kind of thing it is How it relates to cloud telephony
VoIP A way to carry voice as IP packets Almost always used inside it, though VoIP can also run on-site
SIP A signalling protocol One common way to set up its calls
SIP trunk A carrier connection One of the products sold under the label
PBX The function of switching calls inside an organisation Runs at your site, or in the cloud as a hosted PBX
IVR A menu feature on a call A feature that usually runs on the provider's media servers
Cloud telephony A delivery model The umbrella over the products above

So "VoIP or cloud telephony?" is rarely the real choice. The useful question is which layers you want to run yourself.

Which cloud telephony model should you choose?

Start from what you already own and who drives the calls. The map below handles most cases in three questions.

Three situations deserve a second look:

  • You need a contact centre with unusual routing. Ready-made software suits standard flows. Once your routing depends on your own data, a custom contact centre on an API may fit better, at the cost of building the agent interface.
  • You are building voice AI. Your AI platform often decides this for you. SIP or WebSocket streaming each suit different stacks, so check what your platform supports first.
  • You are migrating in stages. Some organisations run hybrid setups during a longer cloud migration. A SIP trunk lets you keep a PBX while you move teams across one at a time.

Where should the media run?

Distance matters more on a phone call than on most web traffic, because neither person can wait for a retransmission. ITU-T G.114, a 2003 Recommendation still listed as in force, says most applications get essentially transparent interactivity below 150 ms of one-way delay. It treats 400 ms as the ceiling for general network planning.

Consider a Frankfurt caller talking to a Frankfurt agent. Both legs of that call meet at the media server, so its location sets the path length.

Only the distance segment is calculated. G.114 gives a planning figure of 5 µs per km for optical fibre. Frankfurt to northern Virginia is about 6,550 km on a great circle, and we assumed routes run 30% longer. The round trip through Virginia therefore covers about 17,000 km and adds about 85 ms. The other segments are round assumptions, so measure your own path before you rely on these totals.

Choosing how agents connect

Agents don't all need the internet. Reaching them over the phone network moves the dependency from your office link to mobile coverage.

Agent connection Network it depends on Best when Watch for
Mobile number over PSTN The agent's mobile coverage Field teams and work from home A second call leg on every conversation, and less control over the handset
SIP softphone or desk phone Your office or home broadband Fixed teams with a managed network Firewall rules and NAT
Browser over WebRTC The agent's broadband Click-to-call inside your CRM Headsets, browser permissions, and Wi-Fi quality
AI agent over SIP or a stream The link between provider and your AI stack Automated conversations AI processing time adds to the network delay above

TRAI's February 2025 numbering recommendations put a SIP call at about 87 kbps with G.711 and 32 kbps with G.729. At those rates, 40 softphone agents on calls at once need about 3.5 Mbps with G.711 or 1.3 Mbps with G.729, by our arithmetic. Budget that in each direction, and leave headroom.

Sizing capacity

Cloud telephony removes hardware limits, but contractual ones remain. Two numbers cap you: concurrent calls and calls per second. Our SIP trunking guide works through the Erlang B math for inbound lines and the rate calculation for diallers, and both apply to any model here.

What rules apply to cloud telephony?

The call flow is the same everywhere, but the rules around it vary by country, and they change often. Check these points for each market you call:

  • Provider authorisation. Many countries license who may sell hosted voice. India, for example, lists cloud-based EPABX under its enterprise communication service authorisation.
  • Number series and telemarketing. Some regulators reserve series by call type. If you're in India, promotions use 140xx and regulated service calls use 1600xx (TRAI, July 2026).
  • Automated calls. Rules such as the US TCPA cover calls started by software. India's Third Amendment adds an advance declaration of application-initiated calls.
  • Where the media runs. Some countries restrict carrying domestic calls abroad or between networks. India's OSP guidelines treat some of this as toll bypass.
  • Recordings and personal data. Privacy laws such as the EU's GDPR, or India's DPDP Rules, set notice and retention duties.

Confirm the current text and take legal advice for your case.

What should you ask a cloud telephony provider?

Feature lists look alike across vendors, so these questions test the parts that are harder to change later. Skip any that don't match your model.

Question Why it matters
Which authorisation or licence covers the service you're selling me? Your supply chain depends on it, and the framework is mid-migration
Where does media run on calls in each country I serve? It sets delay, and it can decide whether a call is allowed
How do I declare A2P use, and who records it? Undeclared calls count as unsolicited once the rule starts
Which number series do I get for each call type? The wrong series is a compliance problem, not only a routing one
What name will my calls display? Caller name display now depends on subscriber records
What happens when my webhook fails or times out? This decides whether a bad deploy drops live calls
Do I get MOS, jitter, and packet loss for each call? You can't fix quality that you can't see
How are concurrency and CPS sold, and what happens at the limit? Callers hear busy tones at the ceiling
Where do recordings live, and for how long? It feeds your retention and consent decisions

How Vobiz handles cloud telephony

Vobiz is a programmable voice platform, so it sits in the voice API and SIP trunking columns of the matrix above. You build the logic and connect the systems you already use.

  • Numbers. Buy a number in the console or over the API. India number KYC comes before renting Indian numbers.
  • Call logic with VobizXML. A Vobiz application ties a number to your server. Vobiz requests instructions from your Answer URL, and it executes the VobizXML you return. A Fallback Answer URL takes over if the primary returns a 5xx error or times out, and the best-practices page asks you to respond within 1 to 2 seconds.
  • Call control over REST. The Call API places, transfers, records, and ends calls authenticated with your Auth ID and Auth Token.
  • SIP trunks. Vobiz SIP trunking connects a PBX, AI agent, or VoIP stack, with trunks for outbound and inbound.
  • Agent legs. The dial instruction bridges to a PSTN number or SIP user. Registered soft-phones and WebRTC clients use endpoints, and the WebRTC Playground lets you try browser calling.
  • Media. Audio Streams forks live call audio to your WebSocket server, with a bidirectional mode for AI agents. Recordings stay available for 30 days, and you can export them as an archive before that window closes.
  • Quality data. Each call detail record reports call-quality scores, jitter, packet loss, and the codec.
  • Capacity. Concurrency and CPS are separate account limits. The CPS and concurrency calculator helps you model a campaign.
  • Campaigns and tenants. Campaigns run bulk outbound dialling with retries and per-attempt logs. Sub-accounts give each customer or team its own credentials, numbers, and usage.
  • Integrations. Vobiz integrations cover CRMs such as Salesforce and HubSpot, and voice AI platforms such as LiveKit and Vapi.
  • India. Calling regulations cover KYC, caller ID, and media anchoring, under which both legs of an Indian call stay in India. A call that breaks this fails with the Violates Media Anchoring hangup cause. The UCC page, 140 and 160 series guide, and DLT registration guide cover commercial calling.
  • Pricing and reach. Current rates are on the Vobiz pricing page.

Test calls and capacity purchases are billed to your account. Run them with your own credentials, and confirm numbers and quantities first.

Frequently asked questions

What is cloud telephony in simple words?

It is a business phone system that a provider runs for you on its own servers. You get numbers, call routing, recording, and reports through a browser or API. Customers still call you on normal phone numbers, and you buy no PBX hardware.

Is cloud telephony the same as VoIP?

No. VoIP is the method of carrying voice as IP packets. Cloud telephony is a way of delivering a phone system, with the provider running it. Most cloud telephony uses VoIP inside, but VoIP can also run on equipment at your own site.

Is cloud telephony legal?

Yes, in most countries, when providers hold the right authorisation and you follow the calling rules. In India, for example, DoT lists cloud-based EPABX under its enterprise communication service authorisation, and TRAI's rules govern number series, consent, and automated calls. Check the current text and take legal advice for your case.

Do I need internet for cloud telephony?

Not always at the agent's end. An agent can take calls on a mobile number over the phone network, with no office data link involved. Softphones and browser calling do need stable broadband. Your application servers also need reliable internet to answer webhooks.

How does cloud telephony differ from a cloud PBX?

A cloud PBX is one product within cloud telephony. It focuses on office extensions and internal calling. Cloud telephony also covers contact centre software, voice APIs, and SIP trunks, which suit customer calling, software-driven calls, and existing phone systems.

Can cloud telephony connect to AI voice agents?

Yes. An AI agent usually joins a call over a SIP trunk or a real-time audio stream over WebSocket. Your AI platform often decides which one to use. In India, automated outbound calls appear to match TRAI's A2P wording, so check that with your provider.

Further reading on Vobiz

  • What is VoIP? · What is SIP trunking? · What is a voice API?
  • What is an IVR? · Build a cloud IVR on Vobiz · Custom contact centre on Vobiz
  • SIP vs WebSockets · India calling regulations · Quick start

Sources

Indian regulators and government

  • DoT, Enterprise Communication Service Authorisation, eServices portal, last updated 7 July 2026.
  • DoT, Circular 01/Licensing Policy/2026: Introduction of calling name presentation service, 13 October 2026.
  • DoT, Revised Guidelines for Other Service Providers, 23 June 2021.
  • TRAI, Press release 119/2026 on the Third Amendment, 18 September 2026.
  • TRAI, Telecom Commercial Communications Customer Preference (Third Amendment) Regulations, 2026, 18 September 2026.
  • TRAI, Press release 91/2026 on the 1600 and 140 series, 10 July 2026.
  • TRAI, Recommendations on Revision of National Numbering Plan, 6 February 2025.
  • PIB, DPDP Rules, 2025 Notified, November 2025.

Legal commentary

  • Khaitan & Co, Update on the miscellaneous telecommunication services rules, June 2026.
  • S.S. Rana & Co., MeitY plans to cut short DPDP compliance timeline, February 2026.
  • ConsentOS, DPDP Rules notification status, updated 9 October 2026.
  • Khaitan & Co, Update on the principal telecommunication services authorisation rules, June 2026.

Standards

  • ITU-T, G.114 (05/2003): One-way transmission time, and its status page.
  • IETF, RFC 3550: RTP: A Transport Protocol for Real-Time Applications, July 2003.
  • IETF, RFC 5853: Requirements from SIP Session Border Control Deployments, April 2010.

Other guides we read

  • TechTarget, Cloud telephony (cloud calling), July 2023.
  • Retell AI, Cloud Telephony: What It Is, How It Works and How To Choose A Provider, July 2026.

For voice AI agents that live in the cloud, Vobiz is AI-native cloud telephony: SIP trunks, numbers and a voice API.

title: IPs públicas sin usar: cuánto cobran AWS y GCP y cómo encontrarlas
description:
Una IP pública parece gratis porque no tiene CPU ni disco. No lo es. Desde el 1 de febrero de 2024, AWS cobra USD 0,005 por hora por cada dirección IPv4 pública, esté asociada a un recurso o no. Son USD 3,65 por mes por dirección (0,005 × 730 horas). Una sola no mueve la factura; cuarenta olvidadas a lo largo de tres años y varias cuentas, sí: USD 146 por mes que no compran nada.

Qué cobra cada nube por una IP pública

  • AWS: USD 0,005 por hora por cada IPv4 pública, incluidas las Elastic IP sin asociar y las IPs públicas que AWS asigna a instancias, balanceadores y NAT gateways. La regla rige desde el 1 de febrero de 2024 y figura en el anuncio oficial de AWS sobre el cargo por IPv4 pública.
  • GCP: una IP externa estática reservada que no está asignada a nada cuesta USD 0,01 por hora; la misma dirección en uso por una VM estándar cuesta USD 0,005 por hora, en regiones de Estados Unidos según la página de precios de red de Google Cloud. Sin usar cuesta el doble: USD 7,30 por mes contra USD 3,65.
  • Azure: la IP pública Standard factura por hora mientras exista, asociada o no. Una IP que quedó colgada de una NIC sin VM factura igual que una en uso.

La diferencia con el resto de los recursos olvidados es que una IP no aparece en ningún panel de rendimiento: no tiene métricas, no dispara alertas y no ocupa espacio. Solo aparece en la factura, como una línea chica que se repite todos los meses.

Por qué quedan IPs huérfanas

Casi siempre por un borrado incompleto. Borrar una VM a mano desde la consola elimina la VM, pero no necesariamente lo que estaba alrededor:

  • En AWS, una Elastic IP sobrevive a la instancia: al terminarla, la dirección sigue asignada a tu cuenta, sin asociar, facturando.
  • En Azure, borrar la VM puede dejar la NIC y la IP pública, salvo que se haya marcado borrarlas junto con la VM. La IP queda asociada a una NIC que no le sirve a nadie, y no se puede liberar hasta desasociarla.
  • En GCP, una dirección reservada como estática queda en estado RESERVED cuando se borra la VM que la usaba.

El otro origen frecuente son las pruebas: alguien reserva una IP para un ambiente temporal, el ambiente se borra y la IP no. La IP es sólo uno de los recursos que nacen con la VM y no mueren con ella; en qué sobrevive cuando borrás una VM está la lista completa, con discos y snapshots, nube por nube.

Cómo encontrarlas, nube por nube

Con permisos de solo lectura alcanza: es mínimo privilegio aplicado, porque buscar no requiere poder borrar. En AWS, las Elastic IP sin asociación (el comando es por región):

aws ec2 describe-addresses \
  --query "Addresses[?AssociationId==null].[PublicIp,AllocationId]" \
  --output table

Hay un caso que este filtro no muestra: una Elastic IP asociada a una interfaz de red (ENI) que quedó suelta, sin instancia. Figura como asociada y no le sirve a nadie. Para verlo, listá las ENI en estado available con aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters Name=status,Values=available.

En GCP, las direcciones externas reservadas que no usa nadie:

gcloud compute addresses list \
  --filter="status=RESERVED AND addressType=EXTERNAL" \
  --format="table(name,address,region,status)"

En Azure, las IPs públicas sin configuración IP asociada, y las NIC que no tienen VM:

az network public-ip list \
  --query "[?ipConfiguration==null].{name:name, rg:resourceGroup, ip:ipAddress}" -o table

az network nic list \
  --query "[?virtualMachine==null && privateEndpoint==null].{name:name, rg:resourceGroup}" -o table

El filtro privateEndpoint==null no es decorativo: la NIC de un Private Endpoint tampoco tiene VM, y sin ese filtro aparece como huérfana una interfaz que está en uso. Borrarla corta el acceso privado a un servicio.

Antes de borrar: huérfana comprobada o desconocida

Una lista de candidatas no es una lista de borrado. Si un comando no pudo leer un campo, por permisos o por una región que no respondió, la respuesta honesta es "no sé", no "está libre". Liberar una IP en uso es peor que pagarla un mes más: la dirección no vuelve, y si estaba en un registro DNS o en la allowlist de un cliente, el corte es inmediato.

Una IP sin usar cuesta USD 3,65 por mes en AWS. Una IP liberada por error puede costar un incidente.

Cómo lo resuelve Control Cloud

Control Cloud lee el inventario de tus nubes con credenciales de solo lectura y marca las IPs huérfanas comprobadas en la página de cada proveedor y en el mapa, con un filtro que deja solo esas: una Elastic IP sin asociar o asociada a una interfaz de red (ENI) sin instancia, una IP estática de GCP que nadie usa, una IP pública de Azure retenida por una NIC sin VM. En GCP, si la lista de usuarios de la dirección no llegó, la IP queda como desconocida: sin marca y fuera del conteo.

No les pone precio: la página de costos muestra solo el gasto que devuelve la API de facturación del proveedor (hoy AWS, Azure y OCI), por servicio, sin estimaciones a partir del inventario. El importe de cada IP sale de las tarifas de arriba y de tu factura. Para estimar lo que se puede recortar en non-prod apagando VMs, la calculadora de ahorro hace la cuenta, y en apagar dev fuera de horario está el detalle de qué baja y qué no.
