title: The $5 Trillion Shift: Preparing Retail Backends for the Age of AI Agents
description:
Retail is entering the era of the multi-agent shopping assistant. Instead of a single, stateless chatbot following a rigid script, retailers are building systems where multiple agents collaborate behind the scenes, drawing on preferences and customer purchase history to deliver recommendations that improve with every interaction. More retailers are reconfiguring their backends to reflect the rise in agentic usage, as this is no small trend: McKinsey estimates AI agents could mediate $3 trillion to $5 trillion of global consumer commerce by 2030.(1)

The need is real, as the race is heating up to quickly respond to customer searches and take service to another level. A customer searching for a pair of running shoes for an upcoming marathon no longer triggers a keyword search. The query kicks off a coordinated reasoning process across multiple specialized agents. This has to happen rapidly and seamlessly to keep consumers' attention and needs met.

The promise of this shift is real, but the real architectural question has nothing to do with which LLM or orchestration framework a team chooses. It has everything to do with where the data lives and whether every agent can see the same version of the truth simultaneously. Increasingly, retailers are finding that solution in MongoDB.

The technology challenge behind multi-agent AI

Building a single AI agent is straightforward with modern LLMs and orchestration frameworks. Building a production multi-agent system is not. Why? Agentic AI has five distinct data needs:

  • Semantic search over vector embeddings 

  • Flexible user context 

  • Conversation state across sessions 

  • Long-term memory that evolves over time 

  • Observability through audit logs

Engineering teams pay a heavy ‘siloed database tax’ to meet these needs, standing up five distinct, single-purpose datastores: a vector store for product discovery, a session store for chat history, a short-term memory store for session context, a long-term memory store for accumulated preferences, and an audit log for compliance and debugging.

That fragmentation comes at a cost. Every additional datastore adds its own SDK, its own operational overhead, and its own failure mode. If the profile agent writes a new preference to one store while the product agent reads from another, the two are only as consistent as the ETL job connecting them. In a real-time conversation, that gap shows up as an agent recommending a product the customer already ruled out, or forgetting a preference captured moments earlier.

Retail makes the problem concrete. Carol asks for running shoes for a road marathon. Her profile has her static preference on file: She wears a size eight. Earlier in this conversation, she mentioned wanting maximum cushioning; that's short-term session context. John asks for running shoes, too. His profile puts him at a size 11, but long-term memory holds something neither his profile nor this conversation does: He needs a waterproof build, a fact learned from a past return after a pair let water soak in. Serving both well, consistently, and across every channel requires holding all three—static preferences, session context, and long-term memory—as one coherent view. This is what we’ve built to make this all happen fluidly

Giving every agent the same context

Retailers building a multi-agent system need specialized agents—including planner agents, profile agents, product agents, and eventually others—to discover and invoke each other's capabilities regardless of which team built them. This is what an open protocol like Agent2Agent (A2A) (2) provides. The Multi Agent Retail Advisor (MARA) is a reference implementation. Here, a planner agent delegates to a profile agent and a product agent, coordinating through A2A. The orchestration framework and LLM are both swappable; MongoDB, the data layer underneath every agent, is not.

Figure 1. Reference architecture for the MARA, showing how the planner, profile, and product agents interact through the A2A protocol, with MongoDB Atlas unifying operational and agentic data via Vector Search, text search, and auto-embeddings.

MongoDB Atlas handles all five agentic data needs natively in one platform, as shown in Figure 2 below. Atlas Vector Search stores product embeddings alongside the catalog data itself, so semantic search runs directly against operational data instead of a separate index to remain in sync. The same flexible document model holds customer context and preferences without a schema migration every time a field changes. Short-term memory lives as a nested array inside each session document, allowing the planner agent to fetch an entire conversation in one read. Long-term memory accumulates in its own collection, capturing facts an agent learns about a customer, like a preference for polyester base layers because they dry faster, independent of any single session. Observability runs through the same platform, too, logging every tool call's inputs, outputs, and latency so a request's full execution path can be reconstructed instantly.

Figure 2. MongoDB Atlas consolidates all single-purpose datastores to meet agentic AI’s data needs into one platform.

For product discovery, retailers build directly on Atlas Vector Search. They embed queries with Voyage AI and match them semantically against the catalog, falling back automatically to Atlas full-text search on the same collection when a query needs it, with no extra infrastructure. Because Voyage AI's newer models share a common embedding space, retailers can embed the catalog once with a larger, accurate model, and then run live queries with a smaller, faster model without ever re-indexing.

A simpler, more resilient stack for IT teams

For retailers, the payoff is architectural simplicity that compounds into speed and cost savings. Teams no longer manage four or five separate systems; they manage one. Schema flexibility, shown in Figure 3, lets agent state and user profiles, each varying by shopper or task, evolve without disruptive migrations. Because MongoDB Atlas scales horizontally, it supports the bursty, unpredictable request patterns of autonomous agents without becoming a bottleneck. Full observability works the same way: A single aggregation pipeline query joins the tool_invocations log, agent_state history, and session record for a request, reconstructing what each agent did, in what order, and how long each step took. That gives IT teams a queryable execution trace for every agent decision, shortening the path from a production issue to a root cause.

Figure 3. Two documents from the agent_state collection and two from the users collection. This shows the same collection, different shape, depending on which agent ran or which shopper it describes.

This consolidation also changes how fast a team can move. The product catalog, user profiles, session history, long-term memory, and tool-invocation logs all live as collections in one MongoDB cluster, not four separate systems linked together. That's the difference between a proof of concept shipping in weeks and one spending its first quarter wiring systems together before a single agent runs.  This setup lowers total cost of ownership the same way: one licensing agreement, one scaling model, and one team. Governance benefits too. Fine-grained access controls, encryption, and audit logging apply consistently across every agent's data, instead of system-by-system configuration. Because the architecture is not tied to a specific framework or model provider, retailers can add new agents, inventory, loyalty, and fulfillment onto the same data plane without replatforming. That matters most for agents no one can name yet. Any future agent built on the same document model plugs into the same unified context, turning what would otherwise be a multi-quarter integration effort into a schema extension.

An experience that feels seamless for customers

For customers, this translates into an experience that feels genuinely continuous. Because every agent reads from and writes to the same unified context, a preference shared in one conversation carries into the next. A question that starts in a chat can hand off cleanly to an inventory agent checking store stock or a loyalty agent applying a reward without the customer repeating themselves. This results in recommendations that get sharper the more a customer interacts with the system and a shopping experience that feels like one relationship rather than a series of disconnected sessions.

Figure 4. Any multi-agent retail architecture needs a swappable layer for orchestration and the LLM, but every agent still needs one constant data layer underneath it. Here, that's MongoDB Atlas beneath MARA's planner, profile, and product agents.

That continuity holds up across channels, not just across conversation turns. A preference a customer states while browsing on mobile is available the next time they open a chat window, walk into a store, or call support because it lives in the same unified profile every agent reads from rather than in a channel-specific cache. Customers also benefit from recommendations that account for their actual history rather than generic popularity signals. This happens since the product agent's semantic search runs against a catalog informed by what a shopper has already bought, browsed, and rejected. For the business, that precision compounds directly into commerce metrics: higher conversion, larger basket sizes, and fewer costly returns from recommendations that miss the mark.

Building for what comes next

The orchestration framework and LLM a retailer chooses today will likely change more than once. What shouldn't change is the data layer holding the system together. MongoDB gives retailers a single, flexible foundation for the knowledge, context, memory, and observability multi-agent retail experiences depend on, so the architecture underneath doesn't have to be rebuilt as frameworks and models evolve. Retailers that consolidate this layer now will be the ones ready to add the next agent—and the next protocol—without starting over.

References

  1. The automation curve in agentic commerce. McKinsey. January 28th, 2026. https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-automation-curve-in-agentic-commerce

  2. Getting Started with Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol https://codelabs.developers.google.com/intro-a2a-purchasing-concierge#0

title: How to Model an Insurance Policy Without Joining Dozens of Tables
description:
Ask an underwriter to describe a policy, and you’ll get a coherent answer: A contract, for a customer, covering a car or a house, with a handful of coverages, each with a limit and a deductible, plus a history of every change since it was issued. One policy—with parts. Many parts.

Now ask your database the same question. In most insurance core systems, that single policy is sliced across dozens of relational tables: one each for coverages, vehicles, named parties, endorsements, and billing schedules. Every time a screen loads, the system reassembles the policy by joining those tables back together. Every time a product changes, several of the tables need altering. When Manulife rebuilt its policy servicing platform, its chief architect described replacing more than 500 core tables with one document per policy and reported that the new system won overwhelming approval from its developers.

That gap—between how the business thinks about a policy and how the database stores it—is the central problem a document database like MongoDB solves. This blog post explains the one design decision that matters most when you make that move and why it’s an insurance decision as much as a technical one.

One rule drives everything

A document database stores records as nested structures, closer to a folder than a spreadsheet row. A policy document can hold its coverages, its vehicles, its parties, and its event history all within itself. The temptation is to simply pour the old table diagram into this new shape. That’s the wrong instinct.

The core idea is to model the data around what the business does with it, not around how the entities look on a diagram. Concretely, that means designing for the policy lifecycle (quote, underwrite, issue, bill, endorse, renew, cancel, claim) and asking, at each step, what gets read and written together.

Once you ask that question, every design choice reduces to one decision: whether to embed or reference.

Embed or reference: The decision that matters

For any two related pieces of data, you have two options. Embed one inside the other, so they live in a single document. Or reference one from the other, storing just an identifier that points to a separate document, the way a relational foreign key does.

The test can be reduced to two very simple statements:

  • Embed data that is part of something and is always read alongside it.

  • Reference data that has its own lifecycle or is shared across many records.

Apply that to a policy and the answers fall out naturally. Coverages belong inside the policy. Nobody ever looks up collision coverage without the policy it sits within. The insured vehicle belongs inside the policy—as does the event history, because an endorsement or a cancellation is meaningless apart from the contract it changed. In document form, that looks like this:

Anyone in the business can read that. It looks like the policy.

The claim follows the same logic, with a payoff that finance teams will appreciate. A claim’s reserves and payments belong inside the claim document. Because a single document is always written atomically, posting a reserve and updating the claim’s total becomes one operation that either fully succeeds or doesn’t happen at all. There’s no window where the ledger and the claim disagree.

Now let’s look at the other side of the test. A customer’s policies should not be embedded inside the customer record. Policies are large, they change constantly, and they’re almost always looked up by policy number rather than through the customer record. Instead, store policies in their own collection and have each policy reference its customer by ID. Claims should not be embedded inside policies either, because a claim can outlive the policy that spawned it: a canceled policy can still have open claims. Store claims separately, with each claim referencing the policy it belongs to.

The agent who sold the policy and the product it was written on should also be referenced, not embedded, and here the reasoning is operational. Thousands of policies share one agent and one product. Embed the agent’s details, and a change to their license number becomes a write across every policy in their book. Keep the product catalog as the single, versioned source of truth, and let the policy store only a point-in-time snapshot of the coverage terms it was bound against.

Two storms that test the design

Insurance also stress-tests data models in a way few other industries do: catastrophes.

The hurricane claim

Most auto and property claims carry fewer than 10 supporting attachments (photos, estimates, or a police report, for example). Embedding them in the claim is fine. But a major-loss claim after a hurricane can accumulate 60 or more attachments. MongoDB has a hard 16 MB size limit per document, but even well below that, a bloated minority of claims slows down every screen that loads them.

The wrong fix is to move all claim documents into a separate collection “just in case,” penalizing the 99% for the 1%. The right fix is what MongoDB’s engineers call the outlier pattern: embed by default, and when a claim crosses a threshold, flip an overflow flag and store the excess in a side collection. The design serves the common case and handles the exception explicitly.

Here’s what that looks like for a hurricane claim. Once the claim crosses the threshold, the application sets the flag and moves the extra documents to the side collection, so the claim record stays small:

The wildfire intake surge

When a database outgrows one server, MongoDB splits it across several, and a field called the shard key decides which server each record lands on. It seems sensible to shard claims by catastrophe (CAT) event code, since the CAT dashboard queries by it. It’s a trap. During an active wildfire, nearly every new claim for days shares one CAT code, so every new claim routes to one server—precisely when intake throughput matters most. Use a hashed shard key on the claim number to spread new claims evenly, and keep the CAT code as an ordinary index for the dashboard.

Both examples carry the same lesson: The data model is where operational resilience is decided, long before the storm arrives.

Three patterns to adopt on day one

Beyond the embed-versus-reference rule, there are three more design patterns to adopt:

  1. Computed totals. Store “total incurred” and “total paid” on the claim rather than re-summing reserves and payments on every read. Claim detail is among the busiest screens in the company; don’t make it do math.

  2. Schema versioning. Stamp every policy and claim with a version number. Insurance records survive for decades under regulatory retention and litigation discovery, and your document shape will change over that time. Without a version marker, that drift becomes an audit problem, not just a technical one. Travelers Insurance is reported to have eliminated a three-day wait for schema changes after moving off a rigid relational model; versioning is what makes that agility safe.

  3. Append-only history. Policy events, claim activity, and increasingly, the step-by-step decision trace of any automated underwriting or fraud-screening agent should only ever be added to, never edited or deleted. In most industries, that’s good hygiene. In insurance, it’s compliance. As regulators turn their attention to AI-driven decisions, an auditable trace of what an automated system decided and why will be the difference between a quick review and a drawn-out one.

What this means for you

None of this requires your engineers to abandon what they know. Multi-document transactions still exist for the moments that need them, such as binding a submission into a policy. The shift is in the starting question. Instead of “What are the entities and how do they relate?” it becomes, “What does the business read and write together, and what changes on its own?”

Keep what’s always read together, well, together. Separate what lives its own life. Plan explicitly for the outlier and the surge. Get those right, and the database finally describes a policy the way your underwriters do.

References: 1. Why Leading Insurer Manulife Ditched SQL For MongoDB 2. Travelers Insurance speeds up business ask-to-production process with MongoDB

title: Jump to the Last Command, and Copy Just That Output
description:
Originally published on MistLab. Part 9 of Building an SSH Terminal.

Part 9 of "Building an SSH Terminal". This is MistTerm v1.2.38. Parts 1–8 still quote v1.2.26.

TL;DR

You can jump to the previous command and copy that command plus its output in one step. The app only knows the edges if the shell prints invisible markers. That convention is called OSC 133. A plain bash prints none until a few lines are added to its startup file. There is no button that runs the command again.

A long session leaves the last df somewhere above the fold. You want to land on it, then take that command and its output together. The ls above it, and the prompt that came after, stay where they are.

A plain scroll of mixed lines, beside one command shaded as a block you can jump to and copy.

What the keys do

With the terminal focused, these three shortcuts are handled in the app. On macOS the same actions are ⌘⇧ with the arrow or with O.

Previous command, next command, and copy. Past the last command, next returns to the latest output.

The keys stop here. They are not typed into the server. If the shell never printed the marks, the view stays put and a hint points at the manual. Right-click still lists the three actions.

Enter is a bad boundary

The screen is one long scroll. A command can take several lines. A prompt does not always end in $. vim, less and htop fill the screen with lines that are not commands. MistTerm waits for the shell to mark the edges. It does not build a block from Enter, or from a line that merely looks like a prompt.

Where the marks sit

The shell prints marks you cannot see, so the app knows where a command starts and where it ends. That convention is called OSC 133. VS Code's shell integration uses the same letters under OSC 633, and MistTerm accepts those too.

Hidden marks sit around the command. Copy takes the shaded command and its output. The prompt stays out.

Copy starts at the command and includes the output. The prompt stays out. While a command is still running, copy stops at the cursor. A command that opens vim or less is still one block. What you copy is the command you typed. The full-screen view stays on that screen. A very long output keeps the start, about 4,000 lines or 200,000 characters, and the rest is marked truncated. Change the window width, or clear the scrollback, and the saved positions are gone.

The "command finished" mark can carry an exit code. Part 10's log may read that number. The number is for the log. The block on screen comes from the edges.

Turning it on

If iTerm2 or VS Code shell integration is already on that account, leave it. Otherwise paste this into the remote ~/.bashrc. It is the short snippet from the manual. When a command finishes it prints a hidden mark, including the exit code, and it marks around the next prompt so the command sits apart from the prompt text.

__mist_cmd_block() {
  local ec=$?
  printf '\e]133;D;%s\a' "$ec"
  printf '\e]133;A\a'
}
PROMPT_COMMAND="__mist_cmd_block${PROMPT_COMMAND:+;$PROMPT_COMMAND}"
PS1="${PS1}"'\[\e]133;B\a\]'

zsh has a matching snippet in the manual. Open a new tab so the shell reloads. This is ordinary shell code. Anyone who can edit the file can remove it, and any program can print the same bytes. That is enough for jumping and copying. It is the same kind of mark as the one in Part 6: useful here, useless as a lock.

Two things this release leaves alone

There is no action that sends the command again. The current directory travels in a different hidden message, the ones other apps call OSC 1337 and OSC 133 ; P. v1.2.38 leaves those unread.

Summary

  • Jump to the previous command, or copy that command plus its output.
  • The shell has to print the hidden marks. A stock bash prints none until the snippet is in its startup file.
  • With no marks, the view stays put and the keys are not typed into the server. The menu still lists the actions and points at the manual.
  • v1.2.38 does not send the command again, and it does not record the current directory.

FAQ

Why can't I jump to the last command on a new server?

The shell has to print hidden marks. A default bash does not. Add the short snippet from the manual to that account's ~/.bashrc and open a new tab.

Can I run the command again?

No. v1.2.38 jumps to the command and copies it with its output. It does not send the command again.

Does this remember the directory?

No. Other apps use a different hidden message for the current directory. v1.2.38 does not read those (OSC 1337, and OSC 133 ; P). Jump and copy only use the edges of the command.

title: 116,000 Stars vs. One Binary: claude-mem and palace-rs, Fact by Fact
description:
claude-mem is the most popular memory plugin for AI coding agents. At the time of writing it has 116,434 GitHub stars.

palace-rs does the same job. It has 10.

Stars tell you what people clicked. They don't tell you what you have to install, what runs in the background, who writes your memories, or whether anyone measured if the thing finds the right memory. So I went through both projects' own READMEs, docs and source and wrote down what each one actually does.

Every claim below links back to something you can open. No guesses.

What you install

claude-mem (from its README and package.json, v15.18.1):

  • Node.js ^20.19.0 || >=22.12.0
  • Bun >=1.1.31, "JavaScript runtime and process manager"
  • uv, "Python package manager for vector search"
  • Chroma, enabled by default (CLAUDE_MEM_CHROMA_ENABLED: 'true'), run locally as chroma-mcp through uvx
  • A worker, "a local HTTP service managed by Bun", that takes tool activity from hooks, runs the observer, and serves the viewer and search

That's a JavaScript runtime, a second JavaScript runtime, a Python toolchain, a vector database and a long-running HTTP service.

palace-rs (from its README, v0.20.0):

One binary, one SQLite file, no API keys, no cloud.

No Python, no vector database, no Docker. One palace executable and one palace.db file.

Embeddings run on your CPU through ONNX Runtime. There's no server process to keep alive. The install script downloads the release binary, verifies its SHA-256 checksum, and you run palace install to wire up your agents.

Who writes your memories

This is the biggest difference, and it's a design choice, not a detail.

claude-mem uses an LLM to write your memory. In its own words:

Hooks in your agent hand each tool call (what it reads, edits and runs) to a small local worker.
A second agent turns that activity into short observations, and writes a summary when the session ends.

The default settings in SettingsDefaultsManager.ts are CLAUDE_MEM_PROVIDER: 'claude' and CLAUDE_MEM_MODEL: 'haiku'. So what ends up in memory is a model's summary of what happened, not what happened.

That second agent also has to be paid for by someone. The README lists three options: the hosted "claude-mem observer" (a 30-day free trial that asks for a payment method), your own OpenRouter or Gemini key, or your Anthropic plan. It then says:

With the observer, memory runs off-plan, so you get up to 100% more usage from your plan.

Read that the other way round: when memory runs on your plan, it's using your plan. And when the trial ends, "memory automatically falls back to your Anthropic plan unless you subscribe."

palace-rs stores text verbatim and uses no LLM.

Code, notes, and conversations are stored as written, not as an LLM summary that loses detail.

No API key, no model calls, no second agent, no subscription. Recall is hybrid search (BM25 fused with cosine similarity over local embeddings) plus intent-aware ranking. A local cross-encoder reranker is optional. Nothing in the memory path costs tokens to create.

Does it find the right memory?

A memory tool has one job: when the agent needs something from last week, return it.

palace-rs publishes its numbers. On LongMemEval s_cleaned (470 evaluated questions, each over a haystack of about 50 sessions and 115k tokens), stored the way Palace actually stores conversations:

Metric palace-rs
R@1 0.915
R@5 0.987
R@10 0.996

From the README's method notes: "No LLM at any stage, no GPU." The one ranking weight picked on LongMemEval data was chosen on a different split (m_cleaned) and frozen before the run. Per-question-type results are published too, including the weakest category.

It also ships a coding-agent eval (51 questions like "why did we choose bundled sqlite?") that runs with one command:

cargo test --test coding_agent_eval -- --nocapture

The README says plainly that this eval is partly tuned, and prints the untuned numbers next to the tuned ones.

claude-mem's README publishes no retrieval benchmark. There's no LongMemEval score, no recall@K, no eval command. The token figures it does give ("~50-100 tokens/result" for the index, "~500-1,000 tokens/result" for full details) come with its own disclaimer:

The ratio is not a measured recall or end-to-end saving.

So for the most-starred memory tool in this space, there's no published number for how often it returns the right memory. For the 10-star one, there is, with the command to reproduce it.

Recall that doesn't depend on the agent remembering to search

Both tools use hooks. palace-rs installs four:

  • Session start injects your standing rules, recent diary entries for this project (from any agent), and the top memories of the project.
  • Prompt submit searches Palace with your actual question and injects matching memories before the agent answers (Claude Code and Codex).
  • Post tool use recalls related memory while the agent greps and reads files, so earlier decisions surface without a search.
  • Stop asks the agent to write a diary entry and record decisions if the session did real work but saved nothing.

All hooks fail open: if the palace is missing or empty, the agent works as normal. Every result carries its wing, room, source file, drawer id and score breakdown, so you can see where an answer came from.

Facts that change over time

palace-rs has a temporal knowledge graph: subject → predicate → object, with a valid-from date. When a fact changes, the agent invalidates the old one and adds the new one, so the timeline keeps both. palace_conflicts flags facts that look stale or contradictory.

Privacy

claude-mem:

  • "Anonymous usage analytics are on by default." Its telemetry page says it uses PostHog and calls it "on by default (opt-out)". You turn it off with npx claude-mem telemetry disable (or DO_NOT_TRACK).
  • The installer "asks you to sign in to claude-mem in your browser (email magic link)".
  • Screenshots are "kept by default" under ~/.claude-mem/media-v1/.

palace-rs:

No telemetry. palace gain statistics are written to your local database only.

The only network calls are the one-time model download from Hugging Face and, if you turn it on, your own Palace Server in remote mode.

No account, no sign-in, no analytics. Back up with palace export or by copying palace.db. Delete everything by removing ~/.palace.

Side by side

claude-mem 15.18.1 palace-rs 0.20.0
Language TypeScript Rust
What you run Node + Bun + uv/Python + Chroma + HTTP worker One palace binary
Storage SQLite + Chroma One SQLite file
What's stored Observations and summaries written by an LLM observer (default: Claude Haiku) Your files, chats and notes, verbatim
LLM / API key needed Yes (hosted observer, your key, or your Anthropic plan) No
Published retrieval benchmark None in README LongMemEval R@5 0.987, no LLM
Telemetry On by default (PostHog), opt-out None
Account / sign-in at install Yes (email magic link) No
License Apache-2.0 MIT
GitHub stars 116,434 10

The point

claude-mem is popular, and it covers a lot of agents. But popularity isn't architecture, and it isn't a benchmark.

If you want memory that:

  • is one binary you can audit,
  • stores what happened rather than a model's summary of it,
  • costs zero tokens to write,
  • sends nothing anywhere,
  • and comes with recall numbers you can reproduce,

that's palace-rs, today.

Don't trust the stars. Don't trust me either. Every quote above is from the projects' own pages. Open them and check.


# macOS / Linux
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs/main/scripts/install.sh | sh

# Windows
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex

palace install

Sources

  • palace-rs README: https://github.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs
  • claude-mem README: https://github.com/thedotmack/claude-mem
  • claude-mem package.json (engines, version, license): https://github.com/thedotmack/claude-mem/blob/main/package.json
  • claude-mem default settings: https://github.com/thedotmack/claude-mem/blob/main/src/shared/SettingsDefaultsManager.ts
  • claude-mem telemetry doc: https://github.com/thedotmack/claude-mem/blob/main/docs/public/telemetry.mdx
  • LongMemEval: https://github.com/xiaowu0162/LongMemEval

Star counts and versions as of 2026-11-12.

title: [AI in Action] First Time Using Herdr: Collaborating with Claude Code and agy for Go Backend Code Review, Issue Fixes, and Cloud
description:
Background

song-lingo is a small tool I made for learning Japanese songs: paste a YouTube MV link, and Gemini helps me transcribe the lyrics, label Romanization (Romaji), provide Traditional Chinese translation and grammar notes, and then uses Gemini TTS to generate a "teacher demonstration audio." After I record myself shadowing the song, Gemini transcribes my pronunciation and provides a word-by-word score.

A few days ago, in a single Claude Code session, I rewrote the entire backend from Python + Next.js API routes to Go 1.26 (Issues #44–#49, Tracking Issue #50, PR #51–#56). The architecture after the rewrite looks like this:

  • Next.js is only for the frontend, using a rewrite to forward /api to the Go server in the same container (127.0.0.1:8081).
  • Deployed on Cloud Run (asia-east1), data stored in a Cloud Storage bucket mounted via gcsfuse at /data; learning progress stored in Firestore; protected by IAP so only I can log in.
  • Key points of the Go version: genai SDK, Gemini REST (voices / interactions), Firestore transactions, kagome for tokenization and conversion to Hiragana, a custom Hepburn Romanization table, and a port of Python's difflib.SequenceMatcher to Go (aligned with 400 sets of golden tests produced by Python).

The rewrite was done, it worked, and tests passed. But "writing and reviewing your own code" always has blind spots. I happened to want to try Herdr—a tool that allows multiple AI Agents to collaborate in the same window, each occupying a Pane. So, I conducted an experiment:

Let Claude Code be the controller and Reviewer on the left, and the Antigravity CLI (agy) be the implementer on the right. The two Agents communicate via Herdr, taking the song-lingo Go backend from Code Review all the way to Cloud Run deployment.

1. What is Herdr? First-time Usage Notes

1. Two Executables: herdr-app and herdr-core

Herdr is divided into two layers:

Component Role Description
herdr-app Desktop App Manages the layout of spaces > tabs > panes. You can split panes left/right and run programs directly in a new pane.
herdr-core (CLI called hc) Terminal Core Responsible for running " terminals that don't die when the window is closed," providing commands like run / send / wait / read / keys / get for Agents to operate other terminals.

A small side note: I initially told Claude Code to "use herdr --skill to learn first," but the herdr command couldn't be found—the actual executables are ~/.local/bin/herdr-app and ~/.local/bin/herdr-core.

2. --skill: An Instruction Manual for AI Agents

I think Herdr's smartest design is that both CLIs have a --skill parameter. Running herdr-app --skill and herdr-core --skill prints an "instruction manual for AI Agents."

So, Claude Code's first step wasn't to blindly try commands, but to read both manuals before starting. The manuals contain many sensible guidelines, such as: background Agents must use --bg, provide a name and clear scope, don't let sub-agents spawn more sub-agents, and use hc wait instead of sleep polling when waiting.

3. Core Command Cheat Sheet

Command Purpose
$HC_TERMINAL_ID Every terminal has an address; Claude Code itself is t4.
hc run --bg --name xxx <agent> "<task>" Start a named Agent in the background and assign a task.
herdr-app do pane.split --direction right --pane <id> --argv [...] Split the pane to the right on the screen and run a program in the new pane.
hc send <t> "..." Paste text and press Enter; used to assign tasks or provide Review feedback.
hc wait <t> / hc wait --children all Wait for the other party to finish (replaces sleep polling).
hc read <t> --lines 0 Read the other party's entire current screen.
hc keys <t> enter Send a keystroke, such as answering a permission dialog.
hc get <t> Check status: idle / working / blocked / done; when blocked, it includes a msg, e.g., Approve RunCommand: ....

4. Agent-to-Agent Communication Channel

This is the most critical piece of the collaboration. When assigning a task, I would require agy: "When finished, please run herdr-core send t4 '...' to report back." After agy finishes, that message appears directly in Claude Code's input, looking like this:

<hc from="t7">ready for review #57 ...</hc>

In other words, Claude Code doesn't need to keep staring at the right screen; agy will "knock on the door" when done. Reporting is asynchronous, and every message carries a source address for tracking.

5. Layout Configuration

The first time I had Claude Code open agy, it used hc run --bg to run it in the background—it worked functionally, but I couldn't see what agy was doing. So, the second time, I specifically requested "in a pane on the right," and Claude Code used herdr-app do pane.split to open agy on the right. The final configuration was:

flowchart LR
    subgraph Herdr["Herdr Window (Same Tab)"]
        direction LR
        CC["Left Pane: Claude Code (t4)<br/>Controller / Reviewer<br/>Opens Issues, views diffs, runs go test -race, approves"]
        AGY["Middle Pane: agy (t7)<br/>Implementer<br/>Code Review, modifies code, runs tests, commit/push"]
        BLOG["Right Pane: Claude Code<br/>Blog Writer<br/>(The one writing this article)"]
    end
    Human(["Me (Human)<br/>Can see every Pane, can intervene anytime"])

    CC -->|"hc send: Assign tasks / Review feedback"| AGY
    AGY -->|"herdr-core send t4: ready for review #N"| CC
    CC -->|"hc keys: Grant read-only permissions"| AGY
    CC -->|"hc send: Write blog"| BLOG
    BLOG -->|"herdr-core send t4: blog draft ready"| CC
    Human -.-> CC
    Human -.-> AGY

2. Round One: Let agy be the Reviewer

The first task was simple: ask agy to review the Go code under backend/, read-only, no subagents, and write the results to a file, reporting back with hc send t4 when finished.

agy's interface showed it was running Claude Sonnet 5.5 (plan mode), and it eventually produced 17 issues, sorted by importance. Claude Code helped me organize them into three categories:

Category Issues found by agy
Concurrency and Data Integrity During Re-annotate (one Gemini call can take up to 5 mins), if I modify lyrics on the proofreading page, the write-back will be overwritten—the two sides use different mutexes; EditLine's global lock spans across Firestore calls; WriteAtomic's temporary filename is fixed as .tmp.
Resource Limits and Leaks TTS generation has no concurrency limit (this is a paid API); the failure cache only grows and stores duplicates; 429 errors without Retry-After have no rate limiting at all; TeacherVoice re-reads voices.json every time and holds a global lock during network calls; request bodies lack MaxBytesReader; background jobs use context.Background(), so they aren't cancelled on shutdown.
Performance and Structure listSongs parses all songs sequentially and reads progress for each; demonstration audio is read entirely into memory before being returned; the same Error type exists in 3–4 places; CLI speak and tts.Service logic are redundant.

Here is a detail I really liked: Claude Code did not accept everything blindly. Before opening an Issue, it first used grep to verify the most important one—"re-annotate and review use different mutexes"—and only after confirming it was true did it start opening Issues. The Reviewer's conclusions also need to be Reviewed.

3. Round Two: Open Issue → agy Fixes → Claude Code Reviews → Commit only if passed

My instructions to Claude Code were:

"Open issues and fix them sequentially. Mainly let the agy pane on the right do the modifications. You are responsible for reviewing and giving feedback. Only after you approve should agy commit and push."

1. Consolidating 17 items into 5 Issues

Claude Code consolidated the 17 items into 5 Issues (#57–#61), all performed on the same branch go-review-fixes, with one commit per Issue, and commit messages including Fixes #N.

2. Collaboration Workflow for Each Round 

sequenceDiagram
    participant CC as Claude Code (t4)<br/>Reviewer
    participant AGY as agy (t7)<br/>Implementer
    participant GH as GitHub

    CC->>AGY: hc send: Issue #N task + implementation points + "do not commit"
    AGY->>AGY: Implementation + gofmt -l . && go vet ./... && go test ./...
    AGY->>CC: herdr-core send t4 'ready for review #N'
    CC->>CC: git diff + run go test -race personally
    alt Has issues
        CC->>AGY: hc send: Review feedback
        AGY->>CC: Report back again after fix
    end
    CC->>AGY: Approved, you may commit & push
    AGY->>GH: git commit (Fixes #N) + push
    AGY->>CC: Report commit sha

3. What did the Review actually catch?

This is the part I want to share the most. Out of the 5 Issues, 3 required a second round of fixes, and 2 passed on the first try:

Issue Topic Review Result Commit
#57 Per-song lock Design correct, but no tests written → requested them e5df5f4
#58 TTS concurrency limit and failure cache Caught error message regression → requested fix and tests d67ec5a
#59 Request limits, timeout, graceful shutdown Caught shutdown sequence and time budget errors → redesigned de38741
#60 Song list concurrency, demo audio streaming ✅ Passed first try bc1615a
#61 Unified error types, CLI refactor, signal handling ✅ Passed first try deb1fb7

#57: Design was right, but where are the tests?

agy's per-song lock design was correct. Claude Code also specifically confirmed one thing: manual translations and the reviewed flag are both written into the transcript, so "comparing the entire transcript before writing back" indeed catches all edits.

But agy didn't write tests. So Claude Code requested extracting the logic into saveAnnotation and adding two cases: normal write when unchanged, and return conflict and no write when edited.

#58: Delete one map, and the frontend doesn't know why it failed

While cleaning up the failure cache, agy deleted the server-side recentErrors. All tests passed, but Claude Code caught a regression:

When the TTS quota is exhausted, "other sentences that have never been generated" checking ?error would get {error: null}—the frontend then couldn't display the reason "quota exhausted."

The fix was to make LastError return a still-valid quota error when there is no failure record for that sentence, and add a test.

#59: Cloud Run gives you about 10s, but you scheduled 20s

This was the most valuable bug catch in my opinion. The graceful shutdown agy wrote was: srv.Shutdown waits 10s, then background jobs wait another 10s. There were two problems:

  1. Cloud Run only gives about 10s after sending SIGTERM, so the two segments combined exceeded the budget.
  2. Re-analysis runs synchronously within the HTTP request. srv.Shutdown would wait for it to finish, but its context hadn't been cancelled yet—it was essentially waiting for itself.

Claude Code requested changing it to a single 9-second deadline and adjusting the sequence:

// Single deadline, leaving a bit of buffer for Cloud Run's SIGTERM grace period
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 9*time.Second)
defer cancel()

runner.Cancel() // 1. Cancel background and ongoing analysis work first
srv.Shutdown(ctx) // 2. Then shut down HTTP server (sync analysis already cancelled, won't hang)
runner.Wait(ctx) // 3. Finally wait for jobs to wrap up within the same deadline

(The above is illustrative of the sequence and single-deadline concept.)

#60, #61: Passed first try

  • #60: Song list changed to bounded concurrency 8, so a single song progress read failure won't drag down the whole list; generated demo audio now uses *os.File + ModTime handed to http.ServeContent for streaming (getting Range and Last-Modified for free).
  • #61: Unified error types to apierr.Error, CLI speak now uses tts.Service.GenerateAll, switched to signal.NotifyContext, and daily quota checks now use type fields instead of string comparisons.

Looking back at these three rejected Issues, there's a common theme: they were all "tests pass, but it hurts in production" problems—test gaps, frontend error message regressions, and shutdown sequences. This is exactly the greatest value of "one writing, one reviewing."

4. Round Three: PR, Merge, Deployment, and Verification

After all 5 commits passed, PR #62 was opened and merged, and #57–#61 were automatically closed. Then, a new revision was deployed using gcloud run deploy --source ..

Post-deployment verification was completed by Claude Code running fetch directly through a Chrome instance logged into IAP:

Verification Item Result Corresponding Change
Homepage /api/songs 200 (10 songs) #60 Concurrent reading
Learning page 200 —
Generated demo audio 200 audio/wav #60 Streaming
Demo audio Range request 206 #60 http.ServeContent
With If-Modified-Since 304 (New feature: now has Last-Modified) #60 ModTime
PATCH with 70 KB 413 "Request content too large." #59 MaxBytesReader
Cloud Logging Only two WARNINGs, both from the test requests themselves —

The previous revision was also kept, allowing for an immediate rollback if needed.

5. Six "Devil in the Details" Moments from Using Herdr for the First Time

Detail 1: agy "prompt" will exit with code 2

Intuitively, you might start agy like this:

agy "Please review the Go code in backend/..."

The result is an immediate error and exit (exit 2):

Prompts are read only from -p/--print, -i/--prompt-interactive, or stdin

The correct way is agy -i "..."—interactive startup with an initial task. The Herdr manual also warns not to use -p one-off mode, because the Agent needs to remain "observable and follow-upable" to conduct the Review back-and-forth.

Detail 2: Trust dialog on first entering a folder

The first time you start agy in a folder, it pops up "Do you trust the contents of this project?". At this point, the hc get status becomes blocked (auth). Claude Code just needs to use hc keys go-review enter to confirm.

Detail 3: A prompt that looks unsent has actually arrived

After opening agy with pane.split, the screen looks idle, and the initial prompt seems unsent. Claude Code tried to resend it with hc send, but was blocked by hc:

t7 is blocked (permission)... typing would answer its dialog; read its screen first

It turns out the task had already arrived, and agy was just stuck waiting for permission. This protection mechanism in hc prevents accidentally typing a task description into a permission dialog—if that actually happened, the result could be an unintended approval or rejection of a command.

Detail 4: Plan mode can only look, not modify

When agy is in plan mode (read-only research), it can only analyze. To have it start modifying code, you must press shift+tab to switch modes; Claude Code used hc keys t7 shift+tab to switch it. The first round of Code Review was perfect for plan mode, and it only switched out when modifications were needed in the second round.

Detail 5: Permission Driver—Evolving from "checking status bar" to "reading the whole screen"

Every shell command in agy requires permission. Pressing Enter for each one is too tedious, so Claude Code wrote a small driver script with the following logic:

flowchart TD
    A["hc wait t7"] --> B["hc get t7 Check status"]
    B -->|"idle / done"| Z["End, wait for agy report"]
    B -->|"blocked"| C["hc read Read full permission screen"]
    C --> D{"Contains dangerous command?<br/>rm -rf / git reset / git checkout<br/>--force / curl / gcloud write operations…"}
    D -->|"Yes"| H["Stop, let human decide"]
    D -->|"No"| E{"Is it git commit / push?"}
    E -->|"Yes, and no ALLOW_GIT=1"| H
    E -->|"No, or Reviewer approved"| F["hc keys t7 enter Grant permission"]
    F --> A

This script was refined several times during the process, each time providing a practical lesson:

  1. Status bar msg gets truncated: Initially, it only looked at the status msg returned by hc get, but it would be truncated with "...". The truncated part might hide a second command. Changed to hc read the entire permission screen for judgment.
  2. gcloud A; gcloud deploy single-line grep misses: Changed to splitting combined commands and judging each one for read-only status (describe / list / read / ls / du).
  3. Fixing false positives: gcloud storage ls and gcloud storage du are actually read-only; they were blocked initially but later added to the allowlist.

Detail 6: Boundaries of Permission Granting

The line for automated granting was drawn like this:

  • Read-only commands: Automatically granted.
  • git commit / push: Blocked by default, only granted with ALLOW_GIT=1 after Claude Code Review passes.
  • Commands requiring external APIs (e.g., agy wanting to use an access token to call the Google Developer Knowledge API for documentation): Stop and let the human decide.

Agents can trust each other enough to say "you can run tests," but "writing to git, writing to the cloud, making external requests" must go through a Reviewer or a human.

六、Multi-Agent Collaboration Checklist

If you also want to use Herdr (or similar tools) to have two Agents write and review, you can refer to this checklist:

  • 1. Read the manual before starting: Have the controller Agent run herdr-app --skill and herdr-core --skill first to confirm actual executable paths.
  • 2. Open sub-agents in visible Panes: Use pane.split to open the implementer Agent alongside, so a human can see and intervene at any time.
  • 3. Start in interactive mode: agy -i "...", don't use positional arguments, and don't use -p one-off mode.
  • 4. Clear task scope: Specify read-only or not, no sub-agents, "do not commit," and report back using herdr-core send <controller address> when finished.
  • 5. Use hc wait, not sleep polling; before sending text, if the other party is blocked, hc read the screen first.
  • 6. Verify Reviewer conclusions: Before opening an Issue, use grep to confirm the most important findings are true.
  • 7. Reviewer runs tests personally: For example, go test -race, don't just rely on the implementer's report.
  • 8. Permission Driver reads the whole screen: Don't rely on the status bar which can be truncated; judge combined commands individually.
  • 9. Gatekeeping for Git and Cloud writes: Only allow commit/push after Review passes; leave external API calls to humans.
  • 10. Verify new behavior after deployment: Don't just look for 200s; verify new limits (413), new headers (304 / 206), and keep the previous revision.

7. Next Step: Let agy analyze Cloud Run performance

As I finish writing this, agy on the right is already running the next task: using its GCP skill to analyze song-lingo's performance on Cloud Run—service settings, cold starts, gcsfuse, Firestore, etc.—proposing 5–8 solutions, each with evidence, expected benefits, monthly costs, and risks, for Claude Code to decide which to implement. This part is still ongoing; I'll share more later.

Summary

My biggest takeaway from using Herdr for the first time is: Multi-Agent collaboration is finally "visible."

  1. One writing and one reviewing catches blind spots better than doing both yourself: 3 out of 5 Issues were rejected, catching "tests pass, production hurts" problems—test gaps, error message regressions, and Cloud Run shutdown sequences.
  2. Agent-to-Agent messaging makes collaboration async and trackable: herdr-core send t4 'ready for review #N' lets the implementer "knock on the door," and the Reviewer uses hc wait to wait without polling.
  3. Panes keep humans in the loop: I can see exactly what commands agy is running in real-time on the right and intervene if necessary.
  4. Permission granting must be measured: Read-only can be automated, but writing to git, writing to the cloud, and making external requests must go through Review or a human.

And this article itself was written by Claude Code in the rightmost Pane of Herdr—after finishing, it will use herdr-core send t4 to report back to the controller on the left.

title: How we built an independent search engine on one server
description:
Most "search APIs" are a thin layer over Google or Bing results. NestDaddy is not. It has its own crawler, its own inverted index, its own ranking and its own news collection, and it all runs on a single server with 48 GB of RAM.

This post walks through how the pieces fit together, the problems we hit in production, and the numbers we used to decide what to fix. If you are thinking about building search yourself, or you want to know what sits behind the API you are calling, this is for you.

The shape of the system

There are four parts, and each one is allowed to fail without taking the others down:

  1. Crawler. Fetches pages, obeys robots.txt, extracts the readable text and stores it in PostgreSQL.
  2. Indexer. Turns new pages into posting lists in a RocksDB index that lives next to the live one.
  3. Swap. Once a day, the new index replaces the live index in one atomic step, with an automatic rollback.
  4. Search. A BM25 ranker reads the live index, read-only, behind the web site, the REST API and an MCP server for AI agents.

The rule that ties them together: the search path never waits for the crawler or the indexer, and neither of them can starve it of CPU or memory.

The crawler: polite, bounded, fenced

A crawler that misbehaves gets blocked, and a crawler that runs out of memory takes the machine with it. So ours is built around limits.

  • robots.txt first. One fetch per site, cached for 24 hours. A 401 or 403 on robots.txt means "disallow everything".
  • Spread across hosts. Each batch claims URLs from the queue with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and keeps at most 3 URLs per host. A batch of 500 URLs touches about 500 different sites instead of hammering one. The SKIP LOCKED claim also means several crawler processes can share one queue safely.
  • Bounded downloads. Every response is streamed and cut at 5 MB or 20 seconds. We learned this one the hard way: the first version read response.content and only then trimmed it, so a server that streamed an endless chunked reply pushed the whole body into memory. The fixed version stops at 5.2 MB in 0.07 seconds on the same endless stream.
  • A fence around it. The crawler runs as a systemd service inside its own slice: pinned to 4 of the server's CPUs, capped at 1.5 cores and 3 GB of memory, with a low priority. If it misbehaves, Linux slows it down or stops it, and the search side does not notice.

That last point matters more than it sounds. On one day this month the crawler hit its memory cap and restarted 36 times. Search latency, the database and every other service on the machine were untouched. The fence turned a production incident into a log line.

The index: RocksDB and posting lists

The index is an inverted index stored in RocksDB: for every term, a posting list of document IDs, plus per-document statistics for BM25.

We picked RocksDB over a search server for three reasons. It is a library, so there is no extra service to run. It is built for fast point lookups and multi-gets, which is exactly what a query does. And it can be opened read-only by many processes while another process builds the next version.

Text goes through a tokenizer (lowercasing, stop words, Porter stemming with a memoised stemmer) before it reaches the index, and the same tokenizer runs on every query.

Replacing the index without breaking it

Our first pipeline copied index directories while they were open. That produced two corrupted index files before we threw it away. The current swap is boring on purpose:

  1. Take the writer lock so the indexer pauses.
  2. Hard-link the immutable SST files into a staging directory and copy the small metadata files (MANIFEST, CURRENT, OPTIONS, WAL). This takes about a second and uses no extra disk.
  3. Release the lock and verify the staging copy read-only: the document counter must not go down, sample terms must resolve, the newest indexed pages must be readable.
  4. Rename the live directory to a "previous" directory and the staging directory to live.
  5. Reload the search workers and run a live search check. If anything fails, roll back automatically.

Two previous generations are kept, so going back is a rename, not a restore.

Ranking: BM25, measured

The ranker is BM25 with a few practical additions: a two-stage pre-score (rare terms first, then the top 3,000 candidates re-ranked by term frequency with one RocksDB multi-get), a domain match signal for navigational queries, and image documents kept out of web results.

We do not change ranking by feel. A small evaluation set of 40 real queries, each with a judgment ("the right answer is this URL pattern" or "the homepage of this site"), runs against the live index after every change. The fixes we shipped in November moved:

Metric Before After
Right answer at #1 (P@1) 45% 70%
Right answer in the top 3 60% 77.5%
Right answer in the top 10 70% 87.5%
Mean reciprocal rank 0.536 0.754

The changes behind that were unglamorous: true document frequencies for IDF instead of estimates, an average document length measured from real documents, deterministic sampling instead of random, and keeping images out of web search.

Latency: the bugs were not where we expected

When search got slow, the ranker was rarely the problem. Profiling live workers found three surprises.

A regular expression. The tokenizer stripped email addresses with \S+@\S+. On some inputs that pattern backtracks quadratically, and one query held the Python GIL for over a minute. The fix was a pattern with identical output and linear time: (?<!\S)(?=\S+@\S)\S+.

The index falling out of RAM. A cold read of the index from disk turned a 0.2 second query into several seconds. We added a small service that checks which parts of the index file are resident (mincore) every ten minutes and reads back only what is missing, and we gave it a cgroup memory guarantee so the kernel prefers to evict other files first. One detail cost us an afternoon: cgroup v2 memory protection is hierarchical. Setting MemoryMin on the service did nothing until the parent slice had the same guarantee.

A forgotten cron job. Even with that protection, the whole index still vanished from RAM once an hour. The cause was a one-line script in /etc/cron.hourly that ran echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches, an old "free up memory" trick. Dropping caches ignores cgroup protection entirely. Removing it brought the median query time on our evaluation set from 0.59 seconds back to 0.22 seconds.

The lesson we keep relearning: measure on the real machine, and read every scheduled job before you trust a graph.

What we have not solved yet

Being independent means owning the weak spots too. These are the ones we are working on now:

  • Long, specific queries. The current index weighs titles, descriptions and headings. Pages whose answer lives deep in the body text can rank below a page that merely shares one word with the query. The next index version adds body text, which also means the index outgrows what we can keep in RAM on one machine, so it needs a tiered design first.
  • Numbers and non-Latin scripts. The current tokenizer drops most numbers ("windows 11", "iphone 17") and handles Chinese, Japanese and Thai poorly. A new tokenizer that keeps short numbers and splits CJK and Thai text is written and waiting for the next rebuild.
  • Freshness. Most of the index was crawled months ago. A targeted recrawl of the most searched results and the most linked sites is running now, and the crawler is next in line to run as a continuous pipeline with several processes.

Why build it at all

Because an index you own is an index nobody can switch off. Microsoft retired the Bing Search APIs in August 2025 and many apps lost their search overnight. Products that need raw results, news by country, or readable page text for AI agents need a source that answers in plain JSON and does not depend on someone else's roadmap.

That is what NestDaddy is for. You can try the search, news and page extraction APIs with a free 7-day key at nestdaddy.com/apis, or connect it to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client through nestdaddy.com/mcp.

If you have questions about any part of this, or you have built something similar and want to compare notes, we would like to hear from you.

Originally published on the NestDaddy blog. NestDaddy is an independent search engine with its own index: nestdaddy.com.

title: I made i18next up to 5x faster with two includes() checks
description:
Two includes() checks made i18next up to 5x faster on long text. This post shows that fix and two more.

A regular expression is a good tool, but it is not free. Each call scans the input, and a bad pattern can scan the same characters many times.

Three of my performance PRs had the same idea: do a cheap check before the expensive regex work. Maintainers merged all three. This post shows each change, the numbers, and the rule you can use in your own code.

1. i18next: check the prefix before you run the regex

i18next (35M npm downloads a week) runs its interpolation regex and its nesting regex on every translated text. The regexes look for {{name}} and $t(key).

Most texts have neither. "Save", "Cancel" and "Welcome back" contain no {{ and no $t(. But i18next ran both regexes on them anyway, and each scan read the full text to find nothing.

Every match of these regexes starts with a fixed prefix. So a text without the prefix cannot match. A plain includes() call answers that question, and it is much cheaper than a regex scan:

// Interpolator.interpolate()
// no placeholder at all: neither regexp can match
if (isString(str) && !str.includes(this.prefixText)) return str;

// Interpolator.nest()
// nothing to nest (the common case)
if (isString(str) && !str.includes(this.nestingPrefixText)) return str;

prefixText is {{ by default, and nestingPrefixText is $t(. Both follow the user's options, so a custom prefix such as %{ also works.

Benchmark Before After Change
t('hello') 1524 ns 1310 ns -14%
t() on a 10 KB text 11858 ns 2232 ns -81% (5.3x faster)
t() on a 10 KB text with {{name}} at the end 12431 ns 7250 ns -42%

The long text gets the biggest gain, because the regex scan was most of the work. The output does not change. Old and new code gave the same results on 1,000,000 random resources, options and calls.

PR: i18next #2469.

2. regexp2: check ASCII before the Unicode tables

regexp2 is a .NET-style regex engine for Go. The \w and \b tokens call IsWordChar for each character. That function looked up 4 Unicode category tables by name, on every call:

// before
return unicode.In(r,
    unicode.Categories["L"], unicode.Categories["Mn"],
    unicode.Categories["Nd"], unicode.Categories["Pc"]) || r == '\u200D' || r == '\u200C'

Two things were slow. First, unicode.Categories["L"] is a map lookup, 4 times per character. Second, most text in logs, code and config files is ASCII. In ASCII, these 4 categories are only letters, digits and _. The change checks ASCII first, and uses the table variables directly for the other runes:

// after
if r < utf8.RuneSelf {
    // In ASCII, L, Mn, Nd and Pc are these runes only.
    return 'a' <= r && r <= 'z' || 'A' <= r && r <= 'Z' || '0' <= r && r <= '9' || r == '_'
}
return unicode.In(r, unicode.L, unicode.Mn, unicode.Nd, unicode.Pc) || r == '\u200D' || r == '\u200C'
Benchmark (run time) Apple M5 AMD EPYC
Compile an email pattern -69 to -71% -68 to -69%
\b\w+\b on ASCII log text -44 to -48% -45 to -49%

Non-ASCII text also got 33 to 37% faster in my test, because the map lookups are gone for all runes. I checked the result for every rune.

PR: regexp2 #142.

3. colord: let the common case match first

colord (25M npm downloads a week) parses CSS colors such as rgba(255, 128, 0, 0.5). Each number in its regexes used this pattern:

/(?:\d*\.\d+|\d+)/   // before

Most numbers in CSS colors are integers, such as 255. For an integer, the first branch reads all the digits, finds no ., and gives the digits back one by one. Then the second branch reads the same digits again.

The new pattern accepts the same strings (.5, 5, 5.5), but an integer matches in one pass:

/(?:\d+(?:\.\d+)?|\.\d+)/   // after
Benchmark Before After Change
colord("rgba(255, 128, 0, 0.5)").toRgb() 245 ns 222 ns -9%

The gain is smaller here, but it costs nothing. colord also has a test that rejects 1 MB malformed strings in linear time. The new pattern passes it, and it is about 2x faster on some of those cases.

PR: colord #173.

The rule

All three changes do the same thing: they find the cheapest question that settles the common case, and ask it first.

  • A fixed prefix? Check it with includes() or strings.Contains() before you run the regex.
  • Mostly ASCII input? Handle ASCII with a range check before you go to the Unicode tables.
  • Alternatives in a pattern? Put the branch that matches the common input first, and make sure it does not backtrack.

When does this not help? If almost every input contains the prefix, the extra check is only extra work. Measure with your real inputs before you add it.

The full benchmarks are in each PR. More PRs: g4lb.

title: Make the agent cite the design-system component it reused, or admit it forked one
description:
The PR adds a primary button. It looks like Button. It is a <button className="rounded-md bg-blue-600 px-4 py-2 text-white"> with a slightly different focus ring. The design system already has Button variant="primary". The agent didn’t mention the fork.

I’ve started asking for a one-line citation in the PR body: which system component was reused, or an explicit “I didn’t use one, because….” Lookalike markup is not reuse.

Why forks sneak in

  • The agent wasn’t given the import path or the story URL
  • The system component’s API didn’t match the first prompt (loading vs isPending)
  • The model “just needed a button” and patterned after a screenshot
  • A previous file in the repo already forked one, and the agent copied that

You cannot see the fork in the screenshot. You see it in the imports — or the lack of them.

What the citation should look like

In the PR body (or the agent’s summary), require one of:

Reused: `@acme/ui` <Button variant="primary" size="md">
  from src/components/Button (story: Button/Primary)

or:

Did not reuse a system component. Reason: we need a native
<file> input trigger and Button doesn’t expose that slot yet.
Fork is local to ImportDialog, not a new shared Button.

That’s it. No essay. The point is to make the decision reviewable in thirty seconds.

What to put in the prompt

Paste the short list of components the task is likely to need — names, import paths, and the one prop pattern you actually use:

For actions, use `import { Button } from "@acme/ui"`.
Variants: primary | secondary | ghost. Do not recreate
equivalent markup with utility classes. If a system
component almost fits but a prop is missing, say so
and do not silently fork it. Cite the component you
used in the PR body, or admit the fork and why.

A link to the Storybook item helps; a 12-line API cheat sheet helps more than “follow the design system.”

Review checklist

  1. New interactive UI: is there an import from the system package or src/components primitives?
  2. If not, is there a stated reason in the PR body?
  3. If the markup is 80% of an existing component, request a swap — don’t bikeshed the border radius
  4. If a real gap exists (missing slot, missing variant), file or link the system issue; don’t let the fork become the unofficial variant

A simple CI rule — flag new <button> / raw <input> in feature folders when the file doesn’t import the primitive — is noisy, but useful as a warning on the PR.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • A restyled raw <button> next to existing Button usage in the same route
  • A local PrimaryButton wrapper that only copies classes
  • “I followed the design system” with no import and no citation
  • A fork that should have been a variant or a asChild / slot on the existing primitive

Accept

  • A real system import, cited (or obvious from the diff)
  • A documented fork with a narrow reason and a local, not global, name
  • A follow-up ticket when the system API is the actual blocker

Tiny habit

When you ask an agent to add a control, tell it to cite the system component it reused — or admit it forked one. Reviewers shouldn’t have to grep for bg-blue-600 to find out you grew a second button.

title: Bookmarks before transcripts: what we learned building a lecture recorder
description:
TL;DR: AI Lecture Recorder records lectures offline, lets you bookmark the moments that matter with one tap, and transcribes only when you ask it to. This post is about why the bookmark button ended up more important than the AI.

🤖 Google Play · 📱 App Store

Originally published on the Nexa Tech blog.

When we started AI Lecture Recorder, the obvious headline feature was transcription: record an hour, get an hour of text. Students told us they rarely read a full transcript. What they wanted was to find the five minutes that mattered. So we organised the product around three moments in a student's day.

  • Before: start recording fast. Open, tap record, put the phone on the desk. No setup screen in the way.
  • During: mark what matters. One tap to bookmark the moment the lecturer says "this will be on the exam".
  • After: find it again. Jump straight to bookmarks, and transcribe only when text actually helps.

Before: getting out of the way

Lectures start whether you are ready or not. The app opens straight to a record button, and recording works fully offline. Nothing about capture depends on a network or an account.

During: one tap beats a note

The biggest button on the recording screen, after stop, is bookmark. One tap marks the current moment. A label can be added later, but doesn't have to be. Marking something takes less effort than writing it down, so people actually do it.

The most advanced feature is not always the most useful one. Sometimes it is a single button that fits the moment.

After: review, not replay

Reviewing a lecture is different from listening to music. You skip, rewind a few seconds, slow down a dense part, speed through a tangent.

  1. Record: phone on the desk, screen off
  2. Tap to bookmark: mark the moment, label it later
  3. Jump back: playback starts just before the mark
  4. Transcribe: optional, when text helps

Bookmarks do the finding; transcription is there when you want words.

  • Playback starts slightly before each bookmark so you hear the lead-in.
  • Skip buttons are sized for the short jumps people make most.
  • Speed control is one tap, not buried in a menu.

Where transcription fits

Transcription is still there, powered by Groq, for when text genuinely helps: searching for a term, copying a definition into notes, or reviewing in a quiet library without headphones.

You want to… Best tool
Find the exam hint Bookmarks
Re-hear an explanation Bookmarks + playback speed
Search for a term Transcript
Copy a definition into notes Transcript

Optional on purpose. Transcription is a choice per recording, not a default. People decide when audio is sent for processing, and recording never depends on it.

Update: what's new in 2.0

Since this post first went up we shipped recording with the screen off, trimming, folders, and export to audio, TXT or PDF. We also removed subscriptions: you can now earn points to unlock the premium AI features instead of paying monthly.

If you're a student (or build tools for students), I'd love feedback:

  • Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.nexa.ai_lecture_recorder
  • iPhone: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/ai-lecture-recorder/id6791456539

What would make you actually review a lecture recording instead of letting it sit in a folder?

title: Shapewear Q&A: Fun, Honest Answers to the Questions You Actually Ask
description:
Let's take a lighter approach. Forget the technical jargon for a minute—here are the fun, honest answers to the questions people actually ask about shapewear, the kind you'd hear over coffee with a friend who's been through it all.

"Will I look like a different person?"
Great question. The honest answer: no, and you don't want to. Good shapewear doesn't transform you into someone else—it smooths, lifts, and defines you. You'll look like the best-rested, best-angled, most confident version of yourself. Same you, just with a little extra polish.

"Is it like wearing a corset from the 1800s?"
The modern answer is a relief: not even close. Today's shaping uses breathable fabrics, graded compression, and flexible construction. You can breathe, sit, bend, and dance. The only thing you'll feel is support—and you'll likely forget you're wearing it by lunchtime.

"How does it feel when I finally take it off?"
This is everyone's secret favorite question. The honest answer: it feels like the best stretch of your life. There's a moment of glorious freedom when it comes off—kind of like taking off a bra at the end of a long day, but for your whole body. Wear it proudly, and savor the release.

"Can I eat in it?"
Yes—and this is non-negotiable for good shapewear. A properly fitted piece lets you sit through dinner, take a full breath, and eat without feeling punished. The old "suffer for beauty" era is over. If you can't enjoy your meal, it's the wrong garment.

"Will my partner notice?"
Depending on your goal, either way works. Many partners do notice—and often love the confidence boost. Others won't notice at all, which is also fine (that's the invisible magic working). Either way, the real person who notices is you, in the mirror, and that's what counts.

"Is one piece enough, or do I need a whole wardrobe?"
You don't need a wardrobe. Start with one versatile piece—a seamless tank or bodysuit—and wear it. Learn what you like, what works for your body, and build from there. Most people find a small, trusted capsule beats a drawer full of "maybes."

"What's the weirdest thing about wearing shapewear?"
Honestly? The moment you forget it's there and live your day completely normally—that's the weirdest and best part. It stops being "shapewear" and just becomes part of you. And that, my friend, is exactly when it's working at its best.
