title: One Clear Call to Action Per Page: A Developer's Guide
description:
As developers, we usually think of a call to action as a button component. It is, but it is also a decision point in the user journey. A visitor lands on a services page, reads the whole thing, likes what she sees, then closes the tab and never contacts the business. Nothing went wrong with the work or the prices. The page simply never told her what to do next. There was no clear button, no obvious next step, just a page that ended. So she left, and a competitor with a big "Request a Quote" button got the enquiry instead.

Behind that missing button is an implementation question. Should the CTA be a semantic button or a link? If it navigates to another page or starts a form, use an anchor element. If it triggers an action on the same page, use a real button element. Screen readers announce both correctly only when the markup matches the behavior, so picking the right element is the first accessibility decision, not a styling choice.

Accessible button markup also means visible focus styles, a descriptive label, and a tap target of at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels on mobile. Add an aria-label only where the visible text is not enough, for example when several buttons on one page all say "Learn more". Keep the primary CTA above the fold and sticky on mobile where it fits, so the next step is always one tap away.

Tracking clicks should be cheap. Fire a single analytics event per CTA, and use a lightweight handler instead of loading a heavy tracking script for one button. And in the component itself, enforce one primary action per view. A CTA component that accepts a single primary action is easier to reuse than one that accepts a list of competing buttons.

This guide covers what a call to action is, why multiple competing CTAs hurt conversions, how to choose the right CTA for every page type, what makes one effective, the common mistakes, and a checklist you can work through this week. The marketing advice is the same as for any business site. The implementation notes are for the developers building it.

What Is a Call to Action on a Website?

A call to action, usually shortened to CTA, is a button, a link, or a short line of text that tells a visitor what to do next. It turns a reader into someone who acts. Without it, a page is a dead end, however good the content is.

Simple examples of website CTAs

You see them everywhere once you start looking. "Request a Free Quote" on a services page. "Book an Appointment" on a clinic website. "Add to Cart" on a product page. "Order on WhatsApp" on a small shop's homepage. "Download the Price List" on a supplier's site.

Each one is specific. It says what happens when you click, and it fits the page it sits on. A product page asks you to buy. A service page asks you to enquire. A blog post asks you to read more or talk to the business. The wording changes, but the job stays the same: give the visitor one obvious thing to do.

Why every page should guide visitors toward an action

People do not arrive on your website to admire it. They arrive with a need. A plumber's number. A price for a wedding dress. A quote for a shop renovation. If the page answers their question but gives them no way to act on it, the visit ends there.

This matters more for small businesses than for big brands. A big brand can afford to lose a visitor and win them back later with ads. A small business in Faisalabad or Lahore usually gets one shot. The visitor found you on Google, read your page, and now decides in seconds whether to contact you or go back to the search results. A clear call to action is what turns that visit into an enquiry.

Why Multiple Competing CTAs Hurt Conversions

It feels logical to add more buttons. If one button brings enquiries, five buttons should bring five times as many. In practice it works the other way round.

We once reviewed a homepage with six buttons above the fold: Contact Us, View Our Services, Book a Meeting, Download Our Brochure, Get a Free Quote, and Chat on WhatsApp. Every one of them was a different colour, every one shouted just as loudly. A visitor who wanted to hire the business had to stop and work out which button to press first. Most did not bother. They scrolled, got confused, and left.

Too many choices create confusion

When everything on a page demands attention, nothing gets it. A visitor scans a page in seconds. If five buttons compete for that scan, the eye lands nowhere and the brain makes no decision. Psychologists call this choice overload, and it shows up on websites exactly the same way it shows up in a shop with too many options on one shelf. People walk away rather than choose.

Primary vs secondary: one job, one button

Every page should have one primary CTA. That is the action you most want a visitor to take on that page. It gets the strongest button, the best spot, and the clearest words.

Secondary actions can still exist. A homepage can link to the services page, the about page, and the contact page. But those links should look like links, not like buttons competing with the main one. The rule we use at aimEncoders is simple: if a visitor can only see one thing clearly in the first five seconds, it should be the primary CTA. Everything else waits its turn.

This is also where website conversion optimization starts. Before you spend money on ads or redesigns, check whether each page even asks for one clear action. Fixing that costs nothing and it often does more than a new homepage ever could.

How to Choose the Right CTA for Every Page Type

Different pages serve different visitors, so they need different CTAs. A first-time visitor on your homepage is not ready for the same action as a returning customer on a product page. Match the CTA to the moment.

Homepage: guide visitors toward your main offering

Your homepage is the front door. Most visitors are meeting your business for the first time. They need a quick sense of what you do, then one clear way forward.

For a service business, that is usually "Discuss Your Project" or "Request a Free Quote". For a shop, it might be "Shop New Arrivals" or "Order on WhatsApp". Pick the one action that matters most to your business and make it the biggest, clearest button on the page. The rest of the homepage can link to services, work samples, and your story, but those links should not fight the main button for attention.

Service pages: encourage visitors to request a quote

A visitor on a service page is already interested. She has read what you offer and she is deciding whether to contact you. This is the easiest enquiry you will ever get, so do not make her hunt for it.

Put a clear button after the service description and again at the bottom of the page. "Request a Website Development Quote" beats "Submit" every time, because it tells her exactly what happens next. The button should lead to a short enquiry form or your contact page, not back to the homepage. When we build fast, SEO-ready websites built to convert, we place the quote button where the reader's interest peaks, right after the service details and the reasons to choose us, not buried in the footer.

For different services, the wording changes but the pattern stays. An ecommerce project gets "Discuss Your Ecommerce Project". A web app gets "Book a Project Consultation". A testing service gets "Request a Testing Consultation". Same structure, matched to the page.

Product pages: make purchasing straightforward

A product page has the simplest job of all. The visitor is deciding whether to buy, so the CTA should make buying easy and immediate.

"Add to Cart" or "Buy Now" should be visible without scrolling, next to the price, and it should work in one tap on a phone. A clothing store in Lahore does not need a clever button. It needs a big, obvious one that a shopper on mobile data can find in a second. Put the price, the size or variant options, and the buy button together. Every extra step between the product and the purchase is a chance to lose the sale.

Delivery and payment details belong near the button too. A shopper who has to search the site for delivery charges will often give up and buy elsewhere. Answer the question next to the action.

Blog posts: turn readers into potential leads

Blog readers are not ready to buy. They came to learn something. A hard sell at the end of a helpful article feels wrong, and readers ignore it.

So connect the CTA to the topic instead. A post about website speed can end with "Is your website losing customers to slow loading? Let's talk about fixing it." A post about online booking can point to our guide on setting up an online booking page and then offer a consultation. The CTA should feel like the next logical step after reading, not an interruption. Readers who found the article useful are exactly the people most likely to enquire, if you give them a gentle, relevant way to do it.

What Makes a Call to Action Effective

A good CTA is not about clever words. It is about clarity, placement, and timing. Get those three right and even a plain button works.

Say exactly what happens next

Vague buttons lose clicks. "Click Here" tells the visitor nothing. "Submit" sounds like paperwork. Compare that with "Send Your Enquiry", "Get My Free Quote", or "Book My Appointment". The visitor knows what happens after the click, and that removes the hesitation.

Use verbs. Start with the action. Keep it short, five words or fewer where you can. And say it in the visitor's language. A Pakistani customer responds to "Order on WhatsApp" far better than "Initiate Purchase Process", because the first one describes something she actually does every day.

Put it where people can find it

A CTA hidden at the bottom of a long page might as well not exist. Put the primary CTA near the top of the page, where it is visible without scrolling. Repeat it after the important information, and once more at the end of the page, so a visitor who reads the whole thing never has to scroll back up.

On mobile, this matters twice as much. Buttons need to be big enough to tap easily, with space around them so a thumb does not hit the wrong link. Test your own site on your own phone. If you have to pinch, zoom, or hunt for the button, your customers are doing the same thing, and most of them will simply leave.

Match it to the visitor

A first-time visitor and a returning customer need different things. Someone who just found you on Google might want to explore your services first. Someone who has already read three of your pages is ready to talk. Your pages can reflect that. The homepage can offer a softer step like "Explore Our Services" alongside the main quote button, as a quiet link rather than a competing button. A service page, where interest is already high, can go straight for the quote.

The test is simple. For each page, ask one question: what is the most likely thing this visitor wants to do right now? Then make that the CTA.

Common CTA Mistakes Small Businesses Make

Most of the problems we see during a website review fall into a few patterns, and all of them are cheap to fix.

First, vague button text. "Learn More" and "Click Here" appear on thousands of business sites, and they tell the visitor nothing about what comes next. Replace them with the actual outcome.

Second, too many equally prominent buttons. A page with four bright buttons is a page with no clear priority. Keep one primary button and let the rest be plain links.

Third, sending visitors to the wrong place. A "Book an Appointment" button that lands on the homepage instead of the booking form breaks trust in one click. Every CTA should land exactly where the visitor expects.

Fourth, hiding the contact options. Some sites put the phone number and WhatsApp button only in the footer, three scrolls down. If contacting you is the goal, the phone number belongs near the top, on every page.

Fifth, forgetting mobile users. A button that looks fine on a laptop can be tiny on a phone, or crowded by other links. More than half of your visitors are likely on a phone, so check every CTA there first.

How to Improve Your Website CTAs This Week

You do not need a redesign to fix this. You need an afternoon and a honest look at your own site.

  • Open every important page: homepage, each service page, the contact page, and your most visited blog posts.
  • For each page, write down the one action you want visitors to take. If you cannot name one, that page has no CTA.
  • Check that the primary button uses specific words, not "Click Here" or "Submit".
  • Make sure the button is visible near the top and repeated at the end of the page.
  • Click every CTA yourself and confirm it lands where it should. Fix any that go to the wrong page.
  • Open the site on your phone and tap each button. If any button is hard to find or hard to tap, fix it first.
  • Remove or quieten any competing buttons so the primary one stands out.
  • Then watch what happens. Count enquiries, calls, and form submissions for a month and compare them with the month before. If a page gets clicks but no enquiries, the form or the page behind the button needs attention, not the button itself.

Small changes here add up. A clearer button on a service page, a working WhatsApp link on a product page, a relevant next step at the end of a blog post. None of this needs new technology. It needs someone to look at each page and ask what the visitor should do next.

Give Every Visitor a Clear Next Step

Your website already does the hard work of explaining your business. A call to action finishes the job by showing visitors what to do about it. One page, one primary action, matched to the person reading it. That is the whole idea, and it is the cheapest conversion improvement most small business websites can make.

If your site gets visitors but few enquiries, start here before you spend on ads or a rebuild. Open your homepage, read it as a customer would, and ask yourself what you are supposed to do next. If the answer is not obvious in five seconds, your visitors are asking the same question, and most of them are leaving without an answer.

At aimEncoders, we check every page for one clear call to action before any website goes live, because a beautiful site that nobody contacts is a brochure, not a business tool. If your website needs the same honest review, talk to us and we will look at it with you.

A Note for Developers

When you build the CTA, start with semantics. Use a real button element for actions that happen on the page, and a real a element for navigation to another page or a form. Do not build a button out of a div with a click handler, because keyboard users and screen readers lose the built-in behavior that real elements provide for free.

Give the button visible focus styles. The default browser outline is a starting point, but a clear custom focus ring that matches your design is better than removing the outline entirely. Never remove focus styles without replacing them.

Add an aria-label only where the visible text is not enough. If three cards on one page each have a button that says "Learn more", a screen reader user hears the same label three times with no context. An aria-label such as "Learn more about website development" fixes that without changing the visual design.

Keep the primary CTA above the fold, and make it sticky on mobile where it fits, so the next step stays within reach while the visitor scrolls. Make sure the tap target is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels, with enough space around it that a thumb does not hit the wrong link.

Track conversions with a single analytics event per CTA. One event per click, fired from one handler, keeps the data clean and avoids loading extra tracking code that slows the page down. Measure the click, the form completion, and the final enquiry separately, so you can tell whether the button or the page behind it needs the fix.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should every page on a website have a call to action?

Yes. Every important page should guide visitors toward a relevant next step. That step might be contacting the business, buying a product, exploring a service, or reading related content. The action changes with the page, but the page should never just end with nowhere to go.

Can a website page have more than one CTA?

Yes, but it should have only one primary CTA. Secondary actions like links to other pages are fine, as long as they do not compete visually with the main button. One clear priority keeps the visitor's decision simple.

Where should I place a CTA button on my website?

Place the main CTA where visitors can find it easily, near the top of the page and again after the important information. The exact spot depends on the page layout, but the rule stays the same: a visitor should never have to hunt for the next step.

How do I know if my website CTA is working?

Track button clicks, completed enquiry forms, phone calls, and purchases. If visitors click the button but do not finish the action, look at the form or the page behind it. The problem is often a long form, a slow page, or a button that lands in the wrong place.

Muhammad Asad Ullah is the founder of aimEncoders, a website development agency in Faisalabad that builds websites designed to turn visitors into enquiries. The aimEncoders team checks every page for one clear next step before launch, so customers always know how to reach your business.

title: How to build, debug, and optimize PostgreSQL code with dbForge Studio and AI Assistant
description:
PostgreSQL development goes far beyond writing and executing queries. It involves optimizing queries for minimal resource usage, refactoring code, and managing database objects such as functions, procedures, and triggers. These tasks require time, attention to detail, and a solid understanding of SQL. Equally important is having the right PostgreSQL development tools to help you work efficiently and maintain the high quality of your output.

This is where we'll explore how a PostgreSQL IDE and its integrated AI Assistant can support your entire development workflow, from writing and refining SQL to debugging issues and improving query performance. You'll see how easy it is to use the Studio's built-in development tools to get cleaner, more efficient database code. What's more, the recent release of dbForge 2026.2 adds a whole lot of new features focused on PostgreSQL and a variety of supported related cloud services.

Now, let's get a more detailed overview of those.

Build PostgreSQL functions, procedures, and triggers

Creating and editing server-side PostgreSQL objects often involves more than crafting SQL statements. Functions, procedures, and triggers help you form business logic, automate database operations, and maintain data consistency. With dbForge Studio for PostgreSQL, you can handle these objects using dedicated visual editors, making your routine database development more structured and convenient than working exclusively with raw SQL scripts.

dbForge Studio provides all you need to develop PostgreSQL functions and procedures, allowing you to define parameters, write logic, and manage database ops in one place. You can also work with PostgreSQL event triggers to respond to database-level events and automate administrative tasks when specific conditions are met.

When it comes to PL/pgSQL development, the Studio's visual object editors make it easier to create database objects while keeping the underlying SQL accessible. You can work with language constructs and data types, including %ROWTYPE, which lets you declare variables based on the structure of an existing table or view. You can work with PostgreSQL composite types, which group multiple fields into a single data type. The Studio's goal here is to help you build maintainable logic and reduce manual coding where possible.

Debug PostgreSQL functions and procedures

Debugging server-side PostgreSQL code can be challenging, especially when a function or procedure produces unexpected results or fails under specific conditions. While logs and RAISE NOTICE statements can offer a glimpse into what is happening during execution, they often require extra code changes and repeated test runs to isolate the root cause.

This is where the latest incarnation of dbForge Studio comes into play, providing a dedicated built-in PostgreSQL Debugger that lets you investigate functions and procedures directly. You can step through code execution, set breakpoints, and inspect variables to understand how your code behaves at different stages. This makes it easier to trace execution paths, identify incorrect values, and pinpoint the source of an error without relying exclusively on messages printed to the output.

By debugging PL/pgSQL code interactively, you can test assumptions, examine how parameters and variables change during execution, and resolve issues more efficiently. The result is a more straightforward debugging workflow that helps reduce troubleshooting time and makes PostgreSQL functions and procedures easier to maintain.

Let's take a closer look.

Debug PL/pgSQL with breakpoints and step-through execution

When a PostgreSQL function or procedure behaves unexpectedly, finding the exact cause can take time if you rely only on logs or RAISE NOTICE statements. dbForge Studio simplifies this process with interactive debugging tools that let you examine PL/pgSQL code as it runs.

You can set breakpoints on specific lines to pause execution at critical points, then step through the code statement by statement to follow the logic. This approach helps you see which operations run, how execution flows through conditional branches, and where the actual behavior starts to differ from what you expect.

The Debugger also lets you inspect the values of variables and parameters during execution. You can check input arguments, monitor changes to local variables, and examine intermediate results to identify incorrect values or unexpected conditions.

By combining breakpoints, step-by-step execution, and live inspection of variables, you can narrow the problem down to the exact statement where incorrect behavior begins. This makes debugging complex PL/pgSQL functions and procedures more precise and reduces the need for repeated diagnostics-only edits.

Debug without manual pldbgapi configuration

Traditionally, the debugging of PostgreSQL functions and procedures could require additional setup, including configuring the pldbgapi extension before developers could start investigating server-side code. Yet again, dbForge Studio simplifies this process with a built-in PostgreSQL Debugger that does not require pldbgapi but does require deploying its debug engine and having the dblink extension installed on the PostgreSQL server.

With the Debugger integrated directly into the IDE, you can start troubleshooting PL/pgSQL code without spending time preparing a separate debugging environment. Set breakpoints, step through statements, inspect variable values, and pinpoint errors in one workspace. This approach definitely helps focus on fixing code without switching context.

Generate and improve PostgreSQL code with dbForge AI Assistant

All recent advances in AI-powered database development boil down to a simple yet vital goal: to save the developer's time and effort, to reduce manual coding, and to deliver results faster without compromising quality. This is where AI copilots enter the stage, having already become must-have features of the best PostgreSQL IDEs. dbForge Studio is no exception with its smart and reliable AI Assistant, well-versed in everything related to SQL and databases. Let us briefly cover its capabilities.

Feature How dbForge AI Assistant helps you
Conversion of natural language to SQL You can describe a task in natural language and let the AI Assistant generate SQL queries based on your requirements. Afterwards, you can modify and run them in the Studio's built-in PostgreSQL query editor.
Database-aware query generation By attaching a certain database, you can provide schema context to help dbForge AI Assistant produce more relevant code. Note that the Assistant does not have any access to your actual table data.
SQL explanations However complex or unfamiliar your SQL statement may be, the Assistant will explain it in simple terms. It's a top feature for quick investigations and for those who are actively learning SQL.
SQL optimization The Assistant is a smart AI SQL optimizer as well. It can review pre-written queries and recommend optimizations to help identify inefficiencies and improve execution. You can select the required code, ask the Assistant to optimize it, then review the suggestions and apply them.
SQL troubleshooting The same applies to unverified SQL code. The Assistant can pinpoint potential issues with it and suggest possible fixes.
Error analysis and clarifications If an error occurs during the execution of your query, the Assistant can inspect it and just as effectively provide you with detailed explanations and the optimal solution.
Attached documents You can attach requirements, specifications, instructions, or technical documentation to AI conversations for extra context.
AI chat with integrated web search The Assistant can become your best guide to everything related to SQL development and databases in general.
Multiple models The recent update brings a selection of models to choose from, including Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, as well as GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.6 Luna.

All in all, dbForge AI Assistant complements the Studio's development and debugging tools rather than replacing them. It helps you move more efficiently from writing SQL to troubleshooting issues and refining database logic—all while keeping you in control of your code.

How to debug PostgreSQL code in dbForge Studio

Let's see how to debug a PL/pgSQL procedure in dbForge Studio for PostgreSQL. We'll keep it as simple as possible.

First, we compile the procedures and functions for debugging. It's done to provide the debug engine with the required information. Next, we double-click our procedure to open it in the editor, then switch to the SQL tab. Then, we'll insert breakpoints in our SQL to pause execution and allow for deeper analysis.

The procedure requires parameter values to rebuild the schedule, so we enter them.

As we approach our functions, we can either step over to run them and move to the next line or step into to enter them and see what happens inside.

As we step into the function, we can check whether it processed the parameter values by adding Watches, expressions that let us track parameter values during debugging.

As we proceed with debugging, we can observe how the values in the Watches window change.

After we let the procedure run to its completion, we need to confirm that our procedure has generated the schedule rows for the period we debugged. The number of rows should match the length of the period we passed to the procedure; in our case, it's 35 rows for a period from 3/1/2026 to 4/4/2026.

The key advantage of it all is that everything works together in one PostgreSQL IDE. You can move from generating code to investigating a problem and applying a fix without repeatedly switching tools or losing the context of your work.

Final thoughts: Why use dbForge Studio with AI Assistant for PostgreSQL development?

Now that you've seen dbForge Studio in action, let's recap the advantages it gives you in your daily work with PostgreSQL databases.

  • Less manual coding: Effortlessly generate SQL and PL/pgSQL code based on natural language prompts and refine the results with smart PostgreSQL AI.
  • Simpler server-side development: Create and edit functions, procedures, and event triggers using dedicated visual editors, without having to deal with raw code at all times.
  • Schema-aware AI: Provide dbForge AI Assistant with real database context to help it generate more relevant code and troubleshoot issues involving actual tables, columns, and relationships.
  • Easy learning: Get explanations of PostgreSQL code and guidance on database logic.
  • Precise debugging: Use the built-in Debugger to find problems in your objects based on their actual behavior.
  • One PostgreSQL development tool to handle everything: Move from code generation and visual object editing to debugging, troubleshooting, and optimization without leaving your primary IDE.

The result is a polished, streamlined, and effective PostgreSQL development process—your key to a better product, shorter time to market, and greater productivity with lower development and maintenance costs.

title: Next.js prefetches got me rate-limited on my own site. Googlebot had been fetching them by the thousand
description:
This article was created with the help of AI. The numbers come from my own site's Search Console and server logs.

On October 8 I opened my own news site, promtime.net, on my phone and got Cloudflare's error 1015 instead of a page. My own rate-limiting rule had blocked me, and all I had done was read posts on it.

The cause was a Next.js feature that exists to make the site feel fast. Two days later Search Console showed me the same feature from Googlebot's side. Between August 10 and October 22 Googlebot made 25,943 requests to the site, and Search Console filed 16,284 of them under "Other file type": not pages, not images, not scripts.

What the router does

When a <Link> scrolls into view, the Next.js router prefetches the page behind it. It requests the same URL with an _rsc parameter and an RSC: 1 header and gets back the React Server Components payload instead of HTML, so the click that follows feels instant. Googlebot renders pages with JavaScript, and the prefetches fire for it as well.

All 990 example URLs Search Console lists for "Other file type" end in ?_rsc=. One page can have many of them, because Next.js derives the value from request headers. On September 28, within two minutes, Googlebot fetched one post with six different suffixes. Here are four:

/c/ru/post/claude-mythos-solves-the-erdos-discrepancy-problem?_rsc=LIEXrFg38zfWwJsj
/c/ru/post/claude-mythos-solves-the-erdos-discrepancy-problem?_rsc=kFwwhQWGfJ28v95A
/c/ru/post/claude-mythos-solves-the-erdos-discrepancy-problem?_rsc=QQ8lwV8YUpwFDVCh
/c/ru/post/claude-mythos-solves-the-erdos-discrepancy-problem?_rsc=vcDMZA7KM_P7ZtS6

Six days in August

Almost all of it happened between August 18 and 23. On August 19 alone Googlebot fetched 8,984 of these URLs, while on an ordinary day it asked for fewer than a hundred URLs of every other kind. By September the row was down to about ten requests a day.

The timing matches one change. On August 17-19 the site got newsroom pages, an archive with a month navigator and an infinite feed. Why the spike started, and why it then stopped on its own, these numbers can't show.

Who paid for it

Right after that week the site's impressions in Google fell almost to zero, and the crawl is the obvious suspect. The data doesn't back it. Google's guide to crawl budget is written for sites with a million pages or more, or ten thousand if they change every day. Mine has a few thousand. The guide's other warning sign, a pile of URLs stuck in "Discovered - currently not indexed", did show up on my site, but in October, six weeks after the spike was over.

The ones who paid were readers, me included.

The rate-limiting rule on my Cloudflare plan sees only the path, not the query string, so to Cloudflare a prefetch looks exactly like someone opening a page. A post page carried more than forty tag and archive links, and the router prefetched each one as it came on screen. One post view could fire up to 58 requests, enough to trip the limit on its own.

What I changed

  • Turned off prefetch on dense link lists: tags, archive months, feed cards. In Next.js that's prefetch={false} on <Link>. Every other link still prefetches.
  • Doubled the Cloudflare rate limit.
  • Blocked the RSC URLs in robots.txt: 
Disallow: /*?_rsc=
Disallow: /*&_rsc=

The first one is now a standing rule in the project's notes: a dense list of links gets prefetch={false} from the start.

How to check your own site

In Search Console, open Settings, then Crawl stats, and click the "Other file type" row in the "By file type" block. The example URLs are at the bottom. If they end in ?_rsc=, you're looking at the same thing.

In your server logs:

grep Googlebot access.log | grep -c '_rsc='

Since the robots.txt rule went in on October 10, my server logs haven't shown a single _rsc request from Googlebot. Then again, it had almost stopped asking for them long before that. The spike ended on its own, back in August.

The site from this story also publishes AI news in English, as Promtime.

title: Reduced motion in Framer Motion: what I learned adding it to 150+ files
description:
Most sites handle reduced motion with one CSS rule. beUI's site has it too:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *,
  *::before,
  *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  }
}

It's worth having, but on a Framer Motion site it isn't enough. Turn on "Reduce motion" with only this rule in place, and drawers still slide in, tabs still spring and counters still roll.

That CSS only shortens CSS animations and transitions. Framer Motion works out each frame of a spring in JavaScript and writes the result to the element's style, so the media query never sees it.

I build beUI, a library of animated React components, and more than 150 of its files now read the reduced motion setting. Here's what I learned doing that.

Start with the hook, and handle null 

import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react";

const reduce = useReducedMotion() ?? false;

useReducedMotion() returns true when the setting is on. It returns null during server rendering, because the server can't know. The ?? false gives you a plain boolean, so you don't have to remember the third case everywhere.

Pattern 1: fade, don't freeze

Reduced motion doesn't mean no animation. People turn the setting on because movement makes them dizzy or sick: sliding, scaling, spinning, parallax. A short fade doesn't cause that, and it still shows that something changed.

So keep the opacity and drop the transform:

<motion.div
  initial={reduce ? { opacity: 0 } : { opacity: 0, y: 12, scale: 0.96 }}
  animate={{ opacity: 1, y: 0, scale: 1 }}
  exit={reduce ? { opacity: 0 } : { opacity: 0, y: 8, scale: 0.98 }}
  transition={reduce ? { duration: 0.15 } : { type: "spring", duration: 0.4, bounce: 0.2 }}
/>

Swap the spring for a short tween too. Even a fade feels odd when it wobbles.

For a component with a lot of motion children, you don't need to branch every one. beUI's tabs wrap the whole thing once:

<MotionConfig transition={reduce ? { duration: 0 } : transition}>
  {/* the sliding pill and every child animation */}
</MotionConfig>

Pattern 2: some interactions need a different design

Turning off a transform works for a toast. It doesn't work for an iOS-style wheel picker, where the whole point is a drum you fling and watch spin.

If you only remove the animation, you get a drum that jumps between values, which is confusing. So under reduced motion, beUI's wheel picker renders something else entirely: a plain list of buttons in a scroll container with CSS snap points. Same options, same value, same onValueChange, and nothing spins.

Even the sound changed. The drum plays a tick for every row it passes. The reduced version has no rows passing, so it plays one tick when the value is picked.

Ask what the movement is for. If it's the interaction itself, design a calm version of it instead of switching it off.

Pattern 3: decoration just turns off

Some motion only exists to look nice. Under reduced motion it goes away completely:

  • Magnetic buttons that follow the cursor stay still.
  • Parallax layers get no transform and scroll with the page.
  • Smooth scrolling (beUI uses Lenis) turns off and falls back to the browser's normal scroll, and scrollTo jumps straight to the target. 
const style = reduce ? {} : { y: drift };

Nobody misses a parallax effect, but plenty of people feel sick from one.

Pattern 4: check everything you start yourself

The hook only helps where you check it. These are easy to miss:

  • Imperative animations. An animate() call inside a useEffect ignores MotionConfig and your variants. Return early when reduce is on.
  • Native smooth scroll. element.scrollBy({ behavior: "smooth" }) is motion too. beUI's tabs use behavior: reduce ? "instant" : "smooth" when scrolling a tab into view.
  • requestAnimationFrame loops. Same deal, check the flag before you start.

What about MotionConfig reducedMotion="user"? 

<MotionConfig reducedMotion="user">{children}</MotionConfig>

This tells Framer Motion to follow the device setting and skip transform and layout animations for everything inside it. It's a good safety net, and you should add it.

But it can't do pattern 2. It doesn't know your wheel picker should become a list. It also doesn't reach the imperative code in pattern 4. Treat it as the floor, and use the hook where a component needs real thought.

How to test it

  • macOS: System Settings, Accessibility, Display, Reduce motion.
  • Windows: Settings, Accessibility, Visual effects, Animation effects off.
  • Chrome DevTools: Command menu (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+P), type "reduced motion", pick "Emulate CSS prefers-reduced-motion: reduce". useReducedMotion picks this up too.

Then click through the whole page, not just the component you changed. Overlays, counters and scroll effects are the usual stragglers.

The short version

  1. CSS can't stop JavaScript springs. Use useReducedMotion() ?? false.
  2. Keep fades, drop movement.
  3. If the movement is the interaction, design a calm version.
  4. Turn decoration off completely.
  5. Check every animation you start by hand.

beUI's components are built with these rules, so if you'd rather not do this work yourself, you can install them with the shadcn CLI:

npx shadcn@latest add @beui/<component>

Source is on GitHub. And if you use reduced motion yourself, I'd like to hear which animations bother you most.

title: Caches, Certificates, Streaming Uploads and a Simulator That Types
description:
The templates this month (a bank, a streaming service, a messenger, a delivery service and a game) all have servers, and every server ran into something a modern web app takes for granted. This post collects what we added to the Codename One backend to fill those gaps. Several of them apply to the client too. Then there's the simulator, which can now show a virtual keyboard and record a video of your app.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

If you write Spring Boot during the day, most of this will look familiar on purpose. When there's no reason to differ, the backend behaves the way Spring does.

A bounded cache

Bastion looks up prices on every quote. Calling the price feed on every quote is slow and burns the feed's quota. Caching forever shows stale prices. The new cache has a size bound, expiry, a removal listener and metrics:

private static final Cache<String, Price> PRICES = Cache.<String, Price>builder("prices")
        .maximumSize(10000)
        .expireAfterWriteMillis(60000)
        .removalListener((sku, price, cause) -> {
            if (cause == Cache.SIZE) {
                System.out.println("evicted " + sku);
            }
        })
        .build();

Tokens for calling other services

Your server calls other servers: a Google API with a service account, a billing service with client credentials. AccessTokenProvider fetches the token, caches it and refreshes it before it expires:

AccessTokenProvider billing(Config config) throws IOException {
    return new AccessTokenProvider(ClientCredentialsGrant
            .builder("https://auth.example.com/oauth/token", "orders-service")
            .clientSecret(config.get("billing.client-secret"))
            .scopes("invoices:write")
            .build());
}

The same change added importing users from an existing identity store, so moving an app's accounts over doesn't mean asking everyone to reset a password.

Certificates without OpenSSL on the command line

Banks and partners love mutual TLS and private certificate authorities. The PKI API parses PEM, validates a chain against your own anchors, creates certificate signing requests and reads and writes PKCS#12:

List<Certificate> anchors = Certificate.listFromPem(KeyFiles.read("/etc/app/partner-ca.pem"));
List<Certificate> path = new CertificateValidator(anchors)
        .forHost("api.partner.example")
        .validate(Certificate.listFromPem(presentedPem));

Errors in one place

@RestControllerAdvice and @ExceptionHandler turn exceptions into responses once, instead of a try and catch in every handler. Interceptors and validation came with the same change.

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiErrors {
    @ExceptionHandler(IllegalArgumentException.class)
    public HttpServer.Response badInput(IllegalArgumentException e, HttpServer.Request request) {
        return HttpServer.Response.text(400, e.getMessage()).header("X-Error", "input");
    }
}

Streaming bodies and a proxy

Reel's uploads are video files. Reading them into memory isn't an option. request.getBodyStream() hands you the body as it arrives, and large uploads, multipart ones included, spool to disk instead of the heap:

@PostMapping("/archive")
public Map<String, Long> archive(HttpServer.Request request) throws IOException {
    long total = 0;
    byte[] buffer = new byte[64 * 1024];
    InputStream in = request.getBodyStream();
    try {
        for (int n = in.read(buffer); n > 0; n = in.read(buffer)) {
            total += n;                 // store, hash or forward each block
        }
    } finally {
        in.close();
    }
    return Collections.singletonMap("bytes", total);
}

HttpProxy forwards a request to an internal service. It reaches only its target and the hosts you allow, so a crafted path can't turn your server into an open proxy:

images = new HttpProxy("https://images.internal:8443")
        .allowHost("cdn.internal");

@RequestMapping("/images/{name}")
public HttpServer.Response image(HttpServer.Request request) {
    return images.forward(request);  // the same path and query, upstream
}

JSON codecs and java.time in the ORM

These two apply to the client as well as the server. JSON mapping gained custom codecs through JsonTypeAdapter, constructor based creators, generics, arrays and explicit null handling. A codec turns a type into JSON and back, here a money amount kept as a decimal string so it never passes through a double:

public final class MoneyAdapter implements JsonTypeAdapter<Money> {
    public Object toJson(Money m) {
        return m == null ? null : m.toDecimalString();
    }
    public Money fromJson(Object json) {
        if (json == null) {
            return null;
        }
        if (!(json instanceof String)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("expected an amount");
        }
        return Money.parse((String) json);
    }
}

Put @JsonAdapter(MoneyAdapter.class) on the field or the class and the mapper uses it.

The ORM now maps java.time without an annotation: Instant and LocalDateTime as epoch milliseconds and LocalDate as an epoch day, so a date column is a number you can index and compare:

@Entity
public class Booking {
    @Id
    private long id;
    private Instant created;        // epoch milliseconds
    private LocalDate checkIn;      // epoch day
    private LocalDateTime pickup;   // epoch milliseconds
}

Tests that start only what they need

@WebMvcTest starts one controller and the beans you list, not the whole application, and MockMvc calls it without a socket:

@WebMvcTest(value = GreetingApi.class, includes = Greetings.class)
class GreetingSliceTest {
    @Autowired
    private MockMvc mvc;

    @Test
    void greetsWithOnlyTheControllerWired() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(get("/greet/{name}", "Ada"))
                .andExpect(status().isOk())
                .andExpect(jsonPath("$.greeting").value("Hello, Ada"));
    }
}

The same change defined a metric schema and probes for observability, so a dashboard means the same thing for every Codename One service.

The backend is still a tech preview. The backend chapters of the developer guide cover each of these, with the code that the snippets above come from.

A simulator that types

Here's a bug you've probably shipped. The login form looks great in the simulator. On a phone, the keyboard slides up and covers the password field, or the layout jumps, and nobody noticed because the simulator never had a keyboard.

Now it does. Simulate > Virtual Keyboard slides up a keyboard styled after the skin's platform, and it behaves the way that platform does:

  • iOS: the screen keeps its size, Display.getInvisibleAreaUnderVKB() reports the keyboard height, and the focused field scrolls into view.
  • Android, resize mode: the form gets a sizeChanged and lays out again.
  • Android, pan mode: the whole screen shifts up.

The simulated iOS keyboard sliding up over a sign up form.Recorded by the simulator itself, driven over MCP by the script below.

By default Android picks a mode per field, the way the real platform does. The Android: Resize and Android: Pan menu items, or the androidSoftInput setting, force one so you can test both.

The simulator also records. It writes MP4, MOV, WebM or an animated GIF, of the screen alone or inside the device skin, on a fixed frame clock so the video doesn't stutter when your machine is busy. Taps show touch indicators and can play a click, and you can add captions. That's a store preview, a bug report or a tweet, without a screen recorder.

Both are also tools in the simulator's built in MCP server, so a coding agent can drive a whole flow and hand you the video:

sim_keyboard_set   {"mode": "ios"}
sim_record_start   {"path": "/tmp/signup.mp4", "frame": "screen"}
sim_record_caption {"text": "The keyboard slides up, the field stays visible"}
ui_snapshot        {}
sim_tap            {"nodeId": 41}
sim_keyboard_type  {"text": "ada@example.com"}
sim_keyboard_key   {"key": "next"}
sim_keyboard_type  {"text": "correct horse"}
sim_keyboard_key   {"key": "done"}
sim_record_stop

It's an emulation of each platform's keyboard behavior, not the native keyboard itself, so do a final pass on a device. But the covered password field shows up on your desk now, not in a one-star review. The simulator keyboard and recording section of the MCP chapter lists every tool.

That's the week

Flutter, Compose, Swing, JavaFX and Android code, a bank, a streaming service, phones without Google and a better backend. Next week, we keep going. The Flutter post links everything from this week in one place.

/**
 * sdm-fichiers.utils.js — des deux fichiers déposés à la sortie attendue par
 * l'aiguillage : `{ ok, format, headers, fr, en }`.
 *
 * Comme Standards, un seul format par référentiel : le fichier officiel
 * (T2.3.21, demande du chef — plus de fichier plat fabriqué à la main) :
 *
 *   source   le référentiel a un traitement Standards (`BUILDERS[ref]`) :
 *            le fichier partagé par l'entreprise, transformé par ce
 *            traitement, appelé comme Standards l'appelle selon sa sorte :
 *              bilingual  deux classeurs FR et EN ;
 *              csv        une extraction CSV (+ la dépendance) ;
 *              workbook   un classeur, les deux langues dedans (+ dépendances) ;
 *              risks      deux extractions, niveaux 1 à 3 puis niveau 4 ;
 *              jobs       une extraction, deux compléments FR / EN facultatifs.
 *            Un fichier plat déposé pour ce référentiel est refusé.
 *
 *   plat     le référentiel n'a pas de traitement : son format officiel est
 *            le plat de Standards, en-tête en ligne 1 portant les colonnes de
 *            structure de la règle (code, parent, discriminant). Lu comme
 *            Standards le lit (`parseImportWorkbook`). Les colonnes EN sont
 *            remises dans l'ordre FR : l'aiguillage partage une seule ligne
 *            d'en-tête.
 *
 * Les extensions acceptées sont celles de Standards (`EXTENSIONS`). Les
 * en-têtes des classeurs FR / EN source sont remis au texte exact que le
 * traitement Standards attend avant de l'appeler : par position pour
 * GOVERNANCE (`headersByPosition`, ligne 4, colonnes A à G), par nom sans
 * majuscules, accents ni s final pour les régulateurs (`alignHeaders`).
 */

const XLSX = require('xlsx');
const standards = require('../../../controllers/admin/settings/settings-standards.utils');
const integrations = require('../../../controllers/admin/settings/standards-integrations.utils');

/**
 * Les fichiers qu'un import peut recevoir : [clé, champ du formulaire].
 * L'ordre fixe celui de la signature : FR puis EN d'abord, comme avant.
 */
const FILES = [
  ['fr', 'fileFr'], ['en', 'fileEn'], ['source', 'file'], ['l4', 'fileL4'], ['stdFr', 'fileStdFr'], ['stdEn', 'fileStdEn'],
];

/** Ce que chaque sorte de traitement attend, pour l'aide et les messages. */
const EXPECTED = {
  bilingual: 'les deux classeurs source FR et EN',
  csv: 'l\'extraction CSV',
  workbook: 'le classeur source (FR et EN dedans)',
  risks: 'les deux extractions : niveaux 1 à 3, puis niveau 4',
  jobs: 'l\'extraction des postes (compléments FR / EN facultatifs)',
};

/** Les sortes dont le traitement lit les référentiels dont il dépend. */
const WITH_DEPENDENCIES = ['csv', 'workbook', 'risks'];

const text = (v) => (v === undefined || v === null ? '' : String(v).trim());

/** Les extensions que Standards accepte, par sorte et par fichier ; `flat` sans traitement. */
const XLS = ['.xlsx', '.xls'];
const EXTENSIONS = {
  flat: { fr: XLS, en: XLS },
  bilingual: { fr: ['.xlsx'], en: ['.xlsx'] },
  csv: { source: ['.csv'] },
  workbook: { source: XLS },
  risks: { source: XLS, l4: XLS },
  jobs: { source: ['.xlsx'], stdFr: ['.xlsx'], stdEn: ['.xlsx'] },
};

/** Les extensions par fichier pour ce traitement (ou le plat sans traitement). */
const extensionsOf = (builder) => EXTENSIONS[builder ? builder.kind : 'flat'] || {};

/**
 * Le premier fichier reçu dont l'extension n'est pas celle de Standards :
 * message de refus, ou null. `received` : [[clé, { originalname }]].
 */
function checkExtensions(builder, received) {
  const allowed = extensionsOf(builder);
  for (const [key, f] of received) {
    const ok = allowed[key] || [];
    const name = text(f.originalname).toLowerCase();
    if (!ok.some((ext) => name.endsWith(ext))) {
      return ok.length
        ? `${f.originalname} : seuls les fichiers ${ok.join(' ou ')} sont acceptés ici`
        : `${f.originalname} : ce fichier n'est pas attendu pour ce référentiel`;
    }
  }
  return null;
}

/**
 * Les en-têtes que le traitement Standards attend dans les classeurs FR / EN
 * source. Ceux de GOVERNANCE recopient `GOV_SOURCE_COLUMNS`, que Standards
 * n'exporte pas ; ceux des régulateurs viennent de `REGULATORS`.
 */
const SOURCE_HEADERS = {
  GOVERNANCE: {
    fr: ['Procédure', 'Processus', 'Règle', 'Exigence', 'Référence Catalogue',
      'Standard(s) associé(s)', 'Modifications vs last version (Y/N)'],
    en: ['Procedure', 'Processus', 'Rule', 'Requirement', 'Catalogue Reference',
      'Associated Standard(s)', 'Modifications vs last version (Y/N)'],
  },
  ...Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(integrations.REGULATORS || {}).map(([code, spec]) => [code, spec.source])),
};

/** Un en-tête comparé sans majuscules, accents, espaces doublés ni s final de chaque mot. */
const loose = (s) => text(s).normalize('NFD').replace(/[̀-ͯ]/g, '').toLowerCase()
  .split(/\s+/).map((w) => w.replace(/s$/, '')).join(' ');

/**
 * Remet au texte exact attendu la ligne d'en-tête d'un classeur dont les
 * colonnes ne diffèrent que par la casse, les accents ou un s final. La ligne
 * est la première des dix premières où toutes les colonnes attendues se
 * retrouvent. Rend le buffer d'origine s'il n'y a rien à changer.
 */
function alignHeaders(buffer, expected) {
  if (!buffer || !expected) return buffer;
  let wb;
  try {
    wb = XLSX.read(buffer, { type: 'buffer', cellDates: false });
  } catch (_) {
    return buffer;
  }
  const ws = wb.Sheets[wb.SheetNames[0]];
  if (!ws || !ws['!ref']) return buffer;
  const range = XLSX.utils.decode_range(ws['!ref']);
  const wanted = new Map(expected.map((c) => [loose(c), c]));
  for (let r = range.s.r; r <= Math.min(range.e.r, range.s.r + 9); r++) {
    const cells = [];
    for (let c = range.s.c; c <= range.e.c; c++) {
      const address = XLSX.utils.encode_cell({ r, c });
      if (ws[address] && wanted.has(loose(ws[address].v))) cells.push(address);
    }
    const found = new Set(cells.map((a) => loose(ws[a].v)));
    if (found.size < wanted.size) continue;
    const changed = cells.filter((a) => ws[a].v !== wanted.get(loose(ws[a].v)));
    if (!changed.length) return buffer;
    changed.forEach((a) => { ws[a] = { t: 's', v: wanted.get(loose(ws[a].v)) }; });
    return XLSX.write(wb, { type: 'buffer', bookType: 'xlsx' });
  }
  return buffer;
}

/**
 * Les classeurs source lus par position, comme le traitement Standards les lit
 * (`GOV_COL`) : la ligne d'en-tête et le nombre de colonnes utiles (A à F).
 * Les titres changent d'une version et d'une langue à l'autre (« Associated
 * Standards », « Référence Catalogues ») : seule leur place compte.
 */
const BY_POSITION = { GOVERNANCE: { row: 4, useful: 6 } };

/**
 * Écrit en ligne `row` les en-têtes attendus, colonne par colonne, quel que
 * soit leur texte dans le fichier. Rend le buffer d'origine si une des
 * colonnes utiles est vide à cette ligne : le traitement le refusera alors.
 */
function headersByPosition(buffer, expected, { row, useful }) {
  if (!buffer || !expected) return buffer;
  let wb;
  try {
    wb = XLSX.read(buffer, { type: 'buffer', cellDates: false });
  } catch (_) {
    return buffer;
  }
  const ws = wb.Sheets[wb.SheetNames[0]];
  if (!ws || !ws['!ref']) return buffer;
  const address = (c) => XLSX.utils.encode_cell({ r: row - 1, c });
  for (let c = 0; c < useful; c++) if (!text(ws[address(c)] && ws[address(c)].v)) return buffer;
  if (expected.every((name, c) => ws[address(c)] && ws[address(c)].v === name)) return buffer;
  expected.forEach((name, c) => { ws[address(c)] = { t: 's', v: name }; });
  const range = XLSX.utils.decode_range(ws['!ref']);
  range.e.c = Math.max(range.e.c, expected.length - 1);
  ws['!ref'] = XLSX.utils.encode_range(range);
  return XLSX.write(wb, { type: 'buffer', bookType: 'xlsx' });
}

/** Les colonnes qui signent un fichier plat pour cette règle. */
const structureColumns = (rule) => [rule.code, rule.parent, rule.column].filter(Boolean);

/** Lit un classeur comme Standards ; `null` s'il est illisible. */
function readFlat(buffer, parse) {
  try {
    const { columns, data } = parse(buffer);
    return { columns: columns.map(text), rows: data };
  } catch (_) {
    return null;
  }
}

/** Appelle le traitement d'une extraction source unique, selon sa sorte. */
function buildSource(builder, { sourceBuffer, l4Buffer, stdFrBuffer, stdEnBuffer, deps = {} }) {
  const dependencies = Object.keys(deps);
  switch (builder.kind) {
    case 'csv': {
      const rows = integrations.parseCsv(integrations.decode(sourceBuffer));
      if (rows.length < 2) return { ok: false, message: 'fichier vide' };
      const dep = dependencies[0];
      return builder.build(rows, dep ? { depFr: deps[dep].fr, depEn: deps[dep].en, dependency: dep } : null);
    }
    case 'workbook':
      return builder.build(sourceBuffer, dependencies.length ? { deps } : undefined);
    case 'risks':
      if (!l4Buffer) return { ok: false, message: `les deux extractions sont attendues : ${EXPECTED.risks}` };
      return builder.build({ l3Buffer: sourceBuffer, l4Buffer }, { deps });
    case 'jobs':
      return builder.build({ mainBuffer: sourceBuffer, stdFrBuffer, stdEnBuffer });
    default:
      return { ok: false, message: `traitement ${builder.kind} inconnu` };
  }
}

/**
 * @param {object} regle     la règle du référentiel (`ruleOf`)
 * @param {object} builder   traitement Standards du référentiel, ou null
 * @param {{frBuffer?, enBuffer?, sourceBuffer?, l4Buffer?, stdFrBuffer?, stdEnBuffer?, deps?, referential?}} fichiers
 *   deux classeurs FR et EN (plat ou bilingual), ou une extraction source ;
 *   `deps` : les référentiels dont le traitement dépend (`loadStandard`) ;
 *   `referential` : pour remettre les en-têtes source au texte attendu
 * @param {Function} [parse] lecteur de classeur plat (injectable pour les tests)
 */
function readOutput(rule, builder, files, parse = standards.parseImportWorkbook) {
  const { frBuffer, enBuffer, sourceBuffer } = files;
  const structure = structureColumns(rule);
  const isFlat = (l) => Boolean(l) && structure.every((c) => l.columns.includes(c));

  if (builder) {
    // Un fichier plat n'est plus le format officiel d'un référentiel traité.
    // Seuls les classeurs FR / EN se contrôlent : une extraction CSV peut
    // porter les mêmes colonnes de structure sans être un fichier plat, et
    // les zones FR / EN n'acceptent rien pour les autres sortes (`EXTENSIONS`).
    const flat = builder.kind === 'bilingual' && [frBuffer, enBuffer].filter(Boolean).some((b) => isFlat(readFlat(b, parse)));
    if (flat) {
      return { ok: false, message: `fichier plat refusé : ce référentiel s'importe avec le fichier officiel — ${EXPECTED[builder.kind] || 'l\'extraction source'}` };
    }
    let output;
    try {
      if (builder.kind === 'bilingual') {
        if (!(frBuffer && enBuffer)) return { ok: false, message: `déposez ${EXPECTED.bilingual}` };
        const expected = SOURCE_HEADERS[files.referential] || {};
        const position = BY_POSITION[files.referential];
        const align = (buffer, names) => (position ? headersByPosition(buffer, names, position) : alignHeaders(buffer, names));
        output = builder.build({ frBuffer: align(frBuffer, expected.fr), enBuffer: align(enBuffer, expected.en) });
      } else {
        if (!sourceBuffer) return { ok: false, message: `déposez ${EXPECTED[builder.kind] || 'l\'extraction source'}` };
        output = buildSource(builder, files);
      }
    } catch (e) {
      return { ok: false, message: `traitement ${builder.kind} impossible : ${e.message}` };
    }
    return output.ok ? { ...output, format: 'source' } : output;
  }

  if (!(frBuffer && enBuffer)) return { ok: false, message: 'déposez les deux fichiers FR et EN au format plat' };
  const [fr, en] = [frBuffer, enBuffer].map((b) => readFlat(b, parse));

  if (isFlat(fr) && isFlat(en)) {
    const missing = fr.columns.filter((c) => c && !en.columns.includes(c));
    if (missing.length) {
      return { ok: false, message: `colonnes absentes du fichier EN : ${missing.join(', ')}` };
    }
    const ordre = fr.columns.map((c) => en.columns.indexOf(c));
    return {
      ok: true,
      format: 'flat',
      headers: fr.columns,
      fr: fr.rows,
      en: en.rows.map((row) => ordre.map((i) => (i < 0 ? '' : row[i]))),
    };
  }
  return { ok: false, message: `format non reconnu : la ligne 1 des fichiers FR et EN doit porter ${structure.join(', ')}` };
}

module.exports = {
  readOutput, structureColumns, alignHeaders, checkExtensions, extensionsOf, FILES, EXPECTED, WITH_DEPENDENCIES,
};

/**

 *   Entités     : arbre par référentiel, éditeur en tiroir, reprise depuis Standards, génération des migrations.
 *   Migrations  : fichiers engendrés, « marquer jouée », vue de compatibilité, écarts à la base.
 *   Imports     : analyse (n'écrit rien), puis intégration ou refus ; reprise des versions Standards.
 *   Liens       : arbre des entités et fiche à droite (E37), déclaration, reprise de l'existant,
 *                 instances des liens déclarés (tiroir), et en tête les liens douteux à trancher

 *   Test API    : les fonctions de l'API Standards, servies par sys-data-model.
 */
(function () {
  const API = '/ajax/sdm';

  const right = (name) => root.dataset[name] === '1';
  const $ = (sel, inside = document) => inside.querySelector(sel);

  const state = { entities: [], referentials: [], importable: [], types: [], roles: [], syndications: ['none', 'user', 'admin'], editing: null };
  /** Ce qu'affiche le parcours ; null = pas encore chargé. */
  const summary = { entities: false, migrations: null, imports: null, links: null, confirm: null };

  // ── Outils ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  async function request(method, url, body) {
    const options = { method: method, headers: {} };
    if (body instanceof FormData) options.body = body;
    else if (body !== undefined) {
      options.headers['Content-Type'] = 'application/json';
      options.body = JSON.stringify(body);
    }
    // Jamais de réponse en cache : l'écran doit suivre la base (TH.5).
    options.cache = 'no-store';
    const response = await fetch(url, options);
    const json = await response.json().catch(() => ({ success: false, error: `Erreur ${response.status}` }));
    if (!json.success) throw new Error(json.error || `Erreur ${response.status}`);

      if (k === 'dataset') Object.assign(n.dataset, v);
      else if (k in n) n[k] = v;
      else n.setAttribute(k, v);
    }
    for (const e of children.flat()) if (e != null) n.append(e instanceof Node ? e : String(e));
