Step 2: Data model and business logic

Every bike has an ID, a station, a status, a ride counter and the version number version, which starts at 1. The business logic is deliberately a pure function without database access. It receives the state that was read and returns the new one – and it leaves version unchanged. As a result, the new state carries the information about which state the decision was based on, and the repository can use exactly that state as its condition.

// src/bike.ts
export type BikeStatus = 'AVAILABLE' | 'RENTED' | 'MAINTENANCE';

export interface Bike {
  bikeId: string;
  station: string;
  status: BikeStatus;
  ridesSinceService: number;
  rentedBy?: string;
  rentedAt?: string;
  note?: string;
  version: number;
}

/** After this many rides a bike has to go to the workshop. */
export const RIDES_UNTIL_SERVICE = 30;

export type RejectReason = 'NOT_AVAILABLE' | 'SERVICE_DUE' | 'NOT_RENTED' | 'WRONG_CUSTOMER';

export class RentalRejectedError extends Error {
  constructor(public readonly reason: RejectReason) {
    super(`Rental rejected: ${reason}`);
    this.name = 'RentalRejectedError';
  }
}

/** Pure business logic: decides based on the state that was read. */
export function rentBike(bike: Bike, customerId: string, now: Date): Bike {
  if (bike.status !== 'AVAILABLE') throw new RentalRejectedError('NOT_AVAILABLE');
  if (bike.ridesSinceService >= RIDES_UNTIL_SERVICE) throw new RentalRejectedError('SERVICE_DUE');
  return {
    ...bike,
    status: 'RENTED',
    rentedBy: customerId,
    rentedAt: now.toISOString(),
    ridesSinceService: bike.ridesSinceService + 1,
  };
}

export function returnBike(bike: Bike, customerId: string, station: string): Bike {
  if (bike.status !== 'RENTED') throw new RentalRejectedError('NOT_RENTED');
  if (bike.rentedBy !== customerId) throw new RentalRejectedError('WRONG_CUSTOMER');
  const { rentedBy: _rentedBy, rentedAt: _rentedAt, ...rest } = bike;
  return {
    ...rest,
    station,
    status: bike.ridesSinceService >= RIDES_UNTIL_SERVICE ? 'MAINTENANCE' : 'AVAILABLE',
  };
}

Step 3: Conditional writes with a version number

The core is the save method. It writes the complete item with version + 1, but only if the table still holds the version that was read. I use PutItem instead of UpdateItem here, because the business logic returns the full new state anyway. Attributes that should disappear, such as rentedBy when a bike is returned, are removed automatically. With UpdateItem you would have to build the SET and REMOVE parts yourself; the condition would stay the same.

When creating a bike, attribute_not_exists(bikeId) makes sure that an existing bike is not overwritten. That matters more than it seems: an unprotected PutItem would recreate an existing bike with version 1 and thereby reset its version history.

I also set ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure: 'ALL_OLD'. With it, DynamoDB returns the current state directly in the exception when a conflict occurs, and according to the API reference this costs no additional read capacity. There is one catch: the document client from @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb does not convert the item in the error object. It arrives in the raw AttributeValue format, which is why the code calls unmarshall. I use the placeholder #version out of habit; version is not a reserved word, but status is.

// src/bike-repository.ts
import { ConditionalCheckFailedException } from '@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb';
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, GetCommand, PutCommand } from '@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb';
import { unmarshall } from '@aws-sdk/util-dynamodb';
import type { Bike } from './bike.js';

export class VersionConflictError extends Error {
  constructor(
    public readonly bikeId: string,
    public readonly expectedVersion: number,
    public readonly current?: Bike,
  ) {
    super(`Bike ${bikeId} was changed in the meantime (expected version ${expectedVersion})`);
    this.name = 'VersionConflictError';
  }
}

export class BikeAlreadyExistsError extends Error {
  constructor(public readonly bikeId: string) {
    super(`Bike ${bikeId} already exists`);
    this.name = 'BikeAlreadyExistsError';
  }
}

export class BikeRepository {
  constructor(
    private readonly db: DynamoDBDocumentClient,
    private readonly tableName: string,
  ) {}

  async get(bikeId: string): Promise<Bike | undefined> {
    const result = await this.db.send(
      new GetCommand({ TableName: this.tableName, Key: { bikeId }, ConsistentRead: true }),
    );
    return result.Item as Bike | undefined;
  }

  /** Creates a bike with version 1 and never overwrites an existing one. */
  async create(bike: Omit<Bike, 'version'>): Promise<Bike> {
    const item: Bike = { ...bike, version: 1 };
    try {
      await this.db.send(
        new PutCommand({
          TableName: this.tableName,
          Item: item,
          ConditionExpression: 'attribute_not_exists(bikeId)',
        }),
      );
      return item;
    } catch (error) {
      if (error instanceof ConditionalCheckFailedException) throw new BikeAlreadyExistsError(bike.bikeId);
      throw error;
    }
  }

  /**
   * Saves the new state only if nobody has changed the item since it was read.
   * `next.version` is the version that was read; the stored item gets version + 1.
   */
  async save(next: Bike): Promise<Bike> {
    const expectedVersion = next.version;
    const item: Bike = { ...next, version: expectedVersion + 1 };
    try {
      await this.db.send(
        new PutCommand({
          TableName: this.tableName,
          Item: item,
          ConditionExpression: '#version = :expected',
          ExpressionAttributeNames: { '#version': 'version' },
          ExpressionAttributeValues: { ':expected': expectedVersion },
          ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure: 'ALL_OLD',
        }),
      );
      return item;
    } catch (error) {
      if (error instanceof ConditionalCheckFailedException) {
        // The document client does not convert the item in the error: it is still in AttributeValue format.
        const current = error.Item ? (unmarshall(error.Item) as Bike) : undefined;
        throw new VersionConflictError(next.bikeId, expectedVersion, current);
      }
      throw error;
    }
  }
}

Step 4: Resolve conflicts with retry and jitter

A conflict is really just the message “somebody was faster”. The right reaction depends on who makes the decision. For a machine decision like renting, the function simply reads again and decides again. The helper withOptimisticRetry does exactly that, with at most three attempts and a random wait in between. You can read why I use full jitter in detail in the article on exponential backoff with jitter.

The comment in the code is the crucial part: the function you pass in has to read again on every attempt. Only then does the conflict turn into a business answer. In the second attempt, customer c-2 does not get “conflict” but “bike not available”, because the business logic now runs on the fresh state.

// src/optimistic-retry.ts
import { VersionConflictError } from './bike-repository.js';

export interface RetryOptions {
  maxAttempts?: number;
  baseDelayMs?: number;
  sleep?: (ms: number) => Promise<void>;
}

const defaultSleep = (ms: number) => new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

/**
 * Runs read -> decide -> conditional write again if another request was faster.
 * Important: `operation` has to read the item again on every attempt.
 */
export async function withOptimisticRetry<T>(
  operation: (attempt: number) => Promise<T>,
  { maxAttempts = 3, baseDelayMs = 20, sleep = defaultSleep }: RetryOptions = {},
): Promise<T> {
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await operation(attempt);
    } catch (error) {
      if (!(error instanceof VersionConflictError) || attempt >= maxAttempts) throw error;
      // Full jitter: random wait between 0 and base * 2^(attempt-1)
      await sleep(Math.random() * baseDelayMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1));
    }
  }
}

Step 5: The Lambda handler

The handler serves five routes. Renting and returning go through the retry helper. Editing a note with PATCH, on the other hand, is a human decision: there is no automatic retry, and the client has to send the version it has seen. Business rejections and final conflicts are answered with 409 Conflict, outdated forms with 412 Precondition Failed.

// src/handlers/bikes.ts
import { DynamoDBClient } from '@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb';
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient } from '@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb';
import type { APIGatewayProxyEventV2, APIGatewayProxyResultV2 } from 'aws-lambda';
import { RentalRejectedError, rentBike, returnBike, type Bike } from '../bike.js';
import { BikeAlreadyExistsError, BikeRepository, VersionConflictError } from '../bike-repository.js';
import { withOptimisticRetry } from '../optimistic-retry.js';

const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({}), {
  marshallOptions: { removeUndefinedValues: true },
});
const repo = new BikeRepository(db, process.env.TABLE_NAME ?? 'bikes');

class NotFoundError extends Error {}

const json = (statusCode: number, body: unknown, headers: Record<string, string> = {}): APIGatewayProxyResultV2 => ({
  statusCode,
  headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json', ...headers },
  body: JSON.stringify(body),
});

const etag = (bike: Bike) => `"${bike.version}"`;

function parseBody(event: APIGatewayProxyEventV2): Record<string, unknown> {
  try {
    return JSON.parse(event.body ?? '{}') as Record<string, unknown>;
  } catch {
    return {};
  }
}

const requireString = (value: unknown): string | undefined =>
  typeof value === 'string' && value.trim().length > 0 ? value.trim() : undefined;

async function loadOrFail(bikeId: string): Promise<Bike> {
  const bike = await repo.get(bikeId);
  if (!bike) throw new NotFoundError();
  return bike;
}

export async function handler(event: APIGatewayProxyEventV2): Promise<APIGatewayProxyResultV2> {
  const bikeId = event.pathParameters?.bikeId ?? '';
  const body = parseBody(event);

  try {
    switch (event.routeKey) {
      case 'POST /bikes': {
        const id = requireString(body.bikeId);
        const station = requireString(body.station);
        if (!id || !station) return json(400, { message: 'bikeId and station are required' });
        const bike = await repo.create({ bikeId: id, station, status: 'AVAILABLE', ridesSinceService: 0 });
        return json(201, bike, { etag: etag(bike) });
      }

      case 'GET /bikes/{bikeId}': {
        const bike = await loadOrFail(bikeId);
        return json(200, bike, { etag: etag(bike) });
      }

      case 'POST /bikes/{bikeId}/rent': {
        const customerId = requireString(body.customerId);
        if (!customerId) return json(400, { message: 'customerId is required' });
        // Machine decision: on a conflict simply read again and decide again.
        const saved = await withOptimisticRetry(async () => {
          const bike = await loadOrFail(bikeId);
          return repo.save(rentBike(bike, customerId, new Date()));
        });
        return json(200, saved, { etag: etag(saved) });
      }

      case 'POST /bikes/{bikeId}/return': {
        const customerId = requireString(body.customerId);
        const station = requireString(body.station);
        if (!customerId || !station) return json(400, { message: 'customerId and station are required' });
        const saved = await withOptimisticRetry(async () => {
          const bike = await loadOrFail(bikeId);
          return repo.save(returnBike(bike, customerId, station));
        });
        return json(200, saved, { etag: etag(saved) });
      }

      case 'PATCH /bikes/{bikeId}': {
        // Human decision: the client has to send the version it has seen.
        const ifMatch = event.headers['if-match'];
        const expectedVersion = Number(ifMatch?.replaceAll('"', ''));
        if (!ifMatch || !Number.isInteger(expectedVersion)) {
          return json(428, { message: 'If-Match header with the version is required' });
        }
        const note = typeof body.note === 'string' ? body.note.slice(0, 500) : undefined;
        const bike = await loadOrFail(bikeId);
        if (bike.version !== expectedVersion) {
          return json(412, { message: 'Bike was changed in the meantime', current: bike }, { etag: etag(bike) });
        }
        const saved = await repo.save({ ...bike, note });
        return json(200, saved, { etag: etag(saved) });
      }

      default:
        return json(404, { message: 'Route not found' });
    }
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof NotFoundError) return json(404, { message: `Bike ${bikeId} not found` });
    if (error instanceof BikeAlreadyExistsError) return json(409, { message: error.message });
    if (error instanceof RentalRejectedError) return json(409, { message: error.message, reason: error.reason });
    if (error instanceof VersionConflictError) {
      const status = event.routeKey === 'PATCH /bikes/{bikeId}' ? 412 : 409;
      return json(status, { message: error.message, current: error.current });
    }
    console.error('Unexpected error', error);
    return json(500, { message: 'Internal error' });
  }
}

Step 6: The CDK stack

The stack is short: a table in on-demand mode, a Lambda function on ARM with an ESM bundle and an HTTP API with five routes. For Node.js runtimes the CDK does not bundle the AWS SDK v3 by default, because it is already available in the runtime; so the package stays at a few kilobytes.

One detail in the repository deserves a second look: I read with ConsistentRead: true. Correctness does not depend on it, because the condition always checks against the current state in the table. A strongly consistent read does, however, reduce the number of unnecessary conflicts, because the function does not start with an outdated state. In return it costs twice as much read capacity as an eventually consistent read.

// lib/bike-rental-stack.ts
import { CfnOutput, Duration, RemovalPolicy, Stack, type StackProps } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import { HttpApi, HttpMethod } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-apigatewayv2';
import { HttpLambdaIntegration } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-apigatewayv2-integrations';
import { AttributeType, Billing, TableV2 } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-dynamodb';
import { Architecture, Runtime } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda';
import { NodejsFunction, OutputFormat } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-nodejs';
import { LogGroup, RetentionDays } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-logs';
import type { Construct } from 'constructs';

export class BikeRentalStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    const table = new TableV2(this, 'BikesTable', {
      partitionKey: { name: 'bikeId', type: AttributeType.STRING },
      billing: Billing.onDemand(),
      removalPolicy: RemovalPolicy.DESTROY, // demo only: in production use RETAIN
    });

    const fn = new NodejsFunction(this, 'BikesFunction', {
      entry: 'src/handlers/bikes.ts',
      handler: 'handler',
      runtime: Runtime.NODEJS_24_X,
      architecture: Architecture.ARM_64,
      memorySize: 512,
      timeout: Duration.seconds(10),
      environment: { TABLE_NAME: table.tableName },
      logGroup: new LogGroup(this, 'BikesLogs', {
        retention: RetentionDays.TWO_WEEKS,
        removalPolicy: RemovalPolicy.DESTROY,
      }),
      bundling: { format: OutputFormat.ESM, minify: true, sourceMap: true },
    });
    table.grantReadWriteData(fn);

    const api = new HttpApi(this, 'BikesApi');
    const integration = new HttpLambdaIntegration('BikesIntegration', fn);
    const routes: Array<[HttpMethod, string]> = [
      [HttpMethod.POST, '/bikes'],
      [HttpMethod.GET, '/bikes/{bikeId}'],
      [HttpMethod.PATCH, '/bikes/{bikeId}'],
      [HttpMethod.POST, '/bikes/{bikeId}/rent'],
      [HttpMethod.POST, '/bikes/{bikeId}/return'],
    ];
    for (const [method, path] of routes) {
      api.addRoutes({ path, methods: [method], integration });
    }

    new CfnOutput(this, 'ApiUrl', { value: api.apiEndpoint });
    new CfnOutput(this, 'TableName', { value: table.tableName });
  }
}

// bin/app.ts
import { App } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import { BikeRentalStack } from '../lib/bike-rental-stack.js';

const app = new App();
new BikeRentalStack(app, 'BikeRentalStack');

Step 7: Tests with Vitest

Conflicts are hard to produce locally, so I simulate them with aws-sdk-client-mock: the first write fails with a ConditionalCheckFailedException, the second one succeeds. This lets you check that the retry really reads again, that it does not overwrite a change made by staff and that the second customer gets a business rejection. The repository also contains tests for the business logic and the handler.

// test/bike-repository.test.ts
import { ConditionalCheckFailedException } from '@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb';
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, GetCommand, PutCommand } from '@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb';
import { marshall } from '@aws-sdk/util-dynamodb';
import { mockClient } from 'aws-sdk-client-mock';
import { beforeEach, describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { rentBike, type Bike } from '../src/bike.js';
import { BikeRepository, VersionConflictError } from '../src/bike-repository.js';
import { withOptimisticRetry } from '../src/optimistic-retry.js';

const ddb = mockClient(DynamoDBDocumentClient);
const repo = new BikeRepository(ddb as unknown as DynamoDBDocumentClient, 'bikes');
const bike: Bike = { bikeId: 'b-17', station: 'harbour', status: 'AVAILABLE', ridesSinceService: 3, version: 4 };

const conflict = (current: Bike) =>
  new ConditionalCheckFailedException({ message: 'The conditional request failed', $metadata: {}, Item: marshall(current) });

beforeEach(() => ddb.reset());

describe('BikeRepository.save', () => {
  it('writes version + 1 with a condition on the version that was read', async () => {
    ddb.on(PutCommand).resolves({});
    const saved = await repo.save({ ...bike, note: 'new bell' });
    expect(saved.version).toBe(5);
    const input = ddb.commandCalls(PutCommand)[0]!.args[0].input;
    expect(input.ConditionExpression).toBe('#version = :expected');
    expect(input.ExpressionAttributeValues).toEqual({ ':expected': 4 });
    expect(input.Item).toMatchObject({ version: 5, note: 'new bell' });
  });

  it('turns a failed condition into a VersionConflictError with the current item', async () => {
    ddb.on(PutCommand).rejects(conflict({ ...bike, version: 5, status: 'RENTED', rentedBy: 'c-9' }));
    const error = await repo.save(bike).catch((e: unknown) => e);
    expect(error).toBeInstanceOf(VersionConflictError);
    expect((error as VersionConflictError).current).toMatchObject({ version: 5, rentedBy: 'c-9' });
  });
});

describe('withOptimisticRetry', () => {
  const noSleep = async () => {};

  it('reads again after a conflict and succeeds on the second attempt', async () => {
    ddb.on(GetCommand)
      .resolvesOnce({ Item: bike })
      .resolvesOnce({ Item: { ...bike, version: 5, note: 'changed by staff' } });
    ddb.on(PutCommand).rejectsOnce(conflict({ ...bike, version: 5 })).resolves({});

    const saved = await withOptimisticRetry(
      async () => repo.save(rentBike((await repo.get('b-17'))!, 'c-1', new Date())),
      { sleep: noSleep },
    );

    expect(saved).toMatchObject({ version: 6, rentedBy: 'c-1', note: 'changed by staff' });
    expect(ddb.commandCalls(GetCommand)).toHaveLength(2);
  });

  it('decides again on the fresh state: the second customer gets a clear rejection', async () => {
    ddb.on(GetCommand)
      .resolvesOnce({ Item: bike })
      .resolvesOnce({ Item: { ...bike, version: 5, status: 'RENTED', rentedBy: 'c-1' } });
    ddb.on(PutCommand).rejectsOnce(conflict({ ...bike, version: 5, status: 'RENTED' }));

    await expect(
      withOptimisticRetry(async () => repo.save(rentBike((await repo.get('b-17'))!, 'c-2', new Date())), {
        sleep: noSleep,
      }),
    ).rejects.toThrow(/NOT_AVAILABLE/);
  });

  it('gives up after maxAttempts and passes on the conflict', async () => {
    ddb.on(GetCommand).resolves({ Item: bike });
    ddb.on(PutCommand).rejects(conflict({ ...bike, version: 99 }));
    await expect(
      withOptimisticRetry(async () => repo.save((await repo.get('b-17'))!), { maxAttempts: 3, sleep: noSleep }),
    ).rejects.toBeInstanceOf(VersionConflictError);
    expect(ddb.commandCalls(PutCommand)).toHaveLength(3);
  });
});

One of the two requests gets the bike, the other a clear rejection (the order of the fields may differ):

{"bikeId":"b-17","station":"harbour","status":"RENTED","ridesSinceService":1,"rentedBy":"c-1","rentedAt":"2026-11-09T14:05:12.345Z","version":2}
{"message":"Rental rejected: NOT_AVAILABLE","reason":"NOT_AVAILABLE"}

Which request wins is random; what matters is that exactly one does. Whether the second one notices the conflict only when writing or already sees “rented” when reading depends on timing. The result is the same in both cases. To clean up, run npx cdk destroy.

ETag and If-Match: optimistic locking over HTTP

For forms, an automatic retry is not enough. Suppose someone from the workshop opens bike b-17 and types a note for three minutes. In the meantime a colleague adds something as well. A retry would simply overwrite her note, because the decision (“this note should be saved”) is based on a state that only a human can re-evaluate.

That is why the handler returns the version as an ETag header. An ETag does not have to be a hash; according to the HTTP standard, a version number in double quotes is a valid value. When saving, the client sends the version it has seen in the If-Match header. If it no longer matches, the API answers with 412 Precondition Failed and the current state, so the UI can show both versions. If the header is missing entirely, the answer is 428 Precondition Required, so nobody bypasses the protection by accident.

curl -si "$API/bikes/b-17" | grep -i etag
curl -s -X PATCH "$API/bikes/b-17" -H 'content-type: application/json' -H 'if-match: "2"' -d '{"note":"Brake squeaks"}'

Comparing the versions in the handler is only a quick pre-check. The actual protection is still the condition in save: if someone changes the bike exactly between reading and writing, the VersionConflictError ends up in the catch block and becomes a 412 as well.

Common mistakes with optimistic locking

Retrying without reading again

The most common mistake hides in the retry. If you take the version from the exception and save the old decision with it once more, you rebuild exactly the lost update you wanted to avoid. A retry always has to repeat all three steps: read, decide, write conditionally.

Increasing the version without a condition

A SET version = version + 1 without a ConditionExpression only counts along and protects nothing. The version number only works in combination with the condition on the value that was read.

Hot items with many writers

Optimistic locking relies on rare conflicts. If hundreds of requests write to the same item at the same time, for example a stock counter during a ticket sale, a large share of the attempts fails, and every failure costs write capacity. Atomic counters with a condition help here, or an SQS FIFO queue whose message group per item processes the writes one after another. To make duplicate deliveries harmless, you then also need idempotency in the Lambda handler.

Old items without a version attribute

If you introduce the pattern later, existing items do not have a version yet. A transition condition such as attribute_not_exists(#version) OR #version = :expected covers both cases if your code treats a missing attribute as version 0. Once all items have been migrated, you can remove the first part again.

Costs and security

Conflicts are not free. According to the DynamoDB documentation, a conditional write consumes write capacity even when the condition is not met, depending on the item size. In on-demand mode you therefore pay for every failed attempt like a successful one. With rare conflicts this is negligible, with hot items it adds up. The return value from ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure, on the other hand, is not charged as read capacity. If you want to estimate what the Lambda side costs at your volume, the Lambda cost calculator helps.

Regarding security: the demo API has no authentication. Before something like this goes into production, it needs an authorizer, for example as shown in the article on Lambda authorizers for HTTP APIs. In addition, grantReadWriteData allows more actions than the function needs; in production I would limit the permissions to GetItem and PutItem on this table and create the table with RemovalPolicy.RETAIN.

My take

To me, optimistic locking is one of the cheapest insurance policies DynamoDB has to offer. One attribute, one condition, one small helper – and a whole class of bugs that otherwise only show up in production, and then usually hard to trace, is gone. For every entity that is edited by code logic or by people, I would plan the version number from day one today. Retrofitting works, but it is more tedious.

What I disagree with is the reflex to use the pattern everywhere. For counters and simple status changes, a condition directly in the update is leaner and saves a read. I am also sceptical of libraries that hide versioning completely, like the @DynamoDbVersionAttribute annotation in the Java SDK. It is convenient, but it moves the most important question out of sight: what should happen on a conflict – decide again or ask the human? That decision should be visible in the code.

FAQ

What does a failed conditional write cost in DynamoDB?

It consumes write capacity like a successful write, depending on the size of the item. In on-demand mode it is billed as usual. With rare conflicts this hardly matters.

What is the difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking?

Optimistic locking locks nothing and detects conflicts only when writing, using a version number. Pessimistic locking locks before reading, and everybody else waits. In DynamoDB the optimistic variant is usually the better choice, because it works without stuck locks.

Does optimistic locking work with DynamoDB global tables?

Within one Region yes, across Regions not reliably. Global tables resolve conflicts between Regions with “last writer wins”, without checking the version condition.

Do I need a transaction for optimistic locking?

No. For a single item, a conditional PutItem or UpdateItem is enough. You only need transactions with TransactWriteItems when several items have to change together.

Your next step

Search your code for places where a GetItem is followed by a PutItem or UpdateItem without a ConditionExpression. Every match is a candidate for a lost update. Then use the table above to check whether a simple condition is enough or whether a version number pays off.

Where do you suspect a lost update in your applications that simply nobody has noticed so far? Feel free to share it in the comments.

Next in the series: Overview “Serverless patterns in practice” · Previous part: SSRF protection for webhooks: call user URLs safely

title: Iceberg catalogs explained: REST, Glue, S3 Tables, Polaris, Nessie
description:
"Iceberg catalog" sounds like a big piece of infrastructure: a metadata service, a governance layer, something with a vendor attached. The core job is much smaller. A catalog keeps one pointer per table, to the table's current metadata.json, and changes that pointer atomically when someone commits. Everything else about the table lives in files.

Once you see that pointer, the choice between REST, Glue, S3 Tables, Polaris and Nessie gets easier. They differ in what they add around the pointer, and in which engines can reach them. I have not run Iceberg in production. To show the catalog concretely, I built a table on my laptop with PyIceberg 0.12.0 and DuckDB 1.5.6, using a SQL catalog on SQLite and then on a throwaway Postgres 16. The rows below are from those runs.

What is an Iceberg catalog?

An Iceberg table is a folder of Parquet data files plus a tree of metadata. The top of the tree is a metadata.json holding the schema, the partition spec and the list of snapshots. Every commit writes a new metadata.json. Nothing is edited in place. So after 50 commits there are 51 of them, and something has to say which one is current.

That something is the catalog. Here is the entire state of PyIceberg's SQL catalog after I created one table and appended 50 batches to it. The catalog database held two tables:

iceberg_tables
iceberg_namespace_properties

and iceberg_tables held one row:

catalog_name                lab
table_namespace             shop
table_name                  events
metadata_location           .../events/metadata/00050-c499c071-....metadata.json
previous_metadata_location  .../events/metadata/00049-bb259239-....metadata.json
iceberg_type                TABLE

That is it. One row, two file paths. The table's schema, its 50 snapshots and its file lists are all in the 50 KB metadata.json that row points to. The catalog holds a few hundred bytes.

A commit is a compare-and-swap

When a writer commits, it writes new data and metadata files, then asks the catalog to move the pointer. The SQL catalog does it with one statement. Simplified from PyIceberg's source:

UPDATE iceberg_tables
SET metadata_location          = '.../00051-....metadata.json',
    previous_metadata_location = '.../00050-....metadata.json'
WHERE table_namespace   = 'shop'
  AND table_name        = 'events'
  AND metadata_location = '.../00050-....metadata.json';  -- the version I started from

If another writer committed in between, the WHERE matches no row, and PyIceberg raises CommitFailedException. I tested it on Postgres: two handles on the same table, both appending. The second append conflicted, PyIceberg retried 108 ms later on top of the new state, and both rows landed.

That check is why the catalog exists. Object storage has no cheap way for two writers to agree on which file is "current". The catalog gives them one place to take turns.

After a delete, a schema change, an append, a rewrite and a snapshot expiry, the same row pointed at 00055-....metadata.json, with 00054 as the previous one. Every operation moved the pointer once.

This is the first part. The full post — including the rest of the working details — is on my site: Iceberg catalogs explained: REST, Glue, S3 Tables, Polaris, Nessie

title: React 19.3 View Transitions: The Suspense Patterns That Keep an App Fast
description:
TL;DR

  • React 19.3 (9 September 2026) made <ViewTransition> stable, and Next.js 16.4 ships it. In the App Router every navigation is a Transition, so boundaries animate with no extra code.
  • An unconfigured boundary animates on every trigger. Start from default="none" and opt into the triggers you want.
  • Follow the Suspense rule: fallbacks appear instantly, the reveal animates, cached content never animates. update="auto" default="none" around <Suspense> does all three.
  • A DOM node above a boundary, a boundary in a layout, or a shared pair without share all disable animations silently.
  • Reduced motion and clicks during animations are your responsibility, not React's.

Most of the View Transition bugs that ship in React apps over the next year will come from animating too much, not too little. React 19.3 made <ViewTransition> stable, Next.js 16.4 bundles it, and the default behaviour is generous: an unconfigured boundary cross-fades on every Transition that touches it. That is pleasant in a demo and tiring in a product. The teams that get this right will treat animation as something each boundary opts into, starting from default="none", and will follow one rule for loading states that the React team spelled out in the 19.3 announcement.

This guide takes that position and builds on it. It covers what became stable and when, which updates can trigger an animation at all, the Suspense rule, shared elements and directional navigation in Next.js, the placement mistakes that switch animations off without an error, and the accessibility and browser-support work that remains your responsibility. It ends with the checks we run on a codebase before View Transitions go to production.

Every API detail below was checked on 9 November 2026 against the React 19.3 release post and reference docs, the Next.js 16.4 release post and view transitions guide, the documentation bundled inside the next@16.4.5 package, and the npm registry. Where two official sources disagree, the section says so.

What React 19.3 made stable, and which versions you need

React 19.3.0 was published to npm on 9 September 2026, and the React 19.3 announcement moved two APIs out of the experimental channel: <ViewTransition> and Fragment refs. Both had been previewed as experimental the year before. The current patch at the time of writing is 19.3.1, published on 14 October 2026, and it is what the latest tag on npm resolves to.

The release also added addTransitionType support for typed animations, a browser() API in react-dom for opting components out of server rendering, Trusted Types support, and the ability for Server Components to render a Context directly. Nothing in the release is listed as a breaking change, which is consistent with it shipping as a minor version rather than React 20.

For Next.js projects, the version that matters is 16.4. The Next.js 16.4 release post, published on 6 October 2026, states that it ships with React 19.3, including stable View Transitions and Fragment refs. If you are upgrading for this reason, go straight to the current patch rather than 16.4.0. On 3 November the team published a security release as 16.4.5 and 15.5.29, fixing one high and several medium severity issues, most of them in Cache Components. If your project is still on Next.js 15, our Next.js 16 upgrade checklist covers the breaking changes to handle first.

Package Version checked Published Why it matters
react, react-dom 19.3.1 14 October 2026 Stable <ViewTransition>, Fragment refs, addTransitionType
next 16.4.5 3 November 2026 Ships React 19.3, transitionTypes on <Link>, security fixes

Keep react and react-dom on the same version. A mismatch is one of the quicker ways to lose an afternoon, because npm refuses the install and forcing it produces runtime errors that look unrelated to the upgrade.

Which updates can trigger a View Transition

A View Transition only runs when an update is marked as non-urgent. The <ViewTransition> reference names three sources: state updates inside startTransition, a <Suspense> boundary revealing its content, and an update coming from useDeferredValue. A plain setState in an event handler never animates, however the boundary is configured.

That design is deliberate, and it is worth understanding before writing any CSS. Urgent updates, such as typing into an input or toggling a checkbox, should appear immediately, and React will not put an animation between the user and the result. Non-urgent updates are the ones where React is already willing to wait, so adding a short animation does not change how responsive the interface feels.

import { ViewTransition, useState, startTransition } from 'react';

function Panel() {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);

  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => startTransition(() => setOpen(o => !o))}>
        Toggle details
      </button>

      {open && (
        <ViewTransition>
          <Details />
        </ViewTransition>
      )}
    </>
  );
}

Remove startTransition from that click handler and the panel still opens, but without animation. When someone reports that "the animation only works sometimes", this is the first thing to check: one code path wraps the update in a Transition and another does not.

In the Next.js App Router, route navigations are already Transitions, so <ViewTransition> boundaries animate during navigation without any extra code. The Next.js view transitions guide makes this point directly, and it is the reason a single unconfigured boundary in a shared component can start animating on every page change.

You also never call document.startViewTransition() yourself. React calls it for you, and calling it alongside React's own handling produces competing transitions.

The four triggers: enter, exit, update and share

React picks an animation based on how the tree changed around each boundary. There are four triggers, and each one can be configured separately:

  • enter runs when the <ViewTransition> is inserted during a Transition.
  • exit runs when it is removed.
  • update runs when DOM inside it changes, or when its size or position changes because of an immediate sibling.
  • share runs when a named boundary is removed in one place and a boundary with the same name is inserted somewhere else.

Each trigger prop accepts "auto" (the browser's default cross-fade), "none", a class name of your own, or an object keyed by transition type. A class name is the usual choice, because it connects the boundary to CSS through the view transition pseudo-elements:

<ViewTransition enter="slide-up" exit="fade-out">
  <Notice />
</ViewTransition>

::view-transition-new(.slide-up) {
  animation: 220ms ease-out both slide-up;
}

::view-transition-old(.fade-out) {
  animation: 150ms ease-in both fade-out;
}

@keyframes slide-up {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(8px); }
  to   { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); }
}

@keyframes fade-out {
  to { opacity: 0; }
}

The React docs recommend styling through these classes rather than targeting view-transition-name values directly. Classes survive refactors and work with React's generated names; hard-coded names do not.

There is also an imperative route. The event props onEnter, onExit, onUpdate and onShare receive the transition instance and the active types, so you can drive the animation with the Web Animations API and return a cleanup function. Only one event fires per boundary per Transition, and onShare wins over onEnter and onExit. Most interfaces never need this, and CSS keeps the animation where designers can find it.

One more detail matters for layouts: React treats each boundary's content as a single image that moves, scales and cross-fades. Child elements inside it do not animate their own positions. If a card's title and image should move independently, they need separate boundaries.

Why default="none" should be your starting point

default="none" turns off every trigger on a boundary except the ones you list explicitly. It is the single most useful prop on <ViewTransition>, and starting from it is the opt-in model this guide argues for.

The problem it solves is not obvious until an app has more than a few boundaries. An unconfigured boundary uses "auto" for every trigger, so it cross-fades whenever any Transition updates it. In the App Router that means every navigation, every router.refresh(), and every Suspense reveal nearby. The Next.js guide puts it plainly: without default="none", every named <ViewTransition> animates whenever any transition runs on the page. Individually, each cross-fade is subtle. Together, they make an interface feel slow even when the data arrives quickly, because the user watches content dissolve rather than appear.

<ViewTransition default="none" enter="slide-up">
  <SearchResults query={query} />
</ViewTransition>

That boundary animates when the results first enter and stays still for everything else. If you later decide that updates should cross-fade too, you add update="auto", and the change is visible in code review instead of being an accident of defaults.

There is one trap. A named pair used for a shared element transition needs an explicit share prop once you add default="none". The Next.js guide warns that with default="none" and no share, the pair silently stops morphing. Nothing errors, and the morph simply disappears.

<ViewTransition name={`product-${id}`} share="morph" default="none">
  <ProductImage id={id} />
</ViewTransition>

As a working rule, we treat any <ViewTransition> without default="none" as something a reviewer should question. Sometimes the generous default is right, for a small, self-contained widget that only ever changes through one Transition. Usually it is a boundary that nobody has fully thought through yet.

The Suspense rule: instant fallbacks, animated reveals

The React 19.3 announcement gives three principles for animating around Suspense, and they are the core of this guide:

  1. Fallbacks should appear immediately, without animation.
  2. A fallback should change to its final content with animation.
  3. Children that do not suspend should appear immediately, without animation.

Each principle protects responsiveness in a different way. An instant fallback tells the user that their click registered; fading it in delays that acknowledgement for no benefit. An animated reveal smooths the jump from skeleton to content, which is the moment where a hard cut feels most jarring. And content that is already cached should never animate, because an animation on data the user has seen before turns an instant response into a slow one.

The default configuration breaks the first and third principles. Wrap a Suspense boundary in a plain <ViewTransition> and the fallback fades in, then content that was already loaded animates again every time the component is shown. The announcement's fix is to switch off everything except updates:

<ViewTransition update="auto" default="none">
  <Suspense fallback={<OrderSummarySkeleton />}>
    <OrderSummary orderId={orderId} />
  </Suspense>
</ViewTransition>

Now the skeleton appears at once, the change from skeleton to summary cross-fades, and once the summary is cached, toggling it is instant. This is a small change with a large effect on how an app feels, and it is the pattern we would put in a team's shared components before anything more decorative.

Suspense boundaries also wait for more than data. Inside a <ViewTransition>, React waits up to 500 milliseconds for fonts and visible images to load before running the animation, and the 19.3 post shows how wrapping images and stylesheets inside a boundary lets them take part in Suspense. That turns the familiar flicker of an image arriving late into a coordinated reveal, as long as the image loads within that window.

Choosing between the update and enter/exit patterns for Suspense

There are two ways to animate a Suspense reveal, and they communicate different things.

The update pattern wraps the whole Suspense boundary in one <ViewTransition>. The fallback and the content share one identity, so React cross-fades from one to the other in place. It suits content that occupies the same space as its skeleton, such as a card, a table or a summary panel.

The enter and exit pattern puts one boundary around the fallback and another around the content. The fallback exits and the content enters, each with its own animation:

<Suspense
  fallback={
    <ViewTransition exit="slide-down" default="none">
      <ArticleSkeleton />
    </ViewTransition>
  }
>
  <ViewTransition enter="slide-up" default="none">
    <Article slug={slug} />
  </ViewTransition>
</Suspense>

This is the pattern the Next.js guide uses for a detail page, with deliberately uneven timing: the skeleton leaves in about 150 milliseconds, and the content's fade waits for that exit to finish before arriving over roughly 210 milliseconds, while its slide runs for 400. The reasoning is sound. Old content should leave quickly so that it does not compete for attention, and new content should arrive gently enough for the eye to register it.

Situation Pattern Why
Skeleton and content occupy the same box Update, one boundary around <Suspense> Reads as the same thing becoming ready
Content is a different shape from its skeleton Enter and exit, one boundary each Avoids stretching one image into another
Content is usually cached Either, with default="none" Cached reveals should not animate
Many small boundaries on one screen Update, or none at all Several entrances at once looks busy

If you are unsure, start with the update pattern and default="none". It is the quieter of the two and the harder one to get wrong.

Shared element morphs and the prefetch condition

A shared element transition makes one element appear to move between two states: a product thumbnail growing into the hero image on its detail page, for example. You create one by giving two boundaries the same name, one in the old tree and one in the new:

// In the grid
<Link href={`/products/${p.id}`}>
  <ViewTransition name={`product-${p.id}`} share="morph" default="none">
    <Image src={p.thumb} alt={p.title} width={320} height={320} />
  </ViewTransition>
</Link>

// On the detail page
<ViewTransition name={`product-${p.id}`} share="morph" default="none">
  <Image src={p.hero} alt={p.title} width={960} height={960} />
</ViewTransition>

Three conditions decide whether the morph actually plays, and each one fails silently.

Names must be unique across the whole app at any moment. Only one boundary with a given name can be mounted at a time. A list where every item uses the same name raises an error about two components sharing a name, which is the easy case. The harder case is a name that collides only when two specific components happen to be mounted together. Build names from a stable identifier, and keep any fixed names in a module of namespaced constants.

Both sides must be in the viewport. If either element is off screen, React does not form a pair, and each side runs an ordinary enter or exit animation instead.

The destination must render in the same commit. This is the condition that catches Next.js teams. The guide explains that the morph plays when the destination content renders in the same commit as the navigation, which is the case for prefetched pages. If the destination suspends into a fallback first, there is no pair, and the content uses its enter animation when it arrives. In practice, a shared element morph is only as reliable as your prefetching. If the detail page fetches uncached data before it can render the hero image, the morph will rarely play, and the fix belongs in your data and caching strategy, not in CSS.

The Next.js guide also adds a short blur to the image pair during the morph. It is a useful trick, because it hides the scaling artefacts that appear when a small image is stretched to a larger size mid-flight.

Directional navigation with transition types in Next.js 16.4

Transition types let one boundary choose different animations depending on why a Transition happened. In plain React you add a type inside the Transition with addTransitionType, for example addTransitionType('next'). In Next.js, <Link> accepts a transitionTypes prop, and the bundled documentation for 16.4.5 records it as added in version 16.2.0. useRouter supports the same option on push() and replace().

<Link href={`/orders/${order.id}`} transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}>
  View order
</Link>

<Link href="/orders" transitionTypes={['nav-back']}>
  Back to orders
</Link>

Each page then maps those types to animations, with everything else switched off:

<ViewTransition
  enter={{ 'nav-forward': 'nav-forward', 'nav-back': 'nav-back', default: 'none' }}
  exit={{ 'nav-forward': 'nav-forward', 'nav-back': 'nav-back', default: 'none' }}
  default="none"
>
  <OrdersTable />
</ViewTransition>

Two details from the Next.js guide decide whether this works. First, put the wrapper in each page.tsx, not in a layout. Layouts persist across navigations, so their boundaries never enter or exit and the directional animation never fires. Second, decide which links count as forward and which as back based on your navigation hierarchy, because Next.js does not infer it. The guide's convention, with forward content sliding in from the right and back content from the left, matches how readers of left-to-right languages expect pages to turn.

Directional slides also need a fixed reference point. If the header slides with the content, the user loses track of what moved. The guide gives the header its own viewTransitionName and disables its animation, so the header stays put while the page content moves beneath it. And it adds pointer-events: none to the ::view-transition overlay, because without it, clicks made during an animation are swallowed by the overlay instead of reaching the page.

::view-transition {
  pointer-events: none;
}

That one rule is easy to miss and fixes a whole class of "the button didn't respond" reports.

A Next.js configuration detail where the docs disagree

Whether Next.js needs a configuration flag for View Transitions depends on which page of its documentation you read. The hosted reference page for experimental.viewTransition, still labelled for version 16.2.3, says to enable the flag in next.config.js and warns that the feature is experimental and not recommended for production. The view transitions guide, last updated on 15 October 2026, says that view transitions work in the App Router with no configuration and that React 19.3 provides everything it uses.

The documentation bundled inside the next@16.4.5 package settles it for current versions. That package contains the guide with the "no configuration" wording and no longer includes a reference page for the viewTransition flag at all. On 16.4 and later, there is nothing to switch on. On 16.2 or 16.3, follow the flag documentation for your installed version, which you can read in node_modules/next/dist/docs. That folder is a reliable tiebreaker whenever the hosted docs and your installed version seem to disagree.

Placement mistakes that silently disable animations

Most "my View Transition does nothing" problems come from where the boundary sits in the tree, not from its props. None of these produces an error.

A DOM node above the boundary. Enter and exit only activate when the <ViewTransition> comes before any DOM node in the part of the tree being inserted or removed. Wrapping it in a <div> breaks it. The fix is to move the boundary outside the element:

// Does not animate on enter or exit
<div className="card">
  <ViewTransition><Card /></ViewTransition>
</div>

// Animates
<ViewTransition>
  <div className="card"><Card /></div>
</ViewTransition>

Boundaries inside layouts. As above, layouts persist, so enter and exit never fire there. Directional and page-level animations belong in pages.

Wrappers inside lists. Nested boundaries receive their own mutations rather than passing them to the parent, and in a list, the update animation applies to each item only when its <ViewTransition> sits directly in the list rather than inside a wrapper element. Reordering also needs stable keys. An index used as a key makes React believe every item changed.

Unstable keys on keyed swaps. The Next.js guide's tab example relies on key={slug} to make React treat old and new content as an exit and enter pair. If the key does not change when the content does, React performs an update in place instead.

This is also where Fragment refs help indirectly. A common reason for a wrapper <div> above a boundary is that some other code needed a DOM node to attach an IntersectionObserver or an event listener. In React 19.3, a ref on a <Fragment> gives you a FragmentInstance with observeUsing, addEventListener, focus and measurement methods that act on the fragment's children as a group, without adding a node. The <Fragment> reference covers the full method list. Removing those wrapper elements is often what lets a boundary sit at the top of its subtree, where it needs to be.

Back navigation, interruptions and flushSync

Three runtime behaviours explain the remaining cases where an animation should play and does not.

Browser back and forward. The React reference says React skips animations for popstate navigations, because scroll and form restoration have to finish synchronously, and notes that routers built on the Navigation API avoid the limitation. The Next.js guide describes the result in its own router slightly differently: back and forward gestures carry no transition type, so directional slides do not play, while a shared element morph still applies if both pages have matching names. The two descriptions are about different layers, but they leave the same advice. Never rely on an animation to explain a back navigation, and test the back button and swipe gestures on each browser you support.

A transition already running. If one View Transition is in progress, React waits for it to finish, and updates that arrive in the meantime are batched. A long animation therefore delays the next one. This is the practical case for short durations: the Next.js guide's timings sit between 150 and 400 milliseconds, and we would treat anything longer on a frequently used screen as a design decision that needs a reason.

flushSync. A flushSync call in the middle of the sequence makes React skip the Transition. Third-party components that call it internally can disable animations in a way that is hard to trace, so when an animation stops working after a library upgrade, search the dependency for it.

Reduced motion and accessibility remain your job

React does not disable View Transitions for users who have asked their operating system to reduce motion. The reference docs recommend always handling the prefers-reduced-motion media query, and the Next.js guide supplies a blunt but effective default:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  ::view-transition-old(*),
  ::view-transition-new(*),
  ::view-transition-group(*) {
    animation-duration: 0s !important;
    animation-delay: 0s !important;
  }
}

With this in place, content swaps instantly, which is what the browser does without view transitions at all. A finer approach keeps cross-fades and removes positional movement, since large horizontal slides are the most likely to cause discomfort, while opacity changes carry far less risk. Whichever you choose, ship the media query in the same pull request as the first animation, not as a follow-up.

The overlay matters for keyboard and pointer users too. Named participants, such as an anchored header, are skipped by hit-testing for the duration of a transition even with pointer-events: none on the overlay, so avoid naming elements that people click quickly and repeatedly. And because animations wait for Transitions, focus management should not depend on an animation finishing: move focus as part of the state change, not in an onEnter callback.

If your products serve customers in the EU, motion and focus behaviour are part of the accessibility picture your team is already assessing, and our guide to European Accessibility Act compliance covers where those obligations come from.

Browser support and progressive enhancement

Same-document view transitions reached Baseline status on 14 October 2025, when Firefox 144 shipped them and all three major browser engines supported the core API. web.dev's announcement also noted that Firefox's first implementation did not include view transition types, which React's integration depends on for typed animations.

The Next.js guide, updated in October 2026, says React's integration uses the newer parts of the API, namely transition types and view-transition-class, and lists them as available in Chromium 125 and later and in recent Safari and Firefox versions, with a warning that some animations may behave differently in Safari. Check the current support tables on the day you ship rather than relying on a version number in an article, this one included. The MDN View Transition API documentation links to them.

The reassuring part is the failure mode. Without browser support, the application works normally and the transitions simply do not animate. View Transitions are progressive enhancement by design, so the risk in an unsupported browser is a plainer experience, not a broken one. That is also the right way to brief a client or product owner: animation is a refinement on top of a working interface, and no user flow should depend on it.

Two adjacent limits are worth knowing. <ViewTransition> works only in the DOM today; React Native support is in progress but not available. And because the browser animates snapshots of the old and new content, a transition that covers the whole page asks more of a low-end phone than one that covers a single card. Animate the element that changed, not the whole page, and measure the screens that matter with real devices. If interaction latency is already a concern on your mobile templates, our piece on mobile-first design and Core Web Vitals is the right place to start before adding motion.

Should you replace your animation library?

For route transitions, loading reveals and simple enter and exit effects, <ViewTransition> is now a credible replacement for a JavaScript animation library, and it has two advantages a library cannot easily match. It is coordinated with React's own scheduling, so animations line up with Suspense and Transitions instead of fighting them. And it runs on a browser API, so there is less JavaScript to download for those effects.

It is not a replacement for everything. Gesture-driven motion, spring physics, scroll-linked effects and animations that must respond continuously to input are still better served by a dedicated library or by CSS scroll-driven animations. That is our view rather than an official position, and it reflects what each tool is designed for: View Transitions animate between two states, while those effects describe motion that has no fixed end state.

A sensible migration moves one category at a time. Route transitions first, because the App Router already treats navigations as Transitions. Suspense reveals second, using the rule above. Leave interactive motion where it is until there is a specific reason to change it.

A test plan before shipping View Transitions

A View Transition that looks right on a fast laptop in Chrome has passed the easiest test available. Before switching them on in production, we work through these checks on every screen that uses them:

  1. Confirm versions. npm ls react react-dom next shows matching React versions at 19.3.1 or later, and Next.js at 16.4.5 or later.
  2. List every boundary. Search the codebase for <ViewTransition and record which triggers each one animates. Anything without default="none" needs a reason.
  3. Check placement. For each boundary that should enter or exit, confirm no DOM node sits above it in the inserted subtree, and that page-level boundaries live in pages rather than layouts.
  4. Test the Suspense rule. Throttle the network in DevTools and confirm fallbacks appear instantly, reveals animate, and revisiting cached content does not animate.
  5. Test shared elements cold and warm. Navigate with an empty cache and with prefetched data. The morph should play when prefetched, and fall back to a clean enter animation when not.
  6. Click during animations. Confirm buttons and links respond while a transition is running.
  7. Use the back button and gestures on every supported browser, and confirm nothing depends on an animation to make sense.
  8. Turn on reduced motion in the operating system and confirm positional movement stops.
  9. Test the browsers you support, including at least one where typed animations may be missing, and confirm the interface still works without animation.
  10. Check keyboard focus after every animated state change.

Each of these, with pass criteria and a readiness score, is in the printable audit worksheet below, so the checks can be split across a team and ticked off screen by screen.

Get the React View Transitions Audit Worksheet

A two-page printable worksheet with 20 checks across setup, behaviour and release, each with clear pass criteria, plus a readiness score that tells you whether a screen is ready for View Transitions in production. No account, no sales sequence.

Get the PDF

FAQ

Do I need a configuration flag to use ViewTransition in Next.js?

Not on Next.js 16.4 or later. The view transitions guide and the documentation bundled with next@16.4.5 say view transitions work in the App Router with no configuration, because React 19.3 provides <ViewTransition> and addTransitionType. Older 16.x versions documented an experimental.viewTransition flag, so check the docs in node_modules/next/dist/docs for your installed version.

Why does my ViewTransition not animate?

The most common causes are an update that is not wrapped in startTransition, a DOM element placed above the boundary, a boundary inside a layout that never enters or exits, and default="none" on a shared pair without an explicit share prop. A flushSync call during the update also makes React skip the animation. None of these produces an error.

Does React ViewTransition work in Firefox and Safari?

The core View Transitions API has been supported in all major browser engines since October 2025. React's integration also uses transition types and view-transition-class, which Next.js lists as available in Chromium 125 and later and in recent Safari and Firefox versions. Where support is missing, the app works normally and simply does not animate.

Does React turn off View Transitions for reduced motion?

No. React does not check the user's motion preference. Add a prefers-reduced-motion media query that sets animation durations and delays to zero on the ::view-transition-old, ::view-transition-new and ::view-transition-group pseudo-elements, or keep only opacity changes and remove movement.

Can I use ViewTransition with React Native?

Not yet. The React 19.3 announcement says <ViewTransition> currently works only in the DOM, and that support for React Native and other platforms is being worked on. Fragment refs and the other 19.3 changes are separate from this limitation.

title: Samestate: one interaction, every device 📱💻
description:
😩 The problem: one site, nine screens, one tab at a time

You ship a responsive layout. Then the ritual starts. Open DevTools, pick iPhone, tap the menu. Switch to iPad, tap the menu again. Switch to desktop, find the menu (it's a nav bar now), click it. Fill a form on mobile, then fill it again on tablet because the state didn't come with you.

Seeing one layout at a time isn't really the pain. The pain is that every interaction has to be repeated on every screen, and the bugs hide in the gaps between them.

So I built ✨ Samestate: you do something once, and every device does the same thing.

📱💻 What Samestate does

Paste a URL and Samestate opens it on nine devices at once, side by side on one canvas: iPhone 11 Pro, Pixel 3XL, a small 320px phone, Nexus 7, iPad Pro 11", MacBook Air, a 1080p desktop and a 1440p large display.

Then you just use the site. Samestate carries what you do to every frame:

  • Clicks and menus: open the hamburger on mobile and the desktop nav opens the matching menu.
  • Typing and forms: fill a field once and it's filled everywhere.
  • Scrolling: scroll to a section and every device lands on the same section, not the same pixel offset.
  • Hover and navigation: change page on one device and the others follow.

Each of these is a toggle, so you can sync only what you care about.

🧠 Same state, not same pixels

The tricky part is that the devices don't share a layout. A click on a desktop nav link has no pixel-equivalent on a phone where that link lives inside a drawer. So Samestate syncs logical state rather than coordinates: it works out what you interacted with (this menu, this field, this section) and finds the equivalent element on each device.

There are two modes:

  • Align: each device reaches the same logical state in its own layout.
  • Mirror: a straight replay, handy when layouts are close.

It also handles the boring-but-necessary bits: rotate all devices to landscape or portrait, reset zoom, and clear storage between runs.

🔍 Detect differences

Syncing shows you the site in the same state everywhere. Detect differences tells you what changed between those states. Pick a baseline device (say, Desktop) and Samestate compares every other frame against it, flagging differences in:

  • images and text that appear on one device but not another
  • fonts, sizes and spacing
  • tables that overflow or collapse
  • navigation that is hidden or unreachable
  • input modes and usability issues, like tap targets that are too small

On my own project, DEV·TV, the first run turned up 10 differences I'd never noticed while clicking through devices by hand. 😅

For now Samestate reports issues. In v2 I'd like it to start suggesting fixes.

🚀 Try it

Samestate runs as a Chrome extension, so there's no localhost or server setup. Install it, open any site, and a short guided demo walks you through syncing and difference detection (or skip it and go straight in).

  • Repo and install steps: github.com/shouvik12/samestate
  • Live demo: [add link]

It's open source and early. I'd love to hear:

  1. Which devices you'd add to the default set
  2. Where the logical sync guesses wrong on your site
  3. Which kinds of differences matter most to you

Drop a comment or open an issue. And if it saves you a round of tapping through nine viewports, a ⭐ on the repo helps a lot. 🙏

title: Small input hints that make web tools easier to use
description:
I maintain the six projects linked in this note. They make useful examples of a recurring interface problem: a short label can hide an important assumption about units, coverage, eligibility, or the result.

The snippets below are proposed copy patterns for developers to adapt. They are separate from the live wording on each site, and they are not results from a user study or a complete product test.

1. Explain what can be represented

A Unicode text tool may use a conservative mapping instead of converting every character. A reader needs to know which input stays unchanged and whether the result suits the destination.

For an interface like my superscript generator, which lists the characters it leaves alone, a useful hint would be:

Some characters may remain unchanged in this mapping. Review the output and its character coverage before copying.

Keep the preview available beside the explanation. A coverage note helps the reader decide whether the result suits a particular name, formula, or caption; it does not establish compatibility with every destination app.

2. Put the interpretation beside the numbers

A ranking page may mix a qualitative recommendation with a numerical comparison. Readers need to understand which question each one answers.

At the tier list where the letter grades are labelled as opinion, the unofficial fan guide includes tier information and starter comparisons. A reusable explanation for that kind of interface is:

Read the tier notes for qualitative context. A raw-stat comparison answers a narrower question and does not capture every interaction in a run.

Put that distinction next to the relevant section. It prevents a score from acquiring a stronger meaning simply because it has a number attached to it.

3. Show the applicable limit at the point of selection

A bulk tool can have different limits for different account states. Show the limit that applies to the current reader.

For a workflow like the batch photo watermark tool where the limit depends on your account, a developer-facing message template could be:

Selected {count} of {limit} photos for this batch.
Your current account limit is {limit} photos per batch.

Here, the braces describe values your application should supply. Keep them tied to the same configuration that enforces the limit. If a new selection is rejected, explain the next useful action, such as reducing the selection, while preserving only state your implementation actually retains.

4. Separate eligibility, processing and retention

Media conversion involves several decisions: whether the source is appropriate to process, whether it fits the service's limits, and how long a completed result remains available.

For a service page such as my YouTube to MP3 converter and its stated limits, keep these messages close to their relevant actions:

  • Before submission: the supported source and current duration limits, together with a clear rights confirmation.
  • During processing: the status that the service actually reports.
  • After completion: the download's actual expiry and the available deletion controls.

Avoid promising automatic retries or preservation of a job unless the implemented behavior supports that promise. A helpful failure message describes the known state and the available next step.

5. Name the unit, then explain the nearby distinction

An image's dimensions and its encoded file size measure different things. A reader trying to meet a byte limit may choose a width control and expect it to enforce that limit.

For a tool like the GIF resizer and its stated limits, clear field labels and a small hint can keep the distinction visible:

Width (pixels)
Height (pixels)
Pixel dimensions and file size are different measurements.
Check the exported file size against your destination's limit.

This explains what the controls address without predicting a compression percentage or a guaranteed export size.

6. Distinguish mixed units from decimal notation

Feet and inches are a familiar example of a formatting trap. Eight feet six inches is 8.5 feet, because six inches is half a foot.

For a feet-and-inches calculator that says what a bare number means, a reusable input hint is:

No unit? Bare numbers start as inches. Check the unit before calculating.

Keep the unit visible beside the input and beside the result. The linked page describes a separate length calculation; calculating room area is a different task.

A small review before shipping copy

For each hint, check that it:

  1. Appears beside the control or result where the reader needs it.
  2. Names the relevant unit, limit or assumption.
  3. Uses the same current values as the enforcing implementation.
  4. Describes supported behavior without adding guarantees.
  5. Gives a practical next step when the current input cannot proceed.

Then test the implementation separately: unsupported characters, account-specific batch limits, rejected selections, failed jobs and mixed-unit inputs are behavior tests. Clear wording helps readers make decisions; it needs working behavior underneath it.

title: Oracle Reports 12c – REP-51002: Bind to Reports Server
description:
I am facing an issue with ms3 failed when accessing showjobsOracle Reports Services while trying to access the Reports Server through the Reports Servlet.

Environment

Oracle Forms and Reports: 12c (please specify exact version)

WebLogic Server: 12c (please specify exact version)

Operating System: Windows / Oracle Linux (specify host OS)

Reports Server Name: rep60_gems3

Reports Servlet URL: http://:9002/reports/rwservlet/

Issue

When I try to access the following URL to view Reports Server jobs:

http://:9002/reports/rwservlet/showjobs?server=rep60_gems3

I receive the following error:

REP-51002: Bind to Reports Server rep60_gems3 failed.

The Reports Servlet is accessible from the browser, but it fails to establish a connection with the specified Reports Server.

What I need help with

What are the possible causes of REP-51002 when accessing the showjobs URL?

How can I verify whether the Reports Servlet can discover and communicate with the Reports Server?

Are there any specific UDP ports or network configurations that need to be checked in rwnetwork.conf?

How can I troubleshoot the connection between WLS_REPORTS and the standalone Reports Server?

Which diagnostic logs should I check to identify the root cause?

Has anyone experienced this issue with Oracle Reports 12c?

Any suggestions or troubleshooting steps would be appreciated.

Thank you!

Solution / Resolution

The issue was identified as corruption in the report_servername.dat file associated with the Oracle Reports Server component. Due to this corruption, the Reports Servlet was unable to bind successfully to the Reports Server, resulting in the error REP-51002: Bind to Reports Server rep60_gems3 failed.

To resolve the issue, we first navigated to the Reports Server component's data directory and renamed the existing report_servername.dat file as a backup, rather than deleting it. This allowed the corrupted file to be preserved for further investigation if required.

Next, we navigated to the Reports Server component's bin directory under the domain and configured the COMPONENT_CONFIG_PATH environment variable to point to the corresponding Reports Server component configuration directory. We then manually initiated the Reports Server using the rwserver.sh script with the appropriate server name:

export COMPONENT_CONFIG_PATH=${DOMAIN_HOME}/config/fmwconfig/components/ReportsServerComponent/<report_server_name>

./rwserver.sh server=<report_server_name>

After executing this command, the Reports Server startup dialog appeared, indicating that the Reports Server engine had successfully started.

Once the manual startup was verified, we shut down the manually started Reports Server to avoid having multiple instances running simultaneously. We then restarted the Node Manager service to refresh the component management and process monitoring mechanism.

After Node Manager was restarted successfully, we started the Reports Server through the standard component management script:

cd $DOMAIN_HOME/bin

./startComponent.sh <report_server_name>

Node Manager then managed the Reports Server startup through its component process management mechanism.

Finally, we verified that the Reports Server was running successfully and accessed the Reports Servlet showjobs URL again. The binding issue was resolved, and the Reports Server became accessible through the Reports Servlet without the REP-51002 error.

**
**

Resolution: Renamed the corrupted data file, manually initialized the Reports Server to validate startup, restarted Node Manager, and brought the Reports Server back online using startComponent.sh.
