title: How to Build Streaming UI for AI Responses in React
description:
AI responses take 5 to 30 seconds to generate. Without streaming, users stare at a spinner the entire time. Streaming UI sends tokens as they arrive so the first word appears in 200 to 500 milliseconds.

How Streaming Works Under the Hood

Most LLM providers stream via Server-Sent Events (SSE) over a single HTTP connection. Each event carries a small chunk:

data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"Hello"}}]}

data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":" there"}}]}

data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"! How"}}]}

data: [DONE]

The frontend reads the response body as a readable stream, decodes chunks, and appends them to the accumulated text:

async function streamResponse(prompt) {
  const response = await fetch('/api/chat', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: JSON.stringify({ prompt }),
  });

  const reader = response.body.getReader();
  const decoder = new TextDecoder();
  let accumulated = '';

  while (true) {
    const { done, value } = await reader.read();
    if (done) break;

    const chunk = decoder.decode(value, { stream: true });
    accumulated += parseChunk(chunk);
    setContent(accumulated);
  }
}

The hard part isn't receiving data. It's rendering partial Markdown, code blocks, and tables without flicker or layout shift.

Rendering Partial Markdown Safely

A naive renderer reparses on every token. That breaks bold tags, leaves code fences unclosed, and invalidates tables. Buffer incomplete structures and only render when you hit a safe boundary.

function StreamingMarkdown({ chunks, isStreaming }) {
  const [rendered, setRendered] = useState('');
  const bufferRef = useRef('');

  useEffect(() => {
    bufferRef.current += chunks;
    const safeContent = sanitizePartialMarkdown(bufferRef.current);
    setRendered(markdownToHtml(safeContent));
  }, [chunks]);

  return (
    <div
      className="prose"
      dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: rendered }}
      aria-live="polite"
      aria-busy={isStreaming}
    />
  );
}

function sanitizePartialMarkdown(text) {
  // Close any open bold/italic tags
  // Close any open code fences
  // Remove incomplete table rows
  // Buffer incomplete list items
  return cleanedText;
}

For code blocks, defer syntax highlighting until the closing fence arrives. Re-highlighting on every chunk is expensive for long blocks.

Streaming Citations

Citations often reference content that appears later in the stream. Render inline markers immediately, then populate the reference panel when full citation objects arrive:

function StreamingWithCitations({ content, isStreaming }) {
  const { text, citations } = parseCitations(content);

  return (
    <div>
      <div className="prose" aria-live="polite" aria-busy={isStreaming}>
        {text}
      </div>
      {citations.length > 0 && (
        <div className="citations-panel" aria-label="Sources">
          {citations.map((citation, i) => (
            <a key={i} href={citation.url} className="citation-card">
              <span className="citation-number">[{i + 1}]</span>
              <span className="citation-title">{citation.title}</span>
              <span className="citation-domain">{citation.domain}</span>
            </a>
          ))}
        </div>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

Stream Controls Users Expect

Stop Button

Visible during streaming. Aborts generation and keeps what arrived.

function StreamControls({ isStreaming, onStop, onRetry }) {
  return (
    <div className="flex gap-2">
      {isStreaming ? (
        <button onClick={onStop} aria-label="Stop generating">
          <StopIcon aria-hidden="true" />
          Stop
        </button>
      ) : (
        <button onClick={onRetry} aria-label="Regenerate response">
          <RefreshIcon aria-hidden="true" />
          Retry
        </button>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

Copy and Format Toggle

Show copy after streaming completes. Let users switch between rendered Markdown, raw Markdown, and plain text without regenerating.

Accessibility Requirements

Streaming content breaks screen readers if handled poorly. Use these patterns for WCAG AA:

<div aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="false" aria-busy={isStreaming}>
  {streamedContent}
</div>
  • aria-live="polite" announces changes without interrupting
  • aria-atomic="false" reads only new content, not the entire region
  • aria-busy="true" holds announcements until streaming completes

Don't steal focus from the prompt input when a response starts. Debounce announcements to 2 to 3 second intervals. Stop, retry, and copy buttons must be keyboard accessible with logical tab order.

Using the Vercel AI SDK

The Vercel AI SDK handles the streaming connection and state. You provide the UI layer:

'use client';

import { useChat } from 'ai/react';

export default function Chat() {
  const { messages, input, handleInputChange, handleSubmit, isLoading, stop } = useChat();

  return (
    <div>
      {messages.map((message) => (
        <div key={message.id} role={message.role === 'assistant' ? 'status' : undefined}>
          <strong>{message.role === 'user' ? 'You' : 'Assistant'}</strong>
          <p>{message.content}</p>
        </div>
      ))}

      <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
        <input
          value={input}
          onChange={handleInputChange}
          placeholder="Ask something..."
          aria-label="Chat prompt"
        />
        {isLoading ? (
          <button type="button" onClick={stop}>Stop</button>
        ) : (
          <button type="submit">Send</button>
        )}
      </form>
    </div>
  );
}

Anti-Patterns to Avoid

Layout thrash: Each token resizes the container and pushes content down. Fix with a minimum height on the response container and scroll the container, not the page.

No loading state before first token: TTFT can be seconds. Show a typing indicator or skeleton immediately on submit.

Flickering Markdown: Re-parsing every token toggles formatting on and off. Buffer and re-render only on whitespace or sentence boundaries.

No stop button: Users can't abort irrelevant long responses. Keep a prominent stop button visible during streaming.

Losing partial responses on error: If the stream fails mid-response, don't discard what arrived. Show the partial content with an error message and retry option.

This is a shorter version of a guide I wrote at Frontkit Studio. The full post has the complete walkthrough.

title: Merge Multiple JPG Files into One in Java - Merge JPG to JPG
description:
Merge Multiple JPG Files into One in Java using REST API.

Merging JPG images can be a time-consuming and challenging task, especially when you have multiple images to merge. Fortunately, GroupDocs.Merger Cloud SDK for Java can help you to accomplish this task quickly and easily. In this article, we will demonstrate how to merge multiple JPG files into one in Java using REST API. So, let’s get started!

The following topics shall be covered in this article:

Java REST API to Merge JPG Images and SDK Installation

GroupDocs.Merger Cloud SDK for Java is a powerful and versatile tool that helps Java developers to merge, extract, rotate, change the document orientation to portrait or landscape, and modify files in the cloud. It is a cloud-based document manipulation and cross-platform API that supports a wide variety of file formats, including Word, PDF, Excel, PowerPoint, HTML, and many more. The SDK is easy to use and can be integrated easily into a Java-based application.

You can either download the API’s JAR file or install it using Maven by adding the following repository and dependency into your project’s pom.xml file:

Maven Repository:

<repository>
    <id>groupdocs-artifact-repository</id>
    <name>GroupDocs Artifact Repository</name>
    <url>https://repository.groupdocs.cloud/repo</url>
</repository>

Maven Dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.groupdocs</groupId>
    <artifactId>groupdocs-merger-cloud</artifactId>
    <version>23.2</version>
    <scope>compile</scope>
</dependency>

Next, you need to sign up for a free trial account or purchase a subscription plan on the GroupDocs website and get your API key. Once you have the Client Id and Client Secret, add below code snippet into your Java application:

# Get your client_id and client_secret from https://dashboard.groupdocs.cloud after registration.

String ClientId = "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx";
String ClientSecret = "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx";
String MyStorage = "test-internal-storage";
Configuration configuration = new Configuration(ClientId, ClientSecret);

How to Combine JPG Files into One in Java using REST API

Merging JPG images in Java using GroupDocs.Merger Cloud SDK is a straightforward process. Here’s how to do it:

Upload the Files

Firstly, upload the JPG files to the cloud using the code example given below:

package com.groupdocsdev.classes;

import java.io.File;
import com.groupdocs.cloud.merger.client.*;
import com.groupdocs.cloud.merger.model.*;
import com.groupdocs.cloud.merger.model.requests.*;
import com.groupdocs.cloud.merger.api.*;
import com.groupdocs.cloud.merger.client.ApiException;

// Upload file to the Cloud Storage using Java
public class App {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        FileApi apiInstance = new FileApi(configuration);
        try {
            File fileStream = new File("H:\\groupdocs-cloud-data\\input-sample-file-one.jpg");
            UploadFileRequest request = new UploadFileRequest("java-testing\\input-sample-file-one.jpg", fileStream, MyStorage);
            FilesUploadResult response = apiInstance.uploadFile(request);
            System.out.println("Expected response type is FilesUploadResult: " + response.getUploaded().size());
        } catch (ApiException e) {

            e.printStackTrace();
        }

}

This section provides step-by-step instructions and an example code snippet for merging JPG images into one:

  • Firstly, import the required classes into your Java file.
  • Secondly, create an instance of the DocumentApi class.
  • Thirdly, create an instance of the FileInfo class.

title: It Was Just a Simple Java Assignment. Or So I Thought.
description:
My first Java GUI application, learning by experimenting, and discovering the effort behind building software.

It started with a college assignment.

Unlike the usual assignments where we write programs, execute them and note down their outputs, this one was a little different. Our Java lecturer asked us to build an actual application using Java.

There were a few conditions, though.

No AI-generated code. We had to sit down, understand what we were doing and build the application ourselves.

And she made one thing very clear: she didn't want a huge application with fancy designs, countless buttons or an impressive user interface. She just wanted something simple, original and functional, with a Java GUI and the concept of layout managers implemented.

Honestly, I thought it would be fairly simple.

I was about to find out otherwise.

Starting from scratch

We had already been introduced to Java basics in class, but building an application was something I hadn't really explored before.

So, I started by setting up Java on my PC. Once I had everything installed, I began researching Java GUI development and exploring Java Swing.

I did take some help from ChatGPT during my research, mainly to understand individual concepts and clear my doubts. But I wasn't asking it to generate the application for me. I wanted to understand the components and experiment with them myself.

My first goal was pretty basic: create a window.

I started with a JFrame, then moved on to creating panels, adding labels and text fields, and eventually experimenting with buttons.

Seeing an actual window appear on my screen was exciting. It was a small thing, but it felt different from writing a program in a console and looking at its output.

For the first time, I was actually putting together something that looked like an application.

From a Student Login Portal to a Lost & Found Portal

Initially, I thought of building a Student Login Portal.

I wasn't entirely sure whether that idea would be enough for the assignment, so I started thinking about something else I could build without making it unnecessarily complicated.

That's when I came up with the Campus Lost & Found Portal.

The idea was simple.

Students could report belongings they had lost or items they had found somewhere on campus.

The application would collect a few basic details:

  • Student Name
  • Item Name
  • Report Type (Lost or Found)
  • Location
  • Description

There would be a Submit Report button and a Clear button.

Nothing too complicated. Just a simple interface that could demonstrate the concepts we were asked to implement.

And that became my first application.

The part that actually took time

This was where things started getting interesting.

Understanding what Java Swing components were was one thing. Figuring out how to use them together was another.

I experimented with different components, including:

  • JFrame – to create the main application window.
  • JPanel – to organise different sections of the interface.
  • JLabel – to display text.
  • JTextField – to collect user input.
  • JTextArea – to accept longer descriptions.
  • JRadioButton – to select whether an item was lost or found.
  • JButton – to perform actions.

I also used ButtonGroup to make sure that users could select either Lost or Found, rather than both.

One thing I particularly remember struggling with was positioning everything.

I had labels, text fields, radio buttons and buttons, but getting them to appear where I wanted them to was a different challenge altogether.

And that's when layout managers came into the picture.

Understanding Layout Managers

Three layout managers were part of my assignment:

1. BorderLayout

I used BorderLayout for the main panel. It divided the application into different sections: North, Center and South.

This allowed me to place the heading at the top, the form in the centre and the buttons at the bottom.

panel.setLayout(new BorderLayout());

panel.add(headingPanel, BorderLayout.NORTH);
panel.add(formPanel, BorderLayout.CENTER);
panel.add(buttonPanel, BorderLayout.SOUTH);

2. GridLayout

I used GridLayout to arrange the different form sections vertically.

formPanel.setLayout(new GridLayout(0, 1));

formPanel.add(studentPanel);
formPanel.add(itemPanel);
formPanel.add(typePanel);
formPanel.add(locationPanel);
formPanel.add(descriptionPanel);

3. FlowLayout

I used FlowLayout inside individual panels to arrange labels and their corresponding input fields.

studentPanel.setLayout(new FlowLayout());

studentPanel.add(student);
studentPanel.add(name);

Initially, these concepts seemed like just another part of the Java syllabus. But when I actually started using them, I understood why they mattered.

I wasn't just adding components to a window anymore. I was learning how to organise them and structure an interface.

And honestly, getting everything positioned properly took more experimenting than I expected.

Making the application actually work

Once the interface was ready, I moved on to the functionality.

I wanted the Submit Report button to collect the information entered by the user and display it in a confirmation message.

For that, I used ActionListener.

Here's a small part of the code:

submit.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {

        String studentName = name.getText();
        String itemName = itemname.getText();
        String itemLocation = place.getText();
        String itemDescription = details.getText();

        // Validate the submitted details
    }
});

I also added basic validation so that users couldn't submit an incomplete report.

If any required field was empty, the application would display a message asking them to fill in all the details.

For successful submissions, I used JOptionPane.showMessageDialog() to display the entered information.

I added a Clear button too, which resets all the input fields and radio button selections.

There was also a small additional touch: I experimented with changing the background colour temporarily when a report was submitted or when required details were missing.

It wasn't necessary for the basic functionality, but it was fun experimenting with it.

A small application, a much bigger realisation

By this point, I had spent quite some time working on something that, at first glance, looked extremely simple.

And that's when I started thinking about something.

If creating a basic GUI prototype with a handful of input fields and buttons required this much time, patience and experimentation, imagine what it takes to build an actual application.

Think about applications we use every day. The interfaces, the functionality, the databases, the backend systems, the error handling and everything else working together.

There's so much happening behind a screen that we usually don't even think about.

Of course, my application was only a prototype. It didn't have a database or backend to store reports permanently. It simply demonstrated the interface and the submission process.

But even building that prototype gave me a completely different appreciation for software development.

I started understanding that building software isn't just about writing lines of code. It's about figuring things out, making decisions, experimenting, fixing mistakes and getting different pieces to work together.

The little achievement that meant a lot

The next day, I submitted my application.

My lecturer awarded me full marks, which was obviously a nice bonus!

But what made me happier was something else.

I had started with very little experience in Java GUI development, spent time researching concepts, experimented with components and layout managers, and eventually managed to put together an application entirely on my own.

I was genuinely excited when I saw everything working. I was also a little surprised that I had managed to build it without relying on AI-generated code.

And that feeling was probably the best part of the entire assignment.

What I'm taking away from this experience

This assignment might not have resulted in some groundbreaking application. It wasn't particularly complex, and it definitely wasn't something that would impress an experienced developer.

But it was my first application-based assignment since joining CSE, and it made me realise how different learning something in theory is from actually implementing it.

I also learnt that you don't necessarily need to start with a huge idea. Sometimes, building something small is enough to understand the process and gain confidence.

I'm still a beginner, and there's obviously a lot more to learn about Java and software development.

But this experience made me genuinely excited to build more things.

And perhaps that's what matters most.

My first application wasn't perfect, but it was mine. And I'm pretty happy with that. ❤️

title: I built a Mac and Windows app so I could share one keyboard and mouse across both
description:
I have a Mac and a Windows PC on the same desk. For a long time the "setup" was just two keyboards, and I kept sliding one out of the way to use the other.

I wanted something closer to Universal Control, but with a Windows PC on the other side. That is what MagicInput is. You push the pointer off the edge of one screen and it continues on the other. Typing, clicking, and scrolling follow it, and so does the text clipboard. If I AirDrop a photo to the Mac, it can land in the PC's Downloads folder.

Pairing is a short code on the local network. There is no account and no cloud. The app stays on the two machines.

It is free for personal use, and the source is public under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0. That is not an OSI open-source license: you can read and build the code, but commercial use is restricted. I want to be clear about that up front.

The Mac build is signed and notarized. The Windows installer is not signed yet. If you install on Windows, expect the usual SmartScreen warning until I finish that work. I would rather say that than pretend the installer looks official.

I wrote it in Rust. The interesting parts for me were crossing the pointer at the screen edge in a way that feels obvious, keeping the clipboard in sync for text, and forwarding an AirDrop arriving on the Mac over to the PC. Multi-monitor layouts are the place I most want feedback, especially from people who already use Synergy, Deskflow, ShareMouse, or Mouse Without Borders.

If you want to try it:

  • Site: https://bullfighterstudio.com/magicinput
  • GitHub: https://github.com/betoxf/Magicinput

I'm Humberto. If the edge-crossing or the pairing feels wrong on your desk, I want to hear about it. Same if the unsigned Windows install is a problem in practice.

title: Responsive type and spacing by changing only the root font size
description:
In print, space was never a number of its own. It was measured in ems, the size of the type being set. The spaces between words were fractions of it. Change the type size, and the space changed with it.

On screen we lost that. Designs arrived as pixel comps, so we wrote pixels: 16px body, 24px gap, 32px heading. Then screens multiplied, and every value got a table per breakpoint:

type: {
  sizes: {
    mobile:  { base: '16px', l: '22px' },
    desktop: { base: '18px', l: '32px' },
  },
}

Nothing in that table says the heading is a step above the body, or that a gap belongs to the text it separates. On mobile l is 1.375 times base; on desktop it's 1.78 times. Nobody decided that. It's just what the numbers happen to be.

Version 4.0 of my design system package, @pindakaasman/design-system, replaces those tables with one relation.

One scale

Every font size and every spacing step is a step on one modular scale. base is 1rem, each step up multiplies by one ratio, and each step down divides by it. The ratio is the token author's choice; the template uses 1.333, a perfect fourth.

type: {
  ratio: 1.333,
  floor: 0.75,
  base: {
    mobile: '100%',
    tablet: '100%',
    tabletLandscape: '106.25%',
    desktop: '112.5%',
  },
}

Spacing uses the same scale as the type, as print did. There is no spacing table to tune. Type has five steps (s to xl); spacing has the same five plus xxs and xs below them.

Step Font size Spacing
xxs 0.4222rem
xs 0.5628rem
s 0.7502rem 0.7502rem
base 1rem 1rem
m 1.333rem 1.333rem
l 1.7769rem 1.7769rem
xl 2.3686rem 2.3686rem

Type stops at s because of type.floor: no font size resolves below 0.75rem. Anything smaller would be raised to the floor and merge with s. Spacing has no floor, so it can go further down.

One root

Per breakpoint, one value changes: the root font size. Everything else is a constant rem value, so it grows or shrinks with the root and keeps its proportions.

This is the CSS the package generates from the tokens above (rootCss()):

:root { font-size: 100%; }
@media (min-width: 768px) {
  :root { font-size: 100%; }
}
@media (min-width: 1024px) {
  :root { font-size: 106.25%; }
}
@media (min-width: 1440px) {
  :root { font-size: 112.5%; }
}
:root {
  --ds-font-size-s: 0.7502rem;
  --ds-font-size-base: 1rem;
  --ds-font-size-m: 1.333rem;
  --ds-font-size-l: 1.7769rem;
  --ds-font-size-xl: 2.3686rem;
  --ds-spacing-xxs: 0.4222rem;
  --ds-spacing-xs: 0.5628rem;
  /* … the remaining spacing steps */
}

Here is the same page at 390px and at 1440px. The sizes are measured in the browser, not typed in.

Step 390px (root 16px) 1440px (root 18px)
s 12px 13.5px
base 16px 18px
m 21.3px 24px
l 28.4px 32px
xl 37.9px 42.6px

Different scale, same relation: at both widths, each step is 1.333 times the one below it.

Using it

Components never see a number. The accessors return CSS variables, so a component describes which step it is on, not how big that is:

const Card = styled.div`
  background: ${({ theme }) => theme.color('background')};
  padding: ${({ theme }) => theme.spacing('base')};
  font-size: ${({ theme }) => theme.fontSize('base')};
`;

Because the values are CSS variables and the root changes through real @media rules, the browser resolves the breakpoint itself. Nothing is measured in JavaScript, so the server's HTML and the client's first render can't disagree about which breakpoint they are on.

The global CSS goes in once, next to the theme provider:

const RootStyle = createGlobalStyle`
  ${({ theme }) => theme.rootCss()}
`;

Rules that keep it honest

The root is a percentage, never px. font-size: 18px on the root overrides the text size the user set in their browser (WCAG 1.4.4). 112.5% scales with it.

The smallest screen is the reference. It stays at 100%, and wider screens grow from there. A phone is held closer than a laptop, so body text shouldn't shrink on it. There is also a practical reason: iOS Safari zooms in when you focus an input with text under 16px.

Touch targets are the exception, and they stay in px. minTarget() is 24px for a mouse or trackpad and 44px when there's a touch input. A finger doesn't shrink with the type. It's meant as a floor: min-block-size: max(${theme.minTarget()}, …).

The trade-off

Everything scales by the same factor. A heading can't shrink more than body text does on a small screen. When one component genuinely needs a different size at some breakpoint, it picks a different step with a media query. It doesn't get a second scale:

const Title = styled.h1`
  font-size: ${({ theme }) => theme.fontSize('l')};

  ${({ theme }) => theme.mq.greaterThan('desktop')`
    font-size: ${theme.fontSize('xl')};
  `}
`;

The relation is still defined once. The exception is visible in the one component that needs it.

Try it 

npm install @pindakaasman/design-system styled-components@^6

The package is on npm, and the source is in RamonGebben/mise.

title: Why Staging SMS as Pending Before Confirming Is Non-Negotiable in Finance Apps
description:
When people discover that FinLedger parses banking SMS messages automatically, one question inevitably follows:

"If the app can read my bank SMS alerts, why doesn't it just insert every transaction directly into my ledger without asking me to confirm anything?"

It is an understandable request. In a world of frictionless digital experiences, asking a user to review and confirm transactions feels like an extra step.

However, in financial ledger design, unsupervised automated insertion is dangerous.

Allowing an automated background process to directly manipulate your authoritative financial accounts without human oversight leads to ledger corruption, phantom expenses, and ultimately, a complete breakdown in personal financial awareness.

Here is why FinLedger treats transaction staging as a non-negotiable architectural boundary, and how the PENDING_CONFIRMATION workflow preserves ledger integrity.

The Real-World Traps of Unsupervised SMS Insertion

Bank SMS alerts are informational messages designed for human eyes; they are not an immutable double-entry accounting API. Treating them as definitive ledger entries creates several failure modes:

flowchart TD
    subgraph FullyAutomatedFailure["The Failure Modes of Unsupervised Ingestion"]
        Alert["Incoming Bank Notification"] --> DirectInsert["Silent Direct Insertion into Live Ledger"]

        DirectInsert --> Trap1["Trap 1: Pre-Authorization Holds
        A hotel or gas station places a Rs. 5,000 hold.
        The hold is never settled, but ledger permanently deducted Rs. 5,000!"]

        DirectInsert --> Trap2["Trap 2: Joint & Family Accounts
        A spouse buys groceries on a joint card.
        The expense silently inflates personal discretionary budget!"]

        DirectInsert --> Trap3["Trap 3: Truncated Merchant Names
        Bank SMS formats 'POS 49102919' with zero context.
        Transaction logged as mysterious unlabeled expense."]
    end

1. Pre-Authorization Holds and Reversals

When you check into a hotel or rent a car, the merchant places a temporary pre-authorization hold on your credit card. The bank immediately sends an SMS: "Debited Rs. 5,000.00 for pre-auth at Grand Hotel". Days later, the hold is released or settled for a different amount.

If an app silently writes that first alert to the ledger, your balance is deducted for money you never actually spent.

2. Joint Accounts and Secondary Cards

Many people share a bank account or credit card with a spouse, parent, or business partner. If your spouse uses the card to buy household furniture, an unconfirmed background ingestion engine logs it as your personal expense, corrupting your individual spending analytics.

3. The Loss of Financial Mindfulness

There is a psychological reason why 100% invisible automation fails.

The primary goal of personal finance software is not simply record-keeping; it is spending awareness. When an application operates entirely in the background without user interaction, you stop looking at your finances. You only notice what happened at the end of the month when your bank account is unexpectedly low.

The Staging Architecture (PENDING_CONFIRMATION)

To solve these problems while still eliminating tedious manual data entry, FinLedger implements a staged confirmation lifecycle:

flowchart TD
    SMS["Incoming Bank SMS"] --> Parser["On-Device Parsing Pipeline"]

    Parser --> Stage["Insert into Staging Table as:
    status = PENDING_CONFIRMATION"]

    Stage --> Isolated["Authoritative Account Balances
    Remain 100% Unpolluted"]

    Stage --> UI["Interactive Pending Review Tray:
    Presents extracted details to user"]

    UI --> Actions{"User Review Action"}

    Actions -->|One-Tap Confirm| Commit["Commit to Master Ledger:
    status = CONFIRMED
    Balance updated atomically"]

    Actions -->|Edit Details| Edit["Adjust Category, Note, or Account
    then Commit to Master Ledger"]

    Actions -->|Dismiss / Swipe| Drop["Delete Staging Record:
    Zero trace left in ledger"]

1. Complete Balance Isolation

When an SMS transaction is detected, it is marked with the status PENDING_CONFIRMATION.

In TransactionDao.kt, queries calculating current account balances, monthly budgets, and historical cash flow ignore pending records by default. An unconfirmed transaction cannot distort your available spendable balance until you explicitly approve it.

2. High-Speed Review Interface

FinLedger makes transaction confirmation effortless.

Rather than forcing you through multi-screen modal forms, pending transactions appear in a consolidated review tray at the top of your ledger feed.

  • The interface displays the merchant, the extracted amount, the assigned account, and the AI-suggested category.
  • If everything is accurate, a single tap confirms the transaction.
  • If you have five pending transactions, you can review and confirm all five in under ten seconds.

3. Immediate Context Enrichment

The moment a transaction is detected is the best time to add context:

  • Did you split this lunch bill with friends? You can split it with a single tap.
  • Did you receive a paper receipt? You can snap a photo attachment immediately before the receipt is lost.
  • Was this payment a loan repayment from a friend? You can reclassify it to your lending ledger with a single click.

Balancing Automation with Control

Automation should eliminate repetitive clerical labor, not strip away human agency.

By automating the tedious work—reading the notification, extracting the numbers, matching the account, and predicting the category—FinLedger saves 95% of the effort of manual tracking.

By staging candidates as PENDING_CONFIRMATION, FinLedger preserves the 5% that matters most: your verification and your financial awareness.

Key Takeaway

Convenience should never come at the expense of accounting correctness.

Staging automated transactions as pending confirmation protects your ledger against pre-authorization holds, shared account confusion, and ambiguous bank alerts. It ensures that every number in your personal finance ledger is there because you approved it.

FinLedger is a privacy-first, offline-first personal finance application for Android that models bank accounts, credit cards, and cash without double-counting.

title: AION Intraday Infrastructure: choosing Full Engine or White-Box integration
description:
A quantitative team can own a strategy and still need the surrounding analytics: options Greeks, indicators, a separate assessment stage and a controlled delivery interface. AION Intraday Infrastructure is our flagship institutional technology project for evaluating those boundaries. Full Engine and White-Box leasing remain proposed contracts, pending legal review and tenant-isolation acceptance. They are not currently orderable services. Current product scope.

Two integration choices

The proposed Full Engine combines Rust computation, five proprietary strategy categories, Edge Heuristics, native Edge ML and approved analytical delivery. The public categories are S1 Intraday Momentum, S2 Mean Reversion, S3 Volatility Breakout, S4 Greeks Scalping and S5 Event-Driven. These names describe capability categories, not disclosed strategy implementations or a verified mapping to private strategy IDs. Public architecture.

The proposed White-Box arrangement is for a customer that keeps its own strategy. It would provide processed Greeks and indicators, with an optional Edge assessment of agreed candidate metadata. Keeping strategy source private does not mean no information is transmitted: the payload, logging and retention boundaries must be agreed. White-Box scope.

A conceptual integration comparison, not an executable endpoint example:

Customer need Proposed arrangement Customer responsibility
Evaluate the complete analytical workflow Full Engine Authorized input, agreed output use and downstream decisions
Retain an existing proprietary detector White-Box Own strategy, source permissions and optional candidate payload
Interpret a supplied financial headline Separate standalone IMI API Supply permitted event text and hold an eligible API key

View the public Full Engine diagram and White-Box diagram.

Exact interface names, with their status

Interface Status
WSS /v1/signals/execute Proposed Full Engine analytical delivery; no broker orders
WSS /v1/stream/greeks Proposed processed Greeks and indicators
REST /v1/edge/evaluate Proposed candidate assessment
REST /v1/edge/historical Proposed licensed replay
POST /v1/analyze Separately published standalone IMI API

Do not construct a public WebSocket hostname from these identifiers. Authentication, schemas, reconnect behavior and delivery guarantees require their own accepted contract. The word execute describes the analytical pipeline, not brokerage execution. Interface documentation.

Deployment is part of the test

AION Hosted, BYOC in an approved AWS, Azure or GCP environment, and On-Premise are intended arrangements. None is a blanket claim of certified isolation or performance. An internal gate measurement is not complete WebSocket latency. Proposed service levels require end-to-end qualification and a signed agreement. Deployment and acceptance.

Data rights remain a separate requirement

AION does not sell, sublicense, distribute, redistribute, publish, broadcast or otherwise provide raw exchange ticks, quote streams, order book records, private brokerage feeds or samples. The prohibition includes free demonstrations, trials, evaluation samples and onward redistribution. Customers must hold appropriate source and processing rights; transformation alone does not create redistribution permission. Data-rights policy.

Access is evaluated for qualified professional developers, verified SEBI-registered Research Analysts and Investment Advisers, and eligible institutional or brokerage technology teams. This is not a retail signal subscription. Documentation grants no data rights, broker credentials, trading permissions or advisory authorization, and promises no financial return, regulatory approval or contractual SLA. Qualification boundaries.

title: 🚀 Building Spring by Example V2: Completing Module 08 - Spring Integration
description:
When I started learning Spring, I noticed something about many of the tutorials I found.

They often showed how to use a feature, but not always why it worked or when you should choose one approach over another.

I learn best by building things and documenting what I discover, so I started a project called spring-by-example.

The idea is simple: instead of building one large application, I’m creating a collection of small, focused examples where each example explores a specific Spring concept with clear explanations, tests, and documentation.

I’m happy to say that I’ve now completed Module 08 - Spring Integration. 🎉

This module introduced me to enterprise messaging and application integration, exploring how different parts of an application can communicate through messages rather than relying entirely on direct method calls.

The module covers:

  • Message Channels
  • Message Endpoints
  • Message Handlers
  • Transformers
  • Filters
  • Routers
  • Service Activators
  • Gateways
  • Channel Adapters
  • Error Channels
  • Integration Testing

One thing I particularly enjoyed about this module was understanding how Spring Integration brings together different messaging components to build loosely coupled application workflows.

I started with Message Channels, which are fundamental to Spring Integration.

A message channel provides a way for components to communicate by sending and receiving messages.

Instead of one component calling another directly, a sender can publish a message to a channel, and another component can receive and process it.

For example:

@Bean
public MessageChannel orderChannel() {
    return new DirectChannel();
}

From there, I explored Message Endpoints and Message Handlers.

Message endpoints connect application code to messaging channels, while message handlers perform the actual processing of incoming messages.

This helped me understand how Spring Integration separates the communication infrastructure from the business logic that processes messages.

Next came Transformers.

Transformers are responsible for converting messages from one representation into another.

For example, an incoming order message might be transformed into an order summary before being passed to another component.

@Bean
public IntegrationFlow orderTransformationFlow(
        OrderTransformer orderTransformer) {

    return IntegrationFlow
            .from("orderChannel")
            .transform(orderTransformer)
            .get();
}

I then explored Filters and Routers, two components that influence how messages move through an integration flow.

Filters determine whether a message should continue through a flow based on a condition.

Routers determine which channel should receive a message based on its content or some routing criteria.

These concepts helped me understand how to build more flexible messaging workflows without putting all the decision-making logic into one component.

Service Activators introduced another important concept.

They connect a message channel to a service method, allowing an existing business service to participate in a messaging flow.

This is particularly useful when integrating messaging with application business logic.

I also explored Gateways.

Gateways provide a higher-level interface for interacting with messaging systems. Instead of working directly with messaging channels, application code can communicate through an interface that hides some of the messaging infrastructure.

Then came Channel Adapters.

Channel adapters help connect external systems and messaging technologies to Spring Integration flows. They provide a bridge between an application's messaging infrastructure and external sources or destinations.

Another important topic was Error Channels.

Not every message-processing operation succeeds. An exception can occur while transforming a message, invoking a service, or processing a message further down a flow.

I explored how Spring Integration handles messaging errors and how applications can route and process error messages through dedicated error channels.

Finally, I completed the module with Integration Testing.

This was an important part of the learning process because understanding how individual messaging components work is different from understanding how they behave together in a complete flow.

I explored testing synchronous and asynchronous messaging flows, verifying message transformations, checking service activators, and testing error handling.

The goal wasn't simply to learn how to configure:

IntegrationFlow

The bigger goal was to understand how messages move through an application, how different components participate in that process, and how Spring Integration helps build loosely coupled systems.

The project is open source, and I'm continuing to build it as I learn:

🔗 GitHub: https://gith.ub/dsAQrAU5

🔗 GitLab: https://gitl.ab/gfDEyGH3

There’s still a long way to go, but completing Module 08 - Spring Integration feels like another important milestone. 🚀

Next up: Module 09 - Spring Cloud - exploring distributed application patterns, including service discovery, configuration management, API gateways, load balancing, resilience, distributed tracing, and declarative HTTP clients.

One focused example at a time. 🚀

If you've worked with Spring Integration before, which component do you find most useful in your day-to-day development - message channels, transformers, routers, gateways, or something else?

title: Designing an honest status screen: four states, including 'we lost the signal'
description:
Most status screens have two states: good and bad. That binary is why people stop looking at them. Real systems spend a lot of time in a third state — I do not know — and a UI that cannot say that will lie instead.

The four states we ship

  1. Moving — something in the room is changing.
  2. Still, present — the room's signature is stable but not the empty baseline.
  3. No one — matches the empty-room baseline.
  4. No signal — the sensor is not reporting.

Two of those four are boring, one is the one families care about, and one exists purely so the other three can be trusted. State 4 gets its own colour, its own icon, and a visible "last seen" age. It is not an error toast you can dismiss, because a dismissed error is indistinguishable from good news.

Why we refuse to compress to green/red

Green/red forces you to collapse "no one is home" and "the sensor died" into the same pixel. One is normal, the other needs a phone call. Colour is a terrible place to hide that distinction.

We also deliberately do not animate a "pulse" or a heartbeat motif. Anything that looks like a vital sign invites the reader to assume vital-sign accuracy, and we would then be answering questions we cannot answer.

Alarm fatigue is the actual enemy

Every feature request in this category is "notify me when X". Each added notification makes the next one less likely to be read. We kept notifications out of the product entirely for the first version: the dashboard shows state, and if you want to look, you look. That is a worse demo and a better product.

The tradeoff is explicit and we say it out loud to customers: this shows you, it does not alert you. If you need someone woken up at 3am, this is not that device.

Physical limits belong on the screen

Wi-Fi sensing degrades with distance and walls, so the UI states the working envelope instead of hiding it: same room up to about 10 metres, through one ordinary interior wall about 5 metres. Outside that, "no signal" appears — which is honest, and also tells you where to move the node. A user who understands the envelope stops trusting the display in the wrong room, which is exactly what you want.

A small test we use for any status UI

Ask: if the data source died right now, what would this screen say? If the answer is anything other than "I lost the signal", the design is not finished.

Live dashboard (a real device in a real apartment, updating about once per second): https://annest.cn/live/

AnNest is a consumer safety display, not a medical device. It does not detect falls, does not measure vitals, and does not call for help. If something is an emergency, call your local emergency number.

title: Introducing WovenUI Components
description:
WovenUI started as an SCSS framework: readable utility classes, an apply() mixin that takes any value, and design tokens for light, dark and high-contrast themes. Core is the foundation layer. It styles plain buttons and form fields, and it stops there.

@wovenui/components is the layer on top: buttons, cards, forms, tables, modals, drawers, dropdowns, tabs, toasts and more, written as plain markup with wu- classes. It needs one companion package, @wovenui/core, which provides the tokens and themes the components read.

This post covers how the kit is built, and one lesson about dialogs that applies to any app, whatever UI kit it uses.

One class on native HTML

The kit leans on what the browser already does. Modals and drawers are <dialog> elements. Dropdowns and popovers use the popover attribute. Accordions are <details> elements, and accordions that share a name keep only one open. Tooltips come from core, through data-tooltip.

Here is a modal, as it appears in the component's own documentation:

<button class="wu-btn" type="button" commandfor="m1" command="show-modal">Open</button>
<dialog class="wu-modal" id="m1" aria-labelledby="m1-title" closedby="closerequest">
  <header class="wu-modal-header">
    <h2 class="wu-modal-title" id="m1-title">Title</h2>
    <button class="wu-modal-close" type="button" commandfor="m1" command="close" aria-label="Close"></button>
  </header>
  <div class="wu-modal-body">Content</div>
  <form class="wu-modal-footer" method="dialog">
    <button class="wu-btn">Cancel</button>
    <button class="wu-btn brand" value="confirm">Save</button>
  </form>
</dialog>

There is no script on that page. The commandfor attribute on a button names the element it controls, and command says what to do (show-modal, close). These are invoker commands. The browser opens and closes the dialog, moves focus and handles the Esc key. showModal() and the command attribute lock page scroll. The body scrolls on its own when the content is taller than the dialog.

closedby decides how the dialog can be dismissed. closedby="any" adds click outside, which suits read-only content. A dialog that holds a form takes closedby="closerequest": a backdrop click with a menu open would otherwise close both and lose the input.

A drawer is the same idea, docked to the inline end by default, with inline-start or bottom to move it. Right-to-left pages mirror the slide.

Menus without a script

A dropdown is a native popover, anchored under its trigger:

<button class="wu-btn caret" type="button" popovertarget="menu1">Actions</button>
<div class="wu-dropdown" id="menu1" popover>
  <a class="wu-dropdown-item" href="/edit">Edit</a>
  <button class="wu-dropdown-item" type="button" popovertarget="menu1" popovertargetaction="hide">Duplicate</button>
  <hr class="wu-dropdown-separator">
  <button class="wu-dropdown-item danger" type="button" popovertarget="menu1" popovertargetaction="hide">Delete</button>
</div>

Esc and a click outside close it. popovertargetaction="hide" on a button item closes the menu after its click handler runs. commandfor with command="toggle-popover" works as the trigger too.

Placement uses CSS anchor positioning. The menu opens under the trigger and flips when there is no room. Where anchor positioning is not available, it is centered in the viewport. The inline-end modifier aligns the menu's inline end with the trigger's, as for the caret of a split button. The popover component works the same way, with a title part and an actions row for an inline confirm.

Where a script is still needed

Most components need no JavaScript. Modals, drawers, dropdowns, popovers and accordions need none. A small optional script, with no dependencies, covers the few that do: tabs, toasts, autocomplete, data table sorting, table row selection and expandable rows, and the input clear button.

The script finds these components by their class and starts them when the page loads. There is no setup attribute. As an ES module it exports init, toast, dismiss and per-component starters:

import { init, toast } from '@wovenui/components/js';

toast('Your changes are live.', { title: 'Saved', variant: 'success' });

Apps built with React, Vue or another framework can skip the script and keep the CSS. State lives in attributes (aria-selected, aria-expanded, aria-sort, hidden), not classes, so a framework sets the same attributes from component state.

Tokens, themes and layers from core

The components read core's design tokens, so they change with the theme. Change colors, spacing, radii or type once in core, and the components follow in light, dark, high-contrast and inverse sections.

Dark-only details use core's dark-mode mixin, which emits CSS @scope. The modal backdrop is one example: 50% black by default, 70% in dark themes, and it applies exactly where the dark tokens resolve, including a dark section inside a light page.

Every component lives in @layer components. The CSS declares the order @layer reset, base, components, recipes;. Core uses the first three; recipes is an extra layer above the components for patterns you build from them, and the package puts nothing in it. Utility classes and your own unlayered CSS win over the components without !important.

Naming stays small. The root carries the prefix, modifiers are bare words, and parts use the root name plus a part:

<button class="wu-btn" type="button">Cancel</button>
<button class="wu-btn brand" type="button">Save</button>
<button class="wu-btn danger subtle sm" type="button">Delete</button>

Modifiers are emitted as compounds (.wu-btn.brand), never alone, so they do not clash with other class names. Color words are core role names: brand, success, danger, warning, info.

Two more defaults: components use logical properties, so they follow dir="rtl" from the same stylesheet with no separate build. And motion is off until you ask for it with the word animated on a component, or wu-animated on an ancestor; it never runs when the visitor has asked the system to reduce motion.

The top layer lesson

Once modals and drawers are real dialog elements, they open in the browser's top layer. That changes the rules for everything that floats. A menu, tooltip or autocomplete list positioned with z-index in the normal page renders behind the dialog, whatever the number. To appear above a modal, it has to be in the top layer too.

The kit's dropdowns and popovers already are, because they are popovers. There is one more rule, which the modal docs state directly: a menu, popover or toast used while a modal is open must be inside the dialog element. A modal dialog makes the rest of the page inert, so anything outside it cannot be clicked. The kit's toast() handles this for toasts: while a modal dialog is open, it moves the toast region into the topmost one, so its toasts can be clicked and are announced, and moves it back when that dialog closes.

We hit this moving an existing Ember app onto the kit. The app had its own tooltip and autocomplete services, each rendering into a portaled container at the end of the body with a high z-index. Once the app's modals became native dialogs, those tooltips and suggestion lists opened behind them.

The fix is small. Give the portaled container popover="manual", call showPopover() when it has content, and hidePopover() when it is empty. A manual popover has no light dismiss, so the service keeps full control over when it closes, and once shown it sits in the top layer above the dialog that opened before it. For an interactive container such as an autocomplete list, the rule above still applies: place it inside the open dialog, as toast() does with its region, so the options stay clickable.

Install 

npm i @wovenui/core @wovenui/components

Load core first, then the components:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="node_modules/@wovenui/core/dist/wovenui.min.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="node_modules/@wovenui/components/dist/wovenui-kit.min.css">

With Sass and a bundler, load both in your global stylesheet:

@use "@wovenui/core";
@use "@wovenui/components";

Every component is on by default. Turn some off with $components, or load one component at a time (@use "@wovenui/components/button";) for CSS modules and component <style> blocks. Pick one path per project, not both, or shared rules are emitted twice.

The kit works in Chrome and Edge 135+, Firefox 144+ and Safari 26.2+.

The package also ships dist/llms-full.txt, an AI guide with every component, its classes, modifiers, variables and examples. Give it to an AI coding assistant so it writes correct markup.

Working with an AI agent

The kit ships a full reference for AI agents. Point your coding agent at it and it writes correct kit markup and SCSS without guessing: every component, its classes, modifiers, variables and examples. Core has its own file for the framework, and the components package has a separate one for the kit. The kit guide is at wovenui.com/components/llms-full.txt and the core guide is at wovenui.com/llms-full.txt.

What is next

The kit and core moved together: the last two kit releases each required a newer core. The next post walks through what changed from core 2.0 to 2.4, and which of those changes the components asked for.

Links

  • Documentation: wovenui.com/components
  • GitHub: github.com/WovenUI/components
  • npm: @wovenui/components
  • Core: wovenui.com

WovenUI Components is MIT licensed.

Html5 semantic tags provide meaningful tags that clearly describe their purpose, improving readability ,accessibility ans SEO for both humans and browsers.

Pixel

title: I got tired of SSH-ing in to run docker ps, so I built a calm web UI for my server (in Rust)
description:
I run a few Docker containers on a small server. Every time something felt off, it was the same routine:

ssh me@server
docker ps -a                  # Restarting (1) 12 seconds ago. Again?
docker logs --tail 50 app     # scroll, squint
nano compose.yml              # which port was it?
docker compose up -d          # did it work?

Five commands to answer three questions: is everything up, what broke, and why?

So I built Server Explorer, a calm web UI that sits on top of Docker and Compose. It doesn't replace them: everything it shows comes from Docker's API, deploys run the real docker compose up, and the stacks it creates are plain compose.yml files.

Small on purpose

Whoever controls Docker controls the whole server, so I kept the attack surface tiny. It only listens on 127.0.0.1 and is reached through an SSH tunnel, never from the network. One admin, an audit log of every change, and stacks built in the app can't use privileged mode, host networking or bind mounts.

Less convenient than a URL on your phone? Yes. That's the trade-off.

What it does

  • A status board: one sentence, one square per container, and a Needs you list with fix buttons
  • Live logs and CPU/RAM per container
  • Stacks from a form: image, ports, storage, env, command, run-as user, then Save & deploy
  • Docker Hub search and pulls with live progress

What building it taught me

  • New volumes belong to root. An image that runs as another user can't write to them, so stacks now have a Run as field.
  • The container port has to match the app. A wrong number fails silently, so reading it from the image is next on the list.
  • Polling can make a page blink. Docker's status text counts seconds, so every refresh looked like new data. Rendering from memos, and rounding the seconds, fixed it.
  • Leptos view! and >: disabled=move || n > 0 closes the tag early. Use braces.
  • () in a reactive block can break hydration. An empty <span hidden> renders the same on server and client.

Built with

Leptos 0.8 (SSR + hydration), Axum, bollard and embedded SurrealDB 3.

What's next

Smarter port checks, Cloudflare Tunnel as a built-in wrapper (the explorer itself stays SSH-only), deleting stacks, and a storage browser.

Try it

Open source (MIT): https://github.com/AeonLogics/aeon-server-explorer

If you self-host: would an SSH-tunnel-only dashboard put you off, or is that exactly why you'd trust it?

description:
Nakodo has 76 public pages, all of them built from the same colour tokens. I have written about the 866 lines of CSS those tokens live in and about the design report that chose them, but I had never actually measured a single contrast ratio. I just assumed the palette was fine, which is the same as not knowing.

So I measured every piece of text on all 76 pages. Here is what came back.

  • 13,403 text runs, of which 15 are invisible on purpose
  • 2,745 distinct combinations of colour, background, size, weight and tag
  • 25 distinct foreground-on-background pairs in the whole site
  • 13,386 of 13,388 visible runs pass WCAG AA
  • 9,257 of them, 69.1 per cent, reach AAA
  • one failure, at 3.48:1, on a 12px badge that appears twice on the home page

Getting a real sRGB value out of the browser

The first problem is that nothing in this app is written in a colour space you can do arithmetic on. The stylesheet declares oklch(), and getComputedStyle in Chrome hands back lab():

"--color-ink-500":    { "css": "lab(56.4751% -1.49497 -5.74161)", "hex": "#818991" },
"--muted-foreground": { "css": "lab(42.5395% -1.93667 -7.83916)", "hex": "#5c6671" },
"--foreground":       { "css": "lab(13.4665% -2.01512 -11.7954)", "hex": "#162433" },
"--background":       { "css": "lab(96.7997% .35131 4.58077)",    "hex": "#f9f5ed" }

The WCAG formula wants sRGB channels. Rather than implement Lab to sRGB and get it subtly wrong, let the browser do it: paint the colour onto a 1x1 canvas and read the pixel back. Canvas accepts any colour syntax the CSS parser does, and getImageData is sRGB bytes by definition.

const cv = document.createElement("canvas");
cv.width = cv.height = 1;
const ctx = cv.getContext("2d", { willReadFrequently: true });
const rgba = (c) => {
  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, 1, 1);
  ctx.fillStyle = "rgba(0,0,0,0)";
  ctx.fillStyle = c;              // ignored if the parse fails, hence the reset above
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, 1, 1);
  const d = ctx.getImageData(0, 0, 1, 1).data;
  return [d[0], d[1], d[2], d[3] / 255];
};

The fillStyle reset matters: an unparseable colour leaves the previous value in place, so without it one bad string silently colours every later measurement.

The background is not a property, it is a stack

The second problem is that backgroundColor is rgba(0, 0, 0, 0) on nearly every element that holds text. The real background is whichever ancestor last painted one, with every semi-transparent layer and every inherited opacity on the way down applied in order.

const bgOf = (el) => {
  const stack = [];
  for (let n = el; n; n = n.parentElement) {
    const s = getComputedStyle(n);
    const c = rgba(s.backgroundColor);
    const op = parseFloat(s.opacity);
    if (c[3] > 0) stack.push([c[0], c[1], c[2], c[3] * (isNaN(op) ? 1 : op)]);
  }
  let base = [255, 255, 255, 1];           // the canvas under the document
  for (let i = stack.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) base = over(stack[i], base);
  return base;
};

Then the text colour is composited over that result, inherited opacity included, and only then is the ratio taken. On this site that detail changes real numbers: the same muted grey measures 5.37:1 on the page background and 5.74:1 inside a card, because the card is a slightly lighter cream.

25 pairs for a whole site

Counting by text runs, these are the ones that matter:

  7.56  #44505e on #f9f5ed   2,965 runs    body text
 14.47  #162433 on #f9f5ed   2,862 runs    headings
 10.98  #2b3847 on #f9f5ed   2,393 runs    strong body text
  5.37  #5c6671 on #f9f5ed   2,271 runs    muted, captions, footer
  6.34  #005ba6 on #f9f5ed   1,195 runs    links
 15.46  #162433 on #fefdf9     605 runs    headings in cards
  5.74  #5c6671 on #fefdf9     524 runs    muted in cards
  8.66  #f9f5ed on #004783     171 runs    text on the dark plate
  9.26  #fefdf9 on #004783     153 runs    headings on the dark plate
  5.69  #a1cdff on #004783      86 runs    muted on the dark plate

Twenty-five pairs, built from about eight token values, is the entire visible range of a site with 76 pages on it. That is the actual product of having no hex codes in the CSS: you cannot introduce a twenty-sixth pair by accident, because there is nowhere to type one.

The muted pair is the interesting row. 5.37:1 clears AA comfortably and misses AAA, and it is used for 2,271 runs of exactly the text a design system is tempted to make quiet: captions, table headers, the footer, "Prices in EUR, including any VAT or sales tax", the line under every heading. Going to AAA would mean darkening one token and losing the distinction between muted and body text, which is the thing it exists for. I am leaving it, and now I know the number instead of assuming it.

The one failure 

  3.48  #818991 on #fefdf9   12px   w400   SPAN   "Email"   2 runs   nakodo.app/

It is the "Email, not published" badge in the example creator cards:

state === "none" && "border border-dashed border-ink-400 text-ink-500",

A dashed outline and text-ink-500 for an absent value. It reads as deliberately faint, which was the intention, and 3.48:1 at 12px is below the 4.5:1 that normal text needs.

The fix is not obviously "darken it", because of where else that token is:

text-ink-500  3 call sites:
  components/ui/input.tsx       placeholder:text-ink-500
  components/ui/textarea.tsx    placeholder:text-ink-500
  components/brand/contact-strip.tsx   state === "none"
--input: var(--color-ink-500)   the border of every input and textarea

So the same value does three jobs, and it is measured against two different bars. As a border it is non-text content and needs 3:1, and 3.48:1 passes. As placeholder text it needs 4.5:1 and fails, on every input in the app, which you can check on the home page: the hero box has a placeholder reading yourbrand.com, and here is what it measures live.

{ "id": "hero-site", "placeholder": "yourbrand.com", "phColor": "#818991",
  "bg": "#fefdf9", "ratio": 3.48, "borderRatio": 3.48 }

One token, two thresholds, one pass and one fail. Placeholder text is not exempt from 1.4.3; only disabled controls and genuinely decorative text are. The honest fix is to stop using the border colour as a text colour: keep ink-500 for borders, and give absent values and placeholders ink-600 or the muted token, both of which already exist and both of which clear 4.5:1.

Thirteen colour pairs that do not exist

My first sweep found 38 distinct pairs and three failures, two of them at 1.30:1 and 2.13:1 on a header link reading "Open the app", on two unrelated pages. I nearly wrote the post around them.

They were not real. The header button carries transition: color 0.15s, background-color 0.15s, and getComputedStyle during a transition returns the interpolated value, so I had caught the same button twice at different points in a 150ms fade. Waiting two seconds after load before measuring dropped the pair count from 38 to 25 and the failures from three to one.

That is the part of this I would tell anyone writing a contrast audit. A computed colour is not a declaration, it is whatever is on screen in that frame, and an audit that does not settle the page first measures the animation.

Fifteen text runs came back at exactly 1.00:1, all three groups of them on the home page: "Reasons, not just a score", "1/5", "Next". Those are the tour notes that are always in the DOM at zero opacity, waiting for the tour to start. Ratio 1.00 is the signature of opacity zero, and it is worth special-casing rather than reporting, because the alternative is an audit that flags every tooltip in the world.

The real accessibility problem is not contrast

The size histogram, in text runs:

 5.5px      1
  11px    696
  12px    815
  13px    423
  14px  5,534
  15px  4,905
  17px     82
  22px    245
  26px    547

1,511 runs, 11 per cent of the text on the site, are 12px or smaller, and all of them pass contrast. Contrast was the thing I was worried about and size is the thing I should have been worried about. 11px is the footer, the table headers and the "On this page" labels, and those are all genuinely secondary, but 11px is small enough that it is a reading problem for a lot of people at any contrast ratio.

The smallest text on the site is a single 5.5px SVG label reading "No. 001", the plate number on a hand-drawn illustration. It measures 8.66:1, which is both pleasing and completely irrelevant, since nobody is reading it. Decorative text is exempt and this is the only element in the audit I would call decorative.

What I am doing about it

Three things, in order:

  1. Stop using ink-500 as a text colour. Two placeholder classes and one badge state move to ink-600, and the token keeps its border job. One commit, two measurable numbers.
  2. Leave the 5.37:1 muted token alone, and write the number down in the design notes next to it, so the next person to pick that colour for a smaller size knows what they are spending.
  3. Look at the 11px cases properly, as a type-scale question rather than a colour question.

Everything above was measured from the public pages, so you can check any of it: open the home page, pricing, the glossary or a guide, paste the canvas trick into the console, and compare. The two numbers I would most like somebody to argue with are the 5.37 and the 3.48.
