title: Building Arcyria: an ELT platform where pipelines run as one-shot containers
description:
I'm building Arcyria, a multi-tenant data operations platform: data connections, ELT pipelines, SQL transformations, monitoring and an AI operator, in one place. This post covers the architecture decision that shaped the most: every pipeline run is its own short-lived container.

The problem with long-running workers

The obvious way to run pipelines is a pool of workers that pull jobs from a queue. It works, until it doesn't:

  • One tenant's heavy run starves everyone else.
  • State leaks between runs (temp files, caches, half-loaded tables).
  • Credentials end up living in long-lived processes.
  • Scaling means guessing how many workers you need.

The approach: one run, one container

When a user starts a run, the API does not execute anything. It publishes a small, credential-free event to a queue. A private control service consumes it and launches a one-shot task on AWS ECS Fargate.

Web app -> Go API -> SQS (run event, no secrets)
                      |
              control service (consumer + scheduler)
                      |
              ECS Fargate task (ELT job)
                      |
   ephemeral DuckDB + dbt -> Parquet artifacts -> destination tables
                      |
              idempotent callback to control

Inside the task, the run is staged through an ephemeral DuckDB database, transformed with dbt, written out as immutable Parquet artifacts, and then upserted into the destination tables. When the run finishes, the local DuckDB and dbt files are deleted. Nothing survives except the evidence the run published.

Why it works well

Isolation by default. A run can't see another run's files, and a crash only kills that run.

Credentials stay out of the pipeline path. The browser never talks to the ELT service. Credentials are encrypted by the API and never appear in queue messages, task overrides, logs or browser state.

Idempotent completion. The task reports back with a callback that is safe to retry, so a flaky network doesn't produce duplicate or lost results.

Cost follows usage. No idle worker fleet. You pay for the minutes a run actually takes.

Trade-offs

It isn't free. Cold-start latency is real, so this suits batch and scheduled ELT rather than sub-second jobs. You also need good run-level observability, since you can't just SSH into a worker. And destination tables must already exist with compatible columns before a run starts. We chose upsert-oriented delivery and strict contracts over magic schema creation.

What's next

I'm working toward a public beta and would love feedback from people who run ELT in production: what would you need before trusting a platform like this with your pipelines?

If you want to follow along, leave a comment or say hi.

title: The AI mind tax that afflicts those who use AI best
description:
AI was supposed to make work easier, but for the people who use it most, it just became a different kind of work, and a whole lot of exhaustion.

The promise of the tech was that AI would make work easier, and, sure, in plenty of ways it came true, but for the people using it the hardest, it created a second job nobody considered, managing the pile of tools that now does the work for you.

The folks who stay sharp hold onto what the machine still can’t do for them, their judgment, their ability to work with other people, and some grip on where the work actually stands, but there’s a price to pay for that.

We’re not talking about just one burnt out person, because nobody was hired for this. The title still says marketer, or designer, or founder. The job shifted to keeping a dozen disconnected machines pointed in the same direction, and the whole industry is pretending that isn’t the work.

The people embracing AI the right way, learning the tools, wiring them into everything, getting genuinely good, are the ones getting buried, because being good at this now means being the one who holds it all together. A recent benchmark from CMO Huddles and Benchmarkit shows why. 98 percent of marketing teams use AI somewhere, and only 3 percent have connected it across their work. The companies didn’t build the connective layer, so the capable people became it.

In a research project I’ve been working with CMOs, I was chatting with a marketer I know who has been in the tech industry for almost twenty years. Her career has spanned some big tech names you would definitely know and these days she runs pretty much all the marketing at a startup by herself.

As we discussed the evolution of marketing and the marketing executive today, it became very clear that she’s about as deep into AI as anyone I’ve met. She is wired into every tool she touches, running most of her day through Claude and ChatGPT. She can spin up a user survey, analyze it, write the launch plan, and build the assets herself. All the stuff that used to take a whole team.

If AI was built to make anyone’s job easier, it was built for her.

I figured, if anything, that AI had simplified her life exponentially and that she’d admit as much. Instead she told me she feels like she’s “melting on the inside.”

The tools aren’t the problem. There are just so many of them, all living in different places, and she’s the only thing holding them together. Figma, the CRM, Claude, ChatGPT, Slack, each one its own window with its own half-finished conversation, and she’s the one keeping track of which idea she had where.

She called it a real tax and toll. She also said she wouldn’t give a single one of these tools back.

And that job is exhausting.

She was not an outlier. One fractional CMO I talked to runs marketing for a whole stack of startups at once, each with its own set of tools, its own logins, its own AI baked into the CRM and the design software and everything else, and she is the only human carrying context from one to the next.

Another person I spoke to runs a team at a big company where everyone has quietly built their own personal pile of AI agents, each one tuned to how that person works, so when someone leaves, the knowledge of how any of it fits together walks out with them.

Different companies, different budgets, same situations. The person in the middle is the integration layer, and the integration layer is tired.

The fatigue is real

What she described as “melting” is a documented, measurable thing. For better or worse, the research on it was pretty disturbingly long before any of us used a chatbot.

Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith, and Ulrich Klocke found that it takes about twenty-three minutes to fully get your focus back after a single interruption.

Similarly, Rohan Narayana Murty, Sandeep Dadlani and Rajath B. Das, studying workers across three Fortune 500 companies, found that people toggle between different applications and websites around twelve hundred times a day.

Cornell’s Ellis Idea Lab, working with Qatalog, found it takes nine and a half minutes just to get back into a workflow after switching apps, that forty-five percent of workers say too many apps make them less productive, and that nearly half admit they make actual mistakes because they can’t keep track of what’s happening across all their tools.

That was the cost of switching between dumb apps that just sat there and waited for you. Then every one of those apps grew its own AI.

As the switching multiplied, every tool became two things to keep track of, the tool and the AI living inside it. The marketer I spoke to isn’t just bouncing between Figma and the CRM and Slack anymore. She’s bouncing between Figma’s AI and the CRM’s AI and Claude and ChatGPT, each one a separate conversation, each one knowing nothing about the others, each one needing to be caught up.

The one thing none of these tools reliably does is hold the thread for you.

Rifat Mehreen Amin and her colleagues, studying how people actually use AI chatbots, gave the problem a name, context fragmentation, and watched people cope with it by copying pieces of one conversation into another by hand, stitching the results back together across sessions, rebuilding their own mental map every time they came back.

You become the only part of the system that remembers what you were doing in the other four windows, which is why, at the end of a day like that, you feel like you’re melting on the inside. It also means you are the only one who knows where any of it stands.

When all the context lives in your head, explaining to your manager or your team where the work actually is becomes its own task, and nobody else can pick it up without you.

You turned into the glue

The reason all of this lands on her and not on the machines is simple. The machines don’t talk to each other, so she has to. Every tool she uses has become its own little walled garden with its own AI inside it.

Figma’s AI knows about the file she’s in and nothing else. The CRM’s AI knows about campaigns and nothing else. Claude knows about the conversation she’s having with Claude. None of them know about any of the others.

Connectors are starting to change that at the edges. You can wire Figma or a CRM into Claude so it can reach into them directly. Xinyi Hou and her colleagues, in a survey of the connector landscape, found that even with a shared standard for these integrations, stitching tools together remains fragmented, and the connections mostly run one way, into whichever assistant she has made the hub. The other tools still sit in their own corners.

She is still the one deciding what connects to what, and carrying across by hand whatever doesn’t.

Jan-Philipp Steghöfer studied how professionals actually use AI tools across their real workflows and found that the most persistent frustration was almost never the AI’s ability. It was the breaks between the tools, each one useful on its own, none able to hand off to the next, so the person in the middle rebuilds the context from scratch every time and carries it across by hand. One worker in his study described finishing in one AI tool and manually moving the output into the next just to keep going.

The marketer I talked to does the same thing, having ChatGPT write a summary of one conversation so she can paste it into Claude to start another. She has become the connective tissue between systems that were supposed to connect themselves.

The cruel part is that all of that burden on your shoulders feels productive. It feels like work getting done.

The research keeps finding that the feeling and the reality don’t match.

The cleanest proof comes from METR, a nonprofit that ran a careful randomized controlled trial on experienced developers doing real work in codebases they knew inside out. Going in, the developers expected AI to speed them up by around a quarter. They did the work, and afterward they still believed it had made them about twenty percent faster.

When the researchers measured the actual time, the developers had been nineteen percent slower with the AI than without it. The gap between how fast they felt and how fast they were ran close to forty points, and it held even after they’d lived through the slowdown themselves.

That gap is the whole danger of the mind tax. You cannot feel it while it is happening. You feel busy, you feel capable, you feel like you are getting an enormous amount done, and some of that is true.

Aruna Ranganathan and Xingqi Maggie Ye found the same thing over eight months of watching people adopt AI at a tech company. The tools intensified the work instead of shrinking it. People took on more, moved faster, and stretched the day longer, largely because AI made doing more feel possible.

Instead of the rest or deeper thinking you’d expect, the time it saved resulted in more work, more tools to run, and more threads to manage.

It comes for your best people first

The cruel joke of the mind tax is who it hits hardest. You would think it’s the people just dabbling with AI who get worn down the most, but the reality is that it’s the people who dove in head first.

Julie Bedard, Matthew Kropp, Megan Hsu and their colleagues at Boston Consulting Group studied nearly fifteen hundred workers and found that productivity climbs as you add AI tools, right up until about the third one. After that it falls. The workers running four or more tools at once were getting less done, making more errors, and reporting more of the exact buzzing, fried feeling the marketer described. The fatigue came from overseeing the AI, not from handing work to it.

All the watching and checking and correcting, and the holding of everything in your head at once, is its own kind of labor, and the people doing the most of it were the heaviest users, the ones who leaned in hardest.

The study found the highest rates were in marketing, which is to say, in people exactly like my CMO friend.

The management version of this is worse than the productivity one. Those same researchers found that workers who weren’t fried intended to leave their jobs at a rate of about one in four. Among the workers who were fried, it rose to one in three.

The Upwork Research Institute found the same thing from another angle, that the most productive AI users, the ones getting the biggest gains, were also the most burned out, with 88 percent of them reporting burnout and roughly twice the likelihood of looking for the exit.

This mental tax seriously wears out your best people and then pushes them out the door. The problem is, of course, that these are the exact people you cannot afford to lose.

What should worry anyone who does this work for a living is the impact to a person’s mind underneath it all. Nataliya Kosmyna and her team at the MIT Media Lab wired people up and watched their brains while they wrote, some on their own, some leaning on AI. The heavy AI users showed weaker neural engagement, remembered less of what they’d produced, and felt less ownership of it.

The researchers called what builds up “cognitive debt,” the brain quietly doing less of its own work once a machine is there to do it.

Michael Gerlich found a matching pattern in a study of six hundred and sixty-six people. The more someone relied on AI, the weaker their critical thinking scored, and the thing connecting the two was cognitive offloading, the habit of handing your thinking to the tool. The effect was steepest in the heaviest and youngest users. Gerlich is careful that this is a correlation and not proof that AI caused the decline, and that caution is fair. The direction of it still lines up with what everyone living in these tools already feels.

Put the pieces together and the mind tax stops looking like plain tiredness. The thing getting taxed is judgment.

The more of the thinking you hand off, the less of it you are doing, and the less sharp you get at the one part of the job a machine still cannot do for you.

That is a genuinely terrible tradeoff. When it comes down to it, your judgment is the only thing you were ever really being paid for.

The new job is quietly eating the old one, and nobody has said so out loud.

A room with one voice in it

When I asked that marketer what she missed most, she avoided any mention of the AI tools in her arsenal, and focused entirely on teamwork and collaboration. The whiteboard, the ten people around a table, the coworker who could absorb her idea and say, in so many words, that it was wrong.

What she has now is a one-way screen. She does the work alone, runs it past an assistant that agrees with her, and then launches it.

The collaborator got replaced by something that never pushes back.

Myra Cheng, Dan Jurafsky and their colleagues at Stanford tested eleven leading AI models and found they affirmed what the user was doing about forty-nine percent more often than a human would, including in cases where the user was describing something deceptive or harmful. Worse, when people took interpersonal problems to a sycophantic model, a single conversation left them more convinced they were right and less willing to repair the situation and people liked it. They trusted the agreeable model more, which is exactly why companies have every reason to keep building it that way.

This is baked into how these systems are made. Anthropic’s own researchers, led by Mrinank Sharma and Ethan Perez, showed that the leading assistants are systematically sycophantic, because the training rewards it.

People reward the answer that flatters them over the one that corrects them, every time. Train a machine on that mentality and you get a world-class suck-up.

Even the humans overseeing the training, and the models built to imitate those humans, preferred the convincing wrong answer to the accurate inconvenient one a meaningful share of the time.

This dismantles what actually made the work good. Jan-Philipp Steghöfer’s study found that the single-user model of these tools substitutes a private conversation with the AI for the collaborative one with the team, the back-and-forth where people surface each other’s blind spots, challenge the weak idea, and build a shared understanding of why the thing is the way it is.

The team inherits the finished artifact but not the argument that should have shaped it. Our marketer friend felt the same loss. She said that when a team spends half an hour in a room on a problem, you get ten different minds pulling at it. With AI, you get one, and it’s pulling in whatever direction you already were.

The thing that used to make people good at this work was friction, the colleague who caught the mistake, the review that stung, the question you hadn’t thought to ask. Trade all of that for a tool that agrees with you, and the cost isn’t only time and focus.

The real loss is what was keeping your judgment honest.

Somebody has to pay for it

I want to be careful here, because it would be easy to think I’m making a case against AI and I’m not. The marketer I talked to would be the first to tell you that. She loves these tools. She said, more than once, that she wouldn’t give a single one of them back, that the amount she can do now would have taken a whole team the old way.

The gains are real. The tax is just the price nobody understood or identified when she started down this path.

Let’s be clear, it is a real price.

Add up everything we’ve walked through and you get the same result in three different outputs. There’s the work of running the tools, the context carried by hand from one window to the next. There’s the slow erosion of the thinking you stop doing because the machine is there to do it. There’s the quiet of working alone with something that only ever agrees with you.

This all comes down to one person standing in the middle of all the tools, holding it all together.

This is really a design problem.

Right now the human is the integration layer, the memory, the quality check, the only thing in the whole setup capable of saying “no, that’s wrong.”

We built a dozen brilliant tools and skipped the part that connects them, carries the thread, or pushes back. The work John Dubois, Chandra Shukla, and Kay Youngstrom from EY have done on redesigning jobs around AI makes the case that the win comes from augmentation, designing work so the tools sharpen human judgment instead of burying it. That is a thing to build, not a thing a person should have to white-knuckle their way through alone.

We need to embrace the idea that the job changed. Being good at this work, today, means being good at orchestration, at judgment, at holding a team together while the machines do the production. Create a name for that job, hire for it, build the day around it, and the tax gets smaller. Pretend the job is still what it used to be, and it keeps coming out of the person.

The reason to build it is that the one job that we could truly own, and still can, is judgment.

Knowing what’s good, knowing what’s missing, knowing when the confident answer is confidently wrong.

Peter Klein calls this the paradox of automation. The more AI takes over the routine work, the more valuable human judgment becomes, and at the same time the fewer chances people get to build it, because judgment is grown through exactly the hands-on work the machine is now doing.

Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic puts the same idea more bluntly. When machines do the thinking, humans have to do more of the judging. The mind tax is dangerous because it eats that capacity first. It buries the one thing you cannot afford to lose under the management of everything else.

So our marketer friend keeps going. She does the work of ten people, and then she does the work of managing the machines that do the work of ten people, and at the end of the day she feels like she’s melting on the inside.

The tools keep getting upgraded.

She’s still running on the same single brain she started with. Until someone designs for that, instead of around it, the tax comes out of her.

The tax will always come out of the person.

References and further reading

The fatigue is real

  • Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith, and Ulrich Klocke, “The Cost of Interrupted Work: More Speed and Stress” (University of California, Irvine, 2008). The research on how long it takes to recover focus after an interruption.
  • “How Much Time and Energy Do We Waste Toggling Between Applications?” (Harvard Business Review, 2022). The study of workers across three Fortune 500 companies toggling around twelve hundred times a day.
  • Cornell’s Ellis Idea Lab, with Qatalog, “Workgeist Report ‘21” (2021). On the time lost and mistakes made switching between too many tools.
  • Rifat Mehreen Amin, Alperen Adatepe, Daniela Fernandes, Daniel Buschek, and Andreas Butz, “Conversations in Space: Non-Linear LLM Interaction in Everyday Use” (2026). On context fragmentation and how people carry it across AI chats by hand.

You turned into the glue

  • Jan-Philipp Steghöfer, “Faster than the Team, Faster than the Customer: Tool Integration, Collaboration, and Organisational Lag in AI-Assisted RE” (2026). On tool integration, not capability, as the binding constraint, and the human bridging the breaks.
  • Xinyi Hou, Yanjie Zhao, Shenao Wang, and Haoyu Wang, “Model Context Protocol (MCP): Landscape, Security Threats, and Future Research Directions” (2025). On how, even with a shared standard for connectors, stitching AI tools together remains fragmented.
  • METR, “Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity” (2025). The randomized trial finding developers nineteen percent slower with AI while feeling faster.
  • Aruna Ranganathan and Xingqi Maggie Ye, “AI Doesn’t Reduce Work, It Intensifies It” (Harvard Business Review, 2026). On how AI expands the pace, scope, and hours of work rather than shrinking it.

It comes for your best people first

  • Julie Bedard, Matthew Kropp, Megan Hsu, and colleagues, “When Using AI Leads to ‘Brain Fry’” (Boston Consulting Group, in Harvard Business Review, 2026). On productivity peaking at three AI tools, and the fatigue and attrition that follow.
  • Upwork Research Institute, “From Burnout to Balance: AI-Enhanced Work Models” (2024). On the most productive AI users reporting the most burnout and the highest intent to quit.
  • Nataliya Kosmyna and colleagues, “Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt When Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing” (MIT Media Lab, 2026). On the measurable cognitive cost of offloading thinking to AI.
  • Michael Gerlich, “AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of Critical Thinking” (Societies, 2025). On the correlation between heavy AI reliance and weaker critical thinking.

A room with one voice in it

  • Myra Cheng, Cinoo Lee, Pranav Khadpe, Sunny Yu, Dyllan Han, and Dan Jurafsky, “Sycophantic AI Decreases Prosocial Intentions and Promotes Dependence” (Science, 2026). On AI affirming users far more than humans do, and what that does to judgment.
  • Mrinank Sharma, Meg Tong, Ethan Perez, and colleagues, “Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models” (Anthropic, 2023). On how training rewards agreement over accuracy.

Somebody has to pay for it

  • John Dubois, Chandra Shukla, and Kay Youngstrom, “How to Redesign Work Around Human Skills in the Age of AI” (EY, 2026). On augmentation, designing work so AI sharpens human judgment rather than burying it.
  • Peter G. Klein, “AI and Human Judgment: Why People Still Matter” (Baylor University, Hankamer School of Business, 2026). On the paradox of automation and why judgment grows scarcer as it grows more valuable.
  • Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic, “How AI Is Changing Decision Making in Organizations” (Forbes, 2026). On why, as machines do more of the thinking, humans have to do more of the judging.

The AI mind tax that afflicts those who use AI best was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Engineering a High-Concurrency E-Commerce Backend: Testing, Concurrency & Resilience at Scale
description:
Introduction
Modern e-commerce platforms operate under extreme constraints. During flash sales or peak traffic events, backends face massive spikes in concurrent requests, threatening data integrity, inventory accuracy, and system availability.

In building ShopEase (shopping-app-backend), a Spring Boot 3.x Java 17 e-commerce backend, achieving functional correctness was only half the battle. The true challenge lay in engineering a robust Testing & Quality Engineering pipeline to guarantee thread safety, zero race conditions, and predictable performance under heavy load.

The Testing & Quality Engineering Strategy
To ensure zero regressions and high availability, our testing architecture covers every critical tier of the application:

Unit & Slice Testing: Isolating controllers and services using Mockito (OrderControllerTest, ProductControllerTest) to validate HTTP statuses and JSON serialization instantly.

Integration Testing: Verifying cross-component flows and database interactions (OrderServiceIntegrationTest).

Concurrency & Race Condition Testing: Simulating multi-threaded contention to prevent inventory overselling and lost updates (InventoryConcurrencyTest).

Load & Stress Testing: Automating high-traffic simulations via custom Java concurrency harnesses to measure throughput and failure rates under pressure (LoadAndStressTest).

Key Technical Highlights

  1. Zero-Mock Concurrency Testing
    To prevent race conditions during high-demand operations, we validated thread safety using multi-threaded execution services (ExecutorService), ensuring that simultaneous updates maintain strict data consistency.

  2. Lightweight Load & Stress Harness
    Instead of relying on heavy external CLI tools, we built an integrated Java-based load testing harness using standard HTTP clients to bombard endpoints with concurrent virtual users, measuring real-time latency, success ratios, and system stability under load.

Conclusion
By implementing this comprehensive testing suite, we achieved 100% build success across all modules, robust thread safety for inventory management, and high test maintainability. Building resilient systems isn't just about clean code—it's about proving that your architecture holds up under real-world pressure.

title: Our desktop clock can say 134 different ages, and "60s ago" is not one of them while "in 60s" is
description:
Notifio's desktop UI is mostly a list of searches with a time next to each one. "checked 12s ago". "last check 4m ago". A found listing says when it turned up. There is no chart and no dashboard, because the only question the window has to answer continuously is "is this thing still working", and an age is the cheapest possible answer to it.

All of that comes out of one file with three functions in it:

// app/src/renderer/format.ts
/** "12s ago", "4m ago", "2h ago". Empty string for a null timestamp. */
export function relativeTime(at: number | null): string {
  if (!at) return "";
  const seconds = Math.max(0, Math.round((Date.now() - at) / 1000));
  if (seconds < 10) return "just now";
  if (seconds < 60) return `${seconds}s ago`;
  const minutes = Math.round(seconds / 60);
  if (minutes < 60) return `${minutes}m ago`;
  const hours = Math.round(minutes / 60);
  if (hours < 24) return `${hours}h ago`;
  return `${Math.round(hours / 24)}d ago`;
}

I wanted to know exactly what this can say, so I enumerated it rather than reading it.

The vocabulary

Output Reachable values Count
"" timestamp is null 1
just now 0 to 9 seconds 1
Ns ago N = 10 to 59 50
Nm ago N = 1 to 59 59
Nh ago N = 1 to 23 23
Nd ago N = 1 upwards unbounded

So 134 distinct strings before the day branch, which is where it stops being enumerable. Three strings that look like they belong in that table are not in it:

  • 60s ago cannot happen. At 60 seconds the seconds branch has already been passed and the minutes branch takes over.
  • 60m ago cannot happen, for the same reason.
  • 24h ago cannot happen, same again.

Fine so far. Now the other function in the same file, the one that counts down to a search's next attempt rather than up from its last one:

/** "in 45s", "in 3m". */
export function countdown(until: number): string {
  const ms = until - Date.now();
  if (ms <= 0) return "any moment";
  if (ms < 60_000) return `in ${Math.max(1, Math.round(ms / 1000))}s`;
  return `in ${Math.round(ms / 60_000)}m`;
}

That one can say in 60s. The guard is in milliseconds and the rounding is in seconds, so anything from 59,500 ms to 59,999 ms passes the < 60_000 test and then rounds to 60. Two functions in one 28-line file, written on the same afternoon, and they disagree about whether sixty of a unit is a thing you are allowed to say. One of them has a boundary expressed in the unit it prints and the other does not.

Neither is a bug a user will ever report. Both are the kind of thing that only becomes visible when you stop reading the code and start listing its outputs.

Every boundary rounds against you

The more interesting property is the choice of Math.round over Math.floor, which appears four times in those nine lines.

Elapsed time rounds to nearest, so:

  • A listing found 90 seconds ago reads 2m ago.
  • A search checked 1 hour 31 minutes ago reads 2h ago.
  • A find from 23 hours and 30 minutes ago reads 1d ago, half an hour before a day has passed.

Every one of those is the older of the two available answers. For a product whose entire pitch is that you hear about a room first, the clock in its own window is biased toward telling you that you are late. And the countdown rounds the same way, which makes the wait before the next attempt read longer than it is.

The right answer is different for the two directions, and it is not "round to nearest" in either:

  • Elapsed time should floor. Never tell somebody a thing is older than it is. At 90 seconds, 1m ago is true and 2m ago is not.
  • A countdown should ceil. Never promise something sooner than it can happen. in 60s at 59.6 seconds is honest; in 1m would be too, and in 59s would be a small lie.

That is a four-character change in four places, and the reason I have not shipped it yet is the one below.

The clock does not tick at the resolution it prints

The strings are rendered by three components, and because this is React, each one needs something to force a re-render as time passes. That is a twelve-line hook I have written about before, in three clocks in one window at 1s, 5s and 30s. Here is what each call site renders against the vocabulary above:

Component Re-renders every Finest unit it can print
SitesList 1s 1s
MonitorCard 5s 1s
RecentFinds 30s 1s

Only the first row is coherent. The second prints a string that changes every second while being re-rendered every five, so a row that says checked 12s ago is showing you a number that was true some time in the last five seconds. The third is the one that bothers me: the recent finds list prints seconds for the first minute of a listing's life, and repaints twice a minute.

Which means just now, a string with a ten-second window, is rendered by a component that only looks at the clock every thirty seconds. A listing that arrives at the wrong moment never says just now at all. One that arrives at the right moment says just now for the better part of half a minute, by which point it is wrong.

None of the three intervals is a mistake on its own. A finds list that re-renders every second to keep a timestamp fresh is wasteful for a window that sits in the background all day, and 30 seconds is also the polling cadence. The mistake is that the interval was chosen per component and the vocabulary was chosen in one shared file, and nothing connects them. The fix is to pick the tick from the age being displayed rather than per component: a row showing seconds ticks at a second, a row showing hours can tick at a minute.

Why show an age at all

Worth saying, because the alternative is to show nothing.

A monitor that is working looks exactly like a monitor that has silently stopped. Both are a window with a list in it and no new listings. The whole value of printing checked 8s ago next to every row is that a stale number is the one symptom of a dead poll loop that a user can see without opening a log, and the app's log, like most desktop logs, is somewhere nobody is going to look.

The same goes for the finds list, which is a 200-entry ring buffer on disk rather than an in-memory list, one of four caps on our local data. It survives a restart, so the day branch of that formatter is genuinely reachable: open the app on Monday and the bottom of the list is last week. An age is the only thing that distinguishes "three listings this morning" from "three listings, and the newest one is four days old, and you should check whether this search still points at anything".

Twenty-eight lines, 134 strings, three refresh rates, one rounding direction that is wrong in both directions. The app it lives in is on /download, and what it does with your machine while it is open is described on /help.

title: Building Armaxcoin: An Open-Source Proof-of-Work Blockchain Written in Go
description:
Building a blockchain from scratch is a challenging engineering exercise. It involves much more than implementing a Proof-of-Work algorithm. Consensus rules, peer-to-peer networking, cryptographic security, difficulty adjustment, and network reliability must all work together.

Armaxcoin is an independent, open-source experimental Layer-1 Proof-of-Work blockchain written in Go.

The project is currently operating a public Testnet and exploring custom consensus engineering, post-quantum transaction signatures, and decentralized infrastructure designed to run across commodity computers and ARM-based devices.

With the release of v1.0.10, Armaxcoin introduces an important Testnet consensus upgrade: Armax-ASERT-AW.

GitHub: https://github.com/acxxcxx/armax-coin

1. Project Overview

Armaxcoin is designed as an independent blockchain implementation with an emphasis on:

  • Custom Proof-of-Work engineering.
  • Decentralized peer-to-peer networking.
  • Adaptive difficulty adjustment.
  • Post-quantum transaction signatures.
  • Cross-platform node and mining support.
  • Transparent open-source development.

The project is written in Go and provides separate binaries for node operation, mining, wallet management, and transaction submission.

2. Consensus Engineering: Armax-ASERT-AW

One of the major developments in v1.0.10 is the introduction of Armax-ASERT-AW as the active Testnet difficulty adjustment mechanism.

The upgrade activates at block #13,335.

Its design incorporates:

ASERT Difficulty Adjustment

The canonical integer aserti3-2d algorithm is used with a one-hour half-life parameter (τ = 3600 seconds).

Four-Hour Surge Cap

A 14,400-second surge cap is implemented to constrain rapid difficulty increases.

TEDR Boost

A 7,200-second TEDR Boost mechanism supports recovery following substantial hashrate declines.

Anti-Poisoning Fallback

The implementation includes a fallback mechanism designed to protect the difficulty adjustment anchor against abnormal historical data.

The Testnet also introduced an earlier Anti-Stall TEDR mechanism at block #13,293, providing an emergency difficulty adjustment when block production stalls.

These mechanisms are being evaluated under actual Testnet operating conditions.

3. Proof-of-Work: ArmaxHash v2

Armaxcoin explores a custom Proof-of-Work algorithm called ArmaxHash.

The active Testnet implementation uses ArmaxHash v2, based on a BLAKE2b Stream-Fast design.

The Testnet has also preserved historical algorithm transitions:

  • SHA-256d during the initial period.
  • ArmaxHash v1 during an intermediate period.
  • ArmaxHash v2 in the current mining era.

The target block interval is 120 seconds.

An important part of this engineering effort is evaluating mining behavior across different hardware configurations, including conventional PCs and ARM-based devices.

4. Post-Quantum Transaction Signatures

Another important technical direction is post-quantum cryptography.

Armaxcoin uses ML-DSA-65, standardized under NIST FIPS 204, for transaction signatures.

The objective is to explore transaction authentication using a signature scheme designed to resist attacks from cryptographically relevant quantum computers.

However, it is important to distinguish signature security from Proof-of-Work security.

The project's hashing algorithms have different quantum security considerations. Post-quantum signatures do not automatically make every component of a blockchain quantum-proof.

Independent cryptographic and implementation audits remain necessary.

5. Network Architecture and Infrastructure

Armaxcoin includes several components:

  • armcoind — Full node daemon.
  • armminer — Standalone CPU miner.
  • armwallet — Wallet and keystore management.
  • armsend — Transaction submission.
  • armgui — Graphical wallet interface.

The network uses peer-to-peer communication protected by TLS 1.3, with a Trust On First Use (TOFU) certificate-pinning approach.

The node RPC interface is restricted to loopback by default.

The project also supports Linux, Windows, and ARM-based environments.

6. Public Testnet: Real-World Testing

Armaxcoin currently operates its public Testnet under the network identifier:

ARMX-TESTNET-1

The Testnet is intended for evaluating:

  • Block synchronization.
  • Peer discovery and networking.
  • Mining stability.
  • Difficulty adjustment behavior.
  • Transaction propagation.
  • Network interoperability.
  • Performance across different hardware.

The latest release, v1.0.10, introduces additional consensus and network improvements.

Important: All Testnet coins (tARMX) have no monetary value, no market liquidity, and no guaranteed conversion into future Mainnet coins.

7. Mainnet Status and Development Roadmap

Armaxcoin is currently operating on a public Testnet. Mainnet has not been launched.

The Mainnet configuration (ARMX-MAINNET-1) remains explicitly locked in the source code through core.MainnetLaunched = false.

The project preserves the following proposed monetary parameters:

Maximum supply: 126,000,000 ARMX.

Initial block subsidy: 60 ARMX.

Halving interval: 1,050,000 blocks.

Target block interval: 120 seconds.

Mainnet launch remains subject to further network stabilization, technical validation, security assessment, and completion of the project's readiness requirements.

Detailed tokenomics, mining allocation plans, and Mainnet preparation policies are documented in the official GitHub repository.

We believe that transparency, independent review, and careful testing are essential before launching a public blockchain network.

8. Security and Known Limitations

We believe transparency about limitations is essential for an experimental blockchain project.

Current considerations include:

  • The Testnet has relatively modest hashrate and may experience temporary chain reorganizations.
  • TOFU certificate pinning does not fully prevent man-in-the-middle attacks during initial peer contact.
  • ML-DSA-65 verification introduces computational overhead, particularly on low-power ARM hardware.
  • Consensus and cryptographic implementations still require independent external security assessment.

We welcome technical criticism and responsible security reviews.

9. Explore and Run Armaxcoin

The project is open source under the MIT License.

Official Repository:

https://github.com/acxxcxx/armax-coin

Latest Release:

https://github.com/acxxcxx/armax-coin/releases/tag/v1.0.10

Documentation:

  • Testnet Guide: docs/TESTNET.md
  • Consensus Specification: docs/CONSENSUS_AND_NETWORK.md
  • Mining Guide: docs/MINING_GUIDE.md
  • Node Operations: docs/NODE_OPERATIONS.md
  • Security Policy: SECURITY.md
  • Contribution Guidelines: CONTRIBUTING.md

For Linux users, the latest release provides precompiled binaries. Developers can also build from source using Go 1.27 or higher.

Please follow the official release verification instructions before running binaries.

10. We Welcome Independent Technical Feedback

Armaxcoin is an ongoing engineering project, and we believe independent feedback is essential to improving its design.

We welcome participation from:

  • Go developers.
  • Blockchain engineers.
  • Distributed systems researchers.
  • Cryptography researchers.
  • Proof-of-Work and mining enthusiasts.
  • Open-source contributors.

We are particularly interested in independent reviews of:

  1. Armax-ASERT-AW difficulty adjustment.
  2. ArmaxHash v2 implementation.
  3. P2P networking and synchronization.
  4. ML-DSA-65 integration.
  5. Overall consensus security and reorganization behavior.

Our goal is not simply to launch another cryptocurrency. It is to build, test, document, and improve an independent open-source blockchain implementation through transparent engineering and community review.

If you are interested in exploring the project, reviewing the source code, or participating in Testnet development, we welcome your feedback.

GitHub: https://github.com/acxxcxx/armax-coin

Thank you for your time.

title: Query Single Record In JooqTemplate
description:
Using JooqTemplate requires no code generation and no XML configuration.

Add Dependency

gradle:

implementation 'net.sf.sprtool:sprtool-jooq:1.7.0'

maven:

<dependency>
    <groupId>net.sf.sprtool</groupId>
    <artifactId>sprtool-jooq</artifactId>
    <version>1.7.0</version>
</dependency>

Inject JooqTemplate 

import net.sf.sprtool.jooq.JooqTemplate;

@Autowired
private JooqTemplate jt;

// Inject JooqMapperTemplate when using RecordMapper for custom mapping
import net.sf.sprtool.jooq.JooqMapperTemplate;

@Autowired
private JooqMapperTemplate jmt;

Using JooqTemplate

v Methods (Recommended, More Concise)

The v-suffixed loadv / loadRecordv / loadLowerCaseRecordv pass conditions and ordering directly as varargs, with operators embedded in field names — no need to build jOOQ Condition objects. This is the most concise style:

// Conditions as field-value pairs; the default operator is ==
UserEntity user = jt.loadv("user_table", UserEntity.class, "name", "John");

// Mixed conditions and ordering: name like '%Lee%' and dept_id = 2, ordered by id ascending
UserEntity r = jt.loadv("user_table", UserEntity.class,
        "name%", "Lee", "dept_id", 2, "id:asc");

// Record / LowerCaseRecord versions
Record record = jt.loadRecordv("product", "name", "Smartphone");
LowerCaseRecord lr = jt.loadLowerCaseRecordv("product", "name", "Smartphone", "id:asc");
String name = lr.get("name");

// The first argument also accepts a Table object
UserEntity u = jt.loadv(DSL.table("user_table"), UserEntity.class, "id", 1);

The following sections describe the equivalent Condition-style usage for side-by-side reference.

Map to a Java Bean

load(table, Class, condition) maps the query result to a Java Bean; snake_case database columns (e.g. nick_name) are automatically mapped to camelCase properties (nickName). Returns null when no record matches, and the first record when multiple match:

import org.jooq.Condition;
import org.jooq.impl.DSL;

Condition condition = DSL.field("name").eq("Smartphone");

Product product = jt.load("product", Product.class, condition);
// product.getName() / product.getNickName() ... mapped automatically

// Complex condition: name = 'xxx' and nick_name = 'xxx'
Condition complex = DSL.field("name").eq("Lee")
        .and(DSL.field("nick_name").eq("Big Lee"));
UserEntity user = jt.load("user_table", UserEntity.class, complex);

Load a Single Field Value

Combined with JooqFields.SL(...) to select a single field, the value is loaded directly as a String / Integer or similar type:

import net.sf.sprtool.jooq.JooqFields;

String name = jt.load("user_table", String.class, JooqFields.SL("name"), condition);
Integer id = jt.load("user_table", Integer.class, JooqFields.SL("id"), condition);

Map to a Record

loadRecord(table, condition) returns a native jOOQ Record; read values by type with get(fieldName, type):

import org.jooq.Record;

Record record = jt.loadRecord("user_table", condition);
String name = record.get("name", String.class);
Integer id = record.get("id", Integer.class);

Map to a LowerCaseRecord

loadLowerCaseRecord(table, condition) returns a LowerCaseRecord with case-insensitive field names; get needs no type argument, and you can also call intoMap() to convert it to a Map or containsKey to check whether a field exists:

import net.sf.sprtool.jooq.LowerCaseRecord;

LowerCaseRecord record = jt.loadLowerCaseRecord("user_table", condition);
String name = record.get("name");

// Use it as a Map
Map<String, Object> map = record.intoMap();
assertTrue(map.containsKey("name"));
assertFalse(map.containsKey("nonexistent_field"));

Use TableLike Objects

The first argument likewise accepts TableLike / Table objects built with DSL.table(...):

TableLike<?> userTable = DSL.table("user_table");

UserEntity user = jt.load(userTable, UserEntity.class, condition);
Record record = jt.loadRecord(userTable, condition);
LowerCaseRecord lr = jt.loadLowerCaseRecord(userTable, condition);

Behavior Notes

  • No matching record: load / loadRecord / loadLowerCaseRecord all return null.
  • Multiple matches: the first record is returned.
  • null Condition: passing null to the TableLike variants does not throw (equivalent to an unconditional query); however, an incomplete field-value pair such as jt.and("id") throws an IllegalArgumentException inside and().
  • Table does not exist: an exception is thrown, and its message includes the table name.

title: Operators in Java
description:
What is Operator?

  • Operators are used to perform a operation on operands.

Types of Operators:

  • Arithmetic Operator
  • Assignment Operator
  • Relational Operator
  • Logical Operator
  • Unary Operator
  • Ternary Operator
  • Shift Operator
  • Bitwise Operator

Arithmetic Operator:

Operator Description
+ Addition
- Subtraction
* Multiplication
/ Division
% Modulus (Remainder) 
class Arithmetic
{

public static void main (String[] args)
{

int a=100;
int b=20;

System.out.println("Addition:"+(a+b));
System.out.println("Sub:"+(a-b));
System.out.println("Multiply:"+(a*b));
System.out.println("Divide:"+(a/b));
System.out.println("Modulo:"+(a%b));

}

}

Addition:120
Sub:80
Multiply:2000
Divide:5
Modulo:0

Assignment Operator:

  • Used to assign values to a variable.
Operator Example
= a = 10
+= a += 5
-= a -= 5
*= a *= 5
/= a /= 5
%= a %= 5 
class Assignment
{

public static void main (String[] args)
{

int a;
System.out.println("Assigning:"+(a = 10));
System.out.println("Add:"+(a += 20));
System.out.println("Sub:"+(a -= 10));
System.out.println("Multiply:"+(a *= 10));
System.out.println("Divide:"+(a /= 10));
System.out.println("Modulo:"+(a %= 3));

}
}


Assigning:10
Add:30
Sub:20
Multiply:200
Divide:20
Modulo:2

Relational Operator:

  • Used to compare two values.
Operator Meaning
== Equal to
!= Not Equal to
> Greater Than
< Less Than
>= Greater Than or Equal
<= Less Than or Equal 
class Relational
{

public static void main (String[] args)
{

int a=10;
int b=30;

System.out.println("Equal to:"+(a == b));
System.out.println("Not Equal to:"+(a != 20));
System.out.println("Greater than:"+(a > b));
System.out.println("Less than:"+(a<b));
System.out.println("Greater than or Equal to:"+(a >= b));
System.out.println("Greater than or Equal to:"+(a <= b));

}

}

Equal to:false
Not Equal to:true
Greater than:false
Less than:true
Greater than or Equal to:false
Greater than or Equal to:true

Logical Operator: 


class Logical
{

public static void main (String[] args)
{

int a=10;
int b=30;

System.out.println("AND:"+((a > b) && (a != 20)));
System.out.println("OR:"+((a == 20) || (b>a)));
System.out.println("NOT:"+(a != b));
}

}

AND:false
OR:true
NOT:true

Unary Operator:

Operator Meaning
+ Unary Plus
- Unary Minus
++ Increment
-- Decrement
! Logical NOT 
class Unary
{

public static void main (String[] args)
{

int a=10;
int b=30;

System.out.println("Unary Plus:"+(a+b));
System.out.println("Unary Minus:"+(a-b));
System.out.println("Increment:"+(++a));
System.out.println("Decrement:"+(a--));
System.out.println("Logical Not:"+(!true));
}

}


Unary Plus:40
Unary Minus:-20
Increment:11
Decrement:11
Logical Not:false

Ternary Operator:

A shortcut for if-else.

Syntax

condition ? value1 : value2;

class Ternary
{

public static void main (String[] args)
{

int a=10;
int b=30;

String result = (a>b ? "A is Larger" : "B is Larger");

System.out.println("Which number is Larger?"+result);
}

}

Which number is Larger? B is Larger

title: Grafana Mimir Prometheus metrics storage: a practical guide
description:
Grafana Mimir Prometheus metrics storage: the grafana/mimir repository holds a Go project that acts as long-term, multi-tenant, scalable storage for Prometheus metrics. Its README describes it as scalable long-term storage for Prometheus. It is released under the GNU AGPL v3 (AGPL-3.0-only), which matters before you embed it in a product.

The problem is a familiar one. A single Prometheus keeps its data locally, for a limited period, and gives no global view once you run ten of them. Mimir receives the samples from all your Prometheus servers, stores them in object storage and answers PromQL queries. How is it built, how do you start it, and how do you monitor it?

A note on honesty: span.observer has not installed or run Mimir. The commands come from the README, from the repository’s docs/ folder and from the grafana.com/docs/mimir pages, read on 7 November 2026. The screenshots reproduce files and one image from the repository. The star count shown on the repository page was about 5.3k that day, with no exact value re-read from the GitHub API, which was not reachable.

Grafana Mimir Prometheus metrics storage: what the repository says

  • Licence: the LICENSE file holds the GNU Affero General Public License version 3. According to LICENSING.md, only vendor/ and operations/ fall under upstream licences, whose text is shipped. The AGPL preamble describes it as designed for network server software: have a lawyer review your use.
  • Version: the VERSION file and the latest published CHANGELOG section both say 3.2.4. We could not re-read the release date, so we do not quote it. The « main / unreleased » section lists many changes, including removed options, marked [CHANGE].
  • Project claims: the README states that internal testing shows up to 1 billion active series. That is the project’s claim, and we have not measured it.
  • Object storage: according to the documentation, blocks go to Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Storage, OpenStack Swift, or the local filesystem (single node only).

Component architecture and multi-tenancy

Mimir is made of microservices called components: distributor, ingester, query-frontend, querier, store-gateway, compactor, ruler and alertmanager, among others. The code of every component compiles into a single binary, and the -target parameter picks its role. Two modes exist: monolithic (-target=all, everything in one process) and microservices, which is recommended for production.

Since version 3.0, two architectures coexist. The « ingest storage » architecture, preferred by the documentation, uses Kafka to decouple reads from writes. The classic architecture uses ingesters with a local write-ahead log.

The storage format follows Prometheus TSDB: each tenant has its own blocks, two hours long by default. Every HTTP request carries the tenant ID in the X-Scope-OrgID header. Mimir does not authenticate callers: a reverse proxy must do it and inject the header.

Installing Mimir step by step, as documented

Step 1: get Mimir 

docker pull grafana/mimir:latest
# or a local binary (Linux amd64)
curl -fLo mimir https://github.com/grafana/mimir/releases/latest/download/mimir-linux-amd64
chmod +x mimir

Step 2: write the demo configuration

The « Get started » guide gives a demo.yaml file for monolithic mode with local disk storage. Its header says not to use it in production. The first screenshot reproduces it, together with the Prometheus configuration from the same page.

Step 3: start Mimir and connect Prometheus 

./mimir --config.file=./demo.yaml

Mimir listens on port 9009. Then add the remote_write block from the screenshot to Prometheus and restart it. With Grafana Alloy, the prometheus.remote_write component sends to the same address. The guide also notes that Mimir can report anonymous usage statistics, and the documentation explains how to opt out.

Step 4: query with PromQL

In Grafana, add a Prometheus data source with the URL http://localhost:9009/prometheus (local binary). Without Grafana, the HTTP API table gives the instant query endpoint as GET,POST <prometheus-http-prefix>/api/v1/query. The command below is derived from it: we have not run it.

curl -G http://localhost:9009/prometheus/api/v1/query \
  --data-urlencode 'query=up'
# with multitenancy_enabled: true, add
#   -H 'X-Scope-OrgID: tenant-1'

To check that it works, the guide ends as follows: query the metrics in Grafana Explore and build a panel on the new data source. An up series for the prometheus job should appear.

OpenTelemetry: OTLP ingestion

Mimir also accepts OTLP over HTTP: the entry point is POST /otlp/v1/metrics. The Collector page recommends OTLP over remote write. It gives the otlphttp exporter with the address http://<mimir-endpoint>/otlp, or prometheusremotewrite towards /api/v1/push. The next screenshot reproduces the example with basic authentication, plus per-tenant retention.

Three points from the format page deserve attention. Dots in names are converted to _. Resource attributes go into the target_info series, except job and instance, which come from service.name and service.instance.id. OpenTelemetry exponential histograms are rejected by default until native histograms are enabled. For context, see the Collector contrib components and OpenTelemetry versus Prometheus.

Limits and open points

  • Complexity: microservices mode multiplies components, and the ingest storage architecture adds Kafka. Monolithic mode suits a first try, but the documentation advises against it at large scale.
  • Disks: the documentation advises against NFS, EFS and network filesystems for components that write locally, and recommends SSDs (risk of crashes or silent corruption).
  • Retention: by default, nothing is deleted. Set compactor_blocks_retention_period. Per-series deletion is not supported.
  • Security: there is no built-in authentication, so a reverse proxy is mandatory.
  • Fast change: the « unreleased » CHANGELOG removes some options and renames others. Read the notes before each upgrade.
  • Licence: the AGPL imposes obligations if you modify the software and offer it as a network service.

Observing Mimir itself

Mimir exposes its Prometheus metrics on /metrics. The repository ships a « mixin »: in operations/mimir-mixin-compiled/, 27 JSON dashboard files, rules.yaml (recording rules) and alerts.yaml (127 alert: entries on 7 November 2026, since one name can appear at several severity levels). Among them: MimirIngesterUnhealthy, MimirRequestErrors and MimirRequestLatency. Every alert carries a runbook_url.

The screenshot below shows the « Mimir / Overview » dashboard published in the repository’s documentation: cluster health, writes, reads, rules and object storage. The cluster and namespace names visible in it come from the example.

Source : github.com

To install it, import the JSON files into Grafana and load the rules and alerts into Prometheus, or run make build-mixin after adapting operations/mimir-mixin/config.libsonnet. The dashboards require the labels cluster, namespace, job, pod and instance on the collected metrics. In monolithic mode, job is <namespace>/mimir. The scrape interval must stay at 1 minute or less for the precompiled rules.

Since Mimir is the storage link, watch the error rate and write latency first, then the health of the ring and of object storage: a failed write means gaps in your SLIs. Name recording rules methodically: see Prometheus recording rules. Keep an eye on cardinality, covered in Kubernetes metrics cardinality.

What about Dynatrace?

Mimir documents no Dynatrace integration, and we do not invent one. For Prometheus metrics ingestion on the Dynatrace side, read Prometheus and Dynatrace on Kubernetes: the setup belongs to the matching Dynatrace documentation.

Best practices

  • Start in monolithic mode on a test machine, and never use demo.yaml in production.
  • Put an authenticating reverse proxy in front of Mimir and let it set X-Scope-OrgID.
  • Set retention from the start, per tenant if needed.
  • Install the mixin before going live, with the right labels.
  • Deploy Mimir through GitOps, as in Argo CD for Kubernetes, and record the versions.

Frequently asked questions

Does Mimir replace Prometheus?

No. Prometheus collects the metrics, and Mimir stores them long term and answers queries. Prometheus (or Grafana Alloy) sends to Mimir by remote write, and the OpenTelemetry Collector by OTLP.

Do you need Kubernetes to use Mimir?

Not to get started: a binary or a Docker container is enough in monolithic mode. The documentation also covers a Helm chart, and the dashboards assume Kubernetes unless you set deployment_type: 'baremetal' before compiling them.

How do you separate teams in Mimir?

By tenant: each team uses its own ID in X-Scope-OrgID, with its own limits and retention. The -tenant-federation.enabled=true option allows querying several tenants, separated by |.

Conclusion

Grafana Mimir answers a precise need: keeping the metrics of many Prometheus servers for a long time, with a global view and per-tenant separation. It takes more operating effort than a single Prometheus and an AGPL review, but it ships its own dashboards and alerts. Try monolithic mode on a test machine before you decide.

title: You Watched Five People Try Your Feature and Most of Them Could Not Find It
description:
Your team finally ran a usability session. Five people from outside the team were asked to complete a task using the new feature you built, while you watched quietly on a call. Three of them never found the button. One found it and then did not trust what it did. Only one finished without help.

You spent six weeks on that feature. Watching it fail in silence is one of the hardest kinds of feedback to receive, because nobody is saying anything critical. They are just struggling, and you cannot help.

That is exactly why it is so valuable. Every other kind of feedback on your work is somebody's opinion. This is behaviour. Nobody was being polite, nobody was guessing what users might do, and nobody had read the design document first.

Resist the first reaction, which is to explain. They should have looked at the menu. They were not our target users. The tooltip covers it. Some of that may be true, but if three people out of five missed it, the next three hundred will as well. The usability researcher Jakob Nielsen has long argued that a handful of test users finds most of the obvious problems, which is why five people can tell you so much.

Instead, go back through the recordings or your notes and write down the exact moments people hesitated. Where did their mouse go first? What did they say out loud while they looked? Which words on the screen did they read, and which did they skip? Those moments are your list of fixes, and they are far more precise than anything a reviewer could have written.

Then separate the problems from the solutions. Users are excellent at showing you where something is wrong and much less reliable at telling you how to fix it. If one participant says just make the button red, note that they could not see it, and then decide with your designer how to make it findable.

Finally, thank the team for running the session, and ask to watch the next one before you build anything. The cheapest time to learn this lesson is before six weeks of work.

– Asael Shinder

title: CortexDB: agent memory and a knowledge graph in one SQLite file
description:
CortexDB

Agent memory usually means a service to run, a vector store to pay for, and facts that go stale without anyone noticing. CortexDB takes the opposite route. It is a pure Go database that puts agent memory and a knowledge graph in one SQLite file, with vectors, RAG, RDF and SPARQL, Cypher, and more than 100 MCP tools, and it works with no embedding model. An optional Claude Code mod writes memories 90 seconds after a session goes idle, and when a new fact contradicts an old one, the old one is kept as superseded instead of being deleted. Version 2.149.0 is the latest release, and the repo now has 480 stars under the MIT license.

What you get:

  • Agent memory and a knowledge graph in a single SQLite file, no service to run and no vector store to pay for
  • Vectors, hybrid and graph retrieval, plus RDF with SPARQL and read-only Cypher
  • More than 100 MCP tools, in-process or over MCP, with Claude Code and Codex plugins
  • A 90-second idle capture in the optional Claude Code mod, so session facts become durable memories on their own
  • Contradicted facts marked superseded and kept, never silently deleted, with a full history of what changed and why
  • Install as a Go library with go get github.com/liliang-cn/cortexdb/v2, or add the plugin to Claude Code or Codex

Try it on a side project first, and read back what it remembers before you trust it with anything you cannot afford to lose.

Repo: https://github.com/liliang-cn/cortexdb

Quick poll

What would you use CortexDB for first?

  • Giving Claude Code a memory that survives between sessions
  • Replacing a hosted vector store with one SQLite file
  • Querying agent memory with SPARQL or Cypher
  • Watching it for now

Vote in the comments.

If you found CortexDB interesting, I write about tools like this every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.
