title: CSS corner-shape: squircles, scoops and notches
description:
This note has an interactive demo. Try it in the original

Since it arrived, border-radius has given us exactly one kind of corner: a quarter of an ellipse. corner-shape changes that. You keep border-radius for the size of the corner and add one property for its shape: squircle, bevel, scoop, notch, or anything in between. Borders, outlines and shadows follow the new outline, and the browser can animate from one shape to another.

Play with the demo above first. Press the chips, drag the K slider, then hit "Morph between shapes". Watch the teal border and the glow: they're not a separate layer, they bend with the box.

Size from border-radius, shape from corner-shape

The property doesn't replace border-radius, it builds on it. MDN puts it plainly: "If a border-radius is not applied to a container, or the border-radius resolves to 0, corner-shape will have no effect."

.card {
  border-radius: 56px;   /* how big the corner is */
  corner-shape: scoop;   /* what the corner looks like */
}

That's the whole of the demo's main shape. The keywords are:

  • square = superellipse(infinity): a normal square corner.
  • squircle = superellipse(2): between round and square, the app-icon look.
  • round = superellipse(1): today's border-radius, and the initial value.
  • bevel = superellipse(0): a straight diagonal cut.
  • scoop = superellipse(-1): a concave quarter circle bitten out.
  • notch = superellipse(-infinity): a concave 90° step.

Because the initial value is round, adding corner-shape to an existing design changes nothing until you pick another shape.

What superellipse(K) really means

Every keyword is a point on one continuous scale. The spec defines superellipse(K) as a quarter of a superellipse "using an exponent of 2^K". A superellipse is the curve |x|^n + |y|^n = 1:

  • With K = 1, n = 2 and you get a circle: round.
  • With K = 2, n = 4: the flatter-sided squircle.
  • With K = 0, n = 1: a straight line, bevel.
  • Negative K mirrors the curve inwards, so superellipse(-1) is a concave circle, scoop.

That's what the small corner plot in the demo draws. It's the same formula I use in the fallback (more on that below): each corner is sampled from the parametric superellipse x = cos(t)^(2/n), y = sin(t)^(2/n) and mirrored inwards when K is negative.

You can also mix shapes per corner, with the same clockwise order as border-radius (top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left):

.launch {
  border-radius: 14px 0;  /* only top-left and bottom-right */
  corner-shape: notch;
}

.tag {
  border-radius: 0 32px 32px 0;
  corner-shape: bevel;    /* the right side becomes an arrow */
}

Those are two of the four small pieces at the bottom of the demo. There are longhands too: corner-top-left-shape, logical ones like corner-start-start-shape, and per-side shorthands like corner-top-shape.

Borders, shadows and animation come with it

This is what makes it more than a clip-path trick. According to MDN, background, border, outline, box-shadow, overflow and backdrop-filter all follow the corner shape. A clip-path just cuts pixels away, so a border gets sliced and a shadow disappears.

There's one nuance in the spec: the inner edge of the border follows the outer curve at a nearly constant distance, but box-shadow doesn't trace the path exactly. It "scales the corner-shape path in an axis-aligned manner". With big spreads you may see a small difference.

It also animates:

.card {
  transition: corner-shape .9s cubic-bezier(.3, .8, .2, 1);
}

The browser interpolates the K parameter, not the keyword. The spec doesn't move K linearly, though. Going from bevel (0) to round (1) to square (infinity) linearly would start fast and crawl at the end, so the spec maps K onto a 0–1 scale first. I checked it in Chromium: 400 ms into a one-second linear transition from round to notch, getComputedStyle reports superellipse(-0.327908), a real in-between shape rather than a jump.

Browser support and gotchas

  • Only Chromium so far. The Chrome 139 release notes list "Corner shaping (corner-shape, superellipse, squircle)", and webstatus.dev shows it in Chrome and Edge since August 2025. Firefox and Safari don't have it yet, so it's far from Baseline.
  • The fallback is free if round is acceptable. In a browser without support, corner-shape is ignored and border-radius still draws round corners. For a squircle button that's a perfectly fine degradation.
  • Concave shapes need a plan B. If your design depends on a scoop or notch (a ticket, a sci-fi frame), round corners aren't the same thing. Detect support with @supports (corner-shape: squircle) or CSS.supports('corner-shape', 'squircle'). The demo then computes the same superellipse as a clip-path: polygon() and shows a notice. It's honest about the trade-off: in Firefox and Safari the shape is right, but the border and shadow no longer follow it, so the demo swaps the shadow for a drop-shadow() filter on a wrapper.
  • Opposite corners can collide. With large radii and concave shapes, MDN notes that "the browser constrains the values to prevent the overlap", so the result may be smaller than what you asked for.
  • Content isn't reshaped. Text and hover areas still belong to the rectangular box. Leave padding near notched or scooped corners.

What to keep an eye on

  • Whether Firefox and Safari pick up corner-shape. Until they do, use it as an enhancement on top of border-radius.
  • The rest of CSS Borders Level 4, where this lives. It's an Editor's Draft that also covers border-shape and partial borders, so details may still change.
  • Design tools exporting squircles. Since superellipse() takes any number, a design system can now name its exact corner curve in CSS instead of shipping an SVG mask.

Sources

  • corner-shape - CSS | MDN
  • CSS Borders and Box Decorations Module Level 4 (Editor's Draft)
  • Chrome 139 release notes | Chrome for Developers
  • corner-shape | Web Platform Status

Originally published at richi.codes.

title: Gradle Under the Hood: Designing a Federated Plugin Architecture for Diverse JPA Providers
description:
Over the first three articles of our Gradle Under the Hood series, we explored incremental source tracking, network-immune classloader harvesting, and compile-only dependency isolation.

Today, in the grand finale of this series, we tackle our biggest architectural challenge: How do you build a cohesive build automation suite that supports three completely different object-relational mapping (ORM) frameworks—Hibernate, EclipseLink, and Apache OpenJPA—without creating a monolithic, tightly-coupled mess of conflicting dependencies?

Let's dive into how we designed a Federated Plugin Architecture in JPersist to orchestrate specialized bytecode transformations while isolating complex provider-specific execution graphs.

The Ecosystem Fragmentation Trap

Compile-time bytecode modification is the holy grail of JPA performance. By weaving change-tracking or lazy-loading hooks directly into compiled .class binaries post-compilation, you eliminate the need for heavy runtime reflection proxies or fragile -javaagent startup flags.

However, each major persistence provider drives its enhancement engine through radically different internal APIs:

  • Hibernate relies on an intensive programmatic cycle (org.hibernate.bytecode.spi.Enhancer) requiring granular execution parameters.
  • EclipseLink uses an offline processor (StaticWeaveProcessor) that consumes raw file paths and streams metadata through explicit directory structures.
  • Apache OpenJPA uses a standalone CLI driver utility (PCEnhancer) driven by command-line arguments.

If you try to jam all three framework dependencies into a single, monolithic Gradle plugin, you create a dependency nightmare. Conflicting versions of bytecode manipulation libraries leak into the global Gradle build daemon classpath, causing silent build-time crashes and memory leaks.

The Solution: A Federated Plugin Architecture

To achieve clean separation of concerns, we designed a Federated Plugin Architecture. Instead of one monolithic plugin, JPersist provides a modular suite of specialized sibling plugins that users can apply independently depending on their stack:

  • io.github.jpersist.jpa (The Core Plugin)
  • io.github.jpersist.hibernate-persistence (The Hibernate Optimization Suite)
  • io.github.jpersist.openjpa-persistence (The Apache OpenJPA Suite)
  • io.github.jpersist.eclipse-persistence (The EclipseLink Static Weaving Plugin)

The core plugin acts as the orchestrator. It manages the central persistence {} DSL extension container, registers global configuration spaces like modelgenProcessor, and auto-discovers annotated entities via a high-speed, lightweight ASM scanner.

The sibling provider plugins then plug directly into this core infrastructure. They read configuration states from the central extension and register their own specialized, framework-native enhancement tasks.

Divergent Execution Strategies: Workers vs. Process Forks

Because the plugins are decoupled, we were free to engineer the exact execution strategy that best fits each framework's unique constraints, rather than forcing a one-size-fits-all model.

1. Hibernate: The ClassLoader-Isolated Worker SPI

Hibernate carries a dual-namespace problem: legacy projects still target the javax.persistence namespace (Hibernate 5), while modern ones target jakarta.persistence (Hibernate 6).

To manage this safely, the Hibernate plugin delegates bytecode transformation to a dedicated Service Provider Interface (SPI) module (persistence-tools-api) executing inside a hermetic Gradle Worker sandbox (classLoaderIsolation):

// Inside HibernateEnhancementPlugin.groovy (v1.8.1)
def enhanceTaskProvider = project.tasks.register(enhanceTaskName, HibernateEnhancementTask) { task ->
    task.jpaVersion.set(activeVersionProvider)

    // Wire the project's native compile classpath directly to satisfy legacy engines
    task.enhanceClasspath.from(enhanceConfigProvider)
    task.enhanceClasspath.from(JakartaPersistencePlugin.resolvePersistenceToolsFiles(project, activeVersionProvider))
    task.compileClasspath.from(sourceSet.compileClasspath)
}

The underlying EnhancementWorker uses Java's native ServiceLoader API inside the sandbox to dynamically discover the correct environment adapter matching the module's target JPA version.

2. EclipseLink & OpenJPA: Lightweight Java Exec Forks

Unlike Hibernate, EclipseLink and OpenJPA drive their weaving routines via standalone main-class CLI processors (StaticWeave and PCEnhancer). Running them inside the main Gradle daemon classpath would contaminate the environment.

Instead of writing complex worker code, our specialized tasks extend Gradle's built-in DefaultTask and use an injected ExecOperations service to fork a completely isolated, short-lived JVM process:

// Inside OpenJPAEnhanceTask.groovy (v1.8.1)
@TaskAction
void enhance() {
    // Stage raw compiled classes into the isolated target output directory first
    project.copy { spec ->
        spec.from(sourceClassesDir).into(targetClassesDir)
    }

    // Fork OpenJPA's PCEnhancer in a detached JVM process boundary
    execOperations.javaexec { spec ->
        spec.mainClass.set('org.apache.openjpa.enhance.PCEnhancer')
        spec.classpath = project.files(enhancerClasspath, compileClasspath, resourcesDir)
        spec.args('-directory', targetClassesDir.get().asFile.absolutePath, ...)
    }
}

This delivers optimal execution speeds. The heavy framework dependencies are loaded exclusively within a transient process fork, keeping the main Gradle daemon completely clean.

The Ultimate Engineering Victory

By adopting a federated plugin layout combined with tailored execution strategies, the JPersist Suite balances developer productivity with bulletproof build engineering:

  1. Absolute ClassLoader Safety: The Gradle daemon remains pristine. It never loads an internal class from Hibernate, EclipseLink, or OpenJPA into its root context, completely eliminating memory leaks and cross-plugin linkage errors.
  2. Tailored Performance: Heavy, namespace-shifting frameworks run inside classloader-isolated worker sandboxes, while CLI-driven frameworks execute via rapid process forks.
  3. Infinite Extensibility: Adding a new ORM provider or updating a framework version requires zero changes to the core plugin code. You simply release a new standalone sibling plugin that reads from the shared core extensions.

This wraps up our Gradle Under the Hood series! We built an automation platform that is blazing fast through source-driven incremental tracking, immune to network drops via ClassLoader harvesting, container-compliant through compile-only scopes, and beautifully modular through a federated plugin architecture.

How do you handle multi-framework automation or isolate conflicting dependency graphs inside your enterprise build engineering pipelines? Let's discuss in the comments below!

🔗 Explore the complete JPersist open-source architecture on GitHub: https://github.com/jpersist/persistence

title: Replacing Standard Go JSON with Low-Allocation Alternatives to Overcome Performance Bottlenecks in Large-Scale Systems
description:
The Performance Wall: Why encoding/json Stalls High-Throughput Pipelines

When data ingestion scales into millions of messages per second or gigabytes of continuous streams, Go's standard encoding/json hits a severe performance ceiling. This bottleneck is not an arbitrary design flaw in the standard library; it is the inevitable physical consequence of how general-purpose deserialization interacts with the Go runtime memory model, CPU cache lines, and garbage collection (GC) cycles.

The Hidden Cost of Runtime Reflection

Every invocation of standard unmarshaling forces the Go runtime to execute extensive dynamic inspection. Because encoding/json is built to handle arbitrary types, maps, and empty interfaces without prior schema knowledge, it relies heavily on runtime reflection via reflect.TypeOf and reflect.ValueOf during the parse cycle.

The causal chain of failure:

  • Impact: Incoming byte streams are scanned token by token while dynamically resolving struct field alignments and JSON tags.
  • Internal Process: This dynamic key lookup and type assertion generates thousands of tiny, ephemeral heap allocations for interface wrappers, map keys, and boxed primitives.
  • Observable Effect: The Go garbage collector is overwhelmed by pointer tracking across millions of short-lived objects. CPU worker threads spend cycles servicing GC sweep phases rather than application logic, causing dramatic latency spikes (p99 tail degradation) and CPU cache thrashing.

The All-or-Nothing Object Graph Allocation Model

Standard JSON parsers operate on an all-or-nothing allocation model. When reading massive files or network frames, encoding/json materializes the complete object graph in heap memory simultaneously. In high-performance systems backed by memory-mapped (mmap) files or zero-copy socket buffers, this behavior neutralizes low-level hardware optimizations.

An mmap buffer allows an application to read directly from kernel page caches with zero initial duplication. However, standard unmarshaling reads these bytes and duplicates every string and nested object into new, disjoint heap locations. This constant memory duplication saturates memory bandwidth and forces the CPU to constantly reload invalidated cache lines.

Decision Dominance: General-Purpose vs. Specialized Parsing

Engineering teams often default to encoding/json out of familiarity, misapplying a universal tool to domain-specific extremes. To eliminate performance bottlenecks, architects must apply strict criteria when choosing a parsing strategy:

  • Use encoding/json when: Handling low-frequency configuration files, handling small, sporadic HTTP request bodies, or dealing with highly dynamic, unstructured schemas where struct types cannot be known at compile time. Under these conditions, the development velocity of the standard library outweighs its allocation overhead.
  • Use pre-registered, low-allocation alternatives when: Processing high-throughput data streams, parsing large arrays from mmap storage, or operating within tight latency SLAs where garbage collection pauses threaten system stability. By shifting reflection to a one-time initialization phase and reusing struct registries, per-parse heap allocations drop toward zero.

The operational rule: If your data pipeline processes rigid schemas at high frequencies and your profiling data shows GC pressure or heap allocation dominating CPU profiles, standard general-purpose parsing is your primary bottleneck. Transitioning to specialized, buffer-reusing parsers is mandatory to restore deterministic performance.

Anatomy of SilentJSON: Engineering for Zero Allocations

When designing high-throughput data pipelines that ingest gigabytes of data from memory-mapped files, standard parsing models break down under the weight of their own abstractions. Go's native encoding/json relies on runtime reflection and an all-or-nothing heap allocation model, which forces the runtime to box primitives, instantiate maps, and generate thousands of ephemeral pointers per payload. This dynamic inspection saturates memory bandwidth, invalidates CPU cache lines, and triggers heavy Garbage Collector (GC) pointer-scanning cycles that degrade p99 tail latencies. SilentJSON circumvents these bottlenecks by shifting metadata extraction to a one-time initialization phase, utilizing pre-registered struct registries, and enforcing zero-copy string slicing over memory-mapped buffers.

Reflection Hoisting and Registry Reuse

The primary performance tax in standard JSON parsers stems from continuous type inspection. Every time encoding/json.Unmarshal encounters a field, it executes dynamic runtime reflection to resolve struct alignments, field offsets, and JSON tag mappings. Under high request concurrency, this constant heap-churn spawns millions of transient interface wrappers that the GC must continuously track, sweep, and compact, starving worker threads of CPU cycles.

SilentJSON solves this by decoupling metadata resolution from the parse loop via pre-compiled registries:

  • Static Registry Generation: The target struct layout is inspected exactly once during application startup using silentjson.BuildRegistry, compiling a flat, type-safe field map.
  • Per-Parse Elimination: During hot-path execution, parsing routines access pre-computed field offsets directly, reducing per-parse heap allocations to absolute zero.
  • Failure Mode and Trade-offs: Pre-compiled registries trade structural flexibility for raw execution speed. If a pipeline requires dynamic schemas or arbitrary map parsing, the registry approach fails because the memory layout cannot be statically bound, forcing a fallback to slower general-purpose parsers.

Zero-Copy Tokenization and Buffer Ownership Risks

For unescaped strings extracted from byte slices or memory-mapped buffers (mmap), SilentJSON bypasses string duplication by returning string slices that point directly to the underlying source memory. Instead of copying byte arrays into newly allocated heap segments—which causes cache line invalidation and memory bandwidth saturation—the parser constructs string headers pointing straight into the input buffer.

However, this performance optimization introduces severe memory management constraints:

  • Buffer Pinning Risk: Because zero-copy strings reference the original input buffer, retaining a single parsed string field in long-term application state forces the Go runtime to keep the entire underlying input block—potentially gigabytes of an mmap file—pinned in memory. The garbage collector cannot reclaim the surrounding segments.
  • Mutation Hazards: If the underlying input buffer is modified while zero-copy string views remain active, memory corruption occurs, manifesting as silent data corruption or unpredictable runtime panics.
  • Mitigation Rule: Developers must enforce strict lifecycle boundaries. If a parsed string must outlive the immediate scope of the parse operation, it must be explicitly cloned using strings.Clone to sever its pointer dependency on the input buffer.

Lazy Materialization via RawMessage

In massive telemetry or event-streaming pipelines, parsing every nested object indiscriminately wastes CPU cycles on data that the application never accesses. SilentJSON utilizes silentjson.RawMessage to defer deserialization of auxiliary fields:

By wrapping unparsed sub-fragments in a raw byte slice, the engine parses only the critical index keys (such as IDs and timestamps) on the hot path, leaving nested attributes untouched. When an operational branch actually requires the auxiliary data, a secondary targeted unmarshal runs locally. This lazy materialization prevents the unnecessary expansion of the object graph, preserving CPU cache locality and eliminating wasted heap allocations for cold-path data.

Streaming and Block-Based Pipeline Control

Loading complete multi-gigabyte JSON files into memory simultaneously saturates physical RAM and triggers violent GC sweeps. SilentJSON provides specialized streaming primitives—StreamDecoder and NextRawBlock—to govern data flow through bounded memory windows:
Strategy Mechanism Optimal Operating Condition Failure Condition
Sequential Stream Reuses a single allocated struct instance across sequential callback iterations, updating fields in-place. Linear processing of large files or network feeds where records can be handled immediately. Retaining references to the passed struct pointer outside the callback without deep-copying leads to data overwrites.
Raw Block Batching Extracts contiguous byte chunks containing N objects (stripped of outer array brackets) referencing internal buffers. Batch-oriented pipelines passing raw byte blocks directly to downstream workers or storage engines. Failing to process or copy the block before the next read operation overwrites the internal buffer window.
Parallel Array Unmarshaling Partitions large in-memory arrays across multiple CPU cores for concurrent parsing. Large, monolithic batch workloads already resident in memory where throughput scales with core count. Applying parallel parsing to small payloads under high HTTP concurrency creates thread coordination overhead and mutex contention, degrading performance below sequential execution.

Conclusion: Architectural Realignment

SilentJSON demonstrates that high-performance JSON parsing in Go is not about micro-optimizing standard reflection loops, but about fundamentally redesigning buffer ownership and memory lifecycles. By aligning parser architecture with the physical realities of memory-mapped storage and cache hierarchies, systems can eliminate the systemic latency tax imposed by general-purpose libraries.

Under the Hood: Benchmarking Memory Footprints and CPU Cycles

When scaling high-throughput data pipelines that ingest multi-gigabyte feeds or interface with memory-mapped storage, Go's standard encoding/json parser introduces severe performance bottlenecks. The root cause lies in its all-or-nothing heap allocation model driven by pervasive runtime reflection. During token scanning, dynamic runtime inspection of struct field alignments and JSON tags spawns thousands of ephemeral interface wrappers and boxed primitives per payload. The resulting causal chain is absolute: dynamic token scanning floods the heap with transient pointers $\rightarrow$ the Go Garbage Collector (GC) pointer-tracking and sweep phases intensify $\rightarrow$ memory bandwidth becomes saturated while CPU cache lines are repeatedly invalidated $\rightarrow$ worker threads experience cycle starvation, triggering severe p99 tail latency degradation.

Specialized alternatives like SilentJSON alter this performance profile by shifting reflection out of the hot path entirely. Through reflection hoisting, target struct layouts are pre-compiled into flat, type-safe field maps exactly once during application startup using silentjson.BuildRegistry. Hot-path execution accesses pre-computed field offsets directly, driving per-parse heap allocations down to near-zero. However, this optimization enforces a strict trade-off: it sacrifices structural flexibility, rendering pre-compiled registries completely incompatible with dynamic schemas or arbitrary map parsing, which still require standard general-purpose tools.

Memory efficiency is further compounded by zero-copy tokenization and buffer ownership mechanics. Standard parsers duplicate every string and nested object into new, disjoint heap locations. In contrast, optimized parsers leverage zero-copy string views that point directly to the source buffer, such as an mmap region. While this eliminates memory allocation overhead, it introduces a critical hazard: buffer pinning. Retaining a single zero-copy string view in long-term application state forces the Go runtime to keep the entire underlying input block pinned in memory, preventing garbage collection of surrounding segments. Developers must enforce strict lifecycle boundaries, explicitly invoking strings.Clone to sever pointer dependencies whenever parsed strings need to outlive the immediate parse scope.

A rigorous evaluation of throughput, latency, and GC pressure reveals distinct operational thresholds across different parsing strategies:

  • Standard Parsing (encoding/json): Optimal for low-frequency configuration files, small and sporadic HTTP request bodies, or highly dynamic schemas where development velocity outweighs runtime allocation overhead. Failure mode: Severe GC pressure and CPU thrashing under high-throughput ingestion.
  • Sequential Streaming (StreamDecoder): Optimal for streaming large files or continuous data feeds where memory footprints must remain bounded. It reuses a single allocated struct instance across callback iterations. Failure mode: Retaining struct references outside callbacks without deep-copying leads to data overwrites.
  • Parallel Array Unmarshaling (UnmarshalArrayParallel): Optimal for massive, pre-loaded in-memory arrays and batch workloads where partitioning payloads across multiple CPU cores maximizes hardware utilization. Failure mode: Applying parallel parsing to small payloads under high HTTP concurrency creates thread-spawning overhead and mutex contention, degrading performance below sequential execution.

Ultimately, the architectural rule is clear: if processing massive arrays or memory-mapped buffers under strict latency SLAs, deploy pre-registered, low-allocation parsers with strict buffer lifecycle management; if handling unstructured schemas or low-concurrency requests, absorb the reflection overhead of general-purpose tools. Treating JSON parsing as a zero-copy stream alignment problem rather than a generic deserialization task is the only way to eliminate allocation churn in large-scale systems.

Real-World Deployment: Integrating SilentJSON into Production Systems

Deploying a specialized parsing library like SilentJSON into a large-scale distributed data pipeline changes how memory moves through your application. When you shift from standard reflection-heavy parsers to pre-compiled registry models, you are fundamentally altering the contract between your application code, the Go runtime, and the underlying storage subsystem—such as a memory-mapped (mmap) key-value engine.

Architectural Patterns for Pipeline Integration

The core challenge in high-throughput ingestion is avoiding the all-or-nothing heap allocation trap of general-purpose parsers. When processing gigabyte-scale datasets, standard unmarshaling instantiates millions of ephemeral pointers, saturating memory bandwidth and triggering heavy Garbage Collector (GC) pointer-tracking phases that degrade p99 tail latencies. Integrating SilentJSON requires aligning your pipeline architecture with its three core execution modes:

  • Pre-Registered Sequential Unmarshaling: By hoisting reflection out of the hot path via silentjson.BuildRegistry, struct layouts are pre-compiled into flat, type-safe field maps once at startup. Hot-path execution accesses pre-computed offsets directly, reducing per-parse heap allocations to zero. This is optimal for pre-loaded slices or structured logs where the schema is static.
  • Sequential Stream Decoding (StreamDecoder): For continuous feeds or large files, StreamDecoder bounds memory consumption by reusing a single allocated struct instance across callback iterations. The internal buffer cycles through reads without allocating new heap objects for every record. However, this introduces a strict ownership constraint: because the decoder mutates and reuses the struct in-place, retaining a reference outside the callback without an explicit deep copy leads to silent data overwrites and race conditions.
  • Raw Block Batching (NextRawBlock): When downstream components require batch payloads rather than individual records, extracting contiguous byte chunks containing $N$ objects separated by commas (stripping outer array brackets) avoids individual struct instantiation overhead entirely.

Managing Buffer Ownership and Zero-Copy Hazards

Performance optimization at this level exacts a toll on safety abstractions, shifting explicit buffer lifecycle management directly onto the developer. SilentJSON’s optimized path for unescaped JSON strings from byte slices allows parsed strings to point directly to the original input buffer—such as an mmap region—without duplicating data in memory.

This zero-copy mechanism creates two distinct failure modes:

  • Buffer Pinning and Memory Leaks: Retaining a single zero-copy string view in long-term application state (e.g., a global cache or long-lived map) forces the Go runtime to keep the entire underlying input block pinned in memory. The Garbage Collector cannot sweep surrounding segments because a single active pointer references the parent buffer, leading to silent, massive memory bloat. Mitigation: You must explicitly invoke strings.Clone to sever pointer dependencies if a parsed string must outlive the immediate parse scope.
  • Mutation Hazards: Because the string slices reference source memory directly, modifying the underlying input buffer while string views remain active causes immediate memory corruption or parser panics. The input buffer must remain strictly immutable throughout the lifecycle of the parsed tokens.

Concurrency Thresholds and Parallel Unmarshaling Trade-Offs

For massive arrays already resident in memory, UnmarshalArrayParallel partitions workloads across multiple CPU cores. While highly effective for heavy batch workloads, applying this strategy indiscriminately to small payloads under high HTTP concurrency backfires.

Spawning parallel worker routines introduces thread-synchronization overhead and mutex contention that far outweighs the cost of a simple sequential scan. Under high request concurrency, parallel parsing saturates CPU scheduling queues and causes thread starvation. Decision rule: Use parallel unmarshaling exclusively for massive, isolated batch workloads; for standard, high-concurrency request paths, rely strictly on sequential UnmarshalSlice. Similarly, when dealing with auxiliary metadata fields that are rarely accessed on the hot path, employ silentjson.RawMessage to defer deserialization, preserving CPU cache locality and eliminating cold-path heap allocations.

The Road Ahead: Next-Generation Parsing and Go's Ecosystem Evolution

As modern data pipelines ingest multi-gigabyte payloads and memory-mapped files under tightening latency service-level agreements (SLAs), standard approaches to data serialization hit a hard physical wall. The traditional reliance on general-purpose reflection and whole-file memory allocation destroys CPU cache locality and floods the heap with ephemeral pointers. Moving forward, the evolution of Go-based data architectures requires shifting away from runtime introspection toward compile-time code generation, strict buffer ownership models, and specialized stream processing primitives.

Generics and Compile-Time Type Dispatch

The introduction of generics in Go changed the economics of parser design by shifting type inspection from runtime to compile time. In a reflection-heavy library like standard encoding/json, the runtime continuously queries field alignments, offsets, and JSON tags, spawning millions of transient interface wrappers. This dynamic inspection creates a causal chain: continuous type interrogation translates to heap-allocated boxing primitives $\rightarrow$ heavy Garbage Collector (GC) pointer-tracking and sweep phases $\rightarrow$ memory bandwidth saturation $\rightarrow$ CPU cache line invalidation $\rightarrow$ severe p99 tail latency degradation.

By leveraging generics, specialized libraries like SilentJSON pre-compile target struct layouts into flat, type-safe field maps exactly once during application startup. Hot-path execution accesses pre-computed field offsets directly, reducing per-parse heap allocations to zero. However, this design enforces a strict trade-off: it sacrifices structural flexibility. Static generics and pre-built registries cannot handle dynamic schemas or arbitrary map parsing without falling back to general-purpose reflection engines.

Compiler Directives and Escape Analysis Control

Optimizing high-throughput parsers also requires understanding Go's escape analysis engine. When a parser allocates temporary byte buffers or string headers on the heap, the Go compiler promotes those variables to ensure memory safety across scope boundaries. This heap promotion creates pointer allocation churn that forces frequent GC cycles.

Engineers can mitigate this by utilizing precise buffer slicing and zero-copy tokenization. By pointing string slices directly to source memory regions—such as memory-mapped (mmap) buffers—the application bypasses string duplication entirely. However, this optimization introduces a severe risk: buffer pinning. If an application retains a single zero-copy string view in long-term state, the Go runtime is forced to keep the entire underlying input block pinned in memory, preventing GC reclamation of surrounding segments. The operational rule is absolute: if parsed strings or blocks must outlive the immediate parse scope, developers must explicitly invoke strings.Clone to sever pointer dependencies and prevent memory leaks.

Next-Generation Stream Processing and Batching Primitives

Loading entire JSON documents into RAM creates memory spikes that easily trigger out-of-memory (OOM) kills in containerized environments. Next-generation data pipelines treat parsing not as a deserialization task, but as a zero-copy stream transformation and memory-mapping alignment problem. Utilizing primitives like StreamDecoder and NextRawBlock bounds memory consumption by processing data within controlled byte-slice windows.

Sequential stream decoding reuses a single allocated struct instance across callback iterations, updating fields in-place. While this eliminates allocation churn, it introduces a dangerous failure mode: data overwrites. Retaining references to struct pointers outside the callback without deep-copying leads to silent data corruption as subsequent stream segments overwrite the memory. Similarly, raw block extraction (NextRawBlock) segments large arrays into contiguous byte chunks containing $N$ objects without outer array brackets. This strips away individual struct instantiation overhead for batch processors, but requires strict lifecycle discipline: blocks must be processed or copied before the next read operation overwrites the internal buffer window.

Architectural Decision Framework: Selecting the Right Parsing Strategy

No single parsing strategy fits every layer of a large-scale system. Choosing the wrong mechanism under high concurrency leads directly to thread contention, lock convoying, and GC thrashing. The following matrix dictates the optimal routing of workloads based on payload scale and concurrency architecture:
Parsing Strategy Optimal Use Case Operational Failure Mode
Standard Parsing (encoding/json) Low-frequency config files, small HTTP request bodies, highly dynamic schemas. GC pressure, heap allocation churn, and CPU thrashing under high-throughput ingestion.
Sequential Streaming (StreamDecoder) Streaming large files or continuous feeds with bounded memory footprints (reuses a single struct instance). Data corruption and race conditions if struct references are retained outside callbacks without deep-copying.
Raw Block Batching (NextRawBlock) High-throughput batch ingestion and pipeline handoffs requiring chunked byte payloads. Memory corruption if internal buffer windows are read after subsequent decoder advancements.
Parallel Unmarshaling (UnmarshalArrayParallel) Massive pre-loaded in-memory arrays and isolated batch workloads across multiple CPU cores. Thread-spawning overhead and mutex contention on small payloads under high HTTP concurrency.

Decision Rule: For massive arrays or memory-mapped buffers under strict SLAs, deploy pre-registered, low-allocation parsers with strict buffer lifecycle management. For unstructured schemas or high-concurrency request paths handling small payloads, fall back to sequential processing or reflection-based parsers. Never apply parallel unmarshaling (UnmarshalArrayParallel) to small payloads under high HTTP concurrency; the thread-coordination overhead and scheduling queue saturation will consistently degrade performance below standard sequential execution.

title: Tired of Weak ISO 8583 Parsers? I Built a Better Java Alternative
description:
Working with payment systems, I kept running into the same frustrations with existing ISO 8583 libraries:

  • Everything comes back as String (then you convert it yourself)
  • Nested subfields (TLV, private fields, etc.) are painful or unsupported
  • Configuration is usually locked in annotations or static XML
  • Fixed-length and ISO 8583 messages often need completely different code paths

I got tired of fighting the tools, so I built alatka-messages.

What is alatka-messages?

It’s a Java library focused on parsing and building both fixed-length and ISO 8583 messages.

Not a full payment switch (like jPOS). Just a clean, modern message definition + pack/unpack layer.

What makes it different?

1. Proper nested subdomain support

Supports TLV, ULV, bitmap subfields, and deep nesting. This is especially useful for UnionPay and other schemes with complex private fields.

2. Real Java type mapping

Fields can map directly to:

  • BigDecimal, Integer, Boolean
  • LocalDate / LocalDateTime
  • List, Map
  • Custom POJOs

No more endless String → type conversions.

3. Flexible configuration + hot reload

Supports:

  • YAML
  • XML
  • Annotations
  • Database tables

YAML, XML, and database configs can be hot-reloaded without restarting the app.

4. Unified API

Same approach for both fixed-length and ISO 8583 messages.

5. Spring Boot Starter + simple Admin UI

Easy to drop into Spring Boot projects.

Quick example 

MessageHolder holder = MessageBuilder.init("iso:cups:common:payload")
    .unpack(hexMessage);

BigDecimal amount = holder.get(4);
LocalDateTime transmissionTime = holder.get(7);

Who might find this useful?

  • Building payment gateways / acquirers / clearing systems
  • Dealing with frequent message definition changes
  • Want better type safety than classic ISO 8583 libs
  • Find jPOS too heavy, but basic libraries too limited

Links

  • Gitee (main): https://gitee.com/asuka2001/alatka-messages
  • GitHub: https://github.com/goGetSomeFries/alatka-messages

It’s MIT licensed and actively maintained.

If you’ve struggled with rigid ISO 8583 configs or weak subdomain support, feel free to check it out. Feedback and issues are welcome.

title: Why our AI asks "which metric?" before drawing a chart
description:
A small design decision we keep coming back to: when a request is ambiguous, PowerDataChat asks a clarifying question instead of guessing.

Example: "Chart revenue and margin by month." Revenue is in currency, margin is a percentage. Put both on one chart and it becomes hard to read. So instead of picking for you, it asks which metric you want, or how you want them shown.

Three related behaviours follow the same idea:

  • Starter questions. An empty chat box is intimidating. After a file is connected, the AI suggests questions based on that file, so a new user has somewhere to start.
  • Honest "missing data" answers. If you ask about a column that does not exist, it says what is missing and suggests alternatives instead of inventing values.
  • Follow-ups keep context. "Now only for 2026" works without restating the whole question.

None of this is clever AI. It is the behaviour you expect from a good human analyst: ask when unclear, say when the data cannot answer, remember what you were talking about.

What do your users do when your product's input is ambiguous? We would like to hear how others handle it.

title: EC2 Image Builder console now integrates with the DevOps Agent for troubleshooting and resource creation
description:
EC2 Image Builder now integrates with the AWS DevOps Agent directly in the Image Builder console, enabling you to troubleshoot failed image pipelines and create resources directly from the console chat panel. You can diagnose up to 50 failed pipelines at once and ask follow-up questions in the same conversation. You can also choose to create resources by describing what you want, and the agent populates the console with values the service has already validated.

With this integration, diagnosing a failed pipeline no longer requires manually inspecting build logs, cross-referencing error codes, or iterating through configuration fixes, saving you significant time and expertise. The agent reads build logs, workflow steps, components, and network configuration, then provides the root cause and the steps to fix it. For resource creation,  the agent verifies the configuration before populating the console for you to review and submit. If you troubleshoot or build with your own AI agents, the new EC2 Image Builder skill in the AWS Agent Toolkit provides you the same troubleshooting and creation capabilities.

This feature is available in all commercial regions. To get started, open the EC2 Image Builder console and use the DevOps Agent from the console panel. For more information, see the EC2 Image Builder documentation and for pricing refer DevOps agent Pricing page.

title: Amazon Route 53 Domains now supports self-service restore for expired and deleted domains
description:
Amazon Route 53 Domains now lets you restore an expired or recently deleted domain yourself, using the Amazon Route 53 console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. Previously, restoring a domain required a request to AWS Support. Now you can recover a domain lost to a missed renewal, an expired payment method, or an accidental deletion, and restore the website, email, and applications that depend on it.

To restore a domain, you enter the domain name, review the restoration price, accept the charge, and submit the request. Route 53 works with the top-level domain (TLD) registry to reactivate the registration and return the domain to your AWS account. Most TLD registries support restoration, and each registry sets how long after expiration or deletion a domain can still be restored. Restoring a domain typically costs more than registering or renewing one.

To learn more, see Restoring an expired or deleted domain in the Route 53 Developer Guide, or visit the Amazon Route 53 Domains page. For a complete list of supported TLDs, see the Route 53 TLD list. For pricing, visit the Route 53 pricing page.

title: AWS Backup now supports resource modifiers for Amazon EKS restores
description:
Today, AWS Backup announces support for resource modifiers when restoring Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) backups. Resource modifiers let you transform Kubernetes resources during a restore, so you can adapt a restored cluster to its target environment.

When you restore an EKS backup that has been copied across accounts or across AWS Regions, the restored cluster can carry references tied to the source environment, such as IAM roles, database endpoints, and Amazon ECR registry URIs. Previously, you had to locate and update these references manually after every restore, which was time consuming and error prone. With resource modifiers, you can define transformation rules once via a YAML file, and AWS Backup applies them automatically as part of the restore, improving the reliability of your cross-account and cross-Region disaster recovery workflows.

AWS Backup support for resource modifiers for Amazon EKS backups is available in all commercial AWS Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To get started, see the AWS Backup Documentation and read the launch blog.

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.22

We've released version 6.22 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Transcript separation for chat

You can now configure Google Cloud CCaaS to deliver a separate transcript file for each participant segment in a chat, instead of one combined transcript per session. Under Settings > Chat > Chat Transcript, select Per Segment in Transcript Separation to generate individual transcript files for each agent, virtual agent, or supervisor who joins the chat—helpful for identifying which participant handled each part of a transferred or escalated conversation. Your consumers still receive a single, full-chat transcript regardless of this setting.

For more information, see Chat transcripts and chat history.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Campaign-based scheduled callbacks

Agents can now schedule a callback during an outbound campaign call. The callback belongs to the campaign, not to an individual agent, and the dialer calls the consumer back in the time slot they chose. Administrators set slot length, capacity, booking window, and expiry for each campaign, and supervisors can track upcoming, completed, and expired callbacks from the campaign list.

For more information, see Campaign management.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where direct access point (DAP) greeting messages played twice when a call was deflected to an internal phone number due to queue overcapacity.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata for top-level menu paths and selected menus was incorrectly displayed in English instead of the user's configured language.

  • Fixed an issue where a failed Salesforce lookup was incorrectly treated as having no matches, which resulted in the creation of duplicate records.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound transfer restrictions remained in force even after being hidden in the administrator interface, causing queues to become silently unreachable for transfers.

  • Fixed an issue where hold music continued to play throughout a call recording after a warm transfer was completed.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound virtual agent audio was prematurely truncated during multi-message turns.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Monitoring Queues report didn't accurately count skill-matched agents for skills-based queues, often displaying zero available agents despite their availability.

  • Fixed an issue where calls deflected to an external phone number after entering a queue were incorrectly recorded as abandoned by the customer.

  • Fixed an issue where the credit card tokenizer was missing from the SmartActions menu during outbound callback calls.

  • Fixed an issue where mandatory call dispositions were discarded if an agent's voice connection dropped but their session remained active.

  • Fixed an issue where the text resize menu in the chat widget wasn't scrollable at 400% browser zoom, which prevented users from accessing all available text size options.

  • Fixed an issue where the system incorrectly prevented saving automatic call redirection settings when the target was a virtual agent-operated queue.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate call records were created for a single inbound call, causing incorrect wait times to appear in the real-time queue view.

  • Fixed an issue where empty data attributes caused an error in the agent interface during call connections.

  • Fixed an issue where the Transfer Restrictions destination picker provided no feedback when a queue was ineligible, making it indistinguishable from a typo or search error.

  • Fixed an issue where incoming calls were rejected with a SIP 603 error due to high database latency and connection timeouts.

  • Fixed an issue where the documentation for the Apps API and call session metadata schema didn't define the top-level parentId and finishReason fields.

  • Fixed an issue where certain inbound call failures were incorrectly reported as a busy signal.

  • Fixed an issue where the event processor service crashed during scaling or rebalancing of the system.

  • Fixed an issue where the conversation ID was missing from chat events during active sessions.

  • Fixed an issue where report exports didn't download or remained stuck in a processing state indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where agents could transfer calls to queues that were already closed if their transfer list was loaded while the queue was still open.

  • Fixed an issue where queued chats were assigned to agents after the end-user had become unresponsive without being prompted to check in.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls cold-transferred to an over-capacity queue generated duplicate reporting records and incorrect queue wait times if the callback leg failed.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls deflected to voicemail during after-hours played three separate audio prompts sequentially.

  • Fixed an issue where a single call was simultaneously assigned to two different agents if the pickup coincided with the cascade timer expiry.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls weren't projected to agents in a breakthrough-enabled status if another call was already waiting in their queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a gray empty area appeared below the chat container in the agent adapter when the iframe width was narrower than 449px.

  • Fixed an issue where several Kubernetes and Google Cloud service accounts were granted overly broad permissions, which could have allowed for unauthorized privilege escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's status sequence was recorded in the incorrect order following a brief connection loss during an active chat.

  • Fixed an issue where selecting a contact during a native campaign call didn't automatically open the corresponding record in the CRM.

  • Fixed an issue where AI-generated Smart Disposition suggestions were inconsistently displayed for outbound calls during the wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings became distorted or garbled when multiple holds were placed during a call.

  • Fixed an issue where audio uploads were accepted based on the file extension rather than the actual file content, which caused call disconnections when incompatible formats were played.

  • Fixed an issue where the call duration timer in the external call adapter didn't match the In-call status timer in the agent desktop for inbound calls.

  • Fixed an issue where the sentiment score was incorrectly displayed in the call adapter for calls escalated from a virtual agent, even when the Sentiment Analysis setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate reporting rows were generated for call and wrap-up durations due to concurrent system events.

  • Fixed an issue where agents couldn't sign in or refresh their status if their account was linked to a deleted or unknown status.

  • Fixed an issue where the Manager API documentation for agent activity logs omitted 17 chat routing and activity values, leading to incomplete reporting data for customers.

  • Fixed an issue where IVR custom callback numbers for certain international regions, including Norway and Denmark, were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix.

  • Fixed an issue where metadata for calls deflected between virtual agent assignment and connection wasn't exported to the Cloud Storage bucket.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent to human chat escalations experienced delays of up to 300 seconds during agent assignment.

  • Fixed an issue where the Answer button didn't appear for dial-by-extension calls when other calls were already waiting in an agent's queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a supervisor's name didn't appear in the chat widget when joining a conversation using the monitor then barge workflow.

  • Fixed an issue where ending a chat session in one browser tab didn't automatically close the chat widget in other open tabs.

Security

Bug ID Description
573663408 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the ingress gateway to patch security vulnerabilities.
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
568535165 Skip main_task_wait_time and nio_task_wait_time metrics for the first 12 Prometheus scrapes during Message Processor startup warmup.
573602919 Fix generated OpenAPI specs' servers[] to carry the Apigee envgroup hostname instead of the backend target host.
562964081 The sgpUserIntentMatchingMode verdict-log field is now always present, including on dry-run policy records, and shows the mode used for the evaluation, including when sgpUserIntentMatching isn't set (CONSTRAINTS_AND_INTENT, or INTENT_ONLY when no policies match the tool call).
524115876 Fix an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests.
572025634 Responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact instead of returning a corrupted body.
549078690 If no SGP policy is attributed for a denial, a customer sees the generic fallback message. This fix short-circuits to show the rationale instead when no matched policy has a configured denial message.
492041991 VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken now set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables only from the LLM operation(s) that matched the request; they are no longer set from unmatched LLM operations or for requests that match no LLM operation.
567244615 Semantic Governance now evaluates LLM requests it previously skipped, such as OpenAI requests whose message content is an array of parts, which can produce new denials and judge-model usage. It considers every system message rather than only the last, and a non-streaming OpenAI or an Ollama tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON is now an evaluation error.
567244615 Semantic Governance no longer evaluates a request or response with a field it cannot read when a tool call is involved. It records verdict ERROR naming the field, with status MODEL_ERROR. The inline SemanticGovernance policy instead raises GovernedLLMResponseParseError or GovernedLLMProviderDetectionFailed (HTTP 500), in DRY_RUN too unless continueOnError is true. It also reads every text part of a Gemini system instruction and Gemini tool parameters given as parametersJsonSchema, and no longer loses the rest of a Claude or Gemini request when one field has an unexpected shape.
560272924 Added continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming support for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Model Armor policies now honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: with it set, Model Armor callouts bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic. Streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
158204922 VerifyJWT now rejects a JWT whose header contains "b64":false, with fault steps.jwt.InvalidToken, as RFC 7797 section 7 requires. Previously, such a token could be accepted if KnownHeaders listed b64, IgnoreCriticalHeaders was true, or the header had no crit.
158204922 GenerateJWS supports RFC 7797 unencoded payloads. GenerateJWS now raises MissingPayload, InvalidPayload or FailedToResolveVariable for payload errors, where it previously raised GenerationFailed. KnownHeaders and CriticalHeaders in the JWS and JWT policies accept names separated by whitespace, such as one per line. A b64 header supplied through AdditionalHeaders is now rejected, with steps.jws.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWS and steps.jwt.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWT. A proxy that set b64 through an AdditionalHeaders variable produced an RFC 7797 JWS before this change, and must move to UnencodedPayload, with DetachContent for the detached form.
158204922 VerifyJWS verifies RFC 7797 unencoded-payload JWS (b64:false), attached or detached. b64 in crit no longer needs a KnownHeaders entry. VerifyJWS rejects b64:false unless crit lists b64, with the new fault steps.jws.UnencodedPayloadNotCritical; IgnoreCriticalHeaders does not change that. DecodeJWS reports the raw payload of such a JWS.
559228730 ext_proc: ImmediateResponse now carries any Content-Type (raw body bytes + preserved Content-Type); replies too large to buffer use StreamedImmediateResponse.
544751120 Semantic Governance Policies marked as dry run are now evaluated and logged without blocking the request. Each dry-run policy adds a second judge evaluation per tool-calling response, whose tokens are billed. Dry-run verdicts are written to the semantic-governance-policy log as separate records flagged sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation=true; queries that count verdicts should add sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation != true to exclude them.
554114419 Fixed: an AssignMessage/HTTPModifier/RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow can now set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers instead of failing with an invalid-header error.
567812025 FILESYSTEM persistence mode makes the synchronizer skip Cassandra entirely (no connections, reads, writes, or datastore health probes).
559009293 Fixed elevated OAuth latency and Cassandra read load for AppGroup apps, including access token verification and token and authorization-code generation, by caching AppGroup lookups in the message processor runtime, matching Developer behavior.
568860869 Fixed RegularExpressionProtection patterns of the form "...." whose middle section contains regular expression syntax (for example, ".?Exception in thread." or "(?i).<script.>.*") being matched as literal text instead of as regular expressions. Such patterns now raise steps.regexprotection.ThreatDetected for all matching input.
564945600 Enhance VerifyAPIKey policy to better handle leading spaces.
502231886 Fixed the default source templates for SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse so a policy that omits the source element extracts content correctly when IgnoreUnresolvedVariables is false.
562964081 Semantic Governance now honors the sgpUserIntentMatching AuthzExtension metadata key (ENABLED or DISABLED) to toggle user-intent matching in policy evaluation; DISABLED evaluates against constraints only.
565004219 Fixed Semantic Governance Policy skipping evaluation for Anthropic requests that send system as a content-block array (the form ADK and LiteLlm emit). Affected agents are now evaluated, which may produce new denials and new judge-model usage on the consumer project.
527517087 SGP policy logs written to your project now identify their originating region. resource.type changes from "global" to "generic_node" and the region appears in resource.labels.location. Anything selecting these entries by resource.type="global" must be updated -- including log-based metrics, sinks, exclusion filters and alerts, which stop matching silently rather than erroring.
575439485 JavaCallout policies that run remotely (per-contract offload) can now pass every value type allowed by the GCP-2025-023 setVariable restriction between policies (collections, maps, arrays, primitive wrappers including Character, Date, BigDecimal, UUID, java.time, atomics, JDK enums, Optional), with their types preserved, instead of failing with steps.remotepolicy.NonSerializableVariable.
575439485 Remotely executed (per-contract offload) JavaCallout policies with continueOnError="true" now continue the flow when the callout faults, instead of returning HTTP 500.
567244901 In enforce mode, Semantic Governance now blocks a tool call when the governance check cannot be completed, instead of letting it through.
573622417 Fixed an issue where istio-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571679067 removes old version of ApigeeTelemetry CRD.
571378258 The Apigee Redis container is now built from the Valkey engine (BSD-3-Clause, Linux Foundation) at version 8.1.10. Wire protocol is unchanged (RESP2) and the redis-server/redis-cli binary names are preserved.

Data Studio

Feature

You can connect Data Studio to a BigQuery Graph or query a graph by using a custom SQL query in the BigQuery connector, which imports graph measures as metrics that you can use in your reports. For more information, see Connect to Google BigQuery.

Firestore

Feature

Data modification language (DML) operations are generally available (GA). Added support for insert and upsert.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Single-user quota limits

Gemini Enterprise administrators can configure single-user quota limits on the Usage & Spending > Usage page in the Google Cloud console to prevent an individual user from using all of an edition's shared subscription quota pool. You can enable a single-user quota limit and set a quota multiplier for each edition and location across the Gemini Enterprise Standard, Gemini Enterprise Plus, and Gemini Enterprise Standard Emerging Market editions.

This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see:

  • Single-user quota limits
  • Configure a single-user quota limit
  • Configure pay-as-you-go usage above quota

Announcement

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon becomes the default model for AlphaEvolve on October 26, 2026

On October 26, 2026, Gemini 4 Argon will replace Gemini 3.8 Flash as the default model for new AlphaEvolve experiments. AlphaEvolve uses the default model when you don't specify a model in the models field of generationSettings.

From that date, new experiments that use the default model are billed at Gemini 4 Argon token prices instead of Gemini 3.8 Flash token prices. To keep using Gemini 3.8 Flash, specify gemini-3.8-flash in the models field.

Experiments created before October 26, 2026 keep the model recorded in their configuration.

For more information, see Default model.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards prerelease notes 6.24

Here are the pre-release notes for updates to the advanced reporting dashboards and other reporting in CCAI Platform. When we release these updates, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Important: The next version of the advanced reporting dashboards could be greater than 6.24.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where call and chat type names were cut off in the Dashboard Reports selector on wide-screen displays.

  • Fixed an issue where the Individual Call History and Individual Chat History reports, run for all agents, left out calls and chats that were never assigned to an agent (for example, abandoned, deflected, or expired calls) when only one agent or no agents had activity in the selected period. The All Call History and All Chat History files are now always included.

  • Fixed an issue where the Interactions Detail by Agent report omitted outbound calls placed without a queue when generated for all agents.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Queue Monitoring and Campaign dashboards incorrectly displayed English queue names for French and Spanish interactions.

  • Fixed an issue where "wrap-up" and "hold" metrics in advanced reporting were displayed with inconsistent and inaccurate French Canadian (fr_CA) translations.

  • Fixed an issue where Spanish chat queues incorrectly displayed English names in Real-time Queue Monitoring and advanced reporting dashboards.

  • Fixed an issue where call disposition fields appeared blank on dashboards when viewing date ranges between 46 and 365 days.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware 1.34.1000-gke.111 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud 1.34.1000-gke.111 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.7-gke.200.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for use with GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.1000-gke.111:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where updating or upgrading a cluster to an advanced cluster failed to join control plane nodes if the cluster's certificate authorities (CAs) were previously rotated. For more information, see Control plane nodes fail to join during an update or upgrade to an advanced cluster after CA rotation.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal 1.34.1000-gke.111 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal 1.34.1000-gke.111 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.7-gke.200.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for installations or upgrades with the GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

Feature

The following features were introduced in 1.34.1000-gke.111:

  • Fixed an issue in clusters using bundled BGP load balancing where control plane upgrades or configuration updates could cause up to 20 seconds of API server connection failures while a control plane node restarted. After the fix, failover to a healthy control plane node completes in approximately 4 seconds.
  • Fixed an issue where the NodePool controller prematurely updated Status.ManagedFields on partial reconciliation failures, causing removed taints and labels to remain stranded on affected nodes.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.1000-gke.111:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed BareMetalMachine conditions during maintenance mode transitions.
  • Fixed an issue where updating control plane configurations caused multiple API servers to restart simultaneously, leading to transient control plane unavailability.

This note is missing a fix included in 1.34.1000-gke.111. See entry for October 26, 2026.

Google SecOps

Feature

Bulk case selection

In the enhanced Investigation Management experience, you can select up to 50 cases at a time in the case queue to perform bulk operations:

  • Range selection: Hold Shift while clicking to select a range of cases.
  • Select all: Click the header checkbox to select up to 50 loaded cases; this action automatically scrolls your view back to the top of the list. Consolidated Settings and Navigation

The Consolidated Settings and Navigation feature is now in public preview. It replaces the separate SIEM Settings and SOAR Settings menus with a single Settings menu, grouped into Administration, Access Management, Investigation, Detection and Data Management, and updates the navigation menu. Each settings page is shown only to users with the correct permissions. Cloud IAM, Viewer and Editor users can now view certain SOAR settings pages in read-only mode. Note that the Google SecOps documentation has been updated to reflect the new navigational changes imposed by the unified Settings menu. For more information, see Navigate the Google SecOps platform.

Looker

Announcement

Looker 26.22 will roll out to Looker (original) instances on the following schedule:

  • Expected Looker (original) deployment start: Monday, October 26, 2026
  • Expected Looker (original) final deployment and download available: Monday, November 9, 2026

The Looker 26.22 rollout for Looker (Google Cloud core) will be announced separately.

Looker 26.22 is expected to include the following changes, features, and fixes.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where table column options menus and search boxes appeared behind drill dialogs, which prevented users from interacting with them. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where configuring a LookML model could trigger unnecessary derived table rebuilds. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the Show filters option was displayed on dashboard tiles that failed to load data in view mode. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where drilling into results that were filtered by string dimensions that contained backslashes returned zero rows. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where pivoted queries in SQL Runner could fail to render or re-pivot unexpectedly. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the View (Expanded / Full Screen) option appeared in the tile action menu on embedded dashboards in view mode. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where custom visualization tiles were truncated in dashboard PDF exports when the Expand tables to show all rows option was enabled. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

Table row group subtotals are now displayed only for sum and count measures. For other measure types (such as averages and count distinct) and table calculations, subtotals are now left blank rather than displaying an inaccurate summed value.

Fixed

The System Activity query_metrics Explore now records connection acquisition time (acquire_connection) for queries that are canceled while waiting in the connection pool.

Fixed

Conversational Analytics DELETE endpoints now return HTTP 404 Not Found instead of HTTP 204 No Content when you attempt to delete nonexistent resources.

Fixed

The System Activity query_metrics Explore has been updated to accurately record model initialization time for models that are loaded from cache.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where adding a new series to a categorical chart, such as adding a new pivot value, could cause category bars to appear ungrouped. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed in the TypeScript and JavaScript SDKs where calling methods that have only optional parameters without passing an empty object could result in compilation or runtime errors. This feature now performs as expected.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.26

We've released version 6.26 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Scheduled callback for IVR overcapacity

Scheduled callback is now available as an overcapacity deflection option for IVR queues. When a queue is over capacity, callers can choose to schedule a callback. Google Cloud CCaaS then hands the call to your configured virtual agent, which books the callback through the Callback call API. Administrators choose the virtual agent, an optional greeting, and the data parameters to pass at the global or queue level. Reporting shows whether each caller submitted a callback or left without one.

Administrators: You can configure scheduled callback for overcapacity deflection globally at Settings > Call > Overcapacity Deflection, or per queue at Settings > Queue > IVR (Interactive Voice Response) > Edit / View > [QUEUE] > Overcapacity Deflection > Configure.

For more information, see Overcapacity deflection per-queue and Callback call API.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Salesforce: PKCE and refresh token rotation support

You can now connect Google Cloud CCaaS to Salesforce apps that require Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) and refresh token rotation. Salesforce turns both settings on automatically for newly created connected apps and external client apps. Google Cloud CCaaS uses PKCE when authorizing Salesforce administrator and agent connections. It also saves replacement refresh tokens returned by Salesforce, keeping connections working across subsequent token refreshes. Salesforce apps that don't use these settings keep working as before. This update adds no new configuration steps in Google Cloud CCaaS.

For more information, see Salesforce integration guide.

Cloud DNS

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

Source of CNAME answer Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) New behavior (starting January 5, 2027)
Cloud DNS public zone Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones.
Cloud DNS private zone Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.
Cloud DNS response policy zone Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.
