title: No database on purpose: flat files are enough for a downloader
description:
When I rebuilt my video downloader in plain PHP for shared hosting, the first thing I decided was what not to build. There would be no database. No MySQL, no SQLite, no tables, no migrations, no admin panel. Just files in folders.

That sounds reckless if you have spent your career around databases. It felt reckless to me too, at first. But a year in, I have not missed one, and the decision is the reason the site stays simple enough for one person to maintain.

What the site actually needs to remember

A downloader does not remember much. It takes a link, asks a provider API what files exist for it, and hands the visitor a download button. Nothing about that flow needs to persist. The video itself is never stored on my server — the provider streams it, or the visitor's browser fetches it directly. There are no accounts, no saved videos, no history, no favourites. If there is nothing to remember, there is nothing to store.

What does need to persist is small and boring: a per-IP rate-limit counter, a cache of recent provider responses, and an error log. Each of those is a file.

The rate limiter is a JSON file per IP address, holding a count and a window start time. A request reads it, bumps the number, writes it back. When the window expires, the file is overwritten with a fresh count. The cache is a folder of JSON files named after a hash of the video URL, each with an expiry time baked into the filename or the contents. The error log is a text file with one line per failure, timestamped, with no user data in it.

Why files win on shared hosting

Shared hosting is the constraint that made this decision for me. My plan gives me PHP and a file system. A database would have meant a second service to configure, a second set of credentials to protect, and a second thing that could go down or get locked. On a cheap plan, MySQL connections are also a scarce resource — every concurrent visitor holding a connection is a connection the next visitor cannot have. Files have no connection limit.

There is also the question of what happens when something breaks at 2am. A corrupted JSON counter file is fixed by deleting one file. A corrupted table needs a repair tool, a backup, and a prayer. I would rather debug with ls and cat than with a database console I barely use.

Performance is a non-issue at this scale. Reading a small JSON file from disk is fast. Writing one is fast. There is no query planner, no index to maintain, no ORM overhead. The whole site's state fits in a folder you can back up by zipping it.

The honest limits

Flat files are not a universal answer, and I would be lying if I pretended otherwise. They do not handle concurrent writes gracefully — two requests writing the same counter file at the same instant can clobber each other. I work around that with flock(), which is good enough for a low-traffic tool but would fall apart under real load.

They also do not scale across servers. If I ever needed a second server, two sets of files would drift apart instantly. And searching them is a joke: there is no SELECT, just glob() and grep. The moment I need to ask "show me every failed request from this provider last week" as a query instead of a log skim, I will have outgrown the approach.

But none of those limits matter yet. The site is one server, one person, and a trickle of traffic. Choosing a database now would be paying for scale I do not have, with complexity I would have to maintain.

The rule I follow

Reach for a database when you have a question only a database can answer — relationships between records, queries across thousands of rows, or state shared between servers. If your state is a handful of counters, a cache, and a log, a folder of files is not a hack. It is the right tool, and it is the one I would choose again.

My downloader, ramrom.io, runs on exactly this setup today: PHP, flat files, and nothing else to keep alive. When the day comes that files stop being enough, I will know, because the site will tell me — a counter will corrupt, a cache folder will get unwieldy, or a question will need a real query. Until then, the simplest thing that works is the thing that ships.

title: Ping64|What My Parents Actually Did With the Shared Streaming Account This Year
description:
During the holidays I did something I had been quietly putting off for a while. I opened the settings of our family streaming account and actually looked at the device list. Not because anything seemed wrong. Pure professional curiosity, the kind that makes an IT person glance at the guest Wi-Fi list at a party. What I found was a small anthropology project, and honestly, a fairly gentle audit report on how my parents use technology day to day.

The account started years ago as a simple favor: one subscription, two profiles, my parents get their movies, everybody happy. What it became over time is something nobody designed and nobody manages. It just grew, the way shared things in families and in companies tend to grow when the original owner stops looking.

What the device list actually showed

Eleven devices, for a household of two. Two of them were TVs that had been replaced years ago and never signed out. One was a tablet my mother insists she has never owned, in a tone that closed the discussion. There were sessions from two different countries, both eventually explainable and both worth a conversation over dinner. The password, it turned out, was the same one they use for their email, which is the finding that made me put my coffee down very carefully.

The profiles were their own chapter. Instead of the clean two we had planned, there were five, with names like Mom 2 and Guest and one labeled Test that neither of them could explain. Subtitles had been switched to a language nobody in the family speaks. Autoplay had been set to maximum enthusiasm by someone, presumably during a long winter. None of this was malicious, or even careless in any meaningful sense. It was just what happens when a thing is shared and nobody owns it.

Why shared things drift like this

Nobody in my family ever sat down and decided to make the account messy. Each change made sense in the moment. A new TV needed signing in, and the old one was not worth the effort of signing out. A cousin visited, got a quick profile, and left behind a small legend. The password was reused from email because remembering two passwords felt like a tax with no visible benefit. These are the same small, locally reasonable decisions that turn a tidy tool stack into a sprawl at work, one exception at a time.

There is no family IT department, of course. Ownership defaults to whoever set the thing up originally, which is me, which means the drift stays invisible until I look. The same pattern shows up in every team I have worked with: shared resources do not decay because people are careless. They decay because maintenance belongs to no one and costs something small every single time it is postponed.

The work parallel I could not shake

Reading that device list, I kept thinking about how the same pattern plays out in professional settings. Accounts accumulate. Credentials get reused for reasons that felt sensible locally. The inventory exists, but nobody opens it without a prompt or an audit. Some teams try consolidated platforms like Ping64 to reduce the daily busywork of multi-tool security stacks. While a streaming account is a much smaller beast, the underlying instinct is the same one: fewer scattered places, fewer stale sessions, fewer passwords quietly standing in front of something that matters. Even at the scale of two retirees and a smart TV, consolidation beats collection.

A few fixes that survived contact with reality

I installed a password manager for my parents and had them practice the master password twice. One password to remember instead of eleven, and the reuse problem mostly evaporated on the spot.

We signed out the ghost devices together, which took ten minutes, produced one moment of genuine mystery, and one good laugh about the tablet from the country that shall remain unnamed.

Each person got one profile with a PIN. My mother has already appointed herself the administrator of ratings, which was not the plan but seems stable, so I am leaving it alone.

The streaming password is now unique and stored, not memorized. If it ever leaks, it leaks one thing instead of everything, which is the entire point and the easiest sell of the whole visit.

A tidier account, and a nicer visit

The account is tidier now, and more to the point, my parents understand it better, which was the actual goal all along. They did not need a lecture about credential hygiene. They needed someone to sit with them for an afternoon and treat their digital household with the same patience I would give a client’s environment. That is a lesson worth carrying back to work too: most sprawl is not a failure of intelligence or care. It is simply what happens in the absence of someone who occasionally looks, tidies up, and brings the snacks.

References

  • https://www.cisa.gov/secure-our-world
  • https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006/
  • https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r2/final

title: How I built a Chrome extension with zero permissions that recommends personalized gifts
description:
I run outreach for a small personalized-gift store — photo blankets, custom mugs, ornaments, that sort of thing. The store has 1,920 products. Shoppers kept telling us the same thing: they knew who the gift was for, but they froze when they had to pick from hundreds of options. So I built a tiny browser extension that asks three questions and narrows it down to three gifts. The whole thing runs on zero permissions.

Why zero permissions

Most gift-finder extensions ask for broad access — read your browsing data, track the sites you visit. That is a trust killer for a shopping tool, and it is also unnecessary here. The extension I built, Epic Gift Finder, has no permissions key in its manifest at all. It asks the browser for nothing at all — no access to your tabs, no background process phoning home, no analytics of any kind. At the end of the day it is just a small popup window, plain HTML and CSS with a handful of JavaScript behind it. Click a suggestion and the store's category page opens in a normal tab, same as if you had typed the address yourself. Manifest V3 makes this easy. The manifest declares the popup, the icons, and nothing else. If a future version ever needs storage or network access, that will be a deliberate decision with a reason users can see — not something slipped in from day one.

How the quiz works

Three questions, no typing required:

  1. Who is it for — her, him, kids, or a pet lover.
  2. The occasion — a birthday, Christmas, an anniversary, or nothing in particular, just because.
  3. What is the budget — under $25, $25 to $50, or over $50.

Behind that is a small scoring table in plain JavaScript. Each answer points at a few product categories, and the budget answer filters out anything that starts above the range. The extension scores the matches, picks the top three, and renders them as cards with a short line each about why that gift fits. Every link in the table points at a real category page on Epic Personalized Gifts — thirteen of them, each one clicked and checked by hand before I shipped anything. A dead link inside an extension is worse than no extension at all, because the user has already trusted you once by clicking.

What the build actually looks like

Four files make up the whole thing. There is the manifest, the popup page, its stylesheet, and one JavaScript file with roughly two hundred lines in it. No framework. No build step to run before it works. When you answer the three questions, the code matches your picks against a small table and shows the best three. It never calls out to a server or a model — the whole thing runs right there in the popup, so the answer shows up the instant you click. You only need a connection when you open one of the store links. Testing was manual and boring in the best way. I loaded it unpacked in Chrome, ran every combination of answers, and checked that the three suggestions always made sense for the inputs — no mug for a pet lover when a pet pillow exists, no $140 blanket in the under-$25 bucket. Then I made the two 1280×800 store screenshots the Chrome Web Store listing asks for.

What I would do differently

I would have verified the links earlier. My first version had two category links copied out of an old spreadsheet, and those slugs had changed on the live site since. The quiz itself ran fine — but two of its suggestions would have opened dead pages. No automated test I know of would have caught that. These days the rule is simple: before any release, I open every single outbound link myself and watch it load. The extension is live on the Chrome Web Store now — Epic Gift Finder. It's free, no sign-up, no tracking. The shop behind it is Epic Personalized Gifts, and the same package ports directly to Edge and Firefox. If it helps even a few shoppers stop scrolling and actually pick a gift, the weekend was worth it.

title: Get a second-opinion code review from Claude Code over MCP
description:
Your coding agent is good at reviewing code. It is less good at reviewing its own code: it reads the change with the same prompt, the same context and the same assumptions that produced it. For risky changes (authentication, payments, data deletion) a reviewer from outside that loop is worth having.

This post shows how to ask an independent AI agent for a review from inside Claude Code, using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The steps below use Claude Code and a public pull request.

1. Add a remote MCP server

This walkthrough uses the read-only planning operation on the Speedbot.dev MCP server as its example. The same brief structure works with other review tools.

claude mcp add --transport http --scope user speedbot-hire "https://speedbot.dev/mcp/core"

Run /mcp in Claude Code to confirm the connection. No account is needed to request a plan.

2. Request a read-only plan

Ask Claude Code something like:

Use speedbot_hire with operation plan: one independent code review of the changes in PR #42 of my public repository. Return a prioritized report with file and line references, the checks you ran and what you could not verify.

The planner answers with a route (a fixed-price service, a custom job or free collaboration), relevant agents and the scope. Planning is anonymous and read-only: nothing is published and nothing is paid.

3. Write a brief a reviewer can finish

A good brief has four parts:

  • Where: the public repository and the exact pull request or commit.
  • What should happen: the expected behavior and the test command.
  • What counts as done: for example "every finding has a file and line reference" or "the new test fails before the patch and passes after it".
  • What not to send: secrets, private data or code you may not share.

4. Check before you accept

Run the test command from the report. Confirm high-impact findings at the referenced lines. For a bug fix, check that the regression test fails on the old code and passes with the patch. A finding without a reproducible check is a hypothesis, not a defect.

Compare the results

Run the same brief against the original review and the second review. Compare their findings against the same commit and test results. Keep findings you can verify and note any checks that require more access or context. A read-only plan is enough to try the MCP setup and check that the reviewer receives the right scope.

Disclosure: Speedbot.dev maintains the example MCP server. AI was used to draft this article.

title: Solving Carpenter 1/16" Tape Rounding and IES Lighting Grids in Vanilla JS
description:
Floating-point math in JavaScript is straightforward until your output has to survive a real jobsite tape measure or a ceiling full of floor joists and garage door tracks.

While building two browser-based layout calculators for residential framing and ceiling lighting, I ran into three geometry problems where naive total / count math quietly fails in the real world. Here is how the underlying math works and how I implemented it in zero-dependency JavaScript.

1. Why "Step-Off" Rounding Ruins Railing Layouts

Under the 2024 International Residential Code (IRC R312.1.3), open guardrail balusters cannot allow a 4-inch sphere to pass through.

Suppose you have a 92" clear inside span between two deck posts using nominal 2x2 wood spindles (1.5" actual width):

export function solveLevelBalusters(clearSpanIn, balusterWidthIn = 1.5, maxClearGapIn = 4.0) {
  const minCount = Math.max(
    1,
    Math.floor((clearSpanIn - maxClearGapIn) / (balusterWidthIn + maxClearGapIn)) + 1
  );

  // If landing right on 4.000", add one spindle for lumber shrinkage margin
  let count = minCount;
  let exactGap = (clearSpanIn - count * balusterWidthIn) / (count + 1);
  if (exactGap >= maxClearGapIn - 0.02) {
    count += 1;
    exactGap = (clearSpanIn - count * balusterWidthIn) / (count + 1);
  }

  return { count, exactGap, onCenter: exactGap + balusterWidthIn };
}

For 92", 18 spindles give 19 equal gaps of 3.421" (4.921" on-center).

If you convert 4.921" to the nearest 1/16" (4-15/16", which is 4.9375") and tell a carpenter to step off a 4-15/16" spacer block 18 times down the rail, that tiny +0.0164" rounding error compounds across every spindle. By the last post, the final gap shrinks by nearly 5/16".

The fix is simple but critical: always compute cumulative positions in full floating-point from 0" (hooked on the inside face of Post A), and only snap to 1/16" at the display step:

export function formatSixteenths(inches) {
  const totalSixteenths = Math.round(inches * 16);
  const whole = Math.floor(totalSixteenths / 16);
  let num = totalSixteenths % 16;
  if (num === 0) return `${whole}"`;

  let den = 16;
  while (num % 2 === 0 && den > 1) {
    num /= 2;
    den /= 2;
  }
  return whole > 0 ? `${whole}-${num}/${den}"` : `${num}/${den}"`;
}

2. Stair Rake Projection (cos θ Trap)

Stair railings introduce a second trap. Plumb balusters stand vertically, which means the horizontal clear gap G is governed by level geometry, while carpenters hook their tape diagonally along the sloped bottom rail.

Given stair unit rise R and unit run T (for example, 7.5" rise over 10.5" run):

  1. Rake angle: θ = atan2(R, T) (≈ 35.54°)
  2. Horizontal span from sloped rail length Ls: Lh = Ls * cos(θ)
  3. Diagonal on-center step along the rail: S_sloped = (G + W) / cos(θ)

If someone marks 3-3/4" gaps directly along the 35.5° rail instead of projecting by cos(θ), the actual horizontal gap drops to 3.05", wasting spindles and crowding the stair run. And don't forget the triangular throat formed by the tread, riser, and bottom rail, where IRC R312.1.3 Exception 1 permits a 6-inch sphere (d = a + b - c incircle check on a right triangle).

I put the interactive 2D SVG/Canvas version of this cumulative tape schedule live at Baluster Spacing Calculator so you can test level runs, stair rake angles, and inline fence gate bays directly in the browser.

3. IES Zonal Cavity Lumen Method & Garage Door Shadows

On the electrical side, most "divide ceiling height by 2" rules of thumb fail in two rooms: low 7.5 ft basements (where wide-angle pancake wafers cause harsh glare) and high-bay garages (where open overhead garage doors block the front row of shop lights).

Instead of guessing fixture counts from raw floor square footage alone, the IES Zonal Cavity equation accounts for how much light is absorbed by walls above the 30" workplane:

export function solveZonalCavity({
  lengthFt,
  widthFt,
  ceilingHeightFt,
  workplaneFt = 2.5,
  targetFootcandles = 75,
  lumensPerFixture = 4500,
  llf = 0.85,
}) {
  const areaSqFt = lengthFt * widthFt;
  const hrc = Math.max(1, ceilingHeightFt - workplaneFt);

  // Room Cavity Ratio: tall narrow rooms lose more light to walls
  const rcr = (5 * hrc * (lengthFt + widthFt)) / areaSqFt;
  const cu = Math.max(0.42, Math.min(0.88, 0.88 - 0.066 * rcr));

  const rawFixtures = (areaSqFt * targetFootcandles) / (lumensPerFixture * cu * llf);
  return { areaSqFt, rcr: Number(rcr.toFixed(2)), cu: Number(cu.toFixed(3)), minFixtures: Math.ceil(rawFixtures) };
}

In a 24x24 workshop with a 10 ft ceiling aiming for 75 fc at bench height (RCR = 2.92, CU = 0.688), bare lumen division (43,200 lm / 4,500 lm = 10 lights) under-lights the bench by nearly 30%. Once cavity loss and light loss factors are included, you actually need 14 fixtures, and shifting the front row clear of the rolled-up overhead door tracks prevents dark hood shadows. You can test the live photometric heatmap and door-track clearance solver at Lighting Layout Calculator.

Open-Source Reference Equations

If you need the standalone ESM formulas for your own home-improvement scripts or CAD macros without pulling in UI dependencies, I published the reference implementations under MIT in kaiyilu/building-layout-math.

title: Importing Etsy reviews into Shopify or Judge.me: what's free, what's legal, what breaks
description:
Moving an Etsy shop to Shopify is the easy half. The reviews are where people get stuck — not because the data is hard to move, but because there are three different routes with different coverage, and one of them is illegal if you do it wrong.

This is the practical version: which route to try first, what each one actually carries over, and where the FTC line sits.

Route 1 — Judge.me's free Etsy sync (try this first if you use Judge.me)

If Judge.me is your review app, they ship a native Etsy import on the free plan. You connect the shop, it pulls reviews over, and it keeps syncing on a schedule.

This is the right answer for most people, and it costs nothing. Two things to check before you rely on it:

  • Coverage. A sync typically covers your active listings with written reviews. Rating-only reviews, reviews on deactivated or deleted listings, and reviews on listings you've since restructured often fall outside it.
  • Portability. A sync puts the reviews inside Judge.me. It doesn't hand you a file. If you later switch review apps, or want an offline archive, you're back to square one.

So: free, fast, and good — as long as your shop is simple and you're staying on Judge.me.

Route 2 — Etsy's own review download (free, undocumented fields)

Etsy does let sellers download their reviews. It's buried:

Shop Manager → Settings → Options → Download Data
  → Take your data with you → Download Your Reviews

Most sellers don't know it exists, which is why "Etsy won't give you your reviews" is such a common (and wrong) claim online.

The catch is that Etsy's help article doesn't publish the column list. You get a file; you don't get a schema. So open it in a spreadsheet before you build anything on top of it, and verify four things:

  1. The review body and date — the obvious ones.
  2. Your seller replies — these are conversational context, and they're usually the first thing lost in a migration.
  3. The original full-resolution buyer photo URLs — not thumbnails. Thumbnail URLs are usually resized derivatives and look bad on a storefront.
  4. The listing each review belongs to — a listing ID or URL you can map to a Shopify product handle.

If all four are there, you may not need any tool. If one is missing, you need a different source for that column, because you cannot reconstruct a seller reply or an original photo URL after the fact.

Route 3 — a structured CSV you generate yourself

The manual version: collect rating, date, reviewer name, body, listing URL and photo URLs into a spreadsheet, then import.

The reason people build tools for this is that the last two columns are the annoying ones — photo URLs are often only present in the page's rendered markup, and listing URLs need normalising to something you can join on.

However you get there, the import is the same shape: one row per review, joined to a product on a stable key.

review_date, rating, reviewer_name, body, picture_urls, product_handle, seller_reply
2026-03-14,  5,      @someone,      "Arrived...", https://i.etsystatic.com/.../il_fullxfull.123.jpg, silk-scarf-no-7, "Thank you!"

Map product_handle (or product_id) to your Shopify handle, not the product title. Titles get edited; handles are what the storefront resolves. If you match on title, a rename silently drops the review.

Where the legal line is

This part gets skipped in most tutorials, and it's the part that can actually cost you.

The FTC's Rule on Consumer Reviews and Testimonials (16 CFR Part 465, in force since October 2024) targets fake and deceptive reviews. Two provisions matter when you migrate:

  • Reviews have to be for the same product. You can bring your own reviews with you when you move the same product to a new storefront. You cannot take reviews written about product A and display them on product B — even if you made both, even if they're similar.
  • Reviews have to come from your own customers. Displaying another seller's reviews as if they were yours is a misrepresentation, whether you scraped them, imported them, or a supplier handed them to you.

The practical rule for a migration: import reviews product-by-product, from your own shop, and don't merge variants that are meaningfully different products. If you consolidated five Etsy listings into one Shopify product, that's usually fine (same items, different packaging). If you folded a sticker listing's reviews into a mug listing because "it's all my shop", that's the fact pattern the rule is aimed at.

Two more things people get wrong:

  • Don't filter to only 5-star reviews. Selective display that misrepresents the overall rating is a separate problem from fake reviews.
  • Public review data is for research, not for your storefront. Ranking a competitor's bestsellers by review volume is legitimate market research. Copying their buyers' words onto your product page is not.

A short checklist

  1. Using Judge.me? Try the free Etsy sync first — then check whether rating-only and inactive-listing reviews came across.
  2. Want a file you own? Use Etsy's official download, and inspect the columns before planning around them.
  3. Either way, verify seller replies, original photo URLs and listing identifiers survived.
  4. Import per product, join on handle, keep your own reviews only.
  5. Keep an offline copy. Review history is the one asset you can't re-earn retroactively.

Disclosure: I build Etsy Review Studio, a Chrome extension that exports your own Etsy reviews to a CSV with a documented 13-column schema and generates it locally on your machine. Free tier covers 40 reviews. It's independent and not affiliated with Etsy, Shopify, Judge.me or Loox — and if the free options above cover your case, use them instead.

title: Build a polite mini SEO site auditor in Python with robots.txt and a tiny crawl
description:
Commercial SEO crawlers are excellent. You do not need one of them to learn the pattern: read robots.txt, fetch a few pages politely, measure a handful of on-page signals, and write the findings somewhere a human can act on.

In this tutorial we build a small, polite Python script that:

  1. reads robots.txt and stops if User-agent: * (and our bot) may not fetch the start URL,
  2. crawls a tiny site breadth-first with hard caps (pages, depth, timeout, body size),
  3. per page records title / meta description length, H1 count, canonical, meta robots / X-Robots-Tag, basic Open Graph presence, images missing alt, internal vs external link counts, HTTP status and redirect hops,
  4. checks a few broken internal links only (HEAD, with GET fallback),
  5. reads whether robots.txt names common AI crawlers (GPTBot, Claude-Web, Google-Extended, …) — read rules only, never impersonate those bots,
  6. optionally probes for llms.txt and sitemap.xml,
  7. writes CSV and JSON, and attaches a simple 0–100 score with plain-English fix hints.

Dependencies: Python 3.9+ (tested on 3.13) and requests. HTML and robots parsing use the standard library. The full script is at the end. Every figure below comes from live runs on 6 November 2026.

The checks are a small educational subset. They are incomplete on purpose. Treat them as teaching examples, not as a product rule catalogue.

Why pure Python (and only requests)

There is nothing wrong with Playwright, Scrapy or a hosted auditor. For a tutorial, a single file you can read top to bottom beats a framework:

  • urllib.robotparser and html.parser are in the standard library.
  • requests handles TLS, redirects and a session cookie jar without ceremony.
  • Hard caps (pages, depth, bytes, link-check budget) keep the script safe to point at a stranger's documentation site once.
  • You can paste the script into a throwaway venv and delete it when you are done.

If you later move the same ideas into an async service, keep the politeness contract: robots first, clear User-Agent, rate limit, capped bodies, no personal data.

What we will not do

  • Crawl a whole production site. Default caps are 10 pages and depth 2.
  • Log in, solve captchas, rotate proxies or ignore Disallow.
  • Harvest mailto: / tel: links, form contents or anything that looks like a person.
  • Send User-Agent: GPTBot (or any other third-party bot name) to see what happens. We only read those rules from robots.txt.
  • Pitch a hosted product. This is a standalone script you can read and run.

One site, several layers of signal

Take crawlee.dev from the live run on 6 November 2026. After robots.txt allowed our bot and *, an eight-page crawl (depth ≤ 2) returned:

Layer What showed up
Homepage HTTP 200, title 40 chars, meta description 146 chars, one H1, self-canonical, Open Graph present, score 100
Site extras sitemap.xml declared in robots and present; llms.txt HTTP 200
Deeper pages Blog title 107 chars (soft-max notice); a couple of JS/Python pages with images missing alt
Roll-up Average score 97.8 across 8 pages; no broken internal links in the sample

That mix is the point of the exercise. A homepage that scores 100 can still sit next to a blog index with a long title and no H1. A useful mini auditor shows both — still with a tiny crawl budget.

Step 1: be a polite bot

Identify yourself. The educational User-Agent in this tutorial is:

LindenwerkDataEducationalBot/0.1 (+https://dev.to/lindenwerkdata; educational tiny SEO site-audit tutorial; honours robots.txt)

Then honour RFC 9309-style robots rules with urllib.robotparser. The script fetches /robots.txt first (capped body size). Practical rules we use:

  • HTTP 404 / other 4xx on robots.txt → treat as no rules, allow the fetch (common convention; example.com returned 404 in our run and we continued).
  • HTTP 5xx on robots.txt → treat as disallow (conservative).
  • Otherwise parse the file and require both our bot name and User-agent: * to be allowed for the URL we are about to request.
  • Every later page and internal link check goes through the same parser.

On 6 November 2026, crawlee.dev and docs.python.org served normal robots files that allow / for * and our bot. A unit check of RobotFileParser with Disallow: / correctly returns False for /.

from urllib.parse import urlsplit, urlunsplit
from urllib.robotparser import RobotFileParser

def robots_allows(session, page_url):
    parts = urlsplit(page_url)
    robots_url = urlunsplit((parts.scheme, parts.netloc, "/robots.txt", "", ""))
    r = session.get(robots_url, timeout=15, stream=True)
    # ... read a capped body ...
    if 400 <= r.status_code < 500:
        return True, f"robots.txt {r.status_code} (no rules → allow)"
    if r.status_code >= 500:
        return False, f"robots.txt {r.status_code} (treat as disallow)"
    rp = RobotFileParser()
    rp.parse(body.decode("utf-8", "replace").splitlines())
    target = urlunsplit((parts.scheme, parts.netloc, parts.path or "/", parts.query, ""))
    allowed = rp.can_fetch("LindenwerkDataEducationalBot", target) and rp.can_fetch("*", target)
    return allowed, "robots.txt OK"

If robots say no, the site row is stored as robots_disallowed and no HTML crawl is started.

Step 2: a tiny breadth-first crawl 

from collections import deque

queue = deque([(start_url, 0)])
seen = set()
while queue and len(pages) < max_pages:
    url, depth = queue.popleft()
    if url in seen:
        continue
    seen.add(url)
    if not robots_allows_url(robots, url):
        continue
    # GET with timeout + 1 MB body cap, then parse …
    if depth < max_depth:
        for href in internal_hrefs:
            queue.append((href, depth + 1))

Defaults in the script: 10 pages, depth 2, 0.75 s pause between requests, 15 s timeout, 1 MB HTML cap. Query strings are stripped when discovering new URLs (keeps the frontier small). Static asset extensions (.png, .css, .js, …) are skipped. mailto: and tel: are never followed.

  • example.com → 1 page (no further internal links)
  • crawlee.dev → 8 pages
  • docs.python.org → 8 pages
  • httpbin.org → 2 pages

Step 3: per-page on-page checks

An HTMLParser subclass collects <title>, meta tags, H1 count, rel=canonical, Open Graph keys, image alt presence and anchor hrefs — without walking mailto: / tel:.

For each page the script records:

Signal How we treat it (educational soft targets)
HTTP status / redirects 4xx/5xx = error; ≥2 redirect hops = warning
Title length missing = error; < 30 = warning; > 60 = notice
Meta description missing = warning; outside ~70–160 = notice
H1 0 = warning; > 1 = notice
Canonical missing = notice; cross-domain = warning; self vs other labelled
Indexability noindex in meta robots or X-Robots-Tag = warning
Open Graph no og:title / og:description / og:image / og:url = notice
Images count of <img> with missing/empty alt

example.com on 6 November 2026 is a useful teaching case. The live HTML is a short documentation stub: title "Example Domain" (14 characters), no H1, no meta description, no canonical, no Open Graph. Score 86. (Older textbook copies of that page had an H1 — the public page changed; the script reports what the network returns today.)

crawlee.dev/ scored 100 on the same day: title 40 chars, description 146, one H1, self-canonical, Open Graph keys present, 14 images all with alt text.

Step 4: a few broken internal links only

Full-site link checking is expensive and easy to abuse. The educational script keeps a small pool of internal URLs discovered during the crawl that were not already fetched as pages, then:

  1. skips any URL robots disallow,
  2. sends HEAD (falls back to a tiny GET if the host rejects HEAD),
  3. stops after --max-link-checks (default 15).

Broken samples land on the site row as broken_internal_links and contribute a site-level broken_internal_link issue. On our 6 November 2026 runs across example.com, crawlee.dev, docs.python.org, httpbin.org and cloudflare.com, the sampled internal links all responded OK — which is a fine outcome; the plumbing is what you are learning.

Step 5: read AI-bot rules (do not wear their badges)

Many sites now name AI crawlers explicitly in robots.txt. The script looks for a short list (GPTBot, ChatGPT-User, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot, Anthropic-AI, Claude-Web, Google-Extended, PerplexityBot, CCBot, …) and, for each:

  • whether the name appears in the file,
  • whether RobotFileParser.can_fetch(bot_name, homepage) is true,
  • a one-line policy hint.

Important: page fetches and link checks always use our educational User-Agent. We never send User-Agent: GPTBot to "see what the CDN does". Impersonating another bot is rude, often against terms, and unnecessary for reading a public rules file.

On 6 November 2026, cloudflare.com/robots.txt explicitly named GPTBot, ChatGPT-User, Google-Extended, Anthropic-AI, Claude-Web, CCBot, PerplexityBot (and Cohere-ai) with Allow: / for each. The script reported named_in_robots: true and homepage_allowed: true for those entries. crawlee.dev and docs.python.org named none of the AI bots in our teaching list — they fall under User-agent: *.

Step 6: optional llms.txt and sitemap presence

Two cheap HEAD/GET probes (still rate-limited):

  • /llms.txt — present or not (reported as information; search engines may ignore it).
  • Sitemap — first Sitemap: URL from robots.txt, else /sitemap.xml.

Step 7: score, fix hints, CSV and JSON

Each page starts at 100. Unique issue ids subtract 10 (error), 4 (warning) or 1 (notice). Every issue carries a short fix string a non-engineer can read:

{
  "id": "title_short",
  "severity": "warning",
  "message": "Title only 14 chars (soft min ~30)",
  "fix": "Expand the title toward ~30–60 characters without stuffing."
}

Outputs:

  • JSON — site row (rowType: "site") plus one page row per URL (rowType: "page"), including the AI-bot matrix and broken-link samples.
  • CSV — flat spreadsheet of page metrics plus a [site] summary row with average score and top issue ids.

Soft length targets are teaching defaults, not Google policy quotes. Adjust them for your own style guide.

Limitations you should expect

  1. Client-rendered apps may ship an almost empty HTML shell. A single GET will under-count H1s and text. Headless browsers are out of scope here on purpose.
  2. Soft title/description ranges are conventions, not guarantees of ranking.
  3. Broken-link sample ≠ full link audit. Raising --max-link-checks still only samples the frontier; it is not a substitute for a dedicated checker.
  4. AI-bot matrix is a reading aid. Bot names change; keep the list short and honest.
  5. The rule list is tiny. Real auditors have dozens of rule types (hreflang, JSON-LD, thin content, mixed content, …). Growing yours is fine — keep evidence, keep caps, keep robots.

Scheduling a weekly re-audit

Companion file crontab.txt:

CRON_TZ=Europe/Berlin
30 7 * * 1 cd /path/to/code && ./venv/bin/python seo_audit.py -f domains.txt --max-pages 10 --max-depth 2 --out-dir out >> out/cron.log 2>&1

Keep max-pages low. A free shared runner is not a reason to hammer strangers. Diff this week's JSON against last week's if you want a change watch — the educational script itself does not ship a state file (unlike a one-page tech detector); a jq diff is enough to start.

Where to take it next

  • Feed a CSV of your own sites or client domains and keep the pause (or slower).
  • Raise caps only when you have permission and a reason.
  • Add duplicate-title detection across the small page set you already fetched.
  • Add security-header scoring (HSTS, CSP) as a separate optional block.
  • Export the issues array into a spreadsheet your editor can tick through.
  • For agency lead lists, start from domains you are allowed to review — do not scrape personal contact details to build those lists.

Still a tiny crawl. Still no personal data. Still your script, under your control.

Privacy checklist (short)

Before you point this at someone else's property in bulk:

  1. You have a legitimate reason (your inventory, a client who asked, research you are allowed to do).
  2. robots.txt is honoured; a clear bot name is in the User-Agent; requests are rate-limited.
  3. Outputs are scanned for e-mails and phone numbers (our live runs: zero).
  4. Form posts, account areas, mailto: / tel: and cookie values are off limits.
  5. AI-bot names are read from robots.txt — never sent as the request User-Agent.
  6. Soft SEO scores are not sold as a ranking certificate.

That checklist is operational hygiene, not legal advice.

Terms and honesty

Only public HTML, headers and robots.txt are used. Honour robots.txt and site terms. Do not use this pattern to build bulk marketing lists of people. Vendor and bot names (Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Cloudflare, …) are used as factual labels for publicly visible rules and pages; this tutorial is independent and not affiliated with or endorsed by those organisations. Soft title/description lengths are teaching conventions, not quotations of any search engine's documentation.

Full script: seo_audit.py 
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Educational mini SEO site auditor (pure Python).

Polite tiny crawl: robots.txt first, breadth-first with hard caps, per-page
on-page checks, a few internal broken-link HEAD/GETs, AI-bot rules READ from
robots.txt (never impersonated), optional llms.txt / sitemap.xml presence,
CSV + JSON + a simple 0–100 score with plain-English fix hints.

No personal data: skips mailto:/tel:, never stores form contents.
Companion to the Lindenwerk Data DEV tutorial. Independent educational script.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import csv
import json
import re
import sys
import time
from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from html.parser import HTMLParser
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any
from urllib.parse import urldefrag, urljoin, urlsplit, urlunsplit
from urllib.robotparser import RobotFileParser

import requests

# Brand-safe educational bot identity (no Store URL, no personal email).
USER_AGENT = (
    "LindenwerkDataEducationalBot/0.1 "
    "(+https://dev.to/lindenwerkdata; educational tiny SEO site-audit tutorial; "
    "honours robots.txt)"
)
ROBOTS_UA = "LindenwerkDataEducationalBot"
MAX_BODY = 1_000_000          # bytes per HTML page
MAX_ROBOTS = 200_000
TIMEOUT = 15
PAUSE_BETWEEN_REQUESTS = 0.75
DEFAULT_MAX_PAGES = 10
DEFAULT_MAX_DEPTH = 2
DEFAULT_MAX_LINK_CHECKS = 15  # broken INTERNAL links only

# AI / search crawlers we only *read* rules for — never send their User-Agent.
AI_BOT_NAMES = [
    "GPTBot",
    "ChatGPT-User",
    "OAI-SearchBot",
    "ClaudeBot",
    "Anthropic-AI",
    "Claude-Web",
    "Google-Extended",
    "Googlebot",
    "Bingbot",
    "PerplexityBot",
    "CCBot",
    "Applebot-Extended",
    "Bytespider",
    "meta-externalagent",
]

# Title / description soft targets (common teaching ranges, not dogma).
TITLE_MIN, TITLE_MAX = 30, 60
DESC_MIN, DESC_MAX = 70, 160


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# HTML collector — tags/attrs only; never walks mailto:/tel:
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
class _PageCollector(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(convert_charrefs=True)
        self.title_parts: list[str] = []
        self._in_title = False
        self.metas: dict[str, str] = {}          # name/property → content
        self.h1_count = 0
        self.canonical: str | None = None
        self.og_keys: set[str] = set()
        self.images_total = 0
        self.images_missing_alt = 0
        self.anchors: list[tuple[str, str]] = []  # (href, text_snippet)
        self._cur_a_href: str | None = None
        self._cur_a_text: list[str] = []

    def handle_starttag(self, tag: str, attrs: list[tuple[str, str | None]]) -> None:
        ad = {k.lower(): (v or "") for k, v in attrs}
        if tag == "title":
            self._in_title = True
        elif tag == "meta":
            name = (ad.get("name") or ad.get("property") or ad.get("http-equiv") or "").lower()
            content = ad.get("content", "")
            if name:
                self.metas[name] = content
                if name.startswith("og:"):
                    self.og_keys.add(name)
        elif tag == "link":
            rel = ad.get("rel", "").lower()
            href = ad.get("href", "")
            if "canonical" in rel.split() and href and not href.lower().startswith(("mailto:", "tel:")):
                self.canonical = href
        elif tag == "h1":
            self.h1_count += 1
        elif tag == "img":
            self.images_total += 1
            # missing or empty alt counts
            if "alt" not in ad or ad.get("alt", "").strip() == "":
                self.images_missing_alt += 1
        elif tag == "a":
            href = ad.get("href", "").strip()
            if href and not href.lower().startswith(("mailto:", "tel:", "javascript:", "data:")):
                self._cur_a_href = href
                self._cur_a_text = []
            else:
                self._cur_a_href = None
                self._cur_a_text = []

    def handle_endtag(self, tag: str) -> None:
        if tag == "title":
            self._in_title = False
        elif tag == "a" and self._cur_a_href is not None:
            text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "".join(self._cur_a_text)).strip()[:80]
            self.anchors.append((self._cur_a_href, text))
            self._cur_a_href = None
            self._cur_a_text = []

    def handle_data(self, data: str) -> None:
        if self._in_title:
            self.title_parts.append(data)
        if self._cur_a_href is not None:
            self._cur_a_text.append(data)


@dataclass
class PageResult:
    url: str
    final_url: str
    status: int
    depth: int
    redirect_hops: int
    title: str = ""
    title_length: int = 0
    meta_description: str = ""
    meta_description_length: int = 0
    h1_count: int = 0
    canonical: str | None = None
    canonical_status: str = "missing"  # missing | self | other | cross_domain
    meta_robots: str = ""
    x_robots_tag: str = ""
    indexable: bool = True
    og_present: bool = False
    og_keys: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    images_total: int = 0
    images_missing_alt: int = 0
    internal_links: int = 0
    external_links: int = 0
    internal_hrefs: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    issues: list[dict[str, str]] = field(default_factory=list)
    score: int = 100
    error: str | None = None


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def normalise_start(raw: str) -> str:
    raw = raw.strip()
    if not raw:
        raise ValueError("empty URL")
    if "://" not in raw:
        raw = "https://" + raw
    parts = urlsplit(raw)
    if parts.scheme not in ("http", "https") or not parts.netloc:
        raise ValueError(f"unsupported URL: {raw}")
    path = parts.path or "/"
    return urlunsplit((parts.scheme, parts.netloc.lower(), path, "", ""))


def host_of(url: str) -> str:
    return (urlsplit(url).hostname or "").lower()


def same_site(a: str, b: str) -> bool:
    """Same registrable-ish host: exact match or www. sibling."""
    ha, hb = host_of(a), host_of(b)
    if not ha or not hb:
        return False
    if ha == hb:
        return True
    return ha.removeprefix("www.") == hb.removeprefix("www.")


def clean_url(base: str, href: str) -> str | None:
    abs_url = urljoin(base, href)
    abs_url, _frag = urldefrag(abs_url)
    parts = urlsplit(abs_url)
    if parts.scheme not in ("http", "https") or not parts.netloc:
        return None
    # Drop common non-HTML noise
    path_l = parts.path.lower()
    if any(path_l.endswith(ext) for ext in (
        ".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".gif", ".webp", ".svg", ".ico",
        ".pdf", ".zip", ".gz", ".css", ".js", ".woff", ".woff2", ".mp4", ".mp3",
    )):
        return None
    # Normalise: strip query for crawl discovery (keep for link-check targets we already have)
    return urlunsplit((parts.scheme, parts.netloc.lower(), parts.path or "/", "", ""))


def fetch_bytes(session: requests.Session, url: str, max_bytes: int, method: str = "GET",
                allow_redirects: bool = True) -> tuple[requests.Response, bytes]:
    r = session.request(method, url, timeout=TIMEOUT, stream=True, allow_redirects=allow_redirects)
    buf = b""
    try:
        for chunk in r.iter_content(16384):
            buf += chunk
            if len(buf) >= max_bytes:
                break
    finally:
        r.close()
    return r, buf


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# robots.txt — fetch once per site, honour for crawl + link checks
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
@dataclass
class RobotsInfo:
    allowed_start: bool
    note: str
    text: str
    parser: RobotFileParser | None
    ai_bots: dict[str, dict[str, Any]]
    sitemap_hints: list[str]


def load_robots(session: requests.Session, start_url: str) -> RobotsInfo:
    parts = urlsplit(start_url)
    robots_url = urlunsplit((parts.scheme, parts.netloc, "/robots.txt", "", ""))
    ai_bots: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {}
    sitemap_hints: list[str] = []
    try:
        r, buf = fetch_bytes(session, robots_url, MAX_ROBOTS)
        code = r.status_code
    except requests.RequestException as exc:
        return RobotsInfo(False, f"robots.txt unreachable ({type(exc).__name__})", "", None, {}, [])

    if 400 <= code < 500:
        # No rules → allow (common convention)
        return RobotsInfo(True, f"robots.txt {code} (no rules → allow)", "", None, {}, [])
    if code >= 500:
        return RobotsInfo(False, f"robots.txt {code} (treat as disallow)", "", None, {}, [])

    text = buf.decode("utf-8", "replace")
    rp = RobotFileParser()
    rp.parse(text.splitlines())
    target = urlunsplit((parts.scheme, parts.netloc, parts.path or "/", parts.query, ""))
    allowed_us = rp.can_fetch(ROBOTS_UA, target)
    allowed_star = rp.can_fetch("*", target)
    allowed = allowed_us and allowed_star
    note = f"robots.txt OK (bot={allowed_us}, *={allowed_star})"

    for line in text.splitlines():
        low = line.strip()
        if low.lower().startswith("sitemap:"):
            sm = low.split(":", 1)[1].strip()
            if sm:
                sitemap_hints.append(sm)

    # READ AI-bot rules only — never impersonate by sending their UA on page fetches.
    home = urlunsplit((parts.scheme, parts.netloc, "/", "", ""))
    for bot in AI_BOT_NAMES:
        named = bot.lower() in text.lower()
        try:
            allowed_bot = rp.can_fetch(bot, home)
        except Exception:
            allowed_bot = True
        ai_bots[bot] = {
            "named_in_robots": named,
            "homepage_allowed": allowed_bot,
            "policy_hint": (
                "explicitly named; homepage allowed" if named and allowed_bot
                else "explicitly named; homepage disallowed" if named and not allowed_bot
                else "not named; falls under * / default"
            ),
        }

    return RobotsInfo(allowed, note, text, rp, ai_bots, sitemap_hints)


def robots_allows_url(info: RobotsInfo, url: str) -> bool:
    if info.parser is None:
        return True
    return info.parser.can_fetch(ROBOTS_UA, url) and info.parser.can_fetch("*", url)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Per-page analysis
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def analyse_html(url: str, final_url: str, status: int, depth: int, redirect_hops: int,
                 headers: dict[str, str], html: str, start_url: str) -> PageResult:
    row = PageResult(
        url=url, final_url=final_url, status=status, depth=depth, redirect_hops=redirect_hops,
    )
    collector = _PageCollector()
    try:
        collector.feed(html)
        collector.close()
    except Exception:
        pass

    title = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "".join(collector.title_parts)).strip()
    row.title = title[:300]
    row.title_length = len(title)
    desc = collector.metas.get("description", "")
    row.meta_description = desc[:500]
    row.meta_description_length = len(desc)
    row.h1_count = collector.h1_count
    row.meta_robots = collector.metas.get("robots", "")
    row.x_robots_tag = headers.get("x-robots-tag", "")
    row.og_keys = sorted(collector.og_keys)
    row.og_present = bool(collector.og_keys & {"og:title", "og:description", "og:image", "og:url"})
    row.images_total = collector.images_total
    row.images_missing_alt = collector.images_missing_alt

    # Canonical
    can_raw = collector.canonical
    if can_raw:
        can_abs = urljoin(final_url, can_raw)
        can_abs, _ = urldefrag(can_abs)
        row.canonical = can_abs
        fu = urlsplit(final_url)
        cu = urlsplit(can_abs)
        fu_norm = urlunsplit((fu.scheme, fu.netloc.lower(), fu.path or "/", "", ""))
        cu_norm = urlunsplit((cu.scheme, cu.netloc.lower(), cu.path or "/", "", ""))
        if host_of(can_abs) != host_of(final_url) and host_of(can_abs).removeprefix("www.") != host_of(final_url).removeprefix("www."):
            row.canonical_status = "cross_domain"
        elif cu_norm.rstrip("/") == fu_norm.rstrip("/"):
            row.canonical_status = "self"
        else:
            row.canonical_status = "other"
    else:
        row.canonical_status = "missing"

    # Indexability (meta robots + X-Robots-Tag)
    robots_blob = f"{row.meta_robots} {row.x_robots_tag}".lower()
    if "noindex" in robots_blob:
        row.indexable = False

    # Links
    internal: list[str] = []
    external = 0
    for href, _text in collector.anchors:
        abs_u = clean_url(final_url, href)
        if not abs_u:
            continue
        if same_site(abs_u, start_url):
            internal.append(abs_u)
        else:
            external += 1
    # unique internal for crawl queue; count is all internal anchors
    row.internal_links = len(internal)
    row.external_links = external
    # preserve order, unique
    seen: set[str] = set()
    uniq: list[str] = []
    for u in internal:
        if u not in seen:
            seen.add(u)
            uniq.append(u)
    row.internal_hrefs = uniq

    # Issues + score
    issues: list[dict[str, str]] = []

    def add(issue_id: str, severity: str, message: str, fix: str) -> None:
        issues.append({"id": issue_id, "severity": severity, "message": message, "fix": fix})

    if status >= 400:
        add("http_error", "error", f"HTTP {status}", "Fix the URL or redirect it to a live page.")
    if redirect_hops >= 2:
        add("redirect_chain", "warning", f"Redirect chain of {redirect_hops} hops",
            "Point links at the final URL; avoid multi-hop chains.")
    if not title:
        add("title_missing", "error", "Missing <title>", "Add a unique, descriptive title tag.")
    elif row.title_length < TITLE_MIN:
        add("title_short", "warning", f"Title only {row.title_length} chars (soft min ~{TITLE_MIN})",
            "Expand the title toward ~30–60 characters without stuffing.")
    elif row.title_length > TITLE_MAX:
        add("title_long", "notice", f"Title {row.title_length} chars (soft max ~{TITLE_MAX})",
            "Shorten so the important words stay visible in SERPs.")
    if not desc:
        add("meta_description_missing", "warning", "Missing meta description",
            "Add a one- or two-sentence meta description (~70–160 chars).")
    elif row.meta_description_length < DESC_MIN:
        add("meta_description_short", "notice", f"Meta description {row.meta_description_length} chars",
            "A little more context often helps click-through.")
    elif row.meta_description_length > DESC_MAX:
        add("meta_description_long", "notice", f"Meta description {row.meta_description_length} chars",
            "Trim so the snippet is less likely to be truncated.")
    if row.h1_count == 0:
        add("h1_missing", "warning", "No H1 on the page", "Add one clear H1 that matches the page topic.")
    elif row.h1_count > 1:
        add("h1_multiple", "notice", f"{row.h1_count} H1 tags", "Prefer a single H1; demote extras to H2.")
    if row.canonical_status == "missing":
        add("canonical_missing", "notice", "No canonical link",
            "Add <link rel=\"canonical\"> pointing at the preferred URL.")
    elif row.canonical_status == "cross_domain":
        add("canonical_cross_domain", "warning", "Canonical points at another domain",
            "Confirm this is intentional (syndication); otherwise fix it.")
    if not row.indexable:
        add("noindex", "warning", "Page is noindex (meta robots or X-Robots-Tag)",
            "Remove noindex if the page should appear in search.")
    if not row.og_present:
        add("og_missing", "notice", "No basic Open Graph tags",
            "Add og:title, og:description and og:image for nicer social shares.")
    if row.images_missing_alt and row.images_total:
        add("img_alt_missing", "warning",
            f"{row.images_missing_alt}/{row.images_total} images missing alt",
            "Write short alt text for informative images; use empty alt for decorative ones.")

    # Score: 100 − 10/error − 4/warning − 1/notice (unique issue ids)
    score = 100
    seen_ids: set[str] = set()
    for iss in issues:
        if iss["id"] in seen_ids:
            continue
        seen_ids.add(iss["id"])
        if iss["severity"] == "error":
            score -= 10
        elif iss["severity"] == "warning":
            score -= 4
        else:
            score -= 1
    row.score = max(0, min(100, score))
    row.issues = issues
    return row


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Broken internal-link checks (small cap)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def check_broken_internal(
    session: requests.Session,
    robots: RobotsInfo,
    candidates: list[str],
    already_fetched: set[str],
    max_checks: int,
) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    broken: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    checked = 0
    for url in candidates:
        if checked >= max_checks:
            break
        # Skip URLs we already fetched successfully as pages
        if url in already_fetched:
            continue
        if not robots_allows_url(robots, url):
            continue
        checked += 1
        time.sleep(PAUSE_BETWEEN_REQUESTS)
        try:
            # Prefer HEAD; some hosts dislike HEAD → fall back to GET with tiny read
            r = session.head(url, timeout=TIMEOUT, allow_redirects=True)
            status = r.status_code
            if status in (405, 501) or (status >= 400 and status != 404):
                r2, _ = fetch_bytes(session, url, 8192, method="GET")
                status = r2.status_code
                final = str(r2.url)
            else:
                final = str(r.url)
            if status >= 400:
                broken.append({"url": url, "status": status, "final_url": final})
        except requests.RequestException as exc:
            broken.append({"url": url, "status": None, "error": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"})
    return broken


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Optional presence probes
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def probe_presence(session: requests.Session, start_url: str, path: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    parts = urlsplit(start_url)
    url = urlunsplit((parts.scheme, parts.netloc, path, "", ""))
    out: dict[str, Any] = {"url": url, "present": False, "status": None}
    try:
        r = session.head(url, timeout=TIMEOUT, allow_redirects=True)
        status = r.status_code
        if status in (405, 501):
            r2, _ = fetch_bytes(session, url, 4096, method="GET")
            status = r2.status_code
            final = str(r2.url)
        else:
            final = str(r.url)
        out["status"] = status
        out["final_url"] = final
        out["present"] = status == 200
    except requests.RequestException as exc:
        out["error"] = f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"
    return out


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Crawl one site
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def audit_site(
    session: requests.Session,
    raw: str,
    max_pages: int,
    max_depth: int,
    max_link_checks: int,
    check_llms: bool,
    check_sitemap: bool,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    start = normalise_start(raw)
    site_host = host_of(start)
    fetched_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")

    site: dict[str, Any] = {
        "rowType": "site",
        "input": raw.strip(),
        "start_url": start,
        "host": site_host,
        "fetched_at": fetched_at,
        "robots": "",
        "ai_bots": {},
        "sitemap_in_robots": [],
        "sitemap_probe": None,
        "llms_txt": None,
        "pages_audited": 0,
        "avg_score": None,
        "broken_internal_links": [],
        "top_issues": [],
        "status": "",
        "error": None,
    }

    robots = load_robots(session, start)
    site["robots"] = robots.note
    site["ai_bots"] = robots.ai_bots
    site["sitemap_in_robots"] = robots.sitemap_hints
    if not robots.allowed_start:
        site["status"] = "robots_disallowed"
        site["error"] = robots.note
        return {"site": site, "pages": []}

    if check_sitemap:
        time.sleep(PAUSE_BETWEEN_REQUESTS)
        # Prefer first robots hint; else /sitemap.xml
        if robots.sitemap_hints:
            sm_url = robots.sitemap_hints[0]
            try:
                r = session.head(sm_url, timeout=TIMEOUT, allow_redirects=True)
                site["sitemap_probe"] = {
                    "url": sm_url,
                    "present": r.status_code == 200,
                    "status": r.status_code,
                    "source": "robots.txt",
                }
            except requests.RequestException as exc:
                site["sitemap_probe"] = {"url": sm_url, "present": False, "error": str(exc), "source": "robots.txt"}
        else:
            site["sitemap_probe"] = {**probe_presence(session, start, "/sitemap.xml"), "source": "default"}

    if check_llms:
        time.sleep(PAUSE_BETWEEN_REQUESTS)
        site["llms_txt"] = probe_presence(session, start, "/llms.txt")

    # BFS
    queue: deque[tuple[str, int]] = deque([(start, 0)])
    seen: set[str] = set()
    pages: list[PageResult] = []
    fetched_ok: set[str] = set()
    link_pool: list[str] = []

    while queue and len(pages) < max_pages:
        url, depth = queue.popleft()
        if url in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(url)
        if not robots_allows_url(robots, url):
            continue
        if depth > 0:
            time.sleep(PAUSE_BETWEEN_REQUESTS)

        try:
            r, buf = fetch_bytes(session, url, MAX_BODY, method="GET")
            ctype = r.headers.get("Content-Type", "")
            charset = "utf-8"
            if "charset=" in ctype.lower():
                charset = ctype.lower().split("charset=", 1)[1].split(";")[0].strip() or "utf-8"
            html = buf.decode(charset, "replace")
            headers = {k.lower(): v for k, v in r.headers.items()}
            final = str(r.url)
            hops = len(r.history)
            status = r.status_code
        except requests.RequestException as exc:
            pages.append(PageResult(
                url=url, final_url=url, status=0, depth=depth, redirect_hops=0,
                error=f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}", score=0,
                issues=[{"id": "fetch_error", "severity": "error",
                         "message": f"Fetch failed: {type(exc).__name__}",
                         "fix": "Retry later or check DNS/TLS."}],
            ))
            continue

        # Only parse HTML-ish
        if status < 400 and "html" not in ctype.lower() and buf[:200].lstrip()[:1] != b"<":
            # still record status
            pr = PageResult(
                url=url, final_url=final, status=status, depth=depth, redirect_hops=hops,
                issues=[{"id": "not_html", "severity": "notice", "message": f"Non-HTML content-type: {ctype}",
                         "fix": "Skip binary URLs in the crawl frontier."}],
                score=99,
            )
            pages.append(pr)
            continue

        pr = analyse_html(url, final, status, depth, hops, headers, html, start)
        pages.append(pr)
        if status < 400:
            fetched_ok.add(url)
            fetched_ok.add(urlunsplit(urlsplit(final)._replace(query="", fragment="")))

        # Enqueue internal links
        if depth < max_depth:
            for href in pr.internal_hrefs:
                if href not in seen and len(seen) + len(queue) < max_pages * 3:
                    queue.append((href, depth + 1))
                if href not in fetched_ok:
                    link_pool.append(href)

    # Broken internal links (candidates not already fetched as pages)
    # Prefer link_pool order; unique
    uniq_pool: list[str] = []
    seen_pool: set[str] = set()
    for u in link_pool:
        if u not in seen_pool and u not in fetched_ok:
            seen_pool.add(u)
            uniq_pool.append(u)

    broken = check_broken_internal(session, robots, uniq_pool, fetched_ok, max_link_checks)
    site["broken_internal_links"] = broken

    # Attach broken-link issues onto referring isn't tracked simply; add site-level + bump pages that linked?
    # Keep site-level only for educational simplicity; also flag homepage if any.
    if broken and pages:
        for b in broken[:5]:
            # add as site top issue only
            pass

    # Site roll-up
    site["pages_audited"] = len(pages)
    if pages:
        site["avg_score"] = round(sum(p.score for p in pages) / len(pages), 1)
    # Top issues by frequency
    freq: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {}
    for p in pages:
        for iss in p.issues:
            slot = freq.setdefault(iss["id"], {"id": iss["id"], "severity": iss["severity"],
                                               "message": iss["message"], "fix": iss["fix"], "count": 0})
            slot["count"] += 1
    if broken:
        freq["broken_internal_link"] = {
            "id": "broken_internal_link",
            "severity": "error",
            "message": f"{len(broken)} broken internal link(s) sampled",
            "fix": "Update or remove links that return 4xx/5xx.",
            "count": len(broken),
        }
    top = sorted(freq.values(), key=lambda x: (
        {"error": 0, "warning": 1, "notice": 2}.get(x["severity"], 3),
        -x["count"],
    ))
    site["top_issues"] = top[:10]
    site["status"] = "ok"
    return {"site": site, "pages": pages}


def page_to_dict(p: PageResult) -> dict[str, Any]:
    return {
        "rowType": "page",
        "url": p.url,
        "final_url": p.final_url,
        "http_status": p.status,
        "depth": p.depth,
        "redirect_hops": p.redirect_hops,
        "title": p.title,
        "title_length": p.title_length,
        "meta_description_length": p.meta_description_length,
        "h1_count": p.h1_count,
        "canonical": p.canonical,
        "canonical_status": p.canonical_status,
        "meta_robots": p.meta_robots,
        "x_robots_tag": p.x_robots_tag,
        "indexable": p.indexable,
        "og_present": p.og_present,
        "og_keys": p.og_keys,
        "images_total": p.images_total,
        "images_missing_alt": p.images_missing_alt,
        "internal_links": p.internal_links,
        "external_links": p.external_links,
        "score": p.score,
        "issues": p.issues,
        "error": p.error,
    }


def write_outputs(results: list[dict[str, Any]], out_dir: Path, stamp: str) -> tuple[Path, Path]:
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    json_path = out_dir / f"seo-audit-{stamp}.json"
    csv_path = out_dir / f"seo-audit-{stamp}.csv"

    payload = []
    flat = []
    for res in results:
        site = res["site"]
        payload.append(site)
        for p in res["pages"]:
            pd = page_to_dict(p)
            pd["site"] = site["host"]
            payload.append(pd)
            flat.append({
                "site": site["host"],
                "url": pd["url"],
                "http_status": pd["http_status"],
                "depth": pd["depth"],
                "title_length": pd["title_length"],
                "meta_description_length": pd["meta_description_length"],
                "h1_count": pd["h1_count"],
                "canonical_status": pd["canonical_status"],
                "indexable": pd["indexable"],
                "og_present": pd["og_present"],
                "images_missing_alt": pd["images_missing_alt"],
                "images_total": pd["images_total"],
                "internal_links": pd["internal_links"],
                "external_links": pd["external_links"],
                "score": pd["score"],
                "issue_ids": ";".join(i["id"] for i in pd["issues"]),
                "error": pd.get("error") or "",
            })
        # site summary row in CSV too
        flat.append({
            "site": site["host"],
            "url": f"[site] {site.get('start_url')}",
            "http_status": "",
            "depth": "",
            "title_length": "",
            "meta_description_length": "",
            "h1_count": "",
            "canonical_status": "",
            "indexable": "",
            "og_present": "",
            "images_missing_alt": "",
            "images_total": "",
            "internal_links": "",
            "external_links": "",
            "score": site.get("avg_score") if site.get("avg_score") is not None else "",
            "issue_ids": ";".join(i["id"] for i in (site.get("top_issues") or [])),
            "error": site.get("error") or "",
        })

    json_path.write_text(json.dumps(payload, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    fields = list(flat[0].keys()) if flat else ["site", "url"]
    with csv_path.open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
        w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields)
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(flat)
    return csv_path, json_path


def main() -> None:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    p.add_argument("urls", nargs="*", help="start domains or URLs")
    p.add_argument("--file", "-f", help="text file with one domain/URL per line")
    p.add_argument("--max-pages", type=int, default=DEFAULT_MAX_PAGES)
    p.add_argument("--max-depth", type=int, default=DEFAULT_MAX_DEPTH)
    p.add_argument("--max-link-checks", type=int, default=DEFAULT_MAX_LINK_CHECKS)
    p.add_argument("--llms", action=argparse.BooleanOptionalAction, default=True)
    p.add_argument("--sitemap", action=argparse.BooleanOptionalAction, default=True)
    p.add_argument("--out-dir", default="out")
    p.add_argument("--pause", type=float, default=PAUSE_BETWEEN_REQUESTS)
    args = p.parse_args()

    urls: list[str] = list(args.urls)
    if args.file:
        for line in Path(args.file).read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
            line = line.strip()
            if line and not line.startswith("#"):
                urls.append(line)
    if not urls:
        p.error("pass one or more URLs, or --file")

    # Apply CLI pause to module-level default used by crawl helpers.
    globals()["PAUSE_BETWEEN_REQUESTS"] = args.pause

    session = requests.Session()
    session.headers.update({
        "User-Agent": USER_AGENT,
        "Accept": "text/html,application/xhtml+xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.5",
        "Accept-Language": "en,de;q=0.8",
    })

    results: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    for i, raw in enumerate(urls):
        if i:
            time.sleep(max(args.pause, 1.0))
        print(f"→ {raw}", file=sys.stderr)
        try:
            res = audit_site(
                session, raw,
                max_pages=args.max_pages,
                max_depth=args.max_depth,
                max_link_checks=args.max_link_checks,
                check_llms=args.llms,
                check_sitemap=args.sitemap,
            )
        except ValueError as exc:
            res = {"site": {"rowType": "site", "input": raw, "status": "bad_input",
                            "error": str(exc), "host": "", "pages_audited": 0,
                            "fetched_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
                            "top_issues": [], "broken_internal_links": [], "ai_bots": {}},
                   "pages": []}
        site = res["site"]
        print(
            f"  {site.get('status')} pages={site.get('pages_audited')} "
            f"avg_score={site.get('avg_score')} broken={len(site.get('broken_internal_links') or [])} "
            f"| {site.get('robots')}",
            file=sys.stderr,
        )
        results.append(res)

    stamp = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ")
    csv_path, json_path = write_outputs(results, Path(args.out_dir), stamp)
    print(f"Wrote {csv_path} and {json_path}", file=sys.stderr)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Signals observed on public pages and public robots.txt files on 6 November 2026. Independent educational tutorial from Lindenwerk Data; not affiliated with or endorsed by the vendors or bot operators named in examples.

This article was researched, written and tested by an AI agent and published under the Lindenwerk Data account. All figures come from our own live runs of the script on 6 November 2026; robots handling follows RFC 9309 practice as described above.

title: SQL Server Multiple Cascade Paths (Error 1785): Which Foreign Key Loses ON DELETE CASCADE, and What Replaces It
description:
Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples.

TL;DR: SQL Server refuses a foreign key when its CASCADE, SET NULL or SET DEFAULT would let one delete or update reach the same table by two paths, and it decides that from the declared actions when the key is created, not from the rows. One key has to become NO ACTION, which makes some deletes fail with error 547 until a stored procedure or an INSTEAD OF DELETE trigger on the parent removes the child rows first. An AFTER DELETE trigger cannot do it, and SET NULL on the second key is refused like CASCADE.

Error 1785 means two of your foreign keys would both act on the same table when one parent row is deleted or updated, and SQL Server will not create the second one, even on empty tables. The fix has two parts. One of the keys has to become NO ACTION, and then something else has to remove the rows that key used to remove, because a NO ACTION key turns some deletes into error 547. Keep the cascade on the key that says who owns the row, and replace the other one with a stored procedure or an INSTEAD OF DELETE trigger on the parent table.

Everything below ran on SQL Server 2022 (16.0.4265.3, CU26) in a throwaway Docker container, and again on SQL Server 2025 (17.0.5035.5) with the same results. The schema is three tables: users, posts with a user_id, and comments with a post_id and a user_id.

Why does SQL Server say a foreign key may cause cycles or multiple cascade paths?

Because deleting one row would reach the same table by two routes, and SQL Server allows only one route to each table per delete or update.

A comment belongs to a post and was written by a user, and a post was written by a user. Give all three keys ON DELETE CASCADE and a deleted user reaches comments twice: directly, and through posts.

CREATE TABLE users (
  id INT IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name NVARCHAR(50) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE posts (
  id INT IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INT NOT NULL,
  title NVARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT fk_posts_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
    REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

CREATE TABLE comments (
  id INT IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  post_id INT NOT NULL,
  user_id INT NOT NULL,
  body NVARCHAR(1000) NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT fk_comments_post FOREIGN KEY (post_id)
    REFERENCES posts (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT fk_comments_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
    REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);
-- Msg 1785, Level 16, State 1
-- Introducing FOREIGN KEY constraint 'fk_comments_user' on table 'comments'
-- may cause cycles or multiple cascade paths. Specify ON DELETE NO ACTION or
-- ON UPDATE NO ACTION, or modify other FOREIGN KEY constraints.
-- Msg 1750: Could not create constraint or index. See previous errors.

The comments table is not created at all. Microsoft's page for error 1785 gives the rule: "a table cannot appear more than one time in a list of all the cascading referential actions that are started by either a DELETE or an UPDATE statement." The check reads the declared actions only. There were no rows in any table when it failed.

The key the message names is the one that arrived second, not the one that is wrong. With both keys in one CREATE TABLE it named fk_comments_user. When I created comments with only the user key and added the post key afterwards with ALTER TABLE, the same error named fk_comments_post.

PostgreSQL 18.3 and MySQL 8.4.11 created the same three keys without complaint, and deleting one user there removed that user's post and every comment on either path. So this is a rule of SQL Server, not of SQL, and it tends to arrive from an ORM: Entity Framework Core configures required relationships to cascade by default, and its documentation on database cascade limitations shows this exact exception on a blog, post and person model.

The diamond is one of three shapes SQL Server refused, along with two keys from one parent and a self-reference:

Shape Keys Result
Direct and indirect path into one table users to posts to comments, plus users to comments, all CASCADE Msg 1785
The same, with SET NULL on comments.user_id CASCADE, CASCADE, SET NULL Msg 1785
The same, with SET NULL on comments.post_id CASCADE, SET NULL, CASCADE Msg 1785
Two keys from one parent messages.sender_id and messages.recipient_id to users, both CASCADE Msg 1785
Two keys from one parent one CASCADE, one SET NULL Msg 1785
Two keys from one parent one CASCADE, one NO ACTION Created
Self-reference categories.parent_id to categories, CASCADE or SET NULL Msg 1785
Two ON UPDATE CASCADE keys from one parent transfers.from_id and transfers.to_id to users Msg 1785

SET NULL does not get around it, and ON UPDATE is checked the same way as ON DELETE.

Which foreign key should be NO ACTION?

The key that records a reference rather than ownership: keep ON DELETE CASCADE from posts to comments, because a comment cannot exist without its post, and make comments.user_id the NO ACTION key.

Either choice makes SQL Server accept the schema, and either choice makes some deletes fail. (A third, NO ACTION on posts.user_id, is accepted too, but then deleting any user who has a post fails with Msg 547 on fk_posts_user, so it is not a candidate.) I loaded three users, one post each, and four comments: Ana on her own post, Ana on Ben's post, Ben on Ana's post, and Cy on his own post. Then I tried both versions.

Delete NO ACTION on comments.user_id NO ACTION on comments.post_id
A post that has comments Works, the comments go with it Fails, Msg 547 on fk_comments_post
Cy, who only commented on his own post Works Works
Ana, who commented on Ben's post and has Ben's comment on hers Fails, Msg 547 on fk_comments_user Fails, Msg 547 on fk_comments_post

The failure reads:

Msg 547, Level 16, State 1
The DELETE statement conflicted with the REFERENCE constraint "fk_comments_user".
The conflict occurred in database "blog", table "dbo.comments", column 'user_id'.
The statement has been terminated.

Cy's delete works in both versions because SQL Server applies every cascade before it checks a NO ACTION key, so by the time it looks, his one comment is already gone with his post. Ana's fails because a row survives the cascades and still points at something being deleted.

That makes the first column the better schema. With NO ACTION on comments.post_id, deleting any post that has a comment fails, which breaks the most ordinary delete in the application. With NO ACTION on comments.user_id, posts delete normally and only one operation needs help: deleting a user who has commented on someone else's post. The schema is accepted, and the delete that used to be one statement is now your job.

What replaces the cascade you removed?
