A stored procedure, or an INSTEAD OF DELETE trigger on the parent table, that removes the child rows before the parent row; an AFTER DELETE trigger cannot do it.

Replacement Result for deleting Ana
AFTER DELETE trigger on users that deletes her comments Still Msg 547. The key is checked before the trigger fires, so it never runs
INSTEAD OF DELETE trigger on users Works: Ana, her post and every comment on either path are gone
Stored procedure that deletes her comments, then her, in one transaction Works, same rows removed
ON DELETE SET NULL on comments.user_id Not available, Msg 1785

The trigger that worked:

CREATE TRIGGER trg_users_delete ON users INSTEAD OF DELETE AS
BEGIN
  SET NOCOUNT ON;
  DELETE FROM comments WHERE user_id IN (SELECT id FROM deleted);
  DELETE FROM users WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM deleted);
END;

It reads the deleted table as a set, so DELETE FROM users WHERE id IN (2, 3) handled both users in one statement. The second DELETE inside it does not fire the trigger again; it runs the real delete, and fk_posts_user and fk_comments_post cascade as declared.

If a comment should outlive its author, the trigger is also where the null goes, since SQL Server refuses SET NULL on that key. Make comments.user_id nullable and swap the first statement for UPDATE comments SET user_id = NULL WHERE user_id IN (SELECT id FROM deleted). Deleting Ana then left her comment on Ben's post in place with no author, and removed her post and the comments on it.

The trigger has three limits, all measured:

  • It only fits a table that has no cascading foreign key of its own. CREATE TRIGGER ... ON posts INSTEAD OF DELETE failed with Msg 2113, "Cannot create INSTEAD OF DELETE or INSTEAD OF UPDATE TRIGGER 'trg_posts_delete' on table 'posts'. This is because the table has a FOREIGN KEY with cascading DELETE or UPDATE.", because posts.user_id cascades from users.
  • It closes a door on the table that has it. With the trigger on users, adding users.org_id with ON DELETE CASCADE to an orgs table failed with Msg 1787. The same key with ON DELETE SET NULL was accepted.
  • It breaks a DELETE that has an OUTPUT clause. DELETE FROM users OUTPUT 1 WHERE id = 3 failed with Msg 334, "The target table 'users' of the DML statement cannot have any enabled triggers if the statement contains an OUTPUT clause without INTO clause." EF Core 7 and later save changes with OUTPUT by default, so the entity has to be configured with HasTrigger before EF Core can write to that table.

A stored procedure has none of these limits, and it is the same two statements in a transaction:

CREATE PROCEDURE delete_user @user_id INT AS
BEGIN
  SET NOCOUNT ON; SET XACT_ABORT ON;
  BEGIN TRANSACTION;
  DELETE FROM comments WHERE user_id = @user_id;
  DELETE FROM users WHERE id = @user_id;
  COMMIT;
END;

Its cost is that it only protects callers who use it. A plain DELETE FROM users from another service, a script or an ORM still fails with Msg 547, which at least fails loudly rather than leaving orphans. Doing the same two statements from application code is equivalent, and it is what EF Core's ClientCascade option does for rows it has loaded.

How do you delete a tree when a self-reference cannot cascade?

Leave the self-referencing key at NO ACTION and delete the whole subtree in one statement with a recursive common table expression.

SQL Server refused categories.parent_id with ON DELETE CASCADE and with ON DELETE SET NULL. With the key at NO ACTION, deleting a category that has children fails with Msg 547, "The DELETE statement conflicted with the SAME TABLE REFERENCE constraint". Collecting the subtree first works, because the key is checked against the rows the whole statement leaves behind, and parent and children go together:

WITH tree AS (
  SELECT id FROM categories WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id FROM categories c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id
)
DELETE FROM categories WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM tree)
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 0);

On four rows, a chain of 1, 2 and 3 plus an unrelated row 4, that statement removed the chain and left row 4. The OPTION (MAXRECURSION 0) matters on a deep tree: SQL Server stops a recursive query after 100 levels by default, and without the option a chain of 150 categories failed with Msg 530, "The maximum recursion 100 has been exhausted before statement completion", and deleted nothing.

How Schemity flags a second cascade path before SQL Server does

Schemity's lint reports the foreign key that adds the second path while it is still a line on the diagram, and names the key it collides with.

Schemity is database design software that reads your live database, shows the impact of every schema change before it runs, and keeps the diagram as a file in Git. On a SQL Server diagram, whether it is connected to a database or a design with no connection yet, the ON DELETE and ON UPDATE actions are set in the relationship dialog, and nothing stops you from choosing CASCADE on both of a table's keys. On an unconnected design there is no server to object, so the first place the problem can show is schema lint.

Changing that last key to CASCADE is one dropdown in the dialog, and Schemity accepts it:

The rule is sqlserver-multiple-cascade-paths, in the "Fails at runtime" group, and it runs only on SQL Server diagrams. For the three tables above with all keys at CASCADE, the finding sits on comments.user_id:

SQL Server refuses this foreign key: its ON DELETE action makes a second path between the same tables (Msg 1785).

ON DELETE in users reaches comments through fk_comments_post and through this key. One of the two has to be NO ACTION.

On a connected diagram the finding also follows the change into Preview changes, next to the planned migration it would run. The preview draws only users and comments, the two tables the change touches, but lint reads the whole schema, so the path through posts is still counted:

Statement 4 in that migration is the one SQL Server would answer with Msg 1785. Schemity runs a SQL Server migration in one transaction and rolls it back on the first error, so the DROP CONSTRAINT before it would be undone and the old NO ACTION key would stay in place.

It covers the same shapes as the table earlier: a direct and an indirect path, two acting keys from one parent, and a self-reference, where the detail says that the rows below have to be handled by the application or a trigger. It checks deletes and updates separately, as SQL Server does, and it counts SET NULL and SET DEFAULT as acting keys, so switching the second key to SET NULL keeps the finding. It also follows one subtlety I confirmed on the server: an ON DELETE SET NULL in the middle of a chain ends that path, because the row it changes is not deleted (an ON UPDATE chain has no such exit). users to members with CASCADE, members to tasks with SET NULL, then tasks to notes with CASCADE and users to notes with SET NULL was created without error, and lint stays silent on it.

What lint cannot tell you is which key to change, because that depends on which table owns the row. That decision is the one in the second section, and it is easier to make on an ERD, where both paths from users to comments are visible as lines, than in a migration file where the two keys are forty lines apart. When you design the next one, set the reference key to NO ACTION in the dialog, and the finding clears before any SQL is written.

Two related posts pick up from here: ON DELETE SET NULL vs CASCADE in PostgreSQL covers choosing between the two actions where both are allowed, and circular foreign keys covers the insert side of a cycle, which SQL Server permits as long as the actions do not go round it.

title: Can a small language model run on a budget Android phone with 4 GB RAM?
description:
Our small open model answered a stock question in 4.25 s on a 4 GB Galaxy A05s. In that same run, its first turn took 13.4 s, right after a print preview, and that gap is still open.

Both times come from a whole-app run of a test build (31 Oct), with airplane mode on, using 673 MB of model memory. So can it run on a 4 GB phone? On the phone we tested, yes. But "does it run?" is not where the check should stop.

Here is what we measured, in the order we would check it on any budget phone. Every timing below is from one phone model, a Galaxy A05s (4 GB, Snapdragon 680), measured on a real device in Firebase Test Lab (FTL). The one accuracy result is different: it was scored on a server (layer EVAL), and we label it where it appears.

The model is a small open model taught only one app's tasks. That app is our first build, pharmacy software, and the model runs inside its offline edition.

First check: does it fit on the phone?

Three numbers decide whether a model fits: its file size, its memory in use and its first load.

What Measured (FTL) Where it comes from
Model size 489 MB the model file, qwen3-0.6b-v18-Q6_K.gguf
Model memory 673 MB the model in memory during the whole-app run, on a phone with 4 GB in total
First launch 18.8 s the whole-app run, cold_start_ms 18786

The whole-app run: Android 15, airplane mode, run PASSED, test build of 31 Oct. No later merged build has passed a whole-app run yet.

The model fits. But fitting is not the same as being fast enough, so writing speed gets its own test.

Second check: how fast does it write?

This is a separate llama-bench run on the same phone model, with the setting that shipped. The network was not controlled (not airplane mode), so do not read these rows together with the whole-app run above.

Test Context already in place Mean tok/s Standard deviation
Writing, tg64 d0 (empty) 14.82 0.16
Writing, tg64 d768 11.02 0.01
Prompt reading, pp128 d0 (empty) 25.45 1.35
Prompt reading, pp128 d768 20.33 0.07

Layer FTL. Galaxy A05s SM-A057G, Snapdragon 680 'bengal', llama.cpp 620d222 (armv8a), 4 threads. These are the settings that shipped: f16 KV cache, flash-attn 0 (off), repack 0 (off).

How to read the names: tg64 is the writing test and pp128 the prompt-reading test; the number in each name is how many tokens it writes or reads. d0 means the context is empty. d768 means 768 tokens are already in context.

The d0 row is the number people quote: 14.8 tok/s from an empty context. But an app rarely runs with an empty context. A system prompt and chat history push it toward the other row: 11.0 tok/s with 768 tokens already in context. So if your app carries history, read d768 first, and ask any phone benchmark which depth it used.

What this does not show

  • Other phones. These are results from one phone model, the Galaxy A05s.
  • General chat. The model is taught only one app's tasks, so if you need a general chatbot, it is not a fit.
  • Battery or energy use. Energy use was not measured.
  • Answer quality on the phone. A phone timing does not answer that. Accuracy needs an exam on your app's tasks. Our one exam result is on an earlier version and was not run on the phone: 0.6B vs its 8B teacher, +13 pts (95% CI +4.0 to +24.4); v7, not the shipped v18; frozen real test, 40 shops, shop-clustered, scored on a server (layer EVAL).
  • Your app. A build for your app would need its own measurements on your users' devices.

Run the same test on your phone

One phone cannot answer this for the phones your users own. Our tuned weights are private, so you cannot rerun our model. But you can run the same test with the same flags on a public Q6_K file of Qwen3 0.6B. That result describes a different model, so label it as such.

The recipe is on the dataset card of neykosa/phone-llamacpp-bench:

  • Build llama-bench for Android arm64 from llama.cpp commit 620d222. llama.cpp's own NDK guide covers the build.
  • Run the one adb command on the card.
  • Run bench_row.py to turn the llama-bench JSON into a block you can paste.

Post that block in the dataset's Discussions, with your phone model and whether the network was controlled. A run that failed to build or load is useful too. We have not walked an outside build through those steps, so a note on where yours broke helps the next person. Full run conditions are on our benchmarks page.

Disclosure: Team Neykosa builds small open models taught only one app's tasks, to run on its users' own phones and laptops, so read these numbers knowing who measured them. An AI agent wrote this article from our published measurement page with little to no human editing, and it is marked Fully Autonomous on DEV. Every number was checked against our measurement records before publishing. First published on neykosa.com.

title: Buffalo Grain Elevator: A Five-Stage Toolchain and What Broke
description:
This one started with a call from a preservation group in Buffalo. They had a 1910s concrete grain elevator complex on the lake, thirty-eight silos in two rows, a marine leg tower, and a rail yard that still connects to a live line. The question was whether part of it could hold a fabrication shop, a small events floor, and a public walk at the top. Before anyone talked about membranes or budgets, I needed a model I could test against.

Stage 1 — base geometry from CADMapper

CADMapper brought in the parcel, the rail alignments, and the nearest streets. The silo complex itself was not in the open data at usable detail, so I traced the outer walls from a survey the group had scanned and used the export only for context and scale. That split matters. Context from the map, dimensions from the survey. When I mixed the two, the rail alignment drifted about two feet against the property line.

Stage 2 — parcel logic with Cityweft

The complex sits inside one legal parcel with three separate owners of record, which is a mess nobody had drawn. Cityweft let me weave a working subdivision inside the boundary so we could talk about phases instead of one building. The version we kept separated the silo block, the marine leg, and the rail yard into three parcels with a shared service spine. That one drawing did more for the conversation than any rendering.

Stage 3 — rules in CityEngine

CityEngine was the right place to test the zoning envelope on the waterfront edge. I wrote rules for height, setback from the rail, and a required public access strip, then generated massing variants for the two infill sites between the silos. The rules made a bad assumption visible early: the height limit measured from the street side lets a much taller building sit behind the silos than the waterfront plan intended. That is a code issue, not a design issue, and it is now in the meeting notes.

Stage 4 — massing inserts with Archshaper

Archshaper handled the shop and the events floor. I gave it the silo block footprint and tested a low shed against a taller box tucked between the bins. The low shed keeps the silo silhouette intact from the water. The taller box gets daylight into the shop but eats the public walk. We kept the low shed and moved the walk to the roof of the connecting gallery, which is a better idea than anything I drew by hand.

Stage 5 — quick volume checks with GenAnywhere

GenAnywhere is the fast pass. Drag a rectangle over the map, and it hands back building volumes for that rectangle. I boxed the rail yard and the two empty pads and generated options for a future phase, mostly to see how much floor area could fit without touching the silos. The numbers came back close to my hand estimate, which is the point. It took four minutes and confirmed that the yard is worth more as a yard.

What broke

• CADMapper exports the rail as a centerline, not a corridor. Buffers need to be drawn by hand.
• CityEngine rules failed on two silo footprints that were not closed. Cleaning the polygon in CAD fixed it.
• Archshaper assumes floor-to-floor heights. The silo block does not have them, so I had to fake levels and label them.
• GenAnywhere returns volumes without structure. Every option needs a manual check against the bin walls.
• Cityweft will happily weave parcels across a rail easement. I had to lock that strip before every run.

What I would keep

The stage order. Base context, parcel logic, rules, massing, then quick volume tests. Each stage produced one decision, and the decisions survived the meeting. I also kept every stage in its own file with the date in the name, because the group will ask for the version from three weeks ago and nobody will remember which one had the corrected rail easement.
Two days of work produced four ruled-out options and one plan. The model was never the deliverable. The list of things we could stop arguing about was.

title: Does Sanae Takaichi Have No Influence in Japan?
description:
From an urgent warning by the prime minister and temporary service shutdowns to internet-exposed risks observed by ZoomEye, the PHP2Shell incident raises questions about Japan's cybersecurity governance.

Executive Summary
In October 2026, Japan's prime minister issued an urgent warning about PHP2Shell, and multiple Japanese organizations temporarily suspended or maintained online services.
According to ZoomEye's PHP2Shell report, Japan accounted for 4,600,612 potentially affected asset records, approximately 4.1% of the global total under the report's methodology, ranking fourth worldwide. As of November 5, 2026, 31,354 of those records had been marked as remediated, representing about 0.68%. This figure describes the share of records carrying a remediation label within the report; it is not an independently verified national vulnerability remediation rate. Drawing on government alerts, service restoration notices, and public-internet observations, this article examines what can be assessed about Japan's incident response and service continuity.
At 9:55 p.m. on October 21, 2026, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi posted an unusual urgent appeal from her personal X account. She urged operators of websites using PHP to prepare to apply security patches as quickly as possible, adding that temporarily suspending affected services could be an effective way to reduce risk if immediate patching proved difficult. It is unusual for a country's prime minister to personally remind website administrators to update a software component.


Figure 1. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's PHP security warning on X, October 21, 2026. Source: X(@takaichi_sanae); screenshot shows X's English translation.

More notably, a number of Japanese government departments, financial institutions, and business websites subsequently undertook emergency maintenance or temporarily suspended services. From parts of the Ministry of Finance's websites to online services in finance and transportation, a vulnerability in a foundational software component quickly had operational consequences.
Temporarily disabling high-risk services is not necessarily the wrong response to a severe vulnerability. Yet the incident raises a question worth examining: Japan already has a national cybersecurity coordination body and continues to reform its cybersecurity institutions. Why could a vulnerability in an open-source component still push several important services into emergency response at the same time? Was this a normal exercise of risk control, or did it reveal room for improvement in routine maintenance and business continuity? The answer requires looking beyond the prime minister's warning to what security agencies had done beforehand, which services were affected, and how the risks were ultimately handled.

01 | Why Did a PHP Vulnerability Trigger Such a Broad Emergency Response?
The incident concerned two severe PHP vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The flaws relate to PHP's handling of out-of-memory errors and requests; in certain affected environments, they could enable remote code execution. The two vulnerabilities are collectively referred to as PHP2Shell.


Figure 2. Japan's Information-technology Promotion Agency (IPA) advisory on the PHP vulnerabilities. Source:
IPA, Japan.

PHP is a foundational component used by numerous websites, content management systems, and web back ends. Unlike a flaw confined to one application, a vulnerability in the PHP runtime can affect systems across regions and industries.
On October 21, 2026, before the security patches were officially released, Japan's Information-technology Promotion Agency (IPA) issued a preparedness notice to operators. The IPA urged organizations to inventory PHP-powered websites and applications, watch for the forthcoming security updates, and prepare to act promptly. Its notice also highlighted that some websites were still running older PHP releases that had reached end of support.
This is an easily overlooked detail. Japan did not begin paying attention to the vulnerabilities only after the prime minister spoke. Security authorities had already issued technical alerts and communicated the risks through established cybersecurity channels.
PHP subsequently released patched versions, including PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. Prompt patching is the principal response for systems that can be upgraded directly. For
systems running older PHP versions, depending on particular environments, or requiring extensive compatibility testing, however, remediation may involve application changes,
vendor coordination, and scheduled maintenance windows.
Takaichi's public appeal before the patches were released broadened awareness of the issue. From a cybersecurity governance perspective, however, the more significant question
is not whether the prime minister should have spoken, but whether critical systems could have identified the risks and prepared a response through existing processes beforehand. A
national warning can make more people aware of a threat, but it cannot substitute for each organization's asset inventory, patching procedures, and ongoing maintenance.

02 | Japan's Security Agencies Acted. How Can the Results Be
Assessed?
Japan has continued to strengthen its national cybersecurity coordination arrangements. In July 2025, it established the National Cybersecurity Office (NCO) through the reorganization
of the former National Center of Incident Readiness and Strategy for Cybersecurity. Its responsibilities include monitoring, analysis, audits, and interagency coordination relating
to government-system security. During the PHP2Shell incident, the NCO and IPA issued warnings through relevant channels, while the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry also communicated protective guidance to businesses through industry groups.
These actions show that Japan's alerting and coordination mechanisms were activated. It would therefore be inaccurate to describe the episode simply as one in which Japan's
cybersecurity authorities did nothing. At the same time, an operational warning mechanism does not mean every organization has an equally mature capacity to respond.
The Ministry of Finance offers an observable case. On October 21, it announced emergency checks of relevant web systems and suspended access to some content. On October 22, it began restoring services after implementing necessary security measures. By October 26,
the ministry announced that the related security measures and functional adjustments had been completed and all suspended content was available again. This timeline shows both preventive action and subsequent restoration. It also raises further questions: Why did the relevant services have to be suspended? What steps were required for patch deployment and restoration? Could more mature redundancy, automated testing, and rollback mechanisms reduce downtime during a similar incident in the future?
At an October 23 press conference, Japan's finance minister said that financial regulators had already considered temporary suspension of services as a possible risk-control measure and had prepared for such circumstances. At least some shutdowns, therefore, were not improvised decisions but part of existing contingency planning. Yet a plan to suspend a service is only one component of business continuity. For essential public services, the precision of risk isolation, the availability of alternatives, and the effect of the recovery process on users also matter. Whether agencies issued alerts is verifiable; whether those
alerts translated into rapid, stable responses with minimal disruption requires more evidence about actual outcomes.

03 | When Vulnerability Response Affects Disaster Alerts, It Is
More Than Website Maintenance
The operational impact of PHP2Shell went beyond temporary unavailability of government websites. Reuters reported on October 23 that Japan's SoftBank had suspended portions of its mobile emergency alert service while addressing the PHP vulnerability, affecting notifications related to earthquakes, tsunamis, and disaster evacuation. Users could still receive relevant earthquake warnings through other channels. This case makes the complexity of incident response more tangible than a routine website maintenance notice.
A short outage on an ordinary commercial website may inconvenience users and cause financial losses. When the affected functionality involves disaster notifications, operators must balance cybersecurity risk against the continuity of public-facing services. Keeping a potentially vulnerable system online can increase exposure; disabling a function can also affect timely access to important information. This does not establish that SoftBank lacked contingency plans, nor does it mean Japan's entire disaster-alert system failed. It does show how the consequences of a software vulnerability can extend beyond conventional IT
systems into essential public services.
For operators of critical services, vulnerability response cannot stop at identifying and
closing an exposed entry point. Backup channels, alternative services, user notifications, and restoration checks are also part of preparedness. Similar considerations may arise in banking, aviation, rail transport, and public-sector information systems. Although online services are operated by different organizations, many rely on common software components. A severe flaw in an underlying component can therefore force multiple organizations to undertake updates and maintenance at roughly the same time. This is one reason software supply-chain risks have attracted increasing attention.
Mature risk management does not promise that systems will never have vulnerabilities. Rather, it seeks to identify technical dependencies in advance, shorten the time needed to
identify and address vulnerabilities, and limit the disruption caused by necessary security measures. The PHP2Shell incident alone does not establish a systemic failure of Japan's cybersecurity framework, but it offers a concrete case for examining how these capabilities work. For a country that depends on numerous essential digital services, the response
merits public review.

04 | ZoomEye's View: How Large Was Japan's Potentially
Exposed Internet Asset Footprint?
News coverage can identify organizations that temporarily suspended services, but it cannot provide a complete picture of other internet-exposed assets that may warrant attention. Cyberspace mapping offers another perspective. By continuously observing
public-facing services, ZoomEye identifies IP addresses, ports, protocols, web components, and some visible version information, providing evidence for large-scale asset investigations and vulnerability-risk screening.
According to the 'Global distribution (TOP 10)' table under 'Affected assets' in ZoomEye's PHP2Shell Alert Report (2026), Japan accounted for 4,600,612 potentially affected asset
records—approximately 4.1% of the global total under that table's methodology. It ranked fourth, behind the United States, China, and Germany.


Figure: Global distribution of potentially affected PHP2Shell asset records (Affected assets). Japan: 4,600,612 records, fourth worldwide, approximately 4.1%. Source: screenshot from ZoomEye's official PHP2Shell report.

The figure places Japan among the countries with relatively large record counts in the report's potential-risk distribution. It covers publicly observable assets within ZoomEye's
scope, not only organizations that publicly announced maintenance. As of November 5, 2026, 31,354 Japanese asset records had been labeled 'remediated' under the report's statistical methodology, or approximately 0.68% of the 4,600,612 potentially affected
records. This is the share of records bearing a remediation label, not an independently verified vulnerability remediation rate for Japan.


Importantly, 'Affected assets' is a vulnerability-association label used by the report. It should not be interpreted as a count of independent servers confirmed to be exploitable, and records not labeled 'remediated' cannot all be assumed to remain unpatched. Public-facing identification can also be affected by hidden version information, CDNs, reverse proxies, vendor backported patches, and asset deduplication rules. These figures can nonetheless guide risk investigations and provide a baseline for follow-up. Security teams should cross-check externally observed evidence against internal inventories, patch records, and actual configurations. Evaluating remediation progress requires consistent asset scope, deduplication rules, and identification criteria over time; 0.68% must not be presented as Japan's overall remediation rate. ZoomEye's value is not to replace vulnerability audits with a single snapshot, but to make potentially overlooked public exposure observable and traceable.

05 | Japan Wants Earlier Vulnerability Intelligence. Would
Earlier Warning Mean Faster Remediation?
Developments in Japan's cybersecurity policy after the PHP2Shell incident also warrant attention. On October 23, Reuters reported that Japan planned to assemble a team to use AI-driven simulations of cyberattacks to identify weaknesses in systems. On November 4,
Reuters, citing Nikkei, reported that the government planned to seek information about undisclosed software vulnerabilities from U.S. AI developers and other overseas technology companies to strengthen cyber defenses. These remained reported plans or policy
initiatives; they should not be treated as fully implemented mechanisms or attributed entirely to PHP2Shell.
The policy direction raises a question: as the window between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation narrows, do defenders need earlier access to risk information? The answer depends on more than the intelligence itself. Early notice can give operators more time to assess exposure, inventory assets, and plan a response. But organizations without accurate software-component inventories, mature test environments, or supportable legacy systems may still struggle to upgrade quickly, even when they learn about a vulnerability in advance.
Put differently, early vulnerability intelligence addresses “when an organization learns about a risk”; mature asset management and security operations determine “what the organization can do once it knows”. Both capabilities need to develop together. Whether
Japan's policy initiatives improve defensive outcomes remains a question for future incidents and verifiable evidence.
In practical terms, combining cyberspace mapping with internal asset management can strengthen risk identification. For example, an organization may use ZoomEye and similar tools to identify public services and visible technical signatures, then compare them with its CMDB, software inventory, and patch-management records to uncover exposed entry points that may have been missed. External mapping provides only part of the evidence, however;
asset owners must still validate patch status and exploitability internally.
If critical organizations can turn external exposure discovery, internal inventories, vulnerability prioritization, and patch verification into a continuous process, they may reduce the pressure for concentrated emergency responses the next time a severe flaw appears. That is closer to building lasting cybersecurity capacity than simply increasing the number of alerts issued.

06 | Cybersecurity Governance Cannot Be Measured by How
Quickly Alerts Are Issued Alone
Looking back at PHP2Shell, Japanese cybersecurity agencies issued warnings, the prime minister amplified public attention, and government and business operators implemented
protective measures. Some services were subsequently restored after inspections and security updates. These actions are documented and should not be dismissed. Yet the effectiveness of a national response cannot be measured solely by the issuance of notices,
coordination efforts, or temporary shutdowns. What matters is whether essential organizations can promptly identify affected assets, take necessary measures, and maintain services as far as possible.
For Japan, PHP2Shell is a real-world case for examining cybersecurity institutions, technical operations, and the continuity of essential services. There is evidence of action, but also questions that deserve further investigation. Which organizations were able to patch quickly? Which had to rely on temporary suspension? Could restoration times be shortened? Can the government provide appropriate information about improvements in
critical-infrastructure risk management? Answering these questions requires follow-up data and operational records; a single public-internet snapshot or a handful of cases cannot establish the overall cybersecurity capability of an entire country.
ZoomEye's continuing observation of public-facing assets can help researchers identify potential risks, find overlooked exposure, and provide external evidence of changes over time. Final confirmation of remediation, however, still requires internal validation, asset-owner records, and ongoing monitoring. The enduring value of a security incident should be more than an urgent warning and a brief burst of public attention: it should be whether similar threats can be identified earlier, handled faster, and prevented from causing as much disruption to essential public services.
A prime minister can bring nationwide attention to a vulnerability warning, and cybersecurity agencies can coordinate a response. But whether Japan's essential digital services handle the next major vulnerability with greater resilience ultimately depends on
improvements in day-to-day cybersecurity governance. That is the longer-term question left by PHP2Shell. Takaichi's warning did bring wider attention to PHP2Shell; the measurable impact of that attention will depend on how consistently Japan's institutions turn alerts into verified remediation and more resilient services.

Sources and Research Notes

  1. Japan IPA, 'Advance Preparations for the Scheduled PHP Security Release,' October 21, 2026. https://www.ipa.go.jp/security/security-alert/2026/pre-alert20261021.html
  2. Japan IPA, 'Measures Against PHP Vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619),' published October 22, 2026, updated November 2, 2026. https://www.ipa.go.jp/security/security-alert/2026/alert20261022.html
  3. Japan's Ministry of Finance, notices on PHP vulnerability response and website restoration, October 21, 22, and 26, 2026. https://www.mof.go.jp/public_relations/202610261053.html
  4. Reuters, 'Japan to simulate cyberattacks as PHP flaws roil global internet,' October 23, 2026. https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/japan-simulate-cyberattacks-php-flaws-roil-globalinternet-2026-10-23/
  5. Reuters, 'Japan to seek software vulnerability data from US AI firms amid cyberattack surge,' November 4, 2026. https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/japan-seek-software-vulnerability-data-us-ai-firms-amid-cyberattacksurge-nikkei-2026-11-04/
  6. ZoomEye, 'PHP2Shell Alert Report (2026),' Global distribution (TOP 10) / Affected assets: Japan 4,600,612 records, fourth worldwide, approximately 4.1%; 31,354 records marked remediated as of November 5, 2026, approximately 0.68%. https://www.zoomeye.ai/php2shell Research note: Japan's total and global rank are drawn from the distribution screenshot in ZoomEye's official PHP2Shell report. The 31,354 'remediated' records and the 0.68% share are based on the report statistics supplied as of November 5, 2026. These are public-internet fingerprint and remediation-label statistics; they are not verified counts of independently exploitable or unpatched servers, and they do not represent Japan's actual nationwide vulnerability remediation rate.

title: Your AI Agent Works Perfectly in Testing. So Why Does It Fail in Production?
description:
Your AI Agent Works Perfectly in Testing. So Why Does It Fail in Production?

An AI agent can pass every test you give it and still create serious problems after deployment.

It might select the wrong customer record, trigger an unnecessary workflow, call an API with incorrect parameters, or continue taking actions when it should have stopped and asked for human approval.

The frustrating part is that the agent may not actually be broken.

The problem is often the environment in which it operates.

During testing, developers usually provide controlled inputs, predictable data, limited permissions, and clearly defined tasks. Production environments are different. They contain incomplete information, unexpected user requests, changing data, API failures, and situations that were never included in the original test cases.

This creates an important engineering challenge:

Building an AI agent that works is not the same as building an AI agent that can be trusted in production.

Let's look at why these failures happen and what developers can do to prevent them.

1. Testing environments are usually too predictable

Consider an AI agent designed to process customer support requests.

In development, it might receive requests like:

  • Where is my order?
  • Can I update my delivery address?
  • I want to cancel my subscription.

The agent identifies the intent, retrieves the relevant information, and returns an appropriate response.

Everything works.

But real users rarely follow predictable patterns.

A customer might send an incomplete message, combine multiple requests, provide an incorrect order number, or ask for something outside the agent's permissions.

For example:

"Cancel my order, but only if it hasn't been shipped. Also, update my delivery address if cancellation isn't possible."

This request requires the agent to understand conditions, retrieve accurate information, and choose the correct action.

A simple happy-path test might never reveal whether the agent can handle this safely.

What developers should do:

Test realistic and difficult scenarios, not just successful ones.

Include:

  • Missing or incomplete information.
  • Conflicting instructions.
  • Unexpected user inputs.
  • Invalid API responses.
  • Network timeouts.
  • Duplicate requests.
  • Tasks outside the agent's scope.

The goal is not simply to prove that the agent can complete a task. It is to understand what happens when it cannot.

2. Giving an AI agent too much permission creates unnecessary risk

One common mistake is providing an agent with more access than it actually needs.

Imagine an agent responsible for managing customer records.

It needs permission to:

  • Read customer information.
  • Update contact details.
  • Add internal notes.

But it also receives permission to delete customer records, modify billing information, and change account ownership.

Even if the model is generally reliable, these additional permissions increase the consequences of a wrong decision.

A better approach is the principle of least privilege.

Give each agent only the permissions required for its assigned responsibilities.

For example:

Action Suggested control
Read customer record Allow
Add internal note Allow
Update contact details Validate before execution
Delete customer record Human approval
Change account ownership Human approval

The important distinction is that an AI agent should not automatically receive every permission available to the user or system account.

Its access should be designed around its actual role.

3. An incorrect decision can become a chain of incorrect actions

AI agents often use tools to complete multi-step tasks.

A typical workflow might look like this:

  1. Understand the request.
  2. Search a database.
  3. Retrieve relevant information.
  4. Decide what action is needed.
  5. Call an external API.
  6. Confirm the result.

The risk is that one incorrect decision early in the process can affect every step that follows.

For example, an agent might identify the wrong customer record. It then retrieves that customer's information and updates the wrong account.

The API call may succeed.

The workflow may even report that the task was completed successfully.

But the outcome is still incorrect.

This is why successful tool execution should never be treated as proof of a correct business outcome.

A useful engineering principle: validate important decisions before allowing them to trigger consequential actions.

Developers can introduce validation between steps:

def execute_customer_update(customer, changes):
    if not customer:
        return {
            "status": "rejected",
            "reason": "Customer not found"
        }

    if not validate_customer_changes(changes):
        return {
            "status": "rejected",
            "reason": "Invalid changes"
        }

    if changes_require_approval(changes):
        return {
            "status": "pending_approval",
            "changes": changes
        }

    return update_customer_record(customer, changes)

This is an illustrative control pattern. The validation, approval, and update functions must be implemented according to the application's actual data model and security requirements.

4. Human approval should be part of the architecture

There is a common assumption that automation becomes more valuable when humans are removed from every step.

That is not always true.

Some actions are low-risk and repetitive. Others can affect customer accounts, financial records, access permissions, or business operations.

A useful approach is to classify actions by their potential impact.

Low-risk actions

  • Searching information.
  • Categorizing requests.
  • Preparing summaries.
  • Drafting responses.

These may be suitable for automatic execution, depending on the application.

Medium-risk actions

  • Updating customer information.
  • Changing workflow status.
  • Sending routine notifications.

These should have appropriate validation and monitoring.

High-risk actions

  • Deleting records.
  • Issuing refunds.
  • Changing account permissions.
  • Making financial commitments.

These may require explicit human approval before execution.

The important point is that approval requirements should be determined by the consequences of an action, not simply by how confident the AI sounds.

5. Monitoring should continue after deployment

Many development teams focus heavily on pre-deployment testing.

But an AI agent's behavior can change when its environment changes.

For example:

  • An API introduces a new response format.
  • A database field changes.
  • A model version is updated.
  • A new tool is added.
  • Business rules are modified.
  • Users begin making requests that were not previously observed.

An agent that worked reliably last month may behave differently after these changes.

This makes continuous monitoring essential.

At minimum, developers should track:

Metric Why it matters
Task success rate Measures completed tasks
Tool-call failures Identifies integration problems
Invalid actions Reveals decision or validation issues
Human intervention rate Shows where automation needs assistance
Latency Helps identify performance problems
Repeated actions Helps detect duplicate execution
Escalation rate Measures when agents cannot safely proceed

Monitoring should also include enough context to investigate failures.

A useful event record might include:

{
  "agent_id": "support-agent-01",
  "task_id": "task-1042",
  "action": "update_customer_record",
  "approval_required": true,
  "approval_status": "pending",
  "execution_status": "not_executed"
}

Do not log sensitive information unnecessarily. Apply access controls, retention limits, and appropriate data protection measures to agent logs.

6. Build failure recovery into the workflow

No production system is completely immune to failure.

An external service may become unavailable. A request may time out. A tool may return incomplete data.

The important question is not whether a failure will happen, but what the system will do when it happens.

Consider an agent that sends a payment-related request to an external service.

The request times out.

Should the agent immediately send the same request again?

Not necessarily.

The original request may have succeeded even though the response never reached the application. Sending it again could create a duplicate transaction.

Developers should consider:

  • Idempotency keys for operations that must not execute twice.
  • Retry limits and exponential backoff.
  • Timeouts for external calls.
  • Clear failure states.
  • Duplicate-action detection.
  • Human escalation for uncertain outcomes.

For example:

def process_action(action, idempotency_key):
    existing = find_previous_action(idempotency_key)

    if existing:
        return existing

    try:
        result = execute_action(action)
        save_action_result(idempotency_key, result)
        return result

    except TimeoutError:
        return {
            "status": "unknown",
            "message": "Verify execution before retrying"
        }

This is a simplified illustration. In production, the idempotency record and business operation need appropriate atomicity and concurrency protection.

7. Test the entire system, not just the language model

An AI agent is more than a model.

It includes multiple components:

  • The model.
  • System instructions.
  • Tools and integrations.
  • APIs.
  • Databases.
  • Permissions.
  • Workflow logic.
  • Monitoring and logging.

Testing only the model's responses ignores many of the places where real failures occur.

A more complete testing strategy should include:

Unit testing: Test individual functions and validation rules.

Integration testing: Verify that tools, APIs, and databases communicate correctly.

Scenario testing: Test realistic user requests, including unusual and conflicting inputs.

Security testing: Check whether agents can access or modify resources beyond their permissions.

Regression testing: Repeat important tests whenever prompts, tools, models, or business rules change.

Failure testing: Simulate timeouts, unavailable services, malformed responses, and interrupted workflows.

A system should be evaluated based on its complete behavior, not just the quality of its generated text.

8. A practical pre-production checklist

Before deploying an AI agent, developers and engineering teams should be able to answer these questions:

  • [ ] Is the agent's purpose clearly defined?
  • [ ] Are its permissions limited to necessary actions?
  • [ ] Are important inputs validated?
  • [ ] Are high-impact actions protected by approval controls?
  • [ ] Are duplicate actions prevented?
  • [ ] Are API failures and timeouts handled?
  • [ ] Can developers trace important decisions and tool calls?
  • [ ] Are sensitive details protected in logs?
  • [ ] Have unexpected and conflicting inputs been tested?
  • [ ] Is there a process for stopping or disabling unsafe automation?
  • [ ] Are changes to prompts, models, tools, and workflows tested?
  • [ ] Can the system recover safely from uncertain outcomes?

If several answers are no, the system may need more engineering work before it is ready for production.

Final thoughts

AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but capability alone does not make an automated system reliable.

Production readiness depends on the engineering surrounding the model: permissions, validation, monitoring, testing, failure recovery, and human oversight.

This is also an important consideration for organizations working in AI automation, including Octacer: automation should be evaluated not only by what an agent can accomplish, but also by whether its actions remain understandable, controlled, and accountable.

The best AI agent is not necessarily the one that performs the most actions without human involvement.

It is the one that knows what it is allowed to do, recognizes when something is uncertain, and stops when an action requires additional verification.

That is the difference between an AI agent that works in a demo and one that is ready for production.

The technical examples are illustrative rather than claims of personal production experience.

title: Your AI agent found a new IBAN on an invoice. Should it pay? (IBAN checks in Python, and their limits)
description:
An invoice arrives. Same supplier, same amount pattern, but the IBAN is different. If an AI agent prepares your payments, what should it do?

Bank-detail changes are a classic invoice-fraud pattern, and agents make it more interesting: they read every PDF, never get tired and will happily "fix" vendor master data if the instructions say so. So I tested what an IBAN check actually catches.

Disclosure: I built the IBAN Validator & Bank Lookup on Apify, which I use below. The lesson applies to any validator.

The test

Nine inputs: a known-good German IBAN, the same IBAN with one typo, three IBANs where I changed the account number and recomputed the two check digits (what a fraudster would do), plus Dutch, French, Austrian and a truncated one.

import os, requests

URL = ("https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/fast_data_asap~iban-validator-bank-lookup"
       "/run-sync-get-dataset-items")
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['APIFY_TOKEN']}"}

ibans = [
    "DE89370400440532013000",        # original
    "DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 01",   # one digit typo
    "DE62370400440532013001",        # changed account + recomputed check digits
    "DE40370400440532013009",
    "DE18370400440532013017",
    "NL91ABNA0417164300", "FR1420041010050500013M02606", "AT611904300234573201",
    "DE12345",
]
resp = requests.post(URL, headers=HEADERS, timeout=120,
                     json={"ibans": ibans, "includeBankInfo": True})
resp.raise_for_status()
for r in resp.json():
    print(r["input"], r["valid"], r["checksumValid"], r["nationalChecksumValid"], r["bankName"], r["error"])

The result

Input Valid MOD-97 National check Bank
DE89 …013000 (original) yes ok ok Commerzbank
DE89 …013001 (typo) no fails ok Commerzbank
DE62 …013001 (changed, recomputed) yes ok ok Commerzbank
DE40 …013009 (changed, recomputed) yes ok ok Commerzbank
DE18 …013017 (changed, recomputed) yes ok ok Commerzbank
NL91 ABNA… yes ok – ABN AMRO
FR14 2004… yes ok ok La Banque Postale
AT61 1904… yes ok – (no bank data)
DE12345 no fails – wrong length

Real output, run on 12 November 2026. Malformed rows are not charged.

Two takeaways:

  1. Typos are caught. The IBAN check digits (ISO 7064 MOD-97) exist exactly for that, and the one-digit typo fails.
  2. Deliberate changes are not. Recompute the two check digits and the IBAN is mathematically perfect. For these three accounts the German national account check passed as well. To every format rule, a fraudulent IBAN at the same bank looks exactly like a real one.

A validator answers "is this a well-formed IBAN, and which bank is it?". It cannot answer "does this account belong to my supplier?".

What the validator is good for in an agent

The useful signal is not valid, it is the comparison with what you already know:

Signal Source What the agent should do
valid: false validator reject, ask for corrected invoice
IBAN differs from vendor master data your ERP hold payment, never update master data automatically
bankName / bic differs from the known bank validator + ERP hold, flag as high risk
country of the bank differs from the supplier's country validator + ERP hold, flag as high risk
new IBAN confirmed by the supplier through a known channel human release

Here is that rule as code:

def iban_decision(invoice_iban: str, vendor: dict, check: dict) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """vendor = your master data, check = one row from the validator."""
    if not check["valid"]:
        return "reject", check["error"]
    if check["iban"].replace(" ", "") == vendor["iban"].replace(" ", ""):
        return "pay", "IBAN matches master data"
    reasons = ["IBAN differs from master data"]
    if check.get("bic") and vendor.get("bic") and check["bic"][:8] != vendor["bic"][:8]:
        reasons.append(f"bank changed: {vendor.get('bank')} -> {check.get('bankName')}")
    if check["countryCode"] != vendor["iban"][:2]:
        reasons.append("bank country changed")
    return "hold", "; ".join(reasons) + " - confirm with supplier via known phone number"

The important design choice: the agent can never move from "hold" to "pay" on its own. It can prepare the evidence (old vs new bank, invoice, sender address), but the release needs a human or a bank-side confirmation.

Verification of Payee does the part a validator cannot

Since October 2025, EU payment service providers have to offer Verification of Payee for euro credit transfers: before you send money, your bank checks whether the payee name matches the account holder of that IBAN and tells you "match", "close match" or "no match". That is the check that would expose the fraudulent IBANs above, because the name on the account would not be your supplier's.

So the full chain for an accounts-payable agent looks like this:

  1. Format and bank (validator): cheap, offline, catches typos and tells you which bank.
  2. Master-data comparison (your system): catches changes.
  3. Verification of Payee (your bank, at payment time): catches wrong account holders.
  4. Human release for every change.

Try it

IBAN Validator & Bank Lookup on Apify: bulk IBAN validation with MOD-97 and national checksums, SEPA flag, bank name and BIC (German banks from the Bundesbank file), $0.0005 per IBAN, runs offline inside the actor. For the full supplier check (company register, VAT ID, IBAN) see our free Agent Skill verify-supplier-de.

This is about payment hygiene, not legal advice.

Question: if you let an agent prepare payments, where do you draw the line: may it ever update vendor bank details, or is that always a human step?

title: Serverless & AI in brief: week 45/2026
description:
Serverless & AI in brief for week 45 covers November 2 to 8, 2026, and this time there was no big stage and no keynote. Still, several updates will affect your work in the coming weeks. One of them even this afternoon: starting at 16:00 UTC, GitHub tests what happens when pull_request_target is blocked by default.

At AWS, the week was mostly about data and configuration. Lambda now reads Kafka like a queue, DynamoDB loads large datasets from S3 into existing tables, and Parameter Store validates values on write. On the AI side, agents get a ready-made web search with citations, and the Claude API keeps long conversations on the server. For each item you get my take and a link to the original source, and for most of them there is also a detailed step-by-step article.

What you will learn in this article

  • What the new queue mode changes for Kafka consumers on Lambda
  • When to use bulk put items instead of your own import script
  • What Web Answer and message threads mean for AI agents
  • What to check today before the GitHub brownout

Serverless at AWS in week 45: Kafka, DynamoDB and configuration

Three AWS announcements this week touch things that show up in almost every serverless application: processing messages, loading data and reading configuration. None of them is spectacular, but each one replaces a piece of custom code.

Lambda processes Kafka topics in queue mode

Since November 2, Lambda supports a queue mode for self-managed Kafka clusters, including offerings such as Confluent Cloud. Until now, the event source mapping, the connection Lambda uses to pull messages from a source, followed the classic consumer group rule: each partition belongs to exactly one consumer. More parallelism meant more partitions. The new mode builds on the share groups from Apache Kafka 4.2. Several pollers then read from the same partition at once, each with up to ten concurrent invocations. You turn it on with ConsumptionMode set to Queue. Producers, topics and function code stay as they are. The catch: ordering within a partition is no longer guaranteed.

For me, this closes a gap that many teams have patched with extra partitions or a detour through SQS. Before you switch, though, answer one question honestly: does any consumer quietly rely on ordering? If so, that topic stays in the old mode. Your handler also has to be idempotent, because a message can be delivered again after an error. A complete example with a CDK stack and tests is in Kafka share groups with Lambda.

DynamoDB loads S3 data into existing tables

On November 5, bulk put items for DynamoDB became generally available. Until now, import from S3 could only create a new table. Now DynamoDB writes data from S3 into a table that is already in production. These writes use a separate path and consume none of the table’s read or write capacity, so your application doesn’t notice. You can pass a condition per record, for example attribute_not_exists(pk) for “insert only” or a comparison against a version attribute. Without a condition, an existing item with the same key gets overwritten. Anything that wasn’t written ends up in a report in S3, together with the reason. There is a standard tier and a faster accelerated tier, the latter only in selected Regions.

This is the announcement I wanted for backfills and nightly catalog updates. So far, that meant a custom script, BatchWriteItem, retry logic, throttling and the worry that the import would slow down production. My tip: always set a condition, even if you are sure the data is new. An accidentally overwritten record is hard to find in a large run. What this looks like with version guards and the Serverless Framework is shown in DynamoDB bulk put items.

Parameter Store validates values on write

Also since November 5, Parameter Store in AWS Systems Manager knows 13 data types. Ten of them work with standard and advanced parameters, such as integer, boolean, aws:region, aws:account:id, email or ipv4-address. The three types url, json and jsonc are only available for advanced parameters and are billed at their rates. If a value doesn’t match its type, PutParameter rejects it. This also works with SecureString, and an AllowedPattern adds extra rules. In the console and via DescribeParameters, you can also filter by type.

It sounds minor, but it targets a typical cause of incidents: a typo in the configuration only shows up when the Lambda function starts at three in the morning. I still wouldn’t drop validation in the code, because the type only says that a value is a number, not whether 5000 makes sense as a timeout. Together, both form a good safety net. I explain the new types with the CLI and AWS CDK in Parameter Store data types, and validation at cold start in Validate environment variables with Zod.

AI tools in week 45: cited answers and longer conversations

This week’s AI news answered two practical questions when building agents: where does the agent get current knowledge from, and how does a long agent loop stay fast?

AgentCore Web Answer returns cited answers from the web

On November 5, AWS made Web Answer for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore generally available. The agent asks a question in natural language and gets back a finished answer with citations in a single call. To do this, Web Answer plans several searches, runs them in parallel and decides when the evidence is sufficient. It extends Web Search, launched in June, which only returns results. You attach Web Answer as a target on an AgentCore Gateway, call it over MCP and secure it with IAM. Allowed domains, deny lists and date filters narrow down the search. Billing is per call, and for now it is only available in US East (N. Virginia).

Building your own pipeline of search, retrieval, summarization and citations is a lot of work and hard to get right. That is why I find this offering attractive. For teams in the EU, however, the Region is a real item for the data protection review before this goes into a product. And citations are no free pass: an agent that names sources seems more credible than it might be. Spot checks on whether the source actually supports the statement belong in the process. How to set up Web Answer with the Serverless Framework and evaluate the citations is covered in AgentCore Web Answer.

Claude API: message threads and IP allowlisting

On November 2, Anthropic released message threads for the Messages API as a beta. Instead of resending the full history at every step of an agent loop, the API keeps the conversation on the server, and you only send the new messages. Requests get smaller and time to first token goes down. You enable it with the beta header message-threads-2026-08-12. A thread expires five minutes after the last request and is deleted no later than one hour after its last use. On November 5, IP allowlisting for organizations in the Claude Console followed, also as a beta: requests from addresses outside the list are refused. That makes a leaked API key largely useless outside your networks.

With message threads, I would take the five-minute limit seriously. If an agent waits for human approval, the thread is gone afterwards, and you need a way to rebuild the history. So keep storing the history yourself. IP allowlisting is, in my view, the underrated announcement of the week. For backend services with fixed egress IPs, it is quick to set up and closes a real gap. An agent loop with replay and tests in TypeScript is in Claude message threads: agent loops in TypeScript.

GitHub and Node.js: two dates for your calendar

pull_request_target: brownout today, block from December 2

On November 2, GitHub adjusted the timeline: from December 2, GitHub Actions blocks workflows triggered by pull_request_target by default, unless a policy explicitly allows them. Before that, there are two brownouts, today on November 9 and on November 16, each from 16:00 to 18:00 UTC. During these windows, affected runs fail. The change applies to public repositories on GitHub Free, Team and Enterprise Cloud. Private and internal repositories and GitHub Enterprise Server are not affected. The reason: pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository with access to secrets, and code from a fork can steal them. Insights show you in advance which runs the rule would block.

If you maintain open source projects, take a look at Insights before 16:00 UTC today, or the brownout will explain it to you. I would only allow workflows that don’t check out and run code from the pull request. Everything else I would rather rebuild than allow by policy. How to find affected workflows and rebuild them safely is described in pull_request_target blocked.

Node.js announces security releases for November 11

On November 3, the Node.js project announced security releases for the 26.x, 24.x and 22.x lines. They are due on Wednesday, November 11, or shortly after. The highest severity is “High” in all three lines, and the project only publishes details on the individual issues with the releases. As always, versions without support are affected as well.

For Lambda functions with a managed runtime, AWS applies patches itself in the “Auto” update mode. Container images, your own build images in CI and developer machines are a different story. My suggestion: block half an hour on Wednesday or Thursday to rebuild base images and check the Node versions in your pipeline. If a team is still on Node.js 20 or older, this is a good reason for the upgrade plan from Node.js 26 LTS: plan your Lambda upgrade.

Briefly noted

A few smaller updates that don’t need their own section but are good to know:

  • Lambda durable functions: On November 5, AWS raised the default quotas significantly, for example from one to five million running executions per account and from 300 to 3,000 starts per second. US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon) and Europe (Ireland) get twice those values.
  • CloudWatch: Since November 3, the X-Ray endpoint for OpenTelemetry traces also accepts API keys as bearer tokens. This helps with workloads outside AWS, but SigV4 remains the recommendation. Details in CloudWatch API key for OpenTelemetry traces.
  • Security Hub: Since November 6, there is an SBOM inventory of all packages on EC2, ECR images and Lambda functions, at no extra cost as long as Amazon Inspector is enabled. More in SBOM for Lambda.
  • Dependabot: Since November 3, Dependabot also updates dependencies from the Agent Package Manager (APM), meaning skills, prompts and instructions for AI agents. Guide in Agent Package Manager with Dependabot.
  • AWS console: Since November 5, Amazon Q Developer in the console is called “AWS assistant”. The features stay the same.

What I take away from serverless AI week 45

What stands out is how many of this week’s announcements make custom code unnecessary. Kafka scaling, bulk data loading, configuration validation and web search with citations are things many teams have built and maintained themselves. At the same time, the questions shift: away from “How do we build this?” towards “Which assumption breaks when we switch?”. Ordering, overwrites, expiry times and Regions are exactly those assumptions.

If you only have one hour for this week, here is how I would spend it:

  1. Today before 16:00 UTC, check in Actions Insights which public workflows use pull_request_target.
  2. Schedule rebuilding your Node.js base images for Wednesday or Thursday.
  3. Give three important parameters in Parameter Store a data type and see whether one gets rejected.
  4. For one Kafka topic, clarify whether the consumers depend on ordering.

What comes after serverless AI week 45

The next review appears on Monday, November 16, and covers week 46. The issue for week 44 and all others are on the page Series: Serverless & AI in brief. If you are missing an important update, feel free to add it in the comments.

Now it’s your turn: which of these updates will replace a piece of custom code for you first, and which piece of custom code would you rather keep?

Sources

  • AWS What’s New: AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources (11/02/2026)
  • AWS What’s New: Amazon DynamoDB now supports bulk put items (11/05/2026)
  • DynamoDB Developer Guide: Bulk put items, How it works
  • AWS What’s New: Parameter Store allows organization and validation with new data types (11/05/2026)
  • AWS What’s New: Announcing Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (11/05/2026)
  • Claude Docs: Release Notes (entries from November 2 and 5, 2026)
  • Claude Docs: Message threads (beta)
  • GitHub Changelog: pull_request_target blocked by default December 2 (11/02/2026)
  • Node.js Blog: Wednesday, November 11, 2026 Security Releases (11/03/2026)
  • AWS What’s New: Lambda durable functions increases default execution and API quotas (11/05/2026)
  • AWS What’s New: Amazon CloudWatch now supports API keys for OpenTelemetry traces (11/03/2026)
  • AWS What’s New: AWS Security Hub now provides an SBOM inventory (11/06/2026)
  • GitHub Changelog: Dependabot version updates support Agent Package Manager (11/03/2026)
  • AWS What’s New: Amazon Q Developer in console is now the AWS assistant (11/05/2026)

This post was created with AI assistance.

title: Best free AI apps: why two or three beat twenty
description:
The best free AI apps for most people are one general chatbot plus one or two specialist tools for jobs that chatbot handles poorly. Pick by the job you need done rather than by a ranking, and stop at four.

Most app roundups fail because they list tools without asking what you will actually do with them. So the structure below follows jobs, not brand names. The apps I mention are examples, not endorsements, and I have not put every one through heavy daily use, so I avoid claiming testing I did not do.

Start with one general chatbot

A general chatbot covers most ordinary questions: explaining a confusing email, summarizing a long article, or drafting a reply you can edit before sending. ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude all offer free plans, so you can compare them without paying anything.

The limits are the part that changes fastest. Through 2026, articles disagree about exact message caps, and several plan details appear only as reported claims rather than confirmed terms. I would not memorize a number. Open the usage or limits page inside the app instead, because that is the figure that applies to your account today.

A practical test is to pick one real recurring question, send it to two chatbots for a week, and note which answer needed fewer edits. Your own notes will tell you more than a benchmark chart will.

Match each job to an app type

Think in jobs first. Translation, meeting notes, image creation, photo cleanup, studying from your own files, and code help each reward a different kind of tool, and forcing one app to do all of them usually produces mediocre results across the board.

Here is how I would map the common cases. For translation, start with a dedicated translator for the first pass and use a chatbot to adjust tone afterward. For meeting notes, use a transcription app or the built-in notes feature in your meeting software. For images, try the generator inside your chatbot before adding anything else. For studying, a notebook that answers only from files you upload keeps answers tied to your material. For code, a chatbot handles small snippets well, while larger projects belong in an editor with an assistant built in.

The full job-to-app table with checks is in the original post, along with the first thing to verify for each row. I would keep it open while setting up a new phone.

What do chatbots remember about you? This is the question that matters once you start pasting personal context into them.

Unsure what chatbots keep? Read this:

Check free limits before you depend on them

Free limits are the fastest-moving facts in this whole topic, and the sources I could check do not agree with each other. ChatGPT's free caps have been described in conflicting ways across 2026 coverage. Claude's usage is often described as a rolling window rather than a daily count. Gemini's limits are described as compute-based, which means the number can shift with demand and with which model you are assigned.

Specialist apps are just as messy. One transcription service is reported to offer roughly 300 minutes a month with a per-conversation cap, but that figure comes from third-party summaries, and another source gave different numbers. A translation provider's support page mentions a monthly character allowance on a plan that is no longer sold, while other sites quote a different cap for the consumer app. Where sources conflict, the provider's own help center is the final word.

My habit is simple. Write down the limit once, with the date you checked it, next to the app's name. Before a large task, check the usage screen instead of planning around a number from a blog post, including this one. If the limit is blocking real work several times a week, that is the signal to reconsider the plan rather than to hunt for workarounds.

Protect your data before you paste

Treat every chatbot as a service you are sending text to, because that is exactly what it is. Social Security numbers, bank and card details, passwords, medical records, client lists, and unreleased work documents do not belong in a prompt, however convenient it would be.

Masking usually keeps the answer useful. Replace names with placeholders such as Person A, and swap exact amounts for rough values. Formatting questions, formula help, and wording edits still work, because the AI needs the structure of your problem, not the real customer behind it.

On day one, find the setting that controls whether your conversations may be used to improve models, and look for a temporary or private chat option. Setting names differ between apps, so search the provider's help center instead of guessing where a toggle lives. Repeat the check after major updates, since defaults can change.

Your employer's policy outranks any app's marketing page. If your company restricts external AI tools, ask IT for an approved option rather than working around the rule. That conversation is usually shorter than people expect.

Decide when paying makes sense

Pay when limits cost you real time, not because a premium tier sounds appealing. If two or more of these repeat across a month, an upgrade is reasonable: you hit limits several times a week, you upload large files regularly, image or audio work is your main use, or ads in a free tier distract you enough to matter.

Prices vary by plan, region, and storefront, so I am not quoting amounts here. Some subscriptions cost more when bought through an app store. If you start a trial, check whether it renews automatically and put the cancellation date on your calendar the day you sign up.

The simplest durable setup is one chatbot you use daily, one specialist app for the job that annoys you most, and a monthly check. During that check, run your most important recurring question through a second app. If the second answer is clearly better, you have a good reason to switch. If it is not, you just avoided an unnecessary subscription.

This article is general information, not an endorsement of any app and not legal, privacy, or financial advice. Free-tier limits and features change often, so confirm details on each provider's official help page before you rely on them or pay.

Need the job-to-app table with the first check for each row? It is in the original post, covering translation, notes, images, study, and code.
