title: ¿Por qué osFoundry obliga a Claude a indicar la pestaña de Slides exacta y a usar una clave en cada cita?
description:
Esta es la llamada de creación que recibe una conexión de Claude para las Notes de osFoundry. Se obtuvo con un tools/list sin autenticar contra el endpoint MCP público el 2026-11-09 y está recortada:

{"name": "create_note_tab",
 "description": "Create a new Slides or Sheet tab in an approved Note. Use the version from list_note_tabs; returns the exact new tab ID for later edits. An optional outline fills a Slides tab. A repeated idempotency key returns the first tab.",
 "inputSchema": {
   "required": ["note_id", "expected_version", "idempotency_key", "tab_type"],
   "properties": {
     "tab_type": {"enum": ["slides", "sheet"]},
     "label": {"type": "string"},
     "slides": {"type": "array", "minItems": 1, "maxItems": 20,
                "items": {"required": ["title"], "additionalProperties": false,
                          "properties": {"title": {}, "body": {}, "notes": {}}}}},
   "additionalProperties": false},
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": false, "destructiveHint": true},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:write"]}]}

Sus dos vecinas para este trabajo:

{"name": "add_note_source",
 "description": "Add an HTTP or HTTPS citation to the Sources tab of an approved Note. Uses the Note version and an idempotency key; returns the new source ID.",
 "inputSchema": {"required": ["note_id", "expected_version", "idempotency_key", "title", "url"]}}

{"name": "list_note_tabs",
 "description": "List every tab instance and its type. A Note may have multiple Slides or Sheet tabs; use the exact tab ID returned here."}

Tres frases sostienen el diseño: "every tab instance", "returns the exact new tab ID" y "a repeated idempotency key returns the first". El resto del post reconstruye las herramientas en Python y mide qué evita cada una de esas frases. El bloqueo optimista sobre la versión de la Note es tema de otro post y aquí solo aparece donde interactúa con las otras dos.

¿Qué puede poner Claude realmente en una diapositiva?

Menos que el asistente propio de la app de escritorio. Dentro de osFoundry, slide_create_deck_from_outline y slide_add_slide del asistente de Notes (en apps/web/src/screens/notes/lib/note-surface-tools.ts) aceptan layouts, viñetas, contenido a dos columnas, tablas, imágenes y uno de cinco temas. El elemento de outline del conector es title, body, notes, con additionalProperties: false. edit_note_tab ofrece slide_add para una diapositiva y slides_add_outline para un array, ambos con los mismos tres campos.

code/note_store.py carga la respuesta guardada de tools/list y valida los payloads contra ella con un validador mínimo (required, enum, additionalProperties, minItems/maxItems). Ocho payloads que un modelo podría enviar perfectamente:

edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slide_add", "title": "Sources", "body": "3 links"}  -> ok
edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slide_add", "title": "Sources", "index": 0}         -> unexpected index
edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slides_add", "slides": [{"title": "a"}]}            -> operation: not in enum
edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slides_add_outline", "slides": [{... "bullets"}]}   -> slides: [0] unexpected bullets
create_note_tab  {"tab_type": "slides", "slides": "[21 items]"}                     -> slides: maxItems 20
create_note_tab  {"tab_type": "markdown"}                                           -> tab_type: not in enum
add_note_source  {"url": "https://example.org/report"}                              -> missing title
list_note_attachments {"kind": "sources", "limit": 100}                             -> ok

El último pasa este validador, pero no el esquema real completo: limit tiene maximum: 50, y la reconstrucción no lo comprueba. slide_add no puede elegir posición, create_note_tab no puede crear una pestaña Markdown y un deck de más de 20 diapositivas necesita más de una llamada. Un esquema estrecho es una decisión sobre quién da estilo al deck: el conector escribe el contenido y una persona en la app de escritorio aplica temas y layout.

¿Por qué un ID de pestaña exacto y no "la pestaña de slides"?

Porque la propia app de escritorio sigue aceptando el atajo, y el atajo elige la primera coincidencia. resolveTabInstanceId() en apps/web/src/screens/notes/types.ts:

if (cfg.some((t) => t.id === rawTabId)) return rawTabId
const byType = cfg.find((t) => t.type === rawTabId)
if (byType) return byType.id

Ese fallback mantiene funcionando enlaces antiguos como …/slides. Para un agente significa que "editar slides" va a parar a la pestaña de Slides que esté primero en la barra. Las pestañas nuevas reciben IDs como slides-9-mh8z1k2a de nextTabId() en NotesContentPanel.tsx, las fijas son markdown, files y sources, y una persona puede añadir tantas pestañas de Slides como quiera, arrastrarlas a otro orden y renombrarlas, incluso con nombres repetidos (handleRename solo hace trim).

La reconstrucción le da a una Note K pestañas de Slides con etiquetas distintas. Un agente scriptado lista las pestañas, elige un deck como objetivo y guarda una referencia a él: su posición en la barra, su tipo, su etiqueta o su ID. Entre turnos del agente, la persona hace de cero a dos cambios aleatorios (mover una pestaña 40%, renombrar una pestaña de Slides con una de las cinco etiquetas 35%, añadir una pestaña de Slides 25%). Después el agente vuelve a listar y resuelve su referencia. 10,000 pruebas por K, seed 7:

K decks referencia correcto deck equivocado no encontrado
2 posición 83.7% 16.3% 0.0%
2 tipo 50.7% 49.3% 0.0%
2 etiqueta 85.6% 2.1% 12.3%
2 ID 100% 0 0
5 posición 82.7% 17.3% 0.0%
5 tipo 19.7% 80.3% 0.0%
5 etiqueta 92.1% 3.0% 5.0%
5 ID 100% 0 0

La referencia por tipo acierta 1/K de las veces, como era de esperar. La posición falla cada vez que un arrastre cruza el objetivo, sea cual sea K. La etiqueta es la tentadora, porque es lo que la persona escribe en el prompt, y acierta la mayoría de las veces. El 2–3% en que falla son los casos malos: otro deck lleva ahora esa etiqueta y el agente escribe en él sin ningún error. "No encontrado" es el fallo seguro. Un ID se asigna una vez y nunca se reutiliza, así que sobrevive a cualquier cambio que la persona pueda hacer en la barra de pestañas.

¿La comprobación de versión no detecta ya una pestaña equivocada?

No. Cada cambio en la barra de pestañas de los de arriba incrementa la versión de la Note, así que una escritura obsoleta se rechaza y el agente vuelve a listar. El nuevo listado le da una versión actual, y entonces resuelve su referencia antigua contra la lista nueva. En la reconstrucción, el 100% de esas escrituras pasa la comprobación de versión, incluidas todas las que apuntan al deck equivocado. La versión demuestra que el agente vio la Note más reciente. No dice nada de si encontró la pestaña correcta dentro de ella. De eso se encarga el ID de pestaña.

¿Dónde va la comprobación de idempotencia, antes o después de la de versión?

Antes, o la promesa de la descripción de la herramienta se rompe. Se ejecuta create_note_tab 50 veces por run con un 30% de respuestas perdidas después de que el servidor hiciera commit, que es como se ve un timeout del host desde el cliente. El cliente reenvía la misma llamada. Tres políticas de cliente, dos órdenes de servidor, seeds 1–3:

el servidor comprueba política de clave del cliente pestañas creadas (llamadas enviadas)
clave, luego versión clave nueva por llamada 63 (76) / 75 (100) / 62 (74)
clave, luego versión misma clave al reintentar 50 (67) / 50 (81) / 50 (62)
clave, luego versión clave nueva tras un conflicto 50 (67) / 50 (81) / 50 (62)
versión, luego clave clave nueva por llamada 63 (76) / 75 (100) / 62 (74)
versión, luego clave misma clave al reintentar 50 (79) / 50 (98) / 50 (72)
versión, luego clave clave nueva tras un conflicto 72 (94) / 73 (96) / 61 (72)

El reenvío lleva la versión de antes del commit perdido. Un servidor que comprueba primero la versión ve una versión obsoleta y devuelve un conflicto en lugar del primer resultado. Un cliente que reacciona a los conflictos de la forma sensata, volviendo a leer y tratando el siguiente intento como una intención nueva con una clave nueva, crea ahora un segundo deck. Incluso un cliente que conserva su clave envía un 16–21% más de llamadas. Con la clave comprobada primero, el reenvío devuelve el ID de pestaña original diga lo que diga la versión. Eso es lo que tiene que significar "a repeated idempotency key returns the first tab".

¿Qué clave debería llevar add_note_source?

La reconstrucción ejecuta 300 sesiones de investigación. Cada una tiene tres turnos, en cada turno se citan 6 de 8 páginas, y una página puede volver en cualquiera de siete formas de escribirla: con barra final, con www., con ?utm_source=…, con un #fragment, con http:// o sin esquema. El 20% de las respuestas se pierde y se reenvía con la misma clave.

clave fuentes guardadas duplicados por sesión
UUID nuevo por cita, reutilizado al reenviar 5,400 3,038 10.13
hash de la URL tal como está escrita 4,814 2,452 8.17
hash de la URL normalizada y el ID de la Note 2,362 0 0.00

Una clave nueva por cita cubre las respuestas perdidas (ninguna fila de esa primera línea viene de un reenvío) y nada más. Una investigación vuelve a citar la misma página en el siguiente turno, y cada turno nuevo es una clave nueva. Hacer hash de la URL tal como está escrita detecta repeticiones exactas, pero no ?utm_source= ni una barra final. La clave que elimina los duplicados nombra la intención, "esta página es una fuente de esta Note", haciendo hash de note_id más una URL normalizada (https, host en minúsculas sin www., sin fragmento, sin utm_*, sin barra final).

El formulario de Sources de la propia app de escritorio hace una versión más ligera de esto. NotesSourcesTab.tsx normaliza el enlace escrito con new URL(...) y rechaza uno que ya esté adjunto ("This source is already attached"). En la reconstrucción, comparar hrefs al estilo del navegador habría detectado 725 de los 3,038 duplicados de la primera fila. El add_note_source del conector no anuncia ninguna comprobación de URL, así que la clave es donde el agente la expresa. Una clave derivada de la URL tiene un efecto secundario: volver a añadir la misma página con una descripción mejor devuelve la primera fila. Editarla es trabajo de la pestaña Sources.

¿Una sola creación con outline o diapositiva por diapositiva?

Coste de un deck de 12 diapositivas, con cada petición validada contra el esquema real:

enfoque escrituras bytes de petición conflictos por deck
create_note_tab con slides 1 1,673 0.070
creación vacía + 12 × slide_add 13 5,237 0.817

La columna de conflictos es un modelo, no una medición de osFoundry: 4 s entre la lectura del agente y su escritura, una persona guardando en algún lugar de la Note una vez por minuto de media (exponencial), 2,000 decks simulados. Cada escritura abre una nueva ventana en la que la versión de la Note puede moverse, así que construir diapositiva por diapositiva exige unas doce veces más relecturas. Mete el deck en el outline (hasta 20 diapositivas) y usa slide_add para la diapositiva que solo descubres después.

La paginación es el otro número que conviene conocer. list_note_attachments limita limit a 50, así que una Note con 120 fuentes necesita 3 llamadas para listarse.

Cómo se ejecutó la reconstrucción

En esta máquina no corre ningún binario de Claude. code/run.py hace de agente y llama directamente a code/note_store.py. El store vive en memoria detrás de un único lock, con un contador como versión. Los nombres de herramientas, campos obligatorios, enums y límites de elementos vienen del esquema real en code/tools_list.raw, y los IDs de pestaña siguen a nextTabId(). La forma de los errores, el ámbito de las claves (aquí, por Note) y el orden de idempotencia son decisiones propias de la reconstrucción, y el segundo orden existe solo para mostrar qué sale mal. Python 3.9.6 en Apple Silicon, los cinco experimentos en 1.0 s de tiempo real. La salida está en code/run.out.

Si lo montas tú mismo

  • Devuelve un ID por instancia en cada llamada de listado y de creación, y haz que las herramientas de edición lo exijan. No resuelvas tipos ni etiquetas en el camino de escritura, aunque tu UI todavía los acepte en las URLs.
  • Comprueba la clave de idempotencia antes que la versión. Un reenvío tras una respuesta perdida siempre lleva la versión antigua.
  • Explica a los agentes en la descripción de la herramienta qué debe nombrar una clave. Para citas, "esta URL en este documento", normalizada, elimina repeticiones entre turnos. Un UUID aleatorio solo cubre los reenvíos.
  • Mantén pequeña la forma de diapositiva del conector (title, body, notes) y deja el diseño a la persona en el editor. Un esquema pequeño significa menos campos en los que un modelo puede equivocarse.
  • Deja que los agentes envíen un outline completo en una sola llamada y ponle un tope (osFoundry usa 20). Menos escrituras significa menos ventanas de conflicto en un documento compartido.
  • Devuelve metadatos de los adjuntos, nunca contenido ni enlaces firmados, por el canal del agente. Un enlace sobrevive a la sesión que lo obtuvo.

Lo que guarda la pestaña Sources del lado de la persona está en la página de la pestaña Sources. El protocolo que hay debajo se resume en la entrada del glosario sobre MCP de osFoundry.

title: How to merge Shift_JIS, UTF-8 BOM, and Windows-1252 CSVs without guessing the encoding
description:
How to merge Shift_JIS, UTF-8 BOM, and Windows-1252 CSVs without guessing the encoding

A shop export from Japan, another from the UK, a third from a US system, and a Chinese marketplace file. You want one table. pandas.read_csv() with the default UTF-8 encoding fails on three of the four files. Dates arrive as 2026/3/2, 20260310, 2026年3月14日, and 3/15/2026. Two rows are exact duplicates, one row is empty, and one amount is written in full-width digits (２４９).

This article walks through that exact problem using sheetstack-lite, a small MIT-licensed Python tool. Every command below was run against the repository's fictional sample files. The output is copied from those runs, not reconstructed from memory.

sheetstack-lite is a free, in-memory merge-and-clean utility. It is not a tax tool, and this article does not claim compatibility with Google Sheets or WPS.

What the sample files actually contain

Clone the repo and install the two dependencies (pandas and openpyxl). Python 3.10 or later is required.

git clone https://github.com/ebhow9986-ctrl/sheetstack-lite.git
cd sheetstack-lite
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

The samples/ folder ships with five fictional CSVs (none of the rows are real customer records):

File What the tool reported What is messy about it
store_us.csv utf-8-sig (UTF-8 with a BOM) Mixed date formats, a blank row, a duplicate US-1002
store_uk.csv cp1252 The word “Café” is a single 0xE9 byte; one date is 3/6/2026; UK-2003 is duplicated
store_jp.csv shift_jis Japanese headers (伝票番号, 日付, 商品名…); dates such as 2026年3月14日 and 20260310; JP-3005 is duplicated
store_cn.csv gb18030 Chinese headers; a full-width amount ２４９; a date written as 2026年3月13日
customers_messy.csv utf-8-sig Duplicate ids, an empty row, mixed dates, a full-width ０８ in the points column

The README describes the four store files as “GBK” for the Chinese export. When the CLI sniffed the same file, it printed gb18030 (a superset of GBK). The rest of this article uses the string the tool actually printed.

Why a default pandas read fails

On the same machine, pd.read_csv(path) with no encoding= argument succeeded only for the UTF-8 BOM file. The other three store exports raised UnicodeDecodeError:

store_cn.csv: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xb6 in position 0: invalid start byte
store_jp.csv: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x93 in position 0: invalid start byte
store_uk.csv: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xe9 in position 67: invalid continuation byte

That last one is the é in “Café”. If you force latin-1 or cp1252 onto the Japanese file, the read may “succeed” and give you mojibake instead of an error. Encoding has to be chosen per file, then the headers have to be lined up, then the dates and duplicates have to be cleaned. Doing that by hand for every export is the tedious part.

This is a well-worn problem — the Stack Overflow thread “UnicodeDecodeError when reading CSV file in Pandas” has been viewed more than a million times. The usual advice is “pass encoding=...”. That works when you already know the encoding and you only have one file. It does not merge four different code pages, or rename 伝票番号 and Order ID into the same column.

Merge the four store exports

The tool is invoked as python3 sheetstack_lite.py. Two subcommands exist: merge and clean.

Point merge at the four store files, ask it to normalize header aliases, and write a single CSV:

python3 sheetstack_lite.py merge \
  samples/store_us.csv \
  samples/store_uk.csv \
  samples/store_jp.csv \
  samples/store_cn.csv \
  -o stores.csv \
  --normalize-headers

Exact output from the run:

Merged 4 file(s), 21 rows, 7 columns
  - store_us.csv: 7 rows / encoding utf-8-sig
  - store_uk.csv: 5 rows / encoding cp1252
  - store_jp.csv: 6 rows / encoding shift_jis
  - store_cn.csv: 3 rows / encoding gb18030
Wrote stores.csv

--normalize-headers maps common aliases onto one English name. In these samples that means, among others:

  • Order ID / 伝票番号 / 订单编号 → order_id
  • Date / 日付 / 成交时间 → order_date
  • Item / 商品名 / 商品名称 → product
  • Quantity / 数量 / 件数 → qty
  • Sales / 売上 / 销售额 → amount
  • Remaining / 在庫 / 库存数 → stock

A source_file column is added unless you pass --no-source. The merged file still has 21 rows, including the blank US row and the three duplicate orders. Dates are not rewritten during merge. “Café mug”, スマホスタンド, and 键盘 all sit in the same product column, and the file is written as UTF-8 with a BOM (utf-8-sig) so Excel on Windows will not treat the CJK text as mojibake.

If you follow the README literally and run python3 sheetstack_lite.py merge samples -o merged.csv --normalize-headers, the tool walks the whole folder. That includes customers_messy.csv, which has a different schema. In that run the CLI reported Merged 5 file(s), 29 rows, 12 columns. For a store-export merge, name the four files (or keep customers in a separate folder).

Clean dates, drop the empty row, remove duplicates 

python3 sheetstack_lite.py clean stores.csv \
  -o stores_clean.csv \
  --date-cols order_date \
  --dedupe-cols order_id

Exact output:

Cleaned 21 rows → 17 rows (empty 1, duplicates 3)
Detected encoding: utf-8-sig
Wrote stores_clean.csv

The 17 remaining order_id values are unique: US-1001 through US-1005, UK-2001 through UK-2004, JP-3001 through JP-3005, and CN-4001 through CN-4003. Every order_date is YYYY-MM-DD. A few examples of what changed:

Input (order_date) Output
2026/3/2 2026-03-02
20260305 / 20260310 / 20260318 2026-03-05 / 2026-03-10 / 2026-03-18
2026.3.9 2026-03-09
3/15/2026 2026-03-15
2026年3月14日 / 2026年3月13日 2026-03-14 / 2026-03-13

Cells are trimmed, and full-width digits are folded to ASCII, so the Chinese amount ２４９ becomes 249. Duplicate keys keep the first row (US-1002, UK-2003, JP-3005).

Ambiguous dates: 3/6/2026 is not obvious

UK-2002 is dated 3/6/2026. Without --dayfirst, the cleaner treated that as 6 March (2026-03-06). With --dayfirst, the same value became 3 June (2026-06-03):

python3 sheetstack_lite.py clean stores.csv \
  -o stores_clean_dayfirst.csv \
  --date-cols order_date \
  --dedupe-cols order_id \
  --dayfirst

Unambiguous values did not flip: 2026.3.9 stayed 2026-03-09, and 3/15/2026 stayed 2026-03-15 (there is no 15th month). If a file is known to be day-first, pass the flag. If a folder mixes US and UK exports, inspect the ambiguous rows before you trust a single convention. sheetstack-lite does not invent a locale per source file during clean; it applies one rule to the column you name.

A second, smaller clean: messy customer dates and duplicates

The customer list is a better illustration of empty rows and full-width numbers mixed with several date styles:

python3 sheetstack_lite.py clean samples/customers_messy.csv \
  -o customers.csv \
  --dedupe-cols customer_id \
  --date-cols signup_date

Exact output:

Cleaned 8 rows → 5 rows (empty 1, duplicates 2)
Detected encoding: utf-8-sig
Wrote customers.csv

The cleaned table is:

customer_id  signup_date  city      notes            points
U001         2026-02-01   Tokyo     paid             120
U002         2026-02-03   Osaka     pending          08
U003         2026-02-08   Nagoya    follow-up        56
U004         2026-02-11   Fukuoka   shipped          230
U005         2026-02-15   Sapporo   address needed   15

2026/2/1, 20260203, 2026年2月8日, 2026-02-11, and 2/15/2026 all became YYYY-MM-DD. The full-width points value ０８ became 08. Leading and trailing spaces (including a full-width space after Nagoya) were stripped. The second U001 and the second U003 were dropped; the blank row was dropped.

One thing not to do: after merging unrelated schemas, do not dedupe on a column that is empty for some of the rows. In a trial clean of the five-file merge, --dedupe-cols order_id treated every customer row (blank order_id) as a duplicate of the first blank key and deleted most of the customer data. Dedupe on a key that actually identifies the row, or clean each kind of file on its own.

What the free tool does not do

sheetstack-lite version 1.0.0-lite loads each file into memory. It will not help if Excel already refuses to open the file, and it has no chunked reads, no split-into-pieces command, and no Excel summary workbook. The tests in the repo (python3 tests/test_lite.py) cover the README examples; they passed on the same machine used for this article.

If you only need to repair a file's encoding and would rather not use the command line, there is a free CSV encoding fixer that runs entirely in the browser. The file never leaves your computer.

If you later need chunked reads for large CSVs, a split into Excel-friendly pieces, an Excel summary with conditional formatting, or a one-step run pipeline, those are in the paid toolkit (Sheetstack on Gumroad). The free repository does not include that source, and the two editions have different licenses.

For the everyday case — a handful of exports, mixed encodings, messy dates, a few duplicates — the commands above are enough, and they stay on your machine.

title: What Does an AI Crawler Actually See? Check Your Page Without JavaScript
description:
A page can look complete in your browser and still deliver very little useful content in its initial HTML response.

That difference matters when a crawler reads the response without running the same JavaScript as your browser. The useful question is not whether a particular AI system always renders JavaScript—crawler behavior varies and can change. Ask instead: does the response contain the content you want a crawler to find?

Here’s a quick way to check.

1. Fetch the page as HTML

Use a real page URL and a crawler-style user agent:

curl -sS -A "GPTBot" https://your-domain.com/page/ -o page.html

This shows what the server returned for that request. It does not prove that every crawler receives the same response, but it gives you a useful first check.

2. Look for the text that matters

Search the response for a phrase that appears in the rendered page:

grep -i -n "a phrase from the page" page.html

If the phrase is missing, compare the response with the page you see in your browser. Check whether the content is fetched only after the page loads, added after scrolling, or hidden behind a client-side route.

You can also get a rough word count after stripping HTML tags:

sed 's/<[^>]*>/ /g' page.html | tr -s ' ' | wc -w

Treat this as a quick diagnostic, not a precise content measurement. Navigation, footer text, scripts, and other markup can affect the result.

3. Compare with JavaScript disabled

In your browser’s developer tools, disable JavaScript for the page and reload it. Then compare what remains with the normal rendered page.

If the article disappears and only the navigation or an empty app shell remains, the content may depend on client-side code for its first render. That is worth investigating, especially for pages you want crawlers to read directly.

Common causes

  • Client-side fetching: the first response contains a loading state, while the article arrives later.
  • Scroll-triggered loading: content is fetched only after a reader scrolls to it.
  • Client-side routing: a deep link returns an app shell without the article in the initial response.
  • JavaScript-injected structured data: JSON-LD is added after the response instead of being present in the HTML.

These patterns can work well for people using a browser. The issue is whether the first response also contains the content a crawler needs.

What this check can—and cannot—tell you

A page with useful text in its initial HTML is easier to inspect and does not depend on a rendering pass just to expose its main content. That is a good baseline.

It does not guarantee a citation, recommendation, or ranking. A crawler may use other signals, and an AI answer engine may choose another source. Even a simple automated word-count check has limits: it may count navigation and footer text rather than the article itself.

For an important page, inspect the actual response and confirm that its main text and structured data are present there. Repeat the check against the deployed URL after changes, because a CDN, consent layer, or bot rule can alter what the origin serves.

I maintain LLMention, a scanner that checks whether a homepage is accessible and readable across a published set of rules. It measures crawl and citation readiness; it does not ask AI systems whether they mention a brand. The complete walkthrough and its limitations are on the original article.

The practical rule is simple: if the content you care about is absent from the response body, do not assume a crawler will reconstruct it the way your browser does.

title: The Gaming Industry Is Doomed
description:
The technological barriers protecting proprietary gaming platforms are collapsing. Emulation is becoming practical, games are being recompiled into native applications, hardware is becoming increasingly unaffordable, and platform holders are responding with increasingly anti-consumer strategies. The economics of the traditional gaming industry are starting to make very little sense.

A few weeks ago, I wrote about how Halo was becoming the new Doom and how most software would soon become effectively open source, whether its owners wanted it or not.

My original argument was that AI had dramatically reduced the cost of reverse engineering, decompilation and software reimplementation. What previously required years of specialist work could increasingly be accomplished by small teams, assisted by coding agents, in days or weeks.

I argued that software was losing its scarcity.

At the time, I was primarily thinking about SaaS, proprietary applications and the economics of software development.

I hadn't fully considered what this would mean for the gaming industry.

Having watched what has happened over the past few weeks, I think the gaming industry might be facing an existential crisis.

And I don't mean gaming itself. People aren't going to stop playing video games.

I mean the traditional business model built around expensive proprietary hardware, exclusive software, digital storefronts, DRM and increasingly expensive AAA productions.

I genuinely believe this business model is approaching a breaking point.

The technological moat is disappearing

For decades, console manufacturers enjoyed a relatively comfortable position.

You bought a PlayStation to play PlayStation games. You bought an Xbox to play Xbox games. You bought a Nintendo console to play Nintendo games.

The hardware was the distribution platform, the security boundary and the commercial moat.

If you wanted to play a particular exclusive, you had to buy the corresponding hardware. There was no practical alternative.

Piracy existed, jailbreaks existed and emulators existed, but there was usually a considerable time gap between a console's release, its security being compromised and its games becoming playable elsewhere.

That time gap was incredibly valuable.

Manufacturers could sell millions of consoles and games before alternative execution environments became practical.

That assumption is now being challenged.

The PS5 is no longer the fortress it once was

The September 2026 release of the Relapse jailbreak significantly expanded the number of exploitable PlayStation 5 consoles.

The exploit works on firmware versions up to 13.60, enabling kernel access and arbitrary code execution.

This is significant because previous jailbreaks often required consoles running considerably older firmware versions.

It opens the door to homebrew, unofficial modifications, backups and alternative software environments.

But the jailbreak itself isn't even the most interesting development.

PS5 emulation is progressing at a remarkable pace.

Consider Demon's Souls Remake.

In early September, it was running at approximately one or two frames per second in the emulator. Within weeks, it had progressed through 30 FPS demonstrations to builds capable of exceeding 60 FPS at 1440p.

By mid-October, my previous article documented custom builds approaching 120 FPS using frame generation.

Read that again.

We are no longer talking about waiting five or ten years for an emulator to become sufficiently mature to run commercial games.

We are talking about going from barely playable to technically impressive performance within weeks.

The historical economics of console exclusivity assumed that emulation would take years to catch up.

What happens when that assumption stops being true?

Nintendo is experiencing the same problem

Nintendo's Switch 2 has also experienced its first significant software jailbreak.

The ns2jb exploit, developed by security researcher Sammy Hajhamid (Pepsipu), demonstrated native code execution through a software-only exploit involving the Switch 1 application SmileBASIC 4.

OpenAI's Codex was reportedly used to assist with the development.

The exploit demonstrated the ability to run homebrew, reverse-engineer and modify games, and access hardware functionality.

Nintendo subsequently patched the vulnerability in firmware 23.5.0.

But patching an individual vulnerability doesn't reverse the underlying technological trend.

The barrier to understanding and modifying proprietary software is falling.

And then came an even more interesting demonstration.

Ocarina of Time: Nintendo's exclusivity problem in miniature

On November 5, Nintendo released its new version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, built from the ground up for Switch 2.

It was a major exclusive release, tied to Nintendo's latest hardware and ecosystem.

Yet independent developers rapidly began working on making the game available outside that ecosystem.

The NX2navi project is a static recompilation of the Switch 2 version into a native x86-64 Windows application, complete with a Vulkan renderer.

This is not traditional emulation.

It translates the game's ARM64 code into native code that runs directly on PC hardware.

The project is already playable in several areas at 60 FPS and above, although it remains under development and has visual issues and occasional crashes.

There is also a broader Switch 2 recompilation toolchain emerging, building on the earlier SwitchRecomp work.

The important point isn't whether every game will be perfectly recompiled overnight.

It's that the technical process is becoming repeatable.

Nintendo released an exclusive game for its proprietary hardware, and independent developers began producing a native PC execution environment almost immediately.

This is the sort of development that should make every console manufacturer uncomfortable.

The moat is no longer necessarily the hardware.

It is becoming increasingly difficult to justify why software should remain tied to the hardware it was originally designed for.

The economics of AAA development are already broken

Now let's introduce another problem.

AAA game development is becoming extraordinarily expensive.

A 2024 Boston Consulting Group report compared the development costs of two major publishers.

Between 2012 and 2021–2023, development costs increased by approximately 360% at one publisher and 449% at another.

Meanwhile, the number of games released by those publishers fell by 73% and 63%, respectively.

This is a worrying combination.

The industry is spending dramatically more money producing fewer games.

The traditional AAA model is based on enormous upfront investments, long development cycles and the expectation that enough consumers will purchase the finished product to generate an attractive return.

But what happens when the market becomes increasingly fragmented?

What happens when consumers have fewer reasons to buy expensive hardware?

What happens when the games themselves become increasingly accessible outside their original platforms?

And what happens when independent developers can use AI-assisted tools to recreate, port or extend software at a fraction of its original development cost?

The problem isn't necessarily that every new game will be pirated.

The problem is that the economic assumptions behind these investments are becoming less reliable.

A publisher spending hundreds of millions developing an exclusive game needs to believe that exclusivity provides a meaningful commercial advantage.

If consumers can increasingly play that game elsewhere, that advantage becomes harder to defend.

The risk is particularly significant for single-player games.

Online games have additional barriers: servers, matchmaking, competitive integrity, live services, player communities and continuous content delivery.

A single-player campaign is fundamentally different.

Once the software exists, the technical challenge is increasingly about understanding how it works and making it run elsewhere.

That distinction matters enormously.

Consumers are running out of money

Technology isn't the only problem.

The economic environment is becoming increasingly hostile to expensive entertainment.

Gaming is a discretionary expense. It competes with housing, food, energy, transportation, healthcare and everything else people need to pay for.

When household budgets become tighter, entertainment expenditure is one of the things people reconsider.

And the gaming industry seems determined to make its products more expensive.

Consoles that historically became cheaper as their hardware matured are now experiencing the opposite trend.

Sony increased the recommended European prices of its PlayStation hardware in April 2026:

  • PS5: €649.99
  • PS5 Digital Edition: €599.99
  • PS5 Pro: €899.99

The PS5 Pro is approaching the price of a capable gaming PC.

And we are already seeing discussions about next-generation consoles potentially approaching €1,000 or even €1,200.

Those figures are not confirmed retail prices, but the possibility itself should concern the industry.

Memory, storage, semiconductor manufacturing, tariffs, energy costs and competition for components all contribute to the pressure.

Meanwhile, geopolitical instability, including the conflicts involving Russia and Iran, creates additional uncertainty around energy prices and household purchasing power.

I don't think it is unreasonable to expect consumers to become increasingly selective about how they spend money on gaming.

Consider what a new console generation could mean for a family:

  • €1,000 or more for the hardware.
  • €80–€100 for individual games.
  • Monthly subscriptions.
  • Additional controllers and accessories.
  • Expensive storage upgrades.

At some point, consumers will simply decide that this is too expensive.

And when people want to play games but cannot justify the price of the official ecosystem, they will look for alternatives.

Some will buy fewer games. Some will wait for sales. Some will move to older hardware, second-hand markets or PC gaming.

And some will turn to piracy.

This is where the technological developments become particularly dangerous for platform holders.

Piracy is no longer necessarily a technically inferior experience that requires waiting years for emulation to catch up.

The gap between the official product and alternative execution environments is shrinking.

That changes the equation.

Piracy is becoming a much more credible alternative

I want to be clear about something: I am not suggesting that everybody will pirate every game.

People pirate for different reasons, and many consumers will continue paying for games they enjoy, particularly when they value supporting developers.

But the gaming industry has historically benefited from a combination of convenience, hardware exclusivity and technical barriers.

Those barriers are weakening.

Imagine buying a PC capable of running modern games.

You can purchase games through Steam, GOG and other storefronts. You can play independent games, older games and modern releases. You can emulate previous generations of consoles. You can use native recompilations where they exist.

You are no longer dependent on purchasing a separate machine every time a manufacturer releases a new generation.

And you aren't necessarily dependent on the manufacturer's storefront to access every game.

The situation becomes even more interesting when games can be recompiled into native applications.

An emulator reproduces the environment expected by the original software.

A static recompilation translates the original executable code into something that can run natively on another architecture.

These are different techniques, but they lead towards the same commercial problem: the original hardware is no longer the only practical place where the software can execute.

There is also an important distinction between technical access and legal ownership. A game becoming playable elsewhere does not make its copyrighted assets or code open source, nor does it automatically permit redistribution.

But that doesn't change the underlying technological development.

The cost of escaping proprietary execution environments is falling.

And if the official ecosystem becomes increasingly expensive and restrictive, the incentive to explore alternatives becomes stronger.

Nintendo should be particularly concerned

Of the three major console manufacturers, Nintendo arguably has the most concentrated exposure to the traditional console model.

Nintendo's business is not literally 100% dependent on hardware. It has substantial intellectual property, licensing, films, merchandise and other activities.

However, its core business remains closely tied to the relationship between proprietary Nintendo hardware and exclusive Nintendo software.

People buy Nintendo consoles because they want to play Mario, Zelda, Pokémon and other Nintendo franchises.

The hardware and software reinforce one another.

This creates an interesting vulnerability.

What happens if the software becomes increasingly accessible outside Nintendo hardware?

Nintendo's competitive advantage isn't simply that it makes consoles.

It is that it controls the primary execution environment for some of the most valuable intellectual property in gaming.

If that control becomes harder to maintain, the business model comes under pressure.

Nintendo can continue making excellent games. Its intellectual property isn't going to suddenly become worthless.

But it needs to consider whether hardware exclusivity will remain an effective way of monetising that intellectual property.

Its latest financial results demonstrate that the company is not currently collapsing: Nintendo sold 6.49 million Switch 2 consoles in the April–September 2026 period and reported higher net profit despite lower overall sales.

That is precisely why this is a forward-looking argument rather than a claim that the collapse has already happened.

The question is whether the economics supporting those sales will remain sustainable.

Sony is fighting the wrong war

Sony's position is different.

PlayStation is an enormously important business, but Sony has other substantial sources of revenue, including music, films, entertainment, image sensors and electronics.

It has more diversification than Nintendo.

However, I find some of Sony's recent strategic decisions particularly difficult to understand.

At exactly the moment when the barriers protecting proprietary gaming ecosystems are weakening, Sony seems increasingly determined to reinforce those barriers.

Consider its recent decisions.

First, Sony increased PlayStation hardware prices in an already expensive consumer electronics market.

Second, it announced that physical disc production for new PlayStation games will end starting in January 2028.

Third, Bloomberg reported that Sony was retreating from its strategy of bringing major single-player PlayStation releases to PC, returning towards console exclusivity.

Individually, these decisions have commercial justifications.

Sony wants higher margins, greater control over distribution and stronger incentives to purchase PlayStation hardware.

But collectively, they are strategically contradictory.

Sony is effectively asking consumers to pay more money for less control at precisely the moment when alternative platforms are becoming increasingly attractive.

Digital-only distribution reduces the second-hand market and makes consumers more dependent on the platform's licensing infrastructure.

Exclusivity makes hardware more important, but emulation and recompilation are undermining the technical barriers that make exclusivity enforceable.

Higher hardware prices make the official ecosystem less accessible, potentially encouraging consumers to explore alternatives.

This is not necessarily a recipe for immediate disaster.

But it is a dangerous combination.

When consumers have no viable alternative, platform restrictions are easier to enforce.

When alternatives become technically credible, economically attractive and increasingly accessible, consumer-hostile practices become a liability.

Sony seems to be operating under the assumption that its ecosystem is indispensable.

That assumption deserves serious scrutiny.

Microsoft might be the biggest beneficiary

There is an interesting irony in all of this.

Microsoft spent decades competing in the console market against Sony and Nintendo.

But Microsoft is structurally different from both companies.

Xbox is a division of a much larger technology company.

Microsoft owns Windows, Azure, Microsoft 365, LinkedIn and a substantial enterprise software business.

Its gaming operations are important, but they aren't the foundation of the company.

In fiscal 2026, Microsoft reported $331.8 billion in total revenue, while Xbox content and services revenue actually declined by 5%.

Microsoft doesn't need the traditional console business to remain successful.

And this puts it in an interesting position.

If the future of gaming increasingly moves towards PC, Microsoft already owns the dominant desktop operating system ecosystem.

If consoles become less relevant, Microsoft can continue participating in gaming through Windows, Xbox Game Pass, publishing, cloud services and its studios.

It doesn't necessarily need everybody to buy an Xbox console.

In fact, Microsoft has increasingly positioned Xbox as an ecosystem rather than just a physical device.

This is strategically significant.

The company that helped create the modern console market could end up benefiting from its decline.

There is another important point here: Microsoft doesn't have to win the console wars to benefit from the outcome.

It just needs Windows and its gaming ecosystem to remain relevant.

The winner is PC

I think the long-term winner is becoming increasingly obvious.

PC gaming.

Not because every consumer will suddenly build a gaming PC, but because PC offers something that traditional consoles increasingly struggle to provide: flexibility.

A PC isn't tied to one manufacturer's hardware generation.

It can run games from multiple storefronts, support emulators, run native recompilations, use mods, preserve older software and offer hardware upgrades without requiring consumers to abandon their existing libraries.

It also benefits from an enormous ecosystem of independent developers and open-source projects.

The PC platform doesn't need to convince consumers to buy a new proprietary device every few years to remain relevant.

And the more games escape their original hardware environments, the more attractive PC becomes.

Windows is particularly well positioned here.

Valve has demonstrated that PC gaming can also flourish through alternative operating systems and distribution models, so I wouldn't claim Microsoft owns the future of PC gaming.

But Microsoft owns Windows, and Windows remains an extremely important part of the gaming ecosystem.

If the industry moves away from closed console environments towards more open execution platforms, Microsoft is already positioned to participate.

Nintendo and Sony have to defend their hardware ecosystems.

Microsoft can participate in the transition regardless of whether Xbox consoles remain commercially important.

The next generation of consoles could be a disaster

Now consider what happens when these trends converge.

The next generation of consoles could become substantially more expensive.

There are already concerns about the cost of memory, storage and advanced semiconductor components.

Consumers are increasingly price-sensitive.

AAA games are becoming more expensive to produce.

Emulation is improving at an unprecedented pace.

Native recompilation is becoming increasingly practical.

AI-assisted reverse engineering is reducing the specialist knowledge required to understand proprietary software.

And the platform holders are still largely operating under the assumption that they can maintain the traditional relationship between hardware, software and distribution.

What happens if the next PlayStation or Xbox costs €1,200?

How many consumers will purchase one?

How many will decide that their existing PC is good enough?

How many will simply stop buying expensive games?

How many will wait for discounts?

And how many will discover that the games they want to play are already available through alternative execution environments?

I think the industry is underestimating the cumulative effect of these pressures.

A console generation is a massive investment for manufacturers.

They need developers to support the hardware, consumers to buy the hardware and publishers to invest in increasingly expensive games.

If any part of that ecosystem becomes significantly less attractive, the entire model becomes harder to sustain.

Why aren't gaming stocks collapsing already?

This is perhaps the question I find most interesting.

If the technological and economic trends are as significant as I believe they are, why aren't investors pricing in a much more dramatic structural change?

I wouldn't pretend that every gaming company is equally exposed.

Nintendo, Sony, Microsoft, Electronic Arts, Take-Two, Ubisoft and independent publishers all have different business models.

Some have valuable intellectual property, recurring revenue, live services and businesses that are much less dependent on console hardware.

But I find it difficult to understand why the market would assume that the traditional economics of the gaming industry will remain intact indefinitely.

The industry is facing several simultaneous risks:

  1. Hardware exclusivity is becoming harder to enforce.
  2. Digital distribution gives consumers less flexibility and control.
  3. AAA development costs are increasing.
  4. Hardware prices are increasing rather than decreasing.
  5. Consumer purchasing power is under pressure.
  6. Emulation and recompilation are becoming increasingly practical.
  7. AI-assisted reverse engineering is reducing the cost of recreating software.

These are not isolated problems.

They reinforce one another.

If I were looking at gaming companies as an investor, I would be asking very difficult questions about their long-term valuations.

I would be particularly interested in understanding how much of their future profitability depends on consumers continuing to accept the traditional console ecosystem.

I wouldn't automatically short every gaming stock. That would ignore differences between individual companies, valuation, existing cash flows and the possibility that these threats take much longer to materialise than expected.

But I would certainly be questioning the assumption that the industry's historical economics are a reliable guide to its future.

Gaming isn't dying. The old gaming industry might be.

I want to finish by returning to the argument I made in my previous article.

Software is losing its scarcity.

AI is accelerating reverse engineering. Decompilation is becoming increasingly accessible. Native recompilation is making proprietary software portable. Emulation is becoming increasingly practical.

Halo running on platforms it was never designed for was an early demonstration.

Demon's Souls running at more than 60 FPS through PS5 emulation is another.

Ocarina of Time being turned into a native Windows application shortly after its Switch 2 release is another.

These are not necessarily isolated curiosities.

They are evidence of a broader technological shift.

The gaming industry has spent decades building business models around the assumption that controlling hardware means controlling software distribution.

That assumption is becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

And the industry is making things worse for itself by increasing prices, restricting consumer choice and doubling down on proprietary ecosystems.

Consumers will continue playing games.

They will continue buying great games, supporting developers and spending money on experiences they value.

But they may become increasingly unwilling to pay the premium demanded by traditional platform holders.

The future could look very different.

PCs become the universal gaming platform. Consoles become optional devices rather than mandatory gateways. Games become increasingly portable. Communities preserve and extend software long after publishers abandon it. Developers monetise convenience, services, communities and continuous experiences rather than relying exclusively on controlling the execution environment.

There will still be successful gaming companies.

There will still be great games.

But the economics of spending hundreds of millions developing a game, locking it to a proprietary platform and expecting consumers to purchase expensive hardware to access it may become increasingly difficult to justify.

The console wars might not end because one manufacturer finally defeats the others.

They might end because consumers simply stop needing the consoles.

And if that happens, the biggest losers won't necessarily be the companies that make the worst games.

They will be the companies that fail to understand that controlling where software runs is no longer the same thing as controlling the software itself.

title: How to Debug an Old noindex Verdict in Google Search Console
description:
You publish a site migration and open a guide at its expected address. It loads. Google Search Console still shows that a crawler found a noindex tag. Before changing the deployment again, check when Google fetched the URL and what the public server sends today.

A noindex directive can come from the HTML or the HTTP headers. A stored indexing report can reflect an older response. Comparing the two versions gives you a specific next action.

Check the first public response

Use the exact URL you want readers to find, including the scheme, host and trailing slash. Save the following script as check_noindex.py. It performs one GET and stops at a redirect so you can see the first status and its Location header.

import argparse
from html.parser import HTMLParser
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.parse import urlsplit
from urllib.request import HTTPRedirectHandler, Request, build_opener


class NoRedirect(HTTPRedirectHandler):
    def redirect_request(self, req, fp, code, msg, headers, newurl):
        return None


class PageMetadata(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.in_head = False
        self.canonicals = []
        self.robots = []

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        fields = dict(attrs)
        if tag == "head":
            self.in_head = True
        if tag == "meta":
            name = (fields.get("name") or "").lower()
            if name in {"robots", "googlebot", "googlebot-news"}:
                self.robots.append((name, fields.get("content") or ""))
        rel = (fields.get("rel") or "").lower().split()
        if self.in_head and tag == "link" and "canonical" in rel:
            self.canonicals.append(fields.get("href") or "")

    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        if tag == "head":
            self.in_head = False


def inspect(url):
    target = urlsplit(url)
    if target.scheme not in {"http", "https"} or not target.hostname:
        raise SystemExit("Enter an HTTP or HTTPS URL.")

    opener = build_opener(NoRedirect)
    try:
        request = Request(url, headers={"Accept-Encoding": "identity"})
        response = opener.open(request, timeout=12)
    except HTTPError as error:
        response = error
    except (URLError, TimeoutError) as error:
        raise SystemExit(f"GET failed: {error}") from error

    with response:
        print(f"GET {response.geturl()} -> {response.status}")
        for name in ("Location", "Content-Type", "Content-Encoding", "X-Robots-Tag", "Link"):
            for value in response.headers.get_all(name, []):
                print(f"{name}: {value}")
        if response.status != 200:
            raise SystemExit("Inspect the status or destination before reading metadata.")
        if response.headers.get_content_type() != "text/html":
            raise SystemExit("Response is not HTML.")
        encodings = response.headers.get_all("Content-Encoding", [])
        if any(value.strip().lower() != "identity" for value in encodings):
            raise SystemExit("Decode the response body before inspecting its HTML.")
        limit = 2_000_000
        body = response.read(limit + 1)
        if len(body) > limit:
            raise SystemExit("HTML exceeds the example's 2 MB inspection limit.")
        page = PageMetadata()
        encoding = response.headers.get_content_charset() or "utf-8"
        page.feed(body.decode(encoding, errors="replace"))
        print(f"Canonical links in head: {page.canonicals}")
        print(f"Robots meta tags: {page.robots}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Show one public HTML response's indexing signals.")
    parser.add_argument("url")
    inspect(parser.parse_args().url)

Run it first on your preferred URL.

python3 check_noindex.py https://example.com/guides/import/

The probe requests an uncompressed response and prints any Content-Encoding header it receives. If a server still sends gzip or Brotli, decode the body before inspecting the HTML. Reading compressed bytes as text can make a page with a noindex tag appear to have no robots meta tags. HTTP content coding

An HTTP 200 can carry both an HTML index, follow tag and an HTTP header such as X-Robots-Tag: googlebot: noindex. That header applies to Google’s main web crawler. Inspect every header and meta tag that applies to your search surface. A none directive also includes noindex. Google's robots tag reference

On a redirect, confirm the first hop, then run the same check on the intended destination. For HTML 200 responses, check the canonical in the document head. If the page also declares a canonical in an HTTP Link header, verify that both signals point to the same preferred URL. The script reports the directives it sees for this one request. Google’s canonical URL guidance

Compare the stored crawl with a live test

In URL Inspection, record the last crawl, page fetch, and indexing allowed fields from the Google Index view. Then run Test live URL for the preferred address and check whether crawling and indexing are allowed there. The live test follows redirects. Check the first hop, then test the intended destination directly. URL Inspection documentation

What you find Next action
Crawl allowed? says No, while Indexing allowed? says Yes Check the robots.txt rule for the exact URL. If the URL belongs in search, correct the matching rule for that path and rerun the live test.
The current response still tells Googlebot noindex Find which layer supplied it. Check the HTML template for meta tags and the server or CDN for response headers. Fix the intended public route and test again.
The stored crawl predates the deployment, and the live test allows indexing Record the deployed version and the old crawl date. Use the existing sitemap and links to support discovery. Request recrawling for an important changed URL if appropriate, then wait for a new stored result.
Google reports a different selected canonical Compare the declared canonical, redirect destination, sitemap entry, and internal links. Decide which URL represents the page and make those signals agree.

Read Crawl allowed? first. When robots.txt blocks the fetch, URL Inspection can show Yes under Indexing allowed? because Google could not read the page’s directives. The public GET above can still succeed in that situation because it does not check robots.txt. Use the live test to confirm that crawling is allowed and the fetch succeeds before interpreting the indexing field. Google’s explanation of the inspection fields

A live test that allows indexing confirms the current response is eligible in the tool. Use the stored result to see whether Google has indexed that URL and which canonical it chose. Google says repeated requests for the same URL won’t make it crawl faster. Google’s recrawl guidance

Check the next stored crawl

In a synthetic UTC timeline, Google’s 09:00 crawl found noindex. The corrected route deployed at 10:00. At 10:10, the public GET returned HTTP 200 with the expected canonical, and Google’s live test allowed indexing. When a newer stored crawl appears, check Indexing allowed and Google-selected canonical. If that crawl still reports noindex, open View crawled page and compare its response headers and HTML with the public GET. Use the two capture times to trace which response supplied the directive.

For several URLs with the same issue, review the affected examples in Page indexing before using Validate fix. A submitted-sitemap filter limits validation to known affected URLs in that sitemap when you start it. Monitor the issue’s validation details and use URL Inspection for each priority URL’s stored indexing status. Google’s Page indexing report

Try a public example

On 11 November 2026, the October Sarv Blog archive returned HTTP 200, declared its own canonical, and sent no robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag on the checked response. I work with Sarv. You can run the same command on the archive and record what the server returns today.

For your own release, keep three pieces of evidence together. Save the first HTTP response, the live test verdict, and the date of the stored Google crawl. Compare them again after Google records a newer crawl.

I used AI for research, drafting, and editing assistance.

title: OpenAI retires gpt-5 and o3 on 11 December 2026: what to change and how to test it
description:
On 11 December 2026, OpenAI removes gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, gpt-5-nano, gpt-5-pro, o3 and o3-pro from the API, together with their dated snapshots. From that day, API calls to these models fail. OpenAI recommends gpt-5.6-sol, gpt-5.6-terra and gpt-5.6-luna as replacements.

Changing the model name takes a minute. Checking that your prompts still give the answers your app expects takes longer, and it can only be done while the old model still answers.

What retires, and what replaces it

OpenAI announced the shutdown on 11 June 2026 on its deprecations page. Both the short name and the dated snapshot stop working:

Model Snapshot Replacement
gpt-5 gpt-5-2025-08-07 gpt-5.6-sol
gpt-5-mini gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07 gpt-5.6-terra
gpt-5-nano gpt-5-nano-2025-08-07 gpt-5.6-luna
gpt-5-pro gpt-5-pro-2025-10-06 gpt-5.6-sol with reasoning.mode: pro
o3 o3-2025-04-16 gpt-5.6-sol
o3-pro o3-pro-2025-06-10 gpt-5.6-sol with reasoning.mode: pro

Fine-tuned models built on any of these follow the same date, so an ID like ft:gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07:your-org::abc123 stops working on 11 December too. o3 and o3-pro don't get an o-series successor: both move to the GPT-5.6 family.

Two other OpenAI shutdowns land just before. On 30 November the Evals platform and the reusable prompts API (v1/prompts) shut down, and on 1 December the older GPT Image models go.

Step 1: find every place your code uses them

Run this in the root of your repository. No install, account or API key; it lists every OpenAI, Anthropic and Google model ID it finds with file, line and retirement date:

npx -y @aidriftline/driftline .

A plain search works too, as long as you remember what it misses:

grep -rnE '"(gpt-5(-mini|-nano|-pro)?|o3(-pro)?)(-20[0-9-]+)?"' .

Places that are easy to overlook:

  • Environment variables and deployment settings, such as OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-5 in a .env file, a Helm chart or your hosting dashboard. These never show up in a code search.
  • Model names stored in a database, for example a per-customer or per-feature setting.
  • Defaults inside libraries and agent frameworks. If you never set a model, check which one your SDK or framework picks.
  • Evaluation scripts, notebooks and cron jobs that only run once a week.
  • Azure OpenAI deployments. Azure has its own retirement schedule, so check Azure's model retirement page for those.

Step 2: test your prompts before 11 December

A new model gives different answers to the same prompt. Usually they're fine, sometimes better. The problems show up where your code depends on the shape of the answer:

  • JSON that no longer matches your schema, or extra text around it
  • answers that are much longer or shorter, which matters for UI limits and cost
  • different tool or function calls for the same request
  • refusals on prompts that used to work
  • a different tone in customer-facing text

The test is simple. Take 10 to 20 real prompts from your logs, including the odd ones, run each on the old model and on the replacement, and compare the answers side by side. Check that every answer your code parses still parses.

The timing matters. After 11 December the old model is gone, so you can no longer see what it would have answered. You can only compare while both models respond. With the Evals platform shutting down on 30 November, OpenAI points to Promptfoo as one way to run such comparisons yourself.

Step 3: switch, then keep it from happening again

Change the model name, deploy well before 11 December, and watch your error logs for the first days. If you use gpt-5-pro or o3-pro, set reasoning.mode: pro on gpt-5.6-sol, otherwise you get the standard mode.

The GPT-5.6 models will retire one day too. A check in CI that flags retired and soon-to-retire model IDs on every pull request saves you from finding out on the day.

I build Driftline, which tracks these retirement dates and runs the scan above. The full list of dates, with one page per model, is at aidriftline.com/models.

title: Before I file for Play closed testing, I run the APK on more than one Android version
description:
I used to treat closed testing like the first real look at a build. That was a bad habit. You spend days rounding up testers, you wait on the clock, and then someone on Android 12 hits a crash you never saw because the only phone on your desk was already on 15.

These days I do a pre-flight pass first. Nothing fancy. I just want the APK to stand up on more than one OS version before I bother anyone else.

I work in growth marketing, close enough to the Android work that a build often lands in my chat before it lands in Play Console. Someone drops an APK and a short note about what changed. I used to install that file on whatever handset I could borrow. The borrowed phone was almost always the newest one in the office, so of course it looked fine. A local emulator missed a crash that only showed up on real ARM. I stopped treating either as the last stop before testers.

The pass I do now looks like this.

I open DuoPlus in the browser. There's a desktop client and a mobile client if I want a native window, but for a morning walkthrough I don't bother installing anything. Each cloud phone is a real ARM Android device, and each one is its own isolated environment. Nicer than a shared lab handset with someone else's test account still signed in.

Android 15 is there, which matters when a targetSdk bump is in the build. Older versions are there too. I usually start an Android 15 phone and at least one older one, often 12, sometimes 11 or 10 if a crash report already pointed at it. I don't spin up a full matrix every time. Two or three versions already catch the stupid stuff.

If the build is meant for a market I'm not sitting in, I pick a local environment from the 150+ country options before I install anything. I got burned once by a paywall that only appeared in a region we hadn't checked. I'm not going to pretend this covers every store quirk. It's still better than testing only on a Singapore handset and hoping.

Then I install the APK. When I've got more than one cloud phone running, I use the bulk install so I'm not doing the same upload three times. Same for launching the app after. Bulk uninstall is what I reach for on the next build, when I want the old package gone.

The pass itself is boring, which is the point. I walk the first-run screens, try a login, background the app and come back. If the changelog mentions a deep link, I hit that too. Purchase screens I take slowly. I keep a notes file open and write the OS version next to whatever I hit. Last week the Android 11 phone stalled on a permission dialog that Android 15 just skipped. Took maybe twenty minutes to notice. That's the kind of thing I want to find before a closed tester files it as a one-off.

If something only happens on one device, I don't try to describe the state in a long message. I use the one-click share and send that same cloud phone to whoever needs to see it. They can open it in a browser even if they haven't installed a client. We've wasted more time rebuilding a state than I want to admit.

A few of our test cases need root. DuoPlus supports that, so I don't keep a separately rooted personal phone around just for those. I only turn it on when the case actually asks for it. There's an API if you want to start devices from a script. I don't do that every morning, but on weeks where the same version matrix keeps coming back, I wish I'd set it up sooner.

Billing is per minute, which I care about because these sessions are often short. A pre-flight pass might be twenty minutes, not a whole afternoon. I'm not going to paste a rate here; look at the official site. I just like not leaving a physical lab powered all day for a walkthrough I could have finished before lunch.

After the pass, I still have to do Play closed testing the normal way. This doesn't replace testers, and it doesn't shorten Google's clock. It just means I stop handing people a build I haven't even opened on Android 12.

If you want to try the same setup I use, it's here:

https://www.duoplus.net/share/market

I still keep one physical phone in a drawer. I just don't let it stand in for every version we claim to support.
