title: Why Great Websites Need More Than Good Development
description:
A website can look impressive in a design presentation and still fail when real people start using it.

Maybe the navigation is confusing. Maybe the mobile layout feels cramped. Perhaps the pages take too long to load, or visitors cannot figure out what the business actually offers.

These problems often happen when website design and development are treated as two separate activities rather than parts of the same process.

Building a successful website requires more than writing clean code or choosing an attractive color palette. It requires a balance between user experience, visual communication, technical performance, and business goals.

  1. Start With the Purpose, Not the Layout

One common mistake in website projects is jumping straight into the visual design.

Before opening a design tool or writing components, understand what the website needs to accomplish.

Ask a few basic questions:

Who is the intended audience?

What problem does the website solve?

What should visitors do after landing on the homepage?

Which information matters most to potential customers?

How will success be measured?

These answers help establish the website's structure and content priorities.

For example, a SaaS company might need visitors to explore product features and request a demo. An ecommerce business needs clear product categories, useful product pages, and a straightforward checkout experience.

The design should support these objectives instead of competing with them.

  1. User Experience Should Guide Visual Decisions

Good design is not simply about making a website look modern.

It is about making information easier to understand and actions easier to complete.

A few principles make a significant difference:

Clear navigation: Visitors should understand where to find important information without having to search through multiple menus.

Readable typography: Font sizes, spacing, and contrast should make content comfortable to read across different devices.

Consistent components: Buttons, cards, headings, and forms should follow a recognizable visual system.

Meaningful calls to action: Every important page should guide visitors toward a relevant next step.

A visually attractive interface is valuable, but usability is what makes people comfortable interacting with it.

  1. Design and Development Should Work Together

A common challenge in website projects is the handoff between designers and developers.

A design might include animations, complex layouts, or interactive elements that are difficult to implement within the project's technical constraints.

When development starts too late, teams may discover these problems after significant design work has already been completed.

A better approach is collaboration from the beginning.

Designers should understand the technical possibilities, while developers should understand the reasoning behind the interface.

This helps teams make practical decisions about:

Responsive layouts

Component architecture

Animation and interactions

Content management systems

Accessibility requirements

Future maintenance

Businesses looking for professional web design and development services should consider whether the team can manage both the creative and technical sides of the project.

Combining these disciplines helps reduce unnecessary revisions and creates a more consistent final product.

  1. Website Performance Is Part of the User Experience

Even a beautifully designed website can lose visitors if it performs poorly.

Performance should be considered throughout the development process, not treated as a final optimization task.

Some important areas include:

Image optimization: Use appropriately sized images and modern formats where supported.

Efficient code: Avoid unnecessary JavaScript and remove unused dependencies.

Responsive implementation: Make sure layouts work across mobile phones, tablets, and desktop screens.

Core Web Vitals: Monitor loading performance, visual stability, and interaction responsiveness.

Accessibility: Use semantic HTML, keyboard-friendly navigation, and sufficient color contrast.

These improvements help create websites that are easier to use and maintain.

  1. Build With Future Growth in Mind

A website should not become difficult to update every time a business launches a new service or changes its messaging.

This is why maintainability matters.

Reusable components, a sensible page structure, and an appropriate content management setup can make future updates much easier.

For development teams, this means thinking beyond the immediate launch.

Consider whether the website can support:

Additional landing pages

New product or service sections

Updated brand guidelines

Marketing campaigns

Third-party integrations

Growing content requirements

A flexible foundation reduces the need for expensive rebuilds as the business evolves.

  1. Test the Website Before Launch

A successful launch requires more than checking whether the homepage loads.

Testing should cover the complete experience.

A practical pre-launch checklist includes:

Test navigation links and buttons.

Check forms and submission confirmations.

Review mobile and tablet layouts.

Test pages across major browsers.

Check image loading and broken links.

Review page titles and meta descriptions.

Validate accessibility basics.

Measure page performance.

Check redirects and important URLs.

It is also useful to ask someone unfamiliar with the project to navigate the website. They may notice usability problems that the development team has overlooked.

Final Thoughts

Great websites are created when design decisions and technical decisions support the same purpose.

A good visual system helps communicate a brand. Thoughtful development makes the experience reliable. Performance and accessibility make the website more usable, while a flexible architecture allows it to grow alongside the business.

For businesses planning a new website or improving an existing one, the goal should not simply be to launch something that looks good.

It should be to build something that works well for the people using it and continues to serve the business over time.

That is the difference between creating a website and creating a useful digital experience.

title: Accept crypto payments in Node.js
description:
A step-by-step Moonvex integration in plain Node.js with the official @moonvex/node SDK: your server creates an invoice, the customer pays on a hosted page, and an HMAC-signed webhook marks the order paid. No framework, just node:http and PostgreSQL.

Step by step

1. Get an API key and a webhook secret

In the Moonvex dashboard go to “Integration” → “Create key” → type “Secret” (sk_live_…). The key is shown only once: store it on your server as MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY. On the same page add a webhook pointing to an https URL on your server and store its signing secret as MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET. The @moonvex/node SDK has no dependencies and needs Node.js 18+.

npm install @moonvex/node pg

# .env — server only, never commit it
MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_...
MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_...
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/shop

2. Create a payment with the SDK

payments.create takes orderId, the amount as a string, currency and network. The second argument is idempotencyKey: a retry after a timeout returns the same payment instead of creating another one. The SDK itself retries network errors, 429 and 5xx with the same key. Errors are thrown as MoonvexError with status, code and detailsCode, for example DUPLICATE_ORDER when the order already has an active payment.

// moonvex.js
import { Moonvex, MoonvexError } from '@moonvex/node';

export const moonvex = new Moonvex({ apiKey: process.env.MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY });

/** Creates an invoice for the order; a retry with the same key returns the same payment */
export async function createPaymentForOrder(order, attempt = 1) {
  try {
    return await moonvex.payments.create(
      {
        orderId: String(order.id),
        amount: order.total, // a string such as "25.00", not a number
        currency: 'USDT',
        network: 'TRON',
        customerId: String(order.userId),
        expiresInMinutes: 30,
      },
      { idempotencyKey: 'order-' + order.id + '-' + attempt },
    );
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof MoonvexError && err.detailsCode === 'DUPLICATE_ORDER') {
      // the order already has an active payment, return it
      const page = await moonvex.payments.list({ orderId: String(order.id), limit: 1 });
      if (page.data[0]) return page.data[0];
    }
    throw err;
  }
}

3. Send the customer to paymentUrl

paymentUrl is a hosted payment page: the exact amount including the fee, the address, a QR code, the official token contract and a timer, with a status that updates by itself. Open it with a redirect or in a new tab; it cannot be embedded in an iframe. A customer returning to your site is not proof of payment: mark the order paid only from a webhook or the status from GET /v1/payments/:id. Answering a POST form with 303 makes the browser open the payment page with a plain GET.

// server.js
import http from 'node:http';
import { db } from './db.js';
import { createPaymentForOrder } from './moonvex.js';

const server = http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  const url = new URL(req.url, 'http://localhost');
  const pay = url.pathname.match(/^\/orders\/(\d+)\/pay$/);

  if (req.method === 'POST' && pay) {
    const { rows } = await db.query(
      'SELECT id, user_id AS "userId", total::text AS total FROM orders WHERE id = $1',
      [pay[1]],
    );
    if (!rows[0]) return res.writeHead(404).end();
    const payment = await createPaymentForOrder(rows[0]);
    // 303 makes the browser open the payment page with a GET
    return res.writeHead(303, { Location: payment.paymentUrl }).end();
  }

  if (req.method === 'POST' && url.pathname === '/moonvex/webhook') {
    return handleWebhook(req, res); // step 4
  }

  res.writeHead(404).end();
});

server.listen(3000);

4. Receive the webhook and verify the signature

Moonvex sends a POST with a Moonvex-Signature header: t=,v1=. The signature is a hex HMAC-SHA256 of the string “t.raw_body” keyed with the webhook secret. Compute it over the body bytes before parsing JSON, compare in constant time and reject events older than 5 minutes. For 24 hours after a secret rotation the header carries two v1 values; either one is valid. verifyWebhook from the SDK does all of this and throws WebhookVerificationError when something is off. It needs the raw body as a Buffer, not an object.

// server.js (continued)
import { verifyWebhook, WebhookVerificationError } from '@moonvex/node';
import { markOrderPaidOnce } from './db.js';

/** Raw request body: the signature covers the bytes, not parsed JSON */
async function readRawBody(req) {
  const chunks = [];
  for await (const chunk of req) chunks.push(chunk);
  return Buffer.concat(chunks);
}

async function handleWebhook(req, res) {
  const raw = await readRawBody(req);
  let event;
  try {
    // checks HMAC-SHA256, both v1 values during a secret rotation and the event age (5 minutes)
    event = verifyWebhook(raw, req.headers['moonvex-signature'], process.env.MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET);
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof WebhookVerificationError) return res.writeHead(400).end('bad signature');
    throw err;
  }

  if (event.type === 'payment.confirmed' || event.type === 'payment.overpaid') {
    await markOrderPaidOnce(event.id, event.data.orderId);
  }
  // any 2xx within 10 seconds, otherwise Moonvex retries the delivery
  res.writeHead(200).end('ok');
}

5. Mark the order paid exactly once

A redelivered event keeps the same id, so store it in a table with a unique key in the same transaction as the order update: a duplicate then changes nothing. Fulfil on payment.confirmed and payment.overpaid, never on payment.detected. Respond with a 2xx within 10 seconds; on failure (5xx, timeout) Moonvex retries the delivery for about three days.

// db.js
import pg from 'pg';

export const db = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

// CREATE TABLE processed_events (
//   event_id   text PRIMARY KEY,
//   created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
// );

/** Marks the order as paid exactly once, even if the event is delivered again */
export async function markOrderPaidOnce(eventId, orderId) {
  const client = await db.connect();
  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN');
    const fresh = await client.query(
      'INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING',
      [eventId],
    );
    if (fresh.rowCount === 1) {
      // first delivery of this event
      await client.query(
        "UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid', paid_at = now() WHERE id = $1 AND status <> 'paid'",
        [orderId],
      );
    }
    await client.query('COMMIT');
  } catch (err) {
    await client.query('ROLLBACK');
    throw err;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

6. Test the integration

Moonvex has no test network: everything runs on mainnets. The “Send test” button under “Integration” sends a webhook.test event, which is how you check the signature. Then pay a small invoice, for example 1 USDT on TRON: it is a regular payment and the money lands on your balance. The delivery log with response codes and a “Retry” button is on the same page.

Pitfalls

  • Pass the original Buffer to verifyWebhook. JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(body)) produces different bytes and the signature will not match.
  • Build idempotencyKey from the order number and attempt (order-1001-1) rather than a random UUID, so a retry after a process restart is safe too.
  • Amounts are strings. Read total from PostgreSQL as numeric::text instead of Number(): floats lose cents.
  • Do slow work (emails, granting access) after responding 200, in a queue. A response slower than 10 seconds counts as a failed delivery.

FAQ

Do I need the SDK, or is fetch enough?

You can skip the SDK: the API is plain HTTPS with JSON and an Authorization: Bearer header. The SDK adds TypeScript types, retries with the same Idempotency-Key and a ready-made verifyWebhook. See the Express guide for a version without the SDK.

Is there a test mode or a sandbox?

No, there is no test network: Moonvex runs on mainnets only. Check the signature with the “Send test” button (a webhook.test event) and the whole payment flow with a real payment of a small amount, for example 1 USDT on TRON.

What if the customer does not pay in time?

The payment moves to EXPIRED and you receive payment.expired. You can create a new payment for the same orderId with a new Idempotency-Key (for example, bump the attempt number at the end of the key). The payment window is set with expiresInMinutes: 5 to 1440 minutes, 30 by default.

Originally published at: moonvex.org/en/guides/nodejs

title: Making AI-Generated Websites Match Your Brand: Structure, Style, and Local Edits
description:
Originally published on We0 on November 11, 2026. This English edition was adapted with AI assistance.

Brand style depends on more than a color palette. Define page structure, spacing, typography, content, and editing rules so that AI-generated pages can evolve without losing their identity.

Conclusion first: whether they look alike depends on how deeply you can edit after generation

Let us answer the two questions directly.

First, AI-generated websites do show obvious homogeneity: many tools by default follow a 'template library + one-shot generation' path, and when the same requirement is put into different tools, the layout rhythm, whitespace ratio, and section order are often highly similar. Second, similarity is not inevitable. When a tool has an independent style layer, an editable design canvas, and element-level and multi-select editing capabilities, the same requirement can produce very different pages, and they can be adjusted repeatedly after launch without being torn down and rebuilt.

In other words, 'AI-made websites all look the same' describes the default way most tools work, not the ceiling of AI website building. What really determines the final result is how deeply you can intervene after generation. The next thing to judge is whether your team needs 'a presentable page launched in three minutes' or 'an official website that carries the brand and must be iterated over the long term.' These two things have completely different requirements for tools.

Why do many AI-generated websites look very similar

Similarity comes from four specific mechanisms, not a vague explanation such as 'AI has bad taste.'

  1. Template libraries set the ceiling. The generation of many tools is essentially 'pick a preset template, then replace the copy and images.' The available structures are limited, and style variation can only stay at this layer.
  2. Prompts do not carry enough information. If you only write 'help me make a company website,' AI can only apply the default aesthetic average: a centered large headline, three-column features, gray-white colors, and card-based cases.
  3. Generation is one-shot, and edits are page-wide. Changing one sentence of copy carries the risk of reflowing the whole page. Users often end up not changing it at all, and homogeneity is preserved.
  4. The content itself is repetitive. Placeholder copy, generic stock images, and a lack of brand-specific cases and data make sites read like the same batch even when the structure differs.

Cross-sectional reviews show the direct consequences of this mechanism. A 2026 AI website builder review, when testing local service sites, pointed out that test sites generated by Durable 'all look like they come from the same template family, just with different colors,' and positioned it as a transition option for fast launch rather than a long-term platform (Nubia Magazine review).

The implication for businesses is direct: the cost of homogeneity is not at the moment of building the site, but in brand recognition and conversion afterward. An official website that does not show industry attributes or brand personality is hard for visitors to remember, and even harder to be cited by AI search as a representative answer in a field.

Can AI choose different design styles based on brand positioning

Yes, but you need to distinguish two kinds of 'style.'

One is just reskinning: change the primary color, change a background image, change a set of default fonts. There is a visual difference, but structurally it is still the same template, and visitors can feel familiarity after scrolling two screens.

The other is structural-level difference: the hero format, the choice and order of sections, the presentation of cases and testimonials, whitespace density, and the closing method all change with brand tone. A brand website cares more about company background and trust building; a marketing page emphasizes focused selling points and a conversion path; a portfolio values visual rhythm and project ordering. The difference must happen at the structure and content organization layer to count as a real style distinction.

The judgment standard is therefore simple: if a tool's 'style' appears only in colors and fonts, it is still giving you a template; if it can change section combinations and content rhythm, you have a chance to make a page that does not look like a template.

Colors, fonts, layout, page structure: to which layer can you specify

Customization granularity is roughly divided into four layers; the deeper you go, the closer you get to actually doing design.

Layer How to describe it to AI Typical failure of doing only half a layer
Visual layer Primary color, secondary color, neutral color, accent color and usage ratios; font family and type scale; corner radius and shadows Changing only the primary color without changing hierarchy is just a skin change
Typography layer Grid columns, container width, section spacing, whitespace density, text-image ratio Changing only colors without changing whitespace leaves the page crowded
Structural layer Page list, section order on each page, sections to explicitly avoid Without a defined list, extra pages are generated or pages are missing
Semantic layer Target customers, core selling points, facts that must appear, and FAQs The copy is all adjectives and lacks citable information

Most complaints that 'AI websites all look the same' are actually stuck at the third layer: users only give first-layer instructions, and tools only open first-layer edits. Raise the description to the structural and semantic layers, and the output difference will immediately become larger. For example, for a finance and tax SaaS aimed at small and medium-sized businesses, you can prompt like this: dark ink green as the primary color with a warm white background and a single high-brightness accent color, no gradients; content area width controlled, section spacing on the larger side, cards no more than two columns; the homepage is fixed as hero + customer pain points + three capabilities + two cases + pricing + FAQ + closing CTA, no carousel; the copy must include the company entity, implementation cycle range, and five FAQs. This passage costs very little, yet it determines whether AI is filling in a template or organizing a page.

If I only want to change one module, do I need to regenerate the whole page?

It depends on whether the tool provides element-level editing. The ideal state is to change it yourself: change one headline, replace one image, adjust one paragraph of description, and only that place moves while the rest of the layout stays unchanged. This kind of interaction is a basic capability in design tools, but in AI website builders it is a key dividing line: tools that support element-level editing turn changes into a matter of seconds, while tools that do not require regenerating the whole page every time and accepting uncontrollable reflow.

When batch adjustments are needed, the gap is even more obvious: unify button copy across the site, lower all card headline font sizes by one step, unify case image ratios, replace a certain type of accent color globally. The value of multi-select editing is not speed, but consistency: changing items one by one is easy to miss and easy to cause style drift; after multi-selecting and submitting one unified change, similar elements change together. There are two things to note when using it: before batch editing, confirm that element types are consistent—one button and one text link usually differ in style, and mixed selection will deform the result; after batch editing, spot-check non-target sections, because a unified font-size adjustment may cause line-break misalignment in a dense section.

Operationally, judge in this order:

  1. First distinguish whether the change is content-level (copy, images, links) or structural-level (adding sections, changing layout).
  2. Content-level changes go through element-level editing and should not trigger regeneration.
  3. Structural-level changes are made by adjusting sections on the canvas, or by targeted redoing of a single section, rather than redoing the whole page.
  4. Only when the overall style needs a new direction is it worth regenerating the whole page.

How to check desktop and mobile effects separately

Typography that looks restrained on desktop often becomes a hero that takes two screens to finish on mobile. It is recommended to fix the checking order:

  1. First look at the overall rhythm on desktop: whether the hero information is fully communicated within the hero, and whether whitespace between sections is even.
  2. Then switch to mobile: whether the hero is squeezed, whether buttons are easy to tap, and whether tables and code blocks overflow horizontally.
  3. Confirm breakpoint behavior page by page: whether card columns drop to a single column as expected, and whether navigation collapses into a menu.
  4. Check long text and mixed Chinese-English typesetting: whether the type scale breaks, and whether line height is compressed.
  5. Recheck on real devices, at least one iOS and one Android device, not just simulators.

Test case: the same requirement, three brand styles

Fix the same content draft—a finance and tax SaaS official website for small and medium-sized businesses, with the same page list (homepage, product capabilities, cases, pricing, FAQ, contact)—and change only the style instructions to generate three versions.

  • Tech brand style: dark background with monochrome highlights; the hero uses a capability-oriented claim; the product capability section is arranged in three columns; cases are presented as data metric cards.
  • Minimal business style: warm white background with dark ink green; the hero keeps only one value proposition and one CTA; section spacing is noticeably increased; cases change to two-column text and images; decorative graphics are removed.
  • Creative design style: asymmetric grid; headline font-size range is larger; cases change to a large-image waterfall layout; FAQ uses two-column accordions.

The biggest difference is not color, but hero information density, section order, and whitespace ratio. When these three change, the same content reads as three brands.

Then do a local modification comparison: before the change, the hero subtitle was a three-line industry description, and on mobile users had to scroll two screens to see the CTA; after the change, the subtitle was compressed into a one-sentence description of just over ten words, and the CTA was moved below the hero, while the other sections stayed unchanged. The result is complete hero information without triggering a full-page reflow—this is exactly the difference between element-level editing and full-page regeneration.

Cross-sectional testing from a designer's perspective also confirms that the gap mainly comes from whether the site can be changed after generation. When the same requirement was given to Squarespace Blueprint AI, Wix AI, Lovable, Webflow AI, and Framer AI for generation, design item scores ranged from 1/5 for Framer to 4/5 for Wix and Webflow; Webflow's output was considered the best designed, but the editor users then enter would deter most business owners (Design by Ency test).

Purchase and acceptance checklist: judging whether an AI website builder can be changed

Use the following checklist during the trial phase; it is much more reliable than watching demo videos.

Check item Specific question Pass standard
Generation method Template replacement or section composition Can specify page list and section order
Style control Can you specify colors, fonts, grid, whitespace Can produce structural-level differences, not just reskinning
Local editing Does changing one piece of copy trigger full-page regeneration Element-level editing, with the rest of the layout unchanged
Batch editing Can multiple elements be selected and adjusted together Supports multi-select and maintains visual consistency
Multi-device acceptance Can you switch device views for checking Desktop, tablet, and mobile can be checked separately
Iteration continuity Is the original design preserved after changes The baseline can continue and can be rolled back
Launch and operations Does it support domain deployment, content management, and SEO/GEO basics Content can be continuously updated after launch

If two or more of the first five items fail, the tool is more suitable for temporary pages than for a long-term official website that carries the brand. After choosing a tool, three more things need to be added: write 'can it be changed' into the selection criteria, not just generation speed; organize brand guidelines into a reusable constraint list (primary color and usage ratio, type scale, corner radius and shadow rules, hero information limit, image style, prohibited elements), and give it to AI together with the requirement each time, so style drift will be significantly reduced; establish a content draft—company entity information, service scope, case data, and FAQs—which serve both visitors and AI search citations.

How we0 supports this 'editable' chain

Generation is not the endpoint. In the three-step process—describe the requirement, multi-Agent real-time building, adjust in the visual canvas and publish to your own domain—adjustment is a default step, not a remedy. Multi-style design turns sections such as hero, advantages, introduction, features, cases, pricing, FAQ, and CTA into a composable page system, with style differences reflected in section selection and page rhythm; the editable design canvas supports element-level editing of text and images, multi-select editing, and switching between device views, so local adjustments do not require redoing the whole page (capability description: we0 official website).

It should be noted that these capabilities solve the efficiency problem of customizability and iterability; they do not promise rankings, traffic, or deal outcomes—those depend on content quality, industry competition, and operational investment.

FAQ

Do AI-generated websites all look the same?
The default output of most tools is indeed similar because they follow a template-library plus one-shot generation path. When a tool supports section composition, style parameters, and element-level editing, the same requirement can produce noticeably different results.

Can I specify colors, fonts, and layout?
Yes, but describe them by layer: colors and type scale at the visual layer, grid and whitespace at the typography layer, page list and section order at the structural layer. If you only give visual-layer instructions, the output usually still looks like a template.

If I only want to change one module, do I need to regenerate the entire page?
No, provided the tool has element-level editing capabilities. Text and image elements can be edited directly on the canvas without affecting the rest of the layout; only a complete style change requires regeneration.

How do I confirm the mobile effect?
Check in a fixed order: desktop hero and section rhythm, mobile hero information volume, breakpoint behavior (card columns, navigation collapse), mixed Chinese-English typesetting and long text, and finally recheck on real devices.

Related Tools

  • We0: an AI intelligent website building and lead growth workspace, covering natural language website building, editable design canvas, content management, and SEO/GEO optimization.
  • Squarespace Blueprint AI, Wix AI, Framer AI, Webflow AI: mainstream AI website builders that appeared in this comparison, which can be used to verify style controllability.

Related Links

  • we0 official website
  • Top 10 Best AI Website Builders In The World 2026 · Nubia Magazine
  • Best AI Website Builders 2026: 5 Tested by a Designer · Design by Ency

Summary

AI-generated websites look similar because template libraries set the structural ceiling, prompts do not carry enough information, one-shot generation cannot be edited locally, and content assets are repetitive—not because of the ceiling of AI capability. Move brand requirements from colors and fonts to section order, page lists, and a citable information layer, and the same content can read as three styles; changing one module does not require regenerating the whole page if the tool has element-level editing; changing multiple places depends on multi-select editing for consistency; desktop and mobile must be accepted separately. we0 uses a composable multi-style page system and an editable design canvas to support the adjustment stage after generation, allowing the official website to iterate continuously while retaining the original design.

title: Running hundreds of Telegram bots on one Node.js server: 8 lessons from production
description:
Most Telegram bot tutorials end at "it works for one bot". Our platform runs a few hundred merchant bots (shops, paid channels, AI assistants) from one Node.js cluster, and almost every hard bug we hit only appeared at that scale. Here are the lessons, in the order they hurt.

1. One process cannot own every bot: shard by bot

A single Node process runs out of event-loop headroom long before it runs out of memory. We run one primary process plus a pool of worker processes, and each bot belongs to exactly one worker. The reverse proxy routes every webhook request to the worker that owns that bot (a stable hash of the bot id), so a bot's updates are always handled in one place, in order, with its in-memory state.

The rule that keeps this sane: anything that must happen once (schedulers, reminders, cleanup jobs) runs only on the primary, and every worker checks "do I own this bot?" before acting.

2. Start bots slowly, or Telegram will rate-limit all of them

On boot, the naive code calls getMe and setWebhook for every bot at once. With hundreds of bots that is a burst of thousands of requests, and Telegram answers with 429 Too Many Requests and a retry_after that can lock bots out for minutes. Every restart degraded every bot.

Fixes that worked:

  • Cache getMe results in the database and only refresh them in the background.
  • Check getWebhookInfo first and call setWebhook only when the URL or settings are actually wrong.
  • Spread the remaining calls over time with a small queue, and honour retry_after when it is short. Give up and retry later when it is long.

3. Answer the webhook fast and do the work after

Telegram waits for your HTTP response. If your handler awaits a database call, an AI model or a file upload before answering, slow requests pile up and Telegram starts retrying, so you get the same update twice.

Reply 200 as soon as the update is validated and queued, then process it. The exception is payments: save a pre_checkout_query or a successful payment durably before you answer, because that is the one place where losing an update costs real money.

4. Deduplicate updates by update_id

Retries, restarts and proxy hiccups all produce duplicates. Keep the last few thousand update_ids per bot (an LRU in memory is enough for most of them) and drop repeats before any handler runs. For anything that moves money, add a second, durable "processed" table keyed by the callback or payment id, so a duplicate can never pay out twice even across a restart.

5. Use secret_token on every webhook

setWebhook accepts a secret_token, and Telegram sends it back in the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header on every request. Check it, and reject requests without it. Also keep the bot token out of the webhook URL: URLs end up in proxy access logs, monitoring tools and error reports. Use an opaque id in the path instead.

6. Be careful what shutdown does

A classic trap is a "clean" shutdown handler that deletes each bot's webhook on SIGTERM. It looks tidy, but a routine restart then unregisters every bot the process owned. Shutdown handlers should stop taking new work and flush queues. They should not change anything on Telegram's side.

Related: wrap startup code so that one bad module cannot crash the process on load. With a cluster, a crash on load is a silent total outage, because every worker dies the same way.

7. Rate-limit per user and per bot

One user tapping a button 50 times a second, or one bot being flooded, should not slow every other bot down. A sliding window per (bot, user) and per bot, checked before any handler, keeps the noise out. Escalate repeat offenders to temporary bans rather than answering every request.

8. Your bot library will silently drop new update types

Telegram keeps adding update types. In November 2026 Bot API 10.4 added widget_query for interactive widget cards. Older libraries only dispatch the types they know, so new ones vanish without an error. If you rely on a library, check how it handles unknown updates, and handle new types yourself before the library's dispatcher. (I wrote up the widget case here: Telegram widgets: interactive cards inside chat messages.)

Also remember allowed_updates: if you ever set an explicit list, new types are not delivered until you add them.

The short version

  • Shard bots across workers, one owner per bot.
  • Run schedulers on one process only.
  • Start slowly and cache getMe.
  • Answer fast, but save payments first.
  • Dedupe by update_id, and durably for money.
  • Use secret_token and keep tokens out of URLs.
  • Make shutdown boring.
  • Rate-limit per user and per bot.
  • Watch for new update types.

These lessons come from building TeleCrow, a no-code platform for Telegram shop bots, paid-channel bots and AI assistants. If you run many bots yourself, I hope this saves you a few late nights.

Disclosure: I work on TeleCrow.

title: Multi-tenant from day one: keeping one customer's chatbot data out of another's
description:
The first version of almost every B2B tool is single-tenant by accident. You build it for one customer, it works, a second customer arrives, and you add a customer_id column.

That column is now the only thing standing between your two customers' data. One forgotten WHERE clause and customer A's chatbot answers a question using customer B's internal pricing document. You will not get a second chance to explain that.

This is what I would set up on day one of a multi-tenant product, in the order the risk actually appears. It is written around a chatbot — vector search makes one of these problems unusually sharp — but most of it is the same for any SaaS.

1. Never pass the tenant id as an argument

The single highest-value change, and it is architectural rather than clever.

If getDocuments(tenantId, query) takes the tenant as a parameter, then every call site is a chance to pass the wrong one, or to forget it in a new function written at 1am. Humans do not reliably remember a rule 400 times.

Instead, resolve the tenant once, at the edge, from the authenticated session — never from a request body, a query string, or a header the client controls — and carry it in a context the data layer reads for itself:

// One place turns a session into a tenant. Nothing downstream takes it as an argument.
app.use(async (req, res, next) => {
  const session = await getSession(req);
  if (!session) return res.sendStatus(401);
  // The tenant comes from the session, never from req.body.tenantId.
  tenantContext.run({ tenantId: session.tenantId }, () => next());
});

// The data layer reads the context itself. There is no overload without a tenant.
function documents() {
  const { tenantId } = tenantContext.getStore() ?? {};
  if (!tenantId) throw new Error('No tenant in context — refusing to query');
  return db('documents').where({ tenant_id: tenantId });
}

That throw matters more than it looks. The failure mode you want for a missing tenant is a loud crash, not a query that quietly returns everything.

In Node this is AsyncLocalStorage. Most ecosystems have an equivalent. The point is not the mechanism — it is that the safe path is the only path, so a new developer cannot write the unsafe one without noticing.

2. Put the same rule in the database

Application-level filtering is one bug away from failing. A second, independent layer means a bug needs two mistakes to become a breach.

In Postgres that is row-level security:

ALTER TABLE documents ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE documents FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;   -- applies to the table owner too

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON documents
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid);

with the setting applied per transaction from the same context as above. FORCE is the line people miss: without it, the owner role bypasses the policy, and your application often connects as the owner.

This is defence in depth, not belt-and-braces theatre. The two layers fail for different reasons — one to a forgotten clause in code, the other to a misconfigured role — and it is unlikely you make both mistakes in the same hour.

3. Vector search is where isolation quietly breaks

Here is the chatbot-specific trap, and it is the one I would check first in anyone else's system.

A vector index does not have a WHERE clause in the way a SQL table does. Approximate nearest-neighbour search walks a graph and returns the k closest vectors it finds. If you then filter those results by tenant, two bad things happen:

  • Correctness: you asked for 20 and got 20 from across all tenants; after filtering, you might have 3 for this tenant, or none. The bot answers badly for no visible reason.
  • Safety: every piece of filtering logic between the index and the answer is a place to get it wrong.

Post-filtering is the wrong shape. The two shapes that work:

An index per tenant. Simplest to reason about, and the cross-tenant bug becomes structurally impossible — a query against tenant A's index cannot return tenant B's rows, whatever the code does. The cost is many small indexes, which is fine for hundreds of tenants and painful for a hundred thousand.

Pre-filtered search, where the tenant is a condition the index applies during the search, not after. pgvector does this naturally, because it is a Postgres query and row-level security already applies:

SELECT id, content, 1 - (embedding <=> $1) AS score
FROM   documents                      -- RLS already scopes this to the tenant
ORDER  BY embedding <=> $1
LIMIT  20;

Managed vector databases support metadata pre-filtering too — but read their documentation carefully and test it, because "filter" in some engines means post-filter, and the difference is exactly the one that matters here.

Write a test for this and never delete it. Two tenants, two documents, one query that would match the other tenant's document far better than its own:

test('a tenant never retrieves another tenant\'s content', async () => {
  await seed(tenantA, 'Our refund window is 30 days.');
  await seed(tenantB, 'Our refund window is 90 days.');

  const hits = await asTenant(tenantA, () => retrieve('how long is the refund window'));

  expect(hits).not.toHaveLength(0);                     // it still works
  expect(hits.every(h => h.tenantId === tenantA)).toBe(true);
  expect(hits.map(h => h.content).join(' ')).not.toMatch(/90 days/);
});

That last assertion is the one that catches a post-filter regression where the leak reaches the prompt but not the response object.

4. Secrets belong to one tenant each

Customers will give you API keys — their own model provider key, a WhatsApp token, an SMTP password. These need handling that plain columns do not give you:

  • Encrypted at rest with authenticated encryption, AES-256-GCM or equivalent, so a database dump is not a credential dump.
  • Decrypted only at the moment of use, never loaded into a general-purpose settings object that gets logged or serialised into an API response.
  • Masked everywhere they are displayed. Show the last four characters. There is no screen that needs to show the whole key, including the owner's own settings page — they have it already.
  • Scrubbed from errors. A provider's error object will happily include the request headers you sent.

5. Make the tenant visible in everything you operate

Isolation that you cannot observe is isolation you are only assuming.

  • Logs carry the tenant id on every line. Debugging a cross-tenant issue without it is guesswork.
  • Metrics and rate limits are per tenant. One customer's traffic spike should not degrade everyone, and a per-tenant limit is also your defence against a runaway loop in someone's integration costing you a fortune.
  • Background jobs carry the tenant explicitly, because they run outside the request that had the context. This is the most common place the whole scheme leaks: a cron job with no session, written months later.
  • Caches are keyed by tenant. A cache key of answer:${hash(question)} will serve tenant A's answer to tenant B, and it will do it intermittently, which makes it nearly impossible to reproduce.

That cache bug deserves emphasis. It is the one that gets shipped by careful teams, because the cache is added later as an optimisation, by someone who is thinking about latency rather than tenancy.

What it costs to do this on day one

Perhaps two days of work: the context plumbing, the RLS policies, the per-tenant index decision, the isolation test, the encrypted-secrets helper.

Retrofitting it onto a live product with real customers is weeks, because every query, job and cache written in the meantime has to be found and re-checked, and you cannot be sure you found them all. The second system is also the one where you are reading your own code wondering whether an untested path ever leaked.

The work is not hard. It is just much cheaper before the second customer than after the twentieth.

I build ChatNory, a multi-tenant AI chatbot that answers from each business's own content. The isolation test in section 3 exists because the post-filtering version looked completely fine until it did not. If you run vector search across tenants, go and check whether your engine pre-filters or post-filters — it is a five-minute check and it is worth doing today.

title: Transactions, Isolation Levels, MVCC, Locking, Triggers, Audit Logs & CAP Theorem in PostgreSQL 🔒
description:
🔒 Isolation, MVCC, Locking, Triggers, Audit Logging & CAP Theorem

This is one of the MOST important database topics for a Full Stack Developer. 💪

Imagine you're building an Instagram-like Social Feed. Thousands of users might like posts, comment, follow people and update profiles at the same time. Now imagine:

  • 🛒 Two users try to buy the last available product
  • 🏦 Two requests update the same bank account
  • ❤️ Someone likes a post while another person deletes it
  • 💥 A transaction fails halfway through
  • 👀 Two people read the same data while a third is modifying it

How does the database prevent incorrect data, conflicts and inconsistent results? That's exactly what we'll learn, from absolute zero, with PostgreSQL examples and connections to FastAPI and SQLAlchemy. 🚀

📚 Table of Contents

  1. What is a transaction?
  2. ACID: Isolation and Durability
  3. What is concurrency?
  4. Dirty read
  5. Non-repeatable read
  6. Phantom read
  7. Isolation levels
  8. MVCC
  9. Row-level locking and deadlocks
  10. Database triggers
  11. Audit logging
  12. CAP theorem
  13. ACID vs CAP
  14. Connecting it all to FastAPI
  15. Revision sheet
  16. Interview questions
  17. Quiz
  18. Practice checklist (two-session lab included!)

1️⃣ What is a transaction?

📦 A transaction is a group of database operations treated as one logical unit of work.

Transfer ₹1,000 from Account A to Account B:

Account Before After
A ₹5,000 ₹4,000
B ₹2,000 ₹3,000

Two actions are needed: subtract from A, add to B. But what if ₹1,000 is deducted from A, the server crashes, and B never receives it? 😱 Money has disappeared. Transactions prevent this.

BEGIN                  → start transaction
  UPDATE Account A     → deduct ₹1,000
  UPDATE Account B     → add ₹1,000
COMMIT                 → save changes ✅
ROLLBACK               → undo changes ❌

BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 1000
WHERE id = 1;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 1000
WHERE id = 2;

COMMIT;

If an error occurs before committing:

ROLLBACK;
Command Meaning
BEGIN Starts a transaction
COMMIT Permanently saves the transaction's changes
ROLLBACK Cancels uncommitted changes
SAVEPOINT Creates a point inside a transaction you can partially roll back to

📍 Bonus: SAVEPOINT 

BEGIN;

INSERT INTO orders (id, user_id) VALUES (1, 10);

SAVEPOINT after_order;

INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id) VALUES (1, 999);  -- suppose this fails

ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after_order;   -- undo only the item insert

COMMIT;                               -- the order itself is still saved

🧠 A transaction is not necessarily one SQL query. It can contain many.

2️⃣ ACID: Isolation and Durability 🧪

ACID is a set of four properties that keep transactions reliable:

  • ⚛️ A: Atomicity. All operations succeed or none do.
  • ✅ C: Consistency. Data follows database rules before and after.
  • 🚦 I: Isolation. Concurrent transactions don't interfere incorrectly.
  • 💾 D: Durability. Once committed, changes survive crashes (under the database's durability guarantees).

You likely know Atomicity and Consistency already. Today we go deep on Isolation and Durability.

2.1 🚦 Isolation: what does it mean?

Two people use the app at the same time:

  • User A wants to update a product price
  • User B wants to read that price

Isolation decides how transactions interact when they run concurrently. The goal: never show users incorrect or incomplete intermediate data.

Product 101 costs ₹500.

Transaction A:

BEGIN;

UPDATE products
SET price = 700
WHERE id = 101;
-- not committed yet!

Meanwhile, Transaction B:

SELECT price
FROM products
WHERE id = 101;

Should B see ₹500 or ₹700? 🤔 It depends on the isolation level, which is the most important part of today's lesson.

2.2 💾 Durability: what does it mean?

Once a transaction is successfully committed, its changes should survive a crash or restart.

  1. User updates their profile name
  2. Database executes COMMIT
  3. Database server crashes 💥
  4. Server restarts
  5. The updated name is still there ✅

How? PostgreSQL uses:

  • 📓 Write-Ahead Logging (WAL): records changes in a log before the data pages need to be written
  • 🔁 Recovery: replays the log after a crash
  • 🏁 Checkpoints: limit how much work recovery must replay
  • 🔄 Storage synchronization: persists required data per configured durability settings

📓 What is WAL?

Think of WAL as a diary kept by the database. Before changes are safely reflected in the main data files, PostgreSQL writes the needed information to its log.

1. Application runs an UPDATE
2. PostgreSQL records the change in WAL
3. COMMIT is acknowledged once required WAL durability conditions are met
4. Data pages are written to their main files LATER
5. If a crash happens → PostgreSQL replays WAL during recovery

🎤 Interview point: COMMIT does not necessarily mean every modified table page has already reached its final location. WAL is what makes crash recovery possible.

⚠️ Durability also depends on correct configuration and reliable storage. For example, weakening synchronous_commit weakens the guarantee.

3️⃣ What is concurrency? 🚗🚕🚙

Concurrency means multiple transactions execute during overlapping periods of time.

Your Instagram-like app at one moment:

  • 👤 User A likes a post
  • 💬 User B comments on the same post
  • ✏️ User C updates their profile
  • 📰 User D views the home feed

All these requests hit the backend at nearly the same time, and your backend sends queries for all of them.

Why is it difficult?

Because transactions may:

  • Read the same row
  • Update the same row
  • Insert new rows
  • Delete existing rows
  • Depend on each other's data

Without proper concurrency control, problems occur. Let's meet the three classic read problems. 👇

4️⃣ Dirty Read 🧟

A dirty read happens when a transaction reads data modified by another transaction that has NOT committed yet.

In simple words: you read someone else's temporary, unconfirmed changes.

Price starts at ₹500.

Transaction A:

BEGIN;

UPDATE products
SET price = 900
WHERE id = 1;
-- not committed

Transaction B:

SELECT price FROM products WHERE id = 1;
-- imagine it reads 900

Transaction A then:

ROLLBACK;
-- price is back to 500

But B already used ₹900, a value that was never permanently accepted. That's a dirty read.

1. A: changes price 500 → 900 (not committed)
2. B: reads 900
3. A: ROLLBACK (price back to 500)
4. ❌ B used data that never officially existed

🐘 PostgreSQL note: dirty reads never happen in PostgreSQL. Even if you request READ UNCOMMITTED, it behaves like READ COMMITTED.

5️⃣ Non-repeatable Read 🔄

A non-repeatable read happens when the same transaction reads the same row twice and gets different values, because another transaction committed an update in between.

Price starts at ₹500.

Transaction A:

BEGIN;

SELECT price FROM products WHERE id = 1;
-- 500

Transaction B:

BEGIN;

UPDATE products
SET price = 700
WHERE id = 1;

COMMIT;

Transaction A reads again:

SELECT price FROM products WHERE id = 1;
-- 700 😮

Same transaction, same SQL, same row, different result.

Transaction A:  first read  → ₹500
Transaction B:  updates to ₹700 and COMMITS
Transaction A:  second read → ₹700   ← non-repeatable read

This matters when your app expects data to stay stable throughout a transaction.

6️⃣ Phantom Read 👻

A phantom read happens when a transaction runs the same query twice and gets a different set of rows, because another transaction inserted, deleted or changed rows matching the condition.

employees

id department salary
1 IT ₹50,000
2 IT ₹60,000
3 HR ₹40,000

Transaction A:

BEGIN;

SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department = 'IT';
-- Employee 1, Employee 2

Transaction B:

INSERT INTO employees (id, department, salary)
VALUES (4, 'IT', 55000);

COMMIT;

Transaction A runs the same query again:

SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department = 'IT';
-- Employee 1, Employee 2, Employee 4  👻

Employee 4 is the phantom row.

⚖️ Non-repeatable read vs phantom read

Problem What changes?
Non-repeatable read A previously read row's values change
Phantom read The set of rows returned by a query changes

🧠 Non-repeatable read = same row, different values. Phantom read = different collection of matching rows.

🐘 PostgreSQL detail: Repeatable Read prevents phantom reads thanks to its snapshot-based MVCC implementation (even though the SQL standard would allow them at that level). Serializable also prevents them, and additionally prevents serialization anomalies.

7️⃣ Isolation Levels 🎚️ (the most important section!)

An isolation level decides how much protection a transaction gets from changes made by other concurrent transactions. The SQL standard defines four:

  1. Read Uncommitted
  2. Read Committed
  3. Repeatable Read
  4. Serializable

7.1 🟥 Read Uncommitted (weakest)

In theory it allows dirty reads. But PostgreSQL treats it as Read Committed, so dirty reads can't occur.

7.2 🟨 Read Committed (PostgreSQL default)

A transaction only sees data committed before the start of each individual SQL statement.

Notice: each individual statement. Every statement gets a fresh snapshot of committed data.

-- Transaction A
BEGIN;
SELECT price FROM products WHERE id = 1;   -- ₹500

-- Transaction B
UPDATE products SET price = 700 WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;

-- Transaction A again
SELECT price FROM products WHERE id = 1;   -- ₹700 (fresh snapshot!)

Therefore:

  • ✅ Dirty reads: prevented
  • ⚠️ Non-repeatable reads: possible
  • ⚠️ Phantom reads: possible
  • ⚠️ Serialization anomalies: possible

Great for: normal web apps, social feeds, ordinary CRUD.

7.3 🟧 Repeatable Read (stronger)

The transaction keeps seeing the same snapshot from its first query onward.

-- Transaction A
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT price FROM products WHERE id = 1;   -- 500

-- Transaction B
UPDATE products SET price = 700 WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;

-- Transaction A again
SELECT price FROM products WHERE id = 1;   -- still 500 ✅

A continues reading its original snapshot. In PostgreSQL this uses MVCC (coming up in section 8).

Repeatable Read prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and (in PostgreSQL) phantom reads. But it does not prevent every anomaly:

🩺 Write skew example: two transactions each read that at least two doctors are on duty, then each marks a different doctor off duty. Both commit, and now nobody is on duty. Only Serializable catches this.

Also, if a Repeatable Read transaction tries to update a row that another transaction changed after its snapshot, PostgreSQL raises:

ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update

and your app must retry.

7.4 🟩 Serializable (strongest)

Successfully committed concurrent transactions produce an outcome equivalent to some serial (one-after-another) execution.

Two users try to buy the last product. Both check stock, both proceed, and boom, wrong result. Serializable detects dangerous interactions and may abort one transaction. The application must retry it.

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;

SELECT quantity FROM products WHERE id = 1;

UPDATE products
SET quantity = quantity - 1
WHERE id = 1;

COMMIT;

On a conflict, PostgreSQL may return:

ERROR: could not serialize access
due to read/write dependencies among transactions

You must retry the complete transaction.

🧠 Serializable does not mean transactions literally run one by one. PostgreSQL runs them concurrently and uses Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) to detect dangerous conflicts.

7.5 📊 Comparison table (interview favorite!)

Isolation level Dirty read Non-repeatable read Phantom read
Read Uncommitted* Possible by the standard Possible Possible
Read Committed ❌ No ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
Repeatable Read (PostgreSQL) ❌ No ❌ No ❌ No
Serializable ❌ No ❌ No ❌ No

* PostgreSQL treats Read Uncommitted as Read Committed.

The table covers these three read anomalies. Serializable also prevents the broader class of serialization anomalies (like write skew).

🪜 Hierarchy 

Read Uncommitted  → weakest protection
Read Committed    → prevents dirty reads
Repeatable Read   → stable transaction snapshot
Serializable      → strongest isolation guarantees

⚖️ Higher isolation generally means more conflict handling, possible retries and extra overhead. It doesn't automatically mean every query is slower.

🛠️ Setting the isolation level 

-- per transaction
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;

-- or right after BEGIN
BEGIN;
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;

In SQLAlchemy:

from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine

engine = create_async_engine(
    "postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@localhost/db",
    isolation_level="REPEATABLE READ",   # applies to the whole engine
)

# or per connection
async with engine.connect() as conn:
    conn = await conn.execution_options(isolation_level="SERIALIZABLE")

8️⃣ MVCC: Multi-Version Concurrency Control 🧬

MVCC lets multiple transactions work with different versions of the same data.

Product 1 costs ₹500. Transaction A updates it to ₹700. Transaction B wants to read it. How can PostgreSQL let both happen without unnecessarily blocking each other? Through MVCC.

Conceptually, PostgreSQL keeps different row versions:

Old row version  (visible to older snapshots)   → Product 1, ₹500
        │  Transaction A updates the price
        ▼
New row version  (visible to newer snapshots)   → Product 1, ₹700

📝 This is a simplified picture. PostgreSQL actually stores tuple versions in table storage along with transaction visibility information.

The key ideas:

  • 👴 An older transaction can keep seeing the old committed version
  • 👶 A newer transaction sees the newly committed version
  • 📖 Readers generally don't block writers
  • ✍️ Writers generally don't block ordinary readers

📸 What is a snapshot?

A snapshot is the database's view of which transactions and row versions are visible to a particular query or transaction.

  • A starts at 10:00
  • B updates a row at 10:01 and commits
  • A (under Repeatable Read) keeps seeing its original snapshot
  • A new transaction starting at 10:02 sees the updated value

🧹 Does PostgreSQL keep old versions forever?

No. A process called VACUUM cleans up obsolete row versions once they're no longer needed. Old versions consume storage, and a long-running transaction can stop PostgreSQL from cleaning some of them, causing table bloat.

💡 Developer takeaway: MVCC improves concurrency, but avoid long-running transactions. Never keep a transaction open while waiting on a user or an external API.

9️⃣ Row-Level Locking 🔐

Two people update the same product at once:

id = 1, quantity = 10

A wants 9, B wants 8. How does the database coordinate? Through locks.

🔒 A lock controls access to database resources while transactions operate on them.

9.1 🧱 What is a row-level lock?

A row-level lock protects a particular row from conflicting operations.

BEGIN;

SELECT *
FROM products
WHERE id = 1
FOR UPDATE;

This locks the selected row. Other transactions trying for conflicting locks on that row may have to wait, but they can still work on other rows.

ID Product Lock status
1 Laptop 🔒 Locked
2 Mouse 🟢 Available
3 Keyboard 🟢 Available

9.2 ⭐ SELECT ... FOR UPDATE

One of the most important commands for backend developers:

BEGIN;

SELECT quantity
FROM products
WHERE id = 1
FOR UPDATE;

UPDATE products
SET quantity = quantity - 1
WHERE id = 1;

COMMIT;

What happens:

  1. PostgreSQL finds the row
  2. It acquires a row-level lock
  3. Other transactions attempting conflicting updates or row locks wait
  4. Your transaction updates the quantity
  5. COMMIT releases the lock

Use it for:

  • 🏦 Banking transactions
  • 📦 Inventory management
  • 🎟️ Booking and ticket reservation
  • 👛 Wallet balance updates
  • 🧠 Any "read a row, then decide based on its value" logic

9.3 🎛️ Row-lock modes

Command Purpose
FOR UPDATE Strong lock; blocks conflicting modifications and row-locking
FOR NO KEY UPDATE Weaker; useful when key columns aren't changing
FOR SHARE Blocks updates/deletes while allowing other shared locks
FOR KEY SHARE Protects key values against changes that affect foreign keys

As a beginner, focus on FOR UPDATE.

🎁 Bonus: NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED 

-- Fail immediately instead of waiting
SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;

-- Skip rows that are already locked (great for job queues!)
SELECT * FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 1
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

9.4 💀 What is a deadlock?

A deadlock happens when two or more transactions wait for each other forever.

  • A locks Row 1
  • B locks Row 2
  • A now wants Row 2
  • B now wants Row 1 
Transaction A: owns Row 1, waiting for Row 2
                  ▲                │
                  │                ▼
Transaction B: owns Row 2, waiting for Row 1

        🔁 circular waiting

PostgreSQL detects the deadlock and aborts one transaction with:

ERROR: deadlock detected   (SQLSTATE 40P01)

🛡️ How to prevent deadlocks

  1. Always acquire locks in a consistent order (for example, lower account ID first)
  2. Keep transactions short
  3. Avoid unnecessary locks
  4. Never wait for external API calls while holding database locks
  5. Retry on appropriate transient errors

If every transaction locks Account A first and Account B second, you reduce the risk of opposite lock ordering.

🔟 Database Triggers ⚡

A trigger is a database mechanism that automatically executes a function when a particular event happens.

Think of it as an automatic reaction. Common events:

  • INSERT
  • UPDATE
  • DELETE
  • TRUNCATE (statement-level triggers)

Real-world example

Whenever a user changes their username, you want to record the old and new username. You could write that in every endpoint. But what if another developer updates the table directly with SQL? That code gets skipped. A trigger enforces it at the database level.

10.1 🔄 How a trigger works 

Database event:   UPDATE users
        ▼
Trigger fires:    PostgreSQL detects the UPDATE
        ▼
Trigger function: records old and new values
        ▼
Audit table:      change history is stored

10.2 🧭 Types of triggers

By timing:

  • ⏪ BEFORE: runs before the operation
  • ⏩ AFTER: runs after the operation
  • 🔀 INSTEAD OF: runs instead of the operation (commonly on views)

By execution level:

  • 🧍 ROW-level: once for every affected row
  • 📣 STATEMENT-level: once for the entire statement 
UPDATE users
SET active = false
WHERE city = 'Bengaluru';

If 100 users match: a ROW trigger fires 100 times, a STATEMENT trigger fires once.

10.3 🆕🆚 NEW and OLD

  • OLD → the previous version of a row
  • NEW → the new version of a row 
OLD.username = deepika
NEW.username = deepika_p
Event Available
INSERT NEW
UPDATE OLD and NEW
DELETE OLD

10.4 🧪 Hands-on: build an audit trigger

Step 1: the users table

CREATE TABLE users (
    id       SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    username VARCHAR(100),
    email    VARCHAR(255)
);

Step 2: the audit table

CREATE TABLE user_audit (
    id           SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id      INTEGER,
    old_username VARCHAR(100),
    new_username VARCHAR(100),
    changed_at   TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

Step 3: the trigger function

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION log_username_changes()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
BEGIN
    IF OLD.username IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.username THEN
        INSERT INTO user_audit (user_id, old_username, new_username)
        VALUES (OLD.id, OLD.username, NEW.username);
    END IF;

    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
  • IS DISTINCT FROM is a NULL-safe "not equal" comparison
  • RETURN NEW; lets the update proceed (required in this kind of trigger)

Step 4: attach the trigger

CREATE TRIGGER username_audit_trigger
AFTER UPDATE ON users
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION log_username_changes();

Step 5: test it

INSERT INTO users (username, email)
VALUES ('deepika', 'deepika@example.com');

UPDATE users
SET username = 'deepika_p'
WHERE id = 1;

SELECT * FROM user_audit;
user_id old_username new_username
1 deepika deepika_p

🎉 The backend developer never manually inserted an audit record in the UPDATE.

⚠️ Important: trigger actions generally run in the same transaction as the statement that fired them. If that transaction rolls back, the audit row rolls back too. Triggers are great for tracking changes, but they are not a substitute for tamper-proof security auditing.

To remove a trigger:

DROP TRIGGER username_audit_trigger ON users;

1️⃣1️⃣ Audit Logging 📝

Audit logging means keeping a record of important actions and changes in a system.

In your social app, you may want to know:

  • Who changed a username?
  • Who deleted a post?
  • Who changed account privacy?
  • When was an email address changed?
  • What was the previous value, and the new one?
User Action Old value New value
101 Username update deepika deepika_p
102 Privacy update Public Private
103 Profile update Old bio New bio

What should an audit log contain? 

audit_id
user_id
action
entity_type
entity_id
old_value
new_value
timestamp
request_id
  • audit_id → unique audit record ID
  • user_id → who performed the action
  • action → what happened
  • entity_type → which kind of resource changed
  • entity_id → which specific resource changed
  • old_value / new_value → before and after
  • timestamp → when
  • request_id → which API request caused it

⚖️ Application-level vs trigger-based logging

Application-level logging Database trigger logging
Written in Python/FastAPI Written in database functions
Captures business context Captures row changes
Flexible for complex workflows Runs automatically on configured DB events
Can be skipped if a code path misses it Runs for applicable changes regardless of entry point
Easy to include API request info Needs extra design to capture request context

In real systems, both are often used together.

🎁 Bonus: giving triggers request context

A trigger doesn't know which app user made the change. One approach: set a transaction-local setting from your backend, then read it inside the trigger.

-- In your app, at the start of the transaction:
SET LOCAL app.current_user_id = '101';

-- Inside the trigger function:
-- current_setting('app.current_user_id', true)

🔐 Security point: don't casually store passwords, raw auth tokens or other secrets in audit logs. Restrict access and protect sensitive logged data.

1️⃣2️⃣ CAP Theorem 🌐

Now we enter distributed systems. Don't worry, we'll start from zero.

12.1 🖥️ What is a distributed system?

One server:

Frontend (React) → Backend (FastAPI) → Database (PostgreSQL)

Now millions of users arrive. One server isn't enough, so you add more:

Users
  ▼
Load Balancer
  ├─ Server 1
  ├─ Server 2
  └─ Server 3
        ▼
Distributed database / replicas

Your application now runs across multiple machines communicating over a network. But networks fail! 💥

  • Server 1 can't talk to Server 2
  • A cable fails
  • A data center loses connectivity
  • A connection becomes extremely slow

These are network partitions, and this is where CAP becomes important.

12.2 📐 What is CAP theorem?

In a distributed data system, when a network partition occurs, you cannot guarantee both strong Consistency and Availability for every request.

CAP = Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance.

🅲 Consistency (in CAP)

Every successful read sees the latest successfully committed write, or an appropriate failure is returned.

A user changes their username from deepika to deepika_p. Your database has Nodes A, B and C. Under strong consistency, once the update is acknowledged, any successful read from any node returns deepika_p, never the old name.

🚨 CAP consistency ≠ ACID consistency. ACID consistency is about constraints and valid states. CAP consistency is about visibility and ordering of data across distributed nodes.

🅰 Availability

Every request received by a non-failing node gets a non-error response, even if that response doesn't contain the latest data.

If Node A is unreachable but Node B can still serve the profile request, the system is available. But an available response isn't necessarily the newest value.

🅿 Partition Tolerance

The system keeps operating despite communication failures between groups of nodes.

Network group A: Node A, Node B
        ✂️  communication broken  ✂️
Network group B: Node C, Node D

The nodes are all running, but they can't talk to each other. That's a partition.

12.3 ⚖️ The CAP trade-off

When a partition occurs, you have two broad choices:

Option 1: prioritize Consistency (CP)

  • Don't allow potentially stale or conflicting reads
  • Some requests may wait or fail
  • Consistency over availability

Example: a strongly consistent banking operation may refuse to proceed without quorum or a valid leader.

Option 2: prioritize Availability (AP)

  • Keep responding to requests
  • Some responses may be stale
  • Replicas reconcile later

Example: a social feed shows a slightly older like count for a moment.

❓ "Pick any two of three?" That's a simplification. The accurate version: when a network partition occurs, a distributed system must trade off strong consistency against availability. Partition tolerance isn't something you can simply switch off, since communication failures are possible. And when there's no partition, the trade-off looks different.

12.4 🌍 Real-world examples

Use case Typical priority
🏦 Bank balance transfers Strong consistency
📦 Inventory reservations Strong consistency
📰 Social media feed Availability (staleness OK)
❤️ Like counts Often eventual consistency
🎯 Product recommendations Availability
🧭 Distributed coordination Strong consistency

These are tendencies, not absolute labels for whole products. One application can use different consistency strategies for different features.

12.5 ⏳ What is eventual consistency?

If no new updates happen and communication is restored, all replicas eventually converge to the same value.

You like a post:

Primary:  Likes = 101
Replica:  Likes = 100     ← hasn't received the update yet

...a moment later...

Primary:  Likes = 101
Replica:  Likes = 101     ← converged ✅
Strong consistency Eventual consistency
Reads reflect the latest committed write Reads may temporarily be stale
More coordination required Allows more independent operation
Good for financial operations Good for feeds, analytics, some counters
May reject/delay requests during partitions Can keep serving during partitions

In your social feed:

  • 📝 Creating a post must reliably save
  • 🔒 Privacy settings need careful consistency
  • ❤️ Like counts can tolerate a small delay
  • 🎯 Recommendations can update asynchronously

Backend developers choose guarantees based on business requirements.

1️⃣3️⃣ ACID vs CAP: don't confuse them! ⚔️

ACID CAP
About transaction reliability About distributed system trade-offs
Atomicity Consistency
Consistency Availability
Isolation Partition tolerance
Durability (no direct equivalent)
  • ACID Isolation → transactions don't interfere incorrectly
  • CAP Consistency → latest values observed across distributed nodes
  • ACID Durability → committed transactions survive failures
  • CAP Partition Tolerance → handling network communication failures

They are not interchangeable concepts.

1️⃣4️⃣ Connecting it all to your FastAPI project 🔌

Imagine users can reserve limited promotional slots. Only one slot is left, and two users try to reserve it simultaneously.

Without concurrency control:

  1. User A reads available_slots = 1
  2. User B reads available_slots = 1
  3. User A reserves it
  4. User B also reserves it
  5. 💥 Overbooked!

✅ Solution 1: row-level locking 

BEGIN;

SELECT available_slots
FROM promotions
WHERE id = 1
FOR UPDATE;

UPDATE promotions
SET available_slots = available_slots - 1
WHERE id = 1
  AND available_slots > 0;

COMMIT;

The lock makes competing transactions wait. Also check whether the UPDATE actually affected a row. If it didn't, no slot was available.

✅ Solution 2: a single conditional UPDATE (often simplest!) 

UPDATE promotions
SET available_slots = available_slots - 1
WHERE id = 1
  AND available_slots > 0
RETURNING available_slots;

This is atomic:

  • Row returned → reservation succeeded ✅
  • No row returned → no slot available ❌

A very useful backend technique. 🧠

🐍 FastAPI + SQLAlchemy version 

from sqlalchemy import select


async def reserve_slot(session, promotion_id: int):
    async with session.begin():
        result = await session.execute(
            select(Promotion)
            .where(Promotion.id == promotion_id)
            .with_for_update()
        )
        promotion = result.scalar_one_or_none()

        if promotion is None:
            raise ValueError("Promotion not found")

        if promotion.available_slots <= 0:
            raise ValueError("No slots available")

        promotion.available_slots -= 1
        return promotion
Code Meaning
session.begin() Starts a transaction
select(Promotion) Builds a SELECT query
.where(...) Filters the requested promotion
.with_for_update() Requests a row-level lock
scalar_one_or_none() Gets one result or None
available_slots -= 1 Updates the value
End of with block Commits on success, rolls back on exception

⚠️ session.begin() raises an error if a transaction has already started on that session (for example, a dependency already ran a query). If your project's session dependency auto-begins, use the explicit await session.commit() / await session.rollback() style instead. Stay consistent with your project's pattern.

🔁 Retrying on serialization failures and deadlocks

Serializable (and Repeatable Read) can abort a transaction by design, so your code should retry:

from sqlalchemy.exc import DBAPIError

MAX_RETRIES = 3

async def run_with_retry(session_factory, work):
    for attempt in range(1, MAX_RETRIES + 1):
        async with session_factory() as session:
            try:
                async with session.begin():
                    return await work(session)
            except DBAPIError as exc:
                # 40001 = serialization_failure, 40P01 = deadlock_detected
                code = getattr(exc.orig, "sqlstate", None) or getattr(exc.orig, "pgcode", None)
                if code in ("40001", "40P01") and attempt < MAX_RETRIES:
                    continue
                raise

💡 Retry the entire transaction, never just the failed statement.

1️⃣6️⃣ Important interview questions 🎤

Q1. Read Committed vs Repeatable Read?
Read Committed takes a new snapshot for every statement. Repeatable Read (in PostgreSQL) uses a stable snapshot for the whole transaction.

Q2. What is a dirty read?
Reading data modified by another transaction before it commits.

Q3. Non-repeatable vs phantom reads?
Non-repeatable reads involve changed values in an existing row. Phantom reads involve changes in the set of rows matching a query.

Q4. What is MVCC?
Multi-Version Concurrency Control. It lets transactions access different versions of rows, improving concurrency between readers and writers.

Q5. What is SELECT FOR UPDATE?
It acquires row-level locks on selected rows so competing transactions can't perform conflicting operations on them until the lock is released.

Q6. What is a deadlock?
Transactions waiting for locks held by each other, so none can progress. The database detects it and aborts one.

Q7. What is a database trigger?
A mechanism that automatically executes a trigger function when a specified database event occurs.

Q8. What is audit logging?
Recording important changes and actions: who did them, when, and what changed.

Q9. What is WAL?
Write-Ahead Logging. PostgreSQL records changes in a log to support crash recovery and durability.

Q10. Explain CAP theorem.
During a network partition, a distributed system must choose between guaranteeing strong consistency for successful requests and guaranteeing availability for every request.

Q11. What is eventual consistency?
Replicas may temporarily differ but converge once updates stop and synchronization succeeds.

Q12. ACID consistency vs CAP consistency?
ACID consistency means transactions preserve database rules and constraints. CAP consistency means reads across distributed nodes respect the latest successful write under the chosen guarantee.

Q13. What is write skew, and which isolation level prevents it?
Two transactions read overlapping data and then update different rows based on what they read, producing an invalid combined result. Only Serializable prevents it.

Q14. Should you retry a failed Serializable transaction?
Yes. Retry the entire transaction, since serialization failures are an expected part of the model.

  • 🐘 PostgreSQL handles isolation, MVCC, locks and triggers
  • 📓 WAL helps with durability
  • 🌐 Distributed architecture introduces CAP trade-offs

Together, these concepts form a major part of backend engineering. 🏆

title: CQRS & Event-Driven Thinking: Commands, Queries, Domain Events & the Outbox Pattern Explained 📨
description:
📨 CQRS & Event-Driven Thinking: Let's Learn from ZERO!

These are important backend architecture concepts, especially with FastAPI, PostgreSQL, SQLAlchemy, repositories, services and a social media app. We'll cover:

  • 🔀 What Command-Query Separation (CQS) means
  • 🧩 What CQRS is and how it differs from CQS
  • ⚔️ Commands vs queries
  • 📣 What domain events are
  • 🌐 How event-driven architecture works
  • 🏢 Real examples using an Instagram-like app
  • ✅ Advantages, disadvantages, use cases and interview questions

We'll start simple and gradually move towards real backend code. 🚀

1. 🤔 First, Understand the Problem

You're building an Instagram-like app. A user can:

  1. Create a post
  2. Like a post
  3. Comment on a post
  4. Follow another user
  5. View their home feed
  6. Search for posts
  7. View someone's profile

All of these touch the database. But are they all doing the same kind of work? No! There are two fundamentally different kinds of operations:

Kind Examples Effect
✍️ Writing / changing data Create a post, like a post, delete a comment, follow a user Changes the database
👀 Reading / retrieving data Get all posts, view comments, get a profile, search posts Retrieves information without changing it

This distinction is the foundation of Command-Query Separation.

2. 🔀 Command-Query Separation (CQS)

  • Command: an instruction to perform an action
  • Query: a request to retrieve information
  • Separation: keeping these two responsibilities apart
