title: How to Create a Next.js App: Your First Project, Step by Step
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

To create a Next.js app, install Node.js, run one command, npx create-next-app@latest, answer a few simple setup questions, then run npm run dev and open localhost:3000 in your browser. That is the whole process. In the next ten minutes you will have a real project running on your own computer, ready to edit.

What You Need Before You Start

You do not need much, and you do not need to be an expert. You need three things: Node.js, a code editor, and some basic React knowledge.

First, install Node.js LTS, the stable long term support version, from the official Node.js website. Next.js needs a recent version, so update old installs now. Then check it in your terminal:

node -v
npm -v

If both print a version number, you are ready. If you see command not found, reopen the terminal or reinstall Node.

Second, install a code editor. Visual Studio Code is free and works well, but any editor is fine.

Third, you need basic React: components, JSX, and props at a simple level. If that feels new, work through this beginner React roadmap for learning React step by step first. An hour there makes this guide much easier.

The One Command That Creates Everything

Open your terminal, move to the folder where you keep your projects, and run this command:

npx create-next-app@latest my-first-app

In short: npx runs a tool without installing it permanently, create-next-app is the official starter, latest means use the newest version, and my-first-app is your folder name. Use lowercase letters and hyphens, not spaces.

The tool downloads what it needs, then asks a short list of questions. When it finishes, you will see a success message.

The full official instructions live in the Next.js installation guide on nextjs.org, which is worth bookmarking because it is updated whenever the setup process changes.

What Each Setup Question Really Means

Beginners often just press Enter repeatedly. The defaults are sensible, but it is better to know what you are agreeing to.

Setup question What it means Recommended for beginners
Would you like to use TypeScript? TypeScript adds type checks to JavaScript and helps catch mistakes early. Yes, if you know a little TypeScript. No is also fine while learning.
Which linter would you like to use? A linter checks your code style and spots common errors as you type. Choose the default option.
Would you like to use Tailwind CSS? Tailwind lets you style pages with small utility classes inside your markup. Yes. It pairs very well with Next.js and is easy to learn gradually.
Would you like your code inside a src/ directory? This puts your app code in a src folder to keep the project tidy. Either works. No keeps the structure simpler for a first project.
Would you like to use App Router? The App Router is the modern way to build Next.js apps, using the app folder. Yes. Always choose this for new projects.
Would you like to customise the import alias? An alias like @/ lets you write short import paths instead of long relative ones. Keep the default.

My advice: choose TypeScript only if you are comfortable with it, say yes to Tailwind and the App Router, and keep the defaults elsewhere. Every option can be added later.

The official Next.js documentation introduction (nextjs.org) — what Next.js is and how the docs are organised.

Run Your App and See It Live

Now move into your new folder and start the development server:

cd my-first-app
npm run dev

The terminal will print a local address, usually http://localhost:3000. Open that address in your browser. You should see the default Next.js starter page. Congratulations, your app is running.

While the dev server runs, every save updates the browser almost instantly. Leave the terminal open while you work, and press Control plus C to stop it. If port 3000 is busy, Next.js will use 3001 instead.

A Quick Tour of Your Project Folders

Open the project in your editor. You only need a few files on day one.

The app folder is where your pages live. This is where you will spend most of your time. Inside it, page.tsx is your home page, layout.tsx wraps every page with shared parts like a header, and globals.css holds your global styles.

The public folder holds static files like images. For example, public/logo.png appears at localhost:3000/logo.png.

The file package.json lists your dependencies and scripts, such as dev, build, and start. You will rarely edit it by hand at first.

Ignore the rest for now; files like next.config are already configured. If you are unsure what Next.js adds on top of React, this explanation of what React is and why it is used for building interfaces will fill in the background nicely.

Edit Your Home Page

Let us make the starter page yours. Open app/page.tsx, or app/page.js if you chose JavaScript, delete the starter content, and try something small like this:

export default function Home() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Hello, this is my first Next.js app</h1>
      <p>I built this in about ten minutes.</p>
    </main>
  );
}

Save the file and check your browser. The page has already changed. A page is just a React component that returns markup, exported as the default export.

Try small changes next: another paragraph, a new heading, a list. Breaking things now is fine, it is how you learn.

Add a Second Page

A real website needs more than one page, and in Next.js adding a page is simply adding a folder. Inside the app folder, create a new folder called about, and inside it create a file called page.tsx:

export default function AboutPage() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>About me</h1>
      <p>This is my second page. No router setup needed.</p>
    </main>
  );
}

Now visit localhost:3000/about. Your new page is live, with no configuration. The folder name becomes the URL. To understand this system properly, read how routing works in Next.js with folders and files when you are ready for links, layouts, and dynamic pages.

To link between pages, use the Link component from next/link. It preloads linked pages, so changes feel instant.

Your Next Steps After Day One

Keep your next steps small. Add a contact page and a projects page, build a shared header in your layout file, and add images from public with a little Tailwind styling.

When you feel comfortable, explore the official Next.js documentation a section at a time. Do not try to learn everything in one weekend. Build one tiny thing, finish it, then build the next.

One last tip: commit to Git early, even if it is messy. It gives you a safety net to return to a version that worked.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Next.js free to use?

Yes. Next.js is free and open source. Creating and running an app on your own computer costs nothing. You only pay if you later choose paid hosting or paid services.

Do I need to know React before Next.js?

You need the basics: components, JSX, and props. You do not need to be advanced. If you can build a small React page, you can start Next.js and learn the rest as you go.

Should I choose TypeScript or JavaScript?

Either is fine for a first project. JavaScript feels simpler at the start. TypeScript helps catch errors as projects grow, and most professional teams use it, so it is worth learning later.

What is the difference between npm run dev and npm run build?

The dev command runs your app for development, with instant updates when you save. The build command creates an optimised production version, ready to put online for real visitors.

Conclusion

Creating a Next.js app is really just three moves: install Node.js, run create-next-app, and start the dev server. Everything else, the folders, the pages, the styling, you can learn piece by piece inside a project that already works. Start today, keep the project small, and change one thing at a time. Your first app does not need to impress anyone. It just needs to exist.

title: What Is MySQL? How the Popular Database Works, Explained Simply
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

MySQL is a free, open-source database system that stores your website's information in organised tables. It lets you save, search, update, and delete that information using a language called SQL. When a WordPress site remembers your posts, a shop remembers its products, or an app remembers its users, MySQL is very often doing the remembering behind the scenes. Think of it as a super-organised digital filing cabinet. Your data lives in neat tables of rows and columns, and MySQL can find any record among millions in a blink. It has been the default database for PHP websites for over two decades.

First, What Is a Database in Plain Words?

A database is an organised collection of information that a program can search and change quickly. Without one, a website would store everything in loose text files. Imagine hunting for one student's marks by opening thousands of files one by one. You would grow old before you found them.

A database keeps data in a strict structure and answers questions fast. Show me all students who scored above 80. Find yesterday's order for this customer. It answers in milliseconds, even with millions of records. MySQL is one specific system, technically called a relational database management system. Relational means data lives in tables that can relate to each other, like a students table linked to a courses table.

What Is MySQL, Exactly?

MySQL was created in Sweden in the mid-1990s and became the favourite database of the early web. Today it is developed by Oracle, the large company that acquired it. Despite that, MySQL remains free and open source for most uses, which is a big reason it spread everywhere.

You talk to MySQL using SQL, short for Structured Query Language. SQL reads almost like plain English. You write SELECT name FROM students, and MySQL knows you want the names from the students table. If that language-versus-system point feels fuzzy, our comparison of SQL vs MySQL and their key differences clears it up. MySQL is also the M in the classic LAMP stack: Linux, Apache, MySQL, and PHP. The official MySQL Reference Manual introduction is the best source for precise technical details later.

The "What is MySQL?" page in the official MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual (dev.mysql.com).

Databases, Tables, Rows, and Columns Explained

Let us build the idea with a school example. At the top level is a database, like one whole filing cabinet. One MySQL server can hold many databases, one for your blog, one for your shop. Inside a database are tables. Each table is like a labelled drawer for one type of thing: students, teachers, courses.

Inside a table are columns and rows. Columns define what is stored: name, age, city, marks. Rows hold the actual records, and one row is one complete student. So a students table could look like this:

id name age city marks
1 Aarav 15 Delhi 88
2 Priya 16 Jaipur 92
3 Rohan 15 Lucknow 76

Each column has a data type. The id and marks columns hold numbers, while name and city hold text. Types keep data clean: MySQL will politely refuse to store the word "banana" in a marks column. The id is usually the primary key, a unique number identifying each row, so two students never share an id, even with the same name.

A Small SQL Example You Can Read Right Now

Enough theory. Here is real SQL that creates the students table and works with it:

CREATE TABLE students (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100),
    age INT,
    city VARCHAR(50),
    marks INT
);

INSERT INTO students (name, age, city, marks)
VALUES ('Aarav', 15, 'Delhi', 88);

INSERT INTO students (name, age, city, marks)
VALUES ('Priya', 16, 'Jaipur', 92);

SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

CREATE TABLE builds the empty table and lists its columns. INT means a whole number, and VARCHAR(100) means text up to 100 characters. AUTO_INCREMENT makes MySQL generate each id itself. Each INSERT adds one new row. The SELECT asks a question: give me the name and marks of students scoring above 80. MySQL instantly returns Aarav and Priya. That pattern, create, insert, select, plus updating and deleting, covers most of what websites do daily. Later, tricks like controlling how many rows come back are covered in our tutorial on MySQL LIMIT and OFFSET explained with examples.

Where Is MySQL Used in the Real World?

The most famous MySQL user in your daily life is WordPress. Every post, page, comment, and user account lives in its MySQL database. When you open a WordPress page, PHP asks MySQL for the content, and MySQL hands it over.

Beyond WordPress, MySQL powers countless PHP applications: shops, school portals, booking systems, and forums. The official MySQL website lists many well-known products built on it. For students the takeaway is simple: if you plan to build websites with PHP, MySQL is the other half of the job. If PHP itself is new to you, start with our guide on what PHP is, explained simply, then return here.

MySQL vs a Spreadsheet: Why Not Just Use Excel?

A spreadsheet also has rows and columns, so why learn a database? For a birthday list, a spreadsheet is honestly perfect. For a website, it breaks down fast. First, teamwork: hundreds of visitors can use MySQL at the same moment, safely. A spreadsheet file was never designed for that. Second, speed: MySQL uses indexes, like the index at the back of a textbook, to jump straight to the right rows. A spreadsheet scans; MySQL leaps. Third, safety: MySQL controls who can change what, and can undo a half-finished change after a crash. A spreadsheet is a notebook on your desk. MySQL is a librarian who never sleeps.

How Does a Website Talk to MySQL?

Your visitors never speak to MySQL directly. A visitor opens a page, and the PHP code connects to MySQL with a username and password. PHP sends an SQL query, receives the rows back, and builds the HTML page from them. The visitor only sees the finished page.

In PHP, the two standard connection tools are called mysqli and PDO. Both are built into PHP itself. A few lines of code can connect, run a query, and loop through results to display products or posts. PDO is usually recommended for new projects, because it makes safe, prepared queries easy. Prepared queries stop a common attack called SQL injection, where a troublemaker types database commands into a form field.

MySQL vs MariaDB in Brief

You will often see the name MariaDB next to MySQL. After Oracle acquired MySQL, some of its original creators made a fully compatible copy, called a fork, named MariaDB. It behaves almost identically and uses the same SQL. Many hosts now install MariaDB by default while still calling the feature "MySQL databases". Good news for learners: everything you learn about MySQL applies to MariaDB too.

Who Should Learn MySQL, and Your First Steps

Learn MySQL if you want to build dynamic websites, work with WordPress or PHP, or aim for a web developer job. Almost every PHP and backend job description lists MySQL or SQL, because almost every real application must store data somewhere. It is also a strong skill for final-year projects.

Your first steps are simple. Install XAMPP, which bundles PHP, MySQL, and a friendly visual tool called phpMyAdmin. Create a database, build the students table above, and practise inserting, selecting, updating, and deleting rows. Then connect a small PHP page with PDO and display your students in a browser. That proud moment, seeing your own data on a web page, is when databases stop being theory.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is MySQL free to use?

Yes. MySQL Community Edition is free and open source, and most websites and learners use it. Oracle also sells paid editions with extra support for large companies.

What is the difference between SQL and MySQL?

SQL is the language used to ask questions and give commands. MySQL is the software that understands that language and stores the data. One is the language; the other is the librarian who speaks it.

Is MySQL hard to learn for beginners?

No. The basic commands read almost like English, and you can do useful work after one afternoon of practice. Advanced topics take longer, but the foundations are beginner friendly.

Does WordPress really need MySQL?

Yes. A standard WordPress site requires a MySQL or MariaDB database. Posts, pages, comments, settings, and user accounts are all stored there.

Conclusion

MySQL is the quiet workhorse behind a huge share of the web: a free, fast, reliable database that stores information in tables and answers SQL questions in milliseconds. You now know how tables, rows, and columns work, and how PHP connects them to your visitors. Install it locally, build the students table, and run your first SELECT today. Small steps, practised daily, make this topic easy surprisingly fast.

title: GitHub Find: A Model Family Built to Be Small Enough to Own
description:
I found jaredpalmer/kev while scrolling trending repos: a small family of decision models built on Qwen3.5, designed to be trained and run on your own hardware instead of called through an API. I haven't tested it, and I'm not going to pretend I have. This isn't a review, it's a case for why the idea deserves attention before anyone opens the code.

Here's the actual point. Most of the model conversation right now is about scale, bigger context windows, bigger parameter counts, bigger bills. Kev bets on the opposite: models small enough that you own them outright. Not "call an API and hope the vendor doesn't change the pricing tier next quarter", something you fine-tune on your own data and keep running when the network is down.

"Decision model" is the phrase worth sitting with. If this means classification-style output, pick an action from a bounded set, route a request, approve or deny, score a lead, that's a different design target than a chat model entirely. You don't need a massive general-purpose model to decide which of five support queues a ticket belongs in. You need something fast, cheap per inference, and predictable enough that you can write tests against its output distribution. Starting from Qwen3.5 instead of pretraining from scratch is the sane move if that's the actual goal.

Who benefits if the idea holds up: anyone running high-volume, low-latency classification or routing behind an API, where a full LLM call is overkill and the cost compounds fast. Teams that need to fine-tune on proprietary decision data and can't ship that data to a third-party endpoint. And agent orchestration generally, a layer of small, cheap "decide what happens next" models sitting in front of one expensive general-purpose model is a pattern that's going to show up more, because it's the only way the economics work once you're running agents at any real volume.

The real test is calibration, not size. "Tiny" plus "trainable on your own data" pushes the burden onto you to prove it isn't just confidently wrong. That's not a flaw in the idea, it's the question anyone should answer before putting a model like this near a production decision path.

Worth tracking if small, ownable models are on your radar: https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev

title: PostgreSQL 14 Reaches End of Support on November 12. What Should You Check First?
description:
The PostgreSQL Global Development Group lists November 12, 2026, as the final release date for PostgreSQL 14. After the final release, the upstream project will stop shipping security patches and bug fixes for the 14.x series. PostgreSQL versioning policy

If you run a managed database, check your provider’s timeline too. Maintenance schedules, supported upgrade paths, and extended support terms vary by service. Confirm when your provider’s coverage ends and whether that date affects your patching or compliance requirements.

If PostgreSQL 14 is still in your stack, start with an inventory. Find out where it runs, which applications depend on it, and how much time you’ll need to rehearse the upgrade and recover if something breaks.

1. Find every PostgreSQL 14 server and assign an owner

Start with your cloud database inventory, deployment manifests, and self-managed hosts. Check production, staging, QA, and disaster recovery environments. A standby replica that only gets attention during a failover is easy to miss.

From an application connection or SQL client, run this command to check the version of the server you’re connected to:

SHOW server_version;

For every PostgreSQL 14 instance, record:

  • The environment
  • The owning team and primary engineering contact
  • Connected applications, including scheduled jobs and BI or reporting tools that query the database outside normal traffic hours
  • Available maintenance windows

If an instance has no clear owner, assign someone to map its dependencies before scheduling changes.

2. Choose a target version your stack can support

Check which PostgreSQL major versions your hosting platform supports and how long each will receive upstream fixes. Then verify compatibility with the extensions, database drivers, and backup tools you rely on. If an application uses PostGIS, for example, confirm that the required extension version is available on your target platform before booking a maintenance window.

For self-managed deployments, pg_upgrade and dump-and-restore are two major upgrade paths. If you plan to use pg_upgrade, run pg_upgrade --check during rehearsal to identify issues the tool can detect before the upgrade. On a managed service, follow your provider’s documented upgrade path and confirm whether you can move directly from PostgreSQL 14 to your target version. PostgreSQL versioning policy

3. Rehearse the upgrade and define your rollback trigger

Rehearse with a representative copy of production data. Time the upgrade, test the application’s critical read and write paths, and run background jobs that execute less frequently. A successful login confirms basic connectivity. Run the nightly reporting job separately to check that it still has the permissions and extensions it needs.

Restore a backup in a test environment, record how long recovery takes, and compare the measured time with your recovery time objective (RTO). Before cutover, agree on two things:

  • When to roll back. Define a measurable trigger, such as an application error rate above an agreed threshold or an upgrade that exceeds the maintenance window.
  • How to handle post-cutover writes. If you redirect traffic to the old PostgreSQL 14 instance after the upgraded database has accepted writes, those transactions will be missing from the old instance unless you have a way to reconcile them.

Your action plan for this week

By the end of the week, aim to give every remaining PostgreSQL 14 instance an owner, a target version to validate, and a scheduled rehearsal date. If you only have time for one step today, verify the server version behind your primary production connection and confirm who owns the upgrade.

If your team has already moved off PostgreSQL 14, what took longer than you expected during the rehearsal?

Author’s note: I work in marketing at Advange and cover enterprise IT news for infrastructure and operations teams. I used AI assistance to draft and edit this post.

title: Optimizing Large-Scale MongoDB Aggregation Pipelines: From Execution Plans to Production Tuning
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

Aggregation pipelines are MongoDB's most powerful query mechanism — and its most performance-sensitive one. A pipeline that runs in 200ms against a million documents can take 45 minutes against a hundred million, with no algorithmic change, only scale. The difference between those two outcomes usually lives in execution plan selection, index coverage, operator ordering, and shard distribution — not in the pipeline logic itself.

This deep-dive examines the MongoDB query engine's approach to aggregation, identifies the specific mechanisms that cause exponential performance degradation, and provides the optimization strategies that matter at scale. We'll trace from wire protocol through the execution engine, then work through concrete transformations that reduce pipeline latency by orders of magnitude.

Table of Contents

  • 1. The Aggregation Execution Engine
  • 2. Pipeline Operator Classification
  • 3. Index-Driven Optimization
  • 4. Operator Ordering and Materialization
  • 5. $lookup and Join Optimization
  • 6. Sharding-Aware Pipeline Design
  • 7. Execution Plan Analysis
  • 8. Data Modeling for Aggregation
  • 9. Production Monitoring and Alerting
  • 10. Comprehensive Optimization Checklist

1. The Aggregation Execution Engine

MongoDB's aggregation engine processes pipelines through a block-based execution model. Each $match, $group, $sort, $project, or other operator is compiled into an execution stage. These stages form a directed acyclic graph (DAG) when blocking operators like $group are present.

Blocking vs. Streaming Operators

The fundamental distinction in pipeline execution is between streaming and blocking operators:

// Streaming operators process documents one at a time (or in bounded batches)
// - $match: filters documents as they arrive
// - $project: transforms each document independently
// - $addFields: enriches each document
// - $sortByCount: wraps $group + $sort (blocking)

// Blocking operators must consume ALL input before producing output
// - $group: accumulates all matching documents into groups
// - $sort: must buffer enough documents to produce sorted output
// - $limit: buffers until enough documents are consumed
// - $skip: discards documents until offset is reached

The engine optimizes streaming pipelines aggressively — it can push $match stages down to the storage layer, enabling index-only scans. Blocking operators force materialization into memory or temporary files, which is where most large-scale pipeline failures originate.

Query Planning and Optimization Phases

When you submit an aggregation pipeline, MongoDB performs several optimization passes:

  1. Stage folding: Adjacent $project stages are merged into a single projection
  2. Match pushdown: Leading $match stages are converted to storage-level filters
  3. Sort optimization: $sort followed by $limit can use an index to avoid full sort
  4. Index selection: The planner evaluates candidate indexes for the first blocking or first stage

The planner's critical limitation: it optimizes the pipeline as a whole but cannot reorder operators across blocking boundaries. A $match that appears after a $group cannot be pushed below it, regardless of logical equivalence.

Wire Protocol and Batch Processing

The $collStats command and explain execution reveal that MongoDB processes aggregation in batches. For sharded clusters, the planning phase fans out to all shards, each shard plans independently, and results are merged at the mongos. This means:

  • Each shard may select different execution plans
  • Merge cost at mongos is proportional to the number of intermediate documents returned
  • Shard-local blocking operators duplicate memory pressure across all shards

2. Pipeline Operator Classification

Understanding which operators do what — and what they cost — is the foundation of optimization.

Cost Classification Matrix

Operator Blocking? Memory Intensive? Index-Usable? Parallelizable?
$match No No Yes (leading) Yes
$group Yes Yes No Yes (shard-local)
$sort Yes Yes Yes (leading + limit) Partially
$project No No No Yes
$addFields No No No Yes
$lookup No Yes Yes (foreign key) Yes
$unwind No No Yes (with $match) Yes
$facet Yes Yes Mixed No
$bucket Yes Yes No Partially
$bucketAuto Yes Yes No No
$sortByCount Yes Yes Yes (count field) Yes
$sample Yes No Yes (with $match) No
$out / $merge Yes No No No
$unionWith No No Depends No

The $group Accumulator Model

$group is the most common source of memory exhaustion. Each accumulator type has different memory characteristics:

// $sum: O(1) memory per group — accumulates into a single value
// $push: O(n) memory per group — stores all elements in an array
// $addToSet: O(k) memory per group where k = distinct values
// $first/$last: O(1) memory per group
// $avg: O(1) memory per group — maintains count + sum
// $min/$max: O(1) memory per group
// $stdDevPop/$stdDevSamp: O(1) memory per group — uses Welford's algorithm

// DANGEROUS AT SCALE:
{
  $group: {
    _id: "$customerId",  // If cardinality = 50M, this materializes 50M groups
    orders: { $push: "$orderData" },  // Each group holds ALL its orders in memory
    total: { $sum: "$amount" }
  }
}

The $push accumulator is the most dangerous at scale. A group with 10,000 documents each containing a 1KB nested object materializes 10MB for that single group. When group cardinality is high AND each group contains many documents, you hit the 100MB default memory limit immediately.

3. Index-Driven Optimization

Indexes are the single highest-impact optimization for aggregation pipelines. The rule: only the leading $match (before any blocking operator) benefits from index utilization.

Compound Index Design for Aggregation 

// Pipeline:
// db.orders.aggregate([
//   { $match: { status: "completed", region: "us-east", createdAt: { $gte: new Date("2024-01-01") } } },
//   { $sort: { amount: -1 } },
//   { $limit: 100 },
//   { $group: { _id: "$customerId", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } }
// ])

// OPTIMAL INDEX (supports $match + $sort + projection):
db.orders.createIndex(
  { status: 1, region: 1, createdAt: -1, amount: -1 },
  { name: "agg_status_region_date_amount" }
)

// This index allows:
// 1. Index range scan for status + region (equality)
// 2. Sorted traversal by createdAt (range)
// 3. Sorted traversal by amount within the range
// 4. Covering projection if all needed fields are in the index

Index-Only (Covering) Scans

A covering index eliminates collection document fetches entirely. The pipeline reads exclusively from the index B-tree:

// If the pipeline only needs fields present in the index:
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "completed", region: "us-east" } },
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
  { $project: { _id: 1, total: 1 } }
]).explain("executionStats")

// Required covering index:
db.orders.createIndex(
  { status: 1, region: 1, customerId: 1, amount: 1 },
  { name: "agg_covering_status_region_cust_amount" }
)

// Verify with explain — look for "IXSCAN" with no "FETCH" stage

The executionStats output reveals whether the pipeline achieves an index-only scan. If you see stage: "FETCH" in the plan, the engine is reading full documents from the collection. Eliminating this stage can reduce I/O by 10-100x depending on document size.

Multikey Indexes and Array Fields

When grouping on array fields, MongoDB creates multikey indexes that expand the index entries:

// Document structure:
// { orderId: 123, tags: ["electronics", "premium", "sale"], amount: 99.99 }

// Multikey index on array field:
db.orders.createIndex({ tags: 1, amount: 1 })

// WARNING: Multikey indexes prevent index-only scans for $group.
// The engine cannot determine which index entry maps to which document
// without fetching the full document. This forces FETCH stage.

// Better approach: pre-compute a non-array grouping field
// or use $unwind + $match before $group

Partial Indexes for Aggregation

Partial indexes reduce index size and improve cache residency:

// Only index documents relevant to the aggregation
db.orders.createIndex(
  { customerId: 1, amount: 1 },
  {
    name: "agg_active_orders",
    partialFilterExpression: {
      status: { $in: ["completed", "refunded"] },
      amount: { $gt: 0 }
    }
  }
)

// Benefit: Smaller index = better B-tree depth = fewer disk pages in cache
// A 500MB index vs a 5GB index can be the difference between
// entirely in-memory scan vs repeated disk I/O

4. Operator Ordering and Materialization

The order of operators in a pipeline determines memory pressure, disk spilling, and execution time. The optimization principle: filter early, transform late.

The Filtering Cascade Pattern 

// ANTI-PATTERN: Group before filtering
// Materializes ALL groups, then discards most
[
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
  { $match: { total: { $gte: 1000 } } },  // Too late — all groups already materialized
  { $sort: { total: -1 } },
  { $limit: 1000 }
]

// OPTIMIZED: Push filtering before grouping where possible
[
  { $match: { amount: { $gte: 1 } } },  // Pre-filter cheaply (uses index)
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
  { $match: { total: { $gte: 1000 } } },  // Post-group filter (unavoidable)
  { $sort: { total: -1 } },
  { $limit: 1000 }
]

The $sort + $limit Optimization

$sort followed by $limit is a special pattern that MongoDB optimizes. Instead of sorting ALL documents, it maintains a bounded priority queue of size N (the limit). This is O(n log k) where k = limit:

// Pipeline: Get top 100 customers by order count in a specific category
// WITHOUT $sort+$limit: sorts ALL matching documents into memory
[
  { $match: { category: "electronics" } },
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", count: { $sum: 1 } } },
  { $sort: { count: -1 } },  // Sorts ALL groups — potentially millions
  { $limit: 100 }
]

// The engine DOES optimize $sort + $limit into a top-N heap,
// but you can reduce input size further with pre-filtering:
[
  { $match: { category: "electronics", orderDate: { $gte: last30Days } } },
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", count: { $sum: 1 } } },
  { $sort: { count: -1 } },
  { $limit: 100 }
]

$facet: Isolation at a Cost

$facet allows parallel sub-pipelines within a single document. It's powerful but forces materialization of ALL input into memory:

// $facet materializes ALL input documents before processing
// Only use when the input to $facet is already heavily filtered
[
  { $match: { region: "us-east", status: "completed" } },  // Heavy pre-filter
  { $facet: {
    revenueByMonth: [
      { $group: { _id: { $month: "$createdAt" }, revenue: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
      { $sort: { _id: 1 } }
    ],
    topProducts: [
      { $group: { _id: "$productId", count: { $sum: 1 } } },
      { $sort: { count: -1 } },
      { $limit: 10 }
    ],
    summary: [
      { $group: { _id: null, totalRevenue: { $sum: "$amount" }, orderCount: { $sum: 1 } } }
    ]
  }}
]

// Memory cost: ALL documents matching $match are held in memory simultaneously
// for ALL sub-pipelines. For 1M documents × 500 bytes = 500MB just for input buffering.

allowDiskUse: When and How

When materialization exceeds the 100MB in-memory limit, MongoDB can spill to disk:

// CRITICAL: allowDiskUse is NOT always safe
// It trades memory for disk I/O — potentially making things 10-100x slower

// Safe with allowDiskUse: predictable, bounded output
// - $group with known cardinality
// - $sort with known input size

// DANGEROUS with allowDiskUse: unpredictable output size
// - $push with unknown group sizes
// - $facet with multiple sub-pipelines on large input
// - $sort on high-cardinality data with no $limit

// Production pattern: set allowDiskUse with monitoring
[
  { $match: { status: "completed" } },
  { $group: { _id: "$region", revenue: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } }
], { allowDiskUse: true }

5. $lookup and Join Optimization

$lookup is MongoDB's equi-join operator. At scale, it behaves like a hash join and can consume enormous memory.

$lookup Execution Models 

// Basic $lookup (hash join on foreign key)
db.orders.aggregate([
  {
    $lookup: {
      from: "customers",
      localField: "customerId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "customer"
    }
  }
])

// The engine builds a hash index on the foreign collection's foreignField.
// For 50M customer documents, this hash index consumes ~2-4GB of RAM.
// This is the #1 cause of OOM in aggregation pipelines.

Optimized $lookup Patterns 

// PATTERN 1: Filter before lookup (reduce hash table size)
[
  { $match: { status: "completed" } },  // Reduce input documents
  {
    $lookup: {
      from: "customers",
      localField: "customerId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "customer",
      // pipeline option allows filtering the foreign collection BEFORE hash build
      pipeline: [
        { $match: { active: true, region: "us-east" } },
        { $project: { name: 1, tier: 1 } }  // Project only needed fields
      ]
    }
  }
]

// PATTERN 2: Replace $lookup with pre-joined embedded data
// If the lookup field is rarely updated, embed it at write time:
// { orderId: 123, customerId: "c1", customerName: "Alice", customerTier: "gold" }
// Eliminates the join entirely — read-only, zero join cost

// PATTERN 3: Use $expr with $in for single-document lookups
// When you only need to verify existence:
{
  $match: {
    $expr: {
      $eq: ["$customerId", "$customerLookup"]  // Pre-resolved
    }
  }
}

Hash Join Memory Analysis 

// Memory consumed by $lookup hash table:
// Formula: numDocuments × (keySize + valueReferenceSize + overhead)
// For 50M customers with ObjectId keys:
//   = 50M × (12 bytes ObjectId + 8 bytes pointer + ~32 bytes overhead)
//   = 50M × 52 bytes ≈ 2.6 GB

// Mitigation: Use the pipeline option to reduce foreign collection size
// BEFORE hash table construction:
db.orders.aggregate([
  {
    $lookup: {
      from: "customers",
      localField: "customerId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "customer",
      pipeline: [
        // This $match runs on the foreign collection BEFORE hash build
        { $match: { _id: { $in: topCustomerIds } } },  // If possible
        { $project: { name: 1, email: 1 } }  // Slim the documents
      ]
    }
  }
])

// Even better: If you know the set of customerIds in advance,
// pre-fetch customer data and use $addFields with $reduce/$arrayElemAt

6. Sharding-Aware Pipeline Design

In a sharded cluster, aggregation pipelines execute as a distributed plan. Understanding the fan-out and merge phases is essential for optimization.

Distributed Execution Model 

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        mongos                                │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │              Global Planning Phase                     │  │
│  │  1. Send pipeline to all shards for planning          │  │
│  │  2. Collect execution plans from each shard          │  │
│  │  3. Select merge strategy based on operator type      │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │              Fan-Out Execution Phase                   │  │
│  │  Send pipeline to Shard 1 → returns partial results    │  │
│  │  Send pipeline to Shard 2 → returns partial results    │  │
│  │  Send pipeline to Shard N → returns partial results    │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │              Merge Phase (at mongos)                   │  │
│  │  Merge all partial results into final output            │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Shard Key Alignment

The shard key determines whether a pipeline can execute entirely on a single shard (no fan-out):

// Sharded collection: orders
// Shard key: { customerId: "hashed" }

// Pipeline 1: SINGLE SHARD (no fan-out)
// $match on shard key routes to exactly one shard
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { customerId: "customer_12345" } },  // Routes to 1 shard
  { $group: { _id: "$category", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } }
])

// Pipeline 2: FULL FAN-OUT (all shards)
// No $match on shard key before first blocking operator
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $group: { _id: "$category", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } },  // ALL shards
  { $sort: { total: -1 } },
  { $limit: 10 }
])

// Pipeline 3: PARTIAL FAN-OUT
// $match on non-shard-key field fans out but reduces per-shard work
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "completed" } },  // All shards, but less data per shard
  { $group: { _id: "$region", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
  { $sort: { total: -1 } }
])

Merge Strategy by Operator

Different operators merge differently at mongos:

Operator Merge Strategy Cost
$group + $sum/$avg Two-phase: shard-local partial groups → global re-group O(shards × groups)
$group + $push/$addToSet Two-phase: shard-local arrays → global concat + dedup O(shards × groups × avgArraySize)
$sort + $limit Partial sort on each shard → merge top-N at mongos O(shards × log(limit))
$sort (no limit) Partial sort on each shard → merge all sorted streams O(totalDocuments)
$count Sum of shard counts O(shards)
$first/$last Cannot merge correctly across shards without global sort Requires special handling

Avoiding Two-Phase $group

The two-phase group merge (partial groups on shards, then global re-group) doubles the grouping work. You can avoid it:

// Two-phase group (default when group _id is not the shard key):
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $group: { _id: "$category", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } }
  // Phase 1: Each shard groups by category → returns partial results
  // Phase 2: mongos re-groups all partial results
  // If 10 shards × 50 categories = 500 intermediate docs to merge
])

// Single-phase group (when group _id IS the shard key):
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { customerId: { $in: allCustomerIds } } },  // Routes to specific shards
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } }
  // Each shard handles its own customerId groups — no merge needed
])

// Alternative: Pre-aggregate in application layer
// Issue N separate queries (one per shard) and merge results in app code
// Gives you explicit control over merge logic and error handling

Zoned Sharding for Time-Series Aggregations 

// For time-series data, zoned sharding keeps date ranges on single shards
db.adminCommand({
  shardCollection: "analytics.events",
  uniqueIndex: {
    key: { timestamp: 1, service: 1 },
    partialFilterExpression: { timestamp: { $type: "date" } },
    shardKeyPattern: {
      timestamp: { $gte: new Date("2024-01-01"), $lt: new Date("2024-02-01") }
    }
  }
})

// Now: monthly aggregations hit a SINGLE shard
[
  { $match: { timestamp: { $gte: new Date("2024-01-01"), $lt: new Date("2024-02-01") } } },
  { $group: { _id: "$service", count: { $sum: 1 } } }
]
// No fan-out, no merge — single shard executes the entire pipeline

7. Execution Plan Analysis

The explain command is the primary diagnostic tool for pipeline optimization.

Reading Execution Plans 

const plan = db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "completed", createdAt: { $gte: new Date("2024-01-01") } } },
  { $group: { _id: "$region", revenue: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } }
]).explain("executionStats")

// Key metrics to examine:
console.log(plan.stages)  // Execution stage tree
console.log(plan.executionStats.totalDocsExamined)  // Documents read
console.log(plan.executionStats.totalKeysExamined)  // Index entries scanned
console.log(plan.executionStats.allPlansExecution[0].stage)  // Selected stage type
console.log(plan.executionStats.executionTimeMillis)  // Wall clock time

Critical Metrics 

// The ratio of docsExamined to nReturned tells you pipeline efficiency:
// docsExamined / nReturned = 1.0 → perfect (index-only, no waste)
// docsExamined / nReturned = 1000 → reading 1000 docs to produce 1 result

// For aggregation pipelines:
const stats = plan.executionStats
const efficiency = stats.totalDocsExamined / Math.max(stats.nReturned, 1)

if (efficiency > 10) {
  console.log(`WARNING: Examining ${stats.totalDocsExamined} docs for ${stats.nReturned} results`)
  console.log("Consider: better index, earlier $match, or covering index")
}

// Check for COLLSCAN (full collection scan — almost always bad):
function hasCollectionScan(stages) {
  for (const stage of stages) {
    if (stage.stage === "COLLSCAN") return true
    if (stage.inputStages && hasCollectionScan(stage.inputStages)) return true
  }
  return false
}

if (hasCollectionScan(plan.stages)) {
  console.log("CRITICAL: Pipeline performs full collection scan")
}

// Check for blocking stages that could be eliminated:
function findBlockingStages(stages) {
  const blocking = new Set(["SORT", "GROUP_BY", "COUNT", "UNION_WITH" ])
  const results = []
  for (const stage of stages) {
    if (blocking.has(stage.stage)) results.push(stage)
    if (stage.inputStages) results.push(...findBlockingStages(stage.inputStages))
  }
  return results
}

The $planCache and plan stability

MongoDB caches execution plans in the plan cache. For aggregation, the cache key includes the pipeline's first operator and its arguments:

// Clear the plan cache for a collection (use sparingly in production):
db.orders.runCommand({ planCacheClear: "orders" })

// Lock a specific plan (MongoDB 5.0+):
db.orders.runCommand({
  planCacheSet: "orders",
  filters: [{
    type: "aggsPlan",
    query: { status: "completed" },
    indexName: "agg_status_region_date_amount"
  }],
  params: "locked"
})

// This prevents the planner from choosing a suboptimal plan
// after cache expiration or workload shift

8. Data Modeling for Aggregation

Sometimes the optimal optimization is not in the pipeline but in the data model.

Pre-Aggregation Pattern 

// Instead of aggregating 10M order documents on every query,
// maintain a pre-aggregated collection updated via triggers or scheduled jobs:

// orders_summary collection (updated every 5 minutes or via change streams):
// {
//   _id: { customerId: "c123", month: "2024-01" },
//   totalRevenue: 5000.00,
//   orderCount: 25,
//   avgOrderValue: 200.00,
//   lastOrderAt: ISODate("2024-01-28")
// }

// Query: instant read from pre-aggregated data
db.orders_summary.aggregate([
  { $match: { "_id.customerId": "c123" } },
  { $sort: { "_id.month": -1 } },
  { $limit: 12 }
])

// Update via change streams:
const changeStream = db.orders.watch([
  { $match: { "operationType": { $in: ["insert", "update", "delete"] } } }
])

changeStream.on("change", async (change) => {
  // Incrementally update orders_summary
  // This trades write amplification for read performance
})

Denormalization for Aggregation 

// ANTI-PATTERN: Join-heavy aggregation
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $lookup: { from: "customers", localField: "customerId", foreignField: "_id", as: "cust" } },
  { $unwind: "$cust" },
  { $lookup: { from: "products", localField: "productId", foreignField: "_id", as: "prod" } },
  { $unwind: "$prod" },
  { $group: { _id: "$cust.region", revenue: { $sum: "$amount" } } }
])
// Cost: 2 hash joins, potentially GB of memory

// OPTIMIZED: Denormalize frequently-joined fields
// Order document already contains:
// { orderId: 123, customerId: "c1", customerRegion: "us-east", productId: "p1", productName: "Widget", amount: 99.99 }

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { customerRegion: "us-east" } },
  { $group: { _id: "$customerRegion", revenue: { $sum: "$amount" } } }
])
// Cost: Single index scan, no joins

Rollup Hierarchies

For OLAP-style queries, maintain multiple rollup levels:

// orders_by_day: 1 document per (customer, day) — updated continuously
// orders_by_week: 1 document per (customer, week) — updated daily
// orders_by_month: 1 document per (customer, month) — updated monthly

// Query strategy: route based on time range
db.orders_by_month.aggregate([
  { $match: { "_id.customerId": "c123", "_id.month": { $gte: "2023-01", $lte: "2024-12" } } },
  { $sort: { "_id.month": -1 } }
])
// Returns 24 documents instead of aggregating 500,000 order documents

9. Production Monitoring and Alerting

Monitoring aggregation pipeline performance requires instrumentation at multiple levels.

Slow Query Log Configuration 

// Enable slow query logging for aggregation operations
db.adminCommand({
  profile: 2,  // Log ALL operations
  slowms: 100  // Threshold: 100ms
})

// In production, use threshold-based:
db.adminCommand({
  profile: 1,
  slowms: 2000  // Only log operations > 2 seconds
})

// Query the system.profile collection:
db.system.profile.aggregate([
  { $match: { op: "command", "command.aggregate": { $exists: true }, duration: { $gt: 5000 } } },
  { $sort: { duration: -1 } },
  { $limit: 20 }
])

Programmatic Pipeline Performance Monitoring 

// Wrapper that measures and logs aggregation performance
async function monitoredAggregate(collection, pipeline, options = {}) {
  const { timeout = 30000, alertThreshold = 5000, label = "pipeline" } = options

  const startTime = process.hrtime()
  const controller = new AbortController()
  const timeoutId = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), timeout)

  try {
    // Get execution stats
    const explainResult = await collection
      .aggregate(pipeline, { ...options, explain: "executionStats" })
      .toArray()

    const stats = explainResult[0]
    const execStats = stats.executionStats || stats.stages?.[0]?.executionStats

    const metrics = {
      label,
      executionTimeMs: execStats?.executionTimeMillis,
      docsExamined: execStats?.totalDocsExamined,
      keysExamined: execStats?.totalKeysExamined,
      nReturned: execStats?.nReturned,
      hasCollectionScan: JSON.stringify(stats.stages).includes('COLLSCAN'),
      memoryBytes: execStats?.memUsage
    }

    // Alert on degradation
    if (metrics.executionTimeMs > alertThreshold) {
      console.error(`[ALERT] Pipeline "${label}" exceeded threshold:`, metrics)
    }

    return metrics
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timeoutId)
  }
}

// Usage:
const stats = await monitoredAggregate(
  db.orders,
  [
    { $match: { status: "completed" } },
    { $group: { _id: "$region", revenue: { $sum: "$amount" } } }
  ],
  { label: "revenue_by_region", alertThreshold: 3000 }
)

Server Status Metrics for Aggregation 

// Current in-progress operations (detects stuck pipelines)
db.adminCommand({ currentOp: true, allOps: false }).inprog
  .filter(op => op.cmd?.aggregate)

// Detect operations exceeding threshold:
const slowOps = db.adminCommand({ currentOp: true, allOps: false }).inprog
  .filter(op => {
    if (!op.cmd?.aggregate) return false
    const elapsed = Date.now() - op.activeSince?.getTime()
    return elapsed > 60000  // Running for over 60 seconds
  })

// Kill a stuck aggregation:
db.adminCommand({ killCursors: "orders", cursors: [cursorId] })
// Or kill by operation:
db.adminCommand({ killOp: opId })

// Cluster-wide aggregation monitoring:
db.adminCommand({ serverStatus: 1 }).metrics.document
// {
//   insert: ...,  // document inserts
//   query: ...,   // document queries  
//   update: ...,  // document updates
//   delete: ...   // document deletes
// }

db.adminCommand({ serverStatus: 1 }).metrics.aggregate
// {
//   scans: ...,        // documents scanned by aggregation
//   resultSets: ...,  // documents returned by aggregation
//   yields: ...        // context switches during aggregation
// }

Alerting Rules 

// Example: Alert when aggregation scan ratio degrades
// scans / resultSets > 100 indicates inefficient pipeline
const aggregateMetrics = db.adminCommand({ serverStatus: 1 }).metrics.aggregate
const scanRatio = aggregateMetrics.scans / Math.max(aggregateMetrics.resultSets, 1)

if (scanRatio > 100) {
  // ALERT: Aggregation pipelines are scanning 100x more documents than returned
  // Action: Review recent pipeline changes, check for index drops
}

// Alert when ops control detects high aggregation load
const activeAggregations = db.adminCommand({ currentOp: true }).inprog
  .filter(op => op.cmd?.aggregate).length

if (activeAggregations > 10) {
  // ALERT: More than 10 concurrent aggregation operations
  // May indicate application bug or thundering herd
}

10. Comprehensive Optimization Checklist

Pre-Deployment Validation

  1. Index existence: Verify all leading $match fields have supporting indexes
  2. Index coverage: Confirm the index covers all projected fields (eliminate FETCH stage)
  3. Cardinality analysis: Measure $group _id cardinality — if > 10M, consider pre-aggregation
  4. Shard routing: Validate whether pipeline fans out or routes to single shard
  5. Memory estimation: Calculate worst-case memory for blocking operators
  6. explain validation: Run explain("executionStats") on representative data

Runtime Optimization

  1. Leading $match: Always place $match before blocking operators
  2. Covering indexes: Design indexes to eliminate collection document fetches
  3. $sort + $limit: Always pair expensive sorts with limits
  4. $lookup pipeline option: Filter foreign collection before hash build
  5. allowDiskUse monitoring: Enable but alert on disk spill events
  6. Plan cache locking: Lock optimal plans for critical pipelines

Architecture-Level Decisions

  1. Pre-aggregation: For sub-second latency requirements, maintain rollup collections
  2. Denormalization: Embed join fields for read-heavy workloads
  3. Shard key alignment: Design shard keys to match query patterns
  4. Read preferences: Route analytics queries to secondary nodes
  5. Query isolation: Use dedicated replica set members for heavy aggregations
  6. Connection pooling: Limit concurrent aggregation operations per node

Ongoing Maintenance

  1. Index rebuild schedule: Rebuild indexes after mass data ingestion
  2. Plan cache monitoring: Alert when plans change unexpectedly
  3. Workload analysis: Regularly review system.profile for regression
  4. Capacity planning: Model growth rates against memory limits
  5. Kill switch: Implement timeout-based circuit breakers for aggregation operations

The optimization landscape for MongoDB aggregation pipelines operates at the intersection of query planning, memory management, distributed execution, and data modeling. There is no single silver bullet — effective optimization requires understanding how the engine plans your specific pipeline, which operators force materialization, and how shard distribution affects the merge phase. The patterns above, applied systematically, routinely reduce pipeline latency from minutes to milliseconds at scale. For teams operating at petabyte scale, invest in execution plan monitoring and automated alerting as infrastructure — pipeline performance degradation is often the leading indicator of broader system issues.

For deeper exploration of query optimization patterns across database systems, see Tamiz's Insights for related deep-dives on distributed systems performance.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my $group operator consume all available memory?

$group materializes one entry per distinct _id value in memory. If your grouping field has high cardinality (millions of distinct values), each entry's memory footprint accumulates. The fix is one of: (1) reduce cardinality by pre-filtering with $match before $group, (2) replace $push with bounded accumulators like $sum/$avg that use O(1) memory per group, (3) enable allowDiskUse: true to spill overflow to disk, or (4) redesign the query to avoid grouping on a high-cardinality field entirely.

How do I determine if my aggregation pipeline is using an index?

Run pipeline.explain("executionStats") and inspect the stage tree. Look for IXSCAN stages — these indicate index usage. If you see COLLSCAN, the pipeline is scanning the entire collection. The specific index used appears in the IXSCAN stage's pattern field. Additionally, check executionStats.totalKeysExamined — if it's significantly lower than totalDocsExamined, you're getting index benefits.

When should I use $facet vs. separate aggregation pipelines?

Use $facet when you need multiple aggregations over the SAME filtered dataset and want to avoid scanning the collection multiple times. However, $facet materializes ALL input documents in memory simultaneously for all sub-pipelines. If the input is already small (post-filter), $facet is ideal. If the input is large, prefer separate pipelines with individual $match stages — each can use its own optimal index and avoids holding all documents in memory at once.

title: Multi-tenant SaaS on PostgreSQL: schema-per-tenant vs row-level security
description:
Every B2B SaaS product eventually gets the same bug report: "I can see another company's invoices." It rarely comes from a sophisticated attack. It comes from a missing WHERE tenant_id = ? in a report query written at 11 p.m., or from a background job that reused a connection with the wrong context.

The way you separate tenant data in PostgreSQL decides how likely that bug is, how painful migrations become at 500 customers, and whether you can move one large customer to its own server later. This post compares the two approaches most teams argue about, schema-per-tenant and a shared schema with row-level security (RLS), with the configs and pitfalls that only show up in production.

The three options in one paragraph each

Shared schema, tenant_id column, RLS. All tenants live in the same tables. Every tenant-owned table has a tenant_id, and PostgreSQL policies filter rows based on a session variable. One set of tables, one migration run, one place to index.

Schema-per-tenant. Each tenant gets its own schema (tenant_0042.orders, tenant_0043.orders), and the application switches search_path per request. Isolation comes from namespaces, not from filters.

Database-per-tenant. Each tenant gets its own database, sometimes its own server. Strongest isolation, highest operational cost. Usually reserved for customers with regulatory or contractual requirements.

Most teams end up with a hybrid: shared schema with RLS for the long tail, and a dedicated database for the few tenants who need it. Keep that end state in mind, because it affects the choice you make on day one.

Shared schema with RLS: a setup that actually holds

Here is a minimal setup that fails closed, meaning that if the application forgets to set the tenant, it sees nothing rather than everything.

CREATE TABLE tenants (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  name       text NOT NULL,
  plan       text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'starter'
);

CREATE TABLE customers (
  tenant_id  uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id),
  id         uuid NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email      text NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, id),
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, email)
);

CREATE TABLE invoices (
  tenant_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  id          uuid NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  customer_id uuid NOT NULL,
  amount      numeric(12,2) NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, id),
  FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, customer_id) REFERENCES customers(tenant_id, id)
);

CREATE INDEX invoices_tenant_created ON invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC);

ALTER TABLE customers ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE customers FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE invoices  ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE invoices  FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON customers
  USING (tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid);

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices
  USING (tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid);

And the application role:

CREATE ROLE app_user LOGIN PASSWORD '...' NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON customers, invoices TO app_user;

Every detail here exists because of a real failure mode.

FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. Without it, the table owner bypasses policies. If your application connects as the same role that ran the migrations (very common in small teams), RLS is silently off. Superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS skip policies regardless, so the app must connect as a dedicated role with neither.

current_setting(..., true) plus NULLIF. The second argument makes a missing setting return NULL instead of raising an error. tenant_id = NULL is never true, so no rows match. The NULLIF matters because once a custom setting has been set in a session and the transaction ends, PostgreSQL reverts it to an empty string, not NULL, and ''::uuid throws an error. Without NULLIF you get intermittent "invalid input syntax for type uuid" errors on pooled connections.

WITH CHECK. USING filters what you read. WITH CHECK stops an insert or update from writing a row with someone else's tenant_id. Skip it and a bug in the API layer can plant data into another tenant.

Composite foreign keys. This one surprises people: referential integrity checks bypass RLS. A plain customer_id REFERENCES customers(id) lets tenant A's invoice point at tenant B's customer, and the database will accept it. Making the key (tenant_id, customer_id) makes cross-tenant references structurally impossible.

tenant_id as the leading index column. Almost every query is "this tenant's rows, sorted or filtered by something". Indexes that start with tenant_id keep those queries on a narrow slice of the table.

Setting the tenant per request, and why SET is a trap

The tenant context must be scoped to a transaction, not a connection:

BEGIN;
SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true);  -- true = local to this transaction
SELECT * FROM invoices ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50;
COMMIT;

In application code, wrap it so nobody can forget:

from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def tenant_tx(pool, tenant_id: str):
    with pool.connection() as conn:
        with conn.transaction():
            conn.execute(
                "SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', %s, true)", (tenant_id,)
            )
            yield conn

A plain SET app.tenant_id = '...' (session level) survives after the request ends. With PgBouncer in transaction mode, the next transaction on that server connection may belong to a different client, and it inherits the previous tenant. That is exactly the "I see another company's data" bug, and it only appears under load, when connections are being reused aggressively. set_config(..., true) or SET LOCAL disappears at commit or rollback, so it is safe with transaction pooling.

Pitfalls that RLS does not cover

  • Views. By default a view runs with the privileges of its owner. If the owner is the migration role, queries through the view skip the policies. On PostgreSQL 15 and later, create views with WITH (security_invoker = true). On older versions, make sure views are owned by a role subject to RLS.
  • SECURITY DEFINER functions. Same problem: they run as their owner. Audit every one of them.
  • Background workers and admin tools. Cron jobs, queue consumers and internal dashboards often connect with a privileged role "just to make it work". Give them their own role with RLS on, and set the tenant explicitly per job. For genuinely cross-tenant tasks (billing runs, platform analytics), use a separate role with BYPASSRLS and keep its credentials out of the web app.
  • Caches and search indexes. RLS protects PostgreSQL only. Redis keys, Elasticsearch documents and files in object storage need the tenant in the key or path, and their own checks.
  • Planner surprises. Policies are added as extra predicates. With simple equality on tenant_id and a good index, the overhead is negligible. If a policy calls a non-trivial function (for example, a lookup of the user's tenants), it may be evaluated per row. Mark helper functions STABLE, wrap them in a subselect so they are computed once per query, and check EXPLAIN ANALYZE on your top queries before and after enabling RLS.

Schema-per-tenant: what it really costs

Schema-per-tenant looks attractive: no tenant_id columns, no policies, and a tenant's data is easy to dump or delete with DROP SCHEMA tenant_0042 CASCADE. The costs appear as tenants grow.

Catalog size. Every table, index, sequence and TOAST table is a row in the system catalogs. A product with 150 tables and 300 indexes, times 2,000 tenants, means well over a million relations. pg_dump slows down sharply, \d in psql becomes sluggish, and each backend's relation cache grows as it touches more schemas, which multiplies memory across hundreds of connections.

Migrations. One schema change becomes N schema changes. A migration that takes 200 ms per schema takes almost 7 minutes for 2,000 tenants, and some of them will fail midway on data you did not expect. You need per-schema version tracking, a runner that can resume, and application code that tolerates tenants being on different schema versions during the rollout.

-- a per-schema version table you will end up writing anyway
CREATE TABLE tenant_0042.schema_version (version int NOT NULL, applied_at timestamptz DEFAULT now());

Pooling. The search_path problem is the same as the SET problem above. Use SET LOCAL search_path TO tenant_0042, public inside each transaction, never a session-level SET, if a transaction pooler sits in front of the database. Also, unqualified names resolve to public if a table is missing from the tenant schema, which can quietly read shared data.

Cross-tenant queries. "Revenue by plan across all customers" becomes a generated UNION ALL over thousands of schemas, or an ETL job into a separate warehouse. With a shared schema it is a GROUP BY.

Schema-per-tenant does have real advantages: per-tenant restores are simple, a missing filter cannot leak data, and per-tenant customization (an extra table for one enterprise customer) is possible. It fits products with tens or low hundreds of tenants, each with substantial data, for example an ERP-like system sold to mid-size companies. It fits poorly with self-serve products that sign up hundreds of small tenants a month.

A rough decision guide

Factor Shared + RLS Schema-per-tenant DB-per-tenant
Comfortable tenant count thousands to millions tens to low hundreds a few to tens
Migration effort one run N runs N runs, N servers
Leak risk from a forgotten filter low with RLS on and forced very low none
Cross-tenant analytics simple SQL UNION or ETL ETL only
Per-tenant backup and restore needs tooling pg_dump -n native
Noisy neighbor control weak weak strong

Note the last row. Schemas share CPU, memory and I/O on one server just as rows do. If one tenant runs heavy reports, schema-per-tenant does not protect the others. Only a separate database (on separate resources) does.

Plan for the hybrid from day one

The design that ages best is a shared schema with RLS plus a routing table:

CREATE TABLE tenant_placement (
  tenant_id  uuid PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES tenants(id),
  dsn_alias  text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'shared-1'
);

The application looks up dsn_alias and connects to the right cluster. Because every row already carries tenant_id, moving one customer to a dedicated database is a scripted export:

COPY (SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE tenant_id = '...') TO STDOUT WITH (FORMAT binary);

followed by an import into an identical schema on the new server and a change to one row in tenant_placement. Going the other way, from thousands of schemas back to shared tables, means adding tenant_id to everything and rewriting the data, which is effectively a re-platform.

Test isolation like a feature

Put a test in CI that connects as app_user, sets tenant A, and tries to read, update and insert rows belonging to tenant B through every table, view and API endpoint. Also run one test with no tenant set and assert it returns zero rows. Add a migration check that fails if any table with a tenant_id column lacks relrowsecurity and relforcerowsecurity in pg_class:

SELECT c.relname
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = c.oid AND a.attname = 'tenant_id'
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE n.nspname = 'public' AND c.relkind = 'r'
  AND (NOT c.relrowsecurity OR NOT c.relforcerowsecurity);

An empty result is the only acceptable one. This catches the most common regression: a new table added six months later by someone who never read the original design notes.

Summary

For most SaaS products, start with a shared schema, tenant_id on every tenant-owned table, forced RLS, composite foreign keys and transaction-scoped tenant context. Reach for schema-per-tenant only when you have few, large tenants who need per-tenant restores or customization. Keep database-per-tenant as an option for the customers whose contracts demand it, and make it reachable through a routing table rather than a rewrite.

Isolation is only one of the decisions that are hard to change later; how plans and limits are counted and what happens to data on non-payment shape the schema just as much. If you are scoping a subscription product and want those questions settled before the first line of code, this overview of how we approach SaaS platform development lists what goes into a first release.
