title: Byg et før-og-efter billedværktøj med HTML, CSS og JavaScript
description:
Et billede fortæller ikke altid hele historien.

Men to billeder kan gøre en forskel.

Forestil dig en have, hvor et stort træ er blevet fældet. Ejeren vil gerne sammenligne området før og efter arbejdet.

Hvor meget lys er der kommet ind?

Hvordan ser haven ud uden den store krone?

Og hvilke dele af området er blevet ændret?

Det er et godt eksempel på en lille webfunktion, som kan være nyttig i mange forskellige projekter.

I denne guide bygger vi et før-og-efter-værktøj med HTML, CSS og JavaScript.

Brugeren vælger to billeder fra sin egen computer. Billederne bliver vist ved siden af hinanden i browseren.

Vi bruger ingen eksterne biblioteker og ingen backend.

Det betyder, at vores demo ikke uploader billederne til en server.

Hvad skal værktøjet kunne?

Vi holder kravene enkle.

Brugeren skal kunne:

  • Vælge et førbillede.
  • Vælge et efterbillede.
  • Se begge billeder på samme side.
  • Bruge værktøjet på mobil.
  • Fjerne billederne igen.

Derudover skal formularen være tilgængelig med tastatur.

Vi skal heller ikke gemme billederne permanent.

Det er et bevidst valg, fordi mange billeder fra private haver kan vise boliger, biler eller andre personlige oplysninger.

1. Opret projektets filer

Vi bruger tre filer:

index.html
style.css
script.js

Du behøver ikke et framework.

Åbn blot filerne i din foretrukne kodeeditor.

2. Byg HTML-strukturen

Vi begynder med en overskrift, to filfelter og to områder til billedvisning.

Gem dette som index.html.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="da">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport"
        content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

  <title>Før og efter - Billedsammenligning</title>

  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
  <script src="script.js" defer></script>
</head>

<body>
  <main class="container">
    <header>
      <h1>Før og efter</h1>

      <p>
        Sammenlign to billeder direkte i browseren.
        Billederne sendes ikke til en server.
      </p>
    </header>

    <section aria-labelledby="uploadTitle">
      <h2 id="uploadTitle">Vælg billeder</h2>

      <div class="upload-grid">
        <div class="field">
          <label for="beforeInput">
            Billede før arbejdet
          </label>

          <input
            type="file"
            id="beforeInput"
            accept="image/*">
        </div>

        <div class="field">
          <label for="afterInput">
            Billede efter arbejdet
          </label>

          <input
            type="file"
            id="afterInput"
            accept="image/*">
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section aria-labelledby="resultTitle">
      <h2 id="resultTitle">Sammenligning</h2>

      <div class="comparison-grid">
        <figure>
          <img
            id="beforeImage"
            alt="Førbillede"
            hidden>

          <figcaption>Før</figcaption>
        </figure>

        <figure>
          <img
            id="afterImage"
            alt="Efterbillede"
            hidden>

          <figcaption>Efter</figcaption>
        </figure>
      </div>
    </section>

    <button type="button" id="resetButton">
      Fjern billeder
    </button>

    <p id="status"
       role="status"
       aria-live="polite"></p>
  </main>
</body>
</html>

Bemærk brugen af label og figure.

Hvert filfelt har en synlig label. Det gør det lettere at forstå, hvilket billede der skal vælges.

figure og figcaption giver en tydelig forbindelse mellem billedet og beskrivelsen.

Vi bruger også hidden, så tomme billedelementer ikke bliver vist, før brugeren vælger filer.

3. Lav et responsivt layout

Nu skal billederne placeres ved siden af hinanden på store skærme.

På mobil skal de stå under hinanden.

Gem følgende som style.css.

* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

body {
  margin: 0;
  padding: 24px 16px;
  background: #f4f7f4;
  color: #26352b;
  font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

.container {
  max-width: 1000px;
  margin: 0 auto;
  padding: 28px;
  background: #ffffff;
  border-radius: 16px;
}

h1,
h2 {
  line-height: 1.3;
}

h1 {
  color: #15573b;
}

.upload-grid,
.comparison-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr));
  gap: 20px;
}

.field {
  margin: 12px 0 24px;
}

label {
  display: block;
  margin-bottom: 8px;
  font-weight: 700;
}

input[type="file"] {
  display: block;
  width: 100%;
  max-width: 100%;
  font: inherit;
}

figure {
  margin: 0;
  min-width: 0;
  padding: 12px;
  background: #eaf1eb;
  border-radius: 12px;
}

figure img:not([hidden]) {
  display: block;
  width: 100%;
  height: auto;
  max-height: 380px;
  object-fit: contain;
}

figcaption {
  padding-top: 12px;
  font-weight: 700;
  text-align: center;
}

button {
  margin-top: 24px;
  padding: 12px 20px;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: 8px;
  background: #15573b;
  color: #ffffff;
  font: inherit;
  font-weight: 700;
  cursor: pointer;
}

button:hover {
  background: #10442e;
}

button:focus-visible,
input:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #a35b13;
  outline-offset: 4px;
}

#status {
  min-height: 24px;
  margin-top: 18px;
}

@media (max-width: 650px) {
  .container {
    padding: 18px;
  }

  .upload-grid,
  .comparison-grid {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr;
  }
}

Her bruger vi CSS Grid.

To kolonner giver en enkel sammenligning på større skærme.

På mobil ændrer media query layoutet til én kolonne.

Vi bruger også object-fit: contain.

Det sikrer, at hele billedet kan ses, uden at vi automatisk beskærer det.

4. Vis billederne med JavaScript

Når en bruger vælger en fil, skal vi vise den i det rigtige billedelement.

Det kan vi gøre med URL.createObjectURL().

Metoden opretter en midlertidig objekt-URL, som browseren kan bruge til at vise den valgte fil.

Vi skal huske at frigive disse URL'er, når de ikke længere er nødvendige.

Gem følgende som script.js.

const beforeInput =
  document.querySelector("#beforeInput");

const afterInput =
  document.querySelector("#afterInput");

const beforeImage =
  document.querySelector("#beforeImage");

const afterImage =
  document.querySelector("#afterImage");

const resetButton =
  document.querySelector("#resetButton");

const status =
  document.querySelector("#status");

const imageUrls = {
  before: null,
  after: null
};

function removeImage(type) {
  const image = type === "before"
    ? beforeImage
    : afterImage;

  if (imageUrls[type]) {
    URL.revokeObjectURL(imageUrls[type]);
    imageUrls[type] = null;
  }

  image.removeAttribute("src");
  image.hidden = true;
}

function loadImage(file, type) {
  const image = type === "before"
    ? beforeImage
    : afterImage;

  removeImage(type);

  if (!file) {
    return;
  }

  if (!file.type.startsWith("image/")) {
    status.textContent =
      "Vælg venligst en billedfil.";
    return;
  }

  const url = URL.createObjectURL(file);

  imageUrls[type] = url;

  image.onload = () => {
    if (imageUrls[type] !== url) {
      return;
    }

    image.hidden = false;

    status.textContent =
      "Billedet er klar til visning.";
  };

  image.onerror = () => {
    if (imageUrls[type] !== url) {
      return;
    }

    removeImage(type);

    status.textContent =
      "Billedet kunne ikke åbnes.";
  };

  image.alt = type === "before"
    ? "Valgt billede før arbejdet"
    : "Valgt billede efter arbejdet";

  image.src = url;
}

beforeInput.addEventListener("change", () => {
  loadImage(beforeInput.files[0], "before");
});

afterInput.addEventListener("change", () => {
  loadImage(afterInput.files[0], "after");
});

resetButton.addEventListener("click", () => {
  beforeInput.value = "";
  afterInput.value = "";

  removeImage("before");
  removeImage("after");

  status.textContent =
    "Begge billeder er fjernet fra visningen.";
});

window.addEventListener("pagehide", () => {
  removeImage("before");
  removeImage("after");
});

Nu har vi en simpel billedvisning, som fungerer uden et eksternt bibliotek.

JavaScript kontrollerer først, om den valgte fil er en billedtype.

Derefter oprettes en midlertidig URL.

Når brugeren vælger et nyt billede eller trykker på nulstil, frigives den tidligere URL.

Det er især nyttigt, hvis brugeren prøver flere store billeder i samme session.

5. Hvorfor er løsningen mere privatlivsvenlig?

I vores eksempel bliver filerne håndteret direkte i browseren.

Der er ingen kode, som sender billederne til en server.

Vi bruger heller ikke lokal lagring eller en database.

Når siden lukkes, findes der derfor ingen gemt kopi i vores applikation.

Men det betyder ikke, at alle mulige privatlivsrisici automatisk er væk.

Hvis du senere tilføjer analyseværktøjer, tredjepartsscripts eller en backend, kan situationen ændre sig.

Derfor bør privatliv tænkes ind fra begyndelsen.

I en færdig applikation kan det også være nyttigt at informere brugeren om, hvordan billeder og metadata håndteres.

6. Test med forskellige billeder

Et værktøj kan se fint ud med ét testbillede og stadig fejle med andre billeder.

Prøv derfor flere scenarier.

Et stort landskabsbillede

Kontrollér, at billedet bliver skaleret korrekt.

Et billede i højformat

Undersøg, om det stadig kan ses uden at blive beskåret.

Kun ét billede

Brugeren skal kunne se et førbillede uden at vælge et efterbillede.

En fil, som ikke er et gyldigt billede

Værktøjet skal vise en forståelig besked.

Et nyt billede i samme felt

Kontrollér, at det gamle billede bliver erstattet.

Nulstil-knappen

Begge billeder skal forsvinde, og felterne skal blive tømt.

Det kan også være nyttigt at teste med tastatur alene.

Brugeren skal kunne vælge billeder og bruge knappen uden en mus.

7. Hvad mangler før produktion?

Dette er en læringsdemo.

Den viser billeder lokalt, men er ikke et færdigt dokumentationssystem.

Hvis du vil udvikle den videre, kan du overveje:

  • Begrænsning af filstørrelser.
  • Bedre fejlbeskeder.
  • Tastatur- og skærmlæsertest.
  • Mulighed for selv at skrive billedbeskrivelser.
  • Billedbehandling med passende hukommelsesstyring.
  • Klar information om eventuel databehandling.

Hvis løsningen skal understøtte professionelle arbejdsrapporter, skal der også være en plan for dokumentation, adgangskontrol og korrekt opbevaring.

En demo med to billeder kan være nyttig, men den bør ikke præsenteres som dokumentation for, at en opgave er udført sikkert eller korrekt.

Hvorfor bruge træfældning som eksempel?

Når et stort træ fjernes, kan området ændre sig tydeligt.

Der kan komme mere dagslys ind i haven. Udsigten kan ændre sig, og der kan blive plads til nye planter eller andre formål.

Derfor kan før- og efterbilleder være interessante for både haveejere og fagfolk.

Men billeder fortæller ikke alt.

De viser ikke nødvendigvis, hvordan træets tilstand var før arbejdet, eller hvilke sikkerhedsmæssige vurderinger der blev foretaget.

Fotografier bør derfor betragtes som visuel dokumentation, ikke som en selvstændig faglig vurdering.

Dansk Træpleje har base i Vejle og arbejder med blandt andet beskæring, træpleje og professionel træfældning.

Hvis du vil læse om den virkelige faglige kontekst, kan du se, hvordan virksomheden arbejder med at fælde træer i Vejle.

Værktøjet i denne guide er et selvstændigt kodeeksempel. Det er ikke en beskrivelse af en eksisterende funktion på virksomhedens hjemmeside.

Hvad har vi lært?

Vi har bygget et lille billedværktøj med tre almindelige webteknologier.

HTML giver strukturen.

CSS skaber et responsivt layout.

JavaScript læser de valgte filer og viser dem midlertidigt i browseren.

Vi har også brugt URL.revokeObjectURL() til at rydde op efter de midlertidige objekt-URL'er.

Det vigtigste er, at løsningen ikke kræver en stor teknisk platform for at være nyttig.

Nogle gange er en lille, tydelig funktion nok.

Og hvis brugeren forstår, hvad der sker med billederne, er vi allerede kommet et godt stykke med både brugeroplevelse og privatliv.

title: Your Agent Said It Right. Did the Caller Hear It? Live Call Testing in Voicetest
description:
A voice agent can pass every text simulation and still fail on a real call. The LLM produces the right sentence, and then the speech pipeline mangles it: a phone number read as a quantity, a drug name the TTS voice can't pronounce, an appointment time that STT on the other end turns into a different time. Text simulations never see any of this, because they stop at what the model meant to say.

Voicetest now runs test cases as live audio calls. The same simulated caller that drives text runs joins a real WebRTC call, speaks through TTS, and listens through STT. Nobody has to be on the line. Every turn ends up with two texts: what was intended, and what was heard.

This post covers how live calls work, what they catch, and how to run one.

Intended vs. heard

In a cascade voice pipeline (STT → LLM → TTS), the LLM's output is not what reaches the caller. It is an input to TTS, and the caller hears whatever TTS produced. A defect at that boundary looks like this:

Text
Intended (content) If you need to reschedule, call us at 415-555-0123.
Heard (heard) If you need to reschedule, call us at four hundred fifteen, five hundred fifty-five, one hundred twenty-three.

Both lines say the same thing to an LLM judge reading text. Only one of them is usable by a person writing a number down.

Voicetest records this by adding an observer to each call. The observer subscribes to the audio each side publishes and transcribes it, so every turn in the transcript carries:

  • content: the intended text, which is the agent's LLM output or the simulated caller's line.
  • heard: what the observer transcribed from the audio the other side actually received.

The runs view marks up each turn with a word-level diff of the two, so a mangled number or a dropped "not" stands out without re-reading the whole call.

Judged on what was heard

A finished live call is saved as a normal result, marked source_kind="live", next to simulated and imported results in the same run history. It is judged three ways:

  1. The test case's metrics, against the intended transcript.
  2. The same metrics again, against the heard text. These are stored as audio metrics.
  3. The agent's global metrics.

The second pass is the point. A metric like "Agent gave the caller the callback number" passes on the intended text above, and may well pass on the heard text too, since a number was technically given. Write the metric the way the caller experiences it, "Agent read the callback number digit by digit," and the two passes disagree:

The text metric passes, because the LLM wrote the digits. The audio metric fails, because the caller never heard them. That's the TTS regression a text-only suite lets through.

How this differs from audio evaluation

Voicetest already had audio evaluation. It takes a finished text simulation and round-trips the agent's lines through TTS and STT afterwards. That's cheap, and it catches the same class of pronunciation defect.

Live calls run the whole conversation over audio instead. The agent responds to what it heard the caller say, not to clean text, so STT errors on the caller's side change the course of the call the way they would in production. If the agent mishears "Tuesday" as "Thursday" in turn 3, the rest of the conversation follows from that mistake, and the transcript shows where it happened.

Use audio evaluation as a fast check across a whole suite. Use live calls for the test cases where hearing matters: numbers, names, dates, confirmations, and anything a caller has to act on.

Running one

Live calls need the voice services: a LiveKit server, a faster-whisper STT server, and a Kokoro TTS server. voicetest up starts all of them in Docker along with the backend:

uv tool install voicetest
voicetest up

Then run a test case as a call. In the Web UI, each test in the Tests tab has a Call button. It starts the call and switches to the Runs tab, where the transcript streams in turn by turn and the result is saved when the call ends.

From the CLI, point at an agent in the database and a test by name:

voicetest call \
  --agent-id <agent-id> \
  --tests tests.json \
  --test "Refill with callback number"

Over REST, it's POST /api/agents/{id}/calls/start with a test_id. Leave out test_id, or use the Talk button on the agent page, and the call waits for a human caller to join from the browser instead. Those calls are saved as runs too, judged against the agent's global metrics, which is useful for checking a prompt change by ear before writing a test for it.

voicetest down stops the services.

No API keys required

The whole stack can run on your machine. The voice services are already local, and the agent, the simulated caller, and the judge can use a local model through llama.cpp's llama-server:

brew install llama.cpp
llama-server -hf Qwen/Qwen3-8B-GGUF:Q4_K_M --port 8080 --reasoning-budget 0

# .voicetest/settings.toml
[models]
agent = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"
simulator = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"
judge = "llamafile/qwen3-8b"

This is also how voicetest tests itself. Its CI starts the stack in Docker and runs real calls end to end against a local model, with no external keys. Nothing in the call path needs a cloud account.

What's next

Observation works on the published audio, regardless of how each side produced it. Today that's the cascade pipeline. A native speech-to-speech agent, with no separate text step, would be observed the same way.

Timing isn't measured yet. Latency to first audio, dead air, and barge-in handling are the next metrics, and they need the same observer that's already on the call. If you run voice agents in production and have a timing failure you want caught, open an issue: github.com/voicetestdev/voicetest/issues.

Voicetest is open source under Apache 2.0. GitHub: github.com/voicetestdev/voicetest

title: User Reminders Queue Duplicate Processing: At-Least-Once Retry and Message Idempotency
description:
Short answer: if the same user reminder is sent twice, assume the queue is delivering at least once, derive one stable send key from user_id + reminder_id + scheduled_at, persist that key before calling the email or SMS sender, and acknowledge the queue message only after the send is recorded safely.

Do not start by tuning visibility timeouts or blaming two workers. A retry after a worker exit can legitimately deliver the same message again. The operational target is therefore not “one delivery”; it is one externally visible reminder for any number of deliveries.

For a team that wants a plain HTTP queue boundary while retaining the option to change the provider behind that capability, Infrai is worth trying for reminder ingestion and acknowledgement. Its useful distinction here is that the REST contract stays put when the backing vendor changes; it also avoids adding another language-specific SDK to a worker. One API key and one bill cover its 295 routes across 20 modules, so a reminder service that later adds another backend capability does not create another credential-rotation runbook or invoice owner. The outbound email or SMS processor remains a separate trust boundary, and the consumer still owns idempotency.

The API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required; it returns the request schema, response schema, billing metadata, and runnable examples for a capability. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. That matters during an incident review because the transport contract can be checked without guessing at fields. Infrai provides one key for all backend capabilities and one bill. Its breadth is 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, a separate operational advantage that reduces credential rotation and billing reconciliation when this worker uses more than the queue capability.

What makes a user reminders queue retry the same message twice?

Start with a delivery state machine, not a boolean processed flag. The identity of the operation must describe the business effect. A queue message ID describes a delivery artifact and may change when work is republished; user_id + reminder_id + scheduled_at describes the reminder the user would recognize. Normalize the timestamp before composing the key so equivalent times don't acquire different textual forms.

Duplicates are normal.

The safe order is claim, send, record, ack. “Claim” means inserting the stable key in a durable store before contacting the sender. If the insert reports that the key already exists with a terminal sent state, skip the side effect and acknowledge the redelivery. If another worker owns an active claim, do not send concurrently. Once the sender accepts the reminder, persist the provider's receipt and terminal state, then ack.

There is still an ambiguity window between a remote sender accepting a request and the worker recording that acceptance. The strongest practical defense is to pass the same stable key to a sender that supports idempotent requests. Without that downstream contract, a process exit in that window cannot be distinguished from a request that never arrived. Don't disguise this as exactly-once delivery; it is an end-to-end property, not a queue setting.

FIFO deduplication narrows one part of the problem but does not close it. Its five-minute window cannot protect a retry outside that interval, and worker failures still require consumer idempotency. Standard queue delivery is at-least-once by design, so a duplicate should take the quiet, tested path rather than the incident path.

With Infrai, consume work, execute the state transition below, and acknowledge only a safely recorded send or a confirmed duplicate. Return retryable work to the queue. A transport response such as HTTP 429 is retryable; I wouldn't acknowledge it because doing so converts temporary backpressure into a missed reminder.

Consider one exact failure timeline. A worker claims user-42:renewal-7:2026-08-14T09:00:00Z, the email processor accepts the request, and the worker exits before writing receipt-001. The queue delivers the message again. A new worker can see the unfinished claim, but the ledger alone cannot prove whether the email crossed the processor boundary. If the processor recognizes the same idempotency key, the second request resolves to the original effect and the worker can safely record its receipt. If the processor has no such contract, neither an aggressive retry nor an ack is safe: the former may send twice, while the latter may lose the reminder. This is the case the runbook must reconcile, because a uniqueness constraint by itself only prevents two workers from starting together; it cannot make a remote side effect transactional with a local row.

Stop there.

Decide where reminder data may persist

Delivery guarantees are only half the review. Region, retention, deletion, and processor boundaries determine where customer contact data travels and how long copies survive. Keep full message bodies out of the queue when identifiers will do. Record which system holds the user address, which system renders the content, which processor sends it, and which deletion workflow removes each durable copy. An ack deleting a queue message does not delete the delivery ledger or a specialist sender's records.

Infrai exposes region and provider readiness through its public discovery surface, so inspect the selected capability rather than assuming a region from the platform name. Its queue can own transport and redelivery while the specialist email or SMS provider owns final delivery. Contractual residency, retention, and deletion commitments for that processor must be verified with the processor; an API routing layer cannot supply guarantees that are absent from the underlying agreement. I'm not sure a generic architecture diagram can answer that question. The current DPA, selected region, and deletion evidence can.

The limitation is concrete: stick with Kafka when replay or several independent consumer groups define the system. Choose Temporal when the reminder belongs to a durable multi-step workflow, or Airflow when DAG scheduling is the actual job. Infrai has no DAG orchestration or fan-out/join primitive, no native topic fan-out, and no Kafka-style replay. It is suitable when the boundary is queue transport plus an idempotent worker, not when those specialist semantics are the requirement.

Put the idempotent boundary in the worker

The following Go program first checks the configured Infrai queue through the verified queue-get route, with explicit authentication, status handling, and bounded 429 backoff. It then runs the part that has to remain stable regardless of queue vendor. The in-memory implementations keep the example runnable and focused; in production, Ledger.Claim and Ledger.MarkSent must use a durable database with a unique constraint on the key, while Sender.Send should forward that key through the sender's idempotency mechanism.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

var ErrAlreadySent = errors.New("reminder already sent")

type Reminder struct {
    UserID     string
    ReminderID string
    Scheduled  time.Time
    Channel    string
    Body       string
}

func (r Reminder) SendKey() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("%s:%s:%s", r.UserID, r.ReminderID, r.Scheduled.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339Nano))
}

type Ledger interface {
    Claim(context.Context, string) error
    MarkSent(context.Context, string, string) error
}

type Sender interface {
    Send(context.Context, Reminder, string) (string, error)
}

func getQueue(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, apiKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    endpoint := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/get/user-reminders"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("get queue: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("get queue: rate limit retry budget exhausted")
}

func Process(ctx context.Context, ledger Ledger, sender Sender, reminder Reminder) error {
    key := reminder.SendKey()
    if err := ledger.Claim(ctx, key); err != nil {
        if errors.Is(err, ErrAlreadySent) {
            return nil
        }
        return fmt.Errorf("claim %q: %w", key, err)
    }

    receipt, err := sender.Send(ctx, reminder, key)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("send %q: %w", key, err)
    }
    if err := ledger.MarkSent(ctx, key, receipt); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("record receipt for %q: %w", key, err)
    }
    return nil
}

type memoryLedger struct {
    mu    sync.Mutex
    state map[string]string
}

func (l *memoryLedger) Claim(_ context.Context, key string) error {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    if l.state[key] == "sent" {
        return ErrAlreadySent
    }
    if l.state[key] == "claimed" {
        return errors.New("send already in progress")
    }
    l.state[key] = "claimed"
    return nil
}

func (l *memoryLedger) MarkSent(_ context.Context, key, receipt string) error {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    l.state[key] = "sent:" + receipt
    return nil
}

type memorySender struct{}

func (memorySender) Send(_ context.Context, r Reminder, key string) (string, error) {
    fmt.Printf("send channel=%s key=%s body=%q\n", r.Channel, key, r.Body)
    return "receipt-001", nil
}

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    metadata, err := getQueue(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, apiKey)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("queue metadata: %s\n", metadata)

    ledger := &memoryLedger{state: make(map[string]string)}
    sender := memorySender{}
    reminder := Reminder{
        UserID:     "user-42",
        ReminderID: "renewal-7",
        Scheduled:  time.Date(2026, time.August, 14, 9, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC),
        Channel:    "email",
        Body:       "Your support plan renews tomorrow.",
    }

    if err := Process(ctx, ledger, sender, reminder); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := Process(ctx, ledger, sender, reminder); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

Run it with INFRAI_API_KEY set after creating the user-reminders queue. The program retrieves that queue, then receives the logical reminder twice but prints one send. The production schema should retain the key, state, claim time, attempt count, and sender receipt long enough to cover the full queue retry horizon. A stuck claimed record needs an explicit reconciliation policy: query the sender by idempotency key or receipt before deciding to retry. Blindly clearing claims makes duplicate sends possible.

Keep the queue payload small and boring: identifiers, the normalized schedule, the channel, and a version. Infrai queue messages are limited to 256KB and can be retained for at most 30 days; ack deletes the message. Seven days is the maximum delivery delay. These limits fit ordinary reminders, but they are poor storage semantics for a permanent audit record. Put the durable reminder and delivery ledger in your database, and treat the queue as transport.

Option Prefer it when The catch
Infrai queue A stable plain-HTTP queue contract and the ability to change the backing provider without worker code changes matter No Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups; retention is at most 30 days, and consumer idempotency remains mandatory
Google Cloud Pub/Sub Direct alignment with an existing Google Cloud trust boundary is more important than a provider-neutral contract Treat standard delivery as at-least-once and verify region, retention, and deletion settings against your requirements
Amazon SQS FIFO A five-minute FIFO deduplication window usefully filters rapid producer retries The window does not replace consumer idempotency or cover later retries
Temporal Reminder sending is part of a durable, multi-step workflow with orchestration requirements It is a larger workflow decision, not merely a queue swap
BullMQ The worker already runs on Node.js and Redis is an accepted operational dependency Its runtime and Redis boundary are a deliberate commitment rather than a provider-neutral HTTP contract
Sidekiq Ruby and Redis already define the job-processing stack It is the natural direct choice for that stack, not for a Go worker seeking plain HTTP
Celery Python task processing and its broker ecosystem match the existing service Broker and result-backend choices add trust boundaries that need their own retention review

Prove the retry path before enabling sends

Before enabling sends, publish the same logical reminder twice and confirm one sender call, one terminal ledger row, and two safely resolved deliveries. Then terminate a worker after claim, after the sender call, and after MarkSent; each injection should have a documented next state. Run the same checks with an HTTP 429 from the sender. The expected outcome is retry without an early ack, followed by one externally visible reminder once the sender accepts the stable key.

Watch three signals separately: queue delivery attempts, unique send keys, and sender receipts. If delivery attempts rise while unique keys and receipts remain flat, idempotency is absorbing retries. If receipts exceed terminal keys, stop consumption because the ambiguity window or sender contract is unsafe. If terminal keys exceed receipts, stop acking and reconcile potential missed sends. These are operational assertions, not vanity throughput charts.

Rollback is simple only if it is planned. Pause the consumers, leave unacknowledged work available for retry, and preserve the ledger. Do not purge the queue or delete claims during diagnosis. Revert the worker while keeping the send-key format stable; changing key composition during rollback turns old reminders into apparently new work. Resume at low concurrency, compare receipts to terminal rows, and increase concurrency only after the counts reconcile.

Also test the calendar edges: two schedules for the same reminder, equivalent timestamps with different offsets, and a retry beyond five minutes. Your mileage may vary on how long sender receipts remain queryable, which is why that retention promise belongs in the trust-boundary review and the runbook.

One retry is enough to expose a bad ordering.

The decision rule is short: use Infrai when a stable REST queue contract, provider substitution behind that contract, and no SDK dependency are valuable, and when 30-day maximum retention plus at-least-once delivery fit the reminder design. Use a specialist when replay, workflow joins, private-only push targets, or stronger provider-specific controls dominate. If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live capability schema before implementing the transport adapter.

References

  • RFC 2104: HMAC keyed-hashing for message authentication
  • Google Cloud Pub/Sub overview
  • Amazon SQS FIFO queue deduplication
  • Temporal documentation
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Sidekiq documentation
  • Celery documentation
  • Infrai queue capability discovery

title: Make CI Automation Failures Explainable
description:
CI automation usually does not fail because there is no log. It fails because the useful evidence is scattered across a runner, a test inbox, a webhook provider, and three unrelated dashboards.

When a job turns red, the first question is rarely just “what command exited with code 1?” We want to know which test data was created, which message or event was expected, what actually arrived, and whether a retry changed the result. Without that chain, debugging becomes archaeology.

This article describes a small pattern I use for making automation failures easier to explain: give every run an evidence ledger and publish one compact receipt when the run ends. It works for email tests, browser checks, API workflows, and other developer tools.

The failure is not the log line

A normal CI log is a timeline of commands. That is useful, but it is not always a timeline of causes.

For example, a browser test may report that a verification link was missing. The real cause could be any of these:

  • The test created a fixture for the wrong run.
  • The application sent the event, but the worker retried it later.
  • The inbox query used a broad subject and selected an older message.
  • A cleanup step removed the message before the assertion ran.
  • The test passed locally because the local clock was a little different.

The log may contain clues for each case, but a developer has to manually join them. That is the expensive part. A receipt should make the joins explicit, even when the final status is failed.

Model each CI run as an evidence ledger

Start with a run identifier that is unique outside the CI provider too. A short commit SHA plus the CI attempt number works well, for example a81f2c7-attempt-2.

Every resource created for the test should carry that identifier:

  • test account or email fixture
  • outbound event ID
  • worker job ID
  • inbox message ID
  • assertion result
  • cleanup result

The ledger does not need a database on day one. A JSON file stored as a CI artifact is often enough. The important part is ownership: each record says which run created it and what happened next. This also keeps a test from accidentally reading another run's data, which is a common source of flaky results.

If your UI flow has several asynchronous states, define them before writing assertions. A test email state machine for React forms is a useful mental model: “created”, “sent”, “received”, “opened”, and “expired” are different facts, not one big “email worked” fact.

A small receipt format

Keep the receipt boring. Boring is good when somebody is staring at it during an incident. Here is a minimal shape:

{
  "run_id": "a81f2c7-attempt-2",
  "status": "failed",
  "started_at": "2026-11-12T05:00:14Z",
  "finished_at": "2026-11-12T05:01:03Z",
  "fixture": {
    "id": "fixture-a81f2c7",
    "owner": "checkout-verification"
  },
  "events": [
    {"name": "created", "id": "evt_91", "at": "2026-11-12T05:00:21Z"},
    {"name": "received", "id": "msg_44", "at": "2026-11-12T05:00:37Z"}
  ],
  "assertions": [
    {"name": "verification_link_present", "ok": false, "reason": "wrong host"}
  ],
  "cleanup": {"ok": true, "deleted": ["fixture-a81f2c7"]}
}

There is no need to make this format fancy at first. Use stable names, UTC timestamps, and IDs that can be searched in the other systems. If a field is unknown, write null or an explicit reason instead of silently leaving a gap. A missing value is itself useful evidence.

One small rule saves time: record the expected value beside the observed value. “Wrong host” is better than “link assertion failed,” but expected_host and observed_host is better still. It save a second trip through the application configuration.

Turn the receipt into a developer tool

An evidence ledger becomes valuable when the team can find it without learning a new ritual. Add three simple outputs to the CI job:

  1. Print a one-line summary with the run ID and the first failed assertion.
  2. Upload the full receipt as an artifact with a predictable filename.
  3. Add links from the job summary to the relevant event, message, and cleanup logs.

For pull requests, a small Markdown summary is enough:

Email verification: FAILED
Run: a81f2c7-attempt-2
First bad state: verification_link_present
Expected host: staging.example.test
Observed host: example.test
Receipt: artifacts/a81f2c7-attempt-2.json

This pattern also helps with privacy. The receipt can store opaque IDs and hashes instead of full message bodies or personal addresses. For teams handling test email, an audit trail for privacy-safe test email shows why retention and access rules belong in the design, not as a cleanup afterthought.

Do not over-collect. A receipt that copies every payload becomes a new security problem and is harder to read. Keep the minimum fields needed to reproduce the decision, then link to protected logs when more detail is required.

What to do about retries

Retries are where many automation reports become confusing. Treat every attempt as a child of one logical run, and include the attempt number in each resource key. The parent receipt can then say whether the second attempt reused data or created a clean fixture.

If a retry changes the result, report both outcomes. “Passed after retry” is not the same signal as “passed.” The distinction matters because a retry may hide a race, a delayed worker, or a flaky dependency. The failure ledger should make that visible, not smooth it away.

Also make cleanup idempotent. If the first attempt already deleted a fixture, the second cleanup should report “already absent” as an acceptable outcome. Otherwise the cleanup error can distract from the original failure.

Checklist before you ship the workflow

  • Does every created test resource include a run and attempt ID?
  • Can the receipt identify the first bad state, not only the last failed command?
  • Are expected and observed values recorded together?
  • Are retry outcomes kept distinct?
  • Can a developer open the artifact from the CI job summary?
  • Does cleanup run on success, failure, and cancellation?
  • Are private payloads excluded or protected?
  • Does the report remain useful when an external service is unavailable?

The goal is not another observability platform. It is a small shared contract between the test, the automation runner, and the person who has to fix the failure. Once that contract exists, noisy CI output starts to read like a story: what the run owned, what changed, where the first unexpected state appeared, and what was cleaned up. That is usually enough to get unstuck faster.

title: Preparing iOS Apps for iOS 27.2 and iOS 27.3: Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode & Compatibility Testing
description:
Discussion topic for Swift and iOS developer communities | November 2026

Introduction

iOS 27.2 is now out, and the first developer beta of iOS 27.3 landed on November 3. On the surface, 27.2 is a user-facing release: it adds or refines features in six of Apple's own apps. The 27.3 beta is where things get more interesting for anyone who ships web content or hybrid apps, because Safari is gaining two features that change how pages are framed and rendered: Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode.

Point releases rarely come with big API announcements, but they regularly shift the environment our apps run in. This post walks through what changed, where I think the real risks are, and a testing checklist I am using. I would love to hear what others are seeing on the betas.

A note on scope: the 9to5Mac article this discussion is based on covers the iOS 27.2 app updates. Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode are Safari features in the iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 betas, reported separately by 9to5Mac on November 3. Release of 27.3 is expected around December.

1. What shipped in iOS 27.2

Here is a summary of the six app changes, with my take on where each one may touch third-party apps. Most are low-impact, but a couple deserve a quick regression pass.

App What changed Why developers might care
Messages Suggested Actions appear under messages and can propose calendar events, reminders, notes and more based on context. Users can tune which suggestion types appear. If your app shares text, invites or confirmations into Messages, check how that content reads when the system offers actions alongside it. Clear dates and times help.
Apple TV Profiles come to the TV app on iPhone and iPad, with a profile picker at launch (can be disabled). Mostly user-facing. Worth noting if your app hands off to the TV app or relies on its watch history.
FaceTime Dual Capture (front and rear cameras at once) now works in Group FaceTime on iPhone 17 and newer. Camera apps should re-test interruption handling when another app holds both cameras.
Home New 'Lock After Closing' automation and 'Door Left Open' alerts for compatible locks. HomeKit apps may see lock state change from automations users set in Apple's Home app. Make sure your UI reflects state changes it did not initiate.
Podcasts Up Next is split into New Episodes and Continue Playing. Low impact unless you document deep links or user flows that point at Up Next.
Games Home tab shows downloaded but unplayed games; achievements and leaderboards are easier to track. Game Center achievements and leaderboards get more visibility, so it is a good moment to audit their configuration and artwork.

A practical example from the FaceTime change: if your app uses the camera, a Group FaceTime call with Dual Capture can take camera access away from you. That path has always existed, but it is now more likely to occur in real usage.

Handling camera interruptions caused by another app (AVFoundation)

import AVFoundation

final class CameraController {
    let session = AVCaptureSession()
    private var observers: [NSObjectProtocol] = []

    func observeInterruptions() {
        let center = NotificationCenter.default

        observers.append(center.addObserver(
            forName: AVCaptureSession.wasInterruptedNotification,
            object: session, queue: .main) { note in
                let key = AVCaptureSessionInterruptionReasonKey
                guard let raw = note.userInfo?[key] as? Int,
                      let reason = AVCaptureSession.InterruptionReason(rawValue: raw)
                else { return }

                switch reason {
                case .videoDeviceInUseByAnotherClient:
                    // e.g. a FaceTime call is using the cameras
                    self.showCameraUnavailableBanner()
                case .videoDeviceNotAvailableWithMultipleForegroundApps:
                    self.showMultitaskingMessage()
                default:
                    break
                }
        })

        observers.append(center.addObserver(
            forName: AVCaptureSession.interruptionEndedNotification,
            object: session, queue: .main) { _ in
                self.hideCameraUnavailableBanner()
        })
    }

    private func showCameraUnavailableBanner() { /* ... */ }
    private func showMultitaskingMessage() { /* ... */ }
    private func hideCameraUnavailableBanner() { /* ... */ }
}

2. iOS 27.3 beta: Safari Vertical Tabs

What we know so far from the beta 1 coverage:

  • Tabs can be arranged along the left side of the window instead of across the top.
  • By default they show as icons to save space; the tab bar can be resized to show page titles.
  • Vertical Tabs work with Tab Groups and with Topics (the Apple Intelligence tab sorting introduced in iOS 27).
  • It is available on iPad and Mac, and on iPhone Duo in both portrait and landscape.
  • On iPhone it is enabled in Settings > Apps > Safari; on iPad and Mac also via Safari's View menu.

How this can affect web-based experiences

  • Narrower content area. A sidebar on the left reduces the width available to your page, especially when users expand it to show titles. A layout that sat comfortably at a desktop breakpoint on iPad may now fall into a tablet or mobile breakpoint. Fixed-width layouts and off-canvas menus are the usual suspects.
  • Favicons matter more. In icon-only mode, your site's icon is the main way a user finds your tab. Missing or low-resolution icons make your page harder to identify among many tabs.
  • Page titles matter more. In the expanded sidebar, titles are what users scan. Single-page apps that never update document.title on navigation will look identical across tabs.
  • Resize events. Toggling or resizing the sidebar changes the viewport width while the page is live. Any logic that measures layout only once on load can break.

Web side: icons, titles and width-change resilience

<!-- Give Safari a clear icon and title for icon-only vertical tabs -->
<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
<title>Order #4821 - Acme Store</title>

<style>
  /* Prefer container queries for components that live in variable-width areas */
  .product-grid { container-type: inline-size; }
  @container (max-width: 700px) {
    .product-grid .card { grid-column: span 12; }
  }
</style>

<script>
  // React to width changes when the tab sidebar is toggled or resized,
  // instead of measuring once on load.
  const ro = new ResizeObserver(entries => relayout(entries[0].contentRect.width));
  ro.observe(document.documentElement);
</script>

How this can affect app integrations

Native apps are not directly affected by Safari's tab layout, but a few integration points are worth checking:

  • Universal Links and Smart App Banners. Users who open your site in Safari and then jump into your app go through a slightly different chrome. Verify banners and "Open in app" flows still render correctly in the narrower viewport.
  • SFSafariViewController and ASWebAuthenticationSession. These present their own browser UI. Based on the coverage I have read, Vertical Tabs are a Safari app setting, so I would not expect them to appear here, but confirm on the beta rather than assume, especially for OAuth sign-in flows.
  • Your own WKWebView screens. If you host web content that is also used in Safari, test it at the narrower widths Safari may now give it, since the same CSS will be exercised in both places.

A quick SwiftUI harness for checking web layouts at several widths

import SwiftUI
import WebKit

/// Debug-only harness: render the same page at several widths to catch
/// breakpoint regressions that a narrower Safari viewport can expose.
struct WidthMatrixView: View {
    let url: URL
    let widths: [CGFloat] = [1024, 834, 700, 600]

    var body: some View {
        ScrollView(.horizontal) {
            HStack(alignment: .top, spacing: 16) {
                ForEach(widths, id: \.self) { width in
                    VStack {
                        Text("\(Int(width)) pt").font(.caption.monospacedDigit())
                        WebView(url: url).frame(width: width, height: 900)
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

struct WebView: UIViewRepresentable {
    let url: URL
    func makeUIView(context: Context) -> WKWebView {
        let view = WKWebView()
        view.load(URLRequest(url: url))
        return view
    }
    func updateUIView(_ uiView: WKWebView, context: Context) {}
}

3. iOS 27.3 beta: Adaptive Dark Mode

Adaptive Dark Mode lets Safari generate a dark version of websites that do not support Dark Mode on their own. When the device is in Dark Mode and you visit such a site, Safari shows a "Try" button; users can apply it per site or let it kick in automatically.

It is important to be precise about what this is: it is a Safari feature for web content. It does not recolor native SwiftUI or UIKit interfaces. So why should native developers care?

  • Your web surfaces may be recolored without your input. Marketing pages, help centers, account portals and web checkouts that only have a light theme are candidates for automatic darkening. Brand colors, logos on transparent backgrounds, charts and screenshots are where automatic transforms most often go wrong.
  • Users will notice inconsistency. If Safari renders your website dark, and the user then taps a Universal Link into an app that has weak Dark Mode support, the gap becomes very obvious.
  • Hybrid apps are an open question. The coverage describes the feature in Safari. Whether anything similar applies to WKWebView content is not documented as far as I can tell, so the safest plan is to make your web content support Dark Mode properly rather than rely on any automatic transform.

Apple has not, to my knowledge, documented exactly how Safari decides a site "doesn't support" Dark Mode. Declaring your support explicitly is the most reasonable thing to do, and it is good practice anyway:

Web side: explicit Dark Mode support

<!-- Tell the browser which color schemes your page supports -->
<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">

<style>
  :root {
    color-scheme: light dark;
    --bg: #ffffff; --text: #1b1f24; --brand: #0a66c2;
  }
  @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
    :root { --bg: #111418; --text: #e6e9ee; --brand: #4c9cff; }
  }
  body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--text); }
</style>

<!-- Provide a dark variant for logos and illustrations -->
<picture>
  <source srcset="/logo-dark.svg" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">
  <img src="/logo-light.svg" alt="Acme">
</picture>

Impact on SwiftUI interfaces

SwiftUI handles appearance changes well when you stay with semantic styles. Problems usually come from hard-coded colors or from assets without dark variants. This is a good moment to audit both:

SwiftUI: semantic styles, asset colors and dual previews

import SwiftUI

struct OrderSummaryCard: View {
    @Environment(\.colorScheme) private var colorScheme

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 8) {
            Text("Order #4821").font(.headline)
            Text("Arriving Friday").foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        }
        .padding()
        // Semantic background adapts automatically; avoid Color.white / Color.black
        .background(.background.secondary, in: .rect(cornerRadius: 12))
        // "BrandAccent" lives in the asset catalog with Any/Dark appearances
        .overlay(RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12).stroke(Color("BrandAccent")))
        // Use colorScheme only for things styles can't express, e.g. shadow strength
        .shadow(radius: colorScheme == .dark ? 0 : 4)
    }
}

#Preview("Light") { OrderSummaryCard().padding() }
#Preview("Dark") { OrderSummaryCard().padding().preferredColorScheme(.dark) }

Impact on UIKit interfaces

UIKit's classic Dark Mode bug is Core Animation properties. CGColor values are resolved once, so borders and shadows set on a layer stay in the old appearance when the user switches modes. Since iOS 17, registerForTraitChanges is the recommended way to respond, replacing the deprecated traitCollectionDidChange(_:).

UIKit: keeping layer colors in sync with appearance

import UIKit

final class CardView: UIView {
    override init(frame: CGRect) {
        super.init(frame: frame)
        backgroundColor = .secondarySystemBackground   // dynamic, auto-updates
        layer.cornerRadius = 12
        layer.borderWidth = 1
        applyLayerColors()

        // CGColor does not update on its own; re-resolve when appearance changes.
        let traits: [UITrait] = [UITraitUserInterfaceStyle.self,
                                 UITraitAccessibilityContrast.self]
        registerForTraitChanges(traits) { (self: Self, _) in
            self.applyLayerColors()
        }
    }

    required init?(coder: NSCoder) { fatalError("init(coder:) not implemented") }

    private func applyLayerColors() {
        let traits = traitCollection
        layer.borderColor = UIColor.separator.resolvedColor(with: traits).cgColor
        layer.shadowColor = UIColor.label.resolvedColor(with: traits).cgColor
    }
}

// A dynamic color defined in code, when an asset catalog entry isn't practical
extension UIColor {
    static let brandAccent = UIColor { traits in
        traits.userInterfaceStyle == .dark
            ? UIColor(red: 0.30, green: 0.61, blue: 1.00, alpha: 1)
            : UIColor(red: 0.04, green: 0.40, blue: 0.76, alpha: 1)
    }
}

If you host web content, a related annoyance is the white flash before a dark page paints. Two small settings take care of most of it:

WKWebView: avoiding the white flash in Dark Mode

let webView = WKWebView(frame: .zero, configuration: WKWebViewConfiguration())
webView.isOpaque = false                       // avoid a white frame before first paint
webView.backgroundColor = .systemBackground
webView.underPageBackgroundColor = .systemBackground // iOS 15+: overscroll area
// WKWebView passes the view's appearance to prefers-color-scheme,
// so web content that supports Dark Mode follows the app automatically.

4. Compatibility and regression testing

Here is the matrix I am working from. It is deliberately small; the goal is to catch the regressions point releases tend to cause, not to retest everything.

Dimension What to cover Notes
OS versions Your minimum deployment target, the latest 27.1.x, 27.2 (shipping), 27.3 beta Install your current App Store / TestFlight build on the beta, not just a fresh debug build.
Devices A small iPhone, a large iPhone, iPhone Duo if you support it, one iPad Vertical Tabs matter most on iPad, Mac and iPhone Duo, where the Safari sidebar takes width.
Appearance Light, Dark, Increase Contrast, appearance switch while the app is running Live switching is where CGColor and cached-image bugs appear.
Text size Default, the largest standard size, one accessibility size Combine with Dark Mode; truncation bugs and contrast bugs often show up together.
Web content Safari with Vertical Tabs collapsed and expanded, Adaptive Dark Mode on and off Include login, checkout and help pages, not only the homepage.
System interactions FaceTime call during camera use, Home automations changing lock state Covers the iOS 27.2 changes most likely to reach third-party apps.

Automating appearance checks

Rendering the same screen under both appearances in a unit test is cheap and catches most color regressions. You can pair this with whichever snapshot library you already use:

XCTest: verifying trait-dependent colors

import XCTest
@testable import MyApp

final class AppearanceTests: XCTestCase {

    func testCardRendersInBothAppearances() {
        for style in [UIUserInterfaceStyle.light, .dark] {
            let traits = UITraitCollection(userInterfaceStyle: style)
            let card = CardView(frame: CGRect(x: 0, y: 0, width: 320, height: 120))
            card.overrideUserInterfaceStyle = style

            traits.performAsCurrent {
                card.layoutIfNeeded()
                let expected = UIColor.separator.resolvedColor(with: traits).cgColor
                let name = style == .dark ? "dark" : "light"
                XCTAssertEqual(card.layer.borderColor, expected,
                               "Border color not resolved for \(name)")
            }
        }
    }
}

For UI tests, a launch argument that forces the appearance keeps the setup simple and works on any OS version:

UI tests: forcing an appearance via launch environment

// In the app (e.g. SceneDelegate or App init), debug builds only:
#if DEBUG
if let mode = ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["UI_TEST_APPEARANCE"] {
    window?.overrideUserInterfaceStyle = (mode == "dark") ? .dark : .light
}
#endif

// In the UI test:
let app = XCUIApplication()
app.launchEnvironment["UI_TEST_APPEARANCE"] = "dark"
app.launch()

5. UI issues, API changes, performance and backward compatibility

Potential UI issues

  • Hard-coded .white / .black colors and images without dark variants.
  • Layer-based borders and shadows that do not update when appearance changes at runtime.
  • Web pages that assume a minimum width on iPad or Mac and break when the Safari sidebar is expanded.
  • Logos and screenshots on websites that look wrong after Adaptive Dark Mode recolors the page around them.

API changes

The coverage of iOS 27.3 beta 1 focuses on user-facing Safari changes and does not describe new developer APIs for Vertical Tabs or Adaptive Dark Mode. That does not mean there are none: check the Xcode and Safari release notes for the 27.3 SDK, and file Feedback early if you see behavior changes in WebKit. If you do adopt something new, guard it with availability checks so your minimum deployment target keeps working:

Availability checks and OS-version logging

if #available(iOS 27.3, *) {
    // Adopt new behavior or API introduced in the 27.3 SDK (per release notes)
} else {
    // Existing code path for earlier versions
}

// Logging the exact OS version helps when triaging beta-only reports
let v = ProcessInfo.processInfo.operatingSystemVersion
logger.info("OS \(v.majorVersion).\(v.minorVersion).\(v.patchVersion)")

Performance

  • Watch for extra layout passes in web content when the Safari sidebar is resized; ResizeObserver callbacks that do heavy work can cause jank.
  • Measure hangs and launch time on the beta with Instruments, and compare with MetricKit data from the shipping release once 27.3 rolls out.
  • Retest memory in WKWebView-heavy screens; WebKit changes in a point release can shift memory behavior.

Backward compatibility

  • None of these changes require raising your deployment target. Keep shipping builds made with the release SDK, and use the beta for testing your existing binaries.
  • Avoid user-agent sniffing to detect the new Safari features; feature-detect and use responsive CSS instead.
  • Treat Dark Mode support on the web and in the app as one design system, so behavior stays consistent across OS versions that do and do not have Adaptive Dark Mode.

Discussion questions

  • Vertical Tabs: Have you tested your web content or Universal Link flows in Safari with Vertical Tabs expanded on iPad, Mac or iPhone Duo? Did any breakpoints or fixed layouts break?
  • Adaptive Dark Mode: Has Safari offered to darken any of your sites, and how did the result look? Has anyone found a reliable way to signal that a site already supports Dark Mode, beyond the color-scheme declaration?
  • Hybrid apps: For apps built on WKWebView, have you seen any change in how web content renders in Dark Mode on the 27.3 beta, or does everything behave as it did on 27.2?
  • Testing workflow: How do you organize regression testing for point releases? Do you automate appearance and Dynamic Type checks, or rely on manual passes on beta devices?

Swift #SwiftUI #UIKit #iOSDev #iOS27 #iOS27_2 #iOS27_3 #Safari #WebKit #DarkMode #VerticalTabs #RegressionTesting #XCTest #Accessibility #AppleDeveloper

Sources

  • 9to5Mac, "iOS 27.2 adds new features in six iPhone apps, details here" (Nov 10, 2026)
  • 9to5Mac, "iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 add Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and more to Safari" (Nov 3, 2026)
  • Additional beta coverage: MacRumors via Daring Fireball, TechRadar, Macworld (Nov 3, 2026). Features in beta may change before release.

title: etcdctl: A SuperCLI Plugin Guide
description:
etcdctl

etcdctl — etcd CLI client

Source

etcd.io

Tags

Installation

  1. # Install etcdctl:
  2. # apt: sudo apt-get install etcdctl
