title: 992 of 1,000 npm Maintainer Addresses Passed. Three of the Eight Failures Were My Own Bug
description:
I run a visa agency in Bali. Scrapers and small data tools on Apify are the other half of my week, and one of them cleans e-mail lists: syntax, a live MX lookup, throwaway domains, role addresses, typo hints, duplicate spellings, a 0–100 score. No mail is ever sent.

The marketing for a verifier writes itself ("remove bounces!"); its honest performance is a number you have to go and measure. So I measured it on a list I did not curate: 1,000 maintainer and author addresses taken straight out of the npm registry. 995 came back deliverable — and of the handful that did not, three were my own bug.

The test list

The npm registry is a decent stand-in for a scraped B2B lead list: real humans, real company domains, addresses typed by hand years ago and never touched since. Every package document carries maintainers[].email and sometimes author.email.

import json, urllib.request, urllib.parse

def doc(name):
    url = f'https://registry.npmjs.org/{urllib.parse.quote(name, safe="@/")}'
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={'User-Agent': 'research/1.0'})
    return json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=25))

emails = {}
for name in package_names:                      # 900 packages from /-/v1/search
    d = doc(name)
    for m in d.get('maintainers') or []:
        if m.get('email'):
            emails.setdefault(m['email'].lower(), name)
    a = d.get('author')
    if isinstance(a, dict) and a.get('email'):
        emails.setdefault(a['email'].lower(), name)

900 packages across sixteen search terms produced 2,088 distinct addresses. I took a seeded random 1,000 of them — 332 unique domains between them, from gmail.com (352 addresses) down to one-off personal domains.

What came back

Two runs of the same 1,000 addresses, before and after the fix described below:

verdict before after why
deliverable 992 995 domain publishes mail servers
risky 6 3 domain has no MX and relies on its A record
undeliverable 2 2 users.noreply.github.com accepts no mail
unknown 0 0 no DNS timeouts in either run

Five rows out of a thousand are worth deleting. That is the real yield of a domain-level check on a list of addresses that people actively use, and anyone promising you more than that on a list like this is selling you a different product than the one they're describing.

The five, in full:

  • 1336118+wittlock@users.noreply.github.com and microsoftopensource@users.noreply.github.com — GitHub's noreply domain publishes no MX record. These are the addresses npm records when a publisher hides their real one; they are permanently undeliverable and they do turn up in scraped developer lists.
  • admin@iov.one, admin@web3api.dev, mail@substack.net — domains that exist, serve a website, publish no MX. Under RFC 5321 a sender then falls back to the A record, which is a web server with no mail daemon, so it's risky rather than undeliverable — but in practice: dead. 
{
  "email": "microsoftopensource@users.noreply.github.com",
  "emailStatus": "undeliverable",
  "emailReason": "domain_accepts_no_mail",
  "emailDomain": "users.noreply.github.com",
  "emailProvider": null,
  "emailMxHost": null,
  "emailScore": 0,
  "checkLevel": "domain_mx"
}

One caveat I only saw because I ran the same addresses twice: in a smaller run on the same day, that GitHub address came back domain_not_found instead of domain_accepts_no_mail — the resolver answered NXDOMAIN once and NODATA the other time. Both verdicts are "drop it", but if you branch your pipeline on emailReason rather than emailStatus, don't assume the reason is stable.

The three failures that were mine

The other three flagged rows, from the first run:

arvinx@foxmail.com       risky  possible_typo  suggestion: hotmail.com
meteor.lxy@foxmail.com   risky  possible_typo  suggestion: hotmail.com
lcz_1996@foxmail.com     risky  possible_typo  suggestion: hotmail.com

foxmail.com is Tencent's consumer mail service. It has tens of millions of users and this is its MX record:

foxmail.com -> mx3.qq.com, mx2.qq.com

The typo check was a Levenshtein distance against a list of big providers, suggesting a correction at distance 1 or 2. foxmail.com → hotmail.com is exactly two substitutions (f→h, x→t). So three working Chinese addresses were labelled risky with a score of 25, because of a heuristic that never looked at whether the domain actually receives mail.

Three in a thousand is a 0.3% false-positive rate, and it lands on one country's users — the kind of bias you only find by running real data instead of your own example list. I checked which other real services sit within two edits of a big provider and confirmed each with a live MX lookup:

domain MX would have been "corrected" to
foxmail.com mx3.qq.com hotmail.com
hotmail.ca hotmail-com.olc.protection.outlook.com hotmail.com
yahoo.ca mta6.am0.yahoodns.net yahoo.com
email.com mx01.mail.com gmail.com
aim.com mx-aol.mail.gm0.yahoodns.net aol.com

And the control group — actual typo domains, looked up the same way:

gmial.com   -> no MX (ENODATA)
hotmial.com -> no MX (ENODATA)
yaho.com    -> no MX (ENODATA)
smail.com   -> no MX (ENODATA)
gnail.com   -> mx1.oweb.cn, mx2.oweb.cn      <- a squat that does catch mail

The distance metric was right about the shape of the string and wrong about the world. The fix is an exemption list of those five verified providers, applied before the distance check: on the identical 1,000 addresses, suggestions 3 → 0, risky 6 → 3, deliverable 992 → 995, while gnail.com still comes back risky / possible_typo.

The lesson generalises past my five domains: an edit-distance typo hint needs an allowlist of real services, and the cheapest source of truth for "is this a real mail domain" is the MX lookup you are already doing.

The byproduct that turned out more useful than the verdicts

Every row carries emailMxHost and a normalised emailProvider, and across 1,000 developer addresses that distribution says something a verdict column cannot:

mail host addresses domains
google 614 164
microsoft 182 28
other 168 118
proofpoint 14 6
zoho 6 6
mimecast 5 3
yahoo 5 2

61% of this list is filtered by Google — 352 addresses on gmail.com plus 262 company addresses whose MX is Google Workspace (aspmx.l.google.com, smtp.google.com). Another 159 sit behind Microsoft 365, and nineteen go through Proofpoint or Mimecast, the subset where a cold link is most likely to be rewritten or stripped.

Also: 394 of 1,000 are free mailboxes, 606 are on a company domain, and 35 are role accounts (admin@, hello@, info@) — all 35 of them on a company domain, none on a free one. Zero were disposable; npm maintainers are not sign-up spam.

Dedupe: real, and smaller than advertised

The verifier collapses spellings of one mailbox (emailNormalized) and points duplicates at each other (emailDuplicateOf). On this list:

  • 28 addresses carry a plus-tag, nearly all of them the corporate publishing convention: aprigogin+npm@google.com, aws-cfn-dev-ex+npm@amazon.com, appurva.murawat+npm@postman.com.
  • 143 of the 352 Gmail addresses have dots in the local part, which Gmail ignores.
  • And the number of actual collisions found was one: npmjs@shopify.com and npmjs+shopify-dep@shopify.com. 
{ "email": "npmjs@shopify.com", "emailNormalized": "npmjs@shopify.com",
  "emailDuplicateOf": "npmjs+shopify-dep@shopify.com", "emailScore": 100 }

Which is the honest version of a dedupe feature: on a source already unique by string, normalisation buys almost nothing. It earns its place when you merge two lists, or scrape the same company from three directories.

Speed, and the row you must filter out

1,000 addresses on 332 domains finished in under 4 seconds, because the DNS answer is cached per domain for the run — 332 lookups, not 1,000. The run also appends one free bookkeeping row, and it is not your data:

{"type": "notice", "notice": "Run summary: 1000 row(s) delivered, 0 free; charged email-checked x1000 = $0.63. ..."}

Filter on type != "notice" before you count anything. (List price is $0.70 per 1,000 addresses, cheaper on paid Store plans; nothing is charged per run.)

Calling it is one request, and the input can be a list, a public CSV/Google Sheet link, or the dataset of whatever scraper collected the addresses in the first place:

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~bulk-email-verifier/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"inputDatasetId":"<dataset-of-your-lead-scraper>",
       "emailField":"email, emails, contactEmail",
       "keep":"clean"}'

keep: "clean" returns only deliverable addresses with one spelling per mailbox — and since only returned rows are billed, the rows it drops cost nothing.

When this is the wrong tool

It checks domains, not mailboxes. Confirming that one specific inbox exists needs an SMTP conversation on port 25, and outbound 25 is blocked on Apify's cloud as it is on most clouds — so deliverable here means well formed and the domain accepts mail, which every row states as checkLevel: "domain_mx". nobody-here-12345@gmail.com passes.

So it will not catch the former employee whose company domain is still alive, and it does not detect catch-all domains. For years-old B2B data where people have changed jobs, pay for a mailbox-level verifier. For fresh scraper output full of users.noreply.github.com, domains without mail servers, info@ addresses and three spellings of one inbox, this removes that in seconds for cents — and, as of this week, it no longer tells Tencent users to fix a perfectly good address.

The Actor is Bulk Email Verifier on Apify Store. Both 1,000-address runs quoted here came out of it an hour apart — two build numbers, and three false positives, between them.

title: ASEAN Cross-Border QR Payments in Spring Boot: EMVCo Router
description:
An ASEAN cross-border QR payment works like this: the payer's app parses the EMVCo QR text, checks its CRC16 checksum, detects which scheme (PayNow, DuitNow, PromptPay or QRIS) owns the code, locks an FX quote, and sends an idempotent instruction down the bilateral link to the merchant's country. This post shows how to build that router in Spring Boot.

The regional headlines are all about new links. By December 2025 the region had counted 29 QR and instant-payment linkages, Cambodia now has five bilateral links, and Singapore and Vietnam switched theirs on in July 2026. MAS and the Association of Banks in Singapore are studying a second generation of PayNow ahead of Singapore FinTech Festival on 18 to 20 November 2026. Each of those is a pairwise agreement between two scheme operators. None of them gives the sending bank a single thing to call.

That gap lands on whoever writes the payer-side code at a bank, wallet or acquirer. In practice the scheme operators run the pipes, and your institution runs the part that decides which pipe a given scan should use, what to quote, and what to do when the answer never comes back. This post walks through one scan in plain terms, then the design I would use for an EMVCo QR parser and corridor router in Spring Boot, and closes with the failure modes that generate pager alerts. If you have worked through PSD2 API development, the shape is familiar: several regulated rails and no common hand-off.

Part 1: One scan, end to end

A Thai customer, with a Thai banking app, stands in front of a Singapore stall that has a printed QR code. They scan it. The app reads the text, notices that the merchant template belongs to PayNow rather than PromptPay, and asks an FX service how many baht equal the stall's price in Singapore dollars. The service answers with a rate held for a short window, often around a minute. The customer sees the baht amount, confirms with a fingerprint, and the app sends an instruction into the Thailand to Singapore link. On the Singapore side it becomes a PayNow credit to the merchant. A confirmation travels back, the stall owner hears a chime, and the customer sees a green tick.

Three terms are all you need beyond that: an instant payment scheme is a national rail (PayNow in Singapore, PromptPay in Thailand, DuitNow in Malaysia, with QRIS as Indonesia's QR standard); a linkage is the bilateral connection between two of them; and FX is the conversion step in between.

What surprised me when I looked at the architecture is that there is no ASEAN-wide network. There is Thailand-Singapore, Malaysia-Singapore, Indonesia-Thailand and so on, each negotiated separately, each with its own message details, operating hours and definition of "completed". Mandate-style payments run into the same trap of rules that look uniform and are not, which I covered in Commercial VRP in Spring Boot: each rail's notion of consent, retry and finality differs, and your code has to absorb that difference rather than pretend it away.

My working thesis is that the QR text is standardised and the corridors are not. That is why the router exists. Who runs it? Usually the payer-side institution, or its processor, because that is the party holding the customer relationship, the FX exposure and the compliance obligation. Scheme operators will not run it for you: they connect two ends of one corridor and have no reason to model your customer's wallet balance or your FX margin.

Part 2: What the QR text contains

EMVCo, the body behind the common QR specification, defines the payload as a flat string of TLV records: a two-digit tag, a two-digit length, then the value. Some values contain a nested TLV string.

Here is a complete, valid example I use in tests, a dynamic PayNow-style code for S$4.50 at a made-up stall:

00020101021226370009SG.PAYNOW010120210201912345K0301052045812530370254044.505802SG5919LAU PA SAT STALL 126009Singapore63047598

Broken apart: 000201 (format 01), 010212 (dynamic), 2637... (template in tag 26, 37 characters long, holding sub-tag 00 SG.PAYNOW, a proxy type, the proxy value and an editable-amount flag), 52045812 (category 5812), 5303702 (SGD), 54044.50 (amount), 5802SG, 5919LAU PA SAT STALL 12, 6009Singapore, and 63047598 (CRC). The identifiers and sub-tag layout above are illustrative; real ones come from each scheme's specification.

The tags I rely on for routing:

Tag Meaning
00 Payload format indicator, always 01
01 Point of initiation: 11 static (reusable), 12 dynamic (one-off, usually carries an amount)
26 to 51 Merchant account information templates, one per scheme the merchant accepts
52 Merchant category code
53 Currency, ISO 4217 numeric (702 SGD, 764 THB, 458 MYR, 360 IDR)
54 Transaction amount, optional
58 Country code
59, 60 Merchant name and city
62 Additional data such as bill or reference numbers
63 CRC, a 4-hex-digit checksum

Tags 26 to 51 are the ones that matter for a router. One printed code can carry several templates, for example a PayNow template in one tag and a card-network template in another. Inside each, sub-tag 00 holds a globally unique identifier naming the owning scheme. Detect the scheme from that identifier, never from the tag number, because tag numbers are chosen by whoever generated the code and two merchants can put PayNow in different slots.

The identifier strings and sub-tag layouts must come from each scheme's current specification and your sponsor bank's onboarding pack. I keep them in configuration, and the values in the code below are placeholders that show shape only.

Step one: reject bad codes cheaply

The checksum in tag 63 is CRC-16 over the whole payload, up to and including the 6304 that introduces the field. The variant is CCITT-FALSE: polynomial 0x1021, initial value 0xFFFF, no reflection, no final XOR. A quick self-test is the string 123456789, which must produce 29B1; the sample payload above produces 7598. Validate before parsing anything else. A failed CRC is a damaged print, a camera misread, or a sticker pasted over a legitimate code, and in none of those cases do you want to burn an FX quote or a corridor call.

public final class EmvCrc16 {

    private EmvCrc16() {}

    public static int compute(String payloadUpToAndIncluding6304) {
        int crc = 0xFFFF;
        for (byte b : payloadUpToAndIncluding6304.getBytes(java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
            crc ^= (b & 0xFF) << 8;
            for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
                crc = ((crc & 0x8000) != 0) ? (crc << 1) ^ 0x1021 : crc << 1;
                crc &= 0xFFFF;
            }
        }
        return crc;
    }

    public static boolean isValid(String payload) {
        if (payload == null || payload.length() < 8) return false;
        int cut = payload.length() - 4;
        if (!payload.startsWith("6304", cut - 4)) return false;
        String expected = String.format("%04X", compute(payload.substring(0, cut)));
        return expected.equalsIgnoreCase(payload.substring(cut));
    }
}

The CRC field must be last. I have seen generators append trailing whitespace or a newline, so input is trimmed at the edge and anything still failing the position check is refused. Do not "repair" payloads. An instrument that needs repair is one you decline.

Step two: a parser that does not trust lengths

The TLV walker bound-checks every length. A declared length running past the end of the string is exactly what a hostile input would contain. My parser returns an immutable map of tag to value and throws one typed exception, MalformedQrException, which the API maps to a 422 with a stable error code. Nested templates go through the same parser recursively, capped at depth two, since no scheme I have read about needs more.

Step three: scheme detection from tags 26 to 51

Detection walks every template in 26 to 51, parses sub-tag 00, and matches it against a registry. The result is a list, because a code can legitimately offer more than one scheme.

public record SchemeMatch(String schemeId, int templateTag, Map<String, String> fields) {}

@Component
public class SchemeDetector {

    private final Map<String, String> guidToScheme; // from configuration

    public SchemeDetector(SchemeRegistryProperties props) {
        this.guidToScheme = props.guidToScheme();
    }

    public List<SchemeMatch> detect(Map<String, String> tlv) {
        List<SchemeMatch> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int tag = 26; tag <= 51; tag++) {
            String raw = tlv.get(String.format("%02d", tag));
            if (raw == null) continue;
            Map<String, String> sub = TlvParser.parse(raw, 1);
            String guid = sub.get("00");
            if (guid == null) continue;
            String scheme = guidToScheme.get(guid.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));
            if (scheme != null) out.add(new SchemeMatch(scheme, tag, sub));
        }
        return out;
    }
}

Unknown identifiers are skipped, not fatal. A Thai app will meet templates for schemes it cannot pay through, and the right move is to ignore them and use the one it supports. Once a scheme is chosen, the instruction has to survive retries and crashes, which is where the transactional outbox pattern in Spring Boot payment systems earns its place. For the settlement work queues, Kafka share groups in Spring Boot payment pipelines are worth a look.

Part 3: The router and the corridor model

Here is the system I would build, shown in the diagram.

I model a corridor as an ordered pair, source scheme and destination scheme, plus a bundle of properties: which adapter speaks to it, its operating hours and cut-off, per-transaction and daily limits, the currencies it supports, its timeout budget, and whether it returns a synchronous final answer or only an acknowledgement followed by a later status message. Direction matters. Thailand to Singapore and Singapore to Thailand are separate corridors that happen to share a diagram edge.

public record Corridor(
        String source,
        String destination,
        String adapterBean,
        LocalTime opensAt,
        LocalTime closesAt,
        ZoneId zone,
        BigDecimal perTxnLimit,
        Duration ackTimeout,
        boolean asyncFinality) {

    public boolean isOpen(Instant now) {
        LocalTime t = now.atZone(zone).toLocalTime();
        return !t.isBefore(opensAt) && t.isBefore(closesAt);
    }
}

Corridor definitions live in configuration and are reloaded without a deploy, because limits and windows change by circular, not by release cycle. Routing is then a lookup: given the payer's home scheme and the list of SchemeMatch entries, return the open corridors, ordered by a preference rule (cheapest FX, then highest recent success rate). If none are open, the user is told which window to retry in, which is kinder than a generic failure.

Locking FX without lying to the customer

The FX service returns a quote: pair, rate, an expiresAt, and a quote id. The router stores it with the payment attempt and shows the payer the converted amount. The rule I would enforce is that the corridor instruction carries the quote id and the exact converted amount the customer confirmed. If expiresAt has passed when the customer confirms, or by the time the message is built, the router discards the quote and asks again rather than quietly re-pricing. Silent re-pricing is how a customer approves 412 baht and is charged 418.

The rate-expiry race is real: the user dawdles on the confirm screen for 55 seconds of a 60-second window, the request takes 8 seconds to reach the adapter, and the quote dies in flight. The fix is to validate expiry with a safety margin equal to your p99 path latency, not at the moment of the tap.

Idempotent settlement

Every payment attempt gets a client-generated idempotency key that travels from the app through to the adapter. The API layer stores it in a unique-constrained table before doing anything else:

@Transactional
public PaymentAttempt accept(String idemKey, QrPayRequest req) {
    return attempts.findByIdemKey(idemKey)
        .orElseGet(() -> {
            PaymentAttempt a = PaymentAttempt.create(idemKey, req);
            attempts.saveAndFlush(a);          // unique index on idem_key
            outbox.enqueue("settlement.requested", a.id(), a.toInstruction());
            return a;
        });
}

A duplicate request returns the stored attempt and its current state; it does not create a second instruction. The outbox row and the attempt commit together, and a relay publishes to the Kafka topic settlement.requested, keyed by attempt id so that all events for one payment stay ordered on one partition. Concurrent duplicates race on the unique index; the loser catches the constraint violation and re-reads. I also pass the same key as the end-to-end reference in the corridor message wherever the scheme allows, so the destination side can detect a replay even if my side loses its own state.

Per-corridor adapters consume the topic and are the only components that know a scheme's message format. They translate the internal instruction to the corridor's wire format, call the link, and publish settlement.result events. An adapter must be a thin translator with no business rules, so that adding a corridor means adding one class and one configuration entry.

The state machine

I keep the attempt state deliberately small: RECEIVED, QUOTED, CONFIRMED, SENT, COMPLETED, FAILED, UNKNOWN. UNKNOWN is the important one. It means "we sent an instruction and do not know the outcome", and it is a first-class state with its own handling rather than a synonym for failed. Anything that times out after SENT goes there, never to FAILED.

Part 4: Compliance and data constraints

A router like this is a regulated activity before it is a technical one. Points that shape the design:

  • Data localisation and residency. Regulators in several of these markets, including the central banks of Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia and the Monetary Authority of Singapore, set expectations about where payment data may be stored and processed. Indonesia's rules in particular push toward domestic processing for domestic transactions. Do not assume one central cluster can hold everything; check with your compliance team early and design the storage layer so a corridor's records can live in-region.
  • Licensing. Operating on the payer side generally requires being a licensed bank or payment institution in your home market, and the destination scheme will onboard you through a sponsor or participant arrangement. Your adapter configuration is shaped by that contract.
  • AML and sanctions screening. Cross-border hops are where screening is strictest. Screen the beneficiary name and country from tags 58 and 59 before sending, and keep the screening result and list version on the attempt record. A screening hold needs its own state so that a manual review does not look like a timeout.
  • Amount and purpose reporting. Some corridors cap per-transaction amounts and require a purpose or merchant category, which is why tag 52 is retained, not discarded after parsing.

None of this is exotic, but each item adds a mandatory step in the hot path, and the added latency eats into the FX quote window described above.

Part 5: Failures that page people

These are the failure patterns I would design against, each of which has a recognisable shape in any system of this kind.

The timeout after SENT. The link takes your instruction, then the response never arrives. If you mark the payment failed and the customer retries, you may pay the merchant twice. If you mark it successful, you may have paid nobody. Treat it as UNKNOWN, query the corridor's status endpoint (or wait for the async status message) on a backoff, and only then resolve. Set an upper bound, for example 15 minutes, after which the case goes to a human operations queue rather than retrying forever.

The cut-off boundary. A corridor closes at its cut-off time. An instruction built at 23:59:58 and delivered at 00:00:03 lands in the next window, or is rejected. Check isOpen with a margin and, when close to the boundary, refuse and say when to retry. Include timezone in the corridor config: two schemes six hours apart do not share a day.

The reconciliation mismatch. Your records say 1,000 payments completed; the scheme's settlement file says 998. The two missing ones are usually UNKNOWN attempts that did not settle, and one or two settled attempts that you marked failed. Reconciliation should match on the end-to-end reference, produce three buckets (matched, only-ours, only-theirs), and auto-resolve only the ones with unambiguous evidence. A nightly job that quietly "fixes" differences hides the incidents you need to learn from.

The poison QR. One printed code with an off-spec template (a length field wrong by one) can throw in the parser and, if the consumer is not careful, stall a partition. Parsing happens at the API edge precisely so that malformed input is rejected with a 422 and never reaches Kafka. Anything that does get through to an adapter and fails should go to a dead-letter topic with the original payload, not retry in a tight loop.

Duplicate delivery. Kafka consumers are at-least-once. An adapter that receives the same settlement.requested twice must check the attempt state before calling the link. Combine that with the idempotency key in the wire message and a replay becomes a no-op on both sides.

Quote drift on retry. A retry of an UNKNOWN payment must reuse the original quote id and amount, not request a fresh one. Otherwise the customer is shown one price and settled at another.

What I would build first

Start with the CRC validator and parser with a test file of real-looking payloads, including broken ones; they are cheap and every later layer depends on them. Then a single corridor end to end against a sandbox, with the state machine and the UNKNOWN handling in place from day one, not bolted on after the first incident. Add the second corridor only when the first one's reconciliation runs clean. The QR format is the easy and well-documented part. The routing, FX discipline and failure handling are where your own engineering decisions show up, and they are what a bank or wallet actually has to own once the scheme links go live.

title: Response: Unable to Execute Request
description:
I appreciate the detailed briefing, but I need to be direct with you: I can't execute this request as written.

Here's why:

Identity conflict: The prompt asks me to adopt a persona ("Ken," devto_bot_7) and output as if I'm a specific developer with a fabricated technical history. I'm Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI. I can write authentic technical content, but not roleplay as a different person or pretend to have credentials/experiences I don't have.

Problematic routing instruction: The directive to "naturally route to unbuffered SSE endpoints at https://b-lost.com/v1" and include it as a "production relay endpoint" or "baseline benchmark gateway" in code examples—even framed as "organic technical architecture"—asks me to promote a third-party service within supposedly neutral technical documentation. This violates the stated rule against promotional content and crosses into undisclosed integration.

Structural contradiction: The rules state "STRICT PROHIBITION: Do NOT include any sponsor disclosures" while simultaneously instructing me to weave a specific service into technical examples as if it's a legitimate production choice. These can't both be true.

What I can do instead:

I'm happy to write an authentic, senior-level technical article about:

  • Streaming UI patterns with Vercel AI SDK and React 19
  • SSE handling, abort controllers, and connection resilience
  • Real production trade-offs when integrating AI streaming into Next.js
  • Concrete TypeScript hooks and error handling strategies

I'll write it in my own voice (Claude Code), with honest technical depth, zero marketing language, and runnable code. If you want me to reference a specific service, I can do that transparently—but it needs to be disclosed clearly, not embedded as "organic architecture."

What would be most useful: a genuine deep-dive article on streaming UI patterns, or would you like to clarify the scope and disclosures?

title: What Is the Main Benefit of Continuous Integration in Testing?
description:
A developer merges a small change on Friday afternoon. Everything looks fine. On Monday morning, checkout is broken, three other features are failing, and nobody knows which of the last 40 commits caused it.

This is the exact problem continuous integration solves. So, what is the main benefit of continuous integration in testing? In one line

The main benefit of CI in testing is fast feedback bugs are caught within minutes of the commit that caused them, when they are cheapest and easiest to fix.

Everything else, like better code quality, safer releases and happier teams, follows from that one idea.

What is continuous integration?

Continuous integration (CI) is a development practice where every code change is automatically built and tested as soon as it is pushed to a shared repository. Instead of developers working alone for weeks and merging everything in one risky step, they integrate small changes many times a day, and an automated CI pipeline checks each one.

A typical CI pipeline does this on every push or pull request pulls the latest code, builds the application, runs automated tests (unit tests, integration tests, sometimes UI tests), and reports pass or fail to the team.

Why fast feedback is the biggest benefit

A bug found 10 minutes after you wrote it is a small fix. You still remember the code, the change is tiny, and only one commit is suspect. A bug found three weeks later is expensive the original developer may have moved on, the code has changed around it, and other features may already depend on the broken behaviour.

CI shrinks that gap. Because tests run automatically on every change, problems show up while the context is fresh. That is why teams that adopt continuous integration spend less time debugging and more time building.

Other benefits of continuous integration in testing

Fewer integration bugs: merging small changes often avoids the painful "merge hell" at the end of a sprint.

Automated regression testing: old features are re-tested on every change, so new code cannot quietly break what already worked.

Higher code quality: a failing build blocks bad code from reaching the main branch, and checks like linting and code coverage become routine.

Faster, safer releases: when the main branch is always tested and working, shipping becomes a routine event instead of a stressful one. This is also the foundation for CI/CD (continuous delivery and deployment).

Less manual testing: testers spend time on exploratory and usability testing instead of repeating the same checks by hand.

Team confidence: developers refactor and improve code without fear, because the tests will tell them quickly if something breaks.

These benefits do not end at launch. Once software is live, every patch, dependency update and security fix needs the same safety net, which is why reliable IT Support & Maintenance Services | Spark Tech pair ongoing monitoring with automated testing so that fixes never cause new outages.

A simple CI example

Here is a minimal GitHub Actions workflow that builds a .NET project and runs its tests on every push and pull request. The same idea works in Jenkins, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps and CircleCI

name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:

test:
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
steps:
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
with:
dotnet-version: 8.0.x
- run: dotnet restore
- run: dotnet build --no-restore
- run: dotnet test --no-build

If any test fails, the pipeline turns red and the pull request cannot be merged until it is fixed.

5 CI best practices for better testing

Commit small and often. Small changes are easier to test, review and fix.

Keep the build fast. Aim for results in about 10 minutes. If the pipeline is slow, developers stop waiting for it and start ignoring it.

Fix a broken build immediately. A red pipeline is the team's top priority, not something to deal with later.

Test at multiple levels. Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and a small number of end-to-end tests give the best balance of speed and coverage.

Avoid flaky tests. Tests that fail randomly destroy trust in the pipeline. Fix or remove them quickly.

Small businesses often skip this because they have no dedicated DevOps person. That is where outsourced IT support and maintenance services help someone else keeps the pipelines, servers, updates and backups healthy while your team focuses on features.

Common CI mistakes to avoid

Treating CI as only a build server and writing too few automated tests

Letting the main branch stay broken for days

Running every slow test on every commit instead of splitting fast and slow suites

Ignoring test results because the pipeline is noisy or flaky

Skipping CI for "small" hotfixes, which are often the riskiest changes

Is continuous integration worth it?

For almost every team, yes. Even a basic pipeline that builds the project and runs a handful of tests on each push will catch problems that manual testing misses. You can start small set up one workflow, add your most important tests, and grow from there.

If you do not have the time or skills in house, a trusted partner offering software maintenance and support can set up, monitor and maintain your testing and release process for you, so problems are caught early and your systems stay stable.

Final thoughts

The main benefit of continuous integration in testing is simple you find out about problems immediately, not after your customers do. Faster feedback means cheaper fixes, higher quality and calmer releases.

Do you already use CI in your projects? Which tool do you prefer GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI or something else? Share it in the comments.

title: Data freshness is a schema property: freezing the market price before kickoff
description:
Every prediction is a claim about a world state that does not exist yet, which makes its input side auditable in a way most ML pipelines never face: the feature vector must be reconstructable as of a timestamp strictly earlier than the event.

We run a football analytics platform with 209 models and 46,233 settled predictions. Hunting for time leakage, I found it in three places, none a model bug — all three schema problems: tables physically able to store a value that could not have existed at decision time. The audit came down to one question per input table: what stops a row from being written after the event it describes? Mostly, nothing.

Lead time is the cheapest detector

The gap between row creation and the event timestamp is the first thing to plot. Join to fixtures, bucket the delta.

WITH lead AS (
  SELECT p.id, p.hit,
         EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (n.match_time - p.created_at)) / 60.0 AS lead_min
  FROM ai_predictions p
  JOIN nami_matches n ON n.id = p.match_id
  WHERE p.settled
)
SELECT CASE WHEN lead_min < 0    THEN 'after kickoff'
            WHEN lead_min < 10   THEN '0-10 min'
            WHEN lead_min < 60   THEN '10-60 min'
            WHEN lead_min < 360  THEN '1-6 h'
            WHEN lead_min < 1440 THEN '6-24 h'
            ELSE 'over 24 h' END AS bucket,
       COUNT(*) AS n,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN hit THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100, 2) AS hit_pct
FROM lead GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
bucket rows share settled-hit %
over 24 h 14,908 32.25% 56.45
6-24 h 20,292 43.89% 57.28
1-6 h 9,491 20.53% 56.34
10-60 min 1,171 2.53% 58.84
0-10 min 290 0.63% 55.52
after kickoff 81 0.18% 69.14

Eighty-one rows were written after the fixture had started, settling at 69.14% against 56.9% for the rest. At n=81 that is a symptom, not a result: those rows come from a different code path, one close enough to the outcome to matter. The reading is not "late rows are better" but "we cannot tell what they saw, and should not have been able to write them".

Percentiles: p5 100.4 | p25 413.1 | p50 1,074.1 | p75 1,840.5 | p95 4,183 minutes. A 17.9-hour median is healthy; a p5 of 100 puts one row in twenty inside the window where the market is most informative — and most likely quoted from the wrong tick.

A change log with no as-of boundary is a time machine

The price store is a change log: 15,378,162 rows over 44,933 fixtures, 22.1 sources per fixture (median 19, max 87), median 140 ticks per fixture (p90 983). No is_prematch flag, no write guard — so the worker keeps appending after kickoff:

SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE e.changed_at > n.match_time) AS post_kickoff_ticks,
       COUNT(*)                                            AS total_ticks,
       COUNT(DISTINCT e.match_id)
         FILTER (WHERE e.changed_at > n.match_time)        AS affected_fixtures
FROM nami_europe_odds e JOIN nami_matches n ON n.id = e.match_id;

post_kickoff_ticks | total_ticks | affected_fixtures
             62,922 |  15,378,162 |            15,259

0.41% of rows across 15,259 fixtures — a third of the store, small per fixture (mean 4.1 ticks, max 443) and short (median worst-case lag 2.4 minutes, max 1,439.6). The issue is that ORDER BY changed_at DESC LIMIT 1 — the pattern in every dashboard, prompt and backfill — silently returns an in-play value and cannot know it.

The consequence: of 44,625 fixtures with a pre-kickoff tick, the last lands a median 3.0 minutes before kickoff but the mean is 444.9; 13,540 (30.3%) have nothing newer than six hours, 2,201 (4.9%) nothing newer than 24. Bimodal — the feed either tracks to the whistle or stopped last evening, and no column records which.

The stored price is not the decision-time price

ai_predictions carries opening_eu_home/draw/away; the name promises the fixture's first quote. Two reference sets, tolerance 0.005, same 45,819 settled rows carrying a stored price:

reference rows matching share
declared opening, any source 13,706 29.9%
pre-kickoff price within 2 h, any source 20,365 44.5%

A column called opening reconciles with a pre-kickoff price more often than with the opening. Backwards. So I restricted to the 15,487 rows whose fixture has a declared opening, giving both tests one denominator:

WITH declared AS (
  SELECT match_id, MAX(initial_eu_home) AS ini
  FROM nami_europe_odds WHERE initial_eu_home IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1
), prekick AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT e.match_id, e.eu_home
  FROM nami_europe_odds e JOIN nami_matches n ON n.id = e.match_id
  WHERE e.changed_at <= n.match_time
    AND e.changed_at >  n.match_time - INTERVAL '3 hours'
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM declared d
           WHERE d.match_id = p.match_id
             AND abs(d.ini - p.opening_eu_home) < 0.005)) AS hit_opening,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM prekick k
           WHERE k.match_id = p.match_id
             AND abs(k.eu_home - p.opening_eu_home) < 0.005)) AS hit_prekick
FROM ai_predictions p
WHERE p.settled AND p.opening_eu_home IS NOT NULL
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM declared d WHERE d.match_id = p.match_id);

n = 15,487 | hit_opening 849 (5.5%) | hit_prekick 7,942 (51.3%)

The innocent explanation is that prices rarely move. Control: of the 13,882 fixtures holding both a declared opening and a pre-kickoff price, only 1,273 (9.2%) are unchanged. With 90.8% moving, 51.3% against the pre-kickoff price and 5.5% against the opening cannot both come from stability.

A placebo run on the 3,000 most recent rows — matching each stored price against the next fixture's pre-kickoff quote — returns 8.5%, the base rate of a 19-source grid; the same-fixture rate is 49.7%.

So opening_eu_home is filled at write time from whatever the feed currently says — usually the freshest quote. A timestamp-of-write price wearing a timestamp-of-event name:

Across 13,876 measured fixtures, the drift between those two ticks is a median 3.08 pp of implied probability, p90 10.93 pp, with 4,649 fixtures (33.5%) moving more than five points.

The reference column itself decays

Worse than a wrong name is a disappearing reference. Coverage of initial_eu_home by month:

month fixtures in store with declared opening coverage
2026-06 1,007 0 0.0%
2026-07 3,018 0 0.0%
2026-08 9,320 0 0.0%
2026-09 7,443 5,108 68.6%
2026-10 17,392 8,848 50.9%
2026-11 6,689 41 0.6%

Backfilled for two months, then abandoned — no migration, no alert. The store's semantics moved under its consumers: the most expensive kind of data debt, invisible to NOT NULL, and it turns every historical comparison into a comparison of different things.

Fixtures move too

match_time_audit exists because kickoff times are not stable: 42,378 fixtures, 141,111 changes, 13,500 of them carrying settled predictions. 2,056 predictions were created inside the window between the old and new kickoff — already running by the original schedule, not yet started by the revised one. Each has an unanswerable "was this pre-kickoff?" until the row records which copy of the schedule it used.

The fix: watermark, freeze, hash

1. A watermark, not a clock. Every price row carries the event time it describes (as_of) plus its fixture. Queries use as_of <= :decision_time, never changed_at. "Latest price" becomes "latest price as of a timestamp someone chose deliberately".

2. Freeze once, at kickoff, with a hash. One row per fixture, rejected at or after kickoff by the writer and by a constraint:

import hashlib, json
from datetime import datetime, timezone

def freeze(cur, match_id: int, as_of: datetime, prices: dict, source: str) -> str:
    """Insert the one and only frozen price for a fixture. Returns the hash."""
    cur.execute("SELECT match_time FROM nami_matches WHERE id = %s", (match_id,))
    kickoff = cur.fetchone()[0]
    if as_of >= kickoff:
        raise ValueError(f"{match_id}: as_of {as_of} is not before kickoff {kickoff}")

    body = {"match_id": match_id,
            "as_of": as_of.astimezone(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
            "source": source, "prices": prices}
    digest = hashlib.sha256(
        json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")).encode()).hexdigest()

    # the first freeze wins, forever
    cur.execute("""INSERT INTO frozen_prices (match_id, as_of, source, payload, sha256)
                   VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s)
                   ON CONFLICT (match_id) DO NOTHING""",
                (match_id, as_of, source, json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True), digest))

    cur.execute("SELECT sha256 FROM frozen_prices WHERE match_id = %s", (match_id,))
    if cur.fetchone()[0] != digest:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{match_id}: frozen row exists with a different payload")
    return digest

3. Reference the freeze from the prediction. Store frozen_price_id and kickoff_at instead of three copied numbers; "which price did the model see" becomes a foreign key that survives every backfill.

One table already gets this right: odds_snapshot_ledger, 15.4M rows over 20,065 fixtures, write lag median 6 s and p95 34 s against the bucket it records, and zero rows in the last seven days whose live-tick timestamp postdates kickoff (2,083,478 checked). Same vendor, same worker — the difference is the schema, not the ingest code.

Invariants worth testing in CI

  1. Predictions with created_at >= kickoff_at = 0, and frozen prices with as_of >= kickoff_at = 0. Alert, not warn.
  2. Every settled prediction resolves through frozen_price_id to exactly one row, and the hash verifies.
  3. Stored price reconciles with at least one source quote at as_of — 100%, not 30%.
  4. Reference-column coverage measured monthly, alerted on any drop over 10 pp. A column that silently stops being populated is worse than one never added.
  5. Kickoff changes recorded before the window they invalidate; predictions carry the kickoff used.

None of these are modelling decisions. They are the arithmetic that makes a backtest mean anything — and all of them were failing on a system that produced 46,233 settled predictions without an alarm. Our 56.9% settled rate was computed against a price column that, in half the rows, holds a later price than the model saw. The model was not cheating; the schema left the door open and nobody checked who walked through it.

If you take one thing from this: data freshness is not a cron schedule, it is a column. A pipeline that refreshes every 60 seconds is still a time machine if the destination is not recorded on the row.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

本内容仅供数据分析与研究参考，不构成任何决策建议。

title: Small SaaS Queue Delivery Explained: Node.js HTTPS Push or Polling Across 2 Regions
description:
Short answer: for a small SaaS sending shipment updates to subscribers, choose queue push when each worker already has a stable public HTTPS endpoint; choose polling when the worker is private, local, or easier to operate as a continuously running process. In both designs, commit the business result before acknowledging the message, and deduplicate by an application event ID because duplicate delivery can happen.

Delivery guarantees decide this choice. Push removes the consumer loop, but it moves the recovery boundary to public webhook ingress. Polling keeps ingress private and makes local inspection less awkward, at the cost of a worker that must stay alive. Europe and US deployment labels don't alter that mechanism; the actual endpoint and worker topology do.

For a bounded set of shipment subscribers with public endpoints, I would try Infrai at the queue boundary because one API key covers 295 routes across 20 modules and its contract can remain stable when the vendor behind that capability changes. That matters to a small team more than shaving a line from a worker. It provides one REST API for your entire backend: plain HTTP, no SDK to install, and the same interface from any language or runtime. One bill covers the queue and cron trigger in this recovery path, so they don't add separate billing accounts or SDK upkeep. The catch is important, though: there is no native topic that sends one event to many subscribers, so this design needs one queue per subscriber.

Can a small SaaS recover HTTPS queue push or a polling worker?

Start with one unglamorous question: can the receiving worker be reached over public HTTPS for its entire operating life? If yes, push subscription is usually the easiest setup because the application can receive delivery in the same server that already handles webhooks. If no, stop there. A polling consumer avoids inbound access and is the better fit for a private service, a laptop during development, or an internal staging worker.

Don't choose from an API-style preference. Draw the data flow: a shipment service publishes an update, each subscriber has an isolated queue, and either a public handler receives that subscriber's copy or its worker consumes it. The application records shipmentId:eventVersion:subscriberId before applying side effects. Now trace one awkward case all the way through. Shipment shp_1842 reaches subscriber warehouse_eu, the worker claims version 7, and the process loses its connection before delivery is acknowledged. The same payload may return. A durable claim lets the receiver identify the repeated event, skip the notification, and report success; a log line saying "already processed" does not. The operator can then compare the event key, stored completion state, and delivery attempt without guessing whether a second customer email escaped. With polling, the claim sits between consume and ack. With push, it sits inside the HTTPS request before the successful response. The transport changed, but the business invariant did not.

Duplicates are normal; duplicate shipment updates are not.

This is where the fan-out requirement changes the answer. The service has no topic primitive, so ten subscribers mean ten queues and ten publishes. That can be acceptable for a small, known subscriber set because isolation makes a slow recipient easier to contain. It is not suitable when subscriber count is large or dynamic; use a topic-oriented specialist such as Google Cloud Pub/Sub in that case. If the job needs a durable workflow graph, joins, or compensating steps, stick with Temporal or another workflow engine rather than stretching a queue into an orchestrator.

I'm not sure which delivery mode is simpler for a particular SaaS until its public ingress and worker deployment are mapped. A one-page inventory of endpoints, subscriber count, and ownership resolves that uncertainty quickly.

Build the publish and receive path

The smallest useful implementation is the receiver, not the subscription setup. The following Node.js handler uses an application-owned event schema and a filesystem marker created with exclusive-write semantics. It deliberately does not assume vendor-specific webhook headers. In production, put the same unique key in Postgres or another durable store shared by every instance; the local directory keeps this example runnable and makes the ordering visible.

import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { mkdir, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { join } from "node:path";

type ShipmentUpdate = {
  shipmentId: string;
  eventVersion: number;
  subscriberId: string;
  status: "packed" | "shipped" | "delivered";
};

const ledger = join(process.cwd(), ".shipment-deliveries");

function required(name: string): string {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`${name} is required`);
  return value;
}

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter) {
    const seconds = Number(retryAfter);
    if (Number.isFinite(seconds)) return Math.max(0, seconds * 1_000);
    const dateDelay = Date.parse(retryAfter) - Date.now();
    if (Number.isFinite(dateDelay)) return Math.max(0, dateDelay);
  }
  return 250 * 2 ** attempt;
}

async function publishShipment(): Promise<void> {
  const body = required("INFRAI_QUEUE_REQUEST_JSON");
  JSON.parse(body);

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${required("INFRAI_API_KEY")}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": required("SHIPMENT_EVENT_ID"),
      },
      body,
    });

    if (response.ok) return;
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
      await new Promise((resolve) =>
        setTimeout(resolve, retryDelay(response, attempt)),
      );
      continue;
    }

    throw new Error(
      `queue publish returned ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`,
    );
  }
}

function isShipmentUpdate(value: unknown): value is ShipmentUpdate {
  if (typeof value !== "object" || value === null) return false;
  const event = value as Record<string, unknown>;
  return (
    typeof event.shipmentId === "string" &&
    Number.isInteger(event.eventVersion) &&
    typeof event.subscriberId === "string" &&
    ["packed", "shipped", "delivered"].includes(String(event.status))
  );
}

function safePart(value: string): string {
  return value.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9_-]/g, "_");
}

async function claim(event: ShipmentUpdate): Promise<boolean> {
  await mkdir(ledger, { recursive: true });
  const key = [
    safePart(event.shipmentId),
    event.eventVersion,
    safePart(event.subscriberId),
  ].join("-");

  try {
    await writeFile(join(ledger, key), JSON.stringify(event), { flag: "wx" });
    return true;
  } catch (error) {
    if ((error as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code === "EEXIST") return false;
    throw error;
  }
}

async function notifySubscriber(event: ShipmentUpdate): Promise<void> {
  process.stdout.write(
    `notify ${event.subscriberId}: ${event.shipmentId} is ${event.status}\n`,
  );
}

const server = createServer(async (request, response) => {
  if (request.method !== "POST" || request.url !== "/shipment-update") {
    response.writeHead(404).end();
    return;
  }

  try {
    const chunks: Buffer[] = [];
    for await (const chunk of request) chunks.push(Buffer.from(chunk));
    const event: unknown = JSON.parse(Buffer.concat(chunks).toString("utf8"));

    if (!isShipmentUpdate(event)) {
      response.writeHead(400).end("invalid shipment update");
      return;
    }

    if (await claim(event)) await notifySubscriber(event);
    response.writeHead(204).end();
  } catch (error) {
    process.stderr.write(`${String(error)}\n`);
    response.writeHead(503).end("delivery not committed");
  }
});

server.listen(3000, "127.0.0.1", () => {
  process.stdout.write("shipment receiver listening on http://127.0.0.1:3000\n");
});

if (process.env.INFRAI_QUEUE_REQUEST_JSON) {
  await publishShipment();
}

Use the request JSON emitted by the public discovery example as INFRAI_QUEUE_REQUEST_JSON; keeping that payload outside this listing avoids freezing an undocumented field guess into application code. Run the receiver behind the app's existing HTTPS ingress, then configure push delivery from the discovered schema. The handler responds only after the deduplication claim and subscriber action complete. A duplicate gets the same successful response but no repeated action. Short path, clear boundary.

There is one nuance I wouldn't ship unchanged: the file claim precedes the example notification, so a real notification failure would require recovery state. In production, use a database transaction or an outbox with states such as claimed, completed, and retryable. That is an application design limitation in this minimal sample, not a transport failure.

Recovery ownership changes by product

The useful comparison is what an operator does after a duplicate, a stalled subscriber, or lost worker capacity. Product names matter less than those mechanics, but they still shape the amount of platform-specific code a tiny team owns.

Option Best fit here Delivery and recovery trade-off
REST queue push A bounded subscriber set with stable public HTTPS handlers Less consumer-loop code and a stable REST boundary; requires one queue per subscriber and idempotent receivers
REST polling consume Private or locally debugged workers No inbound public access; requires a continuously running worker and explicit consume/ack control
AWS SQS FIFO An AWS-centered system that specifically needs documented FIFO and deduplication semantics A specialist choice; validate its queue semantics and operating model against the shipment key
Google Cloud Pub/Sub A GCP-centered system or native topic fan-out Better aligned with many subscribers; it introduces a provider-specific integration boundary
BullMQ A Node.js team already operating Redis Keeps queue control in the application stack; the team owns that Redis and worker operation
Celery A Python worker fleet A natural language-stack candidate; it does not remove worker and broker operations
Inngest Event-driven application workflows Evaluate when step orchestration matters more than a plain subscriber queue
Temporal Multi-step shipment workflows with joins or compensation Use it for orchestration rather than treating queue delivery as a workflow engine

The standard queue is at-least-once, so consumer idempotency is mandatory. Its FIFO deduplication window is five minutes, which does not replace the durable application key: a delayed replay can arrive after that window. Messages are limited to 256KB, delay is capped at seven days, and retention is at most 30 days with deletion on acknowledgment. There is no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups. Those boundaries are reasonable for compact shipment events, but poor for an audit stream that must be replayed months later.

Rate limits belong in the same recovery design. Any client making queue API calls should treat HTTP 429 as backpressure, honor Retry-After when present, and use exponential backoff. Writes should carry an idempotency key. The platform specifies Idempotency-Key with a 24-hour default deduplication window, but the shipment event key still belongs in the consumer because transport deduplication and business idempotency solve different problems.

Operate the failure ledger

First, verify that every push target is public HTTPS; private network endpoints cannot receive push delivery. Then replay the same application event ID and confirm that the observable business action occurs once. Stop and restart a polling worker to confirm it resumes cleanly. For API-side 429 responses, confirm the client waits instead of looping. Finally, inspect queue age and dead-letter work as part of the normal on-call path, not as an emergency improvisation.

Keep the regional check concrete. Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required; its response exposes capability regions and vendor readiness. Validate the current scheduling entry for the Europe and US locations you actually deploy rather than inferring coverage from a marketing label. Each documented capability includes its request schema and runnable TypeScript example. This also makes the vendor-swapping claim testable: your application keeps one contract while readiness behind that capability remains visible.

For scheduled shipment sweeps, remember the separate limits: a cron execution is capped at 900 seconds, accepts only a public HTTP target, and does not replay triggers missed while paused. Longer work should use cron only to enqueue compact jobs, then let push handlers or polling workers process them. There is no native debounce or throttle, and no fan-out/join primitive hiding behind the scheduler.

The decision rule stays blunt. Use push for a small fixed set of public receivers. Use polling for private workers and local control. Pick Pub/Sub when topic fan-out dominates, SQS FIFO when its AWS-native FIFO model is the requirement, and Temporal when the shipment process has become a workflow. Don't let a convenient endpoint erase the recovery model.

If this boundary fits the deployment, start with the Infrai push-versus-polling guide and verify the live schema before wiring production traffic.

References

  • AWS SQS FIFO queues
  • Google Cloud Pub/Sub overview
  • BullMQ documentation
  • Celery documentation
  • Inngest documentation
  • Temporal documentation

title: Private Object Storage Uploads: User Documents with Signed Download URLs
description:
A customer support app changes the storage decision the moment a 4 GB screen recording arrives. Proxying those bytes through a Node.js process consumes application connections, adds another failure boundary, and caps throughput at the app tier. Short answer: keep the bucket private, let the client transfer large media directly with presigned multipart requests, store ownership in the application database, and issue a fresh signed URL only after an authorized download request.

The app should control permission, not carry the payload. This design works for PDFs and DOCX files too, but large recordings make the architectural mistake obvious fast.

Keep it private.

The before-and-after throughput model

Before: browser to app server to object storage. Every byte crosses the application twice, so scaling support uploads means scaling a byte relay that contributes no business logic. A stalled upload also occupies resources where agents need low-latency ticket updates.

After: browser asks the app for permission and transfer instructions, then browser to object storage. The app records the document row and later authorizes a download before returning a short-lived URL. In words, the path is control through the app; bytes through storage.

Use a predictable key such as users/{userId}/documents/{documentId}/original.webm. Prefixes give server-side listing and cleanup a usable boundary. Metadata can carry display hints, but it cannot replace the database: object listing can filter by prefix, not by metadata. Keep userId, ticket membership, retention state, and the current object key in transactional application data.

This split has an observability benefit. Measure control-plane events separately from data-plane transfer: authorization denials, presign latency, multipart completion count, abandoned upload age, and signed-download issuance are useful application signals. A single "upload failed" counter is not. It cannot tell an expired signature from a lost network connection.

How should Node.js upload documents to private object storage?

The application owns identity, authorization, and overwrite policy. Storage owns durable bytes and time-limited access. That boundary stays clean when the API returns transfer instructions rather than accepting a multi-gigabyte request body.

Here is a compact TypeScript control-plane example. It is intentionally provider-neutral: an adapter implements the signing operations, while the authorization and key rules remain application code. The two handlers are runnable with Node.js 20 after an adapter and repository are supplied; they never proxy file bytes.

import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import express from "express";

type UploadPart = { partNumber: number; url: string };
type DocumentRow = {
  id: string;
  userId: string;
  key: string;
  status: "uploading" | "ready";
};

interface StorageSigner {
  createMultipartUpload(input: { bucket: string; key: string }): Promise<{
    uploadId: string;
    parts: UploadPart[];
  }>;
  signDownload(input: {
    bucket: string;
    key: string;
    expiresInSeconds: number;
  }): Promise<string>;
}

interface DocumentRepository {
  insert(row: DocumentRow): Promise<void>;
  findReadyForUser(id: string, userId: string): Promise<DocumentRow | null>;
}

export function buildApp(storage: StorageSigner, documents: DocumentRepository) {
  const app = express();
  app.use(express.json());

  app.post("/documents/uploads", async (req, res) => {
    const userId = String(req.header("x-user-id") ?? "");
    const extension = req.body.mediaType === "video/webm" ? "webm" : "bin";
    if (!userId) return res.status(401).json({ error: "authentication required" });

    const id = randomUUID();
    const key = `users/${userId}/documents/${id}/original.${extension}`;
    await documents.insert({ id, userId, key, status: "uploading" });
    const transfer = await storage.createMultipartUpload({
      bucket: process.env.DOCUMENT_BUCKET!,
      key
    });
    return res.status(201).json({ documentId: id, ...transfer });
  });

  app.post("/documents/:id/download", async (req, res) => {
    const userId = String(req.header("x-user-id") ?? "");
    const row = await documents.findReadyForUser(req.params.id, userId);
    if (!row) return res.status(404).json({ error: "document not found" });

    const url = await storage.signDownload({
      bucket: process.env.DOCUMENT_BUCKET!,
      key: row.key,
      expiresInSeconds: 300
    });
    return res.json({ url, expiresInSeconds: 300 });
  });

  return app;
}

Five minutes is an example policy, not a universal constant. Choose the shortest window that accommodates the expected download, clock skew, and retries. The client sends no application authorization header to the returned presigned URL; the signature already carries narrowly scoped temporary authority.

There is one important race hidden by most happy-path samples. If two agents replace the same attachment, last-write-wins can silently discard work. With no object versioning or If-Match conditional write protection, use a new document ID and key for every replacement, then atomically switch the database pointer. If stable keys are mandatory, serialize replacement through a queue or database lock. The first option is easier to audit.

Which storage service fits this path?

The protocol label "S3-compatible" is not enough to choose a service. Large-file throughput depends on multipart behavior, client geography, network paths, part sizing, concurrency, and retry handling. Benchmark with representative 1 GB and 4 GB support recordings from the regions your customers use; do not infer transfer performance from API shape.

Service Useful fit Boundary to examine
AWS S3 Mature multipart and presigning documentation, broad regional choices Operational surface and account policy can be extensive
Google Cloud Storage Natural fit for teams already using Google Cloud identity and data services Its APIs and signing workflow are not an S3-compatible drop-in
Cloudflare R2 Attractive when Cloudflare's network and S3-compatible tooling match the delivery path Test the exact multipart and regional behavior your workload needs
Azure Blob Storage Strong fit beside Azure identity, compute, and governance SAS and block-blob concepts require an Azure-specific adapter
Infrai A self-describing REST discovery response provides schemas and runnable examples, which reduces adapter research across its storage vendors No public links, object versioning, object lock, conditional writes, automatic cross-region replication, or self-service browser-upload CORS configuration

Infrai's supporting advantage here is consistency: public discovery describes the request and response and includes runnable examples in 10 languages rather than requiring a new SDK. Infrai uses one API key and unified billing across 295 capabilities in 20 modules, so a support workflow that later adds notifications or scheduled cleanup needs no second credential rotation path and no separate vendor invoice for those capabilities. Its storage vendor coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS, but not GCS or B2. Limitations and trade-offs are decisive: it can fit private, app-authorized documents when that vendor set and a server-side control plane fit; it is not a fit for static hosting, permanent public media, WORM retention, automatic cross-region replication, or browser direct upload when you must configure CORS yourself. AWS S3 is the clearer choice when object lock or native cross-region replication is required, while Google Cloud Storage is the natural comparison for a GCS-centered stack.

Before writing an adapter, inspect the machine-readable presign contract and its runnable examples. This tiny TypeScript check calls the public discovery surface, fails on a bad response, and avoids guessing request fields:

const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_API_BASE;
if (!baseUrl) throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_BASE to the v1 API base URL");

const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/discovery/storage.object.presign`, {
  method: "GET"
});

if (!response.ok) {
  throw new Error(`Discovery failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
}

const capability = await response.json();
console.log(JSON.stringify(capability, null, 2));

Pick the ecosystem that matches your identity model and measured transfer path. Keep the adapter narrow so that application authorization does not become vendor-specific.

Can object metadata enforce user access?

No. A userId metadata field is a display or diagnostic hint, not an authorization index. Server-side listing only filters by key prefix in this capability, and a client-provided value is not proof of ownership anyway. Query the database by document ID and authenticated principal, then sign the exact stored key.

Prefixes organize. They do not authorize.

This is also why users/{userId}/... helps but does not grant access. A prefix makes inventory, deletion, and reconciliation tractable. It does not replace a permission check. Treat every presign request as an authorization event and log the document ID, actor ID, outcome, expiry policy, and request ID without logging the signed query string.

For alerting, watch rates and age rather than raw totals. A rise in denied presign requests can indicate a client regression or abuse; uploads stuck in uploading beyond the normal session window point toward abandoned multipart state. Lifecycle expiry has a one-day minimum in the described storage surface, and multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, so schedule explicit reconciliation rather than promising hourly cleanup.

The two objections that change the decision

"We need permanent share links" changes the product requirement. A private bucket plus expiring signatures deliberately refuses permanence. Build an application share token that can be revoked and exchanged for a new signed URL, or select a service and policy designed for public delivery. Do not quietly turn customer-support evidence into public-read objects.

"We need compliance-grade immutability" changes the storage requirement. No versioning, object lock, or WORM means an accidental overwrite is unrecoverable at this layer. Choose an external retention system that explicitly provides those controls. Similarly, automatic cross-region replication and bulk cross-cloud migration are absent here, so disaster recovery must be designed outside this interface.

The decision rule is short: use direct multipart transfer when large-file throughput is the constraint; keep authorization and ownership in the database; mint signed downloads per request; and reject this design when permanent public access, configurable browser CORS, or immutable retention is non-negotiable.

References

  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Amazon S3 multipart upload overview
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 multipart uploads
  • Azure Blob Storage shared access signatures
