title: React Router: Pages That Change Without Reloading
description:
Open a shop site and click a product. The address bar changes, the page changes, and nothing reloads. Visitors expect that smooth switch now, and it is what makes a single-page app feel finished rather than half built. Without a router, the usual workaround is a pile of state: a variable holding the current view, a switch statement rendering one component or another, and links that are really buttons wearing a disguise. It works for two pages, then starts to creak. The address bar never changes, so a visitor cannot bookmark a product, share its link, or use the back button properly. React Router closes exactly that gap, and the question is when it is worth adding.

What I would check before using it

My first check is how many views the app really has. One page with a couple of panels does not need a router, and adding one just adds a dependency to keep updated. Three or more distinct views is where a router starts earning its place. Count the pages before reaching for the library.

My second check is whether the URLs need to mean anything. A shop lives on shareable links: a customer sends a product page to a friend, a search engine indexes it, a visitor bookmarks it. If the address bar never changes, none of that works, and the app is quietly broken for everyone who treats a URL as an address. If nobody shares or bookmarks a view, a router buys little.

My third check is the learning curve, and React Router is gentle here. The example below rests on four ideas: Routes and Route to map paths to components, Link to move between them, and useParams to read a value out of the URL. Anyone who knows React can read that code on the first pass. The cost is a dependency and a little setup.

My fourth check is the layout. Most apps repeat the same header and footer on every page, and React Router lets one layout component wrap the changing content instead of copying it into every view.

My verdict, as judgement: use React Router when an app has several views, when those views deserve real URLs, and when a shared layout would cut repetition. Skip it for a single view or a page that nobody links to. The recommendation flips when the page count drops to one, or the URLs stop mattering, because then the router is a dependency with no job to do.

One small shop, three routes, run end to end

The example is a small shop with three routes: the home page at /, a product list at /products, and a product detail page at /products/:id, where :id is a URL parameter read with useParams. The products are a canvas tote bag at $18, a ceramic mug at $14.50, and a notebook set at $9.25. Everything runs in plain Node with MemoryRouter and ReactDOMServer renderToString, so no browser and no build step are needed. MemoryRouter stands in for the BrowserRouter a real app would use, and every Link and useParams call sits inside it, because a Link rendered outside a router throws a cryptic error about a null context instead of rendering anything.

Here is the whole app:

const React = require("react");
const { renderToString } = require("react-dom/server");
const { MemoryRouter, Routes, Route, Link, useParams } = require("react-router");

const products = [
  { id: "1", name: "Canvas tote bag", price: 18.0 },
  { id: "2", name: "Ceramic mug", price: 14.5 },
  { id: "3", name: "Notebook set", price: 9.25 },
];

function Home() {
  return React.createElement("div", null,
    React.createElement("h1", null, "The Corner Shop"),
    React.createElement("p", null, "Three useful things, fairly priced."),
    React.createElement(Link, { to: "/products" }, "Browse products"));
}

function ProductList() {
  return React.createElement("div", null,
    React.createElement("h1", null, "Products"),
    React.createElement("ul", null,
      products.map((p) =>
        React.createElement("li", { key: p.id },
          React.createElement(Link, { to: "/products/" + p.id },
            p.name + " - $" + p.price.toFixed(2))))));
}

function ProductDetail() {
  const { id } = useParams();
  const product = products.find((p) => p.id === id);
  if (!product) {
    return React.createElement("div", null,
      React.createElement("h1", null, "Product not found"),
      React.createElement("p", null, "No product has id " + id + "."),
      React.createElement(Link, { to: "/products" }, "Back to products"));
  }
  return React.createElement("div", null,
    React.createElement("h1", null, product.name),
    React.createElement("p", null, "Price: $" + product.price.toFixed(2)),
    React.createElement(Link, { to: "/products" }, "Back to products"));
}

function NotFound() {
  return React.createElement("div", null,
    React.createElement("h1", null, "Page not found"),
    React.createElement(Link, { to: "/" }, "Back home"));
}

function App() {
  return React.createElement(Routes, null,
    React.createElement(Route, { path: "/", element: React.createElement(Home) }),
    React.createElement(Route, { path: "/products", element: React.createElement(ProductList) }),
    React.createElement(Route, { path: "/products/:id", element: React.createElement(ProductDetail) }),
    React.createElement(Route, { path: "*", element: React.createElement(NotFound) }));
}

for (const path of process.argv.slice(2)) {
  console.log("=== " + path + " ===");
  console.log(renderToString(
    React.createElement(MemoryRouter, { initialEntries: [path] },
      React.createElement(App))));
}

This is the real output from running it with Node, for the home page and the ceramic mug detail page:

=== / ===
<div><h1>The Corner Shop</h1><p>Three useful things, fairly priced.</p><a href="/products" data-discover="true">Browse products</a></div>
=== /products/2 ===
<div><h1>Ceramic mug</h1><p>Price: $14.50</p><a href="/products" data-discover="true">Back to products</a></div>

Two things are worth noticing. First, the URL parameter did real work: visiting /products/2 rendered the ceramic mug and its $14.50 price, pulled from the same products array as the list, so the list and the detail page can never disagree about a price. Second, the Link components rendered as ordinary anchor tags with the right href, which is why the back button and bookmarks keep working: the router is built on plain links, not on a trick.

The thing that went wrong came from the first version of this app, which had no catch-all route and no guard for a missing product. Visiting an unknown address rendered a blank page, with no error and no message, and visiting /products/999 crashed outright. Here is the real output from that broken run:

=== /nowhere ===

=== /products/999 ===
ERROR: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')

The blank page is the nastier of the two. The crash at least tells you something failed, but a blank page looks like the app loaded and chose to show nothing, so a visitor just leaves. The fix is two small additions: a route with path "*" that renders a "Page not found" message, and a guard in ProductDetail that checks whether the product exists before reading its name. After adding both, the same paths render properly, as the full run showed: /products/999 gives "Product not found" with a link back to the list, and /nowhere gives "Page not found" with a link home. Unknown URLs and unknown ids are normal traffic, not edge cases, so both guards belong in the app from the start.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, leaving out the catch-all route, as in the broken run above. The symptom is a blank page on any mistyped or outdated URL, with no error anywhere to point at. The fix is a Route with path "*" at the end of the Routes list, rendering a helpful not-found page with a link home.

Second, trusting the URL parameter without checking it. The symptom is a crash, "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')", when a visitor opens a product id that does not exist, because find returns undefined and the code reads a property off it. The fix is the guard shown above: look the product up, and if it is missing, render a not-found message instead of the detail view.

Third, using a plain anchor tag instead of Link for navigation inside the app. The symptom is a full page reload on every click, which throws away the app state and defeats the whole point of a router. The fix is to use Link for every in-app move, and save plain anchor tags for links that leave the site.

My call on React Router

React Router turns the address bar into a real part of the app instead of a decoration. The shop above needed four ideas, three routes, and two small guards, and every URL now leads somewhere sensible, including the wrong ones. That is the whole job, and the library does it without asking the app to change shape. Try it on a project with three or more views that people share links to, and watch the back button start behaving. If the app has one view and nobody links to it, skip the router and keep the code plain. The router is worth it when the URL matters, and not a moment sooner.

Further reading

  • React Router documentation, https://reactrouter.com/
  • React docs, Learn React, https://react.dev/learn
  • React docs, Adding Interactivity, https://react.dev/learn/adding-interactivity

Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/react-router-pages-that-change-without.html

title: DTOs, Validation & Pipes in NestJS: Ensuring Data Integrity at the API Boundary
description:
Introduction

When developing backend applications, receiving data from clients is a common operation. However, we cannot always trust the data sent by clients.

For example, imagine building a Task Management API. A client sends a request to create a task:

{
  "title": 12345,
  "description": "Learn NestJS"
}

The title should be a string, but the client has sent a number.

If our backend accepts this data without checking it, invalid information can enter our application and cause unexpected problems.

NestJS provides several features to handle this situation:

  • DTOs (Data Transfer Objects)
  • class-validator
  • class-transformer
  • Built-in Pipes
  • Custom Pipes
  • Global ValidationPipe

These features help ensure that incoming data is validated and transformed before reaching the business logic.

1. What is a DTO (Data Transfer Object)?

DTO stands for Data Transfer Object.

A DTO is a class that defines the expected structure of data transferred between the client and server.

It specifies which properties should be included in a request and their expected TypeScript types.

Example

Consider a task creation request.

Create a file called create-task.dto.ts:

export class CreateTaskDto {
  title!: string;
  description?: string;
}

Explanation:

  • title is a required string property.
  • description is an optional string property.
  • ! tells TypeScript that the property will be initialized elsewhere.
  • ? indicates that a property is optional.

When a client sends a request, the DTO describes the expected data structure.

Why do we use DTOs?

  1. Maintain a consistent request structure.
  2. Separate request data from business logic.
  3. Improve code readability and maintainability.
  4. Make validation easier.
  5. Avoid directly accepting arbitrary client data.

An important point is that TypeScript types alone do not validate incoming JSON at runtime. For runtime validation, we need validation decorators and a validation mechanism.

2. What is class-validator?

class-validator is a library used to validate class properties using decorators.

It allows developers to define rules for incoming data.

Installation 

npm install class-validator class-transformer

Example

Update create-task.dto.ts:

import {
  IsString,
  IsNotEmpty,
  IsOptional,
  MaxLength,
} from 'class-validator';

export class CreateTaskDto {
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  @MaxLength(100)
  title!: string;

  @IsOptional()
  @IsString()
  @MaxLength(500)
  description?: string;
}

Understanding validation decorators

Decorator Purpose
@IsString() Checks whether a value is a string
@IsNotEmpty() Prevents empty values
@IsOptional() Makes a property optional
@IsBoolean() Checks whether a value is Boolean
@IsNumber() Checks whether a value is a number
@IsEmail() Validates an email address
@MinLength() Specifies minimum string length
@MaxLength() Specifies maximum string length

For example:

@IsString()
title!: string;

This tells the validation system that the title property must contain a string.

If the client sends a number instead, validation fails.

3. What is class-transformer?

class-transformer is a library that converts plain JavaScript objects into class instances and can transform values into the required types.

When a client sends JSON, the received body is initially a plain JavaScript object.

However, class-validator works with class instances and their decorator metadata.

class-transformer helps convert the incoming object into an instance of the corresponding DTO class.

For example:

import { plainToInstance } from 'class-transformer';

const requestData = {
  title: 'Learn NestJS',
  description: 'Practice validation',
};

const taskDto = plainToInstance(
  CreateTaskDto,
  requestData,
);

Now taskDto is an instance of CreateTaskDto.

Difference between class-validator and class-transformer:

  • class-validator checks whether data follows the defined rules.
  • class-transformer converts plain objects into class instances and supports data transformation.

They are commonly used together in NestJS applications.

4. What are Pipes in NestJS?

Pipes are special components in NestJS that execute before a controller method.

They are mainly used for two purposes:

  1. Validation – checking whether incoming data is valid.
  2. Transformation – converting incoming data into the required format.

For example, consider this endpoint:

@Get(':id')
findOne(
  @Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number,
) {
  return this.tasksService.findOne(id);
}

When the client sends:

GET /tasks/10

The URL parameter 10 initially arrives as a string.

ParseIntPipe converts it into the number 10.

If the client sends:

GET /tasks/hello

The pipe rejects the invalid value and NestJS returns a 400 Bad Request response.

Why are Pipes useful?

  • Validate incoming parameters.
  • Convert values into appropriate types.
  • Reject invalid data before it reaches the controller.
  • Keep controllers clean and readable.

5. Types of Pipes in NestJS

NestJS provides built-in pipes and also allows developers to create custom pipes.

A. Built-in Pipes

Some commonly used built-in pipes are:

Pipe Purpose
ValidationPipe Validates incoming DTO data
ParseIntPipe Converts a value into an integer
ParseBoolPipe Converts a value into a Boolean
ParseUUIDPipe Validates UUID values
ParseFloatPipe Converts a value into a floating-point number
DefaultValuePipe Provides a default value when input is missing

Example:

@Get(':id')
findOne(
  @Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number,
) {
  return this.tasksService.findOne(id);
}

Here, ParseIntPipe ensures that the ID is a valid integer.

B. Custom Pipes

Sometimes built-in pipes are not sufficient for application-specific requirements.

In such situations, we can create our own custom pipes.

For example, imagine that a task ID must always be a positive integer.

We can create a custom pipe:

import {
  PipeTransform,
  Injectable,
  BadRequestException,
} from '@nestjs/common';

@Injectable()
export class PositiveIntPipe
  implements PipeTransform {

  transform(value: number) {
    if (
      !Number.isInteger(value) ||
      value <= 0
    ) {
      throw new BadRequestException(
        'ID must be a positive integer',
      );
    }

    return value;
  }
}

Usage:

@Get(':id')
findOne(
  @Param('id', ParseIntPipe, PositiveIntPipe)
  id: number,
) {
  return this.tasksService.findOne(id);
}

The value first passes through ParseIntPipe, then through PositiveIntPipe.

If it is not a positive integer, the custom pipe rejects it.

Important: Custom pipes implement the PipeTransform interface and define their logic inside the transform() method.

6. What is ValidationPipe?

ValidationPipe is a built-in NestJS pipe that automatically validates incoming request data against DTO validation rules.

Instead of manually checking every property inside every controller method, we can configure validation centrally.

Global ValidationPipe Setup

Open src/main.ts:

import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';
import { ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);

  app.useGlobalPipes(
    new ValidationPipe({
      whitelist: true,
      forbidNonWhitelisted: true,
      transform: true,
    }),
  );

  await app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
}

bootstrap();

This configuration applies validation to incoming requests across the application.

Understanding the configuration options

1. whitelist: true

Removes properties that do not have validation decorators in the DTO.

2. forbidNonWhitelisted: true

Instead of silently removing unexpected properties, it rejects the request with a 400 Bad Request response.

3. transform: true

Transforms incoming plain objects into DTO class instances. It also enables supported type transformations.

These options help protect the application from unexpected or invalid request data.

7. Practical Example: Create and Update Task DTOs

Let's apply these concepts to a Task Management API.

CreateTaskDto 

import {
  IsString,
  IsNotEmpty,
  IsOptional,
  MaxLength,
} from 'class-validator';

export class CreateTaskDto {
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  @MaxLength(100)
  title!: string;

  @IsOptional()
  @IsString()
  @MaxLength(500)
  description?: string;
}

UpdateTaskDto 

import {
  IsString,
  IsOptional,
  IsBoolean,
  IsNotEmpty,
  MaxLength,
} from 'class-validator';

export class UpdateTaskDto {
  @IsOptional()
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  @MaxLength(100)
  title?: string;

  @IsOptional()
  @IsString()
  @MaxLength(500)
  description?: string;

  @IsOptional()
  @IsBoolean()
  completed?: boolean;
}

Why are all the update properties optional?

Because a client might only want to update the completion status without changing the title or description.

For example:

{
  "completed": true
}

This is a valid partial update.

8. Testing Validation Using Thunder Client

After configuring the global ValidationPipe, we can test our API using Thunder Client.

Valid Request

Method: POST

Endpoint:

http://localhost:3000/tasks

Body:

{
  "title": "Learn NestJS",
  "description": "Practice DTO validation"
}

Expected result:

  • Status: 201 Created
  • Task is created successfully.

Invalid Request: Wrong Data Type 

{
  "title": 12345,
  "description": "Practice NestJS"
}

Expected result:

  • Status: 400 Bad Request
  • The request is rejected because the title is not a string.

Invalid Request: Empty Title 

{
  "title": "",
  "description": "Practice validation"
}

Expected result:

  • Status: 400 Bad Request
  • The title cannot be empty.

Invalid Request: Unexpected Property 

{
  "title": "Learn NestJS",
  "description": "Practice validation",
  "randomField": "unexpected data"
}

Expected result:

  • Status: 400 Bad Request
  • The unexpected property is rejected because forbidNonWhitelisted is enabled.

9. Data Integrity at the Boundary

Data integrity at the boundary means validating incoming data as soon as it enters the backend application.

We should not allow invalid data to travel through the application and reach the business logic or database.

The general request flow is:

Client / Thunder Client
          |
          v
     HTTP Request
          |
          v
     ValidationPipe
          |
          v
     DTO Validation
          |
          v
     Controller
          |
          v
       Service
          |
          v
       Database

If the incoming data is invalid, the request is rejected before reaching the controller method.

This approach improves:

  • Data consistency
  • Application security
  • Error handling
  • Code maintainability
  • Reliability of backend APIs

10. Conclusion

DTOs, Validation and Pipes are important concepts in NestJS backend development.

DTOs define the expected structure of incoming data. class-validator provides validation rules, while class-transformer supports converting plain objects into class instances.

Pipes help validate and transform incoming values before they reach controller methods. Built-in pipes handle common operations, while custom pipes allow developers to implement application-specific rules.

Finally, the global ValidationPipe makes it easier to enforce validation consistently across the application.

The main takeaway is simple: Never blindly trust client input. Validate data at the application boundary before processing it.

Key Takeaways

  • DTO = Defines the expected data structure.
  • class-validator = Validates incoming data.
  • class-transformer = Transforms plain objects into class instances.
  • Pipes = Validate and transform incoming values.
  • ValidationPipe = Automatically validates DTOs.
  • Custom Pipes = Implement custom validation and transformation logic.
  • Data Integrity = Prevents invalid data from entering the application.

title: Linting a DESIGN.md before your AI coding agent reads it
description:
DESIGN.md is a Markdown file with YAML front matter that tells an AI coding agent what your UI looks like: colors, type, radii, spacing and a few components. The tokens go in the front matter, and the Markdown body says how to use them. Google publishes the format along with a CLI, @google/design.md, that lints it.

I wrote a first draft by hand for Northwind Roasters, a fictional coffee shop site I use for demos, ran the linter (v0.4.0), and fixed what it found. Here is what it caught, and what it doesn't check.

The first draft

This is the kind of file you write in five minutes from DevTools:

---
version: alpha
name: "Northwind Roasters"
colors:
  brand: "#c2410c"
  amber: "#f59e0b"
  background: "#fffaf3"
  surface: "#f6eadb"
  text: "#2b1d14"
  muted: "#7a6656"
components:
  button-primary:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.brand}"
    textColor: "#ffffff"
  badge-new:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.amber}"
    textColor: "#ffffff"
  card:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.surfce}"
    textColor: "{colors.text}"
---

Components point at tokens with {colors.name} references instead of repeating hex values, so the agent knows the card background is the surface color rather than a near-identical one.

What the linter found 

npx @google/design.md lint DESIGN.md

The summary: 1 error, 4 warnings, 3 infos. It exits with code 1, so you can fail a CI step on it. The findings, shortened:

Rule Severity Message
broken-ref error Reference {colors.surfce} does not resolve to any defined token.
missing-primary warning No 'primary' color defined. The agent will auto-generate key colors…
contrast-ratio warning textColor (#ffffff) on backgroundColor (#f59e0b) has contrast ratio 2.15:1, below WCAG AA minimum of 4.5:1.
orphaned-tokens warning 'muted' is defined but never referenced by any component.
missing-typography warning No typography tokens defined. Agents will use default font choices…
missing-sections info No 'spacing' section defined. (and the same for 'rounded')

Each one in turn:

  • broken-ref. A typo. Without the linter, the agent gets a card whose background points at nothing and has to guess.
  • missing-primary. I called my brand color brand. The format expects a color named primary, and without one the agent picks its own key colors. Renaming the token was the whole fix.
  • contrast-ratio. White on amber is 2.15:1. Amber is bright, so it works as a fill with dark text on it: #2b1d14 on the same amber is 7.59:1.
  • orphaned-tokens. muted is my caption color, but no component used it. An unused token is just a hex value with no instructions, so I added a caption component.
  • missing-typography. No fonts at all, so the agent would have used its defaults. That is the most visible miss of the lot, since the serif headings are most of this site's look.

The fixed file 

---
version: alpha
name: "Northwind Roasters"
colors:
  primary: "#c2410c"
  amber: "#f59e0b"
  background: "#fffaf3"
  surface: "#f6eadb"
  text: "#2b1d14"
  muted: "#7a6656"
typography:
  headline-display:
    fontFamily: "Fraunces"
    fontSize: 64px
    fontWeight: 600
    lineHeight: 1.04
    letterSpacing: -1.28px
  body-md:
    fontFamily: "Hanken Grotesk"
    fontSize: 17px
    fontWeight: 400
    lineHeight: 1.6
rounded:
  lg: 10px
spacing:
  base: 4px
components:
  page:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.background}"
    textColor: "{colors.text}"
  button-primary:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.primary}"
    textColor: "#ffffff"
    rounded: "{rounded.lg}"
  badge-new:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.amber}"
    textColor: "{colors.text}"
  card:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.surface}"
    textColor: "{colors.text}"
  caption:
    textColor: "{colors.muted}"
---

Lint result: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 info (the token summary). White on #c2410c for the button is 5.18:1, so that pair passes as well.

design.md diff old.md new.md gives a JSON report of what changed: brand removed, primary added, two typography tokens added, page and caption added, three components modified. It also shows the finding counts before and after (errors -1, warnings -4). That's handy for a PR description when someone edits the file.

What a clean lint doesn't tell you

Zero warnings doesn't mean the file is right. Three things I checked by hand:

Contrast is only checked inside a component. The rule looks at a component's own backgroundColor/textColor pair. My caption component only has a text color, so nothing checked it. On the page background, muted is 5.24:1. On a card it is 4.59:1, which still passes, but only just. If your agent puts captions on cards, that's the pair to check yourself.

The values have to be the real ones. The linter can't know that the body text is 17px and not 16px, or that the h1 is tracked to -1.28px. Copy those from DevTools Computed on the real site, not from memory.

Exports drop some things. design.md export --format css-tailwind turns the file into a Tailwind v4 @theme block. For this file it wrote colors, font families, sizes, tracking, weights, radius and spacing, but in v0.4.0 the lineHeight values didn't appear in the output, and the font families came out without fallbacks (--font-body-md: "Hanken Grotesk";). Add those by hand if you use the export.

Short version

  1. Name your brand color primary.
  2. Point components at tokens with {colors.x}, and give every color at least one component that uses it.
  3. Include typography; an agent can't guess your fonts.
  4. Run npx @google/design.md lint in CI, then check contrast on cards and the real values by hand.

I made a Chrome extension, Stylasso, that writes a DESIGN.md from the page you're on: real colors with roles, fonts, type scale, radii and spacing, with components referencing the tokens. The three demo-site files it generates lint with 0 errors; one gets the same white-on-violet contrast warning I'd expect, because that's what the site really uses. There's a short guide here: DESIGN.md from any website. Writing the file by hand, as above, works too.

Written with help from an AI assistant. Every lint result, diff and export above comes from running @google/design.md v0.4.0 on the files shown.

title: Building Real-Time People Tracking for Events & Venues: What Developers Actually Need to Get Right
description:
If you have ever built a check-in system for an event, you know the demo works fine — until 2,000 people arrive at once, Wi-Fi drops, and re-entry breaks your count.
‎
‎Real event & venue people tracking is not just a QR scanner. It is a distributed system problem.
‎
‎Here is the stack that actually holds up in production:
‎
‎1. Entry as an event, not a page load
‎Every scan-in / scan-out should be an immutable event: attendee_id, gate_id, zone_id, timestamp, direction. If the device goes offline, queue it locally and sync later. Never trust a live count that depends on a perfect connection.
‎
‎2. Zone-based counting, not just total headcount
‎Total venue count is useless in an emergency. You need:
‎- occupancy_by_zone
‎- capacity_by_zone
‎- flow_rate_by_gate
‎
‎That is what lets a team open an overflow hall at 85%, not at 110%.
‎
‎3. Idempotency for re-entry
‎The same wristband will be scanned twice. Use a unique scan ID and deduplicate on the server. Otherwise your dashboard will lie to you by 200-300 people, exactly like a paper clicker does.
‎
‎4. A dashboard built for stressed humans
‎During an event, no one reads a table. They need 3 things at a glance: live count vs capacity, which zone is hot, which gate is stuck. Keep it to one screen.
‎

title: Wrapping strings in t() was the easy part of translating my React app
description:
I tried getting an AI agent to internationalize a side project and spent longer checking its diff than it would have taken me to do it myself. It did the work. It also picked the languages, decided where the language files went, and chose Simplified Chinese without asking. None of that was wrong exactly, but I had to read every changed file to find out.

So I started doing it properly, and then I built a tool for it. This post is mostly the first part: the things that make i18n harder than "wrap every string in t()". The tool comes at the end.

The boring part

For a React app that wasn't built with translation in mind, the work looks like this, for every piece of text:

  1. Find the string in the JSX
  2. Make up a key for it
  3. Replace it with t('the_key')
  4. Add the key and the English text to en.json
  5. Get it translated into every other language file

Steps 1 to 4 are tedious but easy. Step 5 is where things break, and mostly not in ways you'd notice by looking at the translated text.

Plurals aren't "one or many"

English has two forms: 1 item, 2 items. So you write two keys and move on. Plenty of languages need more, and Russian shows the problem best: it has four. The form depends on the last digits of the number, so 1, 21 and 101 all use one form, 2 to 4 another, 5 to 20 a third. i18next handles this with suffixed keys, and the Russian file needs all of them:

{
  "items_one": "{{count}} товар",
  "items_few": "{{count}} товара",
  "items_many": "{{count}} товаров",
  "items_other": "{{count}} товара"
}

Arabic has six (_zero, _one, _two, _few, _many, _other). Chinese and Japanese have one.

If your Russian file only has items_one and items_other because that's what English had, nothing errors. For 5 items i18next looks for items_many, doesn't find it, and falls back: depending on your settings, Russian users get the English sentence or a missing-key string in the middle of the page.

Placeholders get translated too

"Hi {{name}}, you have {{count}} messages" contains two things that must come out exactly as they went in. Machine translation, and AI models especially, will sometimes translate the placeholder name along with the sentence: {{name}} becomes {{nombre}}. The JSON is still valid, and the app now shows an empty gap where the name should be.

The fix isn't a better prompt. It's checking every translation against the source: same placeholders, same count, and rejecting it if they differ.

Markup in the middle of a sentence 

<p>By signing up you agree to our <a href="/terms">Terms</a>.</p>

You can't translate "By signing up you agree to our" and "Terms" separately, because other languages put the link somewhere else in the sentence. In react-i18next this becomes <Trans>, and the translation file keeps the tag as a number:

"agree_terms": "By signing up you agree to our <1>Terms</1>."

Translators (human or not) can move <1>…</1> wherever the grammar needs it, as long as they don't drop or rename it. Another thing worth checking automatically.

Not every string is text

A lot of strings in a React codebase look like text and aren't: className="flex items-center", URLs, console.log messages, and product names like "GitHub" or "Markdown" that should stay as they are. Translate those and you get broken styling, or a German UI that talks about "Abschlag".

Choices nobody tells you you're making

  • zh isn't one language for this purpose. Simplified (mainland China, Singapore) and Traditional (Taiwan, Hong Kong) are written differently, and people notice.
  • Where the language files live (src/locales, public/locales) depends on how you load them.
  • If you use Next.js with the App Router, useTranslation() doesn't work in server components at all.

An agent will make these choices for you, quietly. They're all fine to make. I'd just rather make them myself.

What I ended up building

guided-i18n is a VS Code extension that does those five steps with a review in the middle:

  • A parser finds the strings locally and skips the ones that aren't text.
  • You get a checklist of every string and the key it'll get, before anything changes. Untick what should stay hardcoded.
  • It rewrites the code to t() or <Trans>, writes the JSON files, and translates them with your own API key (Anthropic, or anything OpenAI-compatible).
  • Every translation is checked for placeholders, tags and plural forms. A failure gets one retry, then it's reported instead of written.
  • Undo reverts the whole run, code and language files together.

Only the strings and a little context (file path, component name) go to the model, never whole files. A single file usually costs cents. The biggest project I tried it on was about 840 files and cost a few dollars.

Honest limits: React with react-i18next and JSON files only, for now. If you already use an AI agent and don't mind reviewing its diff, it will cover more odd cases than this does. This is for when you'd rather see every change before it happens.

It's free (you pay your AI provider directly), and it's on the VS Code Marketplace and on Open VSX for Cursor and Windsurf.

If you try it on your codebase, I'd like to hear where it gets things wrong: GitHub issues or the comments here.

title: Building a Merchant-to-Category Learning Pipeline That Runs Entirely on Your Phone
description:
When you review your monthly spending, you do not want to see a raw list of bank reference codes like UPI/CR/429810291/SWG*BLR.

You want to see:

  • Food & Dining: Rs. 12,450
  • Groceries: Rs. 8,200
  • Fuel: Rs. 4,100
  • Utilities: Rs. 3,500

To make transaction tracking effortless, an expense tracker must automatically map messy merchant strings into human-readable categories.

Commercial apps solve this by harvesting merchant data in the cloud. Every time millions of users swipe their cards, the app uploads the merchant strings to central servers, where crowdsourced tags categorize the business.

The privacy cost is immense: central servers track which coffee shops you frequent, which pharmacies you visit, and which fitness centers you attend.

Here is how FinLedger architected an on-device merchant-to-category learning pipeline (LocalCategoryIntelligenceEngine.kt, commit e4b4df2) that learns your personal categorization preferences entirely offline.

The Merchant Normalization Challenge

Before a system can categorize a merchant, it must normalize the messy strings generated by payment processors.

Consider how the same merchant appears across different banks and payment channels:

  • "SWIGGY BANGALORE IND"
  • "UPI-SWIGGY-swiggy.payu@icici-429182"
  • "POS 491029 SWIGGY FOODS"
  • "BUNDL TECHNOLOGIES PVT LTD" 
flowchart TD
    RawStrings["Raw Bank SMS Merchant Strings:
    'SWIGGY BANGALORE IND'
    'UPI-SWIGGY-swiggy.payu@icici'
    'POS 491029 SWIGGY FOODS'"] --> Normalizer["Deterministic String Normalizer:
    1. Strip payment rail prefixes (UPI-, POS, NEFT)
    2. Strip VPA handles (@icici, @okhdfc)
    3. Strip terminal IDs and location suffixes"]

    Normalizer --> CleanKey["Normalized Merchant Key:
    'SWIGGY'"]

    CleanKey --> Pipeline["Local Category Engine"]

FinLedger's normalizer strips transaction prefixes (POS, UPI, IMPS, ACH), removes VPA routing handles (@oksbi, .payu@icici), and discards dynamic terminal codes.

This extracts a clean, stable merchant root key—such as SWIGGY, ZOMATO, SHELL, or UBER—in less than 20 microseconds.

The Multi-Tiered On-Device Pipeline

Once the merchant key is normalized, the engine evaluates categorization through a prioritized three-tier hierarchy:

flowchart TD
    CleanKey["Normalized Merchant Key"] --> Tier1{"Tier 1:
    User Personal Overrides
    (Learned Local Relational Map)"}

    Tier1 -->|Found Exact Match| Result1["Apply User Learned Category
    (Confidence: 100%)"]

    Tier1 -->|Not Found| Tier2{"Tier 2:
    Pure Kotlin ML Model
    (TF-IDF + Logistic Regression)"}

    Tier2 -->|Confidence > 75%| Result2["Apply ML Inferred Category
    (Confidence: High)"]

    Tier2 -->|Uncertain| Tier3["Tier 3:
    Default Fallback
    (Flag for Review / Other)"]

Tier 1: The Local Relational Feedback Loop

The user is always the ultimate authority. If a user buys office supplies at a department store and categorizes it under Work & Business, that preference belongs to them, regardless of what a general dictionary says.

In FinLedger, whenever a user edits or confirms a transaction's category:

  1. The app updates an internal Room SQLite entity: merchant_category_preferences.
  2. The record maps the normalized merchant key (normalized_merchant) to the selected category ID (category_id), along with an incremented usage counter and last-updated timestamp.
  3. The next time an SMS arrives with that merchant key, Tier 1 intercepts it immediately. The app applies the user's custom choice with 100% confidence.

Tier 2: The Lightweight Inference Engine

For merchants the user has never encountered before, Tier 2 evaluates the normalized string and surrounding SMS context using FinLedger's pure Kotlin machine learning engine (LocalSmsIntelligenceEngine.kt).

Using sublinear TF-IDF and logistic regression, the engine detects semantic markers:

  • Keywords like "Fuel", "Petrol", "HPCL", or "IOCL" yield Transportation & Fuel.
  • Keywords like "Hospital", "Pharmacy", "Clinic", or "Medicals" yield Healthcare.
  • Keywords like "Supermarket", "Grocery", or "Mart" yield Groceries.

If the top predicted category has a calibrated Softmax probability exceeding 75%, it is assigned as the default suggestion.

Tier 3: The "Never Guess" Fallback

If the merchant is novel and the ML model is uncertain (e.g., an unfamiliar regional shop name like "Guptha & Sons"), the pipeline refuses to guess.

The transaction is assigned to General / Uncategorized and highlighted in the pending review tray with a prompt inviting the user to pick a category. The moment the user picks a category, Tier 1 learns it permanently for all future visits.

Memory and Storage Footprint

Because everything runs on SQLite and in-memory caches:

  • The local merchant dictionary occupies less than 200 KB of encrypted SQLite storage for a typical user over two years.
  • Lookup queries execute against indexed columns in less than 0.3 milliseconds.
  • No background network daemons exist; the database never syncs merchant names to external cloud servers.

Key Takeaway

A smart personal finance app does not need to send your shopping habits to the cloud to understand where you spend your money.

By combining deterministic string normalization, a local relational feedback loop, and a lightweight on-device ML engine, FinLedger creates a categorization pipeline that gets smarter with every transaction you log—without sacrificing your privacy.

FinLedger is a privacy-first, offline-first personal finance application for Android that models bank accounts, credit cards, and cash without double-counting.

Explore FinLedger on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.devanshufinance.app

title: p50, p95, p99 Explained: A Simple Guide to Latency Metrics
description:
Your dashboard says the average response time is 200 ms. Everything looks healthy. But users keep saying, "the app sometimes freezes."

Both things can be true at once. The dashboard isn't broken. The problem is that the average hides the users who are having a bad time.

In this article, we'll learn how to see those users using p50, p95 and p99. We'll start from the basics and build up step by step.

1. What is latency?

Latency is the time a request takes to get a response. You tap a button, the app asks the server for data, and the server replies. The waiting time in between is latency, usually measured in milliseconds (ms).

Lower latency means a faster app. But how do we measure it for thousands of users at once? The obvious answer is the average. Let's see why that goes wrong.

2. Why the average is misleading

Say your app handled 100 requests:

  • 90 requests took 100 ms
  • 8 requests took 500 ms
  • 2 requests took 5,000 ms (5 seconds)

The average comes out to 230 ms, which sounds fine. But look at what really happened: 10 users had a slow experience, and 2 of them stared at a loading spinner for 5 seconds.

The fast majority pulled the average down and covered up the unlucky few. We need a way to look at the slow requests directly. That's where percentiles come in.

3. What is a percentile?

Imagine all 100 requests lined up from fastest to slowest. A percentile simply tells you how fast the request at a certain position in that line was.

For example, if p90 is 300 ms, it means 90% of requests finished in 300 ms or less.

Now let's look at the ones you'll see most often.

p50: the typical experience

p50 is also called the median. Half of the requests are faster than this, and half are slower.

In our example, p50 is 100 ms. This is what a typical user experiences.

p95: the slower experience

p95 means 95% of requests are faster than this value. Only 5% are slower, which is 1 in every 20 requests.

In our example, p95 is 500 ms. So 1 in 20 users waits this long or more.

p99: the worst-case experience

p99 means 99% of requests are faster than this value. Only 1% are slower, which is 1 in every 100 requests.

In our example, p99 is 5,000 ms. The unluckiest 1% of users wait 5 seconds or more.

p99.9 and beyond

p99.9 means 99.9% of requests are faster, so only 1 in 1,000 is slower. Large companies track this too. If you serve millions of requests a day, 1 in 1,000 still means thousands of unhappy users.

All together

Metric Value What it tells us
Average 230 ms Looks fine, but hides the problem
p50 100 ms The typical user is happy
p95 500 ms 1 in 20 users waits 5x longer
p99 5,000 ms 1 in 100 users waits 50x longer

Now we see the real picture. The slow end of this list has a name: tail latency. When engineers say "we need to fix our tail," they mean the p99 and p99.9 requests.

4. "But it's only 1% of users. Why care?"

It's a fair question. There are two good answers.

Answer 1: Your slowest users are often your best users

In the book Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann shares an example from Amazon. Amazon describes the performance requirements of its internal services using the 99.9th percentile, even though that affects only 1 in 1,000 requests.

Why? Because the customers with the slowest requests are usually the ones with the most data on their accounts: the longest order history and the most purchases. In other words, they are often Amazon's most valuable customers.

Amazon has also observed that even a 100 ms slowdown can reduce sales by around 1%. For a company that size, tiny delays cost real money.

Answer 2: Small problems add up

When you open one page of a modern app, it doesn't make just one request. Behind the scenes, it may call dozens of services for your profile, prices, recommendations, stock availability, and more.

Suppose each service is slow only 1% of the time. That feels harmless. But if one page needs 100 calls, the chance that at least one of them is slow is:

1 - (0.99)^100 ≈ 63%

So a "rare" 1% problem becomes a problem for almost two out of three page loads. This is called tail latency amplification. The more services you have, the more your p99 starts to feel like your users' normal experience.

5. Why do some requests become slow?

If your code is the same for every request, why are a few so much slower? Usually the cause is something outside your business logic:

  • Garbage collection pauses that briefly freeze a program
  • Cache misses, where data has to be fetched from a slow database
  • Lock contention, where many requests fight over the same resource
  • Network hiccups like packet loss and retries
  • Queueing, where a few slow requests make faster ones wait behind them
  • Busy neighbors, where other apps on the same server use up the resources

The key point is that these problems are random and rare. That's exactly why they show up in p99 and not in the average.

6. How companies use these metrics

Teams turn percentiles into clear goals, called SLOs (Service Level Objectives). For example:

"99% of checkout requests should finish in under 300 ms."

This is much more useful than "average latency should be low," because it describes what real users feel, and everyone can measure it.

A simple way to remember which metric answers which question:

  • p50: is the app healthy in general?
  • p95: is a noticeable group of users struggling?
  • p99 / p99.9: are there hidden problems like slow queries or overloaded servers?

Companies often go one step further and write these goals into contracts with customers. These are called SLAs, and breaking them can mean refunds or penalties.

7. Common mistakes when measuring

Once you start tracking percentiles, avoid these traps:

  • Don't average percentiles. The average of the p99 from 10 servers is not your real p99. Use histograms instead, which tools like Prometheus, Datadog and OpenTelemetry support.
  • Don't chase perfection. Improving p99.99 gets very expensive. Amazon reportedly decided it wasn't worth the cost. Pick the percentile that fits your business.
  • Use enough data. A p99 calculated from 50 requests isn't reliable. You need enough traffic for the number to be stable.

Summary

  • Latency is how long a request takes.
  • The average hides slow requests, so we use percentiles instead.
  • p50 is the typical experience, p95 shows slower users, and p99 / p99.9 shows the worst cases.
  • The slow end is called tail latency, and it often affects your most valuable users.
  • In systems with many services, rare slowness becomes common.
  • Companies set SLOs on percentiles, not averages.

Next time someone says "our average latency is fine," ask them:

"What's our p99?"
