title: Why Legacy Software Is Slowing Down Your Business Growth
description:
Legacy software modernization is no longer optional, it's a survival strategy. This blog breaks down the real cost of clinging to outdated systems, the most common legacy app issues facing startups and SMEs, and what a smart software migration strategy actually looks like in 2026.

The Software That Built Your Business Might Now Be Breaking It

There's a particular kind of frustration that builds slowly in growing businesses. It usually starts as a minor annoyance: a report that takes too long to generate, an integration that never quite works the way it should, a new hire who needs two weeks just to navigate the internal system. Then, one day, you look up and realize your competitors are moving faster, serving customers better, and shipping features you can't match, not because they're smarter, but because their tools let them move.

That's the legacy software trap. And right now, it's quietly draining resources from thousands of startups and SMEs across Australia and beyond.

Legacy software doesn't announce its failures. It erodes momentum. It chips away at team productivity. It quietly inflates your IT spend while starving the innovation budget. And by the time most decision-makers see it clearly, the gap between where they are and where they need to be has grown considerably.

This article exists to make that gap visible before it becomes a crisis.

What Do We Actually Mean by "Legacy Software"?

It's worth being precise here, because the word "legacy" gets misused. Legacy software isn't simply old software. It's software that has become a liability such as systems that are difficult or expensive to modify, poorly documented, no longer supported by their original vendors, or built on architectures that can't integrate with modern tools and platforms.

For many businesses, legacy systems fall into one of three categories:

  • Custom-built platforms developed years ago that no one fully understands anymore
  • Off-the-shelf products that are end-of-life or have been abandoned by their developers
  • Patchwork stacks or combinations of old and new tools, held together by manual workarounds and a general sense of dread

In each case, the problem isn't just technical. It's strategic. Legacy software limits what your business can do, how fast it can move, and how well it can respond to change.

The Numbers That Should Concern Every Business Owner

This isn't anecdotal. The data on legacy software is striking, and it's getting harder to ignore.

According to industry research tracking legacy modernization costs, organizations typically spend 60–80% of their IT budget just maintaining legacy infrastructure. This means as little as 20 cents in every dollar actually goes toward growth, new features, or competitive innovation.

A 2025 survey of over 500 US IT professionals by Saritasa, as cited by Kissflow, found that 62% of organizations were still relying on legacy software systems, despite acknowledging known security and performance risks. Meanwhile, Gartner estimated enterprises were spending up to 70% of their IT budgets on simply "running the business" and leaving under 30% for anything forward-looking.

For SMEs, the risk profile is even steeper. IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report, as referenced by NinjaOne, put the average global breach cost at $4.88 million, and one of the most common entry points? Outdated systems with unpatched vulnerabilities. That's not a technology problem. That's a business risk.

Five Legacy App Issues That Actively Block Growth

1. Integration Failures That Multiply Over Time

Modern businesses run on interconnected tools including CRMs, payment platforms, analytics dashboards, and communication stacks. Legacy systems were rarely built with open APIs or modern integration standards. Every new tool you adopt requires a workaround, a manual export, or a custom connector that someone needs to maintain. Over time, this creates a brittle web of dependencies that breaks constantly and costs significantly to manage.

2. Security Vulnerabilities You Can't Patch Away

Old software often means unsupported software. No vendor patches. No security updates. No compliance pathway. This is particularly dangerous in sectors like healthcare, finance, and e-commerce, where regulatory obligations are rising alongside the threat landscape. Legacy systems aren't just insecure. In many jurisdictions, running them may expose your business to compliance penalties.

3. Talent Friction and Developer Debt

Developers don't want to work on legacy systems. If you're building a team or trying to attract strong engineering talent, an outdated codebase is a genuine recruiting liability. Beyond hiring, research suggests companies accrue $361,000 of technical debt for every 100,000 lines of legacy code. This pertains to debt that compounds year after year. Before you hire your next developer, it might be worth getting an independent technical health check on your existing codebase to understand exactly what you're working with.

4. Poor User Experience That Costs You Customers

If your customers interact with software you built five or ten years ago, they feel the difference even if they don't articulate it. Clunky interfaces, slow load times, mobile incompatibility, and limited self-service capabilities all create friction. In 2026, users expect the same quality of experience from a regional SME that they get from enterprise platforms. Legacy systems rarely deliver that.

5. Inability to Scale When Opportunity Arrives

Growth is rarely linear. A campaign goes viral, a new market opens up, a large client suddenly comes on board. Legacy systems fail at their worst at these moments when they are unable to scale, unable to adapt, unable to keep up. Worse, knowing this creates a kind of unconscious conservatism where founders avoid pursuing certain opportunities because they already know their systems can't handle them. And it's not just legacy platforms that create this problem. Even newer systems can buckle under pressure if they weren't built with scale in mind. Our post on why scaling your app too early can destroy product performance is a useful companion read if this particular risk resonates with you.

How Legacy Systems Compare to Modernized Alternatives

Here's a practical comparison across the dimensions that matter most to decision-makers:

The contrast isn't subtle. In almost every dimension that drives competitiveness, legacy systems lose, not because they were bad when they were built, but because the world moved on.

The Real Cost of Waiting: Why "If It Ain't Broke" Is Dangerous Thinking

Here's the argument business owners make most often for not addressing legacy app issues: "It still works." And technically, that's true. Your system processes transactions. Reports get generated. Invoices go out. Nobody's panicking. But "working" is a very low bar.

The real cost of legacy software isn't usually a catastrophic failure. It's the slow bleed of opportunity cost. It's the feature your team couldn't ship this quarter. The automation that would have saved 20 hours a week but wasn't possible on your current stack. The customer who tried your product, found it frustrating, and moved on quietly.

It's also worth acknowledging that the longer a modernization is delayed, the harder it becomes. Technical debt compounds. Developers who understood the original system retire or leave. Documentation gets lost. The codebase grows more tangled with every patch. A project that would take three months today may take nine months in two years, and cost significantly more.

According to legacy modernization research published in April 2026, AI-assisted modernization tools are now compressing project timelines dramatically, turning what was once an 18-month migration into a 5–7 month engagement. The window for cost-effective modernization is open right now in a way it hasn't been before.

What a Smart Software Migration Strategy Looks Like in 2026

A good software migration strategy in 2026 looks nothing like the big-bang replacement projects of the past. Nobody's asking you to throw everything out and start from scratch over 18 months. Modern approaches are phased, risk-managed, and designed to keep your business running while the transformation happens underneath.

The typical lifecycle for a well-run legacy modernisation engagement looks something like this:

Phase 1 — Discovery and Diagnosis
This is where you establish the true state of your system. What are the actual bottlenecks? Where is the technical debt concentrated? A structured technical code review at this stage is invaluable; it surfaces the risks before they surface themselves.

Phase 2 — Prioritisation
Not everything needs to be modernised at once. The goal is to identify which components create the most risk or limit the most growth, and address those first. This is strategic triage that’s ruthlessly practical.

Phase 3 — Incremental Modernisation
Component by component, the legacy system is replaced, refactored, or re-platformed. Modern architecture patterns (i.e. microservices, cloud-native deployment, API-first design) create systems that are extensible and maintainable.

Phase 4 — Ongoing Optimization
Modernisation isn't a destination. Once the core migration is complete, the focus shifts to continuous improvement: performance tuning, feature velocity, and building the kind of cross-platform digital experiences that your customers actually expect in 2026.

This is also worth reading alongside our recent post on the hidden costs of skipping a code audit, which digs into the compounding impact of deferred technical decisions, as well as our piece on how to know if your software project needs a rescue team, which is directly relevant if your legacy system has already started to break down in production.

Is Your Software a Bottleneck? A Quick Self-Assessment

Run through this checklist. If you check more than three boxes, your legacy system is almost certainly costing you more than you realize.

Legacy Software Warning Signs Checklist:

□ Your development team spends more time fixing bugs than shipping features
□ New integrations with third-party tools require significant custom work
□ Your system hasn't had a security audit in the last 12 months
□ Mobile functionality is limited, absent, or an afterthought
□ Onboarding new staff takes weeks because the system is unintuitive
□ You've had unplanned downtime in the past year
□ Your vendor no longer actively supports your core platform
□ You rely on manual exports or spreadsheets to bridge data between systems
□ Your developers have flagged the codebase as a risk or a barrier
□ You've delayed a product decision because you weren't sure the system could handle it

If this list feels uncomfortably familiar, you're not alone. Also worth reading: our analysis of the hidden cost of delayed software projects in 2026, which unpacks exactly what inaction costs over a 12-month window.

How Jhavtech Studios Approaches Legacy Modernization

We've worked with startups and SMEs across Australia for over a decade, and the most common thread in our engagements isn't a failed launch or a bad hire. It's a system that outgrew its original design and was never given the attention it needed to evolve.

Our approach to legacy software modernisation is direct and practical. We start with an honest, independent assessment of your current platform after which we’ll tell you what's working, what's fragile, and what's quietly costing you. We don't recommend rebuilding what doesn't need to be rebuilt. We don't sell unnecessary complexity.

What we do is help you create a clear path from where you are to where you need to be, with minimal disruption to your operations and a realistic timeline you can plan around.

When legacy systems have already started failing as indicated by missed deadlines, mounting bugs, failed deployments, our rapid stabilization and project recovery service is designed to stop the bleeding fast and restore confidence in the platform.

And if you need to extend your legacy platform into new channels, our team builds cross-platform applications designed from the ground up to integrate cleanly with both existing infrastructure and modern cloud services.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is legacy software modernization?

It's the process of updating, rebuilding, or replacing outdated software systems so they align with current business needs, security standards, and technology capabilities without necessarily replacing everything from scratch.

How do I know if my software qualifies as "legacy"?

If your system is hard to modify, no longer vendor-supported, incompatible with modern tools, or actively slowing your team down, it is legacy, regardless of its age.

How long does a typical legacy modernization project take?

With modern AI-assisted tooling, timelines have compressed significantly. Many mid-sized projects now complete in 5–7 months. A proper audit at the start gives you a realistic estimate specific to your system.

Do I have to replace everything, or can I modernize incrementally?

Incremental modernization is almost always preferable. Phased approaches let you prioritize high-risk or high-impact components first, while keeping your business operational throughout.

What's the first step if I think legacy software is impacting my business?

Start with an independent technical audit. Book a free code review with Jhavtech Studios to get a clear picture of where your system stands... quickly.

CSS Units Cheat Sheet: px, em, rem, vh, and When to Use Each
description:
Originally published on DevToolsHub — free, privacy-first online tools for developers.

CSS units can be confusing. Should you use px or rem? When does vw make sense? What about ch and ex? Picking the right unit makes the difference between a layout that breaks and one that gracefully adapts to every screen size.

This reference breaks CSS units into two categories — absolute and relative — with clear examples of when to use each. Bookmark this page for your next responsive design project.

💡 Quick Rule of Thumb

Use rem for font sizes, px for borders/shadows, % for widths, vw/vh for full-screen sections, and em for spacing relative to the current font size.

Absolute Units

Absolute units are fixed-length values. They don't scale with the viewport, parent element, or font size. Use them for print stylesheets, borders, and situations where precision matters regardless of screen size.

Unit Name Relative to Best For
px Pixel 1px = 1/96th of 1 inch (screen) Borders, shadows, small precise spacing, images
pt Point 1pt = 1/72nd of 1 inch Print stylesheets, traditional typography
pc Pica 1pc = 12pt = 1/6th of 1 inch Print layouts (rarely used on web)
cm Centimeter 1cm = 37.8px (approx) Print stylesheets, physical measurements
mm Millimeter 1mm = 1/10th of 1cm Print stylesheets
in Inch 1in = 96px Print stylesheets
Q Quarter-millimeter 1Q = 1/40th of 1cm Print, Japanese/CJK layouts

⚠️ When Not to Use px

Avoid px for font sizes in modern responsive design. Users who change their browser's default font size will see no change in pixel-sized text, which creates accessibility issues. Use rem instead — it respects the user's font size preference.

Relative Units

Relative units scale based on the context — the viewport, parent element, or root font size. They are the foundation of responsive and accessible design.

Font-Relative Units

Unit Name Relative to Best For
em Em Font size of the parent element Spacing, padding, margins relative to text size
rem Root Em Font size of the root (<html>) element Font sizes, spacing (accessibility-friendly)
ch Character Width of the '0' character in current font Input widths, line length constraints
ex X-height Height of the 'x' character in current font Vertical alignment, inline spacing
ic Ideograph Width of CJK ideograph character Chinese/Japanese/Korean text layouts
lh Line height Computed line-height of the element Vertical rhythm, consistent spacing
rlh Root line height Computed line-height of the root element Global vertical rhythm

Viewport-Relative Units

Unit Name Relative to Best For
vw Viewport Width 1% of viewport width Full-width elements, hero sections, fluid typography
vh Viewport Height 1% of viewport height Full-height sections, modal overlays, sticky elements
vmin Viewport Minimum 1% of the smaller viewport dimension (width or height) Responsive square elements, safe sizing for all orientations
vmax Viewport Maximum 1% of the larger viewport dimension (width or height) Full-screen backgrounds, decorative elements
svw / svh Small Viewport Viewport size excluding dynamic browser chrome Mobile-safe full-screen layouts
lvw / lvh Large Viewport Viewport size including potential browser chrome When you want the full device screen regardless of UI
dvw / dvh Dynamic Viewport Dynamically updates as browser chrome shows/hides Works like 100vh but handles mobile toolbar changes

⚠️ Viewport Unit Gotcha on Mobile

On iOS Safari, 100vh includes the browser toolbar height, which collapses when scrolling. This causes content to be taller than expected. Use 100dvh (dynamic viewport height) or 100svh (small viewport height) for reliable full-height sections on mobile.

Percentage Unit

Unit Name Relative to Best For
% Percentage Depends on property: width → parent width, height → parent height, font-size → parent font-size, padding/margin → parent width (even for vertical padding) Fluid layouts, responsive widths, aspect ratios

💡 Percentage Padding Quirk

When using padding-top: 50% or padding-bottom: 50%, the percentage is calculated from the parent's width, not height. This is actually useful for creating fixed-aspect-ratio boxes (like a 16:9 container) without JavaScript.

When to Use Each Unit

The table below maps common CSS properties to their recommended units.

Property Recommended Unit Why
font-size rem Respects user's browser font size setting. Avoids compounding issues of em.
padding / margin rem Consistent spacing regardless of nested font sizes.
width / max-width % or rem % for fluid layouts, rem for fixed content widths (e.g., article max-width).
height auto (avoid fixed) Let content determine height. Use min-height with vh for full-screen sections.
border-width px Borders should be crisp and not scale with text size.
border-radius px or rem px for small radii, rem for larger rounded corners that should scale.
box-shadow px Shadow blur and spread should stay crisp.
line-height unitless (e.g., 1.5) Unitless values scale proportionally with font-size changes.
gap rem Grid/flexbox gaps should scale with content size.
hero / full-screen dvh Dynamic viewport handles mobile browser toolbar correctly.
fluid typography clamp() Combine rem + vw with min/max bounds (e.g., clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 2rem)).
icon sizing em Icon scales with surrounding text size automatically.

Practical Examples

Fluid Typography with clamp()

The clamp() CSS function lets you set a font size that scales between a minimum and maximum value. This is the modern way to do responsive typography without media queries.

/* Fluid heading: scales from 1.5rem to 3rem between 320px and 1200px viewports */
h1 {
  font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 2.5vw, 3rem);
  line-height: 1.1;
}

/* Fluid body text */
p {
  font-size: clamp(0.875rem, 0.75rem + 0.5vw, 1.125rem);
  line-height: 1.6;
}

Full-Height Hero Section (Mobile-Safe) 

.hero {
  /* dvh = dynamic viewport height — handles mobile browser toolbar */
  min-height: 100dvh;
  /* Fallback for older browsers */
  min-height: 100vh;
  min-height: 100svh;
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
}

Consistent Spacing with rem 

:root {
  /* Set root font size. Browser default is 16px = 1rem */
  font-size: 100%; /* Respects user preferences */
}

.card {
  padding: 1.5rem;    /* = 24px at default font size */
  margin-bottom: 1rem; /* = 16px */
  border-radius: 0.5rem; /* = 8px */
  gap: 0.75rem;       /* = 12px grid gap */
}

h2 {
  font-size: 1.25rem; /* = 20px */
  margin-bottom: 0.5em; /* relative to h2 font size */
}

16:9 Aspect Ratio Box 

.aspect-16-9 {
  /* Padding % is calculated from parent width */
  /* 9/16 = 56.25% */
  width: 100%;
  padding-bottom: 56.25%;
  position: relative;
  overflow: hidden;
}

.aspect-16-9 > * {
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  width: 100%;
  height: 100%;
  object-fit: cover;
}

Perfectly Centered Modal 

.modal-overlay {
  position: fixed;
  inset: 0;
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  background: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5);
}

.modal {
  width: min(90vw, 600px);  /* 90% of viewport width, max 600px */
  max-height: 90dvh;        /* 90% of dynamic viewport height */
  overflow-y: auto;
  padding: 2rem;
  background: #fff;
  border-radius: 0.75rem;
}

calc() in Practice

The calc() function lets you mix units freely. It's extremely useful for fluid layouts where you need arithmetic operations on CSS values.

/* Sidebar + main: 250px sidebar, rest is main */
.main-layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 250px 1fr;
  gap: 2rem;
}

/* Full-width container with fixed gutters */
.container {
  width: calc(100% - 3rem);
  max-width: 1200px;
  margin-inline: auto;
}

/* Fluid typography alternative */
h1 {
  font-size: calc(1.5rem + 2vw);
}

/* Height minus header */
.content {
  min-height: calc(100dvh - 4rem);
}

/* Background that extends beyond content area */
.hero {
  width: 100vw;
  margin-left: calc(-50vw + 50%);
}

Unit Comparison Table

A quick comparison of how different units behave at different scales. Assumes root font size of 16px and a 1200px wide viewport.

Value px rem em (parent 16px) vw (1200px) %
Small 8px 0.5rem 0.5em 0.67vw 0.67%
Body 16px 1rem 1em 1.33vw 1.33%
Medium 24px 1.5rem 1.5em 2vw 2%
Large 32px 2rem 2em 2.67vw 2.67%
Heading 48px 3rem 3em 4vw 4%

🎯 Summary: Unit Decision Flow

  • font-size → rem (or clamp() for fluid scaling)
  • spacing (padding, margin, gap) → rem (consistent everywhere)
  • widths → % (fluid), rem (fixed content), min() (max bound)
  • heights → auto (preferred), dvh (full-screen)
  • borders / shadows → px (keep them crisp)
  • icon sizes → em (scale with text)
  • line-height → unitless number (always)
  • fluid typography → clamp() with rem and vw
  • full viewport sections → 100dvh (dynamic) or 100svh (small)
  • mixed calculations → calc()

Common Mistakes & How to Avoid Them

CSS units seem simple until a layout breaks. These are the mistakes developers make most often — and the fixes that prevent them.

1. Using px for Font Sizes Hurts Accessibility

px font sizes ignore the user's browser font-size setting, so users who increase their default font size (often for vision reasons) see no change on your site. Use rem for font sizes — it scales with the root font size — and reserve px for borders, shadows, and 1px hairline rules that should stay crisp.

2. Confusing em with rem

rem is always relative to the root element font size (usually 16px), so it is predictable anywhere in the tree. em is relative to the current element's font size, and because it compounds, nested elements can produce surprising sizes: a 1.5em padding inside a 1.5em font becomes 2.25em of effective spacing. Use rem for global spacing and typography; use em deliberately when a component should scale with its own font size (icons, button padding).

3. Using 100vh for Mobile Full-Height Sections

On mobile browsers, 100vh refers to the largest viewport, which includes the area hidden behind the URL bar — so a 100vh section gets cut off or causes scroll jumps when the bar collapses. Use 100dvh (dynamic viewport height) for mobile full-height layouts, with 100svh as a fallback for older browsers.

4. Using vw for Font Sizes Without clamp()

A headline set to 4vw looks great on desktop but becomes unreadably small on phones and comically huge on ultrawide monitors. Wrap viewport units in clamp() with rem bounds: font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 4vw, 3rem). This gives you fluid scaling without ever crossing accessibility limits.

5. Expecting Percentage Heights to "Just Work"

height: 50% only works when the parent has an explicit height (not auto). A common trap is setting a child to 100% inside a parent whose height comes from content — the percentage resolves to auto and the layout collapses. If the parent's height is content-driven, use flexbox/grid stretch, min-height, or viewport units instead of percentages.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between px and rem?

px is an absolute unit — 1px is 1/96th of an inch on screen — so it never changes regardless of browser settings. rem is relative to the root element font size (usually 16px, so 1rem = 16px). Because rem scales when users change their browser's default font size, it is the recommended unit for font sizes, padding, and margin. Use px for borders and shadows that must stay visually identical at any zoom level.

What is the difference between em and rem?

rem is relative to the root element font size, so 1rem is the same everywhere in the document. em is relative to the current element's font size, and it compounds through nesting — a 2em margin inside a 1.5em font resolves to 3em. This makes em great for components that should scale with their own text (icon sizes, button padding) and rem better for site-wide spacing and typography.

When should I use vw and vh?

vw and vh are 1% of the viewport width and height. Use them for full-screen hero sections, overlays, and fluid typography inside clamp(). Avoid raw vh for mobile heights — the URL bar changes the visible viewport, so use 100dvh (dynamic) or 100svh (small) instead. For widths, prefer % when the size should relate to a container rather than the whole viewport.

Should I use px or rem for font sizes?

Use rem. Because rem is relative to the root font size, it respects the user's browser font-size preference — a core accessibility requirement. px ignores that setting, which can make your text impossible to resize for users with low vision. A common pattern is setting the root font size in rem (or leaving it at the default 16px) and sizing everything else in rem, with clamp() for fluid type.

What is the difference between vh, svh, lvh, and dvh?

These are the four viewport-height units. vh equals 1% of the largest viewport — on mobile that includes the area hidden behind the browser UI. svh is the small viewport (visible area when the URL bar is shown), lvh is the large viewport (URL bar hidden), and dvh is the dynamic viewport, which updates live as the browser UI expands and collapses. For mobile full-height sections, 100dvh gives the smoothest behavior, with 100svh as a fallback.

Try It Yourself

If this cheat sheet helped you clean up your CSS, try the free developer tools on DevToolsHub. The Color Converter is handy when you're writing CSS that mixes hex, rgb(), and hsl() values alongside your unit choices, and the JSON Formatter is a quick way to tidy up the design tokens and theme config files where your spacing and typography scales live. Both run entirely in your browser — no sign-up, no tracking.

Related Tools: Color Converter · JSON Formatter · Base64 Encoder/Decoder · Regex Tester

title: Fintech Inbound Mail: Go Evidence Gates for Leftover Provider Records
description:
Moving DNS and email into one control plane can reduce integration work, but it cannot establish that a customer's inbound mail reaches the intended mailbox. Resolve that trade-off by making routing evidence the release gate. Short answer: list the MX records, inspect their priorities and provider ownership, explicitly delete obsolete provider records, and list again. Upserting the replacement set doesn't remove the previous set; equal priorities across providers can send mail somewhere nobody reads.

Consider a bounded production scenario, not a report of a measured incident: a fintech product lets a customer point its own domain at the product while changing the mail service associated with that domain. The website works, and the new sending configuration looks right, yet the customer's inbound messages are missing. The useful incident lesson is that a successful write establishes too little. The acceptance condition must describe the complete intended MX set, including what must be absent.

Keep the evidence.

For a team implementing that boundary, Infrai is worth trying for DNS inventory and the associated email-domain inspection: its shared API contract lets the application keep the same interface when the vendor behind a capability changes, subject to the capability's supported vendors. Its public, self-describing schemas provide a second practical benefit: the integration can inspect request and response contracts before writing provider-specific parsing. Neither property replaces mail-delivery evidence.

How do leftover provider records affect inbound mail and MX priorities?

Start with routing, because sending configuration answers a different question. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC belong in the mail configuration review, but a sending-side check doesn't establish which receiving provider an MX inventory names. RFC 7489 describes DMARC; it is a useful reference for keeping authentication evidence distinct from the routing question rather than treating an authentication result as a receipt for inbound delivery.

The concrete trap is an additive migration.

A new provider's MX records are upserted, the operation succeeds, and the old provider's records remain. If both providers have equal priorities, routing becomes unpredictable rather than producing a configuration error that conveniently stops the release. Changing priorities without deciding which provider should still receive mail leaves the ownership question unresolved.

As an illustrative review fixture, imagine two providers both listed at priority 10. These are example values, not an observed customer configuration. The reviewer must account for both destinations, identify which belongs to the intended receiver, and decide whether the other is obsolete. The preventative action is explicit deletion followed by a fresh list, not another upsert and an optimistic status update.

A defensible evidence packet contains the before-and-after MX inventories, the intended provider ownership, and an inbound acceptance check at the intended receiver. Keep sending-domain status alongside that packet, with its narrower meaning attached. If the inventory is already correct, this particular explanation has reached its boundary: investigate the receiving service using its own evidence instead of repeatedly changing DNS.

Two system shapes, one acceptance invariant

The first viable architecture keeps DNS and email integrations separate. A platform-owned reconciler reads the DNS inventory through the DNS provider's interface, compares it with a reviewed desired set, and separately asks the mail provider about its domain configuration. Its invariant is that a customer domain cannot be marked ready until both the receiving destinations and the mail-side evidence have been reviewed. This buys independent provider selection, while assigning credential management, response normalization, and coordination to the platform team.

The second architecture puts those inspections behind a shared capability API and retains the same reconciler and acceptance rule. Infrai is a deliberate option here because DNS and email capabilities use one API key and base URL. Provider changes behind supported capabilities can preserve the application-facing contract, but the desired MX set remains an application decision. Contract stability doesn't mean arbitrary providers have identical behavior or that existing customer records should be deleted automatically.

For this fintech onboarding workflow, prefer the shared interface when the platform team wants to maintain one evidence-producing controller and the supported provider choices fit its requirements. Prefer direct integrations when a DNS or mail specialist's control surface is itself a requirement. The recommendation turns on evidence ownership and operating work; a shorter integration is valuable only if the release gate remains intact.

The combined approach also concentrates trust, billing, and the outage surface in one vendor.

Say that in the design review before choosing it.

The cross-capability benefit is particularly concrete during SPF or DKIM maintenance. With DNS records and the mail service available through one key, a controller can coordinate inspection instead of relying on a person to copy values between two dashboards and remember to re-check them after a DKIM rotation. This is an integration pattern to implement, not a claim that a shared key automatically reconciles records or proves deliverability.

Buy versus build depends on who owns the evidence

There are several credible stacks.

The table compares the integration boundaries the team would own, rather than asserting that one provider has better measured delivery. No comparative delivery benchmark is established here.

Stack What to buy What the platform still builds Appropriate boundary
Amazon Route 53 + Amazon SES Separate DNS and email service interfaces within AWS The mapping between DNS inventory, mail configuration, and a customer-domain acceptance decision A team deliberately choosing the AWS service boundary
Cloudflare DNS + Resend A DNS service and a separately selected email service Two-provider credential handling, record handoff, and evidence correlation A team that values independent DNS and email selection
Infrai DNS + email One capability interface and one key across the two groups Desired-state ownership, explicit obsolete-record decisions, and the delivery gate A team reducing integration surface while retaining its own acceptance controller

The Cloudflare-plus-Resend alternative requires two provider signups and two credential sets, along with glue that translates the mail service's requirements into DNS changes and correlates the later inspections. Route 53 plus SES can share an AWS account signup, but still introduces two service interfaces and their permission configuration; don't turn that into an inaccurate claim that two AWS accounts are required. Account count and integration count measure different work.

The specialist or direct-provider choice is better when the team's required control or evidence exists at that provider's interface and hasn't been established in a shared contract. Conversely, choosing an independent email service for its sending workflow doesn't, by itself, establish where inbound mail is received. Make receiving ownership explicit in every row of the implementation plan.

A Go gate that carries DNS evidence into the mail check

The preventative code path below is deliberately read-only. It lists DNS records, presents the actual response for review, and permits the email-domain inspection only after the operator has checked MX priorities and leftovers. The first response becomes the evidence input to the second stage; its digest is carried into the mail inspection output so the two cannot be casually detached during review. This is a human approval gate, not an automated interpretation of unspecified response fields.

Use Go with the standard library. Save the block as main.go and run it with go run main.go. Set INFRAI_API_KEY, CUSTOMER_DOMAIN, and DNS_RECORD_LIST_QUERY in the process environment. The query must contain the actual record-list parameters for that domain from the public discovery schema, encoded as a URL query string without a leading question mark. No parameter names or response-envelope fields are assumed here. The operator must verify that the returned inventory belongs to CUSTOMER_DOMAIN before approving it.

Both requests use the same key and base URL. The two API routes appear only in this runnable example. HTTP 429 responses trigger bounded exponential backoff; a Retry-After value, in seconds or HTTP-date form, overrides that delay. Other unsuccessful responses surface their body.

package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const base = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

var client = &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}

func readAPI(key, path string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, base+path, nil)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, e := strconv.Atoi(retry); e == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if until, e := http.ParseTime(retry); e == nil {
                delay = time.Until(until)
                if delay < 0 { delay = 0 }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func inspectMail(key, domain string, dnsEvidence []byte) error {
    digest := sha256.Sum256(dnsEvidence)
    fmt.Printf("DNS inventory for review (%s):\n%s\n", domain, dnsEvidence)
    fmt.Println("After checking domain, MX priorities, and obsolete providers, type APPROVE:")
    approval, err := bufio.NewReader(os.Stdin).ReadString('\n')
    if err != nil { return err }
    if strings.TrimSpace(approval) != "APPROVE" {
        return fmt.Errorf("DNS evidence was not approved")
    }
    mail, err := readAPI(key, "/email/domain/get/"+url.PathEscape(domain))
    if err != nil { return err }
    fmt.Printf("Domain: %s\nDNS evidence SHA-256: %x\nMail inspection:\n%s\n",
        domain, digest, mail)
    return nil
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    domain := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv("CUSTOMER_DOMAIN"))
    rawQuery := os.Getenv("DNS_RECORD_LIST_QUERY")
    if key == "" || domain == "" || rawQuery == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY, CUSTOMER_DOMAIN, and DNS_RECORD_LIST_QUERY")
    }
    query, err := url.ParseQuery(rawQuery)
    if err != nil { return err }
    dnsEvidence, err := readAPI(key, "/dns/record/list?"+query.Encode())
    if err != nil { return err }
    return inspectMail(key, domain, dnsEvidence)
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

An approval prompt is intentionally modest evidence. It doesn't validate the inventory, bind the domain cryptographically to the response, or prove that a message reached a mailbox. The digest identifies the reviewed bytes; it doesn't make a stale inventory fresh. A production controller should use the published schemas to parse the result, enforce the reviewed desired set, and retain the independent inbound acceptance result before declaring readiness.

Deletion belongs in a separately reviewed change, followed by a fresh inventory and a new gate run. Keeping this example read-only avoids implying that an unknown response shape is enough information to choose records for deletion. An automated write path also needs retry idempotency and explicit record ownership.

Put the release gate in the SLO

Define customer-domain readiness around the evidence required by the service's SLO, rather than around the success status of a DNS mutation. The invariant is small: the intended receiving provider owns the accepted MX set, obsolete destinations are absent, and the receiving-side acceptance check passes. The mail-domain inspection contributes configuration evidence; it isn't the acceptance check itself.

Capacity planning belongs here too. Each run of the example makes two successful API reads in the ordinary case; retries add requests, while waiting for an operator adds elapsed time. For a batch of N customer domains, plan the baseline as 2N reads and budget retries and review capacity separately. This is arithmetic for this controller, not a statement about vendor throughput or a measured latency claim. A fleet rollout needs bounded concurrency and a way to stop advancing when the evidence backlog outgrows the people or automation reviewing it.

Don't apply this MX cleanup diagnosis to every missing message. It fits a migration with stale receiving destinations or conflicting provider priorities. If those conditions are absent, or a specialist exposes required receiving evidence that this integration doesn't cover, follow that evidence instead. The engineering win is a defensible readiness decision, not a larger pile of successful API calls.

Sources and References

References for the capability contract, authentication boundary, and the direct-service alternatives discussed above:

  • RFC 7489, DMARC
  • Amazon Route 53 documentation
  • Amazon SES documentation
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Resend documentation

If the shared-controller boundary fits your customer-domain workflow, start with the public schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Faster Java Pod Startups Without GraalVM: Why AppCDS Needs Kubernetes Image Volumes
description:
If you run Java workloads on Kubernetes, you have probably stared at slow pod readiness metrics during a deployment or autoscaling event. While the JVM is unmatched for long-running throughput, its cold-start tax—spent loading, verifying, and linking thousands of classes—can make scaling painful.

The usual advice is to compile your application into a GraalVM Native Image. That delivers sub-second startups, but it comes at a steep operational price: long build times, closed-world reflection constraints, and breaking changes to existing Java agents and libraries.

OpenJDK offers a middle ground: Application Class-Data Sharing (AppCDS) on JDK 21+ and Project Leyden AOT caches on JDK 25+. These features let the JVM dump its internal class metadata into a pre-linked archive file on disk, allowing subsequent restarts to memory-map the classes instead of parsing them from scratch.

When I started building mnemo-warmup—an open-source tool that automates training and sharing AppCDS/Leyden caches inside Kubernetes without changing application source code—I wanted to answer a simple engineering question:

Does a Kubernetes pod actually become Ready sooner once you pay the infrastructure tax of fetching, verifying, and mounting the cache?

After running hundreds of automated cold-restart benchmarks across different JVM architectures, the answer turned out to be: It depends entirely on how you deliver the tooling, and what your application does during its boot cycle.

The Hidden Infrastructure Tax: Init Containers

In a standard Kubernetes setup, injecting a shared cache archive into a stateless pod requires a familiar pattern:

  1. An install init container copies the launcher tools onto a shared emptyDir volume.
  2. A fetch init container pulls the trained archive from an OCI registry and verifies its SHA-256 digest.
  3. The main application container boots the JVM pointing to the shared archive.

On paper, this looks clean. In practice, measuring the end-to-end timeline from pod.status.startTime to Ready revealed a major bottleneck.

In our initial benchmarks running a heavy Spring Boot application (69 JARs, constrained to 1 CPU / 1 GiB), the AppCDS archive successfully cut the JVM's internal startup time from 3.18s down to 1.88s. Yet, total pod readiness remained completely unchanged at 5 seconds.

Even after rewriting our helper utilities from Java into static Go binaries (dropping tool execution time from ~1,050ms down to ~140ms), the pod was still losing nearly 1.75 seconds before the main application even began. The culprit wasn't our code—it was Kubernetes itself. Because the kubelet schedules, initializes, and tears down init containers sequentially, the orchestration overhead was eating 100% of our JVM startup gains.

The Breakthrough: Kubernetes Image Volumes

To eliminate the init-container tax, we pivoted to Kubernetes image volumes (introduced as beta in Kubernetes 1.33+ and supported by containerd 2.1+).

Instead of spinning up sequential containers to copy binaries around, an image volume allows the container runtime to mount the read-only OCI tools layer directly into the application container's filesystem at launch. Our static launcher runs as the entrypoint, fetches the archive directly, and replaces itself with java via exec so the JVM remains PID 1.

Removing the init containers changed the economics overnight:

Workload Profile (1 CPU / 1 GiB) Plain Deployment (none) Init Containers (cached) Image Volume (cached) Net Pod-to-Ready Delta
🟢 Spring Boot (69 JARs) 5 s 5 s 3 s -2 s (40% faster)
🟡 Jenkins LTS (2.492.3) 4 s 5 s 4 s 0 s (Parity)
🔴 SonarQube (26.11) 15 s 17 s Not Run +2 s (Slower)

(Note: Figures are medians over 12 cold restarts on a local kind cluster; Kubernetes pod condition timestamps have a 1-second resolution.)

Three Lessons on Workload Suitability

Testing across three distinct real-world applications mapped out the exact boundaries of where shared class caches thrive and where they fail.

1. Framework-Heavy Apps See Massive Gains (Spring Boot)

Modern microservice frameworks spend the vast majority of their boot cycle scanning classpaths, evaluating conditional annotations, and weaving dependency graphs. On our heavy Spring Boot workload, AppCDS cut JVM initialization by over 40%. Once paired with image volume delivery, total pod readiness dropped from 5 seconds to 3 seconds—with zero changes to the application's source code.

2. I/O and Plugin-Bound Apps Hit Parity (Jenkins)

Jenkins is a massive Java monolith, making it seem like an ideal candidate for AppCDS. However, while the archive successfully loaded 85% of Jenkins' classes and shaved ~300ms off the raw JVM boot, total pod readiness stayed flat at 4 seconds.

Jenkins spends most of its startup timeline performing tasks that class-data sharing cannot accelerate: unpacking bundled archives, parsing XML configurations on disk, and executing sequential plugin initialization hooks. When class loading isn't your primary bottleneck, caching won't move the needle.

3. Multi-Process Wrappers Bypass the Cache (SonarQube)

SonarQube proved to be an important architectural edge case. In our test harness (run at 2 CPU / 3 GiB), training succeeded cleanly and all 12 pods validated and loaded the archive. Yet pod readiness got 2 seconds slower.

The reason lies in how SonarQube boots. Its container entrypoint launches a small Java coordinator process, which then dynamically spawns three separate child JVMs inside the container (one for ElasticSearch, one for the Web Server, and one for the Compute Engine). Because a container wrapper only passes -XX:SharedArchiveFile to the parent entrypoint command, the heavy child JVMs booted completely cold.

The Rule of Thumb

If you are evaluating AppCDS or Project Leyden for your Kubernetes clusters, use these three rules to predict your ROI:

  • Check your delivery mechanism: If you are running on an older cluster that forces you to rely on sequential init containers, the kubelet scheduling overhead will likely cancel out your savings on fast-starting microservices. Target clusters supporting Kubernetes image volumes.
  • Profile your startup bottleneck: If your application spends its first seconds loading classes and wiring frameworks (Spring Boot, Micronaut), expect a 30–40% reduction in pod readiness. If it spends its time running database migrations, unpacking files, or waiting on network I/O, expect parity.
  • Watch out for wrapper scripts: Single-process containers work out of the box. If your container launches a supervisor process that forks downstream child JVMs, those child processes will bypass the cache unless explicitly configured.

What's Next for mnemo-warmup

mnemo-warmup is currently in active alpha. Before tagging our v0.3.0 beta, we are running the next wave of studies: comparing JDK 21 AppCDS against JDK 25 Project Leyden AOT archive sizes, mapping out the application size break-even curve (from 40 MB microservices to 350 MB monoliths), and simulating HPA scale-out bursts against remote cloud registries.

If you want to inspect the raw benchmark CSVs, reproduce the cluster tests on your own hardware, or weigh in on making image volumes our default delivery mode, check out the repository at mnemo-warmup.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is mnemo-warmup and when is it a good fit?

mnemo-warmup is a Kubernetes-native tool that automatically trains and shares OpenJDK AppCDS (.jsa) and Project Leyden AOT (.aot) caches across application pods without requiring source code changes or GraalVM compilation.

  • Best fit: Standard JVM applications (Java 21+) running on Kubernetes—especially framework-heavy microservices like Spring Boot—where teams want faster pod startup and readiness times without migrating to GraalVM Native Image.
  • Not a fit: Workloads running on Java 17 or older, Windows containers, build-time optimized frameworks like Quarkus, or multi-process Java wrappers like SonarQube.

How does mnemo-warmup compare to GraalVM Native Image and build-time AOT?

  • vs. GraalVM Native Image: GraalVM achieves sub-second startups but requires complex build pipelines, closed-world compilation, and breaks dynamic reflection or Java agents. mnemo-warmup keeps the standard HotSpot JVM, requires zero code changes, and preserves full dynamic Java compatibility while still cutting Spring Boot pod readiness by ~40%.
  • vs. Build-Time AppCDS / Leyden AOT (e.g., Spring Boot onRefresh in CI): Baking a cache into a Docker image during CI causes fingerprint drift if production Kubernetes manifests modify -Xmx, GC flags, or environment variables. mnemo-warmup trains asynchronously inside the cluster using the exact live pod fingerprint.

Why does mnemo-warmup recommend Kubernetes image volumes over init containers?

Standard Kubernetes init containers (init-container mode) introduce ~1.75 seconds of sequential kubelet scheduling and container startup overhead, which cancels out the JVM startup savings on fast-booting microservices. Setting warmup.mnemo.io/tools-delivery: "image-volume" (supported on Kubernetes 1.33+ and containerd 2.1+) mounts the tools directly as a read-only OCI layer, eliminating init containers and dropping Spring Boot Pod-to-Ready times from 5 seconds to 3 seconds.

Which workloads see the best and worst performance gains?

  • High Gain (Spring Boot, Micronaut): Single-process applications bottlenecked by runtime classpath scanning and bean wiring see a 30% to 40% reduction in total pod readiness time.
  • Neutral / Parity (Jenkins): Applications bottlenecked by disk I/O, archive extraction, and sequential plugin initialization see minor JVM startup gains (~300ms) but zero net change in pod readiness.
  • Zero Gain (SonarQube): Containers whose entrypoint acts as a coordinator that dynamically spawns child JVM subprocesses (e.g., ElasticSearch, Web, Compute Engine) do not benefit, because the cache flag only applies to the parent coordinator process.

Can a missing, corrupted, or unreachable cache crash a Kubernetes pod?

No. mnemo-warmup is strictly fail-safe. It never passes -Xshare:on (which causes fatal JVM exits on cache mismatch). If the OCI registry is unreachable, the archive digest is corrupted, or a JVM flag changes, the launcher logs the mismatch reason and falls back to an ordinary cold JVM start with exit code 0.

Does mnemo-warmup require a Kubernetes Operator, CRD, or mutating webhook?

No. It operates entirely via a stateless CLI (mnemo-warmup inject) used as a Helm 3 post-renderer or GitOps manifest transformer. Adding three pod template annotations (warmup.mnemo.io/enabled, warmup.mnemo.io/store, warmup.mnemo.io/exit-mode) injects the required volume mounts and generates a standard Kubernetes CronJob and Lease for asynchronous training.

Why must Spring Boot fat JARs be extracted before using mnemo-warmup?

OpenJDK invalidates AppCDS and Leyden AOT archives if the underlying JAR file modification times (mtime) or paths differ between training and runtime. Extracting a Spring Boot 3.3+ fat JAR at container build time (java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract) ensures the trainer pod and application replicas read identical, immutable file layouts.

title: Your White-Label AI Portal Works. Now Make It Usable.
description:
Most white-label developer portals do not fail because the API is broken. They fail in the awkward space between “the endpoint works” and “a new user understands what to do next.”

That gap is easy to underestimate. The team has already spent weeks on model access, metering, and deployment, so changing a logo or rewriting a login screen feels cosmetic. Then the first real users arrive. They cannot tell which tool to open, the domain redirects strangely, the pricing units are ambiguous, and the documentation assumes they already know the product.

A branded AI portal is not just a reskinned dashboard. It is a small product with its own trust signals, information architecture, economics, and support burden. Treating configuration as product design makes the difference between a portal people can technically access and one they can actually use.

The first screen is an interface contract

A visitor should be able to answer three questions almost immediately: What is this site? What can I make here? What should I click first?

A short, specific promise usually works better than a wall of fashionable language. “Generate catalog images and ad variations” gives the visitor something concrete. “An intelligent, all-in-one creative ecosystem” could describe almost anything.

The same restraint helps with branding. A compact logo has to survive a small navigation bar, dark mode, mobile screens, and browser scaling. Fine lettering and elaborate illustrations may look impressive in the source file but turn into visual noise at 32 pixels. Test the exported asset in the actual interface rather than approving it on a design canvas.

This is also where naming matters. The product name should be easy to remember, type, and say aloud. If users have to explain the spelling every time they share it, the brand is creating friction before the application even loads.

Authentication should feel boring

Login is infrastructure from the operator's perspective, but it is a trust test from the user's perspective. People do not care which authentication flow is technically elegant. They care that the option is familiar, the redirect behaves normally, and they return to the page they intended to use.

Pick the default sign-in method around the audience, not around the engineering team's preferences. Then test it without an administrator session. A persistent admin cookie hides exactly the class of problems a first-time visitor will encounter: missing callbacks, unexpected account selection, broken redirects, and pages that silently assume an authenticated state.

A useful habit is to run the whole path in a private browser window. Start at the public homepage, create or access an account, open a tool, and sign out again. Repeat it on a phone. It sounds basic, but this short exercise catches more launch blockers than another hour inside the settings panel.

Your domain is part of the product

A custom domain does more than make a URL prettier. It gives support messages, documentation, and community posts a stable address. It also signals continuity: users are less likely to wonder whether they have been sent to an unrelated service.

Domain setup has two sides. The application needs to know which hostname belongs to the site, and DNS needs to direct that hostname to the platform. For an Ace Data Cloud subsite, the documented target is a CNAME pointing to platform-proxy.acedata.cloud.

A typical record looks like this:

Type:   CNAME
Name:   ai
Target: platform-proxy.acedata.cloud

That would normally make ai.example.com the user-facing hostname. Before adding it, check whether ai already has an A, AAAA, or CNAME record. Conflicting records are a common source of “it works for me” debugging because DNS caches do not all refresh at the same moment.

Do not stop after the DNS panel shows a green status. Open the public hostname, verify that it reaches the intended portal, inspect the TLS certificate, and follow the login flow. A domain is ready when the complete journey works over HTTPS, not when a record merely exists.

A homepage is a decision surface, not an inventory

AI platforms often accumulate capabilities faster than their navigation can explain them. Image generation, editing, chat, video, audio, and developer tools all compete for the same top-level space. Showing every feature may feel transparent, but it transfers the job of product strategy to the visitor.

The homepage should emphasize the jobs users came to perform. If most customers create product visuals, put generation and editing near the front. If the audience is building integrations, make API access and documentation easy to reach. Less common utilities can stay available without occupying the most valuable part of the page.

The hero banner deserves the same discipline. Give it one job. It can introduce the main use case, announce a genuinely important change, or direct newcomers to a starting point. Trying to fit the product pitch, feature matrix, discount, tutorial, and pricing message into one image produces a banner that nobody reads.

Text inside images is especially fragile. It may be cropped on mobile, become unreadable on high-density screens, or remain invisible to assistive technology. Keep critical meaning in HTML whenever possible, and preview the real page at narrow and wide breakpoints.

Pricing is an engineering problem with a copywriting layer

A price table can look polished while still being impossible to reason about. The usual problem is not the number itself; it is the missing unit. Per request, per generated image, per second of video, and per token are very different promises.

Start with the underlying cost model. Include failed-job behavior, retries, storage, support, payment fees, and any free usage you plan to offer. Then present the customer-facing unit in language that does not require knowledge of the upstream provider.

If a request can vary significantly in cost, a single flat label may be misleading. A short example is often more useful than another tooltip:

Standard image: 1 credit
High-resolution image: 2 credits
Ten-second video: 12 credits

These are illustrative units, not universal rates. The important part is that the interface and documentation use the same vocabulary. If the dashboard says “credits” while the help page explains “requests,” users will assume the conversion is being hidden from them.

Pricing changes also need a communication path. Quietly changing the amount after users have built habits around it may save a short announcement, but it creates a much longer trust problem.

Documentation should absorb predictable questions

You do not need a large documentation site on launch day. You need a small one that answers the questions people will actually ask.

A useful starting set covers account access, the first successful task, billing units, common errors, and a visible support route. Write each page in the order the user experiences the product. Screenshots help when they show the exact control being discussed, but they should support the instructions rather than replace them.

Error guidance deserves special attention. “Something went wrong” tells the user nothing. Even when the underlying provider returns a complex response, the portal can explain whether the user should retry, change an input, check their balance, or contact support with a request ID.

Documentation should grow from support evidence. When the same question appears repeatedly, the answer belongs in the product or the docs. This feedback loop is far more valuable than trying to predict every possible tutorial before anyone has used the site.

The quiet settings still shape trust

Analytics, referral rules, and privacy terms are easy to postpone because they are not part of the main creative workflow. They become painful later if they were configured casually.

Analytics should answer a small set of useful questions: where users leave, which tools they open, and whether an onboarding change improves activation. Collecting events without a decision attached to them creates data storage, not insight.

Referral programs need written definitions for attribution, eligibility, rewards, and settlement. Privacy language needs to match what the site actually collects and which third-party services it uses. Copying another company's policy without updating the business name, contact route, or data practices is not a shortcut; it is an inaccurate public statement.

Launch from the user's side of the glass

Before sharing the portal widely, step away from the admin panel. Use a fresh browser session and behave like somebody who has never heard the internal project name.

Can you understand the homepage without a verbal explanation? Can you sign in, find the primary tool, understand its price, complete a task, and locate help? Does the same path work on mobile? Are the logo, banner, and error messages still readable outside the designer's ideal screen size?

This is not a one-time ceremony. A white-label portal should evolve as real usage exposes weak assumptions. The practical goal is not a perfect launch. It is a coherent first experience where the name, domain, authentication, navigation, pricing, and documentation tell the same story.

The API may be the engine, but these details are the controls. Users judge the whole vehicle.

title: I built a local-first API client in Rust and Tauri
description:
At the start of this year I began building Flux, an open source alternative to Postman. The goal was simple: an API client that feels light, runs natively and keeps your work on your own machine.

I launched it in July, and as of today it has a little under 500 downloads, which is more than I expected when I started.

What it is

Flux is a native desktop API client built with Tauri 2, Rust and React. It uses under 30 MB of RAM and the installer is around 9 MB.

It's local-first: your collections and requests live on your machine, and cloud sync is optional, not a requirement.

Besides regular HTTP requests, it has a few things built in that I'd normally need separate tools for:

  • gRPC support
  • Load testing, so you can hit an endpoint hard without installing anything else
  • Mock servers, for when the backend isn't ready yet
  • AI helpers: generating test suites, diagnosing errors, autocomplete, and editing request bodies in plain language

Why Tauri instead of Electron

Electron ships a full copy of Chromium and runs a Node backend inside every app. Tauri takes a different route: it uses the operating system's own webview for the interface, and the backend is Rust. That's where most of the savings in memory and installer size come from.

For an app you leave open all day next to your editor, your browser and everything else, that difference adds up.

It's open source, and I'd love help

Flux is MIT-licensed, and I'm building it in public. If you want to contribute, there's plenty to do: bug fixes, new features, better docs, or just telling me what you'd want from an API client.

If you try it and something breaks, opening an issue helps a lot. And if you're curious how a Tauri app is put together, the code is a decent place to poke around.

  • Website and download: https://fluxapi.dev
  • Code: https://github.com/angeldevmobile/Flux-Post

If you've switched away from Postman or Insomnia, I'd like to know what made you do it, and what Flux would need for you to switch.

title: How Observe.AI Used MongoDB Resharding to Scale Its AI Platform
description:
Launched in 2017, Observe.AI was originally known for its expertise in conversation intelligence and contact center analytics. In recent years, however, the company has grown into a comprehensive agentic AI platform, and now has three core offerings:

  • AI agents for customers that resolve customer requests across voice and chat.

  • AI agents for frontline teams. These include Observe.AI’s recently launched Companion Agent, which provides human team members real-time guidance and automates work before, during, and after customer interactions.

  • AI agents for operations that evaluate interactions, generate coaching, uncover operational insights, and drive continuous improvement across contact centers.

Observe.AI uses MongoDB Atlas as the foundational data layer for its AI platform and relies on it to store raw customer conversations, AI-generated enrichments, model configurations, and agent metadata.

MongoDB's flexible document model enables rapid iteration as AI models evolve, while its scalability—supporting over 100 clusters and 50+ TB of data—has made it the trusted system of record powering our platform's intelligence layer.

Recently, the team wanted to continue scaling with MongoDB in a way that preserved application availability, reduced operational risk, and created a predictable runway for continued data growth.

The team partnered with MongoDB Consulting’s professional services to scale a production-critical MongoDB Atlas deployment to support Observe.AI’s conversation intelligence platform. The project was a joint engineering effort between Observe.AI and MongoDB that used MongoDB resharding as a practical, online mechanism for redistributing large collections across a broader shard footprint.

Expanding a constrained shard footprint

At the time of the project, the cluster had the following characteristics:

  • A sharded MongoDB Atlas deployment with two data shards plus config servers.

  • Approximately 13 TB of compressed data per data shard, representing roughly 50 TB of uncompressed data overall.

  • Each shard runs on the M140 tier with a disk limit of approximately 14 TB, leaving limited available headroom.

  • A sustained ingest rate of roughly 50 GB per day, making proactive capacity expansion important for safe long-term operations.

  • Several multi-TB collections with significant index footprint and production traffic. This setup had worked at an early stage in the company's cycle, but was no longer fit for purpose and could lead to performance issues or service degradation that would directly impact customers.

The engineering objective of the MongoDB–Observe.AI effort was clear: to expand a constrained shard footprint to a healthier horizontal layout, while also keeping the application online and minimizing disruption to production workloads.

Beyond balancer: a faster redistribution for large-scale data movements

After adding new shard capacity, the team evaluated the default balancer-driven redistribution path. They determined that the balancer was the right tool for ongoing incremental balancing, but the volume of data to be redistributed was large enough that relying on chunk migrations alone would have extended the migration window and kept the original shards under elevated pressure for longer than desired.

The team also tackled a number of other constraints. First, the new shard capacity could receive data, but the pace of redistribution was bounded by balancer and range-deletion throughput; range deletion also created additional background load on shards that were already carrying production traffic. Secondly, existing shards periodically experienced high WiredTiger cache pressure, making it important to avoid prolonged competition between application traffic, balancing, and cleanup activity. Finally, the team wanted a controlled, predictable migration path rather than an extended background redistribution process.

They concluded that the balancer should continue to handle incremental corrections, but a faster and more explicit redistribution mechanism was needed for the initial large-scale data movement.

The four-step resharding plan

Instead of relying solely on balancer migrations, the MongoDB–Observe.AI team designed a controlled resharding plan:

  1. Scale out the cluster

    • Increase capacity by adding multiple new shards (not just one) so that, after redistribution, each shard would hold a manageable share of the ~50 TB dataset.

  2. Prepare the cluster for resharding

    • Ensure no ongoing migrations or resharding jobs.

    • Pin the config servers to remain embedded/dedicated as appropriate for this topology.

    • Disable range deletions and disallow chunk migrations for critical collections so that resharding traffic does not compete with the balancer and range deleter for IOPS.

  3. Run resharding on the largest collections

    • For each large collection (collection6, collection7, collection8, etc.), run reshardCollection to redistribute data across the new shard set, keeping the same shard key but changing the ownership distribution.

    • Execute resharding sequentially per collection to avoid overloading donors, recipients, or the config server.

Table 1. Resharding performance metrics.

4. Clean up and return to normal operations

  • Once data has been redistributed:
    • Remove old empty shards from the cluster.
    • Remove temporary zone configurations that were only needed during the migration.
    • Re‑enable balancing and range deletions for the now‑healthy collections.

Resharding driving greater optimization, performance, and reliability

The joint effort gave Observe.AI a safer and more scalable data foundation for continued platform growth.

Thanks to resharding, the cluster moved from a limited disk runway to a healthier multi-month capacity position, while large multi-TB collections were redistributed across the expanded shard footprint using online resharding rather than relying only on extended balancer-driven chunk migration.

Production reads and writes continued during the clone and catch-up phases, with only the final commit phase requiring a brief write-blocking critical section. The team reduced sustained pressure on the original shards and created more room for future ingest growth, maintenance, and operational flexibility.

Finally, after the migration, the MongoDB balancer returned to its normal role of incremental rebalancing, while the heavy data movement was handled through the more appropriate resharding workflow.

The project highlighted how sharding and resharding can be used proactively as part of ongoing capacity management, helping optimize storage utilization, manage growing data volumes, and maintain platform performance and reliability as workloads scale.

Combining horizontal scale-out and resharding: A winning combo

The key idea behind MongoDB’s resharding capability is simple—sharding should not be the last‑resort, once‑in‑a‑lifetime operation you dread. It should be a practical, fast tool you can use whenever your workload outgrows its current shape.

If you treat sharding as “too expensive” and delay it until your primary is holding tens of TBs, you pay that cost back many times in:

  • Oversized single replica sets,

  • Operational risk,

  • And slow, painful balancing when you finally add shards.

By combining horizontal scale-out with resharding, which has been available since MongoDB 8.0 launched in 2024, you can start small, grow organically, and still have a predictable, efficient path to redistribute data when your cluster—and your business—takes off.

Observe.AI’s  platform processes billions of customer interactions each year, so the infrastructure has to scale as seamlessly as the business. Working alongside the MongoDB team enabled Observe.AI to redistribute more than 50 TB of production data with virtually no disruption to customers. MongoDB 8.0 resharding provided  the operational confidence to expand capacity proactively instead of reacting to infrastructure limits, allowing Observe.AI’s engineering teams to stay focused on delivering innovation for customers.
