title: What 1,355 App Store reviews say people want from a Reels/Shorts blocker (2026 data)
description:
Of 1,355 App Store reviews of one Reels and Shorts blocking app (February 1 to September 6, 2026), 466 gave one to three stars. In those low ratings, the most common complaint was that the app was slow, heavy or crashed: 143 reviews, or 30.7%. The complaints most tied to a low rating were rarer: no way to switch between several accounts, Screen Time restrictions reaching unrelated websites, and login problems. In a wider set of 1,405 reviews, the most requested feature was posting Stories and making calls (110 of 266 reviews that asked for something).

I'm Ayumu Kitabayashi. I build a similar app, so I have an interest here; that is disclosed at the end. Below is the data, how I counted it, and what it can't tell you.

What was read

  • App: SocialLite – Block Reels&Shorts (iOS). It is one of the larger apps in this category, so it had enough written reviews to count. All numbers are about this one app.
  • Store: Apple App Store only, all countries in the export. US 600, Canada 148, UK 112, Australia 91, Germany 61, and 54 other countries (59 in all).
  • Period: February 1 to September 6, 2026. 1,355 reviews, no duplicate IDs, none deleted.
  • Stars: 5★ 671 / 4★ 218 / 3★ 166 / 2★ 105 / 1★ 195. Average 3.79.
  • Wishes: counted later on 1,405 reviews (the same 1,355 plus 50 from September 14 to 18).

Complaints in the 466 low ratings

I read all 466 one-to-three-star reviews in full and tagged each with every category that applied, so one review can count more than once. The last column compares how often a complaint shows up in low ratings with how often it shows up in four-and-five-star reviews. A high number means people who write it almost always rate low.

Complaint Reviews Share of low ratings Low vs high
Slow, heavy or crashes 143 30.7% 1.4×
The core job needs payment (e.g. hiding suggested posts) 51 10.9% 3.7×
Long, repeated or pushy onboarding 48 10.3% 5.7×
Too expensive, dislike of subscriptions 46 9.9% 8.8×
Things aren't hidden or slip through 41 8.8% 3.4×
Posting or other features break 36 7.7% 1.3×
Notifications don't arrive 25 5.4% 1.5×
Screen Time limits affect unrelated sites, or can't be removed 20 4.3% 19.1×
Account flagged, suspended or "suspicious login" 18 3.9% 8.6×
Can't log in, or logged out 15 3.2% 9.5×
No switching between multiple accounts 12 2.6% 22.9×
Asked to write a review before using the app 8 1.7% not in high ratings

Two things stand out.

Speed is the most common complaint, but it doesn't decide the rating on its own. At 1.4×, people who liked the app also mentioned it. One reviewer wrote: "Took 5 minutes to open instagram … I understand that the point is to slow down, but 5 minutes is excessive."

The rare complaints are the ones that come with one star. Account switching (22.9×), Screen Time side effects (19.1×) and login trouble (9.5×) are each under 5% of low ratings, but people who hit them rarely gave more than three stars. One reviewer described an unrelated website being blocked in their normal browser; another spent "an hour on the phone with an Apple Specialist" to get access back.

What is free also split the ratings. Low ratings said the free tier still let them scroll because suggested posts came up in the feed. In the later 50 reviews, several five-star reviews praised the opposite: that the main features worked for free.

What people asked for (1,405 reviews)

266 reviews (19%) contained a request. 65% of them came from four-and-five-star reviewers, so they read as "one more thing" rather than anger.

Request Reviews Share of the 266
Post Stories, make calls, send voice messages 110 41%
Notifications for DMs 61 23%
Sleep timer or background playback 27 10%
Dark mode 24 9%
More services (e.g. Pinterest) 19 7%
A one-time purchase instead of a subscription 17 6%
Multiple accounts 14 5%
Opening the official app sends you to the blocker 13 5%

The top two have the same cause: these apps open the web version of Instagram, which has no Stories posting, calls or push notifications. One four-star reviewer put the notification problem plainly: tapping an Instagram notification "opens instagram and not this app, then i start doomscrolling again."

In five-star reviews, the word "friends" appeared 99 times, 8.5 times the rate in one-and-two-star reviews. People don't want to leave social media. They want to keep their friends and lose the feed.

How it was counted

  • The reviews were exported from a review-tracking service as CSV, then merged and de-duplicated by review ID.
  • All 466 low ratings were read by one person. Keyword search was used to find candidates, and each was checked by reading. Keyword counting alone missed whole groups, such as the Screen Time cases.
  • Reviews in German, French, Italian and other languages (about 7%) were read in the original, not translated.
  • The "low vs high" ratio is the share of low ratings with the complaint divided by the share of high ratings with it.

Limitations

  • One app. Other apps in the category may have different problems.
  • Written reviews lean negative. On September 20 the app showed 4.76 stars from 7,317 ratings on the US store, while the written reviews averaged 3.79. Far more people tap a star than write a review.
  • One coder. The categories are my reading. I haven't published the per-review coding sheet, so the counts can't be checked line by line yet.
  • App Store only, iOS only. Nothing here is about Android.
  • Only low ratings were categorized for complaints. Request counts come from all stars.

Disclosure: what I do with this

I'm the developer of minulo, an iPhone app that opens Instagram, YouTube and other services with Reels, Shorts and suggested posts hidden. It is the same kind of app, so read this section with that in mind.

  • Hiding Reels, Shorts and suggested posts is free. Pro is optional ($9.99/month or $39.99/year in the US).
  • You sign in on each service's own page, so minulo never sees your password.
  • It shares the top request's limit: Stories posting, voice messages and calls don't work inside minulo. "Take a break" opens the official app for the minutes you choose.
  • Notifications: while minulo blocks an official app, that app's notifications don't arrive. Instagram DM notifications are a Pro beta exception.
  • It is also a web-view app, so speed is the complaint I watch most.

The full category table is on this page.

title: Introducing the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK Integration: Persistent Memory for AI Applications
description:
We are excited to announce the release of the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK integration, which provides AI applications and agents built with Vercel’s SDK with a persistent memory store in MongoDB Atlas. It's now open source and generally available on npm.

This integration adds MongoDB Atlas as the memory store in the existing Vercel AI SDK code. Once installed, the package connects Vercel AI SDK applications to MongoDB Atlas and automatically stores the application's memories in documents. This allows the application to retain memories about conversations, user facts, and past events that persist across sessions, users, and restarts.

What is the Vercel AI SDK?

The Vercel AI SDK is a TypeScript toolkit for building AI applications. It handles calling models, streaming responses, using tools, and running agents that work through multi-step tasks. The SDK doesn't include a database to persist memories between runs. Without memory, an AI application starts every conversation with no knowledge of the last one. It doesn't know who the user is, what they asked yesterday, or what it learned along the way. It doesn’t have any context.

Today, developers have to build their own tooling to store memories in a layer. That usually means designing a database schema, writing jobs to clear out old data, and setting up vector search so the application can find relevant past information by semantic meaning instead of just keywords. It's a lot of work to build an AI application that can remember context.

What types of memory does an AI application need?

An AI application needs five kinds of memory, each kept for a different length of time and retrieved differently. This integration automatically categorizes each type of memory and stores it in MongoDB Atlas; here are short definitions of the five memory types:

  • Session: The conversation an application or agent has in each session. This helps the application follow what the user just said.

  • Semantic: Facts about people, entities, and preferences, so users don't have to repeat themselves.

  • Procedural: Workflows and instructions, so the application carries out tasks the way you've defined them.

  • Episodic: Key events and outcomes, so the application can recall what happened before. Kept for one year of inactivity by default.

  • Scratchpad: Temporary notes for work in progress. They expire after an hour and can be promoted to episodic memory if they turn out to matter.

Semantic and procedural memories are versioned, so history is preserved when a fact changes. The semantic, procedural, and episodic tiers use MongoDB Vector Search, which finds stored memories by semantic meaning rather than by exact keywords.

This integration automatically creates the vector indexes and detects embedding dimensions at startup. Developers can use any AI SDK embedding model to create vector indexes, including Voyage AI, OpenAI, Cohere, or Google.

Figure 1. How the integration works with MongoDB Atlas and the Vercel SDK interface.

How should memory age?

Each category of memory has its own retention policy, so short-lived notes expire quickly, and long-term facts are stored for longer. The MongoDB Vercel AI SDK integration ships with defaults for every category, which developers can customize if they desire.

Effective memory retention requires a balance. Keeping memories indefinitely can decrease retrieval performance and increase costs, while deleting them too early can cause applications to forget important context. This integration includes features to help developers easily set the right balance:

  • Retention modes: Choose none (never expire), ttl (expire after a set time), ttl+importance (expire after a set time unless the memory is marked important), or dynamic, where you define your own forgetting time period.
  • Model-driven forgetting: With memory_forget, the model can delete a specific memory when a user says "forget that." Removal usually happens within about 60 seconds.

Because the memory is stored in MongoDB Atlas, application operational data, its memory, and the vector search that retrieves it run on one platform. Developers can secure, monitor, and scale a single database without bolting on a separate vector store or memory service alongside it.

What changes when you run the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK Integration in production?

This production release gives developers greater controls over their data and flexibility in how they use the integration:

  • Reliable session history: By default, the model decides when to save and read conversation turns, so it can occasionally skip one. For production, you can use the AI SDK hooks so that the application’s own code loads and saves the transcript at every turn. Every user, assistant, and tool message is saved exactly once.

  • Separate data per customer: Developers can add a filter field, such as tenant_id, to the application’s vector indexes to limit each search to a single customer's memories.

  • Application names and layout: Developers can rename collections and indexes to match the existing application schema or turn off indexing for unused categories. 

  • Open source: The package is licensed under Apache 2.0 and works with any AI SDK model.

Get started today

Developers can add memory to an existing Vercel AI SDK project in three steps. This integration works with AI SDK v6 and v7 and requires a MongoDB Atlas cluster.

  1. Install the package and its peer dependencies: npm install @mongodb-developer/vercel-ai-memory ai mongodb

  2. Create a memory instance with an Atlas connection string and an embedding model.

  3. Pass the memory tools to the application, scoped to a user and session.

From there, the model decides when to save and when to search for memories.

title: How AIClaw Keeps Conversation Search from Rearranging the Sidebar
description:
Searching for an old conversation should not change how the rest of the workspace is organized. A project tree answers where work belongs; a search result answers where a particular piece of work can be found. Treating both as the same list makes switching between them harder than it needs to be.

AIClaw introduced a centered search-and-command panel in 3.9.2. The published 3.10.0 release retains that interaction and moves its search button into the sidebar header. This article covers that shipped behavior, using source pinned to 3.10.0.

Keep the project tree in place

The command panel is a separate Vue component, teleported to the document body. Its backdrop and dialog sit above the workspace instead of replacing project groups with matching conversations.

With an empty query, it offers actions for the current context: start a conversation, rename or archive the selected conversation, create a project, or navigate to a settings category. Rename and archive appear only when there is a current conversation; starting another conversation is disabled while the runtime is unavailable.

Typing filters those command labels and descriptions locally. Conversation results are added separately after the session search returns. Each result includes a workspace label, with extra directory detail when the existing grouping helper provides it. Selecting a result uses the normal conversation-opening action.

The panel does not rebuild project assignments or introduce a second grouping system. Closing it leaves the sidebar available in its existing organization.

Debounce the request, not the local commands

The query watcher clears the previous timer and resets the active selection. For a nonempty query, it schedules the session search after 200 milliseconds. Locally available commands can still match while the conversation search is pending.

The renderer store forwards the query through the existing session-search bridge. It only applies returned results, errors, and loading changes when the stored keyword still equals the keyword associated with that request.

This keeps a response for a different, older keyword from replacing the current results. It is a keyword check, not a unique request-generation check: it does not distinguish two overlapping requests for the same text. Nor does clearing the query cancel an IPC request that has already started.

When the component unmounts, it clears its pending debounce timer and resets session-search state. Those are concrete cleanup guarantees; they should not be described as transport-level cancellation.

A modal interaction needs a return path

The sidebar shortcut handler opens the same panel for Command-K and Control-K. It ignores composing input, already-handled events, and the shortcut when another modal dialog is present.

Opening from the search button records that button as the return target. Opening from the keyboard records the element that had focus. The panel focuses its search input on mount. On unmount, it restores the previous element only if that element remains connected and focus is still within the closing panel or has fallen back to the document body. It does not deliberately take focus away from an unrelated control the user has reached.

Arrow keys move the selected row while focus stays in the input, and Enter executes that row. The markup exposes the dialog, combobox, listbox, and active option relationship. Tab handling wraps the dialog's eligible input and buttons at its boundaries.

Escape closes the panel and stops propagation. This matters because the sidebar also handles Escape: dismissing search should not immediately collapse the navigation underneath it. Clicking the backdrop also dismisses the panel when no command is being executed.

These are keyboard behaviors implemented by the component, not a claim of comprehensive assistive-technology certification.

Reuse the existing actions and failure states

Command execution uses a busy flag to block duplicate execution. Failures remain visible inside the panel instead of being treated as a successful navigation. While a command is running, its controls are disabled and the ordinary dismissal paths are blocked.

Rename delegates to the existing rename form. Archive delegates to the existing archive action and remains a recoverable archive, rather than becoming a new deletion operation. The panel is an entry point to application actions, not a shell-command launcher or a natural-language agent task.

What the checks establish

For this article, I checked a clean checkout at the public 3.10.0 commit, verified the panel's bytes against GitHub's tag-pinned source, rebuilt the desktop app, and ran the release's desktop work UI smoke script. All 375 checks passed.

The relevant checks exercise opening from the header and both keyboard shortcuts, arrow selection, Tab wrapping, Enter into rename, returning focus after cancellation, Escape dismissal, workspace labels in search results, opening a conversation, and backdrop dismissal without changing the workspace groups.

The suite runs an Electron renderer with controlled host responses. It provides interaction regression evidence, not a real-model workflow, a large-history search benchmark, or a screen-reader acceptance test. The broader local validation in the release notes is separate evidence; it was not all rerun for this article.

The improvement is a clear separation of jobs: the sidebar keeps the workspace organized, while a temporary panel helps the user find a conversation or invoke a known action.

title: Business Consulting Website Design
description:
Business Consulting Website Design: A Strategic Approach

In the realm of business consulting, a website is more than just a digital presence – it's a critical tool for establishing credibility, showcasing expertise, and driving conversions. However, standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms often fail to deliver the desired results. This is because they lack the nuanced understanding of the consulting industry's unique needs and the sophisticated design required to resonate with high-value clients.

Off-the-shelf templates are inherently limited by their generic nature, which makes it challenging to convey the distinctive value proposition of a consulting firm. Moreover, these templates frequently prioritize aesthetics over functionality, resulting in a website that may look visually appealing but fails to provide a seamless user experience. Generic forms, on the other hand, can come across as impersonal and unengaging, deterring potential clients from initiating contact.

To create an effective business consulting website, it's essential to adopt a strategic approach that prioritizes both form and function. Here are three concrete engineering takeaways to consider:

  1. Customized Design: A bespoke design that reflects the consulting firm's brand identity and values is crucial for establishing trust and credibility with potential clients. This involves creating a unique visual language, including typography, color schemes, and imagery, that resonates with the target audience.
  2. Intuitive Navigation: A well-structured navigation system is vital for guiding users through the website and ensuring they can easily find the information they need. This includes implementing clear and concise menu labels, minimizing clutter, and utilizing white space effectively to create a sense of clarity and focus.
  3. Conversion-Centric Elements: Incorporating conversion-centric elements, such as prominent calls-to-action, strategic forms, and personalized content, can significantly enhance the website's ability to drive leads and conversions. This requires a deep understanding of the consulting firm's services, target audience, and sales funnel to create a tailored experience that meets the needs of high-value clients.

By adopting a strategic approach to business consulting website design, firms can create a digital presence that truly reflects their expertise and drives meaningful results. Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:
